TI Turning Authorizations into Services: Parent Perspectives on Regional
   Center Utilization for School-Aged Children in California
SO INTELLECTUAL AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE California regional centers; practice; intellectual and developmental
   disabilities; school-age; qualitative research; cultural and linguistic
   diversity
ID EXPERIENCES
AB Program data from a large California Regional Center (RC) showed school-aged clients (5 to <22 years) under-utilized authorized services, with language factors implicated. We conducted semi-structured focus groups/interviews with parents/caregivers (n = 17) from May to August 2024, including a culturally adapted Spanish version. Transcripts underwent modified grounded-theory analysis. Seven themes emerged: advocacy, family stress, positivity/hope, knowledge gaps, obtaining/using services, service coordinators, and school issues. Parents reported persistent advocacy amid time, financial, and administrative burdens; uneven information (often peer-driven); variable coordinator responsiveness; reimbursement/communication gaps; and school shortages. Utilization hinges on navigability, language access, reimbursement design, and RC-school coordination. Recommendations include standardized bilingual onboarding, direct-pay/vendorized options, mentored coordinator onboarding/warm handoffs, and parent-to-parent navigation supports.

TI Introducing Tetrazine Synthesis and Reactivity in Undergraduate
   Laboratory Internship
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate/General; Second-YearUndergraduate; Organic
   Chemistry; Hands-On Learning/Manipulatives; Laboratory Instruction;
   Synthesis; Heterocycles; Oxidation/Reduction; Chromatography;
   UV/VisSpectroscopy; Qualitative Analysis; Dyes/Pigments
ID DIELS-ALDER REACTIONS; CLICK CHEMISTRY; S-TETRAZINES; LIGATION
AB Recent advances in click chemistry have opened promising opportunities for instructional laboratory design, yet heterocyclic compounds such as s-tetrazines-despite their visual distinctiveness and synthetic relevance-remain underutilized in undergraduate education. To meet the instructional need, a short-term undergraduate laboratory internship was designed to introduce first- through third-year students to the synthesis and reactivity of a tetrazine in a collaborative environment. Students learn to synthesize and purify the tetrazine through a straightforward one-pot procedure, followed by performing cycloaddition under ambient conditions. The visually striking transformation, characterized by the disappearance of the red to dark red color, is confirmed by UV-visible absorbance analysis. The experimental protocol is compatible with standard undergraduate laboratory facilities, employing catalyst-free conditions and readily available, inexpensive reagents. The experiment provides students with a structured sequence of reaction setup, purification, and spectroscopic analysis, each reinforcing practical competencies in reaction planning, separation techniques, and instrumental interpretation.

TI Integrating sustainability thinking into microbiology education: a
   conceptual framework for the next generation of environmental scientists
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE sustainability education; microbiology curriculum; ecological literacy;
   problem-based learning; Education for Sustainable Development (ESD)
AB Although microbiology is essential to the global sustainability agenda, its educational focus is still mostly limited to industrial and medical applications. In order to bring microbiological education into line with the tenets of Education for Sustainable Development, this conceptual paper presents a sustainability-focused paradigm. The framework, which is founded on constructivist learning theory and systems thinking, highlights three interconnected educational pillars: interdisciplinary cooperation, ecological literacy, and problem-based learning. These pillars are intended to give students the skills, values, and information they need to relate microbial processes to global issues, including pollution, biodiversity loss, and climate change. The paper describes strategies for encouraging environmental awareness and social responsibility in aspiring microbiologists by combining knowledge from sustainability education and microbiology teaching. In order to prepare graduates to contribute to a resilient and regenerative future, it emphasizes that integrating sustainability thinking into microbiology education is crucial. It ends with strategic recommendations for curriculum reform, educator capacity building, and institutional support, particularly within the Global South.

TI Autonomy-supportive and controlling language in undergraduate biology
   syllabi
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE self-determination theory; attendance; natural language processing;
   emotional tone
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; STUDENTS MOTIVATION; TEACHERS; ENGAGEMENT;
   EDUCATION; STYLE; MODEL; HELP
AB Syllabi are important sources of information for topics covered, how to contact the instructor, and grading and attendance policies. In this study, we used the framework of self-determination theory to better understand how language in the syllabi might reflect autonomy-supportive or controlled style, which has been shown to influence student motivation. In addition, we characterized positive and negative emotion word usage with a natural language processing tool, LIWC. We used qualitative thematic analysis to identify themes in attendance policies under autonomy-supportive or controlled styles, as posited by self-determination theory. Our findings suggested that syllabi tend to be negative in emotional tone, yet somewhat less so in recent years. Furthermore, emotional tone was lower in syllabi of upper-division courses compared to lower-division courses. Controlling language style was most common, with the theme of responsibility appearing in most attendance policies. Our findings provide insights into the undergraduate biology syllabi, and the underlying messages in the text that may impact student motivation. Based on these findings, we provide recommendations for crafting syllabus text that supports student self-directed motivation.

TI Inclusionary leadership and professional learning: Communities of
   practice as catalysts for inclusive schooling in autism education
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE autism education; Communities of Practice; inclusionary leadership;
   inclusive education; primary schools; professional learning; school
ID DEVELOPMENT NEEDS
AB The expansion of autism special classes in mainstream schools has reshaped the demands on principals' leadership and professional learning. This study examines how primary school principals in Ireland enact inclusionary leadership within autism special class contexts with a particular focus on professional learning and collaborative practice. The research uses an interpretive qualitative design, based on semi-structured interviews with fifteen primary school principals responsible for autism special classes. Data were analysed with thematic analysis to explore how principals supported staff learning and inclusive practice. The findings demonstrate that inconsistent preparation pathways for teachers and principals require leaders to actively facilitate professional learning within the school context. Principals supported staff development through mentoring, reflective dialogue and collaborative problem-solving, often embedding professional learning within everyday practice. The study also identified inequitable access to professional learning for Special Needs Assistants, highlighting structural disparities within inclusive education systems. Collaborative practices were present across schools but varied in structure and sustainability, with leadership playing a key role in enabling professional learning environments. This study contributes to leadership and inclusive education scholarship by conceptualising inclusionary leadership as a situated professional learning process. The findings have implications for leadership development, professional learning policy and the sustainable implementation of inclusive education in Ireland and internationally.

TI An investigation into the key factors for implementing total quality
   management within an Irish national agency supporting special education
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE interpretive structured modelling; key implementation factors; special
   education support agencies; total quality management
ID TQM; INSTITUTIONS; PERCEPTIONS
AB This study is conducted within the Irish National Council for Special Education (NCSE). After a decade of extensive change in special education, the Irish Government is enabling the NCSE to undertake substantial reform. Total Quality Management (TQM), a strategic means of improving provision, has been introduced to enhance special education support for students, families and schools. This study investigated the key factors for implementing TQM within the NCSE. Qualitative methods, in the form of semi-structured interviews with the NCSE TQM steering committee, were applied to explore literature review informed education TQM factors. Interpretive Structural Modelling (ISM) was used to generate a TQM key factor implementation framework for the NCSE. 10 key factors of leadership commitment, staff ownership, customer focus, stakeholder engagement, strategic planning, professional development, communication, process management, management information systems and continuous improvement were identified for implementing TQM within the NCSE. A key factor implementation framework was produced. This study presents a suggested framework for TQM within special education support agencies and facilitates further exploration of TQM to improve the reform, research, policy and practice quality dimensions of special education support.

TI Alternative Breakfast Service Models Are Associated With Greater Student
   School Breakfast Participation. Evidence From Middle and High School
   Students Across 8 States
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE alternative school breakfast models; child nutrition; School Breakfast
   Program; universal school meals
ID PROGRAM
AB Background Eating school breakfast has benefits for students, yet participation remains lower than that of school lunch. This study examined associations between school breakfast service models, self-reported participation, and perceived participation barriers, and whether these associations differed by school level (middle vs. high) and universal school meals policy (with vs. without).Methods One thousand ninety-seven middle and high school students were surveyed. Data were analyzed using multilevel logistic regression.Results Most students (67%) reported access only to traditional before-school breakfast. Higher odds of participation and lower odds of time-related barriers were found for breakfast in the classroom (OR 3.88; 95% CI 2.49, 6.03) and "second chance" breakfast (OR 2.07; 95% CI 1.43, 3.00) compared to traditional before-school breakfast only. Grab-and-go options were associated with modestly higher odds of participation (OR 1.29; 95% CI 1.01, 1.67) and fewer barriers among high school students.Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity Breakfast after the bell approaches is associated with higher participation and fewer barriers. These strategies can help ensure more students have reliable access to school breakfast.Conclusions Alternative school breakfast service models, particularly breakfast in the classroom and "second chance" breakfast, may increase participation and support student nutrition, health, and academic performance.

TI A Quality Improvement Initiative to Improve Psychiatry Trainees'
   Knowledge and Confidence in Levels of Care
SO ACADEMIC PSYCHIATRY
LA English
DT Article
DE Psychiatry education; Residency training; Levels of care; Emergency
   psychiatry; Quality improvement
AB Objective To evaluate a brief educational intervention designed to improve psychiatry residents' confidence and knowledge in making level-of-care (LOC) decisions for patients in crisis.Methods Psychiatry residents at Tufts Medical Center participated in a quality improvement initiative consisting of a self-guided didactic session and a structured decision-making tool outlining inpatient, intermediate, and community-based LOC options. Residents completed pre- and post-intervention surveys assessing self-reported confidence and objective knowledge. Data were analyzed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.Results The intervention was associated with increased residents' overall confidence in LOC decision-making. The largest gains occurred in less familiar intermediate and community-based settings, such as crisis stabilization units and partial hospitalization programs. Residents reported greater awareness of alternatives beyond inpatient admission or discharge, and objective knowledge scores showed consistent improvement across domains.Conclusions This quality improvement initiative was associated with increased psychiatry trainees' knowledge and confidence in navigating LOC decisions. This initiative highlighted a potential educational gap in our program and suggests that brief, structured curricula may help increase familiarity with intermediate care options.

TI Learning From People With Disability in University Courses
SO ADVANCES IN NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Inclusive research; Co-design; Lived experience; Disability; University
AB What this paper is about This Easy Read paper talks about two disability courses at Curtin University that were co-designed and co-developed with people with disability. The paper explains how lived experience of disability was prioritised in the design and teaching of the courses to reduce tokenism. Tokenism means including people in a small or non-meaningful way that does not give them real power or influence.What we did People with disability helped plan, write, and teach the learning content. Many lived experience educators were people with high communication and learning support needs. People with disability shared their lived experience and knowledge in authentic ways. The courses focus on what people with disability say matters to them in real life and on the practical skills they need from supporters.What we are doing now People with disability are leading a study on the impact of the courses. The study will explore the long-term effects of lived experience teaching on: Student knowledge and attitudes, and How students work in partnership with people with disability in meaningful and person-led ways. This study will help improve co-designed content creation and further identify examples of tokenism.Take-away messages Universities, and other forms of teaching, still have a long way to go to create learning and resources that are truly co-designed and led by people with disability. The authors, both with and without disability, suggest what needs to change.

TI Social media as a mirror to the sentiment and discourse around Malta's
   2018 assessment changes
SO ASSESSMENT IN EDUCATION-PRINCIPLES POLICY & PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE Continuous assessment; social media; user-generated comments; sentiment
   analysis; discursive strategies
ID NEWS; EDUCATION; TRUST
AB Malta's National Curriculum Framework marked a paradigm shift from prescriptive syllabi to learning outcomes and continuous assessment (CA), challenging a traditional post-colonial testing culture. This study analyses 956 Facebook comments, tokenised into 971 records, concerning the 2018 introduction of CA using a mixed-methods design comprising sentiment analysis (VADER), thematic analysis and critical discourse studies. Findings reveal a heterogeneous sentiment distribution with a marginal positive lead. The dominant discursive strategies, evidentiality, legitimisation and polarisation, reflect experientially grounded public positioning within a divided narrative. Issues of fairness, trust, teaching quality, well-being and power dynamics permeate both positive and negative sentiments. Drawing on the concept of suspension, the study provides a baseline for understanding institutional trust prior the first implementation cycle. The findings suggest that trust remains at a critical threshold, with implications for assessment literacy scholarship, Malta's forthcoming National Assessment Policy, and the role of public discourse in shaping educational reform.

TI Spatial Skills in the Context of K-12 Engineering and Design-Based STEM
   Practices: A Systematic Literature Review
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL OF SCIENCE MATHEMATICS AND TECHNOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Engineering design; Literature review; Spatial skills; Spatial thinking;
   STEM education
ID THINKING; ACHIEVEMENT; INTEGRATION; SCIENCE
AB In supporting K-12 students' cognitive development and twenty-first century skills, there has been a growing focus on promoting engineering design-based science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education. A key relevant skill for success in design-based STEM is spatial skills. Previous research suggested studying how spatial skills and their different types play a role in the context of design-based STEM practices. Such investigations can in turn improve performance in design processes and outcomes. This literature review investigated the associations of spatial skills with engineering and design-based STEM practices and student outcomes in K-12 STEM education. In total, 18 articles were identified using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines. Among the included articles were 15 quantitative or mixed-methods studies and three qualitative studies. The results showed links between the practices predominantly with spatial visualization, mental rotation and mental folding (intrinsic-dynamic), followed by disembedding (intrinsic-static), perspective-taking (extrinsic-dynamic) and with spatial relations (extrinsic-static) skills. Furthermore, the findings revealed factors that play a role in supporting spatial skills and learning outcomes. K-12 STEM education can focus on the identified spatial skills (mental rotation/folding, disembedding, perspective-taking, and spatial relations) and on the instructional factors and support spatial skills development and STEM learning.

TI From Body to Word: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Embodied Vocabulary
   Learning
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Embodied learning; Vocabulary learning; Enactment; Gesture;
   Meta-analysis
ID FOREIGN-LANGUAGE; COGNITIVE LOAD; GESTURES; MEMORY; ACQUISITION; BRAIN;
   BIAS; MIND
AB Embodied cognition posits that cognitive processes are deeply rooted in bodies' interactions with the world. Vocabulary learning is particularly relevant because many lexical meanings can be grounded in motor experiences, making it a compelling context for applying embodied cognition in education. Therefore, the present meta-analysis examines whether embodied instructional designs are effective in supporting vocabulary learning. Studies were identified through searches in databases (i.e., Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, and Scopus), expert consultation, and backward reference in January 2026; ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global was additionally searched in April 2026. Fifty-two studies met the inclusion criteria, and 442 effect sizes were included in the final analyses. A three-level meta-analytic model was employed, followed by moderator analyses to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. Results indicated that embodied learning significantly improved vocabulary learning outcomes compared with non-embodied conditions in both between-subject designs (Hedges' g = 0.65) and within-subject designs (Hedges' g = 0.27). However, publication bias was detected, indicating that the pooled effects may overestimate the true magnitude of the benefit. Moderator analyses indicated that movement-meaning congruency was the only moderator that was consistently observed across research designs, suggesting stronger effects when learners' movements were aligned with the target word meanings. Overall, these findings emphasize the pedagogical potential of embodied learning for vocabulary learning and point to the need for future research to clarify how different forms of embodiment can support vocabulary learning.

TI "Imagination is agency": curricular future-making as an empowering
   framework for teacher professional learning
SO ENGLISH TEACHING-PRACTICE AND CRITIQUE
LA English
DT Article
DE Storytelling; Literature; Teacher professional development;
   Socioecology; Place-based education; Climate futurism
AB Purpose-This study aims to introduce curricular future-making as a framework for transformative professional development (PD). Design/methodology/approach-Drawing on the 2024 National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) Summer Institute, Human/Nature: An Exploration of Place, Stories, and Climate Futurisms, the authors examine how immersive, place-based and speculative approaches can empower educators to imagine literacy not as content delivery, but as a regenerative, socioecological practice. This practice includes the use of cli-fi literature, literacy unbound and other approaches that foreground restorying, or the critical reinterpretation of narratives the authors take for granted (Thomas and Stornaiuolo, 2016). Findings-Conceptual piece includes participant vignettes, anonymous surveys, and curricular action plans. The authors argue that speculative literacy practices such as climate futurism position teachers as curricular world-builders, imagining alternative futures with their students. Collective imagination is not escapism, but agency. Research limitations/implications-The NEH does not allow research as part of Summer Institutes. Practical implications-What does participatory, embodied PD look like? The authors provide an example of an NEH Institute that invites teachers to see curriculum as world-building for hopeful futures. Social implications-Federally funded programs are essential to innovative, experimental work with teachers. This institute created the space for teachers to fully immerse in the content and ideas. Originality/value-This study frames PD as a speculative practice, or "speculative PD." The authors see curriculum design as similar to world-building, which is part of science fiction writing. The authors also push back on the term "empirical" and position teacher and educator voices as experience that counts as knowledge. This study presents a successful model for how to design transformative, immersive PD that opens up possibilities.

AB To enhance students' scientific experimentation skills and facilitate their understanding of careers and culture related to food chemistry, this study designed and implemented a food chemistry experimental project. Rooted in traditional culture and professional principles, this experimental project adopts an interdisciplinary project-based teaching approach. Compared to traditional laboratory classes, this interdisciplinary project-based teaching model in food chemistry helps stimulate students' enthusiasm for learning and improves teaching quality.

TI A level playing field: PLCs as a sustainable model of professional
   learning to support the enactment of inclusive pedagogy to support all
   learners in post-primary schools
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE inclusive education; inclusive pedagogy; post-primary schools;
   professional learning; professional learning communities
ID COMMUNITIES; EDUCATION; IMPACT
AB Despite the strong policy and legislative context for inclusive education worldwide, its definition lacks consensus, and debate exists around its enactment. While there is growing research on how inclusive pedagogy can support teachers to create inclusive classrooms, it mainly relates to primary education. Given the distinct challenges to inclusion in post-primary schools, research explicitly focusing on how to enact inclusive pedagogy in these settings is essential. This is particularly important in the Republic of Ireland in the context of increasing diversity of learning needs and the significant need for teacher professional learning (PL) in this area. This study aims to address gaps in the literature by exploring how professional learning communities (PLCs) in two Irish post-primary schools supported teacher enactment of inclusive pedagogy to meet the needs of all learners through a school-university partnership. Qualitative data from 20 participants revealed that the PLCs were an effective structure for collaboration that supported teachers to enact inclusive pedagogy. This study adds to the limited body of research on inclusive pedagogy in post-primary schools by offering a sustainable PL model to practically support post-primary teachers in creating inclusive classrooms that meet the needs of all learners.

TI A historical reading of language demotion as a settler-colonial
   mechanism: the case of demoting Arabic in Israel
SO LANGUAGE POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Language demotion; Nation state law; Israel-palestine; Historical
   thinking; Language policy; Linguistic citizenship
ID NATION-STATE; LAW
AB This paper examines the demotion of Arabic under Israel's 2018 Nation State Law (NSL) as a historical-legal mechanism through which settler-colonial linguistic hierarchies are constituted and stabilized. Article 4 of the NSL, which revoked Arabic's status as an official language and demoted it to a language of "special status," marks not merely a symbolic or declarative shift but an intensification of long-standing structures that regulate Palestinian presence, visibility, and belonging within the state. Existing analyses of the NSL tend either to interpret language demotion through liberal, rights-based frameworks focused on symbolic inclusion and judicial remedy, or to situate it within a broader structural genealogy of Jewish ethnonational supremacy. I argue that what differentiates these approaches is not only their normative conclusions but the temporal logics through which they narrate the law's emergence and effects. Moving beyond crisis-centered readings of the NSL as an episodic rupture, this article adopts a historical-thinking approach that situates the demotion of Arabic within the longue dur & eacute;e of colonial governance in Israel. Drawing on Supreme Court decisions concerning the NSL, earlier judicial proceedings, and Knesset debates before and after 2018, I conceptualize language demotion as a historically layered technology that governs political subjectivity and the conditions of claim-making. Bringing Christopher Stroud's notion of linguistic citizenship into dialogue with Baruch Kimmerling's critique of futile periodization, the paper shifts attention from formal rights to the cumulative processes through which linguistic and political hierarchies are reproduced.

TI Towards a framework for teaching multiliteracies in the age of
   generative AI
SO PEDAGOGY CULTURE AND SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Multiliteracies; generative AI; critical digital literacy; ethical AI
   literacy; adaptive pedagogy; virtual identity
ID CRITICAL THINKING; MEDIA LITERACIES
AB As generative AI technologies rapidly evolve, they are transforming how students build meaning, presence, and identity across physical and virtual spaces, demanding a rethinking of existing pedagogical frameworks. This paper proposes a reimagined approach to multiliteracies education grounded in three intersecting domains: critical digital literacy, ethical AI literacy, and adaptive, student-centred pedagogy. Situating the argument within debates on pedagogical innovation and virtual identity, it explores how students co-create multimodal texts with AI systems that mediate how they are seen, heard, and recognised online. Methodologically, the paper develops a conceptual framework synthesising scholarship in multiliteracies, critical pedagogy, and sociotechnical AI ethics, illustrated through pedagogical examples. The framework foregrounds learners' need to interrogate algorithmic systems, navigate civic and moral complexity, and leverage AI as a resource for inclusive and creative expression. It demonstrates how multiliteracies pedagogy can support students to read, design, and remix AI-mediated representations of self and others while cultivating reflexive, ethical virtual identities. The paper argues that adaptive AI should function not as an efficiency instrument but as a strategy for justice-oriented inclusion, enabling diverse learners to engage with literacy practices that honour their cultural, linguistic, and virtual lives.

TI Development and Validation of AI Acceptance Scale (AI-AS) for Learners
   in Higher Education
SO TECHTRENDS
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; AI; Scale development; Acceptance; Higher
   education
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; FIT INDEXES; TECHNOLOGY; MODEL
AB The use of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in educational activities is increasing day by day. This situation highlights the need for valid and reliable measurement tools to determine students' levels of acceptance of this technology. This study aims to develop a standard measurement tool to determine students' levels of acceptance of AI. To this end, the systematic scale development steps proposed by DeVellis and Thorpe () were followed. Exploratory factor analysis conducted with 560 participant responses and confirmatory factor analysis conducted with 950 participant responses resulted in a 26-item, 5-factor structure. The factors included in the scale were listed as "usability", "ease of use", "intention and attitude", "facilitating conditions" and "trust and data privacy". The findings revealed that the scale had high internal consistency and exhibited satisfactory model fit indices. The results indicate that the scale is a valid and reliable measurement tool for determining students' levels of AI acceptance. The study offers practical implications for researchers and practitioners and highlights directions for future work on AI adoption in higher education environments.

TI Interventional radiology knowledge among family medicine residents in
   Turkiye: a national cross-sectional survey
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Interventional radiology; Family medicine residents; Knowledge; Medical
   education; Referral patterns; Cross-sectional study
ID ASSOCIATION
AB Background Interventional radiology (IR) provides minimally invasive diagnostic and therapeutic procedures and is increasingly integrated into routine clinical care. Family physicians play a key role in recognizing indications for IR and referring patients appropriately; however, their level of knowledge regarding IR remains uncertain. Aims To assess the knowledge, awareness, and perceptions of interventional radiology among family medicine residents in Turkiye and to evaluate factors associated with knowledge levels. Methods This cross-sectional analytical study was conducted among family medicine residents between August and October 2023 using a structured 21-item online questionnaire. The survey assessed sociodemographic characteristics, exposure to IR training, and knowledge of IR procedures. Knowledge scores were calculated using ten items. Statistical analyses were performed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVA, and chi-square tests, with significance set at p < 0.05. Results A total of 413 residents participated in the study. Overall, 60.6% of participants reported having an adequate level of knowledge regarding interventional radiology (IR), whereas only 25.5% stated that they directly referred patients to IR units. Commonly performed procedures, such as image-guided biopsy and drainage, were correctly identified by most participants; however, misconceptions were noted regarding several other interventional procedures. Residents who had completed clinical rotations associated with IR, particularly in cardiology and obstetrics and gynecology, demonstrated higher knowledge scores compared with those without such experience. Conclusions Family medicine residents demonstrated moderate awareness of interventional radiology, with knowledge gaps remaining in specific procedural areas. Clinical exposure through rotations may improve understanding. Incorporating structured IR education into residency training may enhance appropriate referral practices.

TI Factors Associated with Students' Outcome Expectations Toward Technical
   and Vocational Education and Training (TVET): A Social Cognitive Career
   Theory Study in Phnom Penh, Cambodia
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE TVET; outcome expectations; self-efficacy; Social Cognitive Career
   Theory; Cambodia
AB Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) is central to Cambodia's skills-development agenda, but limited evidence explains how students form expectations about public TVET pathways. Grounded in Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), this study examined the factors associated with students' outcome expectations in public TVET institutions in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 616 bachelor's-degree students, measuring self-efficacy, perceived social support, perceived government and institutional support, and outcome expectations. Data were analyzed using hierarchical multiple regression and stratified subgroup regressions by sector-based major group. Outcome expectations were positively correlated with all three predictors. Controlling for age and gender, the full model explained 64.9% of the variance in outcome expectations, with perceived government and institutional support showing the strongest association, followed by self-efficacy and perceived social support. In the stratified analyses, self-efficacy and perceived government and institutional support were significant within every sector-based subgroup, whereas perceived social support was significant only in the Engineering/Industrial Technical subgroup. These findings provide associational support for SCCT in a Southeast Asian, lower-middle-income setting and indicate that institutional and government credibility may carry particular weight where a public TVET system is still being established.

TI Low-Overhead Learning Analytics: A Parsimonious Early Warning System for
   At-Risk Students in Chilean STEM Courses
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE early warning systems; logistic regression; student retention; STEM
   education; learning analytics
ID DROPOUT
AB Early warning systems grounded in learning analytics offer a practical route to identifying students at risk of failing, yet their adoption in Chilean undergraduate STEM courses is constrained by limited infrastructure and data availability. This study proposes a parsimonious methodology based on univariate logistic regression with the first partial grade as the sole predictor-a deliberate choice prioritising interpretability, actionable timing, and replicability without specialised analytical infrastructure. The approach was tested on two introductory mathematics courses (Linear Algebra and Mathematics I) at two Chilean universities across 2022 and 2023 cohorts. Models trained on 2022 data were externally validated on 2023 data without retraining. Discrimination was high at both institutions (AUC 0.85-0.93 in external validation). At the institution where approval prevalence remained stable across cohorts, operational metrics (PPV, NPV, balanced accuracy) were consistent between years. At the institution where prevalence shifted markedly-because the second semester is composed mainly of students who previously failed-the model preserved its discriminatory capacity but PPV and NPV inverted substantially, illustrating that operational metrics are functions of prevalence rather than indicators of model failure. A gender equity audit revealed systematically lower sensitivity for female students, indicating under-identification of at-risk women under a uniform threshold and underscoring the need for periodic equity monitoring in any deployment. The methodology offers a replicable, low-overhead floor for early warning practice in comparable courses.

TI Exploring factors influencing employer satisfaction with BPharm
   graduates: Evidence from a private university in Vietnam
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Employer satisfaction; BPharm graduates; Graduate outcome quality;
   Learning outcomes; Private university
AB Background Employer feedback is widely recognized as an important mechanism for evaluating graduate outcome quality in higher education, particularly in the health sciences. However, empirical evidence on employer satisfaction with undergraduate Bachelor of Pharmacy (BPharm) graduates in developing countries, including Vietnam, remains limited. Objective This study examined factors influencing employer satisfaction with BPharm graduates from Thanh Do University. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 127 employers from September 2025 to March 2026. The questionnaire consisted of 17 observed variables developed based on the Vietnam National Qualifications Framework, the Vietnamese Pharmacist Competency Standards, and the learning outcomes of the pharmacy program at Thanh Do University. Data were analyzed using Cronbach's alpha, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and multiple linear regression. Both factors were positively associated with employer satisfaction and jointly explained 59.2% of the variance in overall satisfaction. The mean satisfaction score was 3.76/5, indicating generally positive evaluations, although gaps remained in higher-order competencies. No significant difference in satisfaction was observed between public and private sector employers (p > 0.05). Conclusion Although overall employer satisfaction was favorable, gaps persist in graduates' practical application competencies. The findings indicate the need for competency-based curriculum reform and stronger alignment with labor market demands.

AB Background In the modern digital era, computational thinking (CT) is a fundamental skill that has been influenced by advances in artificial intelligence (AI). TI Analysing student engagement in breakout rooms in an online language
   course
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Online student engagement; Small groups; Breakout room; Language
   learning; Video-mediated interaction
AB As the popularity of online courses in higher education keeps increasing, the importance of student engagement gets highlighted. In an online learning environment, peer interaction gets emphasised when students work in small groups in breakout rooms. In this case study, qualitative content analysis and discourse analysis were used to analyse breakout room recordings (458 min in total) of two small groups in a 14-week synchronous online language course. The study focused on how engagement at small group level seems to emerge from the group's interaction, which is a primordial site for language learning, and what kind of collaborative engagement practices seem to support it. The findings suggest that affective, behavioural, and cognitive engagement often cooccur and that they may either support or hinder each other. Also, the group members may be engaged in diverse ways at the same time. Three collaborative engagement practices were identified: participation in group discussions, making and negotiating proposals, and collaborative writing. Participation in group discussions highlighted the importance of both verbal and nonverbal communication and the importance of equity in participation. When making proposals, the role of tentativeness was emphasised as that seemed to open space for interaction in the small group. Finally, collaborative writing was found to engage students specifically from the language learning perspective. The findings suggest that small group interaction and collaboration play a key role in group level engagement. It is suggested that small group level should be taken into consideration when operationalising the concept of engagement in online learning environments.

AB Introduction: Clinical simulation is a widely used strategy in health education, whose effectiveness depends on the pedagogical processes that frame it. TI Class size as a pedagogical challenge
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Class size; Large classes; Cognitive skills; Teaching methods; Active
   learning; Student-teacher relationships
ID STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; MASSIFICATION
AB This study examines when class size becomes a pedagogical challenge in management education, shifting the focus from numerical thresholds to the pedagogical conditions under which difficulties arise. Drawing on a survey of 217 faculty members across disciplines in a Canadian business school, the findings show that while challenges occur in both classes perceived as too small and those perceived as too large, they are more frequently associated with large classes. No universal threshold was identified; instead, a hierarchy of challenges emerged, indicating that class size matters most when faculty aim to develop higher-order cognitive skills, implement active learning methods, and foster meaningful pedagogical relationships. The study contributes by examining student cognitive skills, teaching methods, and pedagogical relationships simultaneously, showing that class size becomes a pedagogical challenge under specific pedagogical conditions rather than at specific numerical thresholds. More broadly, it reframes the debate from "how big is too big?" to "under what pedagogical conditions does class size become a challenge?" It also invites researchers and business schools to consider the longer-term consequences of large classes for pedagogical relationships, which may erode not only student engagement but also the development of the interpersonal skills that management education seeks to cultivate.

TI Comparing the use of linking adverbials in academic writing by L1 and L2
   English student writers: A corpus-based study
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE Corpus-based; Linking adverbials (LAs); Academic writing; University
   students; Learner corpus
AB This study investigates the usage of linking adverbials (LAs) and their semantic types in the academic essays of L1 and L2 English university students in the British Academic Written English (BAWE) corpus across four academic levels (e.g., first-year, second-year, third-year undergraduate, master) and three disciplinary groups (e.g., Arts and Humanities, Social Sciences, Life and Physical Sciences). Findings show that L2 writers employed more LAs in their academic essays than their L1 counterparts, although both groups relied predominantly on a limited subset of this linguistic feature in academic writing. Configural Frequency Analysis (CFA) reveals another important finding: while disciplinary variations in LA usage were observed for both L1 and L2, there was no significant difference in the use of LAs across academic levels. Notably, L1 students showed a preference for adversative adverbials (e.g., yet, however), whereas L2 students tended to use additive adverbials (e.g., moreover) more frequently. The findings offer insights into the differential cohesive strategies employed by L1 and L2 writers. Ultimately, these findings have important implications for targeted academic writing instruction aimed at enhancing essay cohesion for undergraduate students in diverse disciplinary contexts.

TI "When results become striking": Promotional adjectives in STEM research
   articles (1995-2025)
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE Promotional adjectives; Promotion; STEM disciplines; Diachronic study;
   Academic writing
ID EVALUATIVE ADJECTIVES; LANGUAGE
AB Promotional language has become increasingly prominent in academic discourse, yet diachronic evidence from STEM research writing remains limited, particularly with respect to adjectives. Based on a corpus of 360 research articles from Biology, Computer Science, Engineering, and Mathematics, this study examines changes in promotional adjectives (PAs) across 1995, 2010, and 2025, focusing on evaluative orientation, syntactic realization, and rhetorical target. PA use remained broadly stable between 1995 and 2010, but increased markedly from 2010 to 2025 across all four disciplines. By 2025, rates were highest in Computer Science and lowest in Mathematics. The increase was driven mainly by significance-oriented evaluation, while utility and novelty followed more discipline-specific trajectories and emotion showed no sustained rise. Syntactically, the change was realized chiefly through the expansion of noun-premodifying patterns, indicating a growing tendency to package evaluation in more compressed forms; in Mathematics, this trend was accompanied by a decline in extraposed-it constructions. Promotion also became increasingly associated with research-oriented targets, whereas topic-oriented patterns varied across disciplines. These findings reveal that recent promotion in STEM research writing is widespread but discipline-specific. These patterns extend current understanding of evaluative language in academic discourse and offer useful implications for EAP instruction.

TI Evaluating virtual reality training for law enforcement officers to
   respond to autism-related calls: A replication and extension☆
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism spectrum disorder; Law enforcement officers; Training
ID SPECTRUM; YOUTH; INDIVIDUALS; PREVALENCE
AB Previous research has found that law enforcement officers (LEOs) have limited knowledge of autism, and most have not received formal training. Researchers aimed to replicate and extend previous findings on the impact on and experiences of LEOs participating in an autism training that included virtual reality (VR) simulation. Training components included an interactive presentation, VR simulation, and think-pair-share activities. LEOs' perceived confidence when responding to calls involving autistic individuals was the primary outcome. A total of 401 sworn LEOs attended one of 20 training sessions. Participants completed pre- and post-training surveys assessing perceived confidence in responding to related calls. LEOs also provided positive feedback on their experiences with the VR simulation, though a small number shared negative experiences such as reported motion sickness. LEOs reported significant increases in perceived confidence in responding to calls. The vast majority indicated that the training would positively influence their professional interactions with autistic individuals. Notably, LEOs without prior autism training and those without a personal relationship with an autistic individual demonstrated the greatest gains in confidence. Future research should examine the long-term effects of such training on officer behavior and call outcomes.

TI The impact of organizational inertia on teacher well-being under the
   background of educational digital transformation: The chain mediating
   role of techno-overload and techno-inefficacy
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teachers; Technostress; Well-being; Organizational inertia
ID USERS; CONSEQUENCES; ANTECEDENTS
AB Educational digital transformation often causes technostress, diminishing teacher well-being. However, the impact of organizational inertia remains underexplored. Drawing on the Stressor-Strain-Outcome model, this mixed-methods study investigates the chain mediating roles of techno-overload and techno-inefficacy. Quantitative data from 2000 Chinese teachers were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). Qualitative data from 100 semi-structured interviews underwent reflexive thematic analysis. SEM results indicate that organizational inertia negatively correlates with teacher well-being, mediated by the independent and serial paths of techno-overload and techno-inefficacy. Crucially, qualitative findings reveal that organizational inertia manifests as redundant administrative workflows and inadequate training, directly exacerbating teachers' cognitive burden and sense of incompetence. Breaking structural inertia and providing tailored support are imperative for sustaining teacher well-being in the digital era.

TI Creativity in preschool education and its relationship with self-esteem
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creativity; Self-esteem; Childhood; School
ID CHILDREN
AB Introduction: Fostering creativity and self-esteem in childhood are very important factors in child development, and the relationships between the two are established throughout the different stages of development. The objectives of the research were (a) to analyse creativity in children aged 3 to 6; (b) to understand how gender, geographical context, school year, age and participation or non-participation in extracurricular activities influence the development of creativity; and (c) to determine whether there is a relationship between levels of self-esteem and creative ability. Methodology: This study analyses creativity and its relationship with self-esteem in 137 children in early childhood education. A sample from two schools (urban and rural) in Granada, Spain, was evaluated using the Creative Thinking Test and the Questionnaire for the Assessment of SelfEsteem in Childhood. After verifying the normality of the data, inferential analyses were performed (Mann-Whitney U test and Kruskal-Wallis test), calculating the effect size. Results: The results showed that girls and rural students scored higher in creativity. Furthermore, creativity increased with age, school year and participation in extracurricular activities. Correlations have been established between creativity and self-esteem, especially in the academic and general dimensions. Conclusions: The study concludes that fostering creativity and self-esteem from an early age is key to children's emotional, cognitive, and social development. As practical implications of the study, the importance of fostering development by providing a safe and motivating environment, both at school and at home, was highlighted. Limitations of the study included sample size and the specific context of the study.

TI Indonesian students' performance in cryptarithm problem-solving: Rasch
   analysis
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Cryptarithm; Problem-solving; Item analysis; Student performance; Rasch
   analysis
ID ALGEBRAIC THINKING; GENDER; MATHEMATICS; DIF
AB Cryptarithm problem-solving promotes algebraic thinking and supports students' cognitive development, particularly in enhancing logical reasoning skills. This study examined the validity and reliability of a cryptarithm test using the Rasch measurement model to assess students' cryptarithm problem-solving abilities and to investigate potential Differential Item Functioning (DIF) across gender and area. The study involved 281 senior high school students from four schools in Aceh, Indonesia, consisting of two rural and two urban schools. Students completed a six-item cryptarithm test, and the data were analyzed using the Rasch analysis method through WINSTEPS and SPSS 25. The findings indicated that the test items were valid and reliable, with no evidence of DIF. In terms of students' problem-solving abilities, most participants demonstrated a moderate level of proficiency, with female students outperforming their male counterparts. Moreover, students from urban schools generally showed better performance than those from rural schools. These findings invite further discussion on the underlying factors contributing to gender and regional differences in performance on cryptarithm problems.

TI Comparison of Rasch Preequating and Postequating When Item Parameters
   Drift
SO APPLIED MEASUREMENT IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID IRT; IMPACT; STABILITY
AB Test equating is commonly applied in psychological and educational assessments to ensure score comparability across multiple test forms. However, item parameter drift (IPD) poses a threat to equating, potentially impacting the validity, fairness, and reliability of test scores. This study investigates the effects of IPD on true-score preequating and postequating within the Rasch framework, commonly used in certification and licensure testing programs. Through a simulation study, we examined various scenarios, including IPD direction, percentage of items exhibiting IPD, magnitude of IPD, and examinee sample size. Our findings indicate that postequating consistently outperforms preequating in the presence of IPD, demonstrating greater robustness in maintaining equating accuracy and fairness. The results highlight the importance of considering IPD in equating processes and suggest that postequating may be preferable in contexts where IPD occurs. These insights are valuable for test practitioners managing assessments susceptible to IPD, ensuring more accurate and reliable score interpretations.

TI Improving international medical students' communication skills in
   psychosomatic care through a communication training seminar: a natural
   language processing-based analysis
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE International students; Natural language processing; Communication
   training; Patient-centered communication
ID ETHNICITY; PERFORMANCE; PROGRAM; EMPATHY
AB Background International students face numerous challenges in both their academic and social lives when relocating to a new country for their university studies. The foreign language can have an impact on international medical students' performance in patient encounters. Particularly in the context of psychosocial medicine, a deficiency in communication skills can negatively impact the doctor-patient-relationship. This is the first study that uses natural language processing (NLP) as well as traditional rating scales to assess the improvement of international students' communication skills after attending a communication training seminar.Methods N = forty-two international students participated in the study, which followed a pre-post-design. Diagnostic interviews with standardized patients (SP) were videotaped before and after the three-day training seminar, which was comprised of short lectures and communication trainings with SPs regarding the topic of psychosomatic medicine. Transcripts of diagnostic interviews were analyzed with NLP. Videotaped clinical encounters were assessed by three raters with binary and global rating instruments. For the comparison between pre- and post-assessment of all NLP communication parameters and rating results, two-way ANOVAs and Wilcoxon tests were calculated, respectively.Results NLP communication parameter results showed a decrease in talk-turns, interruptions, number of questions and talking over, and an increase in talk-turn-length in post-assessment compared to pre-assessment. There were no significant pre-post changes observed in binary checklist results. Significant pre-post changes were observed in global rating score and ratings from global rating domains 'interview structure' and 'verbal expression'.Conclusion International students significantly improved their communication style in psychosomatic medicine towards a more patient-centered approach. Changes in NLP communication parameters and improved interview style and verbal expression suggest that international students may have listened to patients more carefully. Furthermore, NLP has shown to be a viable tool to evaluate communication parameters in a doctor-patient-relationship and assess the effectiveness of communication training for international students.

TI Observations of relational reasoning and strategic processing in an
   interdisciplinary team

LA English

AB The purpose of the current study was to determine the extent to which relational reasoning and strategic processing were evident in the discourse of an interdisciplinary team. Emergent patterns in the co-occurrence of these processes and changes in their frequency over the course of collaborative work were analyzed. TI Learning Chemistry in the Kitchen: Designing Flavored Photonic
   Hydroxypropyl Cellulose Gels as Food Colorant
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Hands-on experiment; First-year undergraduate students; Hydroxypropyl
   cellulose; Self-assembly; Structuralcolor
AB Structural colors are widely observed in nature. In this laboratory experiment, we designed a hands-on experiment for first-year undergraduate students that involves the fabrication and characterization of edible food gels with vibrant structural colors. In this experiment, food-grade hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) powder and commercial beverages, such as coffee, coke, and red wine, are mixed to obtain photonic gels via the self-assembly of HPC molecules into a cholesteric liquid crystalline phase. During the experiment, students can observe the shifting of structural colors, from red to green to vivid blue, when increasing the HPC concentration. Additionally, the obtained flavored photonic gels can be encapsulated within chocolate as photonic fillings to increase students' interest in their application. This hands-on experiment is safe, convenient, and adaptable to most undergraduate laboratory courses. Through this practical class, students can evaluate the optical behavior of the photonic gels using UV-vis/NIR spectroscopy and optical microscopy, enhancing their skills in structural characterization and providing a hands-on experience in materials science. By presenting this concept, we aim to inspire students to explore structural color through the bottom-up self-assembly process, which can further stimulate students' interest and devotion to scientific research in the future. Detailed instructions for assessing student learning, step-by-step protocols, and a student survey are provided, supporting educational value and easy integration into undergraduate teaching.

TI Spanish-Speaking Secondary Students Reading and Spelling in English as a
   Foreign Language
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE English; foreign language; reading; Spanish students; spelling
ID VISUAL WORD RECOGNITION; MIDDLE SCHOOL; ACQUISITION; CONSISTENCY;
   LITERACY; CHILDREN; ACCURACY; ERRORS; TRANSPARENCY; ORTHOGRAPHY
AB Proficiency in English reading and spelling is essential, as many professional environments require both spoken and written skills. Literacy development in English as a foreign language poses challenges for learners whose first language is transparent, such as Spanish, due to the complexity and inconsistency of English orthography. Spanish-speaking students often struggle with these inconsistencies, adversely affecting their reading and spelling abilities. While prior research has primarily focused on primary students, this study investigates the reading and spelling processes of 78 Spanish-speaking secondary school students, aiming to highlight their lexical processing, sensitivity to rime consistency, and the relationship between reading and spelling performance. Participants completed reading-aloud and spelling-to-dictation tasks using English monosyllabic words with different values of lexical frequency and rime consistency. The analysis revealed that reading accuracy improved with grade level and higher feedforward rime consistency. Although reading speed did not show significant differences across grades, reading latencies were shorter for high-frequency and high-rime consistency words, while older students articulated high feedforward rime consistency more slowly. Increased lexical frequency reduced the influence of rime consistency. Spelling accuracy in secondary education remained low, influenced by grade level and feedback rime consistency. Writing latencies were affected by lexical frequency, and writing durations were influenced by both grade and frequency, with fourth graders benefiting more from high-frequency words. A positive relationship between reading and spelling accuracy indicates that proficient readers are generally proficient spellers. Overall, increased exposure to English enhances students' reading and spelling performance of high-frequency words and sensitivity to rime consistency.

TI Effects of Preservice Teachers' Perception and Professional Knowledge on

   Noticing

AB This study investigated the influence of mathematical knowledge for teaching (MKT) and perceptual attention on preservice teachers' (PSTs) attending to students' mathematical thinking when the prompts scaffolding their noticing differed. TI An Undergraduate Laboratory Module Using a Ternary Nitride
   Electrocatalyst to Teach Structure-Property Relationships in
   Electrocatalytic Hydrogen Evolution
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Undergraduate laboratory; Hydrogen Evolution Reaction; Triple-Phase
   Nitrides; Alkaline Water Splitting; Hands-On Learning;
   Structure-Property Relationships
AB The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in alkaline media is central to sustainable hydrogen production but is limited by sluggish kinetics and catalyst instability. To connect fundamental chemistry, electrochemistry, and materials science with hands-on learning, we designed a laboratory experiment for undergraduate students to synthesize and evaluate a Mo3N2/Ni3Mo3N/Co3Mo3N triple-phase nitride electrocatalyst, composed of three integrated nitride phases. The ternary structure provides abundant active sites and efficient charge-transfer interfaces, which achieve a low overpotential of 33 mV at 10 mA cm-2, surpassing binary analogues and approaching the HER performance of the benchmark platinum-on-carbon (Pt/C) electrocatalyst. Students prepare working electrodes, characterize catalyst structure using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy, and perform electrochemical HER measurements. Analysis of polarization curves, Tafel plots, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy data, and electrochemically active surface area, combined with guided comparisons between ternary and binary systems, enables students to relate structural features to the HER activity. This integrated approach demonstrates how multiphase design enhances HER activity, offering students insights into rational electrocatalyst design and sustainable energy research.

TI Scaling access to education: Identifying enablers and barriers using
   outlier national comparisons
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cross-national comparisons; education inequality; educational access;
   outlier countries; SDG4
AB Despite ongoing global efforts, access to education remains a significant challenge with major disparities across countries and population groups. This paper examines the main factors affecting educational access worldwide. It identifies key enablers and obstacles through comparing selected national cases. Drawing on reliable international databases and national education statistics, the study analyzes patterns of educational access, enrolment, and participation, with particular emphasis on the contextual factors that shape educational opportunities. The findings show that high-performing countries often have strong political commitment, effective governance, consistent public investment, inclusive education policies, and targeted support for marginalized groups. On the other hand, low-performing countries struggle with persistent poverty, weak governance, limited institutional capacity, political instability, conflict, and social and cultural barriers that hinder participation, especially among girls and other disadvantaged groups. The analysis further reveal that educational access is influenced not by one factor alone but by the interaction of policy effectiveness, governance quality, contextual adjustments, institutional capacity, and resource use. By highlighting these dynamics, the study adds to discussions on global educational inequality and offers practical insights for policymakers and practitioners seeking to scale equitable access to education in support of Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4).Context and implications Rationale for the study: Despite ongoing commitments, educational access remains uneven across countries and population groups, with persistent disparities by region, socio-economic status and gender. This study uses outlier national comparisons to identify the key factors that facilitate or hinder educational access. Why the new findings matter: The results clarify which enablers and barriers are most likely to explain cross-national differences, providing a more actionable basis for targeting future scaling efforts. Findings also reveal that access depends not only on resources but also on governance quality, inclusiveness and contextual responsiveness, highlighting the need for context-sensitive, evidence-based policies rather than one-size-fits-all approaches. Implications for policymakers, practitioners, researchers and funders: Policymakers should adopt evidence-based, context-responsive reforms, ensure equitable resource distribution and implement inclusive frameworks to expand access and reduce educational disparities effectively. Practitioners (school leaders and educators) can utilize insights from diverse national experiences to adapt and implement scalable solutions in their communities. Researchers can adopt this outlier analysis framework for future studies on causal relationships and diverse learning contexts. Donors and development organizations should focus their investments on targeted interventions that effectively address the root causes of educational inequities.

TI Modelling Sound in Primary Education: A Qualitative Case Study of a
   STEAM-Based Didactic Sequence
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE school scientific model of sound; scientific modelling; STEAM education;
   music and science; scientific practices; science education
ID STUDENTS; INQUIRY
AB Teaching sound in Primary Education poses specific challenges because students are required to explain an everyday phenomenon whose physical functioning is not directly observable. This study examines how fifth-grade Primary Education students construct and transform their understanding of sound through a STEAM-based didactic sequence implemented in a real classroom context. A qualitative case study was conducted with two fifth-grade classes from a public school in Zaragoza, Spain, involving 41 students. Three sources of evidence were collected: students' productions, observational records kept by the first author acting as teacher-researcher, and the final product of the sequence. The corpus comprised 97 meaning units, defined as segments of student discourse representing distinct explanatory ideas. Qualitative content analysis revealed a progression from phenomenological, substantialist, or poorly articulated explanations towards formulations closer to the school scientific model of sound. Progress was especially evident in students' understanding of vibration as the origin of sound, the need for a material medium for sound propagation, and the application of the model to new situations. This study contributes to science education by showing how a STEAM-based modelling sequence can support the progressive development of scientific explanations in Primary Education. Overall, the findings suggest that integrating physical exploration, listening, sound production, and the construction of a final product can effectively support school modelling processes related to sound.

TI The Intersection of Music Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and
   Occupational Health: A Job Demands-Resources Analysis of Technostress,
   Burnout, and Engagement Among Music Students
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Job Demands-Resources; music education; technostress; cultural identity;
   burnout; engagement; AI differentiation; music student subgroups
ID PERFORMANCE; IMPACT; EXPERIENCES; TYPOLOGY; MODEL
AB This study applies Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory to music student psychology, with particular attention to the differentiated impacts of artificial intelligence across music student subgroups. Background: Music education requires intensive cognitive, motor, emotional, and social training. Methods: Employing a narrative literature review and conceptual framework approach, this paper draws on JD-R theory, technostress research, and cross-cultural scholarship to identify demands and resources in music education and examine their relationships with burnout and engagement. Results: Seven demands: technical, physical, temporal, performance, social-emotional, technostress, cultural identity. Resources: teacher support, peer collaboration, instruments, AI tools, curricula, and intrinsic motivation. Critically, AI-related demands and resources differ substantially across subgroups: composers face direct demand shocks (job displacement) and resource opportunities (creative augmentation) that vary by career stage, while performers experience more indirect impacts through recording market disruption and emerging self-media opportunities. Singers face a unique paradox whereby AI voice cloning creates short-term recording opportunities while potentially enabling long-term vocal replacement. Cultural identity demands arise from heritage-Western tensions in East Asia. Conclusions: This JD-R framework provides a nuanced lens for understanding music students' well-being that accounts for subgroup-specific vulnerabilities and opportunities.

TI Negotiating belonging: a constructivist grounded theory of transfer
   students' experiences in STEM
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Community college transfer students; STEM education; Sense of belonging;
   Non-traditional students; Neuroscience education
ID SENSE; PERSISTENCE; ENGAGEMENT; MOTIVATION; 1ST-YEAR; SCIENCE; GENDER;
   WOMEN; RACE
AB Background A sense of belonging has been identified as a crucial predictor of persistence in undergraduate degrees. This construct is especially significant within the chilly environment of STEM fields since students' sense of belonging and recognition as rightful members of the academic community ultimately shape their educational trajectories. However, it has rarely been studied among community college (CC) transfer students attending highly selective universities. This population is of interest because CCs enroll students from underrepresented backgrounds at higher rates than four-year institutions, making transfer students a critical component in efforts to diversify the STEM workforce. Additionally, these students often face unprecedented challenges as compared to their "traditional" peers. We addressed this research gap by conducting semi-structured qualitative interviews with thirteen community college transfer students one and two years after transferring. Analyses applied constructivist grounded theory methodology to examine how these students described a sense of belonging and what experiences they drew from to assess their level of belonging in academic environments.Results Transfer students described their sense of belonging as a negotiated process involving internal motivators, values and perceptions, and the messaging received from external institutional, familial, and social factors. Particularly, participants' experiences of belonging were first marked by an orientation toward building it with some more concerned about their level of fit than others.Conclusion By theorizing belonging as a negotiated process, this study shows how community college transfer students in STEM actively interpret academic environments, drawing from both internal motivation and external signals to negotiate a sense of belonging, with students' orientations toward belonging and internal alignment comprising a major contributing paradigm in the process. This work emphasizes the need to include opportunities for disciplinary exploration in transfer students' academic trajectories. Potential implications include the design of transfer pathways and advising structures that recognize belonging as dynamic, supporting students' identity work as central to academic success.

TI Assessment of Five Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools in Theory of
   Machines and Mechanisms Through Bloom's Taxonomy
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Bloom's taxonomy; educational assessment; generative artificial
   intelligence; mechanical engineering education; theory of machines and
   mechanisms
AB Background: The rapid development and adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools, particularly following ChatGPT's release, have created new opportunities and challenges for engineering education. While several studies have explored AI capabilities in mechanical engineering, systematic analysis across different cognitive skill levels remains limited. Purpose: This study evaluates and compares the performance of five conversational AI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, LeChat) in Theory of Machines and Mechanisms (TMM), analyzing their capabilities across the six cognitive levels of revised Bloom's taxonomy: L1-Remember, L2-Understand, L3-Apply, L4-Analyze, L5-Evaluate, and L6-Create. Methods: A set of 48 TMM questions was developed, with eight questions targeting each of Bloom's taxonomy levels. Four mechanical engineering professors interacted with the five AI tools using standardized prompts. Responses were anonymized and independently evaluated by two graders using a 5-point Likert scale across three aspects: technical quality, accuracy and completeness, and quality of writing. Statistical analysis was performed through ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis test, and linear mixed-effects models, to examine differences among AI tools and cognitive levels. Results: AI tools demonstrated generally good performance, with mean scores ranging from 3.76 to 4.22 for technical quality and 3.79 to 4.27 for accuracy and completeness. Writing quality scores consistently exceeded 4.65. LeChat performed significantly worse than the other tools. Performance was notably weaker at the L6-Create level compared to all other cognitive levels. Conclusions: GAI tools show promise as educational resources for TMM, particularly at lower cognitive levels, though significant limitations persist in creative tasks requiring higher-order reasoning and synthesis.

TI Enhancing Motor Competence in Rhythmic Gymnastics: Effects of the
   Overlapping Waves Strategy in School-Based Physical Education
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE cooperative learning; fundamental movement skills; motor competence;
   motor development; physical literacy; rhythmic gymnastics; school-based
   intervention
AB Background: Rhythmic gymnastics offers a context for motor development. This study examined the association between the Overlapping Waves Strategy and traditional instruction in fundamental club skills. Methods: A cluster-allocated quasi-experimental design (16 sessions) was implemented among 64 fifth-grade female students. Participants received Overlapping Waves Strategy (n = 32) or conventional instruction (n = 32). Four skills were assessed by certified judges. Results: Two-way mixed ANOVA revealed significant group & times; time interactions (all p < 0.001). The experimental group exhibited greater pre-post performance gains than the control group. Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity: The strategy provides a structured pedagogical framework for physical education, suggesting potential feasibility, though limited by the specific single-setting and demographic parameters, and policy recommendations remain premature without broader replication. Conclusion: Preliminary findings indicate greater short-term execution of club skills in the experimental classroom. Classroom-level confounding cannot be excluded. Replication in cluster-randomized designs with retention measures is required.

TI Beyond Medical Absence: Grade-Related and Year-To-Year Persistent
   Patterns of Parent-Reported Psychological/Functional Absence in Routine
   School Attendance Records
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE absenteeism; attendance records; mental health; psychological/functional
   absence; school health
ID ABSENTEEISM; SYMPTOMS; PSYCHOPATHOLOGY; DEPRESSION; CHILDREN; STRESS
AB Background Psychological/functional absences may be obscured within broad medical leave categories in routine attendance records. This study examined whether parent-reported psychological/functional absence is patterned and persistent in a Chinese secondary school context. Methods We analyzed retrospective attendance records from 2183 students and 26,092 absence events across the 2022-2025 academic years. Parent-reported reasons were coded into 8 categories. Event-level logistic regression with student-clustered robust standard errors examined associations with grade, sex, cohort, academic year, and month; student-year lagged models examined recurrence. Results Psychological/functional absence accounted for 5179 events (19.8%). In the fully adjusted event-level model, Grade 11 students had higher odds of psychological/functional absence than Grade 8 students (OR = 2.62, 95% CI [1.45, 4.72], p = 0.001). Prior-year psychological/functional absence predicted current-year occurrence (OR = 3.50, 95% CI [2.67, 4.59], p < 0.001), and prior-year count predicted current-year count (IRR = 1.06, 95% CI [1.04, 1.07], p < 0.001) Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity Repeated psychological/functional absences may help schools identify students needing timely, non-punitive follow-up. Conclusions Psychological/functional absence appears to be a recurring administrative signal, but should not be interpreted as a clinical diagnosis.

TI Raciolinguistic Autobiographies With Intermediate Elementary Learners
SO READING TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
ID LANGUAGE; LITERACY
AB We propose raciolinguistic autobiographies as a developmentally appropriate multimodal composition authored by intermediate elementary learners (Grades 3-5) that promotes critical consciousness around how language, race, and signs are interwoven to form hierarchies of power and belonging. We provide learning objectives, concrete pedagogical strategies, and examples that educators can implement in their intermediate elementary classrooms. The pedagogical outline is informed by raciolinguistic and raciosemiotic perspectives. Raciolinguistic autobiographies provide crucial tools for [minoritized] young learners to denaturalize the raciolinguistic and raciosemiotic signs that seek to devalue them, their communities, and their practices of belonging.
