TI Crystallization beyond Purification: A Teaching Laboratory Experiment on
   the Counter intuitive Occlusion of Nanoparticles within Calcium
   Carbonate Crystals
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE crystallization; nanoparticle occlusion; calcium carbonate;
   multisession; undergraduate
ID BIOMINERALIZATION
AB Crystallization is traditionally presented in undergraduate laboratories as a thermodynamically driven purification process in which impurities are excluded from the growing crystal lattice. In this Multisession Laboratory Experience, students investigate a counterintuitive phenomenon: the efficient occlusion of nanoparticles within calcium carbonate (CaCO3) crystals during growth. The experiment can be implemented in an upper-level undergraduate laboratory course using a simple ammonia diffusion method with assistance from an instructor. By comparing CaCO3 crystals grown in the absence and presence of various diblock copolymer nanoparticles, students observe that crystallization can operate as an inclusion process rather than solely as a purification step. This reproducible outcome challenges conventional assumptions and provides a concrete platform for discussing interfacial compatibility, kinetic trapping, and nonclassical crystallization pathways. The experiment is well-suited for undergraduate inorganic or materials chemistry laboratories, effectively bridging foundational crystallization concepts with contemporary materials science and promoting the development of students' critical thinking skills.

TI A Meta-Analysis of Cognitive Complexity and Judgment Accuracy in
   Clinical Decision Making
SO JOURNAL OF COUNSELING PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE clinical judgment; cognitive complexity; judgment accuracy;
   meta-analysis
ID COUNSELOR CONCEPTUAL LEVEL; BETA COEFFICIENTS; ROBUSTNESS; EXPERIENCE;
   MODELS; POWER
AB Cognitive complexity refers to a multidimensional information-processing style hypothesized to enhance clinical decision making. Extending the Meta-Analysis of Clinical Judgment project (Spengler et al., 2009), we reviewed 55 years of research examining the association between mental health clinicians' cognitive complexity and judgment accuracy. Nine studies (N = 915) met inclusion criteria. The mean random-effects correlation was r = .17 (95% CI [.11, .24], p < .01) indicating a small but statistically significant positive association. Mixed effects and meta-regression moderator analyses revealed no statistically significant effects, though trends suggested stronger associations among more experienced clinicians and in higher quality studies. Findings provide modest support for cognitive complexity as a beneficial clinician characteristic while highlighting the need for further research.

TI "They exploit us, but we still have to respect them": Rethinking Latin
   Cultural Values Through a Critical Lens
SO JOURNAL OF COUNSELING PSYCHOLOGY

DT Article

   Ricans
ID CRITICAL CONSCIOUSNESS; THEMATIC ANALYSIS; PUERTO-RICANS; MENTAL-HEALTH;

AB Because cultural values are believed to shape the identities, attitudes, and behaviors of societies, the study of Latine cultural values holds a prominent place in Latine psychology. TI Differentiation-related tensions in the thinking and instruction of
   Eritrean elementary and middle school mathematics teachers
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article

ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; INCLUSIVE EDUCATION; IMPLEMENTATION;

AB Differentiated instruction is key to implementing inclusive education and addressing the individual needs of all students. This study explores the pedagogical tensions related to differentiation in Eritrean elementary and middle school mathematics teachers' thinking and instruction practices. TI When r and β disagree: suppression-aware interpretation of
   personality-learning links in Vietnamese EFL classes
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Big five inventory; Learning preferences; Sign reversals; Suppression;
   Zero-order
ID HIGHER-ORDER FACTORS; PERFORMANCE; ANXIETY; STYLE
AB Personality effects in English as a foreign language (EFL) studies are often read from zero-order correlations even though Big Five traits and classroom outcomes are both intercorrelated. Using data from 103 first-year Vietnamese EFL students, this study examines whether such bivariate readings can obscure suppression-compatible patterns. Students completed the BFI-44 and a classroom-adapted inventory of group, individual and kinesthetic preferences, together with a collaboration-oriented self-regulated learning scale. Simultaneous five-trait regressions yielded two notable r -> beta divergences. Agreeableness was essentially unrelated to individual preference at the zero-order level (r approximate to .02) but became negative after the other four traits were controlled (beta approximate to - .15). Neuroticism showed the complementary pattern for group preference, moving from a near-zero bivariate association (r approximate to - .02) to a positive unique coefficient (beta approximate to .17). Given the modest sample and self-report design, these results are interpreted as pattern-validating rather than parameter-final. The study's contribution is therefore methodological as much as substantive: it shows why EFL personality research should report zero-order correlations, multivariate coefficients and sensitivity checks together rather than relying on bivariate associations alone.

TI Dyslexia, School-Connectedness, Depression, and Anxiety During the
   Transition From Primary to Secondary School
SO DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
DE dyslexia; mental health; peer relationships; school transition;
   school-connectedness
ID REVISED CHILD ANXIETY; READING DIFFICULTIES; MENTAL-HEALTH; STUDENTS;
   SCALE
AB Children with dyslexia are at elevated risk of depression and anxiety. The transition from primary to secondary school may be particularly challenging given increased educational demands. Past research indicates school-connectedness may be a protective factor across this transition. We tested longitudinal relationships between dyslexia, school-connectedness, depression, and anxiety over the secondary school transition. Children (N = 208, M age = 12.16, 58% girls, 61 with dyslexia) and their caregivers (95% mothers) completed standardised measures of school-connectedness, depression, and anxiety in Year 6, and again in Year 7 after the transition to secondary school. Mediation models tested direct and indirect effects of dyslexia on Year 7 depression and anxiety through domains of school-connectedness (whole school, peer, friend, and teacher). After adjusting for Year 6 depression, anxiety, and gender, there were no significant direct effects of dyslexia on depression or anxiety in Year 7. However, dyslexia was indirectly associated with both depression and anxiety via school- and peer-connectedness. These findings support the role of school-connectedness in supporting mental health, and suggest peer-connectedness might be an important protective factor post-transition to secondary school. Future studies should explore further change across adolescence and mental health promotion targeting school- and peer-connectedness among children with dyslexia.

TI From fear to innovation: a case study of transformative faculty
   development for ethical AI integration in higher education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL FOR EDUCATIONAL INTEGRITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Higher education; Faculty development;
   Universal design for learning; Bloom's taxonomy; Design thinking;
   Academic integrity; Inclusive pedagogy; Professional learning;
   Educational technology
AB As artificial intelligence (AI) technologies increasingly permeate educational spaces, the need for structured and reflective faculty development becomes critical. This study presents a comprehensive case study of a six-week faculty institute designed to support higher education instructors in thoughtfully integrating AI into their pedagogical practices. Framed by Universal Design for Learning (UDL), Bloom's Taxonomy, and design thinking methodologies, the institute explored the tensions between innovation and academic integrity while promoting inclusive, critical adoption of AI tools. Drawing on session materials, pre/post surveys, participant reflections, and capstone projects from ten interdisciplinary faculty members, this paper examines the experiences and evolving mindsets of educators navigating AI integration. The findings reveal a transformative journey from fear and resistance to collaborative innovation, demonstrating that AI integration, when scaffolded by inclusive design, ethical literacy, and practical application, can enhance faculty agency, curriculum responsiveness, and student engagement. The study identifies four key themes: shifting from fear to curiosity, the desire for ethical clarity, inclusive design as an equity amplifier, and the evolution of faculty from gatekeepers to guides. However, significant challenges persist around policy clarity, institutional support structures, and AI's perceived legitimacy in teaching and learning. This case study contributes to emerging scholarship on faculty AI literacy and offers a replicable model for sustainable professional development design in a rapidly evolving technological landscape. The research provides practical implications for institutions seeking to bridge the divide between administrative enthusiasm and faculty skepticism, ultimately arguing that AI in higher education transcends fashion or fantasy to become a reality demanding thoughtful pedagogical engagement.Clinical trial numberNot applicable.

TI Scaffolding Success: Redefining HSI Servingness and Belonging for the
   Hispanic Graduate Student Population
SO JOURNAL OF LATINOS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Servingness; graduate students; belonging; representation
AB While Hispanic-Serving Institutions (HSIs) are growing, research disproportionately focuses on undergraduates. This study utilizes Garcia et al.'s (2019) servingness framework and Yorke's (2016) belonging scale to examine Hispanic-identifying graduate students' lived experience at a large northeastern HSI. Student-led survey findings (n = 24) reveal a "service gap": despite high academic agency, only 16.7% of student respondents knew of demographic-specific resources. For graduate commuters, belonging relies on faculty representation and professional mentorship over campus social programming. Discussing these finidings within the 2025-2026 federal political climate, we argue that graduate-level HSIs must scaffold success, and implement servingness models prioritizing structural diversity and inclusive professional pathways.

TI Enhancing Legal Literacy and Active Citizenship Through Gamified
   Creative Learning in Higher Education
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE active citizenship; creative-based learning; gamification; higher
   education; legal literacy
AB Active citizenship is a key goal of higher education. However, limited empirical evidence exists on how learning management approaches support legal literacy and citizen participation among university students. This research lacuna was addressed by examining whether a legal literacy enhancement program, incorporating creativity-based learning and gamification, was related to changes in legal literacy and active citizenship using a quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test design with follow-up assessment. The sample comprised 40 undergraduate students, obtained by purposive sampling. The classroom was divided into the experimental group (n = 20) and the control group (n = 20) based on their timetables and the lecturer's readiness. The experimental group received activities as scheduled for four weeks. The program was designed to enhance their experience-based learning, problem-solving, and enthusiastic participation through creative learning activities and gamification elements. Legal literacy forms and a self-assessment form on active citizenship were used to collect the data with mixed-design ANOVA used for data analysis. The results revealed that legal literacy and active citizenship in the experimental group were significantly higher than those in the control group. There was a significant coeffect between group and time (Group & times; Time interaction effect) on legal literacy, was well as on active citizenship. Changes were observed in the post-test and follow-up phases. This provided preliminary evidence that the program was associated with increased legal literacy and active citizenship during the short-term follow-up period. The experimental group also showed a higher awareness of civic responsibility and participation in social issues.

TI To Be or Gan a Bheith: An Instructional Coaching Intervention for Irish
   Secondary Science
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE instructional coaching; culturally responsive and sustaining teaching
   (CREST) practices; secondary science; Ireland; Gaeilge language
   learning; initial teacher education
ID TEACHERS; PEDAGOGY
AB In Ireland, most school-aged students are required to take Gaeilge (the Irish language) as a compulsory subject. For some, this is not a favourable experience. This study was designed and structured to help support student teachers who wish to deliver secondary school science through Gaeilge. Specifically, this study used a dynamic and iterative instructional coaching intervention that was designed to be relevant, useful, and meaningful in applying culturally responsive and sustaining teaching practice. Over the course of one university semester, eleven student teachers voluntarily agreed to attend Gaeilge workshops in how to use their Gaeilge in their teaching practice. These ten workshops focused on collaboration between peers using effective pedagogy in meaningful contexts. This research suggests that these student teachers found instructional coaching based on culturally responsive and sustaining teaching practice to be effective. Specifically, it was these student teachers working in collaborative relationships both student teacher to coach and student teacher to student teacher, which improved their confidence and willingness to use Gaeilge. There has been no research into how instructional coaching is able to support Irish student teachers in using Gaeilge in teaching secondary science. This study addresses this gap in the research literature concerning Gaeilge-speaking teachers in secondary science.

TI Microlearning in medical histology: a longitudinal evaluation of
   faculty-created five-minute videos using five theoretical frameworks and
   Kirkpatrick assessment
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Microlearning; Medical histology education; Kirkpatrick evaluation;
   Faculty-created five-minute videos; Generation Z; Cognitive load theory;
   Multimedia learning theory; Variation theory; Spaced repetition theory;
   Self-regulated learning theory
ID COGNITIVE LOAD THEORY; EDUCATION; ANATOMY
AB Background Medical histology education worldwide faces a documented crisis: curriculum compression has dramatically reduced laboratory instructional time while content expectations remain unchanged. Microlearning, in the form of faculty-created five-minute histology review videos, offers a pragmatic and evidence-based contribution, but empirical evidence for its value in tissue identification remains limited. This study provides rigorous longitudinal evidence across three Kirkpatrick levels to address this gap.Methods This longitudinal study followed first-year medical students across three time points within one semester at Alfaisal University, Saudi Arabia. Performance was assessed using a mock-OSPE on blood vessel histology. Students had access to 11 faculty-created five-minute histology review videos covering cardiovascular and renal histology. Four hypotheses were tested across Kirkpatrick levels 1-3, guided by five theoretical frameworks: Cognitive Load Theory, Multimedia Learning Theory, Variation Theory, Spaced Repetition Theory, and Self-Regulated Learning Theory. Two hypotheses addressed Kirkpatrick Level 3 behavior. Two frameworks - Variation Theory and Self-Regulated Learning Theory - were applied to histology video education for the first time, to the best of the author's knowledge.Methods This longitudinal study followed first-year medical students across three time points within one semester at Alfaisal University, Saudi Arabia. Performance was assessed using a mock-OSPE on blood vessel histology. Students had access to 11 faculty-created five-minute histology review videos covering cardiovascular and renal histology. Four hypotheses were tested across Kirkpatrick levels 1-3, guided by five theoretical frameworks: Cognitive Load Theory, Multimedia Learning Theory, Variation Theory, Spaced Repetition Theory, and Self-Regulated Learning Theory. Two hypotheses addressed Kirkpatrick Level 3 behavior. Two frameworks - Variation Theory and Self-Regulated Learning Theory - were applied to histology video education for the first time, to the best of the author's knowledge.Results Mock-OSPE scores were significantly higher in the post-intervention assessment, with a large effect size. The majority of students watched the videos multiple times across both organ systems. Positive perceptions remained consistently high across all three time points, while negative perceptions remained low overall. Faculty-created videos exhibited a 17-fold adoption increase, becoming students' primary out-of-class learning method. Students valued both videos and face-to-face microscopy, consistent with Generation Z's blended learning profile.Conclusions Faculty-created five-minute histology review videos are an effective and reproducible microlearning component of a broader strategy to mitigate the effects of curriculum compression. They extended learning beyond limited laboratory hours through 24/7 access, were associated with higher tissue identification scores, and showed high voluntary adoption - complementing rather than replacing hands-on learning.

TI Developing augmented reality and virtual reality digital pop-up books to
   foster a reading culture in elementary schools
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF CHILDHOOD EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital pop-up book; augmented reality; virtual reality; reading
   culture; primary school
AB Background: Developing a reading culture among elementary school students is important for supporting literacy development and meaningful learning in Indonesia. Digital learning media may help teachers to provide more engaging and contextual reading materials. Augmented reality (AR)-and virtual reality (VR)-based digital pop-up books offer a possible direction for instructional media development, but such development should be grounded in teachers' perceived needs. Aim: This study described elementary school teachers' perceptions and instructional needs regarding AR-and VR-based digital pop-up books to support reading culture in elementary education. Setting: The study involved 137 elementary school teachers from Pandeglang Regency, Indonesia. Methods: This descriptive quantitative survey collected data through a 25-item structured questionnaire. The instrument was developed as a content-reviewed needs assessment tool covering seven dimensions: reading culture achievement, authenticity, technological integration, functionality, communicative learning, contextuality and assessment. Data were analysed using frequencies, percentages and descriptive statistics. Results: The mean agreement rate across the seven indicators was 85.14%. The highest agreement rates were found for technological integration and communicative learning, each at 88.00%, while the lowest agreement rate was for functionality at 80.00%. Conclusion: The findings show that many teachers perceive the need for reading materials that are technologically integrated, communicative, contextual, authentic, functional and assessment-oriented. Contribution: This study provides a descriptive needs assessment to inform the early development of AR-and VR-based digital pop-up books for elementary reading instruction. The findings represent teachers' perceived needs, not evidence of media effectiveness. Further research should develop, validate and test the media in classroom settings.

TI A model for diagnosing and preventing burnout in inclusive education
   teachers with elements of artificial intelligence
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE burnout; diagnostics; elements of artificial intelligence; model;
   prevention; teacher
ID EFFICACY; STRESS
AB Introduction: In the era of the rapid development of artificial intelligence, the problem of teacher burnout is taking on new substantive characteristics. Ignoring teacher burnout will ultimately negatively impact the quality of education. Therefore, the development of effective teacher support measures is crucial for the development of the education system in Kazakhstan. The aim of this study is to develop a structural and substantive model with elements of artificial intelligence for diagnosing and preventing burnout in teachers working in inclusive education settings. Methods: This article presents a study and assessment of the level of professional burnout among teachers at higher education institutions, colleges, and general secondary schools in Shymkent. The sample consisted of 200 teachers, of whom 84% were women (n = 168) and 16% were men (n = 32), reflecting the gender imbalance characteristic of the teaching profession in Kazakhstan. Results: The mean total score M = 28.13 (SD = 9.01), which corresponds to a high level of burnout and exceeds the threshold used for diagnosis. Analysis of the distribution by levels revealed a pronounced asymmetry towards high values: 74.0% of teachers (n = 148) demonstrated a high level of professional burnout, 24.5% (n = 49) -moderate, and only 1.5% (n = 3) -low. Overall, the analysis confirms that the used diagnostic scale has satisfactory characteristics (alpha > 0.80) and can be used in further studies of the professional well-being of teachers in inclusive education. Discussion: The proposed structural and substantive model is aimed at diagnosing and preventing teacher burnout in inclusive education settings. A SWOT analysis was conducted to assess the internal and external factors involved in implementing the developed model. A comprehensive architecture for an intelligent chatbot was developed, enabling automated screening, forecasting, and personalized recommendation processes. The integration of artificial intelligence tools and digital platforms opens up new possibilities for preventing personalized professional burnout. A specialized training course, "Preventing Teacher Burnout in Inclusive Education", was developed. The proposed model demonstrated the effectiveness of a comprehensive approach to preventing teacher burnout.

TI Developing pre-service EFL teachers' professional competences for
   digital adaptive learning: a quasi-experimental validation of a training
   model
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI in teacher education; competence-based education; digital adaptive
   learning; digital pedagogy; pre-service EFL teachers
AB The growing integration of artificial intelligence into language education necessitates a corresponding evolution in teacher preparation, yet existing competence models remain largely unvalidated within the specific context of digital adaptive learning. This study designed and experimentally validated a training model for developing professional competence among pre-service EFL teachers, comprising four interrelated dimensions: conceptual, digital, methodical, and organizational. Using a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control group design, 106 third-year pre-service EFL teachers (experimental, n = 54; control, n = 52) participated in a 15-week intervention. The experimental group engaged in an elective course structured around the proposed model, while the control group followed conventional methodology training. Competence was assessed across motivational, cognitive, and performance domains using validated instruments. Mixed ANOVA revealed significant Time & times; Group interaction effects favouring the experimental group across all dimensions: motivation [F(1,104) = 24.82, p < .001, eta(2 )= .19, d = 0.97], cognitive competence [F(1,104) = 111.34, p < .001, eta(2 ) = .52, d = 2.05], and instructional performance [F(1,104) = 228.34, p < .001, eta(2 )= .69, d = 2.94]. These findings provide empirical validation for a training model, demonstrating that structured, competence-based preparation is associated with significantly enhanced pre-service teachers' readiness to integrate adaptive technologies into language instruction. The study contributes both a replicable pedagogical framework and evidence of its effectiveness for teacher education programmes responding to AI-mediated educational contexts.

TI From Plausibility to Auditability: Generative Systems, Synthetic
   Scholarship, and the Epistemic Risks of AI-Mediated Research
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-mediated research; auditability; epistemic forensics; generative AI;
   methodological transparency; peer review; prompt framing; research
   integrity; scholarly publishing; synthetic scholarship
ID IMPACT
AB GenAI is now capable of producing journal articles that look like human work, raising the question of whether the scholarly credibility might be misinterpreted as evidentiary validity. This research investigates AI-generated scholarship by shifting attention from the detection of AI-generated content to its critical appraisal and evaluation. To achieve this, a split-paper audit procedure was applied to a fully AI-generated mixed-methods manuscript that was independently reviewed by three university faculty members. Findings indicate that the model can simulate academic style and coherence with a high degree of surface plausibility; however, this superficial rigor was combined with ungrounded content, unsupported contextualization, selective reporting, and inconsistent methodological details. Reviewers' comments also highlighted the formulaic language and narratives that confirmed their prior expectations, and questioned whether prompt structures may be channeling outputs towards pre-existing assumptions and masking areas where evidence is scant. The study defines synthetic scholarship as an epistemic condition where plausibility may supplant verification, and suggests a transparent audit process to facilitate the assessment of AI-mediated scholarship. It argues that ensuring research integrity in the era of generative AI will rely on more than just disclosure of generative AI use; it will also require auditable trails to assist in examining, verifying, and substantiating claims.

TI Literacy Before It Counts: Legibility and Recognition of Adult Literacy
   Beyond Standardized Assessment
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE adult basic education; adult literacy; legibility; literacy assessment;
   multimodality; New Literacy Studies; recognition; standardized
   assessment; translation labor
AB Within dominant policy discourses, adults who score poorly on standardized assessments are often positioned as deficient or lacking because they do not conform to institutionally valued forms of reading and writing. Although these adults often use literacy in complex ways in their daily lives, these vernacular (everyday, out-of-school) literacies do not count. Drawing on New Literacy Studies, recognition theory, and scholarship examining literacy across prisons, transnational families, historically marginalized communities, and multimodal contexts, this article examines how literacy becomes institutionally legible and socially recognizable. We argue that adults' sophisticated everyday literacy practices are institutionally undervalued because they do not align with dominant forms and expectations. Central to this analysis is a distinction between legibility and recognition: literacy may be institutionally illegible because it appears in forms institutions do not know how to read, or it may become legible while still being socially misrecognized and devalued. Adults must engage in costly translation labor to convert their literacies into institutionally acceptable forms and to access recognition, legitimacy, and opportunity. This article argues that literacy exists prior to institutional recognition and that adult literacy education must move beyond deficit-based frameworks toward broader understandings of literacy while still supporting adults' access to dominant literacies. Implications for adult literacy policy, assessment, instruction, and research are discussed.

TI Understanding Student Dependency on AI: The Role of AI Literacy,
   Academic Self-Efficacy, and Resource Management Strategies
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE AI dependency; AI literacy; academic self-efficacy; generative
   artificial intelligence; self-regulated learning; higher education
ID MOTIVATED STRATEGIES; COLLEGE-STUDENTS; INTERNET; PROCRASTINATION;
   APPROPRIATE; PERFORMANCE; AUTOMATION; MODEL
AB The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education raises important questions about how students engage with these technologies and what shapes that engagement. This study examined how AI literacy, academic self-efficacy, and self-regulated resource management strategies are associated with students' reported AI dependency. Participants were 478 students from Israeli higher education institutions who completed a cross-sectional online survey assessing AI dependency, AI literacy (four subscales), academic self-efficacy, and resource management strategies (time and study management, effort regulation, and help seeking). Multiple regression and K-means cluster analysis were used. The skill-based dimensions of AI literacy were positively associated with AI dependency, whereas AI self-efficacy and academic self-efficacy were both negatively associated, suggesting a unified compensatory self-efficacy mechanism. Effort regulation also predicted lower dependency, while general academic help seeking predicted higher dependency. The model explained 27.3% of the variance in AI dependency. Cluster analysis identified four learner profiles differing in literacy-dependency combinations and in self-regulatory resources. The findings suggest that fostering AI literacy alone is insufficient. Developing students' self-efficacy beliefs and self-regulated learning practices appears equally important for promoting balanced and intentional AI engagement in higher education.

TI Design and Content Validation of a Questionnaire on Teachers' Training
   Needs to Promote the School-Family Relationship (EVANEFEF)
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article

   relationship; teacher training
ID ENGAGEMENT; EDUCATION; COMMUNICATION; PARTNERSHIPS; VALIDITY; TRUST
AB This study relates to the growing recognition of the school-family relationship as a key factor in equity, inclusion, and educational success, highlighting the need to strengthen teacher education in this area. TI Perceived usefulness of institutional repositories for research outputs
   among Arabic language undergraduates in Kwara state, Nigeria
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Arabic language; institutional repositories; Kwara state; Nigeria;
   perceived usefulness; research outputs; undergraduates
ID USER ACCEPTANCE
AB Institutional repositories (IRs) are critical platforms for preserving scholarly outputs in higher education, yet undergraduate students' awareness of and utilisation of IRs remain concerns in Nigerian universities. This study investigated the perceived usefulness of IRs for research outputs among Arabic language undergraduates in Kwara State, Nigeria. A descriptive survey design was adopted, involving 300 students selected through multi-stage sampling from federal, state, and private universities. Data were collected using a validated questionnaire with a reliability coefficient of 0.79 and analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics at a 0.05 significance level. Findings revealed that students perceived IR usefulness (grand mean = 3.04). IRs were valued for exploring previous research, accessing publications, enhancing literature reviews, and refining methodologies. No significant differences were found based on gender (t = 1.714, p = 0.122) or institution type (F = 1.724, p = 0.072). The study recommends that universities develop robust IRs and mandate research deposits, that librarians provide training programmes, that departments integrate IR use into curricula, and that the National Universities Commission establish IR guidelines and accreditation standards.

TI When mathematics remains trade-blind: recontextualization and workplace
   mobilization in Ghanaian welding and fabrication education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competency-based education; didactic transposition; Ghana; situated
   learning; trade-blind instruction; TVET; vocational mathematics; welding
   and fabrication
AB Mathematics is essential to vocational competence, yet its occupational relevance may remain obscured when taught as generic academic content. This study examines a specific form of mathematics-vocational misalignment in Ghanaian Welding and Fabrication education: the gap between the formal inclusion of mathematics in the curriculum and its functional integration into trade-specific practice. Using an interpretive qualitative case-study design, the study draws on semi-structured interviews with 12 participants across two technical institutes and 10 workplace observation sessions involving two recent graduates. Data were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis informed by abductive reasoning. The findings show that mathematics was embedded in fabrication activities, including measuring, cutting, spacing, estimating, forming angles, and constructing artifacts. However, respondents described the implemented curriculum as a shared TVET mathematics syllabus that was commonly taught and assessed as general, examination-oriented mathematics rather than as trade-specific occupational reasoning. Vocational instructors, therefore, frequently reconstructed the occupational meaning of mathematics during workshop activities, a process the study conceptualizes as retrospective repair. Workplace observations further revealed uneven mathematical mobilization: graduates acknowledged that mathematics was involved in all 48 recorded activities, but varied in their ability to identify and articulate the concepts used. The study contributes by distinguishing formal inclusion from functional integration, conceptualizing workshop mediation as retrospective repair, and proposing trade-blind mathematics instruction as a sensitizing concept for examining weak recontextualization in vocational mathematics education.

TI Relational coordination as a driver of student satisfaction in higher
   education: a nonlinear structural equation modelling analysis
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; nonlinear structural equation modelling; perceived
   institutional improvement; relational coordination; student
   satisfaction; university management
AB Introduction Student satisfaction is a strategic indicator of higher education quality and is closely related to retention, engagement, and students' overall evaluation of their university experience. Previous research has often examined academic, administrative, social, and participatory dimensions separately, leaving limited evidence on how relational coordination with different university actors is jointly associated with satisfaction. This study examines whether relational coordination with lecturers, administrative staff, peers, and student representatives is associated with overall student satisfaction, and whether perceived institutional improvement moderates these relationships.Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 593 undergraduate students at a Spanish public university during the 2024-2025 academic year. Data were analysed using nonlinear structural equation modelling with WarpPLS, allowing the estimation of direct associations, latent interaction terms, and potential nonlinear patterns.Results The model explained 46.9% of the variance in student satisfaction. Coordination with administrative services, lecturers, and peers was positively associated with student satisfaction, while coordination with student representatives was not significant as a direct predictor. Perceived institutional improvement selectively moderated the relationship between relational coordination and satisfaction: it strengthened the associations involving lecturers and student representatives but did not significantly moderate the relationship involving administrative coordination. The interaction involving peer coordination was positive but did not reach the conventional level of statistical significance.Discussion The findings suggest that student satisfaction is closely linked to the quality of everyday relational coordination, particularly in administrative and academic domains. They also show that perceived institutional improvement does not operate as a universal enhancer, but rather as a selective contextual condition that strengthens some relational pathways more than others. The study contributes to higher education research by clarifying how relational ecosystems and institutional perceptions jointly shape student satisfaction, while also offering practical guidance for university managers seeking to improve the student experience.

TI Mechanisms of resilience and meaning in teacher well-being: a serial
   mediation model derived from professional self-efficacy
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE resilience; self-efficacy; teacher subjective well-being; teachers;
   Venezuela; work meaning
ID JOB DEMANDS; RESOURCES
AB Background Professional self-efficacy shares a complex relationship with teacher subjective well-being (TSW) through proximal psychological resources like work meaning and resilience. This study examined the sequential associations connecting professional self-efficacy to TSW through work meaning and resilience among Venezuelan teachers.Methods A cross-sectional design was used with a multi-regional sample of 1,088 primary and secondary education teachers. The proposed sequential framework was tested using structural equation modeling and bias-corrected bootstrapping for indirect associative pathways.Results Professional self-efficacy was positively associated with TSW at the bivariate level, but its direct association was not significant after work meaning and resilience were included in the model, indicating an indirect-only associative pattern. The results suggest that teacher development programs should go beyond technical skills and include strategies that strengthen work meaning, emotional regulation, and resilience, particularly in high-demand educational contexts such as Venezuela.

TI Heart rate variability, psychological variables, and executive
   performance in teachers: an exploratory cross-sectional study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE burnout; executive functions; heart rate variability; perceived stress;
   social support; Stroop; teachers; verbal fluency
ID NEUROVISCERAL INTEGRATION; SOCIAL SUPPORT; WHOQOL-BREF; STRESS;
   PERSPECTIVE
AB Objective Teaching is a high-demand occupation in which sustained stress may impair wellbeing and self-regulatory processes. Within the neurovisceral integration framework, heart rate variability (HRV) is used as an indicator of autonomic modulation relevant to self-control. To examine the relationships among perceived stress, social support, resting HRV, and executive function performance (Stroop and verbal fluency) in teachers, considering burnout and quality of life as concurrent variables.Methods Cross-sectional correlational study (N = 49). Participants completed the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10), Maslach Burnout Inventory-Educators Survey (MBI-ES), WHO Quality of Life-BREF (WHOQOL-BREF), and the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS). HRV was recorded for 5 min at seated rest using a Polar H10 chest strap and processed into time-domain indices (mean RR, SDNN, RMSSD) and frequency-domain indices (LF, HF, LF/HF). Executive performance was assessed with the Stroop test and phonemic and semantic verbal fluency. Associations were modeled using hierarchical multivariate Bayesian regression adjusted for potential confounders.Results Multivariate models suggested that global variability markers (e.g., SDNN and mean RR) were associated with better Stroop interference performance, whereas indices reflecting parasympathetic predominance (e.g., HF and a parasympathetic nervous system index) were associated with poorer interference performance. Higher perceived stress and higher depersonalization were associated with poorer verbal fluency (semantic and phonemic) and poorer inhibitory control as measured by Stroop.Conclusion In this exploratory study, preliminary associations suggested that executive performance in teachers may relate to both psychological state (perceived stress and burnout) and resting autonomic modulation. Notably, higher resting parasympathetic indices showed a tendency toward negative associations with executive performance, a pattern that contradicts simple interpretations of neurovisceral integration and warrants replication. These findings should be regarded as hypothesis-generating signals pending confirmation in larger, longitudinal samples.

TI Evaluating peer discussion in calculus-based mechanics using a
   cluster-randomized crossover design
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID STUDENT PERFORMANCE; INSTRUCTION
AB Peer discussion (PD) is widely used as an active-learning strategy in physics education, yet most prior research has focused on conceptual multiple-choice questions. Much less is known about how peer discussion functions when applied to mathematically structured problems typical of calculus-based mechanics courses. To address this gap, we compared the effects of PD and instructor explanation (IE) during short in-class exercise sessions in a calculus-based introductory mechanics course (N 1/4 87). Using a cluster-randomized crossover design with two course sections, instruction alternated between PD and IE across weekly exercise topics. After each lesson, students completed a 16-item post-test; 12 of these items were also administered on the final exam. Across the 16 post-test items, we found no statistically significant evidence that PD outperformed IE on any single item. In unadjusted item-level analyses, four items that required greater abstraction and multistep mathematical reasoning showed a trend favoring IE, although none of these differences remained statistically significant after Holm correction for multiple comparisons. On the final exam, no statistically significant differences were observed between conditions. These results suggest that, within the instructional conditions of this study, PD did not produce consistent performance gains relative to IE, and any item-level differences may depend on task characteristics such as mathematical abstraction, novelty, and multistep reasoning demands.

TI Can citations indicate performance levels? An investigation of
   integrated argumentative writing tests
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Citations; Integrated reading-to-write tests; Argumentative essays;
   Writing Performance; L2 writing assessment research
ID PERCEPTIONS
AB Citation is an essential feature of source use in integrated writing. However, scarcely any research has investigated test-takers' citation performance on timed integrated writing tests. This study addressed this gap by investigating undergraduate students' citation performance on a timed integrated reading-to-write argumentative essay test. The study recruited 204 undergraduate participants, who completed an integrated reading-to-write essay based on five source texts. Their writing samples were manually coded to generate statistics on citation density, accuracy, distribution, formats, and functions, which were compared across three performance levels, source texts, and part genres (i.e., introduction, body, and conclusion) to identify features of citation patterns in timed integrated writing tests. The study provides valuable information for understanding citations, source use, and their potential as performance indicators of writing performance in integrated writing tests and research.

TI Causal attributions and engagement in class: a daily diary study of
   success and failure experiences
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Causal attributions; Behavioral engagement; Daily diary study; Academic
   beliefs; Intensive longitudinal data; School performance; Grades
ID SINGLE-ITEM MEASURES; ADOLESCENTS ATTRIBUTIONS; SELF-ESTEEM;
   HIGH-SCHOOL; MOTIVATION; PERFORMANCE; DISAFFECTION; PERSPECTIVE;
   PREDICTORS; TRANSITION
AB Throughout the world, students typically receive grades as an evaluation of their schoolwork. Students' subjective interpretations of the causes behind these grades - their causal attributions - can influence their educational experiences, including their engagement in class. While previous research has thus far mostly studied attributions as relatively stable dispositions, the current study addresses their situational nature by employing intensive longitudinal methods to examine attributions and their daily associations with engagement. Across two weeks, 623 7th grade students (Mage = 13.13; 49.8% female) in 49 classrooms across six Dutch secondary schools provided daily assessments of their behavioral engagement alongside attributions for their daily grades. Variance decomposition analyses revealed substantial variation both within and between students, indicating that students exhibit both a general tendency in their attributions as well as daily fluctuations. Multilevel modeling showed that between-student differences in attributions rather than daily attributions were mostly associated with differences in engagement in class. Attributing success to luck proved to be an exception. On days when students attributed their successes more to luck, they tended to be less engaged in class. The findings suggest that students who experience their good performance as being out of their control may be less likely to engage in class. By examining students' daily attributions as they unfold in their natural environment, this study makes a valuable contribution to enhancing the understanding of attributions in real-world contexts.

TI Teaching beyond the prescription: A survey evaluating a cultural
   humility course in pharmacy education
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Cultural humility; Pharmacy education; Cultural competence; Purnell
   model; Active learning; Health disparities
ID COMPETENCE
AB Objective To evaluate the impact of a structured cultural humility course on first-year PharmD students' self-reported confidence in cultural knowledge, cross-cultural communication, and culturally responsive patient care, anchored in the Purnell Model for Cultural Competence. Methods A 2-credit cultural humility course was integrated into the P1 pharmacy curriculum, aligned with ACPE Standards 2025 (Standard 2.1.d). Using a quasi-experimental, non-randomized pretest-posttest design, students completed an anonymous 16-item survey before and after the course rated on a 4-point Likert scale (1 = not at all confident to 4 = very confident). Active learning strategies included take-home quizzes, a structured Padlet reflection activity, and a culminating group cultural presentation applying the Purnell Model framework. Survey reliability was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, and paired comparisons evaluated pre-to-post confidence changes. Results Twenty-five students completed the pre-course survey; 11 completed the post-course survey. Internal consistency was high (alpha = 0.93 pre-course; 0.95 post-course). Mean pre-course scores ranged from 2.16 to 3.36; post-course scores ranged from 3.36 to 4.00. All 16 items showed significant improvement (p < 0.0001). The largest gains were in eliciting patients' illness perspectives (+1.21), accurately describing culturally competent care (+1.17), and effectively using interpreters in patient encounters (+1.20). Conclusion A structured cultural humility course incorporating the Purnell Model and active learning strategies significantly improved PharmD students' self-reported confidence across cultural knowledge, communication, and patient care domains. These findings support intentional curricular design as an effective approach to preparing future pharmacists to address health disparities in alignment with ACPE Standards 2025.

TI Building pharmacists' research-to-practice capacity through
   province-wide continuing education: Baseline readiness, immediate
   effects, and an implementation model
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacists; Continuing education; Research capacity; Pharmacy
   education; Implementation; Medication use
ID HOSPITAL PHARMACISTS; ATTITUDES; CONFIDENCE
AB Introduction: Pharmacists increasingly need practice-based research skills, but workforce readiness, educational response, and posttraining support needs remain under-described in resource-constrained health systems. Methods: A baseline survey with a nested one-group pre-post educational evaluation was conducted during a one-day continuing education program in Dong Thap Province, Vietnam. Eligible pharmacists worked in public or private healthcare facilities and completed electronic questionnaires. Analytic samples included 193 pretraining pharmacists, 135 unique posttraining pharmacists, and 104 conservatively matched pre-post pairs. Outcomes included knowledge, attitudes, confidence, satisfaction, intention to apply learning, perceived barriers, and support needs. Paired analyses used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for total-score changes and exact McNemar tests for item-level knowledge changes. Results: At baseline, 48.7% had never participated in medication-use or quality-improvement research, 72.5% had no related output in the previous three years, and 53.9% had never used research to change practice. Leading barriers were insufficient workforce (77.7%), limited mentorship (66.8%), lack of time (64.2%), limited interprofessional collaboration (62.2%), and difficulty using English-language or international evidence (61.1%). In matched analyses, knowledge changed from 6.09 to 6.43 of 8 (mean change, 0.35; Wilcoxon P = 0.059; Cohen dz = 0.21), attitude from 32.91 to 33.92 of 40 (mean change, 1.01; Wilcoxon P = 0.004; dz = 0.22), and confidence from 28.12 to 30.36 of 40 (mean change, 2.24; Wilcoxon P < 0.001; dz = 0.36). Satisfaction was high, while 63.7% indicated possible participation in at least one medication-use improvement or research activity within three months and 85.9% reported needing a posttraining support focal point.<br /> Discussion: The largest immediate gains were affective and self-efficacy related; imple-mentation readiness remained conditional on workplace supports. Conclusion: Sustaining pharmacist research capacity may require education combined with mentoring, protected time, standardized tools, and feedback into medication-use governance

TI Behind screen time: An examination of parents' decisions on young
   children's screen time
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Screen time; Early childhood; Attitudes; Subjective norms; Intentions;
   Perceived; Behavioral control
ID MEDIA USE; BEHAVIOR; EFFICACY
AB The aim of the present study was to examine the decision-making processes that lead parents to allow screen time for their children. To this end, screen time among children aged 1 to 48 months was examined through a survey of 129 parents using an online questionnaire. In line with the framework of the Theory of Planned Behavior, findings indicate that parents' subjective norms about screen time are linked to their attitudes toward children's screen time. A more positive attitude toward children's screen time was in turn linked to a higher intention to permit screen time, which was associated with a higher level of children's screen time. Perceived behavioral control was not found to play a strong role in this process. Moreover, the age of the child was linked to more favorable subjective norms and attitudes toward screen time as well as to all other aspects of the decision-making process. These results suggest that children's age and subjective norms might play an important role in children's screen time.

TI Epistemic in/justice and theories of multiple source use: A narrative
   review and emerging sociocultural model
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGIST
LA English
DT Article
ID INJUSTICE; REPRESENTATIONS; COMPREHENSION; PLAUSIBILITY; CREDIBILITY;
   INFORMATION; DOCUMENTS; FRAMEWORK; CONTEXTS; BELIEFS
AB Multiple source use (MSU) is a common phenomenon in everyday literacy tasks, and learning environments. A subset of MSU tasks implicates justice concerns, in requiring readers to engage with contested or contentious issues, or/and issues of power and in/equity in source and content evaluation and underlying topics of foci. Epistemic in/justice provides a conceptual frame to understand some of these issues, relating to testimonial and hermeneutic in/justice in how sources are treated and the interpretive resource available for epistemic communities to build knowledge. This article introduces a novel emerging account of epistemic in/justice in theoretical models of multiple source use, through a narrative review of both literatures that highlights areas of intersection in MSU tasks. We provide an exemplification of the account through discussion of a vignette describing a typical MSU task, and possible sites for closing, opening, and activating opportunities for engagement with epistemic justice in this task. Our approach has implications both in the use of MSU in research (as instantiating, probing, or challenging epistemic justice), and in MSU task design for pedagogic contexts.

TI Academic procrastination at three levels: The DEferral dispLAY (DELAY3)
   framework
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGIST
LA English
DT Article
ID SELF-REGULATION; EMOTION REGULATION; UNDERSTANDING PROCRASTINATION;
   TRAIT PROCRASTINATION; SCHOOL SUBJECTS; MOTIVATION; PERFORMANCE;
   EFFICACY; MODEL; TIME
AB Procrastination-the voluntary and unnecessary delay of an intended personally important action, despite awareness of negative consequences and accompanied by subjective discomfort-is a widespread phenomenon and has typically been conceptualized as a result of self-regulatory failure. Existing theoretical approaches propose various mechanisms underlying procrastination, yet these have not been integrated into a comprehensive framework. Moreover, prior research tends to focus either on state aspects of procrastination or on more stable interindividual differences; it rarely addresses different levels simultaneously. With the proposed DEferral dispLAY (DELAY3) framework, we aim to move the field forward in four respects. First, we integrate currently dominant approaches to more fully describe the (lack of) self-regulatory process underlying procrastination behaviors. First, we integrate currently dominant approaches to more comprehensively describe the (lack of) self-regulatory processes underlying procrastination. Second, we extend previous theoretical approaches by explicitly considering three different levels of procrastination, including situation-specific processes, domain-specific person characteristics, and general traits. Third, we take contextual factors of procrastination and their potential moderating role for individual behavior into account. Fourth, feedback cycles across levels, and regulatory processes on a state level are described. The DELAY3 framework provides a comprehensive framework for procrastination research. It offers guidance for future research and allows the derivation of targeted interventions.

TI Possibility mindset: A theory of motivation under constraint, with
   neurodivergence as a revealing interpretive case
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGIST
LA English
DT Article
ID MEASUREMENT INVARIANCE; SELF-DETERMINATION; IMPLICIT THEORIES;
   ACHIEVEMENT; AUTISM; EMOTIONS; INTERVENTIONS; DISABILITIES; STUDENTS;
   ADULTS
AB Growth mindset has reshaped how educational psychology explains persistence under challenge by showing that self-change beliefs influence how students interpret difficulty and respond to setbacks, particularly when learning conditions make improvement feasible. For disabled and neurodivergent learners, however, effort and strategy often cannot fully remove high-impact barriers, raising questions about how motivation operates under enduring constraint. Possibility mindset is proposed as a complementary construct for understanding motivation in such contexts. It is defined as a learner's context-specific appraisal of "room to move," grounded in three belief dimensions: self-change beliefs, environment-change beliefs, and pathway-flexibility beliefs. Although especially salient for disabled and neurodivergent learners, the framework applies more broadly to educational contexts in which effort alone cannot reliably secure access. The central claim is that self-change beliefs are most likely to sustain engagement when learners also expect environments to respond and pathways to remain viable. The framework specifies predicted belief configurations, outlines a research agenda for measurement and incremental validity testing, and identifies aligned interventions that combine psychological messages with visible structural flexibility. Drawing on attributional traditions, the framework shows how attributions about systems-not solely about the self-shape motivational decisions under enduring constraint.

TI Remodeling methods for researching self-regulated learning: Randomized
   controlled trials vs. N=me
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGIST
LA English
DT Article
ID INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES
AB This invited essay adapts my address delivered on the occasion of receiving the American Psychological Association Division 15 Career Achievement Award. I summarize my conceptualization of self-regulated learning (SRL) and, relative to that account, I identify deficiencies of today's gold standards for research, the randomized controlled trial (RCT) and meta-analyses of RCTs. Studies adopting that paradigm misconstrue how learners practice SRL in their individual ways, garble how SRL relates to outcomes, and cannot validly ground generalizations about practices individual learners should adopt to regulate learning more productively. Software can be engineered to gather fine-grained, precise trace data documenting what each learner does as they study and which information they process via each of those events. Leveraging trace data, I propose an alternative to the gold standard for researching SRL (and other constructs), the N=me approach. I describe that approach, how it rectifies shortcomings of RCTs, and note some of its limitations.

TI Practicing defending in virtual reality: A feasibility study among
   primary school children
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual reality; Defending behavior; Bullying prevention; Feasibility
   study; Shyness, Self-efficacy, Bystander intervention
ID BYSTANDER INTERVENTION; SOCIAL WITHDRAWAL; FACE VALIDITY; METAANALYSIS;
   ANXIETY; CHILDHOOD; BEHAVIOR; THERAPY; PEERS
AB Most children say they want to help peers who are bullied, but in real bullying situations, they often remain passive bystanders. Existing anti-bullying programs have led to modest improvements in defending, but they typically provide limited opportunities for children to practice defending in realistic, emotionally charged bullying situations. Immersive Virtual Reality (VR) may offer a promising tool to let children rehearse defending in controlled ways in such scenarios. This practice might be particularly helpful for children who experience stronger inhibitions to defend because they are shy. This feasibility study examined whether a brief VR-based training could strengthen defending behavior and defending self-efficacy in bullying situations, and explored whether children who are more shy would benefit in particular. Participants were 22 children aged 6-10 years (Mage = 8.41, SD = 0.96; 77.3% boys), from two Dutch primary schools and an after-school care. In a within-subjects pre-post design, children completed two VR bullying scenarios with individualized coaching in between. Observed defending behavior in VR was coded, and children reported defender self-efficacy, tension, VR experience, shyness, and perceived bullying in their classroom. Children showed a substantial increase in observed defending from pre-to post-training, alongside a significant increase in defending self-efficacy, while reported tension remained stable. Shyness did not moderate observed defending at baseline, nor defending improvements. However, more shy children showed a larger gain in defender self-efficacy than their less shy peers. These findings, obtained in a small, age-heterogeneous sample, suggest that immersive VR can be used to elicit measurable changes in defending behavior and perceived defending ability among young children, and that children with higher levels of shyness may be especially responsive in terms of self-efficacy, but they require replication in larger, age-stratified samples. The study, thus, initially illustrates the potential of VR as a tool to study how bystander defending develops and how children's defending behavior in perceived socially risky situations can be supported.

TI Pedagogical stratification in kindergartens: Evidence from Hong Kong
   quality review reports
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Early childhood education; Pedagogy; Text-as-data; Structural topic
   model; Semi-market governance; Hong Kong
ID EARLY-CHILDHOOD EDUCATION; CLASSROOM QUALITY; CARE; PROGRAMS;
   METAANALYSIS; ACHIEVEMENT; PERCEPTIONS; PARENT
AB Equity in early childhood education is often debated in terms of access; however, the pedagogical content that children experience may be unequally distributed even when access and accountability are formally standardized. This study examined whether pedagogical emphases varied systematically across kindergartens operating under a common quality-assurance regime. Drawing on 720 publicly available kindergarten inspection narratives from Hong Kong (2015-2024) as an empirical proxy for documented practice, this study used structural topic modeling to identify six common pedagogical themes: Regulation and Monitoring, Child Choice and Play, Experiential and Constructive Learning, Physical Development, Moral Socialization, and National Socialization. Neighborhood educational composition, rather than income, differentiated Moral from National Socialization. The findings suggest that documented pedagogy is stratified along institutional and socioeconomic lines even within a standardized accountability framework, which has implications for assessing equity in children's enacted learning opportunities.

TI AI-supported scenario-based learning in entrepreneurship education: A
   comparative classroom study of learning processes and outcomes
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrepreneurship education; AI-supported learning; Scenario-based
   learning; Situated learning; Cognitive apprenticeship
ID GENERATIVE AI
AB Entrepreneurship education is often limited by the difficulty of providing students with authentic, consequence-driven practice. This study examines how different forms of AI-supported scenario-based learning shape student learning and teaching in an entrepreneurship course. Using a quasi-experimental, three-condition classroom design, we compared regular instruction, static AI-assisted interaction, and a multi-agent dynamic simulation. The study involved 42 students, comprising 30 undergraduates and 12 graduate students, and adopted a mixed-methods approach that integrated pre-and post-tests, instructor-evaluated performance, reflection logs, and interviews. Quantitative analyses were used to compare learning outcomes and mechanism-related measures across groups, while qualitative data were coded and thematically analyzed. Results indicated that the static AI support condition was associated with only modest benefits, whereas the multi-agent dynamic simulation condition was associated with stronger gains in entrepreneurial self-efficacy, opportunity competence, and instructor-evaluated decision quality, as well as higher perceived scaffolding, authenticity, and engagement. Qualitative findings further indicated deeper reasoning and reflection in the multi-agent dynamic simulation condition, while also revealing reduced interpersonal communication and greater ambiguity in instructors' roles. Because this condition combined several instructional features, the findings suggest that the value of AI in entrepreneurship education depends on the design of the broader instructional package rather than on technology alone.

TI Enhancing professional vision with annotation tools
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional vision; Teaching videos; Annotation tool; Instructional
   strategies; Pre-service teachers
ID COGNITIVE-LOAD; TEACHERS; PRESERVICE; VIDEO; KNOWLEDGE; PROMPTS;
   ACQUISITION; STRATEGIES; FRAMEWORK; BENEFITS
AB Background: Professional vision is conceptualized as a situation-specific competence that involves noticing (i.e., attending to relevant classroom events) and knowledge-based reasoning (i.e., describing and interpreting events using learning and teaching principles). Whereas video analysis is widely used to foster pre-service teachers' professional vision, it is not always effective. Possible ways to enhance its impact include the use of technological tools and instructional support. Aims: We examined whether technological support through annotation tools improves professional vision compared to post-viewing analysis (Study 1), and whether the effectiveness can be improved by instructional support (prompts, video modeling example, or their combination; Study 2). Samples: We collected data from pre-service teachers who participated in university courses (NStudy1 = 122; NStudy2 = 164). Methods: In Study 1, participants were randomly assigned to either an annotation tool or a post-viewing comment condition. In Study 2, all participants used an annotation tool but were randomly assigned to receive a video modeling example, prompts, both, or no instructional support. Outcome measures included the quantity of classroom events noticed and the quality of knowledge-based reasoning. Subjective cognitive load measures were collected. Results: In Study 1, annotation tools enhanced noticing but did not affect reasoning. In Study 2, modeling improved reasoning over time, whereas prompts alone showed no impact. Conclusions: The findings indicate that annotation tools can facilitate noticing of classroom events, but improving reasoning necessitates structured instructional scaffolds. Video modeling examples effectively enhance pre-service teachers' development of professional vision and promote elaborated reasoning.

SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY

   student; Quality; Scale
ID LEARNING-ENVIRONMENT; SUPERVISION; NURSES
AB Background: Clinical practicum quality is shaped by the learning environment, supervision, and student-patient relationship. Although clinical placements provide valuable learning opportunities, barriers remain. While accreditation programs improve healthcare processes and outcomes, research on nursing students' experiences is limited. Aims: To compare the quality of clinical practicum for nursing students among Magnet hospitals, Magnet-aspiring hospitals, and non-Magnet hospitals, and to identify the background characteristics associated with the quality of clinical practicum in these hospitals. Methods: A comparative cross-sectional study design was used. Implications for practice: Integrating Magnet model components into clinical practicum development can enhance students' skills, learning experiences, and interest in the unit. TI Artificial intelligence literacy, attitudes, and behaviors among nursing
   educators: A latent profile and mediation analysis

DE Nursing educators; Artificial intelligence; Literacy; Attitudes;

AB Background: Nursing educators play a pivotal role in the effective integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into nursing education. Investigating the heterogeneity of their AI literacy and its impact on attitude and behavior is a prerequisite for developing targeted interventions. Objective: This study aimed to identify latent profiles of AI literacy among nursing educators and to examine the mediating role of AI attitude in the relationship between literacy and behavior. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 339 nursing educators in China. Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed in Mplus to identify distinct AI literacy subgroups. TI Rethinking robot-assisted autism interventions: A developmental
   misalignment framework in ethics, cognition, and context
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Pedagogical effectiveness; Robot-assisted instruction; Critical
   interpretive synthesis (CIS); methodology; Naturalistic teaching; Social
   interaction
ID AUTOMATIC IMITATION; CHILDREN; INDIVIDUALS; EDUCATION; THERAPY
AB This study aims to critically examine robot-assisted instructional practices from a pedagogical perspective concerning the developmental and social-cognitive needs of children with autism. Using the Critical Interpretive Synthesis (CIS) methodology, this critical review analyzes findings from 29 studies. According to the studies, robots mostly exhibit benefits in short-term, organized, low-demand interactions; however, these benefits do not translate to natural social circumstances. The findings further suggest that robots' limited capacities for gesture, facial expression, prosody, and intentionality restrain their ability to support the multi-layered processes underlying social cognition. Moreover, mechanical language use and interaction patterns raise theoretical concerns regarding communication and language development in children with autism that warrant careful empirical scrutiny. Given these findings, the current evidence base supports positioning robotassisted instruction as a time-limited, supplementary tool targeting specific, structured subskills rather than as a primary method for broad social-cognitive development. Evidence-based practices that emphasize naturalistic, relationship-based, and contextually embedded learning are identified as better aligned with the developmental and contextual requirements of children with autism for supporting long-term developmental outcomes. Accordingly, this paper proposes the Developmental Mismatch Framework (DMF), which conceptualizes the structural incongruence between robots' social representational capacities and the natural social-cognitive requirements of children with autism across interactional, cognitive, and contextual dimensions.

TI Classroom management in vocational schools - A multilevel analysis of
   class context, class composition, and classroom management

ID OF-FIT INDEXES; TEACHING QUALITY; STUDENTS; TEACHERS; PERCEPTIONS;

AB Given the lack of studies on the topic of classroom management in vocational schools, we used student ratings to analyze the factors that contribute to effective classroom management in vocational schools. TI Development and evaluation of a student feedback agency scale
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Writing feedback; Feedback agency; Student agency; Scale development;
   Chinese international students
ID SOCIAL COGNITIVE THEORY; OF-FIT INDEXES; L2
AB Feedback agency is a key concept in enhancing student writing performance. While growing attention has been paid to student feedback agency, existing research remains largely theoretical and qualitative. As a result, there is a lack of psychometrically supported instruments to measure this construct. To address this gap, the present two-phase study aimed to develop and evaluate Student Feedback Agency Scale (SFAS), drawing on social cognitive theory. In the development stage, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was conducted on a sample of 235 Chinese international postgraduate students. The results yielded a 23-item SFAS comprising six components: Action Taking, Goal Setting, Processing, Generating, Self-efficacy, and Seeking. Using an independent sample of 349 participants from the same population, Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) conducted in the evaluation stage. The results supported a good model fit (RMSEA = .055, IFI .923, TLI = .908, and CFI = .922). Multi-group CFAs further confirmed the structural invariance across gender, academic level, and discipline. Overall, the findings provide psychometric dence to support the interpretation and use of the SFAS scores to measure student agency writing feedback processes. Based on these results, the factor structure and subscales of the SFAS are discussed, and implications are outlined.

TI Fair and explainable educational recommendations with a hybrid Graph-GRU
   framework
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational recommender systems; Heterogeneous graph; Neural networks;
   Sequential modeling; Fairness-aware learning; Explainable AI;
   Counterfactual robustness; Re-ranking diversity; Responsible AI
AB Artificial Intelligence (AI) recommender systems are increasingly used in education to personalize learning and help students navigate large collections of digital learning resources. However, many existing approaches emphasize predictive accuracy over fairness, robustness, diversity, and transparency. This creates an important educational challenge. The students with limited participation histories may receive less reliable support, while highly popular resources may dominate recommendation lists and limit access to other useful learning materials. To address this challenge, this study aims to develop and evaluate a responsible educational recommender framework that supports personalized learning resource navigation while making recommendation behavior more fair, stable, diverse, and explainable. This study introduces the Hybrid Heterogeneous Knowledge GraphGated Recurrent Unit (Hybrid HKG-GRU) framework, which combines heterogeneous graph embeddings with sequential modeling to capture both the relational structure of course materials and the temporal dynamics of learner interactions. The framework integrates three contributions: (i) multi-objective training with Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (GroupDRO), (ii) Maximum Marginal Relevance (MMR) reranking to reshape exposure patterns, and (iii) built-in, model-centric explainability through path-based and counterfactual analyses. The empirical evaluation shows strong predictive performance with HR@10 = 0.68 and MRR = 0.41 on Moodle LMS logs dataset that comprises of 152 students, 59 resources, and approximately 150k interactions. The model also achieves high intra-list diversity and moderate catalogue coverage, while showing moderate counterfactual stability for many learners (median CR@10 = 1.0), although catalogue-level popularity bias remains evident. The framework provides model-centric interpretability and verification intended to support more transparent educational recommendation. The study positions the framework as a technically auditable approach for improving how learning resources are recommended, inspected, and monitored in educational settings. By integrating fairness, robustness, and explainability as coequal design objectives, the Hybrid HKG-GRU provides a methodological foundation for more responsible and accountable recommender systems in education and related high-stakes contexts.

TI Developing L2 writing student self-assessment literacy through
   AI-generated feedback and AI chain-of-thought: An action research study
   with lower-proficiency university EFL learners
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student self-assessment literacy; AI chain-of-thought; AI-Generated
   feedback; L2 writing; Action research
ID TEACHER FEEDBACK; EDUCATION
AB Student self-assessment literacy (SSAL) is crucial for second language (L2) writing proficiency and learner autonomy. However, lower-proficiency English as a foreign language (EFL) learners often struggle to apply assessment criteria independently and remain reliant on teacher feedback. Although generative AI is increasingly used to provide writing feedback, its potential to support SSAL development through explicit evaluative reasoning remains underexplored. In this study, AI chain-of-thought (AI-CoT) refers to learner-visible, criterion-guided evaluative reasoning that externalizes the processes of planning, monitoring, and evaluation during supported selfassessment. In this sense, AI-CoT was used alongside AI-generated feedback to make the reasoning linking assessment criteria, textual evidence, and revision priorities more transparent. This study traces SSAL development across four dimensions among lower-proficiency university EFL learners, analyses the complementary roles of AI-generated feedback and AI-CoT, and proposes a dual-loop interaction framework explaining how teacher-led instructional design and student-led AI-mediated self-assessment jointly shape SSAL. Employing a three-cycle action research design over 12 weeks, this study involved 30 lower-proficiency university EFL learners. Data included think-aloud protocols, semi-structured interviews, drafts with tracked revisions, AIgenerated feedback and AI-CoT logs, SSAL checklists, and teacher reflective journals. Findings showed that AI-generated feedback primarily supported criterion application and text revision, whereas AI-CoT supported learners' comprehension and interpretation by making evaluative reasoning more visible. Across the three cycles, students became increasingly self-directed in their self-assessment, although critical engagement and independent enactment remained uneven. The proposed framework offers pedagogical guidance for integrating generative AI into reflective, criterion-guided self-assessment to support metacognitive growth in L2 writing.
