TI Implementation of Shiny-R in active learning strategies for teaching
   statistics in engineering education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE active learning; cognitive load theory; engineering education; Shiny-R;
   statistics education
AB The digitalization of engineering education demands pedagogical strategies that go beyond passive instruction. While R is a standard tool for data science, its steep learning curve often creates a "syntax barrier" that hinders conceptual understanding, leading to cognitive overload for novice students. This study evaluates ShinyStats-ESPE, an interactive web-based environment designed to bridge the gap between statistical theory and computational practice. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory, our approach isolates conceptual exploration from coding mechanics using a "Predict-Observe-Explain" pedagogical cycle. We employed a quasi-experimental design (N=44) to compare learning outcomes between a control group (n=19) using traditional script-based methods and an experimental group (n=25) utilizing our interactive modules. The results, analyzed via Welch's t-test, indicate a significant improvement in the experimental group (t=2.21, p=0.018), with pass rates doubling from 37% to 76%. These findings suggest that temporarily bypassing syntax through interactive GUIs allows students to scaffold deeper statistical reasoning, offering a scalable model for engineering curricula.

TI Beyond formal equality: institutionalizing inclusion in Kazakhstan's
   higher education through policy and student perceptions
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE formal equality; higher education; models of inclusion; reasonable
   accommodations; Universal Design for Learning
ID UNIVERSAL DESIGN
AB Inclusion in higher education has become a fundamental necessity in contemporary educational settings. In Kazakhstan, universities tend to institutionalize inclusion primarily through the lenses of formal equality and a medical-compensatory approach, whereas students themselves associate inclusivity with flexible learning, support mechanisms, and elements of Universal Design for Learning (UDL). The study examines inclusion in higher and postgraduate education institutions in Kazakhstan through a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods, including a content analysis of universities' internal regulatory documents and an empirical sociological survey conducted among students from five Kazakhstani universities (n = 372). The findings reveal a noticeable gap between the institutional formalization of inclusion and the way inclusion is perceived by university students. The study demonstrates that Kazakhstani inclusive higher education requires a shift from compensatory approach toward the systemic integration of Universal Design for Learning and substantive equality at the institutional policy level.

TI Clinical ultrasound competencies for undergraduate medical education in
   Spain: A national consensus using a modified Delphi study
SO EDUCACION MEDICA
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Medical education; Clinical ultrasound; Professional compe-tence;
   Curriculum; Medical students; Point-of-Care Ultra-sound (POCUS)
ID STUDENT EDUCATION; ANATOMY; CURRICULUM; STATEMENT
AB Introduction: Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS) has become an essential diagnostic tool in contemporary medical practice. However, its integration into medical degree curricula in Spain is uneven and lacks a standardized competency framework. Objective: To define, by expert consensus, the cross-cutting competencies in clinical ultrasound that medical students in Spain should acquire during their undergraduate training. Material and methods: A modified Delphi study was conducted, coordinated by the Interuniversity Working Group on Clinical Ultrasound of the Spanish Society for Medical Education (GTEC-SEDEM). Thirty expert teachers from 20 Spanish universities participated. Eighty-nine statements distributed across 14 thematic blocks were evaluated using a 1-to 9point Likert scale. Consensus was established following the RAND/UCLA criteria in two rounds conducted between October and December 2025. Results: Eighty-five competencies were validated (81 with strong consensus and 4 with moderate consensus). The consensus supports a longitudinal curriculum model, beginning with basic sciences and culminating in supervised clinical application. The technical management of the ultrasound machine, the application of the ALARA principle, ethics and confidentiality, and the systematic examination of organs and systems were identified as core competencies. Invasive procedures in patients and applications specific to the postgraduate field were excluded; simulation training for basic skills was maintained. Conclusion: This study provides a nationally agreed competency framework for POCUS teaching in Spanish undergraduate medical education, amenable to local adaptation and future updates. TI Understanding Student Engagement in AI-Assisted Learning in Higher
   Education: The Roles of AI Support, Teacher Support and Flow
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-assisted learning; flow; student engagement; teacher support;
   university students
AB With the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education, this study examined how AI support, teacher support and flow are associated with student engagement in AI-assisted learning in higher education. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, a cross-sectional survey was conducted with 677 university students from multiple institutions who had prior experience using AI-enabled tools for learning. Data were analysed using structural equation modelling with AMOS 26.0 to examine the hypothesised relationships among the study variables. The results showed that AI support and teacher support were both positively associated with student engagement. In addition, both forms of support were positively associated with flow and flow was positively associated with engagement. Mediation analyses further indicated that flow mediated the associations between AI support and engagement and between teacher support and engagement. These findings suggest that student engagement in AI-assisted learning is linked not only to the availability of technological and interpersonal support, but also to the extent to which students experience learning as focused, absorbing and meaningful. The study contributes to current research by integrating technological support, teacher support and experiential processes into a single framework for understanding engagement in AI-assisted learning in higher education.

TI Validation of the adolescent-adults sensory profile (AASP) in the
   Spanish population
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE AASP; Sensory processing; Validation; Spanish population; Psychometric
   properties
ID CROSS-CULTURAL ADAPTATION; PROCESSING PATTERNS; CHILDREN; AUTISM;
   MODULATION; DISORDER; LIFE
AB Purpose: There is a need to validate culturally adapted assessment tools that can identify sensory reactivity problems in adolescents and adults. Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate the psychometric properties of the Spanish version of the Adolescent/Adult Sensory Profile (AASP) according to current COSMIN recommendations, and to explore the structural validity of the instrument in a large Spanish adult sample. Materials and methods: A total of 806 adults participated in this study. A confirmatory factor analysis was performed. Cronbach's alpha coefficients were calculated for all items and for each of the quadrants. An intraclass correlation coefficient analysis was performed on a sample of 134 participants with a 1-week interval. Convergent validity was evaluated by assessing the relationships among the quadrants of the exploratory 42-item solution, AASP-60, and ASQ. Results: Index for confirmatory factor analysis were satisfactory for a version of 42 items (the exploratory 42-item solution). Cronbach's alpha was 0.82, and McDonald's omega was 0.86 for all items; the Intraclass correlation coefficient for each of the four quadrants was 0.90, 0.90, 0.90, and 0.83, respectively. The original version of the AASP-60 items was compared with the new Spanish adaptation of the exploratory 42-item solution, and the correlation levels were high (r = 0.88-0.97; p < 0.01). Conclusions: The psychometric analyses supported acceptable reliability and preliminary evidence of structural validity for an empirically derived 42-item version (AASP-42). This shortened version should be considered exploratory until replicated in independent samples.

TI Mapping the synergistic interaction of L2 learners' writing
   self-efficacy and writing performance: The serial mediating effects of
   writing anxiety and motivation
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE L2 learners; Writing performance; Writing motivation; Writing anxiety;
   Writing self-efficacy
ID 2ND-LANGUAGE; VALIDATION; ENGLISH
AB While writing self-efficacy has long been acknowledged as a determinant of L2 writing performance, the mechanisms through which it translates into meaningful differences in learners' writing achievements remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, our research investigated the synergistic relationship between L2 learners' writing self-efficacy and writing performance, with particular attention to the serial mediating effects of writing anxiety and motivation. A total of 327 Iranian L2 learners were recruited from various universities through a maximum variation sampling technique. Participants first responded to three validated self-report questionnaires and then took the CUNY assessment test in writing (CATW), a standardized instrument that evaluates preparedness for college-level study through an integrated writing task. A structural equation modeling (SEM) was conducted to examine the interactions of the variables under investigation. The SEM results revealed a significant positive correlation between writing self-efficacy and performance. More importantly, writing anxiety and motivation were found to mediate this relationship both independently and sequentially. The study underscores the multifaceted essence of writing development by integrating psychological, affective, and motivational factors into a single framework. It highlights the importance of viewing writing performance not as a static outcome but as the result of interactive psycho-emotional processes that evolve in tandem.

TI Preparing undergraduate education majors to make and use accessible
   digital instructional materials
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital accessibility; Technical accessibility; WCAG standards; Digital
   inclusion; Disability diversion; Critical accessibility
ID STUDENTS
AB Challenges in meeting accessibility needs for K-12 students during the COVID-19 pandemic bring new urgency to teaching accessibility to teachers. While some educators had been able to learn some aspects of accessibility through frameworks such as the Universal Design for Learning, new mandates in the U.S. and Europe are more technical and specific. The purpose of this study was to document and analyze responses undergraduate educators made alongside efforts to teach them about making and using accessible digital instructional materials. Education majors came from a university in the southwest U.S. across three semesters. Implications for practice, research, and policy include the need not only to teach technical skills but help educators (re)conceptualize responsibilities for more careful thinking about educational justice.

TI Filling the fellowship gap: A structured program for pharmacy students
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Fellowship; Mentors; Postgraduate training
AB Background: Postgraduate fellowships for Doctor of Pharmacy students are diverse in their nature and expectations. Although fellowships have long been an avenue for advanced training, the lack of a centralized accreditation process means students are often navigating these opportunities on their own. The objective of this paper is to describe the structure and preliminary outcomes of the fellowship portion of a novel Fellowship and Residency Advising Program (FRAP) at an urban public university. Educational activity: The fellowship portion of FRAP facilitates progression to postgraduate training programs in industry, academia, government, and professional organizations. Students receive support in identifying programs of interest, preparing application materials, and mentorship from a faculty member and an alumnus in the field. Additional activities have been added to increase fellowship preparation over the years. Student fellowship placements are tracked. Data is available for the graduating classes of 2016 to 2025. Evaluation findings: FRAP has evolved since it was first introduced in 2015 with the addition of a formal fellowship pathway in 2019. Forty-six students have successfully obtained fellowships since the program's inception. Summary: The FRAP framework of dual mentorship, a repository of resources, and industry panels for pharmacy students pursuing fellowships may be useful for other institutions to implement.

TI Tracing the origins of teacher gender bias
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher bias; Gender; STEM; Cross-subject skills
ID SUBJECT CHOICE; TEST-SCORES; PERFORMANCE; DISCRIMINATION; ACHIEVEMENT;
   OUTCOMES; WOMEN; GAPS
AB This paper examines whether teachers form gendered expectations that deviate from students' actual academic performance. We exploit a unique institutional setting in England, where university admissions rely on teacher-predicted grades, and use rich administrative data linking student performance and teacher assessments across multiple STEM and non-STEM subjects. We find that, conditional on achieved grades, teachers systematically predict lower grades for boys relative to observationally similar girls within the same school across all subjects. In the second part of the analysis, we examine the extent to which observable student characteristics account for this pattern. We find that including measures of students' cross-disciplinary skills reduces the gender gap in predicted grades by up to 70% in non-STEM subjects and fully explains or even reverses it in STEM. These results indicate that what appears to be a pro-girl bias is, at least in part, associated with students' broader competencies rather than necessarily reflecting differential treatment by teachers. These findings have important implications for the fairness and effectiveness of teacher-based assessments in high-stakes contexts such as university admissions.

TI Exploring changes in high school teachers' culturally sustaining
   pedagogy after training for and implementing an ethnic-racial identity
   curriculum
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Culturally sustaining pedagogy; Ethnic-racial identity; Reflexive
   thematic analysis; Longitudinal qualitative research; Teachers
ID RELEVANT; HEALTH
AB Culturally sustaining pedagogy (CSP) is an approach to teaching and learning that values and sustains students' understanding of and engagement with their identities, cultures, and communities within broader systems of social stratification; it also expands students' understanding of local and global oppressive systems and structures. Yet, little is known about how teachers move toward transformative CSP. This qualitative study employed longitudinal reflexive thematic analysis to explore if and how 14 teachers (13 White, 1 Teacher of Color) changed in their CSP understanding, praxis, and self-efficacy across the span of 16 months during which they were trained on an ethnic-racial identity curriculum and implemented it with their students. Five profiles of CSP change were identified: Transformative Change, Progressive but Nascent Change, Surface-level but Symbolic Change, Interested and Engaged but Limited Change, and Negligible Change and Affirmed in their Practice. Additionally, mechanisms for change that either facilitated or inhibited teachers' movement toward CSP were identified at the teacher and program level. Findings highlighted the variability in how and why teachers advance in their knowledge, practice, and confidence related to CSP. Furthermore, teachers' willingness and depth of critical reflection on their ethnic-racial identity, positionalities, and power dynamics emerged as foundational to CSP change.

TI Long-term Impact of a Surgical Innovation and Training Program for High
   School Students: A 12-Year Follow-Up Study
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE surgical education; innovation; program evaluation; high school students
AB OBJECTIVE: The University of California, Irvine (UCI) Summer Surgery Program (SSP) was founded in 2012 to empower high school students to learn surgical skills, experience surgery in the operating theater, and participate in the surgical innovation process. The 2-week program includes endoscopic, laparoscopic, robotic, open surgical skills training, and a group innovation requirement. Our objective was to assess the impact the SSP on subsequent career paths. DESIGN: We sent a REDCap-based postactivity survey to all 555 program participants to assess the long-term impact of the program. Associations between demographics and survey responses, and career outcomes between cohorts, were determined using chi-square analysis and false discovery rate (FDR) correction. SETTING: The summer surgery program is located at UCI Medical Center, Orange, CA. PARTICIPANTS: Of the 313 survey respondents, 10 were excluded due to virtual participation between 2020 and 2024. A total of 303 individuals were included in the study. RESULTS: Of the 555 participants in the SSP between 2012 and 2024, 303 (54.6%) completed the follow-up survey. Among respondents, 301 (99.3%) reported an increase in their knowledge of healthcare, 93.1% indicated enhanced interest in studying medicine or the sciences in college, 94.1% reported an increased understanding of the importance of innovation, and 83.5% gained a clearer understanding of the innovation process. Overall, 84.2% reported greater confidence in their ability to succeed in a healthcare career, with these students being significantly more likely to report high confidence in becoming a healthcare professional (p = 0.00020). Among the 58 respondents with longterm results (students from 2012-2015), 32 (55.2%) reported being currently enrolled or having completed an MD/DO program and 54 respondents (93.1%) reported pursuing or completing any health-related graduate degree (MD, DO, PhD, RN, etc.) CONCLUSIONS: The 2-week UCI summer surgery program exerted a significant and long-lasting influence on participants' academic trajectories and career aspirations. TI Gendered investments and literacy gaps: Evidence from rural China
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender disparity; Reading performance; Parental educational expectation;
   Parental investments; Rural education
ID CHILDRENS READING-SKILLS; MOTIVATION; INEQUALITIES; STUDENTS; PARENTS;
   HOME
AB This study examines how gendered family practices influence children's reading performance in rural China. Using three waves of panel data from 3486 primary school students, we apply two-way fixed effects models to examine gender differences in reading achievement while accounting for time-invariant unobserved factors. Results show that girls outperform boys across multiple reading outcomes throughout the observation period. We further find that parental reading attitudes and literacy-related investments differ by child gender and are positively associated with children's reading outcomes, partly accounting for observed gender differences. These associations persist over time, though the magnitude of change remains modest. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that gendered patterns in family attitudes and investments are more pronounced among families with lower socioeconomic status. The findings suggest that family beliefs and practices are systematically associated with gender differences in reading development, underscoring the importance of home literacy environments in understanding literacy disparities in resource-constrained rural settings. Educational relevance and implications: This study highlights that gendered patterns in family attitudes and literacy-related practices are systematically associated with children's reading development, suggesting that home environments represent an important, though partial, context for understanding gender differences in literacy outcomes. From a policy perspective, these findings indicate that efforts to promote gender equity in reading may benefit from complementing school-based initiatives with programs that support parents in fostering inclusive and supportive reading environments at home. In rural settings, where families often play a central role in children's learning, providing guidance on reading practices may be particularly relevant for supporting boys' engagement with reading. At the same time, the modest explanatory power of family-level mechanisms underscores the need for coordinated approaches that also consider school practices and broader institutional contexts, especially for children from socioeconomically disadvantaged households.

TI Adaptivity as a core principle of cognitive stimulating instruction:
   Conceptualization and future directions
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
ID LITERACY INSTRUCTION; LOAD THEORY; CLASSROOM; ARCHITECTURE; ADAPTATION;
   FRAMEWORK; STUDENTS; QUALITY; DESIGN; PLAY
AB Attending to student differences during classroom instruction is a central challenge in education and has been addressed through concepts such as individualized instruction, differentiated instruction, personalized learning, and adaptive teaching. Despite differences in terminology and emphasis, we argue that these concepts share a common core instructional principle-adaptivity. In this editorial to the special issue 'Adaptivity as a Core Principle of Cognitively Stimulating Instruction', we define adaptivity as the fit between instruction and student characteristics that effectively stimulates student's cognitive learning processes. We propose that two largely separate research strands provide insights into the concept of adaptivity: experimental research on cognitive foundations of instruction and research on instruction in authentic classroom settings. While experimental research provides robust evidence on cognitive mechanisms underlying instructional effectiveness, classroom research captures the social, motivational, and contextual complexity of teaching and learning. We suggest a conceptualization of adaptivity that integrates insights from both strands. Building on this synthesis, we position the contributions of this special issue along their respective degrees of proximity to these two research strands, illustrating how empirical research from both research strands contributes to the understanding of adaptivity. Finally, we outline future directions for research on adaptivity. Overall, the aim of this special issue is to advance our understanding of how instruction can effectively support learning in heterogeneous classrooms.

TI Articulating a sociocultural framework for designing for learning
   computational thinking
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sociocultural framework; Computational thinking; Greeno; Design for
   learning; Sociocultural conceptualization of; computational thinking
AB This conceptual paper develops a socioculturally informed theoretical framework for designing for learning Computational Thinking (CT); with the wider purpose of providing guidance for educational practice. Existing understandings of CT broadly fall into three categories, which have been termed the cognitive, the situated, and the critical approaches. Implicitly, they agree to an engagement condition for CT activities: CT activities necessarily involve engagement with algorithms. All approaches have an individualist focus, even the so-called "situated" one, which emphasizes individual sense-making and personal expression. The individualist focus of prevalent CT understandings is a problem, not least because of its practical implications: Educational activities based on understanding CT individualistically do not adequately support students in learning the cultural practices of developing, using, and critiquing algorithms in interaction with others; practices that are, however, crucial in our highly digitalized contemporary societies. Instead, such support requires a sociocultural conceptualization of CT, focusing on learners' negotiation of meaning in shared practices, development of patterns of participation and of shared repertoires of informational resources, and negotiation of interactional identities. The present article provides this. Drawing on the work of Greeno, CT phenomena are reconceptualized at four levels of increasing time-scale and complexity. For each level, it is explicated what engagement with algorithms consists in from a sociocultural perspective, and what criteria for demonstrating engagement are. The framework encompasses learning activities highlighted by existing approaches to CT but reconceptualize them as interactional practices. Examples of learning activities at each level are provided.

TI Influence of nursing interns' moral sensitivity on patient safety
   competency: The mediating effect of ethical action
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing interns; Moral sensitivity; Patient safety competency; Ethical
   action
ID EDUCATION; STUDENTS
AB Background: Nursing interns play a dual role in clinical practice, acting as both potential risks to and defenders of patient safety. Although moral sensitivity is recognized as a foundational element for patient safety, the specific mechanism translating it into actual safety competency, particularly the mediating role of ethical action, remains underexplored. Aim: To examine the mediating effect of ethical action on the relationship between moral sensitivity and patient safety competency among nursing interns. Methods: A cross-sectional study was reported following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. This study was conducted with 311 nursing interns recruited via cluster sampling from a tertiary Grade A hospital in central China (Henan Province). Data were collected using the Moral Sensitivity Questionnaire, the Ethical Action Subscale of the Judgment About Nursing Decision, and the Patient Safety Competency Scale. Structural Equation Modeling was employed to test the hypothesized relationships and the mediating effect. Results: Moral sensitivity was positively correlated with both ethical action (r = 0.509, p < 0.001) and patient safety competency (r = 0.480, p < 0.001), while ethical action was also positively correlated with patient safety competency (r = 0.603, p < 0.001). Structural equation modeling demonstrated that moral sensitivity exerted both a direct positive effect (beta= 0.34, p = 0.001) and an indirect positive effect through ethical action (beta = 0.28, p = 0.001) on patient safety competency, with the mediating effect accounting for 44.8% of the total effect. Conclusion: Ethical action serves as the pivotal mechanism translating moral sensitivity into patient safety competency. Nursing education should integrate ethics curriculum and clinical practice through action-oriented training in authentic clinical settings, thereby empowering interns to convert moral sensitivity into patient safety competency.

TI Undergraduate nursing students' co-construction of learning spaces in a
   bioscience course: A qualitative study with an ecological perspective on
   the learning environment
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Bioscience; Cooperative learning; Ecology; Learning environment;
   Learning spaces; Motivation; Nursing education
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; MOTIVATION; CURRICULUM; PHYSIOLOGY
AB Background: To ensure patient safety, nursing students must acquire sufficient bioscience knowledge. Previous research has emphasized the importance of high-quality learning environments and opportunities for students to act upon their learning needs. However, to our knowledge, no studies have examined nursing students' construction of learning spaces in bioscience from an ecological perspective. Aim: This study explores how undergraduate nursing students use elements in their learning environment and construct their learning space within a bioscience course. Methods: A qualitative descriptive design was employed. Three focus group interviews were conducted in April 2024, facilitated by an interview guide, to collect qualitative data from 17 first-year nursing students. Results: Three categories emerged from the data analysis: 1) high expectations and a belief in succeeding, 2) standing together, even when alone, and 3) freedom within established frameworks. Conclusions: The findings underscore the importance of a supportive and flexible learning environment that acknowledges students' agency and social dynamics. Drawing on ecological theory, we posit that learning spaces are co-constructed through interactions among students, resources, and institutional structures. Elements in the learning environment should therefore balance structure with flexibility, foster competence through optimal challenge, and promote inclusive relatedness to sustain motivation and meaningful engagement.

TI From awareness to application: Unveiling the interplay between
   dependence on artificial intelligence and achievement motivation among
   nursing students: A multicenter study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Achievement; Motivation; Nursing; Students
AB Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative, fundamentally reshaping how we access and apply knowledge. Achievement motivation (AM) remains a critical component of students' academic and personal development. Examining the association between nursing students' dependence on AI and their AM is a pertinent area of research, particularly in light of the growing incorporation of AI within educational settings. Aim of the study: To explore the association between undergraduate nursing students' dependence on artificial intelligence and achievement motivation. Methods: A multicenter descriptive correlational study was conducted across five nursing faculties affiliated with Port-Said, Damietta, Alexandria, Mansoura, and Sohag universities, involving 1412 nursing students. Data were collected using a Personal and Academic Characteristics Questionnaire, the Achievement Motivation Scale (AMS), and the Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Scale (DIA). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression. Results: Nursing students demonstrated a moderate level of dependence on AI (M = 19.46, SD = 11.33) and a moderate level of AM (M = 6.32, SD = 2.13). A statistically significant moderate negative association was found between AI dependence and AM (r = -0.389, p < .001). This indicates that increased dependence on AI is associated with lower achievement motivation. Regression analysis indicated that AI dependence accounted for 19.6% of the variance in AM (R-2 = 0.196), while the remaining variance is likely influenced by other unmeasured factors. Conclusion: Nursing students exhibited moderate AI dependence and achievement motivation. The findings indicate a significant negative association between AI dependence and achievement motivation, emphasizing the need to consider students' technology usage patterns concerning academic motivation. Implications for practice: Educational programs should promote informed and balanced use of AI by clarifying its benefits and limitations as a learning support tool. Learning strategies should also be formulated to foster independent thinking, self-regulation, and goal-directed behavior to support students' achievement motivation.

TI Autistic identity dimensions correlate with wellbeing and daily living
   in autistic adults
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Identity; Self-esteem; Stigma; Quality of life; Flourishing
ID SELF-ESTEEM; SPECTRUM DISORDER; SOCIAL IDENTITY; MENTAL-HEALTH; SCALE;
   MODEL; LIFE; NEURODIVERSITY; PRIORITIES
AB Autistic adults vary in how they identify with being autistic, which may influence their quality of life and flourishing. TI Interpersonal synchrony in caregiver-child dyads with autism spectrum
   condition: A scoping review
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Interpersonal synchrony; Autism spectrum condition; Caregiver-child
   interaction; Biobehavioral synchrony
ID INFANT-MOTHER ATTACHMENT; YOUNG-CHILDREN; INTERACTIONAL SYNCHRONY;
   SOCIAL ENGAGEMENT; RESPONSIVENESS; PRESCHOOLERS; COMMUNICATION;
   INTERVENTION; COREGULATION; BEHAVIORS
AB Purpose: Interpersonal synchrony (IS), the temporal alignment of behavior and biological processes between interaction partners, is a key mechanism for social engagement and co-regulation. While well-studied in neurotypical populations, its nature in caregiver-autistic child dyads remains fragmented. This scoping review maps the current knowledge on IS in these dyads across behavioral and biological levels and identifies methods and interactional contexts used for its measurement. Methods: A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on October 12, 2024, with an updated search on September 30, 2025, following PRISMA guidelines. Quantitative studies examining behavioral and/or biological interpersonal synchrony in caregiver-child dyads involving autistic children or children with an elevated likelihood of autism were included. Studies were screened using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. A total of 39 studies met all eligibility criteria and were included in this review. Results: Across studies, IS in caregiver-autistic child dyads shows substantial heterogeneity. IS is neither uniformly reduced nor enhanced relative to caregiver-neurotypical child dyads but varies across modalities, interactional contexts, and developmental periods. Variability in IS has been associated with individual (child and caregiver), relational, and contextual factors. Evidence from longitudinal and intervention research suggests that synchrony is modifiable over time and may be linked to downstream developmental outcomes. Conclusions: Findings highlight IS as a multidimensional, context-sensitive, and dyadically constructed process in caregiver-autistic child interactions. Advancing the field will require theoretically integrated, multimodal and longitudinal approaches that move beyond deficit-based models and support mutually attuned and meaningful social engagement in neurodiverse populations.

TI Unscripted, unofficial, unseen, and uncontained: The social and digital
   life of teacher reflection
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher reflection; Informal professional learning; Digital professional
   networks; Communities of practice; Networked publics
ID COMMUNITIES; BOUNDARIES; EDUCATION
AB Teacher reflection is widely positioned as central to professional learning, yet it is most often examined within formal, institutionally structured settings. This study investigates how teachers in Ghana engage in reflection across informal and digital contexts. Using a qualitative interpretive design, data were collected from twelve teachers through semi-structured interviews and focus groups. Findings indicate that reflection emerges as a relational and socially mediated process, enacted through storytelling, peer dialogue, and shared interpretation. TI The effect of AI-supported reading comprehension instruction on
   students' 4C skills: A systematic review
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Reading comprehension; 4C skills; 21st-century
   skills; Systematic review
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; THINKING SKILLS; CREATIVITY; EDUCATION
AB In this systematic review, we aimed to comprehensively evaluate the relationship between artificial intelligence-supported reading comprehension education (AISRCE) and the skills of creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, and communication, and to present trends, methodological characteristics, and results from a holistic perspective. This study addresses the fragmented structure of the existing literature and the fact that 4C skills are generally examined separately, offering a comprehensive synthesis that integrates all four skills within a single analytical framework in the context of AISRCE. Based on our search of the Web of Science (WoS), Scopus, and Education Resources Information Center (ERIC) databases according to our criteria, 29 studies were included in our analysis. Based on the descriptive analysis, we identified each of the 4C skills as a theme to examine the relationship between AISRCE applications and the 4C skills. Our results indicate that AISRCE applications generally have a positive effect on creativity and collaboration skills, with particularly pronounced effects on critical thinking and communication skills. However, these effects vary depending on the educational level, pedagogical design, and methods of use. We found that the impact of AISRCE applications on 4C skills is not onedimensional but rather context-sensitive, dependent on pedagogical design, and shaped by learner characteristics, constituting a multi-layered structure. The results revealed that the guided and purposeful use of AI strengthens higher-order cognitive, communicative, and collaborative processes, whereas unguided and excessive use may lead to risks such as superficial learning, loss of creative effort, and a decline in collaboration quality. Therefore, the effect of artificial intelligence-supported reading applications on 4C skills needs to be addressed with more holistic models that explain the forms of integration between AI, reading, and cognitive skills at all educational levels, considering developmental differences, pedagogical design, and technological diversity.

   and insecurities in psychotherapy education
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Virtual patients; Psychotherapy training;
   Clinical skills
ID COGNITIVE LOAD; MENTAL-HEALTH; REALITY; TECHNOLOGY; VALIDATION;
   ACCEPTANCE; EXPERIENCE; IMPACT
AB Background Preparing psychotherapy trainees for clinical complexity is a persistent educational challenge. Virtual patient (VP) simulations enabled by artificial intelligence (AI) may enhance training by offering practical, hands-on experience. This study examined their effectiveness in improving training outcomes and reducing insecurity in future psychotherapists.Methods Psychology students and psychotherapy trainees (N = 87) were randomly assigned to four online 2D-VP sessions with automated feedback or pre-recorded role-play videos. TI Innovating informatics education: A TikTok-integrated learning activity
   for pharmacy students
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Social media; Informatics; Medication safety; Pharmacy education;
   Integrated laboratory
AB Purpose: This study evaluated the implementation of a social media-integrated learning activity by examining student perceptions, engagement, and EO-aligned performance to determine whether this approach is a feasible, enjoyable, and effective strategy for supporting informatics skill development in pharmacy students. Methods: This descriptive observational study assessed a TikTok (R) informatics activity implemented in an integrated laboratory skills course for 55 third-year student pharmacists in Spring 2025. Students worked in 14 small groups to create informatics-themed TikTok (R) commercials. After the activity, students completed a brief demographic and perceptions survey. Faculty evaluated videos using a 36-point analytic rubric aligned with AACP educational outcomes: Scientific Thinking (EO 1.1), Problem-solving (EO 2.1), Communication (EO 2.2), and Population Health Impact (EO 2.8). Descriptive statistics summarized performance, and Kruskal-Wallis H and chi-square tests examined grade differences. Results: All students participated in and completed the survey. The cohort was 73% female (n = 40) and 27% male (n = 15), with most identifying as white (84%) or Black (11%). Students reported the activity encouraged an innovative mindset (76%), and 96% enjoyed watching their peers' commercials. Student performance was strong at 32.1/36 (89%), with scores ranging from 26 to 35. Compared to Communication and Population Health domains, Problem Solving (EO 2.1) and Scientific Thinking (EO 1.1) demonstrated significantly lower performance, indicating opportunities for instructional refinement. Conclusion: This pilot study demonstrates that an activity using TikTok (R) can successfully support key competencies in informatics and medication safety while fostering creativity and student engagement.

   Study of a Brief Metacognitive Workshop in General Chemistry
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student Mental Health; Depression; Anxiety; Expectations; Higher
   Education; Chemistry Students; Interventions; STEM Students; In-Class
   Activities
ID ANXIETY DISORDER; MENTAL-HEALTH; ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; DEPRESSION;
   VALIDATION; SELF; PERFECTIONISM; PREVALENCE; STUDENTS; BURNOUT
AB Student mental health in large, high-pressure STEM courses is a persistent concern. This pragmatic, practice-based classroom study mapped the mental-health landscape in first-year students taking a General Chemistry course and piloted a brief, in-class metacognitive workshop that names common pressures (perfectionism, comparison), reduces stigma, and offers simple regulation and reflection tools. Pre-Post surveys (anonymous; treated as independent samples) assessed anxiety (GAD-7), depression (PHQ-8), and perfectionism (SAPS). Confirmatory factor analyses supported the internal structure of the measures, and composite and subscale scores were used to summarize response patterns. Across survey administrations, distributions varied between respondent pools, while overall patterns remained stable, indicating cross-sectional variation rather than intervention effects. Under authentic teaching conditions, the workshop was feasible, low-burden, and compatible with routine instruction. Ready-to-use materials and practice-based evidence are provided to support adoption and inform future confirmatory work

TI Artificial intelligence literacy of nursing students: A cross-sectional
   study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing student; Artificial intelligence; Artificial intelligence
   literacy; Cross-sectional study; Survey
AB Background: With the rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the nursing field, AI literacy has emerged as a critical competency for nursing students. However, evidence regarding the current status and influencing factors of AI literacy among Chinese nursing students remains limited. Aim: This cross-sectional study aimed to examine AI literacy levels across four dimensions (Awareness, Application, Evaluation, Ethics) among Chinese nursing students, identify its independent influencing factors, and generate localized empirical evidence for AI curriculum construction in vocational nursing education. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted between November 1, 2025 and January 20, 2026. The research institution has not set up an institutional ethics committee; the whole protocol was ethically reviewed by the supervisor team in line with the Declaration of Helsinki before recruitment. A total of 178 sophomore nursing students from Henan Vocational University of Science and Technology were enrolled via convenience sampling. Data were collected using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (AILS, Wang et al., 2023). This scale is publicly accessible for non-commercial academic research; the original authors have granted open-use permission for educational cross-sectional surveys without additional formal written authorization. After data cleaning, 155 valid questionnaires were included (effective response rate = 86.9%). Nonparametric tests and ordinal logistic regression were performed via IBM SPSS 27.0 for statistical analysis. Results: Participants demonstrated a moderate level of overall artificial intelligence literacy (Median = 60.00, IQR = 21.00, SD = 13.18). The Application dimension scored highest. Gender and interest in AI were independent influencing factors. Strong positive correlations were identified among all four dimensions. Conclusions: Study findings suggest that nursing education should integrate AI content and targeted training to strengthen students' AI awareness, critical evaluation, and ethical awareness, while providing tailored support for female students and boosting AI interest.

TI Does more mean better? Evaluating faculty-to-resident feedback in
   general surgery
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Resident assessment; Feedback quality; Surgical education; Entrustable
   professional activities
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION
AB Purpose To test the hypothesis that surgical faculty who submit more Entrustable Professional Activity (EPA) micro-assessments to general surgery residents provide higher quality feedback. Methods We utilized EPA micro-assessments for gallbladder disease, appendicitis and inguinal hernia to analyze narrative feedback submitted by faculty to general surgery residents for the 2023-2025 academic years. Two independent raters evaluated the narrative feedback for quality using the QuAL (Quality of Assessment for Learning) rubric, to score the assessments on a zero-to-five-point scale based on evidence, suggestion and connection. Interrater reliability was assessed. Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, correlation testing, and regression modeling using an alpha < 0.05. Results 661 EPA micro-assessments from 26 faculty members were analyzed for quality. Interrater reliability was 0.85. The median QuAL score was 3. The median word count was 60 and positively correlated with QuAL scores (rho = 0.81, p < 0.001). Faculty with < 25 evaluations had a median QuAL score of 2.88 vs. 3.25 for those who submitted >= 25 evaluations (p = 0.034). Faculty years in practice ranged from one to 37. Regression analysis using generalized estimating equations showed that the number of evaluations submitted, narrative feedback word count and more faculty years in practice were independently associated with higher quality feedback (all p < 0.05). Conclusions Quality of EPA narrative feedback submitted to residents by general surgery faculty was associated with longer word count feedback, faculty years in practice, and submitting more EPA micro-assessments. These findings suggest targets for faculty development to improve the quality of EPA micro-assessment narrative feedback.

TI Student-Centered Teaching of the Electron-Transfer Chain in
   Biochemistry: Integrating Anime Analogies and Microbial Fuel Cell
   Concepts
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE electron transfer chain; biochemistry; undergraduate; student-centered;
   anime storyline analogy
ID TRANSFER MECHANISMS
AB Teaching the electron transfer chain (ETC) in biochemistry is challenging due to both its challenging nature and high cognitive load for students. In this study, we developed a student-centered instructional model that uses an anime storyline analogy and a microbial fuel cell (MFC) demonstration to enhance students' interest, engagement, and understanding of the ETC. The model was implemented with junior undergraduate biology majors. In the experimental class, key steps of the ETC were illustrated through an adventure narrative featuring the anime character Pikachu, and a real-world bioelectricity generation example by MFC was incorporated. Interactive activities such as a jigsaw-puzzle game were used to reinforce knowledge integration. A control class was taught the same content using traditional lecture-based methods. Pre- and post-test scores, a student feedback questionnaire, and classroom observations were used to evaluate learning outcomes. The experimental class showed a significant improvement in post-test scores compared to the control class. The increase indicates a deep understanding of the ETC. Questionnaire responses also revealed that the anime analogy and gamified activities both increased student motivation and lowered their perceived cognitive load. Introducing the MFC case made the challenging concept of electron transfer tangible by linking it to observable electrical current generation. This integrated approach, blending cutting-edge science, core biochemical concepts, and students' pop-culture interests, proved to be an effective and replicable way to teach an abstract biochemistry topic. It not only improved learning outcomes in the ETC chapter, but also helped foster students' interdisciplinary thinking. Further adaptation of this model to different classroom settings and other abstract topics is recommended to explore its broad applicability.

TI Photonic Chocolate:A Sweet Holistic Playground To Explain
   Crystallization, Phase Transitions, Rheology, and Optics
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE General Public; Public Understanding; Hands-On Learning; Materials
   Science; Crystallography; Optics; Rheology; Phase Transitions;
   Nanoimprint Technology
ID PARTICLE-SIZE DISTRIBUTION; NANOIMPRINT LITHOGRAPHY; COCOA BUTTER;
   MOLTEN CHOCOLATE; FAT; POLYMORPHISM; BEHAVIOR; SCIENCE; LUBRICATION;
   CRYSTALS
AB Traditional methods for teaching scientific principles such as crystallization, phase transitions, rheology, and optics frequently struggle to engage younger audiences or individuals lacking a strong and broad scientific background. Many educational tools do not incorporate the tactile, visually engaging, and relatable elements necessary to stimulate curiosity in complex scientific phenomena. To address this gap, we propose the use of photonic chocolate, an educational tool that integrates diffraction grating technology, material structures, and their processing with the familiar appeal of chocolate. By imprinting commercial diffraction gratings onto the surface of tempered chocolate, striking photonic effects emerge through the light diffraction. These vibrant, iridescent colors are not only captivating but also serve as an instructive function, providing an accessible gateway to advanced scientific concepts. The fabrication of photonic chocolate introduces learners to cocoa butter crystal chemistry and polymorphism, the principles of non-Newtonian rheology, nanoimprinting techniques, and the optics underlying diffraction and interference. The scope of this work is 2-fold: first, providing a comprehensive theoretical background on the topic to support teachers in preparing the learning experience; and second, presenting a practical approach for designing engaging seminars and hands-on activities, emphasizing the connection between scientific fundamentals and everyday experiences.

DT Article
ID PRESERVICE TEACHERS; KNOWLEDGE; ACQUISITION; FOUNDATION; TIME
AB The present study examined the impact of participation in an annual 60-h national in-service program called Building Blocks (BB), focusing on strengthening teacher knowledge of basic language constructs for teaching literacy in English as a foreign language (EFL). We employed an online questionnaire developed to evaluate teachers' beliefs and self-reported practices regarding the teaching of reading and writing amongst 50 teachers who had participated in the BB program and 150 teachers who had not. Results using Mann-Whitney nonparametric tests and ordinal regressions indicated that BB participants reported greater confidence in using differentiated instruction methods for teaching literacy to children from diverse backgrounds than non-BB teachers (z = -2.83, p = 0.005). The BB participants also reported greater self-efficacy for teaching reading to students with diverse needs with higher frequency levels than non-BB teachers (z = -3.10, p = 0.002). These findings are significant because in order to differentiate instruction and teach students with diverse needs, a teacher must possess a particular skill set that includes awareness of different English ability levels and knowledge about how to match instructional methods to individual student literacy needs. The current results highlight the potential of participation in a professional development program focusing on literacy acquisition for EFL teachers.

TI Mapping Multilingual Voices: Comparing Teacher, Parent, and Child
   Perspectives on Bilingual Children's Social Networks
SO EARLY EDUCATION AND DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
ID ENGLISH; INPUT; PSYCHOPATHOLOGY; EXPOSURE
AB Research Findings: This study explores similarities between how different informants characterize language interactions in childhood bilingual educational settings. Spanish-English bilingual children (n = 120, 45.8% female) from pre-kindergarten through second grade (age range: 4-9 years; M = 6.33 years, SD = 1.09 years) were recruited from four elementary schools in central Texas. Three network assessments were employed: (1) teacher-reported classroom language use networks, (2) family reports of children's language use in and out of school, and (3) child reports about their language use in and out of school. Network characteristics included group size, gender composition, language use patterns, interaction frequency, and perceived relationship closeness. Correlation analyses were used to examine similarities across informant perspectives. Teacher network measurements revealed complex linguistic patterns not captured by other informants. Notably, language use perspectives showed moderate correlations, with the strongest alignments in concrete network characteristics like gender composition and network size. Parent-child differences emerged, with school networks showing less agreement than out-of-school. Practice or Policy: Findings underscore the importance of multi-perspective approaches in understanding bilingual children's social-linguistic networks. Different informants provide unique and complementary insights, suggesting comprehensive network assessment requires integrating perspectives from multiple social contexts and observers.

TI Moment-to-Moment Dynamics of Foreign Language Enjoyment: An Idiodynamic
   Study of Conversational Topics Among Young Language Learners
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE complex dynamic systems theory; conversational topics; English as a
   foreign language; ergodicity; foreign language enjoyment; idiodynamic
   method; young learners
ID COMPLEX-SYSTEMS; EMOTIONS; ANXIETY
AB Foreign Language Enjoyment has received increasing attention in second language acquisition due to its role in fostering engagement and communication. Although previous research has often treated enjoyment as a relatively stable trait, perspectives informed by Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST) suggest that emotions are dynamic, non-ergodic, and fluctuate over time. Drawing on CDST, the present study adopts an idiographic approach to investigate second-by-second changes in foreign language enjoyment during conversational tasks. Six young language learners participated in recorded interactions on four different conversational topics, followed by idiodynamic self-ratings and stimulated recall interviews to explain emotional fluctuations. The findings revealed nonlinear, individualized trajectories of enjoyment, highlighting substantial within-person variability. Fluctuations were closely linked to topic familiarity and interest, idea availability, perceived task difficulty, and cognitive effort. Familiar and meaningful topics generally facilitated higher enjoyment, whereas unfamiliar or cognitively demanding topics led to declines; however, moderate challenge occasionally enhanced engagement. This study highlights the dynamic and context-sensitive nature of foreign language enjoyment. These results also underscore the importance of examining emotional experiences at a micro-temporal level and demonstrate the value of the idiodynamic method in capturing fine-grained affective dynamics during language use. The study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how contextual (e.g., conversational topics) and cognitive-linguistic factors shape learners' emotional experiences during real-time communication.

TI The relationship between peer experience and college students' math
   achievement: the moderating role of intrinsic value and the mediating
   role of math self-efficacy
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer experience; Math achievement; Math self-efficacy; Intrinsic value;
   College students
ID SCHOOL-STUDENTS; REGULATORY EFFICACY; SCIENCE; MATHEMATICS; BELIEFS;
   MIDDLE; ELEMENTARY; EXPECTATIONS; PERFORMANCE; EDUCATION
AB This study primarily investigates gender differences in peer experience, mathematical self-efficacy, intrinsic value, and mathematical achievement, as well as the prospective associations among these variables. First-year students from two Chinese colleges participated in this research. Data were collected across three waves over the course of one academic year. Initially, 800 first-year students completed scales measuring peer experience and intrinsic value. Six months later, 660 students completed a mathematical self-efficacy scale during the second phase of the study. Eight months later, data on mathematical achievement were collected from 647 students. The first finding indicated that there were gender differences in peer experience, intrinsic value, and mathematical self-efficacy, with males' average values being significantly higher than those of females. The second finding revealed that peer experience positively and significantly predicted mathematical self-efficacy; however, it had no direct predictive effect on mathematical achievement. Furthermore, intrinsic value significantly moderated the relationships between peer experience and both mathematical self-efficacy and mathematical achievement. The mediated moderation model accounted for 4.3% of the variance in mathematical achievement. These findings have practical implications for understanding how peer experience relates to college students' mathematical achievement and suggest that more attention should be paid to enhancing college students' intrinsic value and math self-efficacy, which are associated with their mathematical achievement.

TI Understanding the role of competition beliefs and learning orientations
   in Duolingo learners' engagement: the mediating effects of autonomy and
   motivation
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Competition beliefs; Competitive orientation; Cooperative orientation;
   Engagement; Autonomy; Motivation
ID ACHIEVEMENT; SELF; COOPERATION; SCALE; MODEL
AB This study examines how learners' beliefs about competition (positive vs. negative) and learning orientations (cooperative vs. competitive) shape engagement in language learning on Duolingo, with autonomy and motivation serving as mediators. Although competition is often viewed as either motivating or debilitating, little is known about how differing competition beliefs and orientations jointly influence engagement in digital learning contexts. Accordingly, a sample of 191 multilingual Duolingo users, recruited via convenience sampling, completed self-report scales assessing competition beliefs, learning orientations, autonomy, motivation, and engagement. Structural equation modeling indicated that positive beliefs about competition significantly and positively predicted both autonomy and motivation, whereas negative competition beliefs negatively predicted motivation. Moreover, competitive orientation significantly predicted autonomy, motivation, and engagement, whereas cooperative orientation showed only a direct positive path to engagement. Mediation analysis also revealed that both positive and negative beliefs about competition, along with competitive orientation, were indirectly associated with engagement, whereas cooperative orientation had no indirect effects. These findings suggest that cooperative and competitive dynamics promote engagement through different mechanisms, highlighting the value of supporting both orientations in digital learning environments. This study contributes to understanding how individual differences in learners' beliefs and orientations interact with motivational processes to shape engagement, offering practical implications for designing adaptive, inclusive, and motivating language learning platforms that cater to diverse learner profiles.

TI Research on Preparing Pre-service Teachers for Leading Mathematical
   Discussions: A Systematic Literature Review
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mathematical discussions; Mathematics teacher education; Pre-service
   teacher; Systematic literature review
ID NOTICE; DISCOURSE; KNOWLEDGE; SKILLS
AB Activities designed to prepare pre-service teachers (PSTs) to lead high-quality mathematical discussions are a crucial element of teacher education. However, the research literature presents teacher education activities that are designed in a wide variety of ways to support PSTs effectively. This study synthesizes research to map and characterize teacher education activities focused on preparing PSTs to lead high-quality mathematical discussions and the discussion-leading practices these activities aim to develop. Studies were identified through searches in Scopus, Web of Science, and Education Research Complete, and selected based on inclusion criteria focused on mathematics teacher education and PSTs' preparation to lead discussions. Data were analyzed using an iterative thematic synthesis approach informed by our conceptual framework. The findings, based on 23 studies, indicate that research has emphasized teacher education activities supporting PSTs in analyzing or planning for ambitious discussion-leading practices, although descriptions of what PSTs are expected to do during these classroom practices vary in specificity. A notable gap in the literature concerns limited attention given to how teacher education activities provide opportunities for PSTs to enact discussion-leading practices. While many studies report on PSTs' opportunities to analyze or plan for discussions, fewer examine how they gain experience with the interactive, in-the-moment aspects of leading mathematical discussions. Together, these findings clarify how the literature has conceptualized and described teacher education activities and the discussion-leading practices they aim to support, as well as relations between them, offering insights for designing learning opportunities that better support PSTs in enacting high-quality mathematical discussions.

TI Reimagining global citizenship education: Decolonial dialogues across
   Australia, Colombia and Mexico
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Global citizenship education; Global North and South dialogue;
   international comparative research; Colombia; Australia; Mexico;
   critical and decolonial perspectives
AB This article presents a comparative analysis of global citizenship education (GCE) in three national contexts: Australia, Colombia and Mexico. The systematic examination of these contexts contributes to understanding GCE through a critical and decolonial lens. The comparative study analyses national education policy discourse as a starting point for systematising experiences. It engages in an epistemic dialogue between the Global South (specifically Latin America/Abya Yala), represented by Colombia and Mexico, and the Global North, represented by Australia. Despite Australias predominantly Global North-oriented education policy, the study also examines student mobilisations and discusses issues such as Indigenous rights and planetary responsibility. These dialogues open avenues for alternative visions, rooted in critical interculturality and planetary care. Methodologically, the study draws on Stephen Balls heuristic approach to analyse education policy through a poststructuralist sociological lens, considering policy context and the influence of policy as discourse. The investigation identifies official pedagogical discourse across the three nations and examines references to GCE and its interpretations in texts, including policy documents and teacher training programmes. It also shares advancements, opportunities, challenges and policy insights in relation to GCE within each national context. The article argues for a plurality of perspectives on GCE and for recognising alternative conceptualisations beyond neoliberal approaches, which are based in epistemologies of the Global North and the capitalist global order.

TI Firework Research:A Twist on a General Chemistry Laboratory Practical
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate/General; Laboratory Instruction; Curriculum;
   Hands-On Learning/Manipulatives; Inquiry-Based/Discovery Learning;
   Testing/Assessment; Aqueous Solution Chemistry; Metals; Stoichiometry;
   Precipitation/Solubility; Qualitative Analysis
ID TEST ANXIETY; NURSING-STUDENTS; UNDERGRADUATE; STRATEGIES
AB Due to their striking colors and rapid progression, precipitation reactions and flame tests are two quintessential phenomena commonly showcased in general chemistry. This work presents a multipart experiment centered on these classic phenomena that is designed as a low-stakes midterm laboratory practical exam during a 150 minute laboratory period in the first semester of general chemistry. In an effort to reduce anxiety associated with high-stakes assessments and increase student enjoyment, this original laboratory practical exam has been reframed as a mini research project where students identify unknown metal salts that are used as firework colorants through flame tests, chemical color trends, and precipitation reactions. The experiment consists of six short parts that assess students' understanding of various skills developed as part of a scaffolded curriculum in the first half of the laboratory course. The topics assessed include scientific vocabulary, glassware identification, Bunsen burner operation, stoichiometric calculations, standard solution preparation, qualitative observations, precipitation reactions, solubility, and gravity filtration. Instructional materials and information on implementation are presented. The efficacy of the experiment was shown by positive changes in student confidence and correctness when completing comparable questions over the course of the semester.

TI Prevalence of Psychotropic Use and Psychotropic Polypharmacy in a
   Finnish National Cohort of Persons With Intellectual Disabilities
SO JOURNAL OF INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID MEDICATION USE; ADULTS; HEALTH; INDIVIDUALS; BEHAVIOR; DRUGS
AB Background Psychotropic use and psychotropic polypharmacy are common in people with intellectual disabilities, but representative population-based studies on this topic are scarce. We evaluated the prevalence of psychotropic use and psychotropic polypharmacy in a Finnish nationwide cohort of people with intellectual disabilities aged 0-97 years.Methods The annual prevalence of psychotropic use in 2019 was studied among 37 196 individuals with intellectual disabilities and an age- and sex-matched comparison cohort with no diagnosis of intellectual disabilities. Psychotropics included antipsychotics, antidepressants, anxiolytics, hypnotics and sedatives and antiepileptics indicated for bipolar disorder (carbamazepine, valproic acid, lamotrigine, pregabalin and clonazepam). A likely indication was identified for 52.9% of psychotropic users with intellectual disability (major psychiatric comorbidity 38.1%, challenging behaviour 22.1%). Psychotropic polypharmacy was more common in the intellectual disability cohort (18.2%), than in the comparison cohort (3.6%).Conclusions Our findings highlight concerns about psychotropic polypharmacy and potential overmedication. Using a comprehensive, nationwide cohort, this study emphasises the need for more evidence-based, person-centred approaches, including careful diagnostics, non-pharmacological interventions and regular treatment reviews.

TI The role of achievement goals in the association between classroom life
   and creative personality
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Creativity; Goal orientation; Learning environment; Performance-approach
   goals; Student motivation
ID MOTIVATING CREATIVITY; LEARNING-ENVIRONMENT; PERFORMANCE GOALS; MODEL;
   ORIENTATION; PERCEPTIONS; MASTERY
AB This study examines the complex interrelations between students' perceptions of their classroom environment, achievement goals, and creative personality traits. Employing an ex-post-facto correlational survey design, the research examines the indirect roles of distinct achievement goals, including mastery-approach, performance-approach, mastery-avoidance, and performance-avoidance, in the association between classroom life perception and creative personality traits. Data were collected from a sample of 461 tenth-grade students in Turkey via validated self-report measures assessing perceptions of the classroom environment, creative personality traits, and achievement goals. The proposed theoretical model was analyzed using structural equation modeling. The findings indicate a significant positive association between students' perceptions of the classroom environment and their creative personality traits. Furthermore, the results indicated a pattern consistent with partial statistical mediation, with performance-approach goals showing a significant negative indirect association between classroom life perception and creative personality traits. These results suggest that supportive classroom environments are positively associated with creativity-related dispositions, whereas performance-approach goals may be less compatible with the expression of such dispositions in this sample. The study highlights the relevance of considering classroom climate and achievement goals together when examining students' creativity-related dispositions in secondary school contexts.

TI Development and validation of a writing self-assessment practice
   questionnaire for self-regulated learning
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-assessment; Self-regulated learning; EFL writing; Instrument
   development; Questionnaire validation; Self-reported practices
ID EXPLORATORY FACTOR-ANALYSIS; ASSESSMENT CRITERIA; FEEDBACK;
   RECOMMENDATIONS; COEFFICIENTS; VALIDITY; FLUENCY; NUMBER
AB Self-assessment (SA) is central to self-regulated learning, yet scalable instruments for capturing learners' self-reported SA practices in domain-specific writing contexts remain limited. This study developed and validated the Writing Self-assessment Practice Questionnaire for EFL Learners (WSAPQ-EFL), designed to measure how learners report establishing evaluative standards, monitoring writing quality, and forming judgments during English writing self-assessment. Drawing on process-sensitive qualitative findings from a preliminary phase using think-aloud protocols and stimulated-recall interviews (Ou, 2026), the questionnaire was administered to 1,180 Chinese university English majors in the psychometric validation phase. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses on independent subsamples (EFA, N = 661; CFA, N = 519) supported a 61-item, 14-factor structure organized within three stages: Determining Standards, Monitoring/Cue-seeking, and Cognitive Judgment. This structure captures reported dimensions of self-regulated learning and dual-process-informed judgment by distinguishing learners' reported reliance on criterion sources, internal monitoring cues such as processing fluency and sense of familiarity, and three judgment patterns involving intuitive reliance, consistent intuitive-rational alignment, and intuitive-rational conflict. A theory-driven hierarchical regression on an independent criterion-validity sample (N = 687) showed that the final 14-factor model explained 44.0% of variance in writing performance (R & sup2; = 0.440, adjusted R & sup2; = 0.429), with all three theoretically defined blocks contributing significant explanatory variance at entry. Internalized knowledge and internal monitoring cues showed stronger unique associations with writing performance than external resources. The WSAPQ-EFL provides a theoretically grounded, psychometrically validated tool and a scalable complement to process-based methods for researching and diagnosing EFL writers' reported SA practices.

AB This study examined the associations between parental attitudes and developmental outcomes among preschool children aged 2-6 years in T & uuml;rkiye. TI Teacher Educators as Sustainability Change Agents: Identity, Agency, and
   Disciplinary Cultures in EFL and Social Sciences Programmes
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE disciplinary culture; Identity-Agency-Disciplinary (IAD) framework;
   professional agency; professional identity; sustainability education
   (SE); sustainability implementation; sustainability literacy; teacher
   educators
AB Sustainability education (SE) is increasingly recognized as a critical aspect of higher education and teacher education due to global environmental, social, and economic challenges. However, limited research has examined how teacher educators in developing countries, including Iran, conceptualize and implement sustainability in their teaching practices. This qualitative narrative study explored how Iranian English as a Foreign Language (EFL) and Social Science (SS) teacher educators interpret and enact sustainability through the Identity-Agency-Disciplinary (IAD) framework. Twenty semi-structured interviews were conducted with teacher educators from four public universities in Iran, and thematic analysis was performed using NVivo software. Findings indicate a complex, recursive relationship between sustainability literacy and sustainability implementation. EFL teacher educators exhibited strong awareness of sustainable practices' outcomes but reported limited integration of sustainability into their professional identity, enacting only partial sustainable practices. Conversely, SS teacher educators demonstrated conceptual understanding of sustainability but experienced identity fragmentation and resistance to practical implementation. Across both disciplines, identity tension and constrained professional agency exceeded institutional constraints, while disciplinary culture both facilitated and hindered transformative practices. Overall, the study reconceptualizes teacher educators as conditionally empowered actors who implement sustainability only when identity, agency, and disciplinary culture align. These results highlight that effective sustainability reforms in teacher education require systematic support for professional identity development and opportunities for agency, rather than reliance solely on policy mandates. This study contributes to literature on teacher identity, professional agency, and disciplinary culture, offering theoretical and practical insights for fostering transformative, sustainability-oriented pedagogical practices in diverse educational contexts.

AB This study examined the heterogeneity of professional identity among Chinese teachers and estimated the predictive effects of demographic and psychological factors on professional identity profiles based on the self-determination theory (SDT). TI Procedural adaptations of the good behavior game for Brazilian public
   schools: a narrative review and Elos 2.0 program description
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCHOOL & EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Good behavior game; procedural adaptation; elementary school;
   school-based intervention; Elos 2.0
ID PREVENTIVE INTERVENTIONS; DISRUPTIVE BEHAVIOR; UNIVERSAL; IMPACT;
   1ST-GRADE; DISORDER; OUTCOMES
AB This article presents a two-part analysis of procedural adaptations of the Good Behavior Game (GBG) for Brazilian public schools. Part I is a structured narrative review of 34 randomized controlled trials implementing GBG internationally, mapping adaptations in game structure, reinforcement contingencies, teacher autonomy, feedback, and fidelity support. Part II describes how these findings informed Elos 2.0, a Brazilian adaptation designed for large, heterogeneous, and resource-constrained classrooms. Across trials, recurrent procedural patterns included explicit classroom rules, heterogeneous teams, interdependent group contingencies, visible monitoring, a gradual shift from punishment-based procedures toward positive reinforcement, flexible rewards, and simplified teacher supports. Elos 2.0 translates these principles into a feasible classroom model emphasizing cooperative teams, neutral feedback, positive reinforcement, low-cost rewards, and structured teacher support. Its feasibility and effectiveness were subsequently tested in a cluster randomized controlled trial in 22 Brazilian public schools, showing improvements in attention (d = 0.254; 95% CI [0.038, 0.469]) and prosocial behavior (d = 0.436; 95% CI [0.139, 0.734]) and higher odds of no disruptive behavior (OR = 4.88; 95% CI [1.89, 12.60]). Together, the review and program description show how core GBG mechanisms can be preserved while adapting procedures for scalable classroom-based prevention.
