TI Examining Clinical Educators' Readiness for Artificial Intelligence in
   Medical Education: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; medical education; faculty development;
   technology acceptance; clinical teaching; qualitative research;
   healthcare education; UTAUT
ID TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE
AB Artificial intelligence (AI), treated in this study as an umbrella term for AI-enabled clinical and educational technologies rather than as a single platform, is reshaping medical education, including how diagnostic skills, treatment planning, and patient care are taught. This study examines AI integration in medical education through the perceptions and readiness of clinical educators. Guided by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, the study explores factors influencing AI adoption in medical training, including performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions. In this exploratory study, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 clinical educators in the south-central United States who supervise third-year medical students. Findings suggested six recurring themes: the technological learning curve, the need for hands-on learning, institutional support, mentorship, preservation of human elements, and generational differences in comfort with AI. While some AI-enabled applications may support adaptive and personalized learning, educators expressed concerns about maintaining empathy, patient interaction, and human-centered care. The findings suggest that effective AI integration may require strategic institutional support, ongoing training, and pedagogical change. This study provides insight into developing AI-ready medical education models that balance technical competence with humanistic values.

TI Higher Education for Sustainability-Intergenerational Comparative
   Analysis of the Perceptions of Students at the University of the Basque
   Country Regarding Socioecological Transitions
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education for sustainability; socioecological transitions;
   students' perceptions; Education for Sustainable Development; IraMuTeq
ID ENVIRONMENTAL-EDUCATION
AB Higher education plays a crucial role in equipping citizens to tackle contemporary socio-ecological challenges. However, little research has examined how different generations of university students understand socioecological transitions, or the implications of these differences for sustainability education. This study compares the perceptions of older learners (aged 55-70) enrolled in the 'Classrooms of Experience' programme with those of undergraduate students (aged 18-28) from the Faculty of Economics and Business at the University of the Basque Country (UPV/EHU). Qualitative data were collected from approximately 250 participants during the 2023/24 and 2024/25 academic years. The data were analysed using the Grid Elaboration Method and the IRaMuTeQ (Version 0.8 Alpha 7) text analysis tool to identify semantic structures, symbolic associations and patterns of meaning across the two age groups. The findings reveal significant generational differences in understanding socioecological transitions. Older learners tend to frame transitions as regulated processes linked to institutional action, public policy, welfare, and quality of life. In contrast, younger students interpret socioecological transitions as responses to interconnected ecological and social crises, emphasising socioecological justice, responsibility, sustainability, and technological innovation as key drivers of transformation. These results suggest the coexistence of complementary yet distinct socioecological imaginaries within the university context. The study highlights the pedagogical value of intergenerational dialogue and learning in higher education. By bringing together diverse perspectives on sustainability, universities can promote more critical, reflective, and transformative educational processes that are capable of addressing the complex challenges of contemporary socioecological transitions.

TI From Teacher Workshop to Self-Study Online Module: Developing a
   Video-Based Resource for Diagnostic Accuracy in Primary Mathematics
   Teacher Education
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE primary mathematics teacher education; initial teacher training;
   continuous professional development; diagnostic competence; design-based
   research; video-based training; digital self-study
ID JUDGMENTS; KNOWLEDGE
AB Diagnostic competence is central to primary mathematics teacher education but existing approaches tend to depend on individual personnel and module structures, limiting their sustainability. This study combines a research-informed design approach with quasi-experimental intervention cycles: a fully asynchronous, video-based Moodle self-study module was developed to foster diagnostic competence in early arithmetic, consistently grounded in an empirically validated cognitive-developmental model. The module was implemented and iteratively refined across four phases-an in-service teacher workshop, a module pilot, and two quasi-experimental intervention cycles with pre-service primary teachers, including matched control groups. Across phases, the most consistent finding was a significant pre-post improvement in diagnostic accuracy for a below-average-performing pupil profile in the intervention group, while effects for average- and above-average profiles were less uniform. Log-data analyses showed that actual engagement with video vignettes, rather than structural completion, was the active ingredient of learning gains. Three design principles are proposed: model-based mathematical design, vertical connection of in-service and pre-service contexts, and guided asynchronous self-study with structured feedback. The study provides promising, context-bound evidence that a theoretically grounded, personnel-independent digital module can be integrated sustainably into primary teacher education and can foster diagnostic accuracy under the institutional and sample conditions investigated, while yielding initial design knowledge for comparable development efforts.

TI Sustainable STEM teacher learning: The role of college principals in
   Ghana
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE college principals; Ghana; STEM education; teacher professional
   learning; transformational leadership
ID SCHOOL LEADERSHIP; PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; DISTRIBUTED LEADERSHIP;
   HIGHER-EDUCATION; PERCEPTIONS; COMMUNITIES; MODELS; SYSTEM; REFORM;
   IMPACT
AB This study explores how principals in Ghanaian Colleges of Education (CoEs) perceive their roles in promoting STEM education and the strategies they employ to sustain STEM initiatives. It aims to understand how leadership practices contribute to sustainable teacher learning within resource-constrained educational environments. A qualitative multiple-case study design was adopted, drawing insights from four principals, five STEM teacher educators, and five student-teachers through semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions. Data were analysed thematically using Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework, with transformational leadership theory serving as the analytical lens to interpret how principals inspire vision, motivate staff, and build institutional capacity. Principals demonstrated a strong commitment to articulating vision, supporting professional development, and fostering innovation within their colleges. However, sustaining STEM initiatives was hindered by coordination challenges, limited resources, and insufficient mechanisms for feedback and follow-up. The study reveals that while transformational leadership behaviours such as idealised influence and intellectual stimulation promote teacher motivation and collaboration, long-term sustainability requires stronger systemic alignment and participatory structures. By examining leadership practices within a reform-driven teacher education system in the Global South, this study extends understanding of how STEM leadership is enacted under conditions of institutional change, resource constraints, and evolving policy demands. The Ghanaian context reveals how principals align professional learning, organisational routines, and STEM priorities to sustain innovation, offering broader insights into the systemic and relational nature of STEM leadership across diverse educational contexts.

TI Finding voice through memoir writing: An exploration of the expression
   of grief in undergraduate students' narratives
SO READING & WRITING-JOURNAL OF THE READING ASSOCIATION OF SOUTH AFRICA
LA English
DT Article
DE autobiography; bereavement; grief; memoir; memoir writing; voice
AB Background: Memoir writing can be a powerful tool for authors to reflect on past events and express their emotions, especially those related to grief. Research suggests that, beyond narrating stories, memoir writing can fulfil a therapeutic purpose when based on personal experiences. Objectives: This article explores how first-year undergraduate students utilise memoir writing as a therapeutic means to express grief. In this article, memoir writing is employed not merely to recount events drawn from personal memories but also as a coping strategy that involves reflection upon traumatic experiences through written expression. It acts as a means for emotional expression and interrogation of thoughts. Method: Data were collected using qualitative approach aligned with a case study research design. The data collection process involved memoirs written by five first-year undergraduate students who participated in a Memoir Writing Project. In addition, thematic analysis was used to analyse the data. Results: The findings indicate that some students utilised the memoir writing process as a means of reflecting on their past traumatic experiences. In addition, the memoir writing process contributed to enhancing metacognitive skills which are a requirement in selfreflection. It afforded them an opportunity to connect their past, present, and future and consequently, they gained a broader perspective into how loss shaped their personal identities. Conclusion: This article demonstrates that memoir writing can provide a haven for first-year students to express deep emotions which they might not previously have shared with others. It provides a space in which students feel secure enough to disclose personal experiences and understand that others may have experienced similar life challenges. Contribution: This article provides a broader understanding of how memoir writing functions as an important tool to help students develop confidence to express their perspectives through writing. It also shows how collaborative writing creates a space where writers feel safe to express themselves without fear of judgement.

TI Characterizing elementary science teachers' understanding of language as
   an epistemic tool
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE discourse analysis; epistemic tools; generative learning; language;
   science teacher education
ID STUDENTS; LITERACY; CONSTRUCTION; AGENCY; TALK
AB Central to scientific literacy is the cultivation of students' engagement in scientific practices, including the generation and justification of scientific knowledge. Critically, teachers' understanding of epistemic tools predicts their likelihood of facilitating such knowledge-generation activities. This study examines elementary science teachers' conceptualization of language as an epistemic tool to learn science in a two-year professional development (PD) program focused on the Science Writing Heuristic (SWH) approach. Gee's discourse analysis with inquiry tools of situated meanings and figured worlds was utilized to analyse teachers' written responses to characterize their language uses as a learning tool. On the other hand, teachers with lower questionnaire scores showed pedagogical understanding of language by explaining procedural use of language in science classroom. These results provide evidence for the role of the language questionnaire in supporting rich PD workshops at a large scale and informing the movement toward understanding that language is fundamental to all science learning.

TI The self-regulatory paradox of learning analytics: student expectations
   and the conditions for fair algorithmic assessment in higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE algorithmic transparency; data literacy; fairness; higher education;
   learning analytics dashboards; self-regulated learning; student agency;
   student expectations
AB Learning Analytics (LA) are increasingly positioned as tools to foster self-regulated learning (SRL) in higher education. As assessment-related data are progressively processed, interpreted, and acted upon through algorithmic systems, the fairness, transparency, and perceived legitimacy of these systems depend not only on their technical design but on whether students recognise themselves as agents within them. Yet students' own expectations regarding the institutional use of LA remain underexplored, particularly in face-to-face university contexts. This study investigates the service and feature expectations of 1,020 undergraduate students at a large Spanish research university, using the Student Expectations of Learning Analytics Questionnaire (SELAQ). Descriptive analyses and between-group comparisons were applied to seven items rated on a five-point Likert scale. Findings reveal a consistent asymmetry: students most strongly expect professors to act on analytics when academic risk is detected, and show comparatively lower expectations for LA to support their own decision-making. This pattern-expecting LA to function as a teacher-mediated intervention tool rather than a learner-directed resource-constitutes what we term a self-regulatory paradox: students endorse the outcomes of self-regulated learning while simultaneously delegating its data-informed enactment to their instructors. A direct within-student comparison confirmed that instructor- and institution-oriented expectations exceeded student-oriented ones (paired-samples test, medium effect). Gender-based differences were statistically significant for all seven items but small in size and, after Bonferroni correction, robust for five of them (Cohen's d = 0.18-0.29), female students consistently reporting higher expectations. These findings have direct implications for the design of LA dashboards, data literacy training, and institutional strategies aimed at repositioning students as active, data-informed agents of their own learning. More broadly, the paradox specifies an empirical precondition for fair and transparent algorithmic assessment: systems cannot be considered legitimate by virtue of being technically accessible to learners if those learners do not recognise themselves as entitled to interpret and act upon their own assessment data. We argue that perceived fairness and transparency in automated and AI-assisted assessment are contingent on building, rather than presupposing, students' data-informed agency.

TI Engineering technology through a constructivist lens: student
   motivations and experiences
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE constructivist learning theory; engineering technology students;
   postsecondary STEM education; student academic pathways; student support
   structures
ID BLACK-MALE; RACIAL IDENTITIES; ACHIEVEMENT; EDUCATION; IMPOSTOR;
   BARRIERS; DIVERSE; SCIENCE
AB Introduction Engineering Technology (ET) students construct belonging, identity, and academic persistence within predominantly white institutional environments where representation and recognition shape academic confidence. This study examines how constructivist learning processes operate within ET programs and how social and structural contexts influence student persistence.Methods Guided by constructivist learning theory, the study employed a qualitative design consisting of an eligibility survey and two focus groups with currently enrolled ET majors at Purdue University. Participants discussed motivations for selecting ET, perceptions of program culture, interactions with peers and faculty, and experiences of inclusion and exclusion across campus.Results Students were drawn to ET for its applied, hands-on learning model, early exposure to discipline-specific coursework, and perceived alignment with their learning preferences. Belonging operates as both a social and cognitive resource, enabling students to integrate prior experiences with new learning demands and persist despite structural or interpersonal challenges. Institutions should validate ET as a rigorous STEM pathway, strengthen mentorship and advising structures, and create inclusive learning environments that recognize the diverse backgrounds and strengths ET students bring to applied STEM education.

TI Digital equity and socioeconomic gradients in PISA 2022 mathematics: an
   integrated equity-diagnostic framework for Latin America and the
   Caribbean
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR); digital equity; explainable AI
   (SHAP); PISA 2022; socioeconomic gradient (ESCS)
AB This study develops and applies an integrated equity-diagnostic framework to examine mathematics achievement in PISA 2022, with Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) as the focal comparative case. Using public-use PISA 2022 microdata covering 613,744 students across 80 participating countries and economies, the analysis organizes evidence into complementary diagnostic layers: baseline regional performance, socioeconomic dependence of achievement, ESCS-linked point gaps, multilevel variance structure, and model-based interpretation of socioeconomic, digital, and school-level correlates. Design-consistent estimates were computed using final student weights and Balanced Repeated Replication with Fay's adjustment, while multilevel models and LightGBM/SHAP analyses were used as complementary robustness and interpretation layers. Results show that LAC has the lowest regional mean mathematics score among the classified regions, 56.9 points below the global descriptive mean. However, this disadvantage is not reducible to a single regional average or a uniform socioeconomic gradient. ESCS gradients vary substantially within LAC, from comparatively steep gradients in Chile, Uruguay, and Argentina to flatter gradients in Guatemala and Paraguay. ESCS-linked point gaps further show that socioeconomic dispersion changes the magnitude of inequality expressed in score points. Variance decomposition indicates that achievement differences are structured across country, school, and within-school levels, supporting a system- and school-level interpretation of equity. Across weighted and multilevel models, socioeconomic background, home possessions, disciplinary climate, language background, and digital-resource indicators show relevant but specification-sensitive associations with achievement. SHAP results are compatible with this interpretation by showing that digital-resource indicators contribute to prediction variability within broader socioeconomic and institutional contexts, rather than providing evidence that these indicators function as stand-alone equalizers. Overall, the study contributes a reproducible, survey-aware framework for monitoring educational equity and interpreting LAC's mathematics disadvantage as a multidimensional equity profile.

   cheating behaviours

   norms; theory of planned behaviour
ID PLS-SEM
AB Introduction Academic cheating remains a persistent ethical concern within accounting education, with implications for professional integrity and public trust. Guided by the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB), this study examines the extent to which attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control predict cheating behaviour among accounting students in Ghanaian higher education institutions.Methods Using a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 404 accounting students at a higher education institution in Ghana. TI Bridging Nanoscience and Chemistry as a Lever for Developing
   Higher-Order Questioning Skills Among High School Students
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE critical thinking; quality of questions; question asking ability (QAA);
   nanoscience education; scientific text
ID GENERATED QUESTIONS; THINKING; SCIENCE; NANOTECHNOLOGY; EDUCATION
AB Developing higher-order thinking skills in general, and question-asking skills in particular, is considered a cornerstone for fostering critical and cognitive thinking skills. Question-asking is a key component in student engagement toward understanding complex scientific concepts. This study investigates two innovative dimensions in chemistry education: the integration of nanoscience and nanotechnology aspects into chemistry instruction, and its impact on development of question-asking skills among 11th-grade high school students. Using a quasi-experimental design, 120 students were divided equally into experimental and control groups. Both groups read a simplified scientific text on redox reactions; the control group's text addressed redox reactions only, while the experimental group's text had nanoscience aspects embedded within the same redox context. Students' questions were evaluated by five judges using a validated four-level questioning hierarchy, ranging from factual to complex integrative knowledge. Results revealed significant differences in both the number and cognitive level of questions generated by the two groups. Students exposed to the nano-integrated text demonstrated markedly higher question-asking skills. In conclusion, integrating nanoscience into chemistry instruction was shown to be a powerful gateway to developing higher-order thinking, enabling students to ask more cognitively advanced questions, deepen their scientific understanding, and engage more meaningfully with scientific content.

TI Generative Learning and Student Motivation in Middle-School Science:
   Evidence from a Quasi-Experimental Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative learning; science achievement; motivation to learn science;
   science learning; middle school students
ID CONSTRUCTIVIST; MODEL
AB The present study examined whether seventh-grade female students in Oman who were taught through the generative learning model showed higher posttest science achievement and motivation to learn science than students who received regular instruction. The study used a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design with non-equivalent groups. There were 56 student participants, with 28 in the experimental group and 28 in the control group. The experimental group was taught using a teacher's guide organized around the stages of the generative learning model, whereas the control group received regular instruction for the same Grade 7 science unit. Student outcomes were assessed using an academic achievement test covering knowledge, application, and reasoning, and a motivation toward learning science scale. Pretest evidence indicated baseline equivalence between the two groups on achievement, Wilks' Lambda = 0.939, F(3, 52) = 1.13, p = 0.346, and motivation, Wilks' Lambda = 0.943, F(6, 49) = 0.489, p = 0.807. Posttest comparisons showed higher achievement and motivation scores for the experimental group under the conditions of the study. The findings provide preliminary context-specific evidence that generative learning may be associated with stronger cognitive and motivational outcomes in middle-school science, although the intact-class design warrants cautious interpretation.

TI Reframing Gifted Education: From Sorting Students to Cultivating
   Classroom-Based Opportunities
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE talent development; gifted education; advanced content; intellectual
   stimulation; interest-based learning
ID ACCELERATION; INEQUALITY; BELIEFS; ABILITY; TALENT
AB This article argues that gifted education is at a critical turning point, shaped by persistent conceptual fragmentation and the limitations of identification-centered systems. Despite decades of refinement, identification practices remain inconsistent, inequitable, and weakly aligned with the educational experiences they are intended to support. At the same time, the field continues to be divided between competing paradigms, most notably the Gifted Child Paradigm and the Talent Development Paradigm, resulting in incoherence in research, policy, and practice. Drawing on recent empirical and theoretical work, this article contends that these dual challenges undermine the effectiveness and equity of gifted and creative programming. In response, this article advances a reconceptualization of gifted education grounded in the talent development framework, which views ability as dynamic and emergent rather than fixed. Central to this vision is the Three Legs of Talent Development model, which emphasizes (a) access to advanced content, (b) intellectually stimulating instruction characterized by depth and complexity, and (c) interest-based authentic learning opportunities. Importantly, this framework situates the majority of gifted education services within the general classroom, positioning classroom instruction as the primary site for talent development rather than relying on separate or pull-out programs. Together, these elements form an integrated, system-level approach that shifts the focus from identifying gifted individuals to designing opportunity-rich, classroom-based environments that cultivate talent broadly.

TI Brief Science Teaching Self-Efficacy Scale for Pre-Service Teachers:
   Educational Implications of Science Teaching Self-Efficacy in Relation
   to Anxiety Toward Experimental Sciences, STEAM Familiarity, and Academic
   Achievement
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE anxiety toward experimental sciences; science teaching self-efficacy;
   STEAM approach; emotional well-being; pre-service teacher education
ID FIT INDEXES; CRITERIA
AB Anxiety toward experimental sciences may hinder learning, confidence in teaching science, and the professional development of pre-service teachers. Science teaching self-efficacy and familiarity with the STEAM approach have been identified as protective factors, although evidence examining these variables together remains limited. The purpose of this study was to analyze the validity and reliability of a brief measure of science teaching self-efficacy among pre-service teachers through its relationships with anxiety toward experimental sciences, familiarity with the STEAM approach, and academic achievement in science. A quantitative, cross-sectional study was conducted with 325 students enrolled in Early Childhood and Primary Education programs at the University of Ja & eacute;n, with a mean age of 21.05 years (SD = 2.79). Greater self-efficacy was associated with lower anxiety, greater STEAM familiarity, and higher academic achievement.

TI How Rare and How Stable? Resilient and Vulnerable School Profiles in
   Hungary Before and After the COVID-19 Pandemic
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE educational resilience; resilient schools; vulnerable schools;
   pedagogical value-added; school effectiveness; educational inequality;
   school climate; COVID-19 pandemic; Hungary
ID ROMA
AB Educational resilience commonly refers to better-than-expected academic outcomes among socioeconomically disadvantaged students or schools. However, little is known about its temporal stability, particularly in highly stratified and selective education systems such as Hungary's, especially following major disruptions like the COVID-19 pandemic. This study investigates the prevalence and stability of resilient and vulnerable elementary school profiles in Hungary using data from the National Assessment of Basic Competencies (NABC). School-level pedagogical value-added (PVA) indicators were estimated separately for mathematics and reading comprehension and aggregated across two three-year periods: the pre-pandemic period (2017-2019) and the post-pandemic recovery period (2023-2025). Schools were categorized into resilient and vulnerable groups based on the intersection of social disadvantage and performance. The profile analyses included 2048 schools; regression models included 192-201 cases depending on data completeness. Results show that resilient schools are rare and only partially stable, with fewer than one-quarter maintaining this status after the pandemic. Logistic regression analyses show that prior resilience, lower levels of disciplinary problems, and maintainer type were associated with a higher likelihood of post-pandemic resilience, while school size, regional location, disadvantage level, and teacher shortages lost explanatory power. Overall, the findings support a dynamic, context-dependent interpretation of school resilience.

TI Design and Evaluation of Interactive Matrix-Based Algorithm
   Visualizations in Introductory Programming: A Student Perception Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE algorithm visualization; programming education; interactive learning
   environments; matrix algorithms; educational visualization tools;
   student perception
ID COGNITIVE-LOAD; ANIMATIONS; SYSTEM
AB Algorithm development and its implementation by novice programmers in their first or second year of programming education can be difficult to teach because they often involve two-dimensional data structures, such as matrices. The use of these data structures requires both the ability to use nested iterations and the ability to coordinate row and column indices correctly. While algorithm visualization is commonly suggested as a method for externalizing intermediate program states and enhancing the understanding of algorithms, empirical studies have primarily focused on one-dimensional structures, such as sorting vectors using various algorithms. This study investigates the pedagogical potential of theory-informed, interactive, matrix-based algorithm visualizations implemented with the MatrixVis JavaScript library, a reusable web-based framework that provides step-by-step execution, visual highlighting of matrix operations, and synchronized source code display. The visualizations were demonstrated during introductory programming lectures and evaluated using a structured questionnaire (N = 48). Students evaluated the visualizations positively. The perceived usefulness of animations for understanding algorithms received a mean rating of M = 4.56, while the clarity of the visual presentation (M = 4.58), step-by-step execution (M = 4.54), and synchronized code highlighting (M = 4.69) were rated as particularly supportive. Visualizations of aggregation algorithms were perceived as the clearest (M = 4.58), whereas visualizations of structural transformations were slightly more difficult to follow (M = 4.08). These findings suggest that theoretically grounded, interactive visualizations of algorithms on matrices can provide meaningful pedagogical support in introductory programming education.

TI Student Advocacy in Higher Education: The Roles of Institutional DEI,
   Online Brand Community Engagement, and Service Quality
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education marketing; student advocacy; diversity; equity; and
   inclusion (DEI); online brand community engagement; brand attitude;
   student-university identification
ID BEHAVIORAL INTENTIONS; DIVERSITY CLIMATE; SATISFACTION; MODEL;
   IDENTIFICATION; ATTACHMENT; REGRESSION; INCLUSION; LOYALTY; CONTEXT
AB This study examines how perceived institutional diversity, equity, and inclusion, online brand community engagement, and service quality shape student advocacy in higher education through brand attitude and student-university identification. Drawing on the S-O-R framework and social identity theory, the study develops a model in which institutional signals influence student advocacy through evaluative and identity-based mechanisms. TI Navigating publication: chemistry faculty and graduate students'
   conceptions of copyright and fair use
SO CHEMISTRY EDUCATION RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
ID KNOWLEDGE; INFRINGEMENT
AB Copyright literacy is an important component of responsible and ethical research training and scholarly research in higher education. Chemistry faculty and graduate students routinely create copyrighted works and reuse copyrighted materials in publications, presentations, and instructional settings, yet little research has examined their understanding of copyright and fair use within this discipline. This pilot study developed and deployed a survey of chemistry graduate students and faculty at colleges and universities in the northeastern United States to assess their knowledge of copyright and fair use concepts. The instrument included multiple-choice, open-ended, and self-assessment questions, and the responses were analyzed using quantitative and qualitative methods. Results indicate both groups demonstrate a limited and incomplete understanding of key copyright principles. Participants commonly described copyright as ownership of intellectual property but rarely referenced concepts such as copyright transfer or duration. Understanding of fair use was similarly superficial, with no respondents identifying all four factors used in fair use analysis. These findings highlight the need for targeted copyright education in chemistry graduate programs.

TI Flexible Work Arrangements in Pharmacy Academia: An Overdue Imperative
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID LIFE
AB The COVID-19 pandemic fundamentally altered how faculty and staff in higher education, including schools and colleges of pharmacy, experience their work. As pharmacy schools navigate a postpandemic landscape marked by increasing workloads, workforce attrition, and growing burnout, the question of how to define, implement, and equitably distribute flexible work arrangements (FWAs) has become urgent and complex. This commentary examines FWAs in pharmacy academic settings: what they are, why they matter, and how they can be implemented in ways that serve the full workforce. We intentionally extend the conversation beyond faculty to include staff colleagues, who face many of the same pressures but have historically been left out of these discussions. Drawing on pharmacy and higher education literature, as well as broader organizational behavior research, we describe the spectrum of FWA types and summarize evidence on their impact on well-being, job satisfaction, and productivity. We also examine the unique complexities of pharmacy academia (including clinical obligations, accreditation constraints, and satellite campus dynamics)that make one-size-fits-all policies unrealistic. In addition, we address the risks of poorly managed flexibility, including erosion of collegiality, boundary permeability, and uneven impacts across roles and career stages. We close with a call to action for pharmacy school leaders to audit and publish their current FWA policies, engage faculty and staff in designing equitable approaches, and invest in the research needed to advance the field.

TI Assessing entrustability to performance: A longitudinal effort to evolve
   assessment in advanced pharmacy practice education
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Experiential education; Advanced pharmacy practice experiences;
   Assessment; Entrustable professional activities; Practice ready
AB Problem description: The experiential advanced pharmacy practice experience assessment tool needed to be revised and validated to incorporate new guidance from the Accreditation council. One direct patient care assessment was created that included practice-ready questions and entrustable professional activities (EPAs). QI methods: A stepwise approach was taken over a five year period to first educate preceptors on a new EPA rating scale, test formatively how the EPA scale performed, and then create a new assessment tool mapping to the new COEPA guidance published in 2022, paying careful attention to domains and questions from the previous APPE evaluations. Further analysis was done once the tool was implemented to compare performance and scores generated. Results: EPAs performed well in the pilot phase, with very few "not observed" scores. Preceptors showed a 98% agreement to the grades generated by the new tool in the 2024-25 fiscal year. Conclusion: A new single patient-care APPE assessment tool encompassing practice readiness skills and EPAs that performed accurately and very closely to the previous evaluation was successfully implemented for grading performance on APPEs across different practice settings.

TI Effects of game-based learning on student outcomes in mathematics
   education: A second-order meta-analysis
SO EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE GBL; Mathematics education; Second-order meta-analysis; Student
   outcomes; Cognitive skills; Affective outcomes
ID DIGITAL GAME; ACHIEVEMENT; SCIENCE; IMPACT
AB Game-Based Learning (GBL) has increasingly been used in mathematics education as a pedagogical approach intended to support student engagement and learning processes through interactive learning environments. This study employs a second-order meta-analysis to synthesize findings from nine first-order meta-analyses examining the effects of GBL on student outcomes in mathematics education. The findings indicate that GBL is generally associated with positive but relatively modest effects across both cognitive outcomes (e.g., academic achievement and problem solving) and affective outcomes (e.g., motivation and attitudes). The overall mean effect size was calculated as ES = .45 [LL = .25, UL = .65, p < .05]. However, a high level of heterogeneity was observed across studies, suggesting that the effects of GBL may vary considerably depending on contextual and methodological conditions. While cognitive outcomes tended to yield relatively more stable positive effects, findings related to affective outcomes appeared to be more limited and variable across studies. The findings further suggest that factors such as intervention duration, game type, implementation context, and methodological characteristics may contribute to variations in reported effect sizes. Overall, the findings suggest that GBL may offer a potentially supportive but context-sensitive contribution to mathematics education, while also highlighting the need for methodologically rigorous and pedagogically detailed future research.

TI The Impact of Preference Signaling on Orthopedic Surgery Residency
   Interviews
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Orthopedic surgery; Residency inter-views; Signal; Medical education
ID APPLICANTS
AB OBJECTIVE: This study examines whether the effectiveness of preference signaling in obtaining interview offers for orthopedic surgery residency varies by program type and size. DESIGN: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of orthopedic surgery applicants in 2024 using the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) Residency Explorer Tool. The primary outcome was the "interview offer rate," defined as the number of interviews given to applicants who signaled the program divided by the number of signals sent. Programs were analyzed by type (academic or community) and size (small = <= 5 residents, medium = 6-8, large => 9). Data were evaluated via Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn post hoc tests. SETTING: This study was performed at Duke University Medical School in Durham, North Carolina. There was no clinical care provided. PARTICIPANTS: We incorporated data from all MD, DO, IMG, and non-IMG applicants invited to interview at orthopedic surgery residency programs in 2024. Inclusion criteria were residency programs in the AAMC database which reported the rates of interviews offered to applicants who did and did not send a preference signal (120 programs total). RESULTS: Of 210 programs, 90 were excluded due to incomplete data, leaving 120 (57.1%). Across all institutions, applicants who signaled a program were significantly more likely to receive an interview offer (median 22% versus 1%, p < 0.001). For applicants who sent a signal, there was no significant difference in interview offer rate by program type, size, or type and size combined. There were also no significant differences across these metrics for applicants who did not signal a program. CONCLUSIONS: Interview rates for signals were consistent across program types and sizes, suggesting similar effects wherever signals are sent. All programs were unlikely to interview applicants who did not signal, highlighting the importance of careful signal selection. ( J Surg Ed 83:104066. TI Fostering conceptual change by comparing correct and incorrect solutions
   - The role of individual misconceptions☆
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Conceptual change; Cognitive analysis; Learning from errors; Worked
   solutions; Problem solving prior to instruction
ID RATIONAL NUMBERS; INSTRUCTION; STRATEGIES; EXAMPLES; ERRORS; MODEL;
   POWER; TEXT
AB Background: Conceptual change emerges from cognitive conflicts between new information and prior understanding. Confronting learners with their incorrect solutions and asking them to compare these to correct solutions can facilitate successful acquisition of new concepts. This learning process of committing errors and comparing solutions occurs, for instance, in problem-solving prior to instruction (PS-I). However, it is not clear how well this comparison has to be aligned to students' individual errors. Aims: We examine if conceptual change is more effectively supported by comparing a correct solution to an individually aligned incorrect solution rather than to a typical incorrect solution example. Sample: Participants were 184 sixth graders. Methods: In a computer-based learning environment, learners solved a fraction problem. They then received: 1) the correct solution only (control condition), 2) a correct and an individually aligned incorrect solution (alignment condition), or 3) a correct and non-aligned incorrect solution (contra-alignment condition). Results: Unlike in previous studies, using both correct and incorrect solutions (i.e., regardless of the alignment) did not outperform the correct solution only approach. However, learners in the alignment condition had the highest learning outcomes, supporting conceptual change theories. Intermediate knowledge after the problemsolving phase (visible in students' solutions) significantly influenced learning outcomes. Prior knowledge predicted learning outcomes only in the alignment and the control condition, a trend not observed in the contraalignment condition. Conclusions: This study highlights that comparison processes can support conceptual change when tailored to individual misconceptions.

Sample: Participants were 293 undergraduate students in the northeastern United States. Methods: Students completed a scenario-based integrative essay task using multiple textbook chapters and ChatGPT-3.5. We analyzed students' conversation logs qualitatively to develop a coding scheme. We then quantified the frequency of each strategy and used multiple regression analyses to examine whether strategy use predicted four dimensions of integration task performance. Results: Writing improvement was the strongest positive predictor across essay-quality dimensions. More specifically, task-based framing, learner-based generation, linguistic refinement, and referencing were linked to higher scores for some dimensions, whereas monitoring was negatively associated with several dimensions. Conclusions: The findings suggest that the educational value of GenAI in learning from multiple sources depends not simply on whether students use it, but on how they use it. Prompting strategies appear to be one observable way students strategically engage with GenAI within these environments.

TI Re-mapping the geopolitical imagination: From "Euro-Consumer" to
   "Techno-nationalist producer" in Turkish as a foreign language textbooks
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical discourse analysis; Multimodality; Textbooks; Geopolitical
   imagination; Techno-nationalism; Mental maps; Turkish as a foreign
   language
ID POLICY
AB Language instruction extends well beyond the simple conveyance of grammatical principles. Through it, states cultivate their self-image and affirm their status within the international order; language instruction, in this sense, functions as an instrument of statecraft. T & uuml;rkiye serves as a notable illustration in this context. Over the course of roughly two decades, T & uuml;rkiye's cultural diplomacy has transitioned from an "EU-centered integration" goal to a paradigm of "strategic autonomy." This paper examines how that transition has shaped Turkish teaching materials at the C1 level. The study utilizes a specialized dataset of approximately 86,0 0 0 tokens, integrating Multimodal Analysis and Corpus-Based Critical Discourse Analysis to compare C1-level textbooks produced by T & uuml;rkiye's principal cultural diplomacy organizations: the Yunus Emre Institute (YEI) and the T & uuml;rkiye Maarif Foundation (TMV). A page-level analysis of the images shows the same split, while a civilisational and Silk-Road vocabulary turns out to be heavier in the 2015 YEI volume. (c) 2026 Elsevier Inc. AB In this article, we explore how international students from diverse linguistic, racialized, and educational backgrounds at a U.S. university make sense of race and language and how these understandings shape their communication practices across academic and social spaces. TI Latent profile analysis of professional commitment among undergraduate
   nursing students and its association with interprofessional
   collaboration competence
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing students; Professional commitment; Latent profile analysis;
   Interprofessional collaboration; Professional identity
ID SELF-EFFICACY; SIMULATION
AB Background: Professional commitment is a key factor influencing nursing students' sense of professional identity, learning motivation, and future retention. However, most existing studies treat it as a single continuous construct, overlooking the dimensional combinations and internal heterogeneity within student groups. The relationship between commitment profiles and interprofessional collaboration competence (IPCC) remains unclear. Aim: To identify latent profiles of professional commitment among undergraduate nursing students and examine differences in their IPCC and related influencing factors. Design: Cross-sectional study. Settings: Six public undergraduate universities in Guangxi, China. Participants: A total of 492 undergraduate nursing students across all academic years. Methods: Data were collected using structured questionnaires measuring professional commitment and interprofessional collaboration competence. Latent profile analysis (LPA) was used to identify commitment profiles. Chi-square (chi(2)) tests, ANOVA, and multinomial logistic regression were employed to explore associated factors and group differences in collaboration competence. Results: Three distinct profiles of professional commitment were identified: Low Commitment (27.8%): Weak affective and idealistic commitment, with a high risk of attrition; Moderate Commitment (53.3%): Strong in normative commitment but low in intrinsic motivation; High Commitment (18.9%): Balanced development across all four dimensions and strong professional identity. Satisfaction with the nursing major significantly predicted profile membership (P < 0.001). A gradient association was found between commitment profiles and IPCC, with the High Commitment group showing significantly higher scores in value alignment, role understanding, communication, and teamwork (P < 0.001). Conclusions: Professional commitment among undergraduate nursing students exhibits clear heterogeneity. Commitment profiles effectively predict collaboration competence. Educators are encouraged to apply tiered interventions based on commitment levels and integrate identity development into interprofessional education to enhance students' collaborative capacity and career development potential.

TI Who lost the most? COVID-19 school closures, PISA achievement, and
   socioeconomic gaps
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE COVID-19 school closures; Learning loss; Educational inequality; Remote
   learning
AB This paper examines how COVID-19 school closures were associated with student achievement and social inequalities using data from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) for 2018 and 2022. The analysis examines how different remote learning methods were associated with the relationship among school closures, educational inequality, and learning outcomes in mathematics, science, and reading. To estimate both direct and indirect associations, the study employs a Generalized Structural Equation Model (GSEM) and a Triple Difference-in-Differences approach. This method enables the simultaneous estimation of correlates of remote learning modality usage and their associations with proficiency outcomes, while accounting for students' socioeconomic backgrounds. The results show clear differences between advanced and emerging/developing economies. In advanced economies, school closures were associated with moderate average learning losses, but a significant increase in social inequalities. In emerging/developing economies, school closures were primarily associated with larger average learning losses rather than with increased socioeconomic gaps. This may be due to the limited spread of digital learning technologies that could help create advantages. In summary, the results suggest that school closures were associated less with a uniform disruption to learning and more with a redistribution of educational opportunities along socioeconomic lines, with the type of remote learning available to students associated with much of who lost the most.

TI Impact of flipped classrooms on higher education student outcomes: A
   second-order meta-analysis
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Flipped classroom; Teaching/learning strategies; Meta-analysis; Higher
   education; academic performance; pedagogy
AB Although current theoretical models and empirical studies have clarified the mechanisms of the flipped classroom, its overall effectiveness remains contested. This study examined the impact of the flipped classroom (FC) on student outcomes in higher education. A second-order meta-analysis was performed on 25 first-order metaanalyses. A random-effects model was employed for the statistical analysis. The overall effect of FC on student outcomes was moderate (ES = 0.75; 95% CI [0.62, 0.87]). The effect size varied across contexts, as indicated by significant heterogeneity and moderation by discipline, geographical location, research design, sample size, and number of primary studies. FC effects may vary across student outcome categories, although this pattern should be interpreted with caution due to potential dependence among subgroup estimates. We conclude that FC is an effective pedagogical approach in higher education, although the magnitude of its effect depends on contextual and methodological conditions.

TI A structural topic modeling analysis of positive psychology in EFL
   teacher education from 2010 to 2025
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL teacher education; positive psychology; Structural topic modeling;
   Teacher well-being
ID EMOTIONS
AB This study investigates how positive psychology discourses have evolved within the EFL teacher education literature between 2010 and 2025. Using Structural Topic Modeling (STM) on 619 journal articles, the study maps the thematic, temporal, and contextual dimensions of the field. Results reveal twelve latent topics clustered around three overarching domains: individual psychological resources (e.g., self-efficacy, resilience, mindfulness), emotional-relational dimensions (e.g., motivation, feedback, autonomy), and professional-organizational contexts (e.g., identity, commitment, job satisfaction). Geographical and methodological analyses reveal that quantitative approaches are more prevalent in the East Asian context, while qualitative and mixed methods in other regions focus more on issues such as teacher agency and pedagogical well-being. Overall, the study demonstrates that positive psychology in EFL teacher education functions not as a universal framework but as a culturally and epistemologically diverse discourse that integrates well-being, pedagogy, and professional sustainability.

TI Cognitive diagnosis of EFL integrated writing under interactive noise
   input conditions: A G-DINA model approach
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Integrated writing assessment; Cognitive load; Textual complexity;
   Interactive noise input; G-DINA model
ID INSTRUCTIONAL-DESIGN; SYNTACTIC COMPLEXITY; ARCHITECTURE; ACCURACY;
   STUDENTS; LEVEL; TASKS
AB This study investigates how isolated and combined reading complexities affect EFL learners' specific cognitive skills in integrated writing tasks. The experiment introduced three types of textual interference (syntactic complexity, lexical difficulty, and logical structure complexity) as reading "noise." The G-DINA cognitive diagnostic model was then applied to analyze the writing performances of 540 EFL learners under single- and dual-noise conditions. Results indicate that traditional holistic scores often obscure critical cognitive vulnerabilities. By visualizing these fine-grained diagnostic results through radar charts, the study provides a practical tool to shift from general score-based grading to targeted skill interventions.

   bimodal teaching format
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking; Secondary education; Design-based research; Science
   mediation; Metacognition; Pedagogical design
ID COGNITIVE REFLECTION; NEUROSCIENCE; VALIDATION; BELIEFS
AB Critical thinking is now widely recognized as a major educational goal. Among the emerging responses to this challenge are teaching formats that seek to combine rigor, engagement, and compatibility with school constraints. This article examines a lecture-performance, The Critical Moment, designed for school audiences aged 15 to 18, as a bimodal pedagogical device situated at the intersection of lecture and stage performance. The article offers a design-based analysis of the conception of the device. ID LEARNING ANALYTICS; USER ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY; SCIENCE; MYTH
AB This study examines the intellectual evolution of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) from 2000 to 2024 by integrating scientometric analysis and BERTopic-based semantic modeling. Drawing on 2340 peer-reviewed records from the Web of Science, we mapped publication patterns, journals, institutions, authors, and thematic structures, and interpreted the results through a macro-meso-micro analytical framework. Findings reveal rapid growth in AIED research, with marked acceleration after 2022, alongside a gradual reorientation of research agendas. At the macro level, early work was shaped by online learning and MOOCs, while later research increasingly reflects the importance of data-intensive educational systems, especially learning analytics and educational data mining. These developments raise institutional implications related to data regulation, privacy, transparency, accountability, and ethical oversight. At the meso level, teacher digital competence and organizationally supported professional capacity function as key mediating hubs that connect institutional agendas with curriculum design, assessment, and organizational support. At the micro level, research attention moves beyond performance prediction toward learner engagement, affective experience, and interactive forms of AI-supported learning. By linking these clusters through an institutional-organizational-individual coupling framework, the study shows that AIED knowledge has evolved not as a set of isolated themes, but as a cross-level structure in which institutional priorities, organizational arrangements, and learner experiences mutually shape one another. The synthesis offers implications for data-informed governance, institutional capacity building, teacher professional development, curricular integration, and sustainable support structures for user-centered AI adoption in education.

AB This content analysis examined U.S. prekindergarten oral language state standards to illuminate the interactive, linguistic, and conceptual dimensions of children's language development. We sought to examine the structure and organization of oral language standards as well as the guidance for setting-specific language practices and samples of children's language. TI From abstract concept to concrete insight: Visualizing mass transfer
   with a rotating disk electrode in the chemical engineering curriculum
SO EDUCATION FOR CHEMICAL ENGINEERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Chemical Reaction Engineering; Mass transfer; Intrinsic kinetics;
   Reaction rate; Rotating disk electrode
ID OXYGEN REDUCTION REACTION; TAFEL SLOPE
AB This article presents a laboratory module that uses a rotating disk electrode (RDE) to transform the abstract principle of mass transfer into a tangible and investigable phenomenon for upper-level undergraduates. The module centers on two controllable experimental parameters-electrode rotation speed (omega, which tunes convective transport) and reactant partial pressure (p, which sets the bulk concentration)-that govern the mass-transfer-limited rate. Through real-time linear sweep voltammetry of the hydrogen oxidation and oxygen reduction reactions, students observe how these variables control the limiting current plateau and trace the transition from kinetic to transport control. The laboratory sequence guides students from qualitative observation (Levich validation) to quantitative analysis (Kouteck & yacute;-Levich deconvolution), enabling them to separate intrinsic kinetics from mass-transfer effects. A tutorial session reinforces learning through comparative analysis of catalysts, challenging students to explain why similar limiting currents can mask distinctly different intrinsic activities. Implementation with chemical engineering students demonstrated substantial learning gains, particularly in diagnostic reasoning and model-based analysis, as evidenced by pre-and post-test assessments. Complete student handouts and instructor notes are provided to facilitate adoption, offering a hands-on strategy for teaching transport-limited reactions within the critical context of electrochemical energy technologies.

TI Reconstructing the Teaching of Activity and Activity Coefficients
   Centered on Intermolecular Forces: Progressive Modular Teaching
   Reconstruction and Practice Based on Physical Mechanism Classification
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Activity Coefficient; Intermolecular Forces; Physical Mechanism
   Classification; Progressive Modular Teaching; Local Composition Model;
   Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics; Teaching Reconstruction
ID CHEMICAL-EQUILIBRIUM; GIBBS ENERGY; THERMODYNAMICS; DESIGN
AB Activity and activity coefficients in chemical engineering thermodynamics feature both in-depth microscopic molecular mechanisms and intensive macroscopic engineering calculations, representing a core teaching pain point where students struggle to internalize concepts and tend to solve problems mechanically. Traditional teaching generally introduces activity coefficient models-ideal solution, Margules, Van Laar, Flory-Huggins, Wilson, NRTL, etc.-in chronological order of their development, leading to severely fragmented knowledge points, disconnected physical mechanisms, and a situation where students only apply formulas without understanding engineering model selection. This article breaks away from the outdated teaching paradigm of "listing models by era" and innovatively adopts a new perspective of classification by physical mechanisms. All activity coefficient models are uniformly categorized into four physical types: enthalpy-effect-dominated, entropy-effect-dominated, local composition microscopic enrichment, and energy-volume coupling. An integrated cognitive chain is constructed: "root of molecular forces -> two core mechanisms of nonideality -> progressive physical classification of models -> precise selection for engineering scenarios". Taking the typical polar-nonpolar ethanol-cyclohexane mixture system as a case throughout the course, the reform is supported by problem-oriented modular teaching, molecular dynamics microscopic visualization demonstrations, and an integrated "prediction-validation-modeling" reform of vapor-liquid equilibrium experiments. This achieves a cognitive leap for students from "memorizing formulas for numerical calculation" to "understanding mechanisms for model selection". Teaching practice shows that the proportion of students who grasped the physical essence of activity coefficients rose from 12.2% to 88.0% after the reform and that the score rate of students' ability to select and apply engineering models increased by 38.9%, as verified by standardized pretests and post-tests covering three dimensions, including conceptual understanding, phenomenon interpretation, and engineering application, as well as an independent sample t test. This provides a directly replicable paradigm reference for the advanced teaching reconstruction of core concepts in chemical engineering thermodynamics in universities and is mainly applicable to senior undergraduate students and graduate students majoring in chemical engineering.

This Research into Practice paper reports on a staged instructional workflow implemented in a graduate EAP writing course in Taiwan, where selected NotebookLM features were integrated as pedagogical scaffolds to support proposal development. TI Vibe coding in nursing education: From user to creator
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing education; Generative artificial intelligence; Vibe coding;
   Digital co-design; Critical AI literacy; Nursing innovation; Nurse
   educators
AB The rise of generative artificial intelligence has begun to transform how digital tools are created, shifting development from conventional programming toward natural language prompting, iterative refinement, and AI-assisted generation. Popularly described as "vibe coding," this informal practice refers to building applications, interfaces, automations, or prototypes by describing desired outcomes conversationally and revising outputs until they function as intended. Although the term is playful, it signals a significant shift in who can participate in digital creation and what forms of expertise now matter. This paper argues that "vibe coding" provides a useful contemporary lens for examining an important issue in nursing education: the transition from nurses as users of educational technologies to potential co-designers of digital learning tools. Nursing education has increasingly incorporated simulation, learning management systems, virtual cases, electronic documentation, and AI-enabled supports, yet nurses have often remained positioned as adopters rather than designers of these systems. AI-assisted creation may begin to alter that relationship by lowering barriers to prototyping and enabling educators and students to translate pedagogical ideas into functional tools more quickly. This shift holds promise for more contextually grounded, practice-informed, and responsive educational innovation. At the same time, it raises critical concerns regarding accuracy, bias, accessibility, privacy, pedagogical quality, and the illusion of expertise. As a Contemporary Issues conceptual commentary, the paper explores the educational possibilities and ethical tensions associated with AI-assisted creation in nursing education and argues that the issue should not be approached with either uncritical enthusiasm or outright rejection. Instead, nursing education may need to cultivate critically informed digital co-design capacity. This includes moving beyond basic digital literacy toward critical AI literacy, supporting educators in responsible experimentation, and ensuring that relational, reflective, and equity-oriented commitments remain central. Ultimately, nursing education must prepare future nurses not only to use digital systems, but also to question, evaluate, and, when appropriate, help shape them.

TI Teachers' transformative professional agency: Inspiration and means for
   promoting educational change in the context of digitalization
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digitalization; Networking; Professional development; Teacher
   collaboration; Transformative professional agency
ID IDENTITY; SELF; COMMUNITIES; KNOWLEDGE; NETWORKS
AB This study examines teachers' transformative professional agency during their participation in the Learning and Teaching in Digital Environments Professional Specialization program. It explores what inspires teachers to develop educational practices and how they drive educational change in the context of digitalization. Data, comprising teachers' application letters and final interviews (n = 28), were analyzed qualitatively using content analysis. The findings reveal teachers' transformative professional agency at four levels: teacher, student, work community, and network. This study contributes to academic research by demonstrating how transformative professional agency unfolds across ecological levels and clarifying the relationship between teachers' motivations and their practices in driving educational change.

TI Harnessing the Power of Lived Expertise: Evaluating a Majority
   Autistic-Led Autism Sabbatical Program
SO ADULT LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE adult learning; autism; inclusion; neurodiversity; universal design
AB Does Autistic-led instruction influence adult learners' knowledge and beliefs? A neurodiverse team, including instructor-facilitators and educator-students in a year-long autism sabbatical program, evaluated the primarily Autistic-led program. Four Autistic instructor-facilitators shared what they believed worked well in their teaching, challenges they experienced, how they addressed feedback, and recommendations for the future. We used content analysis to examine potential shifts in 24 student-educators' beliefs, knowledge, and intended teaching practices, coding their open-ended responses to surveys administered at three points across the program. Findings suggest that Autistic-led instruction promoted meaningful perspective shifts among both instructor-facilitators and educator-students, including increasing focus on meaningful, hands-on learning opportunities among instructor-facilitators and greater respect for Autistic stimming, communication, and interests among educator-students. Educator-students shared that the program taught them to be more flexible and student-centered. Some indicated that they planned to teach their students self-advocacy skills to empower students to spark changes that will make classrooms more equitable and inclusive for all. Some planned to advocate for systems changes themselves, including by teaching their colleagues how to adopt more neurodiversity-affirmative practices. Some Autistic instructor-facilitators and some educator-students described Autistic instructors as key agents of perspective transformations. Others indicated that qualities that make someone a strong educator, like flexibility and responsiveness, may be orthogonal to autism. Tangible outcomes of the program include educator-students' portfolios which include concrete tools such as innovative assignments that have been refined through ongoing dialogue between instructor-facilitators and educator-students.

TI Staffing and Resource Allocation in College Access Reform: How Dual
   Credit Shifts Educational Costs
SO COMMUNITY COLLEGE REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE dual enrollment; early college high schools; college access; cost
   analysis; education finance
ID ENROLLMENT; BENEFITS; IMPACT
AB Objective: Dual credit (DC), or dual enrollment, is college-level coursework that confers credit toward both high school graduation and a postsecondary degree. As DC has grown rapidly across the country, this study provides needed evidence about how these courses shift resources and cost burdens among community colleges, school districts, and families.Methods: We use economic evaluation methods to assess the cost of DC across three delivery models, where DC is administered in (a) traditional comprehensive high schools; (b) Early College High Schools (ECHS); and (c) school-within-school ECHSs. We draw on statewide administrative datasets combined with a smaller qualitative data sample.Results: We find that implementation of DC requires substantial investment in existing staff personnel time as well as new staff positions, professional development costs, and other costs, across both K-12 and postsecondary sectors. In addition to requiring new resources, DC shifts the cost burden of educating high school students from school districts to community colleges. We find community colleges bear a disproportionate share of costs, especially in delivery models where community college faculty serve as the instructor of record-a model that is common in ECHSs.Contributions: The study informs the design of tuition agreements and instructor and student course assignment policies that promote equitable and sustainable distribution of costs and resources for students, school districts, and community colleges. Future research may explore how costs compare to measures of impact, especially for low-income and global majority students, who are historically underrepresented in higher education.

AB This paper explores the relationship between mindfulness practice and slow relational pedagogy in early childhood education, drawing on insights from a qualitative study with early childhood educators. TI Linking Chemistry Learning to Careers: Impact of Career-Based
   Differentiated Instruction (CBDI) on STEM Students' Self-Efficacy and
   Outcome Expectations
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Differentiated instruction; Career relevance; General Chemistry; Outcome
   expectations; Senior high school; STEM education; Self-efficacy
AB Despite efforts to achieve Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) Target 4.4, which seeks to increase the number of youth and adults with vocational skills for employment, STEM education in the Philippines continues to face gaps in career relevance that link classroom learning with workforce needs. This study aimed to develop and validate a career-based differentiated instruction (CBDI) resource package in General Chemistry 1 for teachers and evaluate its impact on STEM students' self-efficacy and outcome expectations. The development phase entailed applying chemistry concepts to fields in engineering, technology, and health. Experts affirmed the relevance of CBDI in these career fields. The implementation phase used a quasi-experimental design with 161 grade 12 STEM students using pre- and post-tests through Career Decision Self-Efficacy (CDSE) and Vocational Outcome Expectations (VOE) scales. Paired samples t-test showed no significant changes in the control group, while the experimental group achieved significant improvements in self-efficacy [t(84) = -9.30, p < 0.001] and outcome expectations [t(84) = -5.95, p < 0.001] after eight (8) weeks of intervention. Independent samples t-test confirmed significantly greater gains for the experimental group in self-efficacy [t(155) = -5.26, p < 0.001] and outcome expectations [t(158) = -4.08, p < 0.001]. Reflexive thematic analysis from classroom observations and student reflections further supported these results, highlighting career-based laboratory experiments, collaborative activities, problem-solving, and case studies as mechanisms of improvement. The study concludes that the developed CBDI resource package is valid and that its implementation significantly improved students' self-efficacy and outcome expectations. It recommends classroom adoption, school integration, and policy-driven pilot implementation.

TI Molecular Orbital Theory for Octahedral Complexes:Playing with Cards
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Card Game; Second-Year Undergraduate; Inorganic Chemistry;
   Collaborative; Cooperative Learning; Molecular Orbital Theory
ID LIGAND GROUP ORBITALS; GAME
AB Teaching Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT) is often challenging due to its abstract concepts and mathematical formalism, which can make it difficult for students to grasp. To make this content more accessible and engaging, we developed a card game based on MOT principles. In this game, each card represents either a metal orbital, a group of ligand orbitals, or the resulting molecular orbitals generated through Linear Combination of Atomic Orbitals (LCAO). The objective is to form trios of cards that represent and require the evaluation of orbital combinations involved in the bonding interactions of octahedral coordination complexes. The activity was implemented in an Inorganic Chemistry II course at the Federal University of Espirito Santo (UFES). A five-question multiple-choice test was administered before and after the game to explore its potential impact on student understanding. Results suggested trends consistent with improvement in student performance, with an increase in the number of correct answers and a reduction in "I don't know" responses. In addition, a postactivity questionnaire revealed highly positive student perceptions: students highlighted that the game made learning more enjoyable, interactive, and collaborative, while also supporting the understanding of complex concepts. These findings are consistent with the integration of strategies, such as this low-cost and easily reproducible card game, supporting student engagement and contributing to the learning of abstract concepts in coordination chemistry and beyond.

TI Thin-Layer Electrochemistry:Visualizing the Diffusion Layer During
   Chronoamperometry and Cyclic Voltammetry
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Hands-on Illustration; Hands-on Learning/manipulatives; First-Year
   Undergraduate/General; Upper-Division Undergraduate; Electrochemistry;
   Oxidation/Reduction; Redox Indicator; Diffusion Layer; Diffusion
   Coefficient; Chronoamperometry; Cyclic Voltammetry
ID METHYL VIOLOGEN; REDUCTION; GUIDE
AB The phenomena that occur in the diffusion layer play a central role in electrochemical processes but are often challenging for students to understand. Here, we present a demonstration and activity to directly observe and analyze the changes in diffusion layer during chronoamperometry and cyclic voltammetry. Methyl viologen (MV2+), a redox indicator with distinct color changes upon one-electron reduction, was used to generate an observable color change. The reaction was carried out in a homemade thin-layer cell, and the color changes were monitored and recorded using an optical microscope equipped with a digital camera. In chronoamperometry, students examined the time dependence of current decay and diffusion-layer growth, then calculated the diffusion coefficient of the methyl viologen radical cation (MV+ center dot). In cyclic voltammetry, students visually tracked the appearance and disappearance of the colored diffusion layer during forward and reverse potential scans. Linking these visual observations to the electrochemical responses enhanced students' ability to comprehend the underlying processes. This activity offers a versatile and visually engaging tool for teaching electrochemistry in both introductory and advanced courses.

TI What Makes the Best Educator? A Qualitative Analysis of Emergency
   Medicine Resident Perspectives
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
ID GUIDE
AB Background Effective clinical educators are essential to emergency medicine (EM) residency training, and the pace and dynamics of the emergency department require them to have a unique educational skillset. Most existing literature defining educational excellence in EM reflects educator rather than learner perspectives, and there is limited contemporary, resident-centered work that describes the teaching practices of exceptional EM educators. This study aimed to identify EM resident-defined practices that characterize the "best" EM educators.Methods We performed a qualitative thematic analysis to analyze open-ended survey responses from residents at a large, urban, 3 year EM residency program. All 78 residents were invited to complete an anonymous survey containing a single prompt to describe their best EM educator. Data were collected over 72 h in March 2025. Three investigators performed iterative open coding and applied constant comparative methods to identify themes. Postgraduate year (PGY) class was unblinded after analysis to explore patterns by training level.Results Thirty-eight residents responded (48.7% response rate). Five themes emerged: (1) growth orientation, (2) psychological safety, (3) shares clinical burden, (4) educational expertise, including optimal timing and setting of teaching, knowledge translation, and fostering independence; and (5) clinical expertise, including content expertise and role modeling. In a secondary descriptive analysis, PGY-1s emphasized psychological safety, growth-oriented feedback, and autonomy, while PGY-2 and PGY-3 residents prioritized approachability, timely teaching, shared workload, and clinical expertise.Conclusions Residents identified outstanding EM educators as growth-oriented, supportive, skilled teachers and expert clinicians, with preferences varying by training level. These themes may guide faculty development, coaching, and feedback as well as future studies on resident-centered educator training.

TI Understanding school stress/distress: moving beyond the functional model
   of school attendance
SO CAMBRIDGE JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE School distress; school attendance; school safety; student voice
ID REFUSAL BEHAVIOR
AB This study explored the lived experiences of children aged 8-12 and their caregivers navigating school can't (SC), an emotionally based school non-attendance driven by a stress/distress relationship, rather than defiance. Using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA), six neurodivergent children and young people shared how school environments influenced feelings of safety, belonging and overwhelm. Findings revealed that the distress that resulted from school-based stressors was often embodied through physical symptoms and exacerbated by inconsistent school supports and unmet sensory needs.
