TI "It's not magic, it's logic": a case study of pedagogical content
   knowledge in teaching reaction mechanisms in organic chemistry
SO CHEMISTRY EDUCATION RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
ID CHEMICAL-EQUILIBRIUM; TEACHERS; STUDENTS; SCIENCE; REPRESENTATIONS;
   ACIDS/BASES; MODELS; NOVICE; EXPERT; PCK
AB Reaction mechanisms are central to organic chemistry and function as explanatory models that link electron density and reactivity through electron flow, supporting the development of mechanistic reasoning. While chemistry education research has extensively documented students' persistent difficulties with reaction mechanisms, comparatively little work has examined how instructors shape this learning through their instructional decisions, despite teaching and learning being fundamentally co-constructed processes. This work examines an experienced organic chemistry instructor's topic-specific pedagogical content knowledge (TSPCK) and its enactment in classroom practice. A qualitative case-study design (N = 1) was used to develop a detailed account of instruction over a semester of introductory organic chemistry. Data sources included semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and instructional artifacts used to construct and develop the content representation (CoRe) and pedagogical and professional-experience repertoires (PaP-eRs). Classroom observations were guided by an enacted PCK framework focusing on curricular saliency, knowledge of student thinking, conceptual teaching strategies, and their integration. Findings indicate that the instructor's TSPCK is organized around three "big ideas": (1) thinking at the atomic level, (2) mechanistic logic and generalizable patterns, and (3) representations as meaningful rather than decorative. PaP-eRs for each "big idea" were developed through exemplar teaching moments noted during classroom observations. For instructors, these findings emphasize the importance of aligning instructional goals, representations, and assessment practices. For researchers, this work demonstrates the value of using the CoRe and PaP-eR tools to capture both articulated and enacted dimensions of PCK.

TI "Residents-as-teachers": a survey on perceptions and experiences of
   surgical and orthopedic residents in teaching medical students
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Residents as teachers; Medical education; Internship and residency;
   Teaching hospital; Orthopedics; Surgical specialties
ID SKILLS; TIME
AB Introduction Surgical and orthopedic residents are tasked with teaching medical students, despite heavy clinical workloads and limited formal training. While previous literature has demonstrated positive feedback from medical students, little is known about resident surgeons' perspectives on their teaching duties. This study investigates the perceptions and experiences of surgical and orthopedic residents as clinical teachers.Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among resident and resident specialist grade doctors in the surgical and orthopedic department of a single university teaching hospital. Participants with prior teaching experience were asked to complete an online survey that collected background data, experiences in clinical teaching, and opinions on clinical teaching, including perceptions and beliefs rated on a Likert scale of 1 to 5.Results 40 residents across all training grades completed the survey. All had been taught by residents during medical school, with 65% rating those experiences as good or very good. Most residents enjoyed teaching (65%) and 47.5% expressed a desire for greater involvement in teaching. 75% believed teaching enhanced their own knowledge and learning. However, only 25% received formal teaching training and 12.5% had protected time for teaching from clinical duties. Feedback on quality of teaching was also limited (25%), and only 20% felt valued by their institution for their teaching contributions.Conclusion Surgical and orthopedic residents reported positive experiences and recognized the benefits of undergraduate clinical teaching, but identified barriers such as inadequate training, minimal feedback and institutional support. Institutions should address these issues to improve resident engagement in teaching.

TI Instrumental Genesis of Learning Trajectories in Professional Noticing:
   Comparing Expert and Novice Teachers' Competencies in Fractions
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Fractions; In-service teachers; Learning trajectory; Pre-service
   teachers; Professional noticing
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; MATHEMATICS
AB Professional noticing, encompassing attending to, interpreting, and responding to students' understanding, is a vital skill for effective mathematics teaching. This study investigated how novice and expert primary school teachers developed instrumental relationships with fractions learning trajectory (LT) knowledge during professional noticing processes. Data were collected from 64 participants (30 novice teachers and 34 expert teachers) through tasks requiring them to analyse students' fractional reasoning strategies and propose developmentally appropriate instructional activities. Results revealed that expert teachers exhibited significantly higher skills in interpreting and responding to students' understanding compared to novice teachers, while showing minimal differences in attending capabilities. The study identified four levels of instrumental genesis-artifact role, using specific LT components, partial instrumentation, and full instrumentation-revealing that expert teachers consistently achieved higher levels of LT transformation from theoretical artifacts to practical instruments. Expert teachers demonstrated instrumental resilience, maintaining stable performance across varying cognitive demands, while novice teachers showed systematic regression as task complexity increased. These findings demonstrated that expertise enables robust instrumental relationships with theoretical frameworks, suggesting that teacher education programs must support systematic instrumental genesis rather than simple framework exposure to develop effective professional noticing capabilities.

TI Unpacking the heterogeneity of pre-service teachers' ChatGPT acceptance:
   a latent profile analysis across STEM and non-STEM disciplines
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; Pre-service teachers; TAM; UTAUT2; Latent profile analysis;
   STEM
ID DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY; UNIFIED THEORY; PERSPECTIVE; VARIABLES; EDUCATION;
   ADOPTION; SYSTEM
AB Background Pre-service teachers' acceptance of generative AI is highly heterogeneous, yet most studies rely on variable-centered approaches that cannot reveal qualitatively distinct subgroups. This study adopted a person-centered latent profile analysis (LPA) to identify pre-service teachers' ChatGPT acceptance profiles and to compare STEM and non-STEM teachers in terms of profile distribution and behavioral intention. Data were collected from N = 128 pre-service teachers in Taiwan (68 STEM, 60 non-STEM). Building on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2), five constructs were used as LPA indicators, with behavioral intention treated as a distal outcome. Results The analysis identified four highly distinguishable profiles (entropy = 0.985): Pragmatic Evaluators (47.66%), Environmental Observers (11.72%), Technology Pioneers (26.56%), and Resistant Skeptics (14.06%). Notably, Resistant Skeptics demonstrated relatively high perceived ease of use but very low behavioral intention, indicating that perceived technical ease does not guarantee behavioral intention. Disciplinary background was strongly associated with profile membership (chi & sup2; = 36.20, p < .001, Cramer's V = 0.532), with STEM teachers concentrated in Technology Pioneers (47.1%) and non-STEM teachers overrepresented in Environmental Observers and Resistant Skeptics. The four profiles also differed substantially in behavioral intention (F = 109.00, p < .001, eta & sup2; = 0.726). Conclusions These findings demonstrate that person-centered approaches can uncover heterogeneous acceptance patterns and that disciplinary background systematically shapes profile membership. Practically, the study proposes a differentiated AI literacy training framework, emphasizing that profiles such as Resistant Skeptics require targeted interventions that extend beyond operational skills training.

SO JOURNAL OF APPLIED RESEARCH IN INTELLECTUAL DISABILITIES

AB Background Promoting self-determination during adolescence is crucial for enhancing academic engagement and social inclusion. This study examined the effects of the Self-Determined Learning Model (SDLMI) on the self-determination of students with and without intellectual disability (ID).Methods A randomised parallel-group trial involved 90 adolescents aged 13-17 years (M = 14.05, SD = 1.39), including students with (n = 41, 45.6%) and without ID (n = 49, 54.4%). TI Differential Motor System Activation in Chemistry Problem Solving:
   Gesture-Based Versus Model-Based Instruction
SO MIND BRAIN AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE embodied cognition; fNIRS; gesture; organic chemistry; problem-solving;
   working memory
ID COGNITIVE LOAD THEORY; EMBODIED COGNITION; SPATIAL THINKING;
   WORKING-MEMORY; CONCRETE; BRAIN; SCIENCE; DESIGN; MATH; FMRI
AB Gesture-based instruction enhances spatial problem-solving accuracy, yet the underlying neurocognitive mechanisms remain unclear. This study examines whether gesture enhances spatial problem-solving in organic chemistry through activation patterns more consistent with offloading cognitive effort or coupling motor and working memory systems. Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), we compared students (68 recruited; n = 64 with usable fNIRS data) trained to translate between molecular diagrams using gesture-based or model-based instruction. Behavioral data revealed higher accuracy in the gesture-based compared to the model-based condition. In the fNIRS data, although channel-level condition effects did not survive FDR correction, exploratory ROI-level analyses showed increased activation in premotor and motor planning regions (BA 6) for the gesture group, whereas the model-based learners exhibited greater dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (BA 46) activation to suggest higher executive control demands. These findings provide preliminary neurocognitive evidence consistent with offloading and show that gesture and physical models promote different problem-solving strategies after embodied STEM instruction.

TI Comparing feedback learning and arousal responses in Down, Fragile X,
   and Williams syndromes
SO NPJ SCIENCE OF LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
ID REACTIVITY; ATTENTION; REWARD
AB Mechanisms underlying feedback learning in intellectual disability (ID) remain poorly understood. Down syndrome (DS), Fragile X syndrome (FXS), and Williams syndrome (WS) are genetic syndromes associated with ID, with distinct attention and arousal regulation profiles. Pupil dilation is a well-established index of feedback processing in typical development; little is known about these processes in non-social learning in these syndromes. Participants with DS (n = 13), FXS (n = 13), WS (n = 27), and typically developing (TD) individuals (n = 56) aged 6-60 years completed a reward contingency reversal task while eye-tracking recorded pupil dilation and gaze allocation. Data were analyzed using Bayesian mixed-effects models. All groups effectively learned from feedback, staying with rewarded options and switching after losses. WS participants performed similarly to TD participants. DS and FXS individuals showed more variable behavioral performance, indicating potential individual differences in feedback processing that warrant further investigation. Physiologically, TD individuals showed greater pupil dilation following losses than wins, whereas WS individuals showed no difference, suggesting attenuated physiological sensitivity to feedback valence. All groups tended to fixate on the previously rewarded options. This research highlights the value of combining behavioral and physiological approaches in ID research.

TI Educational expansion and inequality of opportunity in Ghana, 1945-1994
   cohorts
SO CAMBRIDGE JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational expansion; educational transitions; inequality of
   educational opportunities; Ghana; Maximally Maintained Inequality
ID MAINTAINED INEQUALITY; PARTICIPATION; AFRICA
AB This study examines whether five decades of educational expansion in Ghana have reduced or exacerbated inequality of educational opportunity. Using nationally representative data from the Ghana Living Standards Survey (wave 3-7), it analyses educational transitions across birth cohorts (1945-1994) through sequential logit models, complemented by cumulative attainment measures. The results show substantial gains in educational attainment, particularly at the basic level. However, inequalities persist at key transitions. Females remain 12.9% less likely to transition to senior high school, while northern students face a 32.9% disadvantage in primary completion. Parental education and poverty exert strongest effects at post-basic levels. The findings support the Maximally Maintained Inequality hypothesis: expansion shifts inequality to higher levels rather than eliminating it, a pattern shaped by Ghana's colonial legacies, economic volatility and capacity constraints. Policies must address structural barriers, including rural school quality and capacity constraints, which cumulatively disadvantage students across the educational pipeline.

TI Screen exposure and sleep in preschool-aged children
SO EDUCATIONAL MEDIA INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Screen exposure; sleep patterns; sleep problems; social jetlag;
   preschool-aged children
ID MEDIA USE; HABITS QUESTIONNAIRE; SOCIAL JETLAG; DIGITAL MEDIA; IMPACT;
   CHILDHOOD; DURATION; QUALITY; TIME
AB Recent research has shown the negative impact of screen exposure on children's sleep outcomes. However, knowledge remains limited regarding specific screen exposure patterns and little attention has been given to social jetlag. Guided by the Ecological Systems Theory, this study aims to: (1) characterize screen exposure patterns in preschool-aged children; (2) identify child, family and environment-related factors associated with screen exposure; and (3) examine differences in sleep patterns and problems according to screen exposure. A total of 271 Portuguese caregivers of preschool-aged children completed measures of screen exposure and sleep problems. Findings revealed that more than half of preschool-aged children exceed national screen time recommendations, with television remaining the most used device, although mobile devices are also prevalent. Screen exposure often occurs in the presence of caregivers and outside the child's bedroom, aligning with current recommendations. Only children's age was significantly associated with screen exposure. More prolonged screen exposure is associated with later bedtimes, shorter sleep duration, increased social jetlag, and more sleep problems. These findings reinforce the importance of promoting healthy media habits from early childhood. Public health strategies through multiple channels should prioritize screen time management to support optimal sleep and overall well-being in preschool-aged children.

TI Investigating a structured ChatGPT-assisted instructional routine and
   its association with intolerance of uncertainty and emotion regulation
   in higher education: insights from Situated Learning Theory
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Structured ChatGPT-assisted instructional routine; Artificial
   intelligence; Higher education; Situated Learning Theory; Intolerance of
   uncertainty; Emotion regulation
ID BASE-LINE; EFFECT SIZES; TRIALS; POWER; BIAS
AB The accelerating integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education offers clear opportunities for learning support while also raising concerns that bear directly on student well-being; in particular, although AI-enabled tools such as ChatGPT can widen access to information and on-demand assistance, their implications for students' emotional well-being, especially their capacity to tolerate uncertainty and regulate emotions, have yet to be examined in sufficient depth. Guided by the concepts of Situated Learning Theory, the present study investigated the possibilities of a structured ChatGPT-assisted instructional routine through an individually randomized experimental pretest-posttest control-group design, drawing on a convenience sample of 60 undergraduate students from a state university. Participants were randomly allocated to an experimental group (n = 30), which engaged in an instructor-orchestrated ChatGPT-assisted learning routine over a 12-week semester, or to a control group (n = 30), which received traditional instruction. Data were collected via pre- and post-tests assessing intolerance of uncertainty (IU) and emotion regulation (ER). Independent samples t-tests were used to examine pretest group comparability, and ANCOVAs controlling for pretest scores were used as the primary analyses of posttest group differences. The baseline-adjusted results indicated lower posttest IU and higher posttest academic ER among students in the experimental condition. These findings indicate that participation in a carefully structured ChatGPT-assisted instructional package can support cognitive growth and strengthen students' emotional resilience, with potential to ease anxieties that often accompany higher education and to encourage the deliberate integration of AI tools in ways that foster more supportive and emotionally intelligent learning environments.

TI Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite
   experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific
   argumentation
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Feedback design; Higher education;
   Digital learning; Scientific argumentation; Self-regulated learning;
   Epistemic agency
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used for feedback in higher education, yet evidence remains limited on how alternative human-AI feedback designs shape learning processes and durable outcomes. This study addresses that gap through a multisite, cluster-randomized, longitudinal field experiment comparing four feedback designs in introductory university science courses: peer feedback only, direct GenAI-supported feedback, reflective GenAI-supported feedback, and a hybrid design combining self-evaluation, peer feedback, and GenAI critique. The analytic sample comprised 1,176 first-year undergraduate students from 48 course sections across four universities and three science domains. Primary and secondary outcomes were argument-quality gain on four shared rubric dimensions-claim quality, evidence relevance and sufficiency, coherence of reasoning, and treatment of limitations or alternative explanations-conceptual learning, and delayed AI-free transfer; feedback uptake and self-regulated learning during revision were modeled as process mediators. Direct GenAI-supported feedback improved immediate argument-quality gain relative to peer feedback, whereas reflective and hybrid designs produced stronger feedback uptake and self-regulated learning. The hybrid condition yielded the highest adjusted mean for immediate argument-quality gain and showed the clearest advantage on conceptual learning; the reflective condition showed a positive but non-significant adjusted contrast on conceptual learning relative to direct GenAI-supported feedback. Both reflective and hybrid conditions outperformed direct GenAI-supported feedback on delayed AI-free transfer. Multilevel mediation analyses indicated that feedback uptake and self-regulated learning partially explained these advantages. By comparing four feedback designs, modeling revision processes, and assessing delayed AI-free transfer in a multisite field experiment, the findings suggest that the educational value of GenAI in higher education may depend less on AI access per se than on whether feedback environments preserve student agency, evaluative judgment, and ownership during revision.

TI Daily Ageism and Negative Affect as a Function of Older Adults' Sexual
   Orientation
SO JOURNAL OF COUNSELING PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE daily ageism; sexual orientation; well-being; sexual minority
   populations
ID MENTAL-HEALTH; MINORITY STRESS; GAY; VULNERABILITY; ISSUES; RISKS; MODEL
AB Although the link between ageism and poorer well-being is well-established, little is known about how this association fluctuates daily or whether it varies as a function of sexual orientation, due to the double jeopardy of age and sexual minority stigmas. In this article, we examined the daily coupling of ageism and negative affect (NA) among sexual minority and heterosexual older adults in Israel, a context historically characterized by sexual minority stigma. For this purpose, community-dwelling lesbian, gay, bisexual, and heterosexual middle-aged and older adults (N = 151, M-age = 59.73, range = 50-79) completed measures of daily ageism as indicated by ageist messages, experiences of age-based discrimination, internalization of ageist beliefs, and NA over 14 consecutive days. Results showed that participants reported higher daily NA on days when they experienced higher levels of ageism. The daily association between ageist messages and the internalization of ageist beliefs (both descriptive and prescriptive) and NA was stronger among older adults belonging to sexual minorities compared to their heterosexual counterparts. No such interaction was found for experiences of age-based discrimination. Investigating daily fluctuations in ageism and well-being among older adults from diverse sexual orientation groups is essential, as it captures the context-dependent and recurring nature of age-related stigma in everyday life. From an applied perspective, this research helps identify daily vulnerabilities in well-being faced by an understudied sexual minority population, namely, older sexual minority adults. It underscores the importance for practitioners to recognize these day-to-day challenges and consider timely, context-sensitive interventions to support their well-being.

TI Influence of entrepreneurial leadership on proactive work behavior among
   head nurses
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Egypt; entrepreneurial leadership; head nurses; nursing management;
   proactive work behavior
AB Introduction Entrepreneurial leadership (EL) has been linked to proactive work behavior among healthcare professionals. However, limited research has examined its influence on proactive work behavior (PWB) among head nurses. This study aimed to examine the relationship between entrepreneurial leadership (EL) and proactive work behavior (PWB) among head nurses in Alqalubia, Egypt. Methods A cross-sectional design was conducted with 55 head nurses from Central Toukh Hospital, Alqalubia Governorate, Ministry of Health, Egypt. Participants were recruited using a census sampling technique. Data were collected using a personal and job characteristics sheet, an entrepreneurial leadership questionnaire, and a proactive work behavior scale. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 27. Result More than half (53%) of the head nurses demonstrated a high level of entrepreneurial leadership, while 25% showed a moderate level and 22% a low level. Regarding proactive work behavior, 38.2% exhibited a high level, 40% a moderate level, and 21.8% a low level. A highly statistically significant positive correlation was found between total entrepreneurial leadership and total proactive work behavior (p < 0.001). Conclusion There was a significant positive correlation between entrepreneurial leadership and proactive work behavior among head nurses. Establishing an educational program to enhance head nurses' awareness of entrepreneurial leadership is recommended as a potential approach to strengthen proactive work behavior. However, given the single-site design and small sample size, these findings should be considered preliminary and context-specific, limited to Central Toukh Hospital; caution is warranted against broad generalization to other healthcare settings or populations.

TI Understanding student experiences in a mentorship-driven summer research
   program: a mixed-methods evaluation of program design and student
   satisfaction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE medical education; medical student research training opportunities;
   medical student satisfaction; qualitative assessment; quantitative
   survey; summer research program
ID MEDICAL-STUDENTS; ATTITUDES
AB Background: Medical students increasingly recognize the need for research competencies but often lack mentorship, institutional support, and structured training. The Medical Student Summer Research Program (MSSRP) addresses these gaps through an 8-week, faculty-mentored research experience with guided projects and structured learning activities. Its innovation is a transactional, semi-structured, mentorship-driven model integrating guided project selection and staged reporting to support early research skill development. Methods: The MSSRP pairs MS1 students with clinical or basic science faculty and provides structured deliverables and oversight to support early research training. Mentor-mentee matching occurs through an information session where faculty present ongoing projects, followed by guided student selection to ensure alignment. Students submit project applications outlining background, objectives, methods, analytic approach, and anticipated outcomes. Applications undergo review by the program coordinator for completeness and the MSSRP Research Committee for scientific merit. Students complete a mid-term progress report and a final two-page summary. All participants receive a $2,240 stipend funded jointly by mentors or departments and the Dean's Office. Students present findings at Student Research Week and complete a program evaluation survey. Results: Among 237 evaluations from 2020 to 2022, findings showed consistent, high-quality program implementation. Students reported working an average of 19.3 h/week, with most projects involving analysis of existing datasets. Survey responses were highly positive, citing strong mentorship, increased research knowledge and skills, enhanced self-efficacy, and project relevance to career goals. Qualitative feedback identified areas for improvement, including mentor-student matching, access to research resources, mentor dependability, clarity of expectations, and administrative processes. Conclusion: The MSSRP offers a feasible, effective model for early research training, with engaged mentorship as a key contributor to student satisfaction. Student feedback highlights opportunities for refinement that will guide ongoing program improvement.

TI The role of transformative learning in the development of higher-order
   thinking skills in junior high school students: a qualitative study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE transformative learning; higher-order thinking skills; mathematics
   education; epistemic dialogue; junior high school; qualitative study
AB The development of Higher-Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) is an important agenda for 21st-century education, but pedagogical mechanisms explaining how HOTS develops in junior high school classroom practices, particularly in mathematics learning, are still limited. This qualitative study explores the role of transformative learning in mediating students' HOTS development through critical reflection, epistemic dialogue in the classroom, and the meaning of learning experiences. The study used an interpretative-constructivist paradigm with an instrumental qualitative case study design. Data were collected through learning observations of 77 students (grades VII = 27; VIII = 25; IX = 25), in-depth interviews with three teachers (G1-G3), semi-structured interviews with 15 students, and analysis of learning documents. Thematic-reflective analysis resulted in four themes: (1) the gradual and contextual development of HOTS across levels, (2) critical reflection as the main trigger for analysis and evaluation, (3) epistemic dialogue as a space for testing and assessing arguments, and (4) the transformation of learning orientation from a focus on answers to the quality of thinking processes and justification. The findings suggest that HOTS develops through a spiral trajectory influenced by the intensity of reflective scaffolding, norms of classroom dialogue, and a classroom culture that is safe for experimenting and revising reasoning. This study contributes by mapping the mechanisms of how and why transformative learning facilitates HOTS in a junior high school context while also offering practical implications for the design of sustainable reflective and dialogic learning.

TI Behavioural engagement patterns in an AI-powered student support
   chatbot: an exploratory learning analytics study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; chatbots; digital transformation; engagement
   sustainability; higher education; learning analytics
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; ACCEPTANCE
AB Introduction The increasing adoption of AI-powered conversational systems in higher education has created new opportunities for scalable student support and digitally mediated engagement. However, limited research has examined how students behaviourally engage with these systems using real-world interaction data, particularly within resource-constrained institutional contexts. This study investigates patterns of student engagement within an institutional chatbot-supported student support environment using an exploratory learning analytics approach. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as an interpretive framework, it conceptualises engagement sustainability as a behavioural lens for understanding continued interaction beyond initial system use.Methods An exploratory descriptive learning analytics design was employed to analyse 1,495 chatbot interaction records collected from a hybrid AI-assisted student support system deployed at a South African University of Technology between July and November 2025. Behavioural interaction data were analysed using Microsoft Power BI to identify engagement patterns, interaction persistence, support-query trends, and system-classified resolution outcomes.Results The findings indicate that chatbot-supported student engagement occurs within a hybrid interaction environment combining automated conversational processing with human-assisted institutional support. Student interaction patterns were highly uneven, with a small proportion of users accounting for a disproportionately large share of system activity, while many users disengaged after initial interactions. Chatbot usage was concentrated primarily within administrative support domains, and system-classified completion rates were high for structured queries. However, extended response times associated with escalated interactions reflected institutional workflow processes rather than chatbot processing performance.Discussion This study demonstrates the value of behavioural interaction log analysis for understanding AI-mediated student engagement in higher education. By interpreting engagement sustainability as an observable behavioural phenomenon, it extends existing applications of the Technology Acceptance Model beyond adoption intentions to actual usage behaviour. The findings further highlight the importance of considering interaction patterns, institutional context, and hybrid human-AI support models when evaluating the effectiveness and sustainability of chatbot-supported student engagement in higher education.

TI Direct and indirect assessment of practical skills: longitudinal
   associations and performance variation in secondary science
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE direct assessment; indirect assessment; internal assessment;
   longitudinal associations; performance variation; practical skills;
   science education; secondary education
ID WORK
AB This study examines how the transition from direct external assessment in Grade 10 to indirect external assessment in Grade 12 is associated with longitudinal patterns of student performance in secondary science education and how internal laboratory-based assessments relate to performance continuity across assessment formats. Longitudinal data were analyzed for Biology (n = 368), Chemistry (n = 206), and Physics (n = 983), including external assessments in Grades 10 and 12 and internal assessments in Grades 11 and 12. Sequential regression models for longitudinal associations, mixed-effects clustering and distributional analyses for performance variation, and robustness and sensitivity tests were conducted, with confidence intervals for all estimates. Resultsshowed consistently greater score dispersion in Grade 12 across all subjects, indicating differences in observed score distributions under the indirect assessment format. Prior external achievement was a significant predictor of Grade 12 outcomes, while internal assessments, particularly in Grade 12, were positively associated with external assessment performance and improved model explanatory power. Mathematics achievement was also positively associated with science outcomes, with the strongest relationships found in Chemistry and Physics. These findings indicate longitudinal associations between prior achievement, internal assessments, and later external outcomes across assessment formats. However, because the Grade 10 and Grade 12 assessments differ in construct emphasis, task structure, and cognitive demand, the results should not be interpreted as evidence of psychometric superiority, construct equivalence, or causal effects. The results highlight the value of combining laboratory-based internal assessment with externally assessed scientific reasoning and interpretation in science education.

TI From gatekeeper to architect: operationalizing AI as a cognitive partner
   in higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; dual-process theory; epistemic cognition;
   higher education; prompt engineering; zone of proximal development
ID INSTRUCTION; COMPREHENSION; KNOWLEDGE
AB In higher education, debates about Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) often polarize around academic integrity risks and efficiency gains. A growing body of post-2023 work has begun to move beyond this dichotomy, proposing constrained tutoring systems, Socratic dialogue agents, and adaptive pedagogical scaffolds built on large language models (LLMs). However, these efforts typically target a single instructional function (e.g., Socratic questioning, problem-by-problem scaffolding, or guardrailed answer generation) and treat the cognitive demands of learning as undifferentiated. An instructional architecture that explicitly aligns distinct LLM configurations with the qualitatively different cognitive operations required across learning phases is not available in the literature yet. We address this gap by presenting a simulator-based framework that decomposes instruction into three functionally distinct, sequentially gated simulators: (i) structured comprehension with explicit depth regulation, (ii) schema-based application and analysis under progressively increasing demands, and (iii) evaluation and creation under instructor-defined epistemic uncertainty. Each simulator is grounded in a specific cognitive theory (Zone of Proximal Development, dual-process accounts of cognition, and epistemic cognition, respectively) and is operationalized through explicit constraints, transition criteria, and non-normative diagnostic rubrics. The framework conceptualizes LLMs as constrained instructional simulators whose pedagogical value derives from how they are configured, bounded, and sequenced by the instructor. The primary contribution is therefore not a new tutoring paradigm but a theory-aligned architecture for sequencing multiple, functionally distinct LLM configurations within a single instructional design. Rather than asserting a solution to Bloom's 2-Sigma Problem, the framework demonstrates how LLMs can scale the specific instructional mechanisms associated with individualized tutoring while preserving disciplinary standards and pedagogical authority. The framework is conceptual and design-oriented; empirical validation is identified as a necessary next step.

TI Analogical Alignment for Teaching Feedback Loops
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE feedback loops; analogical reasoning; mutual alignment; systems
   thinking; geoscience education; spatial thinking
ID STRUCTURAL ALIGNMENT; SYSTEMS THINKING; MENTAL MODELS; SIMILARITY;
   DYNAMICS; STUDENT; CLIMATE
AB Feedback loops are fundamental to understanding complex systems across the sciences, yet undergraduate students consistently struggle to correctly identify and distinguish positive and negative feedback loops. Traditional instructional approaches, which typically provide a definition and a single example, often fail to produce robust understanding. We tested an alternative pedagogical approach grounded in cognitive science research on analogical reasoning: mutual alignment of analogies. In this approach, students compare two feedback loop examples drawn from different domains (e.g., Earth science and economics) and identify their shared structural features, thereby extracting the abstract schema of a feedback loop. We compared student performance across two consecutive offerings of an introductory geoscience course at a large urban university. In the first year (Year 1, n = 71), feedback loops were taught using a traditional definition-plus-example approach. In the second year (Year 2, n = 100), a mutual alignment activity was introduced. Students in the mutual alignment condition outperformed those in the traditional instruction condition at all three time points following instruction, with a large effect size on the immediate assessment (Cohen's d = 0.86) that persisted at three months (Cohen's d = 0.51). We also identified two factors that may impede feedback loop understanding: the perceived desirability of a loop's outcome and the readability of the loop description.

TI Comparing Generative AI-Supported Instruction and Strategic Dictionary
   Use in Upper Elementary Students' Receptive and Expressive Vocabulary
   Development
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence (GenAI); strategic dictionary use;
   receptive vocabulary; expressive vocabulary; bilingual learners
ID 2ND-LANGUAGE; ACQUISITION; EXPOSURE
AB This study compares the effectiveness of Generative AI-supported instruction and strategic dictionary use on upper elementary students' receptive and expressive vocabulary development. A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design was employed with 136 students aged 10-12, including monolingual and bilingual learners, who were assigned to three conditions: Generative AI-supported instruction, strategic dictionary use, and a control group. Receptive vocabulary was assessed with the LEXiS standardized test, while expressive vocabulary was measured using the Greek adaptation of the Renfrew Word Finding Vocabulary Test. Both interventions focused on climate change vocabulary and were implemented over four weeks, incorporating parallel receptive and productive vocabulary-learning activities. General Linear Models revealed significant effects of intervention type on receptive vocabulary development, with both the AI-supported and dictionary-based groups outperforming the control group. No significant differences emerged between the two experimental conditions. For expressive vocabulary, no overall intervention effect was observed; however, a significant interaction between intervention type and bilingualism indicated that bilingual students in the dictionary-based condition achieved significantly greater productive vocabulary gains than their peers in the AI and control groups. The findings suggest that Generative AI and strategic dictionary instruction support different dimensions of lexical development and should be viewed as complementary rather than competing pedagogical approaches.

   Slovakia: A Critical Case from J. Selye University

DT Article
DE internationalisation of higher education; internationalisation at home;
   internationalisation of the curriculum; minority higher education;
   reflexive internationalisation; case study
AB This article examines the internationalisation of higher education in a semi-peripheral system through the concept of a minority higher education space, focusing on the implementation of internationalisation of the curriculum (IoC) at J. Selye University. Drawing on world-system theory and approaches to global inequalities in knowledge production, the study conceptualises minority higher education space as a structurally constrained, symbolically marginalised, and epistemically subordinated institutional configuration. The concept is operationalised through three dimensions: structural peripherality, epistemic partial subordination, and symbolic limitation. The article introduces the concept of reflexive internationalisation to explain changing patterns of international engagement in minority academic contexts.

TI Ethical Considerations of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Use in
   Qualitative Research: Evidence from TESOL and Applied Linguistics
   Scholars
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence (AI); qualitative research; ethics; applied
   linguistics research; TESOL research; Saudi Arabia
AB This study investigates views on the ethical considerations of artificial intelligence (AI) in qualitative TESOL and Applied Linguistics research in Saudi Arabia. A mixed survey design (n = 99) was adopted to explore attitudes to AI use during the main research stages of transcription, coding, analysis, and academic writing. The quantitative data showed that AI is moderately accepted to perform mechanical activities, such as transcription, but is less accepted in the performance of higher-order tasks, for example, generating findings and writing research papers. Meanwhile, the content analysis of the open-ended questions showed concerns surrounding authenticity, over-reliance on technology, and the risk of losing human interpretive authority in qualitative inquiry. This study therefore makes a valuable contribution through providing exploratory empirical evidence of researchers' perceptions of ethical AI use in TESOL and Applied Linguistics. It seeks to provide suggestions to balance between technological efficiency and the possible ethical considerations in AI implementation in qualitative research.

TI Do AI Grading Systems Systematically Differ from Human Teachers'
   Grading? Evidence of Bias and Consistency in Educational Assessment
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; automated assessment; educational evaluation;
   grading consistency; human-AI collaboration
AB The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced new possibilities for transforming educational assessment processes. Among these developments, AI-assisted grading systems have attracted increasing attention due to their potential to improve efficiency, consistency, and scalability of student evaluation. The present study examines the role of artificial intelligence in student grading by comparing AI-generated scores with human teacher evaluations and by exploring teachers' perceptions regarding the use of AI in educational assessment. The research adopts a quantitative comparative design. Student-written responses were independently evaluated by teachers and AI systems, and the resulting scores were statistically analyzed to examine the level of agreement between the two grading approaches. In addition, a structured questionnaire was administered to teachers to investigate their attitudes toward AI-assisted grading. The findings indicate that while some AI systems produce scores comparable to human evaluators, others exhibit statistically significant differences, highlighting variability across models. Furthermore, AI systems were found to produce more consistent grading outcomes in relation to the corresponding human evaluators. Nevertheless, teachers recognized the potential of AI to reduce the time required for assessment tasks. However, concerns related to fairness, transparency, and the interpretation of complex student responses remain important considerations. Overall, the results suggest that artificial intelligence can effectively support educational assessment when implemented within hybrid evaluation models that combine automated analysis with human pedagogical oversight.

TI Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement Emotions in an Engineering
   Emergency Management Module
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE achievement emotions; disaster education; emergency management;
   self-regulated learning
ID PERFORMANCE
AB This study examined engineering students' intrapersonal factors, self-regulated learning (SRL) and achievement emotions, and their prior emergency, disaster, and crisis management (EDCM) knowledge, within a three-week EDCM module embedded in an engineering course. We collected data at three points during the implementation of the EDCM module N = 53). First, before the module began, students completed a demographic questionnaire, the SRL motivational orientation questionnaire, and an EDCM knowledge pretest. Second, during module implementation, students completed the SRL learning strategy questionnaire. Third, after the module was completed, students completed the achievement emotion questionnaire. TI Teachers' Socio-Emotional Competencies in the Digital Era:
   Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Psychometric Validation of the BESSI in
   Kazakhstan
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE socio-emotional skills; teachers; BESSI; psychometric validation;
   Kazakhstan; teacher well-being; cultural adaptation; educational
   assessment
ID SKILLS
AB Teachers' socio-emotional competencies are increasingly recognized as essential for professional well-being, adaptive teaching, and effective participation in digitally transforming educational systems. However, valid and culturally appropriate instruments for assessing these competencies among teachers remain limited, particularly in multilingual and underrepresented educational contexts. This study aimed to adapt the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI) for teachers in Kazakhstan and to examine its preliminary psychometric properties and socio-emotional competency profiles. The instrument was translated and culturally adapted into Kazakh and Russian using a TRAPD-based (Translation, Review, Adjudication, Pretesting, and Documentation) procedure involving translation, review, adjudication, pretesting, and documentation. Data were collected from 1458 school teachers across Kazakhstan representing different subject areas and language groups. After data-quality screening, the final analytic sample included 918 valid observations. Reliability analyses demonstrated excellent total-scale internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.92; McDonald's omega = 0.94), while domain-level reliability ranged from moderate to acceptable (alpha = 0.60-0.76; omega = 0.73-0.81). Exploratory factor analysis suggested an empirical eight-factor structure rather than a direct replication of the original BESSI framework, indicating that socio-emotional competencies may be organized differently in teacher populations. Model-based clustering identified four exploratory teacher profiles reflecting different configurations of self-management, emotional regulation, interpersonal, and innovation-related competencies. The profiles differed not only in overall competency levels but also in specific patterns of strengths and developmental needs. The findings provide preliminary evidence supporting the use of the adapted BESSI as a promising research and diagnostic instrument for assessing teachers' socio-emotional competencies in Kazakhstan. At the same time, the results indicate the need for further confirmatory validation, measurement invariance testing, and external validity evidence before broader application.

TI Capstone Projects as Preparation for Engineering Practice: A
   Graduate-Based Evaluation of Supervision and Industry Readiness
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE capstone projects; engineering education; capstone supervision;
   project-based learning; industry readiness; graduate perceptions;
   professional practice
AB Capstone projects in undergraduate engineering education are widely regarded as a central bridge between academic learning and professional practice, enabling students to integrate disciplinary knowledge, design processes, teamwork, and problem-solving skills in a project-based learning experience. This study examines how 131 engineering graduates and practicing engineers retrospectively evaluate capstone supervision and its contribution to industry readiness. Correlation analysis and multiple regression were used to examine relationships between the supervisor's approach, perceived industry preparation, supervision satisfaction, and capstone project quality. Regression models including supervisor's approach and perceived industry preparation explained substantial variance in both supervision satisfaction (R-2 = 0.75) and project quality (R-2 = 0.78). Follow-up analyses identified connection to engineering work as the strongest retained predictor of supervision satisfaction (beta = 0.34), and cognitive factors as the strongest retained dimension associated with project quality (beta = 0.52). However, 60.3% of graduates perceived the capstone project as making little or no contribution to finding engineering employment, suggesting a gap between this intended bridging role and its perceived value after graduation. These findings highlight the need to strengthen the connection between supervision practices and professional engineering work and contribute a graduate-based perspective to capstone project evaluation in engineering education.

TI Teacher Usability and Utility Needs for a Professional Development
   Passport
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE professional development; computer science; education; tracking;
   recording; impacts; shared measures; teachers
ID DESIGN; IMPACT
AB Policy makers and educators have increasingly recognized the importance of K-12 teacher professional development (PD) in computer science (CS) to foster student growth and academic achievement. In this exploratory mixed-methods study (focus groups n=23 , survey n=661 ), we addressed two research questions: (1) What features and data do teachers think will enhance the usefulness of an application designed to keep track of their PD-related data?and (2) Which demographic factors are most predictive of teacher ratings? Based on a survey, teachers identified several features and data-related elements that would make the platform useful and usable and add value to their experiences. Further, we noted statistically significant differences in teachers' ratings across various demographic subgroups (i.e., race/ethnicity, teaching experience, disability, gender, and locale) for all potential platform features and data items. This indicates the importance of considering the perspectives of various subgroups when developing a platform that meets the needs of all teachers.

TI Balancing Livelihoods and Conservation Under Uncertainty: A Case Study
   of Artisanal Chitala Fisheries in West Bengal, India
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE conservation; small-scale fishers; natural stock; sustainability
ID HAMILTON
AB Chitala (Chitala chitala) fisheries in middle stretch of River Ganga, India, represent an important seasonal livelihood activity for small-scale fishing communities. This study examines a locally developed seed collection practice in the middle stretch of the river near Farakka, West Bengal, and explores its implications within a socio-ecological systems (SES) framework. The findings indicate that this practice provides a significant supplementary source of seasonal income, while also reflecting adaptive responses to ecological variability and market demand. The study highlights the need for context-specific management approaches that balance livelihood needs with ecological sustainability. The study contributes to understanding locally driven innovation in small-scale fisheries and identifies pathways for integrating conservation with livelihood resilience.

TI Valuing Biodiversity Conservation in Manu National Park: A Choice
   Experiment Case Study Conducted During the COVID-19 Pandemic
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE biodiversity conservation; choice experiment; Manu National Park;
   species interaction networks; Peru
ID VALUATION
AB This case study analyzes public preferences for biodiversity conservation in Manu National Park, Peru, using a choice experiment. The study evaluates how respondents assess different representations of biodiversity, including threatened species of flora and fauna, habitat loss, and ecological functionality expressed through networks of species interactions. The survey was implemented online during the COVID-19 pandemic among residents of Metropolitan Lima. A total of 1,005 respondents completed the survey, generating 4,020 choice observations. Preferences were estimated using mixed logit (MLM) and latent class (LCM) models to account for heterogeneity in respondents' valuations of biodiversity attributes. Results indicate that ecological functionality is the most influential attribute in respondents' choices. Improvements in species interaction networks generate the largest marginal utility gains and the highest willingness to pay (WTP) estimates relative to traditional biodiversity indicators such as species counts and habitat loss. These findings suggest that functional ecological indicators may be more easily interpreted by respondents in megadiverse contexts where the complexity of biodiversity is difficult to communicate. However, the results reflect the preferences of an urban sample from Metropolitan Lima and therefore should not be interpreted as nationally representative. Overall, the findings provide insights for conservation policy by suggesting that functionality-based biodiversity indicators may help communicate ecological change more effectively in megadiverse ecosystems.

   BENEFITS; WELFARE; IMPACT; BIRDS
AB Conservation practitioners need to effectively engage the public in nontraditional, informal settings to go beyond conventional models of education and engagement. Influencers live-streaming conservation content on social media offer unique lessons on how this can be done effectively, particularly when it comes to the use of animal ambassadors: animals trained for public interaction to facilitate conservation messaging. TI Spatial Inequities in Addressing Hunger: A Case Study of Public and
   Private Food Assistance Resources in Hawai'i
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE hunger; food assistance; GIS; food bank; food insecurity; food pantry
ID SOVEREIGNTY
AB The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals seek to create a sustainable future, including the second goal to "end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture." While the world has more than enough food for everyone, inequality leads to unnecessarily high levels of hunger and food insecurity. Even in wealthy nations like the United States, more than 1 in 8 people live in food-insecure households. The United States is one of the few countries that does not uphold the right to food, leaving people to rely on a combination of weak public assistance programs and charities. The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program is the most expansive federal food program and food banks are the largest private food assistance provider, but both have geographic inequities and insufficiencies. This case aims to help students understand the spatial inequities in food assistance programs that hinder our ability to end hunger and provides related teaching resources to teach students to geocode and map public and private food assistance to visualize the limitations of existing food assistance programs in Hawai'i. This case study is designed to be incorporated in an introductory GIS class or can be modified to introduce mapping in a food or environmental class. This article provides context on approaches to ending hunger, focusing on how wealthy nations need to devote resources to achieving Sustainable Development Goals within their borders.

TI Impact of Leader Academy Training on Growth Mindset and Impostor
   Phenomenon
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Leadership training; Impostor phenomenon; Growth mindset; Pharmacy
   students
ID HEALTH
AB Objective To assess the impact of a cohort-based leadership training program on growth mindset and impostor phenomenon (IP) experiences among student and pharmacist participants. Methods Pharmacy students and pharmacists enrolled in the Phi Lambda Sigma Leader Academy completed online surveys before and after the 5-month program. Surveys included the Clance IP scale (CIPS), the implicit theories of intelligence scale (ITIS), and demographic questions. Only participants who completed the presurvey and postsurvey were included in the final analysis. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and paired comparisons. Results Of 53 initial participants, 45 completed the Leader Academy program, with 43 and 42 completing the CIPS and ITIS assessments, respectively. No significant changes were observed between the preprogram and postprogram ITIS and CIPS median scores according to the Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (Z < -0.61, p >.51) or in their respective categories according to the McNemar's tests (p >.99). Subgroup analyzes revealed a significant decrease in growth mindset (from 100% preprogram to 46% postprogram, McNemar's test, p =.03) among older participants but not among younger participants. Conclusion In our study, the Leader Academy program did not significantly affect growth mindset or IP experiences in the short term. Cohort-based leadership training may foster self-awareness, but more targeted interventions may be necessary to meaningfully affect mindset development and IP.

TI Enhancing Surgical Performance: The Need for a Holistic View on Surgical
   Skills
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE surgery; education; teamwork; technical skills; nontechnical skills
ID NONTECHNICAL SKILLS; OPERATING-ROOM; SIMULATION; SURGEONS; NOTSS
AB Objective Recent studies suggest surgeons rely on both technical (TS) and nontechnical (NTS) skills simultaneously, while others have suggested interdependence of the skills. On a practical level, a correlation between the skillsets is yet to be established. The present study investigates whether a relationship between TS and NTS exists on an overall level and on the level of the individual operating room (OR) team. Design This cross-sectional single cohort simulation-based study took place during 3-days of laparoscopic interventions. Laparoscopic and OR video recordings were obtained during the interventions. Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills (OSATS) and Nontechnical Skills for Surgeons (NOTSS) scores focusing on the operating surgeons were subsequently assigned, and Pearson's correlation analyses were performed to assess the association between skill sets. Setting The intervention took place at the surgical laboratory facilities for animal research at Aarhus University Hospital. Participants Three surgical teams participated in the study. Each team consisted of 2 OR nurses and 2 surgeons in post graduate year 3 to 5 undergoing specialist training. Participants of each team were recruited from separate sites across the Central Denmark Region. Results A total 27 operations were carried out, resulting in 63 recordings that were sent for evaluation. Overall, a weak positive correlation (r = 0.336, p < 0.05) was found between OSATS and NOTSS scores. One team showed a moderate positive correlation (r = 0.497 p < 0.05), while correlations for the other teams were nonsignificant (r = 0.338 p = 0.218), and nonlinear (r = -0.036 p = 0.872), respectively. Conclusions This study demonstrated an overall relationship between TS and NTS for surgeons during laparoscopic surgery in a simulated setting. The correlation on team level was inconsistent, indicating the dynamics of the individual teams may be of essence. A holistic view on surgical skills may be crucial in enabling surgeons to reach their potential in the OR.

TI The (In)congruence between creative family and school environments and
   Chinese adolescents' creative self-efficacy: The mediating role of
   growth mindset
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative self-efficacy; Creative family environment; Creative school
   environment; Growth mindset; Response surface analysis; Adolescent
   creativity
ID OF-FIT INDEXES; LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS; POLYNOMIAL REGRESSION; STUDENT
   CREATIVITY; TEACHERS; PERSPECTIVES; ANTECEDENTS; INVOLVEMENT;
   MOTIVATION; CONFUCIAN
AB Family and school contexts are central to adolescent development, yet their joint and nonlinear contributions to creative self-efficacy remain underexamined. Based on the Ecological Systems Model of Creativity Development, this study investigates how the creative family environment and the creative school environment jointly predict adolescents' creative self-efficacy, with growth mindset as a potential mediator. We analyzed data from 10,291 secondary students in Hong Kong and Macao from PISA 2022 (48.3% female; Mage = 15.73 +/- 0.44) using response surface analysis and structural equation modeling. Three findings stand out. First, both family and school contexts positively predict creative self-efficacy, and when support is high in both contexts the increase follows an accelerating nonlinear pattern, consistent with positive curvature along the line of congruence. Second, under contextual incongruence, the school context shows a compensatory effect and can offset weak family support. Third, growth mindset partially mediates the effects of family and school contexts on creative self-efficacy. No significant gender differences emerged in either mean levels or structural pathways. These results highlight the importance of coordinated efforts between families and schools, identify growth mindset as a central psychological mechanism, and offer actionable guidance for building aligned ecosystems that reliably strengthen adolescents' creative self-efficacy.

TI Fostering inclusion in healthcare: a systematic review of collaborative
   teaching with individuals with disorders of intellectual development
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Co-teaching; Intellectual disability; Inclusive education; Healthcare
   training; Educational inclusion
ID SERVICE USER INVOLVEMENT; MEDICAL-STUDENTS; LEARNING-DISABILITIES;
   PEOPLE; EDUCATION
AB Background Enhancing healthcare professionals' knowledge and skills through co-productive educational programs aligns with the UN's rights for people with disabilities. Collaborative teaching approaches, where individuals with Disorders of Intellectual Development participate as co-teachers, are increasingly recognized as effective strategies for improving healthcare training and fostering inclusion.Methods This review examines interventions involving individuals with Disorders of Intellectual Development as co-educators in higher education, focusing on studies published from 2009 to 2024. Inclusion criteria required: Co-teachers with Disorders of Intellectual Development, teaching in higher education, publications after 2009, university or medical school settings. Exclusion criteria eliminated studies without co-teachers with Disorders of Intellectual Development, those involving Disorders of Intellectual Development only as students or patients, and non-university settings. Literature searches were conducted across major databases (PubMed, Cochrane, Psyndex, Web of Science, FIS Bildung, peDOCS, and Google Scholar), between April 25th and November 29th 2024, and articles were screened according to predefined criteria.Results Out of 21,327 records identified, 10 met the inclusion criteria, 2 articles were further included for additional consideration. In total, seven empirical studies, three literature reviews, one guideline and one case study were included. Most research focused on the impact of inclusive teaching on students, with some examining the qualification and participation processes for educators with Disorders of Intellectual Development. The evidence supports the value of co-teaching models involving individuals with Disorders of Intellectual Development, highlighting benefits for both students and co-teachers. However, the literature notes that systemic barriers and insufficient structural support can limit the effectiveness and sustainability of such approaches. Standardization among interventions proved insufficient.Conclusions Inclusion of co-teachers with Disorders of Intellectual Development is an emerging and important field in higher education as could be shown by this literature review. There is a need for standardized, evidence-based guidelines and adequate institutional resources to support co-teaching involving individuals with Disorders of Intellectual Development in healthcare education. Although inclusive teaching indicates benefits for both, students and educators, their success depends on institutional commitment and overcoming persistent barriers. Ongoing research and policy development are essential to fully realize the potential of co-productive educational models in fostering genuine inclusion and improving healthcare outcomes.

TI Student nurse anesthetists' learning during clinical practice: a

SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION

DT Article

   Student Nurse Anesthetist; Mixed-Methods
ID OPERATING-ROOM; PSYCHOMETRIC EVALUATION; ENVIRONMENT; SUPERVISION;
   TEACHER; BIAS
AB Background Clinical practice is essential for student nurse anesthetists to integrate theory with practical skills; however, the demanding clinical environment can impact both stress and learning outcomes. Responsibilities and expectations differ across healthcare systems, and research in the Swedish context remains limited. Addressing this gap is essential for understanding how clinical practice contributes to the development of professional readiness and competence. This study, therefore, aimed to describe the learning experiences of students and newly graduated nurse anesthetists, with a focus on the clinical learning environment and the stress it entails.Methods A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was used. In the quantitative strand, student nurse anesthetists were recruited using convenience sampling to complete a web-based survey that included the two instruments, "Clinical Learning Environment Supervision and Nurse Teacher evaluation scale" and "Perceived Stress Scale" (with 10 items). Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, while free-text answers were analyzed using summative content analysis and word frequencies. In the qualitative strand, newly graduated nurse anesthetists were recruited using purposive sampling to participate in individual semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed with content analysis. After separate analysis, the pillar integration process was used to integrate quantitative and qualitative data.Results The analysis included data from 63 surveys (63/225, 28%) and 13 interviews. Although stress levels varied, the average Perceived Stress Scale score remained low.

TI Balancing AI responsibility with privacy, safety, and utility:
   Unlearning in large language models for mathematics education
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Unlearning; AI privacy; Responsible AI; Large language models; Online
   math education
AB Online mathematics learning platforms are increasingly adopting large language models (LLMs) to provide scalable, on-demand support, but these models may reproduce private information from training data or generate harmful language. This raises concerns about responsibility in educational settings regarding the use of pretrained models. LLM unlearning is an emerging area for reducing a model's ability to produce specific unwanted content and remains underexplored in educational research. This study aims to investigate how LLM unlearning reduces the model's reliance on personally identifiable information (PII) and inappropriate content in the math tutoring context, while maintaining the model's utility on both single-label and multi-label downstream math tasks. We applied a gradient-based LLM unlearning approach to three different models, which were pretrained on approximately 3 million data points from an Algebra I online discussion forum between students and professional tutors. PII and harmful content were detected on this training data and used for unlearning in two different orders (PII and harmful content unlearning). Then, the generated outputs from these two unlearning models were compared with those of the pre-trained model in terms of PII-containing output rate and harmful rate. Moreover, unlearned models were evaluated on two different math classification tasks. The results showed that the rates of PII-containing output rate and harmfulness substantially decreased compared to the pretrained models, and the utility of the unlearned model was still maintained. These findings demonstrate how LLM unlearning can be applied to pre-trained models to behave them more responsibly, while maintaining strong model performance on math-related tasks.

TI Educational prompt engineering self-efficacy scale (Ed-PESS):
   Development and psychometric validation
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Prompt engineering; Educational prompt engineering; Prompt engineering
   self-efficacy; Scale development; AI
ID NUMBER
AB Pre-service teachers' confidence in designing pedagogically purposeful prompts for generative AI tools remains an underexamined construct in teacher education. This study developed and validated the Educational Prompt Engineering Self-Efficacy Scale for Pre-service Teachers (Ed-PESS) to address the absence of a psychometrically sound instrument measuring this domain. Scale development followed Boateng et al.'s three-phase framework, grounded in a systematic literature review and expert review procedures. Two independent samples of pre-service teachers were recruited: an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) sample (n = 300) and a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) sample (n = 305). The final 26-item scale comprises four dimensions: Basic Prompt Engineering, Pedagogical Prompt Engineering, Ethical Prompting Practice, and Continuous Professional Development. Internal consistency was high across all subscales. The Ed-PESS provides a valid, reliable instrument for assessing prompt engineering self-efficacy in pre-service teacher education. It supports formative curriculum evaluation and targeted intervention design.

TI Presence and pragmatism: Implementing co-located extended reality (XR)
   in hybrid online education
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION: X REALITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Social presence; Virtual reality; Augmented reality; Mixed reality;
   Hybrid education; Language learning; Online learning
ID MEDIA RICHNESS THEORY; SOCIAL PRESENCE; TECHNOLOGY; CHALLENGES;
   DISTANCE; DESIGN
AB The widespread adoption of video conferencing for hybrid learning has exposed significant limitations in its ability to foster equitable and embodied interaction between remote and in-person students. As an alternative approach that addresses these limitations through spatially grounded embodiment, this study investigated colocated mixed reality (MR) as a medium to enhance social presence and reduce transactional distance in synchronous hybrid activities. We developed a cooperative MR platform where on-site students wearing MR headsets shared a single, synchronized virtual space within their physical classroom, enabling collaboration with each other and with a remote student embodied as an avatar. Critically, implementation revealed substantial pragmatic barriers. While MR shows clear potential for transforming hybrid learning, technical challenges remain, indicating the technology requires significant maturation before it is viable for widespread adoption.

TI Predicting digital reading enjoyment among 10,979 Chinese children in a
   summer program: A machine learning approach
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital reading enjoyment; Motivation; Goals; Family; Machine learning
ID ACHIEVEMENT GOALS; INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; LITERACY; HOME; MODEL
AB Reading enjoyment is crucial to students' reading performance and behaviors. Digital reading is common in the digital era. Educators attempt to identify the factors that predict children's digital reading enjoyment. We utilized five machine learning algorithms to investigate the impact of demographic variables, reading motivations, achievement goals, and family reading environment factors on digital reading enjoyment among 10,979 Chinese children participating in a summer digital reading program. Gradient Boosting was selected as the optimal model with its strong predictive performance (R2: 0.6627, MSE: 0.4152, RMSE: 0.6443, MAE: 0.4530). SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis (SHAP) revealed that the six features with the largest positive contributions to the model's prediction of digital reading enjoyment were intrinsic motivation, social motivation, mastery goal, self-efficacy, extrinsic motivation, and parental reading autonomy support. In contrast, performance-avoidance goals and performance-approach goals were found to be negative contributors. Further subgroup SHAP analyses revealed differences in feature importance across gender, grade, and area. These findings provide internally validated, modelbased evidence that may inform future hypothesis validation and the design of targeted strategies for enhancing children's digital reading enjoyment.

TI The role of intelligence in the development of metacognitive knowledge
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Metacognitive knowledge; Intelligence; Motivation; Mathematics;
   Longitudinal study
ID INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; INTELLECTUAL ABILITY; HIERARCHICAL MODEL; GOAL
   ORIENTATION; FIT INDEXES; SELF; ACHIEVEMENT; STRATEGIES; SKILLS; TASK
AB This study investigated individual differences in students' metacognitive knowledge development in mathematics. Conditional metacognitive knowledge of 1050 German students (40% female, MAge = 10.97) was assessed at the beginning and end of grade 5, and at the end of grade 6. Initial intelligence was examined as a predictor of later metacognitive knowledge development while controlling for students' initial mathematics knowledge, math-related motivation, gender, and class-type (i.e. regular vs. gifted classes). Latent growth curve analysis revealed a general increase but also high variability in metacognitive knowledge development. Intelligence was associated with greater increases in metacognitive knowledge over time (beta = 0.32), suggesting that higher intelligence accelerates metacognitive knowledge development. Additionally, girls demonstrated a greater increase in metacognitive knowledge than boys over time. Math knowledge, motivational variables, and class-type were not associated with metacognitive knowledge development. These findings highlight the variability in metacognitive knowledge development and underscore intelligence as an important predictor of this differential development.

TI Correlates of adolescents' profiles of cognitive emotion regulation
   strategies in the school context
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Emotion regulation; Adolescents; Latent profile analysis; Test anxiety;
   Academic buoyancy
ID TEST ANXIETY; ACADEMIC BUOYANCY; PERFORMANCE; QUESTIONNAIRE
AB Emotion regulation is crucial for managing academic failures. Little research has explored adolescents' emotion regulation strategy profiles and their correlates at school. Through a person-centered approach, we identified profiles based on four emotion regulation strategies (self-blame, catastrophizing, positive reappraisal, and positive refocusing) and examined their predictors (gender, socioeconomic status, and prior achievement) and outcomes (test anxiety, academic buoyancy, and later achievement). We involved 535 British students in Year 12 (Mage = 16.40 years, 71% girls). A subsample of them (n = 318, 74% girls) was also involved in Year 13. Latent profile analysis revealed four profiles: low self-blame and catastrophizing, balanced average strategy use, high positive reappraisal and positive refocusing, and high self-blame and catastrophizing. The latter profile was more common among girls and associated with higher test anxiety and lower buoyancy. Despite limitations, these findings inform interventions to enhance school-related emotion regulation by considering individual differences. Educational relevance statement: This study revealed that adolescent students could be clustered into different profiles based on the ways they used to regulate the emotions resulting from academic failures. Members of a profile marked by high self-blame and catastrophizing were predominantly female and showed elevated levels of test anxiety along with limited ability to cope with everyday school-related stressors. These findings underscore the importance of implementing interventions in schools to promote adaptive emotion regulation strategies.
