TI Chinese nursing master's graduates' perceptions of pursuing a doctoral
   degree after graduation: A qualitative study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing master's graduates; Doctoral degree; Qualitative study; Early
   career nurses; China
ID EDUCATION; INTENT; ISSUES
AB Background: The shortage of doctoral-prepared nurses is a global challenge. Understanding the factors that influence the decisions of newly graduated nursing master's students is critical to fostering the next generation of nursing scholars. Objective: This study aimed to explore the perceptions of Chinese early- to mid-career nursing master's graduates regarding pursuing a doctoral degree. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted. Data were collected through in-depth, semi-structured interviews with 20 nursing master's graduates from four tertiary hospitals in Nantong, China, from September to November 2024, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Results: A total of 20 participants were interviewed in this study. The analysis identified three primary themes shaping the participants' perceptions: (1) The Allure of the Doctorate (Career Advancement and Professional Identity, Pursuit of Academic Interest and Intellectual Fulfillment, Positive Reinforcement and Encouragement); (2) Weighing Commitments (Calculating the Investment, Academic Self-Confidence and Preparedness, and Alignment with Life Goals and Stage); and (3) Perceived Structural Barriers (Scarcity of Admission Opportunities and Intense Competition, The Closed Loop of Supervisor Resources, Concerns over Admission Process Fairness). Conclusion: The decision to pursue a Ph.D. is influenced by a complex interplay of personal aspiration, perceived risk, and structural barriers. Our findings suggest that effective interventions must address not only individuallevel support but also, and more critically, systemic reforms to ensure a transparent and equitable admissions process.

TI Effects of group-based music therapy combined with speech therapy on
   language and social skills in preschool children with autism spectrum
   disorder: An exploratory randomized controlled trial
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism spectrum disorder; Music therapy; Speech therapy; Language
   development; Social skills
AB Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by early difficulties in language and social communication. While speech therapy is a core early intervention, music therapy has been increasingly applied to support social-emotional development. However, evidence regarding the additive effects of group-based music therapy combined with speech therapy in preschool children with ASD remains limited. Method: This exploratory randomized controlled trial enrolled (RCT) preschool children aged 3-5 years with ASD and language delay. Participants were randomly assigned to a Music Therapy group receiving group-based music therapy (60 min/week) plus individual speech therapy (30 min/week), or a Control group receiving speech therapy alone, for 8 weeks. The primary outcome was week 8 language performance assessed using the Preschool Language Scale (PLS). Secondary outcomes included autism-related characteristics, emotional and behavioral functioning, and parenting stress, assessed using the Checklist for Autism Spectrum Disorder-Chinese Version (CASD-C), Pervasive Developmental Problems scale of the Child Behavior Checklist for Ages 11/2-5 (CBCL 11/2-5 PDP), and Parenting Stress Index-Short Form (PSI-4-SF), respectively. The primary treatment effect was evaluated using a multiple imputation-based intention-to-treat (ITT) adjusted analysis accounting for sex and baseline outcome measures. Secondary outcome analyses were interpreted with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons. Exploratory within-group analyses and generalized estimating equation (GEE) models were used to characterize observed changes over time. Results: Forty participants were randomized, and 38 participants completed the week 8 assessment. The ITT analysis included all randomized participants. Observed PLS total scores increased significantly within both groups. Exploratory within-group analyses also showed reductions in CASD-C social interaction issues and emotional difficulties in the Music Therapy group, and CBCL 11/2-5 PDP T-scores decreased within both groups. However, the primary adjusted ITT analysis did not demonstrate statistically significant superiority of adjunctive group-based music therapy over speech therapy alone for the primary language outcome (adjusted between-group difference, -1.65; 95% confidence interval, - 7.52-4.21; p = 0.569). No statistically significant adjusted between-group differences were observed for secondary outcomes. Exploratory GEE analyses indicated time-related changes in PLS total score, CASD-C sensory difficulties, and CBCL 11/2-5 PDP T-score, but no significant group-by-time interactions. Conclusion: In this exploratory RCT, group-based music therapy was feasible to integrate with speech therapy and was not associated with intervention-related adverse events. Although language performance and selected autism-related behavioral features showed improvements over time, adjunctive group-based music therapy did not demonstrate statistically significant superiority over speech therapy alone. Larger adequately powered trials are needed to evaluate its incremental benefit.

TI Translation and assessment of psychometric properties of the French
   version of the Adult Developmental Coordination Disorder/Dyspraxia
   Checklist (ADC)
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Motor difficulties; Neurodevelopmental disorders; Evidence of validity;
   Evidence of reliability; Questionnaire
ID DISORDER; CHILDREN; ALPHA
AB Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that emerges during childhood, affecting approximately 5-8% of school-age children. Although it often persists into adulthood, there is a lack of standardized and validated tools for assessing DCD in adults in France. The Adult Developmental Coordination Disorder/Dyspraxia Checklist (ADC) is the most widely used questionnaire in DCD studies with adults and has been adapted in several countries. This study aimed to translate the ADC into French and to evaluate its psychometric properties. The questionnaire was translated following literature recommendations. A total of 209 participants aged 18-58 years were included (138 females, mean age: 24.49 +/- 7.87 years, mean laterality quotient: 71.41% +/- 45.85%), including 13 with a reported diagnosis of DCD or probable DCD. The psychometric properties related to evidence of validity and reliability were then assessed. The test of the questionnaire structure led to a 28-item modified version instead of the 40-item original one. Analyses of the other psychometric properties provided initial evidence based on test content, internal structure, relations with validated motor tests, and sensitivity to DCD. The ADC also showed acceptable to excellent internal consistency and test-retest reliability. Preliminary French thresholds and minimal detectable change values (e.g., following an intervention) were calculated. This article represents a first step in the validation process of the French ADC, in line with French and European recommendations on DCD. It also contributes to harmonizing diagnostic tools and supporting international research on adults with DCD.

TI Teaching quality, average outcomes, and within-classroom dispersion: A
   variance function analysis of Japanese ninth-grade mathematics
   classrooms
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teaching quality; Math self-efficacy; Math achievement; Equity;
   Within-classroom dispersion; Socioeconomic status
ID SELF-EFFICACY; SCHOOLS
AB Research on teaching quality has typically focused on average student outcomes rather than on within-classroom distributions. Using OECD Global Teaching InSights data from Japanese ninth-grade mathematics classrooms, this study examined whether four student-perceived teaching-quality indicators-cognitive activation, classroom management, student support, and instructional clarity-were associated with the conditional mean and residual dispersion of post-unit math achievement and self-efficacy, with SES as a moderator. Variance function regression showed that these indicators were not uniformly associated with average outcomes or residual dispersion. Several associations involving student support remained statistically significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction in the conditional mean models, whereas evidence from the dispersion models was more limited. SES moderation indicated selected context-dependent associations. These findings suggest that student-perceived teaching-quality indicators should be examined in relation to both average outcomes and equity-relevant distributional patterns within classrooms.

TI Uniting generic and content-specific instructional quality: A profile
   analysis of pre-service teachers' learning experiences and its relevance
   for TPACK development
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; FIT INDEXES; USE ICT; EDUCATION;
   FRAMEWORK; IMPACT; ACHIEVEMENT; TECHNOLOGY; READINESS; CRITERIA
AB Promoting TPACK in teacher education programs is a current imperative. One approach to foster TPACK is focusing on instructional quality (INQ), which offers two perspectives on effective learning experiences: generic and content-specific INQ. Past studies have examined both INQ perspectives separately, whereas our study aims to unite both perspectives by investigating the extent to which their combined influence shapes the development of pre-service teachers' TPACK. Therefore, we first explore heterogeneous experiences with INQ by using latent profile analysis, and second use multi-group latent change models to examine the TPACK development across identified profiles. Our sample consists of 248 pre-service teachers from one German University. Notably, pre-service teachers in profiles defined by high satisfaction with all INQ dimensions also had significant TPACK development, emphasizing the central role of both generic and content-specific INQ to foster TPACK development for pre-service teachers.

AB This study investigates how history teacher education in Japan, Korea, and Taiwan has prepared pre-service teachers to teach difficult knowledge. Using a case study design, this research explores the experiences of seven history teacher educators. The findings reveal an inherent tension between the need to address challenging historical narratives and a systemic lack of institutional preparation across these cultural contexts. Despite the differing contexts, history teacher educators in Japan, Korea, and Taiwan independently made their curriculainstructional decisions, navigating these challenges beyond their traditional roles. They encountered distinct yet overlapping struggles in their efforts to integrate difficult knowledge into teacher education. This comparative analysis illuminates the shared educational challenges faced by post-colonial and democratizing societies, highlighting a collective struggle to balance educational innovation with systemic constraints.

TI Implementing a High-Relevance Redox Course in Everyday-Life Contexts:
   Effects on Motivation, Attitudes, and Perceived Relevance among Middle
   School Science Teachers and Pre-Service Teachers
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE redox chemistry; relevance-based instruction; chemistry teacher
   education; teacher professional development; context-based learning;
   mixed methods
ID SYSTEMS THINKING; CHEMISTRY; EDUCATION; STUDENTS
AB Oxidation-reduction chemistry is central to chemistry education, yet it remains difficult because learners must coordinate visible change, particulate explanation, symbolic notation, and electron transfer. This mixed-methods study examined a high-relevance redox course delivered to two intact Arab-majority teacher cohorts in northern Israel: 50 preservice science teachers and 60 in-service middle school science teachers. The course joined everyday and societal contexts with explicit representational work, misconception analysis, demonstrations, guided discussions, and instructional design tasks. Quantitative measures assessed attitudes toward chemistry, science learning motivation, and perceived relevance before and after the course. Final projects and ten semistructured interviews were used to interpret the quantitative patterns. Paired comparisons showed significant motivation gains in both cohorts and a significant perceived-relevance gain only among preservice teachers. Attitude changes were positive, but not statistically significant. Project scores indicated that participants produced contextually grounded redox tasks under course conditions, although the study did not establish their classroom effectiveness. Qualitative evidence suggests that preservice teachers tended to describe relevance as an expansion of chemistry's civic and explanatory purpose, whereas in-service teachers more often evaluated relevance through feasibility, curricular pressure, and differentiated student needs. The findings are interpreted cautiously because the design lacked a comparison group, and the qualitative sample was limited.

TI Proper Use of Parentheses and Square Brackets in Describing
   Cycloaddition Reactions: A Discussion on Normative Practices
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cycloaddition Reactions; Bracket Symbols; Pedagogical Standardization;
   Organic Chemistry; IUPAC Nomenclature
AB Cycloaddition reactions constitute a crucial chapter in organic chemistry education and remain a perennial frontier of chemical research. This article addresses the nonstandardized use of bracket symbols commonly observed in current teaching materials and research literature concerning cycloaddition reactions. It systematically clarifies the appropriate contexts and chemical significance represented by parentheses "()" and square brackets "[ ]" in the notation of cycloaddition reactions based on IUPAC recommendations and authoritative teaching practices. Through an analysis of textbook examples and contemporary research articles, we document the prevalence of inconsistent usage. To assess the practical impact of this inconsistency, we conducted a controlled study of organic chemistry students. The results revealed significant initial confusion regarding symbol interpretation, which was effectively remediated by explicit instruction on the IUPAC convention, confirming the pedagogical importance of the standardized notation. Our aim is to provide clear guidelines for the use of these symbols in chemical pedagogy and academic writing, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the instructional expression and the standardization of scholarly communication.

TI The French-Speaking Chemists Tournament: A Laboratory-Based Team Debate
   Competition to Foster Research Skills through Challenge-Based Learning
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Graduate Education;
   Interdisciplinary/Multidisciplinary; Laboratory Instruction;
   Collaborative/Cooperative Learning; Hands-On Learning/Manipulatives;
   Communication/Writing; Inquiry-Based Learning; Problem Solving/Learning
   Theories; Research-Based Learning; Challenge-based learning
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; INQUIRY; STUDENTS; MOTIVATION; OLYMPIAD; EFFICACY;
   IMPACTS; NEXUS; WORK
AB In the context of teaching laboratory skills, research- and challenge-based approaches are increasingly valued for fostering inquiry, collaboration, and authentic (real-world context) problem-solving. The Tournoi Francophone des Chimistes (French-speaking Chemists' Tournament, TFChim) implements these approaches through a laboratory-based team debate competition in which senior undergraduate and early graduate students from 13 French-speaking institutions develop and defend original experimental solutions to open-ended chemistry problems. These problems use a challenge-based learning approach, providing authentic opportunities for research, design, and interdisciplinary exploration in real-world or imaginary contexts. Over several months, teams design these solutions before presenting them and critiquing others in structured debates during a two-day tournament. A survey has been administered to the participants at the conclusion of the tournament. Its responses indicate strong perceived gains, particularly in research competencies such as inquiry skills, with most gains occurring during the extended preparation phase. Analyses also show no significant differences between teams, highlighting the consistency of the learning experience across numerous institutions. TFChim offers a novel research-based learning format for laboratory work, and provides a solid framework for developing international online versions or institution-level competitions that engage multiple disciplines in addressing complex problems implemented in authentic situations.

TI Reimagining inclusive education through challenge-based learning:
   Opportunities and barriers for students with learning disabilities
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Challenge-Based Learning; Learning Disabilities; Inclusive Education;
   Universal Design for Learning; Student Agency; Neurodiversity
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; WORKING-MEMORY; DYSLEXIA; IMPACT; BRAIN
AB Inclusive education increasingly emphasizes pedagogical approaches that promote participation, autonomy, and meaningful engagement for all learners. Challenge-Based Learning (CBL), an educational framework that engages students in addressing authentic, real-world challenges through collaboration, inquiry, and action, has gained attention as a promising approach for fostering academic, social, and transversal skills. CBL should therefore be understood as a pedagogical framework rather than an assistive technology, even if, when combined with assistive and digital tools, it can support information access, planning, collaboration, communication, and multimodal expression. However, its potential application to students with Learning Disabilities (LD) remains largely underexplored. In this short narrative review and position paper, we examine the theoretical foundations of CBL and discuss its relevance for inclusive educational settings. Drawing on evidence from the broader literature on challenge-, project-, and problembased learning, we explore how key features of CBL, including student agency, collaborative learning, and multimodal engagement, may align with the learning profiles and strengths of students with LD. At the same time, we identify key challenges related to executive functioning demands, self-regulation, cognitive load, assessment practices, and the need for appropriate scaffolding and teacher support. We argue that CBL offers a valuable opportunity to move beyond deficit-oriented approaches and toward strength-based models of inclusion that recognize and value the diverse competencies of learners with LD. Building on the limited attention given to CBL in relation to students with learning disabilities, we propose a research agenda focused on how CBL can be implemented in accessible and supportive ways, drawing on Universal Design for Learning principles and evaluating outcomes related to academic achievement, selfdetermination, and participation.

TI Strategies for enhancing creativity among geography elective students: A
   multilevel linear analysis of student teamwork, learning motivation, and
   teachers' instructional innovation
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Multilevel linear models; Creativity; Teamwork; Learning motivation;
   Teacher instructional innovation
ID SCHOOL-STUDENTS; PERFORMANCE
AB This study created a moderation model to investigate the relationships between student teamwork, learning motivation, and teacher instructional innovation and student creativity, as well as the moderating role of teacher instructional innovation, in order to comprehend the relationship between student teamwork, learning motivation, and teacher instructional innovation and their connection to student creativity as well as the possible psychological processes underlying this relationship. This study investigates the connection between student creativity and multiple characteristics, not only theoretically transcending the limitations of unidirectional causality but also providing insights for educators to cultivate student creativity in teaching practice.

TI Learning, play, and the shifting expectations of childhood: insights
   from young children in Australian schools
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Early years; Learning; Play; Children's voices; Neoliberal reform; Early
   childhood education
ID POWER; PERSPECTIVES; RIGHTS; YOUTH
AB The experience of childhood is not static. It is subject to changing social, cultural, and economic demands. In 2009, the Australian Government heeded the advice of internationally acclaimed economists and 'reconceptualised' childhood as a critical period for investment to secure a stronger economic future. In response, a revised school-based childhood emerged, echoing neoliberal ideology through a national curriculum that heightened focus on the "well-being" and "well-becoming" of young children. Alteration to the expectations of school-based childhood in Australia beckons researchers to examine the undiluted perspectives of young children. Using a qualitative approach, visual-dialogic methodology supported by children's drawn and embodied expressions were used to capture and understand the views of 17 public school children aged 5 and 6 years old in Western Australia. The children explained their experience of childhood and then their understanding of how children learn. They celebrated play as what children do. Schoolwork was considered important, but for an undetermined future rather than for now. An underlying disconnect between children's own 'being' and 'becoming' as they transition to a school-based childhood was revealed, suggesting immediate application of learning to what children do in childhood may augment learner engagement. The study adds to evidence that children's contributions are relevant to ongoing processes of pedagogical decision-making and policy development in early childhood.

TI From prompt engineering to modeling: secondary science teachers' use of
   generative AI to engineer sweetener molecules
SO CHEMISTRY EDUCATION RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
AB Scientific modeling is a core epistemic practice in chemistry, yet supporting learners in visualizing and making sense of abstract molecular structures and functions remains a challenge. While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new representational capabilities, it remains unclear how text-based prompt engineering intersects with established theories of scientific modeling. This study addresses this gap by reconceptualizing prompt engineering as a form of molecular modeling within AIMS, a chemistry-specific GenAI-supported molecular modeling environment. Through a qualitative case study, 11 secondary science teachers used GenAI embedded in AIMS to design novel sweetener molecules. Applying the CLEAR and REFINE analytic frameworks through the lens of Halloun's Modeling Theory, the study examined how participants translated disciplinary knowledge into iterative prompt-based molecular designs. The analysis concludes with three key findings. Participants' prompts functioned as externalized models that embedded assumptions about molecular structure-function relationships and design constraints within explicit chemical and theoretical requirements. As iterations progressed through model testing, reasoning shifted from broad appeals for scientific accuracy to precise, mechanistic constraints, including spatial arrangements and molecular properties. Revisions operated as controlled experiments where participants tightened or relaxed constraints to test the plausibility of GenAI outputs. These findings advance chemistry education by demonstrating that a chemistry-specific GenAI-supported modeling tool can function as a modeling assistant rather than an answer engine, scaffolding the core epistemic practices of construction, evaluation, and refinement in chemistry education. This reconceptualization positions prompt engineering as a source of written evidence for how learners articulated, tested, and revised chemical constraints, offering educators new ways to support and assess student modeling practices.

TI State-Trait Duality of Self-Efficacy in Mathematical Problem-Posing and
   Solving: Insights from Chinese Eighth Graders
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Problem-posing; Problem-solving; Self-efficacy; State-like
   characteristic; Trait-like characteristic
ID MODEL; CRITERIA; FIT
AB This study investigates the state-like versus trait-like nature of self-efficacy among 1,767 Chinese eighth-graders in the context of mathematical problem-posing and problem-solving. The investigation utilized problem-posing and problem-solving tasks developed by Cai et al., alongside task-specific self-efficacy instruments based on Bandura's social cognitive theory. Using both Linear Regression and Generalized Additive Models, the analysis revealed that the correlation between self-efficacy and performance was consistently stronger for problem-solving than for problem-posing. A key finding was that task-specific self-efficacy was not always the strongest predictor. Specifically, self-efficacy for posing easy problems emerged as the most robust predictor for all levels of problem-posing performance. Conversely, self-efficacy for solving easy problems was the strongest predictor only for easy and moderate problem-solving tasks. These results suggest that self-efficacy exhibits a "State-Trait Duality," simultaneously functioning as a temporary state shaped by situational factors and a stable trait consistent across tasks. This dualistic framework provides a more nuanced understanding of how self-efficacy influences students' mathematical engagement and achievement.

TI Pick Your Own Adventure: Orthogonal Methods for Analyzing Polyphenols
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Second-Year Undergraduate; Analytical Chemistry; Laboratory Instruction;
   Inquiry-Based/Discovery Learning; Chromatography; Phenols; Quantitative
   Analysis; UV-vis Spectroscopy; Titration/Volumetric Analysis
ID UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH EXPERIENCES; QUANTITATIVE-ANALYSIS; VANILLIN
   ASSAY; CHEMISTRY; DESIGN; QUANTIFICATION; CATECHINS; FRUIT
AB The analytical chemistry classroom is naturally poised to demonstrate the use of orthogonal techniques to quantify different molecules such as polyphenols. Using food science as a lens and a molecule-centric, inquiry-based approach, this article describes a semester-long laboratory experience for students to adapt and use potentiometric titration, spectrophotometric, and chromatographic methods to analyze polyphenols (i.e., catechin and gallic acid) in instructor-provided samples. Students then are given the agency to select a sample of interest which (theoretically) contains the target analytes (or not) and justify the appropriate method for that sample. The implementation of this experience provides students with many opportunities to authentically engage in scientific practices, such as designing experiments, evaluating their results, and making evidence-based decisions about how to modify procedures and what samples to study. After completing this laboratory experience, students reported significant gains in learning laboratory techniques and moderate gains in designing experiments and analyzing data, while engaging in authentic analyses (including variability) in a supportive environment. Peer evaluations also indicated that students had positive experiences working in groups. Furthermore, the experience is incredibly flexible. Each standard method module (titration, spectrophotometry, chromatography) can be completed independently, or more orthogonal techniques (e.g., gas chromatography) could be added to expand the molecule-centric semester experience.

TI Toward Linguistic Justice: Immigrant Students' and Families' Languaging
   as Pedagogical Disruption of School-Based Literacy Instruction
SO READING TEACHER

DT Article
ID PERSPECTIVE
AB In this article, we examine immigrant families' language and literacy practices against the backdrop of school-based literacy instruction in two dual language bilingual education (DLBE) programs: Vietnamese/English and Portuguese/English. TI Academic Freedom in Austria de jure and de facto: Concepts
   and Challenges
SO TERTIARY EDUCATION AND MANAGEMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Austria; Academic freedom; Freedom of research; Institutional autonomy;
   Liberal democracy
AB This article examines the legal foundations and practical realities of academic freedom in Austria, situating its analysis within the broader European context. Austria's robust constitutional protection of academic freedom, rooted in Article 17 of the Basic Law of 1867, is complemented by European legal safeguards and the explicit autonomy granted to public universities under Article 81c of the Federal Constitutional Law. The study clarifies conceptual distinctions between academic freedom, freedom of scientific research, and institutional autonomy, referencing contemporary European models and legal interpretations. Inspired by Popper's critical rationalism, the paper underscores the intrinsic link between science and democracy, advocating for universities as centres of contestable ideas and rational discourse. The Austrian experience offers valuable insights for the evolving European doctrine of academic freedom, emphasising the need for vigilance against gradual erosion and the collective responsibility to safeguard academic freedom as a cornerstone of liberal democracy.

TI Reconceptualizing Educational Assessment Integrity for Sustainable
   Development: A Multilevel Validity Modeling Approach
SO APPLIED MEASUREMENT IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB Assessment integrity is essential for ensuring fairness, validity, and reliability in education and for advancing sustainable development goals in Ghana. This study employed a quantitative, cross-sectional, correlational design to examine the multidimensional nature of educational assessment integrity within sustainable development frameworks. Guided by Messick's Unified Validity Theory, data were collected from a stratified multistage sample of 2,400 stakeholders, including students, teachers, administrators, and assessment officers across all 16 regions. Multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM) was used for analysis. Descriptive results indicated high perceptions of assessment integrity (M = 4.00-4.30), with Consequences, Fairness, and Content Relevance rated highest. Reliability and validity indices were strong (Cronbach's alpha = 0.82-0.90; AVE = 0.58; CR = 0.87), supported by robust factor loadings (0.75-0.83). Model fit indices demonstrated excellent fit (CFI = 0.94, TLI = 0.92, RMSEA = 0.045, SRMR = 0.035). Regression findings showed that teacher-related factors significantly predicted Structural Fidelity (beta = 0.32, p < .001) and Content Relevance (beta = 0.28, p < .001), while female respondents reported higher perceptions of ethical and social consequences (beta = 0.15, p = .004). Institutional characteristics, particularly private school status, significantly influenced Generalizability (beta = 0.25, p = .002). The model explained up to 14% of variance in key constructs. The findings confirm the multidimensionality of assessment integrity and underscore the influence of contextual and individual factors.

   Sino-Latin American and Caribbean community with a shared future

AB Purpose - To properly understand China's partnership diplomacy towards Latin American and Caribbean (LAC) states within its ambition to promote a Global Community of a Shared Future for Mankind (GCSFM), a new conceptual approach is required. Design/methodology/approach - Drawing on dominant international relations theories, including relational approaches to global politics, this research is grounded in the hypothesis that a GCSFM as both a theoretical framework and a practical model is shaping Chinese partnership diplomacy in Latin America and the Caribbean by promoting cooperative initiatives, aligning development goals and managing asymmetries in economic and political power. The GCSFM is operationalized through three key initiatives: global development initiative, global security initiative and global civilization initiative. Originality/value - This paper provides a novel analytical framework for examining the precise scope and patterns of China's partnership diplomacy toward the LAC region.

TI Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate,
   review strategies, and learning implications
SO INSTRUCTIONAL SCIENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Primary education; Studying rate; Reading rate; Multimedia learning;
   Video; Learning strategy
ID TIME-COMPRESSED INSTRUCTION; COGNITIVE-LOAD; TRANSIENT INFORMATION;
   EYE-MOVEMENTS; LEARNERS PERCEPTIONS; SEDUCTIVE DETAILS; LISTENING RATE;
   READING RATE; COMPREHENSION; MODALITY
AB Despite the prevalence of videos and illustrated texts in primary education, there is a limited understanding of how children study and review these materials, and how this impacts their learning performance. This study examined 97 tablet screen recordings, which captured the learning behaviors of fifth graders as they studied illustrated texts and videos in a within-subjects experiment. The screen recordings were coded frame-by-frame to assess the children's studying rates and learning strategies. These factors, and their connection to prior learning performance data, were analyzed using mixed-effects models and stepwise regression. The results show that videos were studied significantly faster than content-equivalent illustrated texts. Furthermore, this faster studying was associated with better learning outcomes and lower cognitive load. As the children scarcely used the navigation options in the videos, they were mostly studied and reviewed linearly at their designed rate, which was especially beneficial for slower readers. In comparison, both the studying rate and the review strategies were more varied in the illustrated texts. In both conditions, children devoted more time on the slides that had more text content and were positioned early in the presentation. The type of pictures on the slide did not influence time spent. These results indicate that children tend to watch and review videos linearly at their designed rate and sequence, leading to faster studying rates, better learning outcomes, and lower cognitive load compared to illustrated texts. In particular, slow readers benefit from videos.

TI Navigating AI in STEM: what secondary students actually do with
   generative AI-driven tools
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Secondary STEM education; AI
   literacy; Disciplinary epistemology; Cognitive mediation; Educational
   governance; Student practices; Integrated STEM
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; SCHOOL STUDENTS; EDUCATION
AB Background The rapid proliferation of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into secondary education has outpaced formal institutional guidance, creating an expansive array of unsupervised, independent student digital practices. Moving beyond simplistic assumptions of technological affordances, this cross-sectional study empirically analyses the self-reported behavioral distributions of secondary students' interaction with generative AI-driven tools across four STEM subjects: computer science, mathematics, natural sciences, and economics. Using a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, we synthesized survey data (n = 416) and thematic reflections from business-oriented secondary schools in the Czech Republic to examine how institutional regulation and subject-specific environments shape student adoption.Results Quantitative findings reveal a stratified, divergent adoption model characterizing distinct academic fields when treated as structural and environmental proxies for varying disciplinary epistemologies and task environments. While applied and computational disciplines demonstrate normalized integration, theoretically rigorous subjects like mathematics exhibit a transparency gap characterized by high perceived prohibition and persistent clandestine use. We map the self-reported functional roles of AI in the student workflow, finding that students predominantly position AI as an instrumental scaffold for explanation and procedural verification rather than a direct substitute for independent reasoning. However, qualitative evidence uncovers a critical evaluation gap that exposes a behavioral asymmetry within the student workflow: operational prompting loops and epistemic verification are shown to function not as independent psychometric traits, but as interdependent workflow phases where continuous prompt modification heavily overshadows external factual validation. Although students frequently encounter algorithmic errors and procedural dissonance, where AI logic diverges from curricular standards, systematic cross-verification remains reported at low frequencies.Conclusions The study suggests that AI integration is currently evolutionary rather than disruptive, often functioning as a cognitive mediator that accelerates workflow while shifting the behavioral layout toward operational dependency. These associational patterns highlight the need to transition from restrictive governance, which faces distinct reverse-causality reporting biases, to a framework that formally integrates overlapping operational and epistemic workflow competencies, emphasizing the need for subject-sensitive guidance that ensures AI enhances rather than displaces disciplinary rigor.

TI Wording, structure, and design of plain language policies in legislative
   drafting across common law jurisdictions
SO LANGUAGE POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Plain language; Language policy; Legislative drafting; Language
   standardisation; Common law jurisdictions; Legal communication
AB ISO 24495-2 standardises plain legal language as an international benchmark; however, its implementation is hindered by the lack of clear evaluative criteria for assessing the clarity of wording, structure, and design in new legislation. Drawing on an ISO-inspired categorisation of these three dimensions, this study undertakes a structured examination of governmental policies from six major common law jurisdictions: Canada, Australia, Hong Kong, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Findings reveal both similarities and differences in standardisation patterns. The wording and structure dimensions demonstrate strong stability and convergence, particularly in micro-level features such as modal verb usage, whereas the design dimension exhibits significant variability, operating as adaptive supportive practices rather than compulsory requirements. Based on convergent principles in plain-language policies across six jurisdictions, this study constructs a Three-Dimensional Framework of Plain Language Principles in Legislative Drafting. This framework aims to promote the standardisation of plain legal language within common law traditions and provide a valuable tool for legal drafters seeking to align new legislation with ISO 24495-2. Furthermore, it is believed to offer practical benchmarks for civil law jurisdictions by translating laws into English for international audiences. Eventually, this study contributes to legal linguistics and language policy by elucidating the institutionalisation of plain-language policies across analogous legal systems.

TI Impact of Artificial intelligence tools on learning motivation in
   English instruction: a network meta-analysis
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Network meta-analysis; Artificial intelligence; English-medium
   Instruction; Learning motivation; Computer-assisted language learning
AB The rapid expansion of English-Medium Instruction (EMI) programs and the growing demand for English language proficiency have introduced significant motivational challenges for EFL learners who face linguistic barriers. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools offer a potential solution by providing personalized scaffolding and interactive support. This study conducts a network meta-analysis (NMA) of 16 empirical studies (N = 1,923) to compare the effectiveness of three AI interventions, including Generative AI Chatbots, AI Writing Assistants, and AI Language Learning Applications, on the learning motivation of K-12 and university EFL students in English instruction contexts. Results indicate that all AI tools significantly outperform traditional instruction. AI Language Learning Applications (g = 0.907, k = 2) showed the largest effect, followed by Generative AI Chatbots (g = 0.824, k = 11) and AI Writing Assistants (g = 0.692, k = 3). These findings suggest that interactive and adaptive AI tools are particularly effective in fostering motivation by fulfilling students' basic psychological needs of autonomy and competence. The study provides evidence-based recommendations for the strategic integration of AI into English instruction curricula to optimize student engagement and academic success.

TI From recognition to response: investigating brief video intervention on
   misinformation engagement among University students
SO EDUCATIONAL MEDIA INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Social media; media literacy; video-based intervention; misinformation;
   university students
ID MEDIA LITERACY; FALSE NEWS
AB While many educational efforts teach people to identify misinformation, research shows individuals often recognize but fail to respond to false content on social media. TI Outspoken emotions - Emotion regulation during emotional challenges in
   collaborative learning
SO INSTRUCTIONAL SCIENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Collaborative learning; Emotional challenges; Emotion regulation
   strategie; Qualitative analysis; Video data
ID INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; SOCIAL REGULATION; PROCESS MODEL; STUDENTS;
   MOTIVATION; COREGULATION; SITUATIONS; CONFLICT; QUALITY
AB This study examines emotion regulation during emotional challenges in mathematics group tasks among teacher education students (N = 62). The data consisted of 87 hours of videotaped group interaction and students' pre- and post-evaluations of their group experiences. The results show that emotional challenges and regulation varied across groups and tasks. Pre-evaluations were associated with the level of regulation, whereas post-evaluations were associated with the level of challenge but not with regulation. These results have implications for the design and support of collaborative learning: beyond helping students stay on task, groups may benefit from increased awareness of the nature of their challenges and sufficient time to address them through negotiated interaction.

   outcomes: a single-institution retrospective cohort study in China
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION

AB Background Licensing examinations provide an external reference for selected knowledge, skills, and professional standards required for entry into clinical practice. TI The Game Café: Exploring Students' Perceptions of Learning Experiences
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE game-based learning; analog gameplay; higher education; student
   engagement; motivation; sense of belonging
ID SENSE
AB Game-based learning (GBL) has increasingly been recognized as a valuable approach for supporting student engagement, motivation, and skill development in educational settings. However, comparatively little research has examined analog gameplay within informal, co-curricular higher education environments. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this exploratory study examined students' perceptions of their experiences at a university's Academic Skills Centre's (ASC) Game Caf & eacute; (not course-based), with particular attention to motivation, social engagement, and perceived academic skill development. Using a descriptive, cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 44 student participants through a researcher-developed survey consisting of Likert-scale and open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative responses were thematically coded. Internal consistency analyses demonstrated acceptable to strong reliability across survey scales (Q6 alpha = 0.70; Q7 alpha = 0.89). Findings indicated that students perceived a consistent association between the Game Caf & eacute; and positive emotional experiences, collaboration, peer interaction, and the perceived development of transferable skills such as communication, critical thinking, and problem-solving. Participants also described the caf & eacute; as a low-pressure and socially supportive environment that fostered motivation and informal learning beyond the classroom. Overall, the findings suggest that analog, co-curricular game-based environments may support students' perceived engagement, belonging, and learning within higher education contexts.

TI The Structure Paradox: How Parental Belief About Structured Life Shapes
   Children's Play Engagement
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE parental beliefs; structure; child routines; play; play engagement; home
   environment
ID FAMILY ROUTINES; SELF-DETERMINATION; SCHOOL READINESS; CHOICE
AB This study investigates a paradoxical association between parental beliefs about structured life (PBSL) and children's play engagement. We conceptualize this association as the structure paradox: although structure is often viewed as potentially constraining free play, parents' stronger endorsement of structured and organized everyday life may instead be positively related to children's engagement in play. The sample included 299 parents (94% mothers) of typically developing 6-year-old children. Parent-reported measures included the Parent Play Beliefs Scale and single-item assessments of PBSL, children's play engagement, and the presence of a dedicated play space at home. Data were analyzed using correlation, multiple regression, and mediation analyses. Results showed that PBSL was positively associated with children's play engagement: parents who more strongly endorsed the importance of structured and organized everyday life reported higher levels of play engagement in their children. Parental play beliefs were not significantly associated with children's play engagement. Among the examined family factors, the presence of a dedicated play space at home showed the strongest association with children's play engagement. A significant positive indirect association was also found between PBSL and children's play engagement via the presence of a dedicated play space at home. However, the observed direct and indirect associations involving PBSL were small in magnitude. These preliminary findings contribute to the understanding of PBSL and the organization of the home play environment as family factors associated with preschool children's play engagement. For parents and teachers, the findings suggest that predictable daily routines, clear rules, and the inclusion of play in preschool children's everyday routines may be associated with more sustained engagement in play.

   comprehension; prompt fading
ID GRADERS
AB Students with learning disabilities (LD) and dyslexia often struggle with a variety of literacy skills, including reading comprehension. Generating questions can be challenging for all students, especially those with disabilities. Systematic prompt fading (i.e., gradually removing instructional prompts) is a way to teach students to generate their own questions. TI Modeling the reading-to-writing pipeline: Knowledge graph and LLM-based
   assessment framework for source-based writing
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Automated writing evaluation; Source-based writing; Comprehension
   modeling; Knowledge graphs; Large language models; Multiple-document
   comprehension
ID TEXT; REPRESENTATION
AB Source-based writing requires integrating information across multiple documents, yet most Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) systems evaluate only the final written product, overlooking the comprehension processes that precede the writing. We propose a comprehension-sensitive AWE framework that makes the reading-to-writing pipeline visible through knowledge graphs (KGs) and large language model (LLM) inference. The framework comprises three layers (artifact representation, inferential linking, and idea tracing) that together trace how students' ideas move and transform across source texts, process artifacts, and final essays. As a proof of concept, we applied the framework to archival data from 132 students completing a source-based writing task. Integrated KGs were constructed for each student, tracing idea flow across four source texts, constructed responses, and final essays. Graph-based metrics correlated significantly with human rubric scores across multiple measurement configurations, providing evidence that the representational structures capture systematic variation in writing quality. A diagnostic case analysis demonstrates how graph representations make specific patterns of source engagement and idea transfer visible, revealing meaningful differences between two students who received identical holistic scores. Cohort-level analyses further reveal systematic variation in how students engage with and transform source ideas. The framework is designed to adapt across genres, task structures, and educational contexts, and offers a foundation for diagnostic feedback that is sensitive to the comprehension processes source-based writing demands.

TI Evaluating AI-based visual privacy through Cartoonification: Impact on
   expressive participation and consent for data retention

DT Article

ID STUDENT PERCEPTIONS; ONLINE; ENGAGEMENT; CLASSROOM; PRINCIPLES;
   PROTECTION; ANALYTICS; PROJECT; ISSUES; FACE
AB Learning analytics tools embedded with video devices are increasingly prevalent for capturing student interactions during learning activities. This approach is useful for classroom observation and analyzing students' emotional expression and perceived confidence during discussions. However, students expressed concern about how their identities could be represented, interpreted, and misused during these analytic and research processes. TI From spreadsheets to storybooks: How the skill requirements of mothers'
   occupations relate to activities with their children
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Occupational skills; Occupations; Parenting; Parental involvement;
   Parental engagement
ID LITERACY SKILLS; EARLY NUMERACY; SELF-EFFICACY; EDUCATION; PARENTS;
   ASSOCIATIONS; ACHIEVEMENT; INVOLVEMENT; MOBILITY; SUPPORT
AB This study examines how the skill requirements of mothers' occupations influence their parenting practices during early childhood. We used data from the UK Millennium Cohort Study (MCS), a nationally representative longitudinal survey of children born in 2000-2002, linked to occupation-specific skill profiles derived from the British Skills Surveys. Parenting behaviors were measured when children were ages 5 (N = 12,892) and 7 (N = 11,265), capturing the frequency of seven cognitively and recreationally oriented activities. TI A Practical Approach for Implementing Holistic Review for General
   Surgery Resident Recruitment
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE diversity; holistic review; residency; recruitment; surgery
AB OBJECTIVE: To describe the implementation of a holistic review process in an academic general surgery residency program. TI Comparing the effects of GenAI-assisted and facilitator-led debriefing
   on knowledge and non-technical skills in immersive virtual reality
   simulation in nursing education: A quasi-experimental study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE GenAI; Debriefing; IVR; Knowledge acquisition; Simulation; Nursing
   education; Non-technical skills
ID INTERVENTIONS
AB Background: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) simulation is increasingly used in nursing education to support experiential learning and the development of non-technical skills. Debriefing is integral to simulation-based education; however, shortages of qualified facilitators and variability in delivery can constrain scalability and quality. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may offer a standardised and scalable approach to post-simulation debriefing, yet comparative evidence in nursing education remains limited. Aim: To compare the effectiveness of GenAI-assisted versus facilitator-led debriefing on nursing students' knowledge acquisition and self-reported non-technical skills following an IVR nursing simulation. Design: Quasi-experimental, two-group pretest-posttest study. Setting: A higher education institution in Hong Kong. Participants: Undergraduate nursing students with less than four weeks of clinical internship experience. Methods: Participants were allocated by subject enrolment to either GenAI-assisted debriefing plus a 10-minute facilitator summary (experimental group) or facilitator-led debriefing (control group) after an IVR hospital simulation. Knowledge was measured using a multiple-choice questionnaire at baseline (T0) and post-intervention (T1), while self-reported non-technical skills were assessed at T1. Results: A total of 178 students participated (experimental n = 102; control n = 76). Baseline knowledge scores were comparable (experimental: M = 10.98, SD = 2.27; control: M = 11.03, SD = 2.56; p = .899). Knowledge increased significantly from T0 to T1 in both groups (experimental: M = 12.71, SD = 2.71, d = 0.79; control: M = 12.68, SD = 2.44, d = 0.72; both p < .001). After adjustment for baseline knowledge, there was no significant between-group difference in post-intervention knowledge (F = 0.03, p = .871). Non-technical skill domain scores did not differ significantly between groups (all p = .272-0.876). Conclusions: GenAI-assisted debriefing produced outcomes comparable to facilitator-led debriefing for knowledge and self-reported non-technical skills. These findings warrant further investigation of GenAI-assisted debriefing as a complement to existing approaches.

ID MALE BRAIN
AB Despite growing awareness, autism identification remains hindered by historical biases linking the condition to male populations and a limited understanding of the subtler female phenotype, which can delay timely educational referrals in schools. This study investigated how student gender (perceived binary gender: boy or girl) and autism phenotype (male or female behavioral profiles) affect autism identification by pre-service teachers. Using vignettes depicting children showing either a male or female autism phenotype, 709 pre-service teachers from six countries (Chile, Ecuador, France, Latvia, Spain, and the USA) considered possible diagnoses, confidence levels, and ranked likelihoods. Results revealed that student gender significantly influenced identification: autism was more frequently, confidently, and highly ranked when the vignette described a boy rather than a girl. The autism phenotype itself did not affect identification rates, though teachers showed greater confidence when judging the male phenotype. No interaction effects emerged between gender and phenotype. These findings suggest that pre-service teachers are still influenced by the stereotype of autism as a predominantly male condition. This study shows how teacher education training on gender bias in autism could be re-designed to promote earlier recognition and support for autistic girls who are often underdiagnosed or diagnosed late.

TI Navigating language learning choices: How Chinese students adapt
   out-of-school English learning choices in a constrained EFL context
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Out-of-school language learning; English private tutoring; Language
   policy constraints; Rational choice theory; Double reduction policy
ID EDUCATIONAL DECISION; SHADOW EDUCATION; SECONDARY-SCHOOL; POLICY;
   DIFFERENTIALS; INEQUALITIES; MODEL
AB Out-of-school language learning, a crucial supplement to formal schooling, is shaped by many sociopolitical factors, such as macro-level policies that determine the availability of language resources. China's ongoing Double Reduction Policy (DRP) has substantially reduced English private tutoring (EPT), reshaping out-of-school language learning landscapes. While existing research has largely examined impacts on the supply side (tutors and institutions), the decisionmaking processes governing students' strategic adaptations, i.e., the demand side, remain relatively understudied. Findings reveal that, within the sampled Chengdu schools, social origin is inextricably associated with out-of-school English learning disparities, while policy attitudes show a statistically significant relationship with EPT demand, suggesting the policy's limited effectiveness in curbing entrenched motivations for EPT. By bridging macro-level policy constraints with micro-level decision-making, this study offers insights into students' strategic decision-making under complex sociopolitical context.

AB Pre-service physical education teachers commonly show stronger technical instructional competence than needsupportive behaviors addressing students' needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. TI Using explainable artificial intelligence to investigate key factors
   predicting students' creativity
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY

DT Article
DE Creativity; Post hoc interpretation; PISA; Explainable artificial
   intelligence
ID SOCIOECONOMIC-STATUS; PERSONALITY; MODEL; ACHIEVEMENT; ENVIRONMENT;
   REGRESSION
AB Investigating factors predicting students' creativity informs the development strategies of fostering creativity. Most previous studies have used linear regression-based methods to investigate a small subset of prediction factors on students' creativity in a small to medium sample, failing in capturing complex nonlinear relationships and limiting the generalizability of the findings. Grounded in the PISA Creative Thinking Framework, with the Investment Theory of Creativity as a supplementary perspective, this study employed explainable artificial intelligence to investigate the prediction of 44 factors on 423,685 students' creativity. SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander education; Cultural interface;
   Indigenous education; Migrant teachers; Multiculturalism; Diversity
ID EDUCATION; EXPERIENCES; AUSTRALIA
AB Multicultural diversity in settler-colonial Australia impacts the way that the growing number of migrant teachers in Australia's teaching workforce engage in Indigenous education. Foundational ideas of multiculturalism promote diversity and inclusion yet can inadvertently perpetuate the narratives of settler colonialism. The impact is that the important decolonial work required to prevent Indigenous erasure is further impeded. Drawing on Nakata's (2007) concept of the cultural interface, this paper illustrates how migrant teachers navigate complex knowledge-power dynamics shaped by Indigenous sovereignty, white colonial privilege, and multicultural diversity. Literature from these fields illustrates the knowledge contestations required for migrant teachers to engage effectively in Indigenous education. Multicultural diversity, when uncritically aligned with white colonial privilege, can reinforce systemic barriers to Indigenous representation and sovereignty in education. Ultimately, the paper recommends ways to support migrant teachers to engage in the contested knowledge space at the Western/Indigenous cultural interface and develop intercultural responsiveness in order to advance reconciliation and ensure that Indigenous knowledges and perspectives are valued as integral to Australia's educational future.

TI GenAI-supported collaborative project-based language learning: effects
   on EFL undergraduates' achievement and autonomy
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI); Project-based language

ID TECHNOLOGIES
AB Despite growing interest in Generative AI (GenAI) in language education, empirical evidence examining its pedagogical integration within project-based language learning and its influence on measurable learning outcomes remains limited. Many studies emphasize learner perceptions or short-term tool interaction rather than sustained classroom interventions grounded in instructional design. Addressing this gap, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study investigated the extent to which participation in GenAI-supported collaborative PBLL was associated with changes in English language achievement and learner autonomy among EFL undergraduates. Participants were 53 Saudi female first-year university students assigned to experimental and control groups. Learner autonomy development was also significantly greater in the experimental group across dimensions, with especially strong growth in motivation and self-regulation. Qualitative findings suggested that collaborative engagement, peer interaction, and GenAI-mediated scaffolding supported strategic learning behaviors, confidence, and reflective awareness, while highlighting challenges related to digital literacy, tool selection, and potential over-reliance on AI outputs. Overall, findings suggest that GenAI-supported PBLL may contribute to language development and autonomy when embedded within structured and socially mediated learning environments.

TI When Can AI Models Explain Learning? Validity Criteria for AI as
   Cognitive Models in Education
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Artificial neural networks; Education;
   Cognitive science; AI for cognitive science
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; NEURAL-NETWORKS; ACT-R;
   SYSTEMS; ARCHITECTURE; FRAMEWORK; TUTORIAL; SCIENCE; PLACE
AB Traditional verbal theories in educational psychology often remain underspecified at the mechanistic level. While they offer rich descriptive constructs and conceptual insights, they provide limited accounts of how learning processes unfold dynamically and causally. Here, "verbal" denotes theories stated in prose and qualitative relations rather than as formal, computational process models. This lack of mechanistic precision constrains rigorous theory testing, limits integration across levels of analysis, and reduces the potential to design interventions grounded in explanatory understanding of learning processes. In this Review, we synthesize an emerging paradigm that treats artificial intelligence (AI) systems not merely as predictive tools or instructional technologies, but as cognitive models of learners, explicit, runnable instantiations of theoretical assumptions about cognition and learning. Our central question is not whether AI systems can serve as cognitive models, but when they should be allowed to count as such. We therefore organize the Review around explicit validity criteria, theoretical grounding, construct validity, mechanistic transparency, alignment with human learning trajectories, error-signature matching, causal-intervention tests, ecological validity, and instructional usefulness, that an AI system must satisfy before its cognitive-model status is granted rather than assumed. We examine how major families of AI models, including neural networks, reinforcement learning agents, cognitive architectures, and large language models, have been used to operationalize core educational constructs such as memory, strategy use, motivation, self-regulation, and social learning. Across these approaches, we highlight how mechanistic transparency, interpretability, and alignment with human learning trajectories and error patterns are essential for explanatory validity. We further discuss methodological tools, such as representation analysis, ablation, and trajectory-level comparison, that enable causal inference about learning mechanisms within models. Finally, we outline key challenges and future directions, including construct validity, ecological realism, individual differences, and ethical accountability. By positioning AI as a theoretical instrument rather than solely an engineering solution, this Review argues that AI-based cognitive models can, when they satisfy these criteria, help transform abstract learning theories into precise, testable, and educationally actionable accounts of how students learn.

TI Goals of Well-Being in the Context of Finnish Comprehensive School
   Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE discourse analysis; education policy; school; well-being; well-being
   goals
ID COMPETENCE; SATISFACTION; LEADERSHIP; HEALTH
AB One of the central aims of education and educational policies is to promote well-being. Laws and norms oblige Finnish schools to formulate the goals for improving the well-being of the entire school community in the documents guiding the school's operations. However, little is known about how the policy shows up in the school-level goals related to well-being, and how the ambiguous concept of well-being has been understood. This article examines the well-being discourses that emerged in the documents guiding the operations of Finnish comprehensive schools. We collected 379 school-level documents from 20 municipalities and analysed the data using discourse analysis. As a result, four discourses were identified: the individual-centred, competence-related, collaboration-related, and development-supporting discourses. Our results indicated that well-being at school is not an unambiguous or universal goal. Goals related to well-being are often described at an abstract level. The trends in education policy affect the discourses that emerge and produce goals in the plans that partly follow the paradigms related to schools and society.

TI Before and After Remedial Classes: Students' Attitudes, Perceived
   Learning and Behavioural Intentions in Higher Education Accounting
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE accounting education; higher education; perceived learning; remedial
   classes; structural equation modelling; student attitudes
ID UNIVERSITY ONLINE EDUCATION; ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; MOTIVATION;
   ENGAGEMENT; DETERMINANTS; SATISFACTION; OUTCOMES
AB This study examines the role of remedial classes as a pedagogical intervention in higher education accounting. Specifically, it analyses how students' attitudes, perceived learning, continued-use intention and word-of-mouth communication are shaped before and after participation in remedial classes. A quantitative pre- and post-intervention design was adopted, with data collected from accounting students at two moments: before the implementation of the remedial classes and after their completion. The study used previously validated scales to measure reciprocal benefits, social influence, recognition, motivation, attitude, continued-use intention, word-of-mouth and perceived learning. Structural equation modelling was used to test the relationships among the constructs at both time points. The descriptive results showed that students' evaluations became more moderate after the intervention, suggesting a shift from expectation-based perceptions to experience-based evaluations. The structural results revealed that reciprocal benefits, social influence, and recognition positively influenced students' attitudes both before and after the remedial classes. However, reciprocal benefits and social influence became stronger predictors of attitude after the intervention, whereas the effect of recognition decreased but remained statistically significant. Motivation did not significantly influence attitude at either time point. Attitude, in turn, had strong positive effects on continued-use intention, perceived learning and word-of-mouth communication in both models. These findings suggest that remedial classes should not be understood only as a mechanism for content recovery. Their pedagogical value also depends on whether students perceive them as useful, socially supported, and positively connected to their learning experience. The study contributes to the literature by reframing remedial classes as a pedagogical intervention and by distinguishing perceived learning from objective academic success. Since the study relies on self-reported perceptions rather than grades or test scores, future research should combine perceived learning measures with objective indicators of academic performance.

TI Employment Related Self-Determination: Construct Validation Through
   Psychometric Evaluation of the Vocational Fit Assessment
SO INTELLECTUAL AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Intellectual disability; self-determination; assessment; transition;
   employment
ID INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; INDIVIDUALS; CONTEXT; MODEL; INTERVENTIONS;
   PREDICTORS; CHOICE; SCALE
AB Self-determination (SD) of young adults with intellectual disability (ID) is necessary to their success beyond high school, but our understanding of the construct of SD does not sufficiently invoke environmental factors or context. We explore employment-related SD of young adults with ID using psychometric methods. This cross-sectional study examines the construct validity and internal consistency of the Vocational Fit Assessment (VFA)-SD (n = 309), then concurrent validity of the VFA-SD with the Self-Determination Inventory: Parent/Teacher Report (SDI-PTR; n = 233). Ordinal exploratory factor analysis strongly suggests that VFA-SD items measure one unidimensional construct. The mean inter-item correlation was 0.61, ordinal alpha = 0.97, and McDonald's omega = 0.87. The VFA-SD and the SDI-PTR were positively and moderately correlated, R = 0.61, p < .001. Taken together, these complementary psychometric results validate the use of the VFA-SD but also indicate potential benefits of item refinement and the opportunity to align with widely accepted Causal Agency Theory. This work highlights the critical need for all transition professionals to consider the context when selecting appropriate assessments to measure young adults' SD, as well as the need for future research that considers employment as a relevant contextual factor.

AB This article draws on Afrodiasporic thought and practices in the Andes to question educational structures that continue to dismiss Black lives, knowledge, and ways of knowing. TI Conceptual frameworks in designing learning environments: a typology
   guiding the dialogue between education and space
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Education; Architecture; Learning environments; Educational spaces;
   School design; School architecture
ID SCHOOL; CLASSROOM; IMPACT; PLACE
AB The architecture and design of learning environments have been recognized in the last two decades for their intrinsic effect on educational practice. This recognition has led to massive investment in the (re)design, (re)planning, and (re)building of learning environments. However, while changes are occurring, little is known about the conceptual frameworks that guide these planning and design processes. Therefore, this interdisciplinary study asked: What are the conceptual frameworks behind the planning and design of learning environments? And how do these conceptual frameworks articulate a dialogue between education and space? These questions were examined through a qualitative content analysis of architectural and educational scholarship on processes of planning and design of learning environments. We present five typological conceptual frameworks that underpin these processes: the engineering-industrial, the scientific, the patterns, the hermeneutic-interpretive, and the user experience frameworks. The typology is based on the classification of different paradigmatic assumptions that lead to various forms of dialogue between education and space, and between learning and environment. The conceptualization presented enables a more systematic discussion between architects, designers, and educators involved in the planning and design of learning environments.

TI Understanding student satisfaction in their online learning: a student
   demands-resources model of engagement and burnout
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Online learning; Student engagement; Student satisfaction; Technological
   demands; Technology resilience
AB This study examined how study resources and technological demands jointly shape engagement, burnout, and satisfaction in Indonesian online higher education. Drawing on the Study Demands-Resources (SD-R) framework, four key resources-teaching and course design, institutional digital support, peer climate, and technology resilience-were evaluated alongside four techno-cognitive demands: cognitive switching demand, system complexity, technology overload, and connectivity burden. Using survey data from 531 undergraduate students and PLS-SEM analysis, the results show that strong pedagogical design and adaptive digital coping skills play central roles in sustaining engagement and satisfaction, while fragmented multitasking and digital overload are major contributors to burnout. Satisfaction is most strongly explained by engagement, whereas burnout exerts a smaller yet negative influence. These findings highlight the need for a coherent instructional structure, reduced platform fragmentation, and strengthened digital resilience initiatives to enhance student experiences in blended and online learning environments.

TI The Effects of Contextualized Construction Play on the Development of
   Executive Function in 4-5-Year-Old Preschoolers: A Three-Arm
   Quasi-Experimental Study with a 2-Month Follow-Up
SO EARLY EDUCATION AND DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
ID INHIBITORY CONTROL; SCHOOL READINESS; CHILDREN; SKILLS; HOT
AB Research Findings: Using a 12-week, three-arm quasi-experimental design, this study examined whether Contextualized Construction Play (CCP)-block-building projects embedded in narrative storyline-enhances executive function (EF) among 90 Chinese preschoolers (Mage = 55.8 months). Children were allocated to CCP, Non-Contextualized Construction Play (NCP), or Business-As-Usual control (BAU) conditions. EF was assessed at three time points (pretest, posttest, and a 2-month follow-up) using a multi-task battery targeting cognitive flexibility, working memory, inhibitory control, and delay of gratification. Relative to BAU, both intervention conditions showed greater EF gains at posttest, and these gains were maintained at the 2-month follow-up. In addition, CCP yielded larger improvements than NCP at posttest, with the advantage persisting at follow-up. Findings provide preliminary support that embedding cooperative construction play in meaningful narrative contexts may strengthen preschoolers' EF beyond non-contextualized construction activities. Practice or Policy: CCP offers a feasible, low-cost way to enrich everyday classroom play with structured opportunities for planning, rule use, and collaborative problem solving. Practitioners can anchor weekly builds in familiar picture books or locally relevant stories and use brief prompts to support goal setting, turn taking, and reflection.

AB The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has created a practical problem for virtual higher education: universities must distinguish legitimate AI-supported learning from undisclosed delegation of academic work, while maintaining valid, fair, and privacy-sensitive assessment. This study compared student and faculty perceptions of AI use and academic integrity at the Technical University of Machala, Ecuador. A descriptive-comparative cross-sectional survey was administered to 1660 students and 34 faculty members during the second academic semester of 2024. The student questionnaire examined AI-use frequency, perceived academic benefit, readiness for non-assisted assessment, observation of dishonest online practices, perceived efficacy of virtual assessment, and attitudes toward proctoring. The faculty questionnaire examined suspected AI-generated submissions, responses to suspected use, perceived assessment efficacy, training, control tools, ethical judgments and proctoring. Findings indicate a transitional integrity landscape: students view AI mainly as a useful academic support, whereas faculty interpret it primarily through authorship, evidence and assessment-security concerns. Both groups report limitations in current virtual assessment, suggesting the need for AI-resilient assessment design, explicit disclosure rules, faculty development, student AI literacy, and proportional use of proctoring. The article argues against both blanket prohibition and permissive ambiguity, proposing a governance model grounded in transparent policy, authentic assessment, due process and human-centered AI literacy.
