TI Comparing Human and ChatGPT Performance on the Force Concept Inventory:
   An Item-Level Analysis Through Rasch Modeling and the Theory of
   Conceptual Fields
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE theory of conceptual fields; generative artificial intelligence; force
   concept inventory; alternative conceptions
AB This exploratory study compares the conceptual performance of human respondents and ChatGPT on the Force Concept Inventory (FCI), a widely used assessment designed to diagnose alternative conceptions in Newtonian mechanics. Rather than relying exclusively on overall performance scores, the study investigates whether item-level analyses reveal qualitative differences between human and AI responses. The dataset comprised responses from fourteen Belgian pre-service physics teachers and eleven independent ChatGPT sessions generated through different user accounts. A Rasch model was employed to estimate respondent proficiency and item difficulty, complemented by an item-by-item comparison of success rates and analyses of Item Characteristic Curves (ICCs). The findings indicate that although ChatGPT achieved an overall level of performance comparable to that of several human participants, substantial discrepancies emerged on conceptually demanding items requiring the coordination of multiple physical relationships. These discrepancies are interpreted through Vergnaud's Theory of Conceptual Fields as suggesting that successful human performance may involve richer coordination of operational invariants than can be inferred from ChatGPT response patterns. Because of the exploratory design, the small sample size, and the asymmetry between human and AI testing conditions, these interpretations should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. The study illustrates how item-level analyses, combined with a conceptual framework grounded in physics education research, may provide a more informative perspective on human-AI comparisons than global scores alone.

AB Technology is changing the way in which gifted students are identified and supported. In the past, the focus has been on acceleration and enrichment. The cultivation of 21st-century skills among talented students has become a global goal, including in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). To enhance the creative problem-solving skills of academically talented high-school students in the UAE, the College of Education at a leading institute launched an online mentoring program for several students based on the Real Engagement in Active Problem Solving (REAPS) model. This innovative experience showed that the REAPS model is an effective method for teaching creative problem-solving skills, and online mentoring is a promising strategy for gifted education to develop future and life skills.

TI Bridging the Education-Employment Gap: Linking Labour Market Needs with
   University Programmes Through AI-Assisted Insights and Micro-Credentials
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence (AI); labour market analytics; skills mismatch;
   micro-credentials; digital transformation of education; curriculum
   development; employability
ID SKILLS MISMATCH
AB This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI)-driven labour market analytics can support the alignment of university curricula with emerging skill demands and inform the development of targeted micro-credentials. A mixed-methods approach was applied, combining AI-assisted analysis of approximately 30,000 online job advertisements in Latvia with ESCO-based skill mapping, curriculum analysis, and expert interviews. The study develops and validates a three-layer analytical framework integrating labour market demand, professional standards, and programme learning outcomes. Three occupations-Personnel Specialist, Finance Manager, and Organisation Manager-were analysed at Riga Technical University as proof-of-concept cases. The findings demonstrate that strict one-to-one ESCO matching overestimates curriculum gaps because labour market and educational actors often describe competencies at different levels of abstraction. Composite matching significantly improves alignment estimates by identifying functionally equivalent competencies embedded across curricula. Nevertheless, the analysis reveals a persistent under-representation of digital competencies across all programmes, confirmed by industry experts. Interviews further identify a "pedagogical transfer gap", where formally acquired competencies are insufficiently applied in practice, and highlight employer support for high-quality micro-credentials focused on technical upskilling. The study contributes an AI-assisted curriculum-monitoring framework that combines large-scale skill extraction, semantic alignment, and stakeholder validation, offering universities a practical tool for evidence-based curriculum renewal and lifelong learning development.

TI Engaging Adults with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities as
   "Citizen Scientists" to Transform Health Care Accessibility
SO INTELLECTUAL AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD); health care
   accessibility; citizen science; primary care; community-based
   participatory research (CBPR)
ID PHOTOVOICE; PEOPLE
AB Adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (AIDD) experience persistent barriers to accessing and participating in health care yet are rarely engaged as partners in efforts to improve accessibility. This study used the evidence-based Our Voice (OV) citizen science approach to engage AIDD in identifying barriers and facilitators to primary care access and generating actionable solutions. Twelve participants (six AIDD and six adults without IDD) documented accessibility conditions across three medical clinics using photographs and narratives. Analysis of 170 photographs and 154 narratives identified five themes: (1) sensory considerations, (2) informational materials, (3) signage and wayfinding, (4) accommodations, and (5) physical accessibility. Findings demonstrate the feasibility of engaging AIDD in structured, clinic-based accessibility assessment and suggest a participatory framework that may inform research and quality improvement initiatives aimed at promoting disability-inclusive health care.

TI Developing fine-tuned prompt literacy in EAP: Graduate students'
   experiences with customized GPT for academic inquiry
SO JOURNAL OF ENGLISH FOR ACADEMIC PURPOSES
LA English
DT Article
DE Fine-tuned prompt literacy; AI-Assisted academic inquiry; Generative AI
   in EAP; Learner agency; Critical AI literacy; Digital literacies
ID AI
AB Given the limited research on AI interaction competencies in advanced academic contexts, this qualitative case study examines how graduate students develop fine-tuned prompt literacy-the ability to strategically craft and refine prompts-while using customized GPT-based tools (MyGPT) for academic writing and research. Four graduate students in an English for Academic Purposes (EAP) context participated in iterative interactions with personalized MyGPT tools tailored to discipline-specific tasks. Data came from semi-structured interviews, open-ended survey responses, prompt-writing practices, and AI-generated outputs. The findings reveal four themes: (1) the development of prompt literacy through iterative experimentation and reflection, (2) the strategic customization of MyGPT to support research workflows and academic writing, (3) critical engagement with AI outputs, including the identification of limitations, inaccuracies, and ethical concerns, and (4) shifts in learner identity and cognitive-emotional responses, including increased confidence, agency, and ambivalence. The study positions fine-tuned prompt literacy as a sustained, discipline-sensitive, and evaluative form of academic AI literacy in contemporary L2 contexts. Pedagogically, it suggests that EAP instruction should scaffold sequenced prompting, prompt diagnosis, and verification routines to support reflective human-AI collaboration. Future research should examine broader samples and longer-term development. Ultimately, when guided by explicit scaffolding and ethical awareness, customized AI tools like MyGPT can support not only academic writing development but also the cultivation of critical digital literacies among graduate EAP learners.

TI Cultural representation in Arabic textbooks: unveiling intercultural
   gaps and pedagogical implications in Indonesian Islamic higher education
SO MULTICULTURAL EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Arabic textbooks; cultural representation; content analysis; higher
   education; intercultural communicative competence
AB Cultural representation in Arabic textbooks is essential for fostering students' intercultural awareness, yet critical studies in Indonesian universities remain limited. This study examines cultural representation in six Arabic textbooks in Indonesian Islamic universities and their contribution to students' intercultural awareness. Using Krippendorff's content analysis of verbal and visual texts, the study applies a framework of cultural elements (people, products, practices, perspectives) and cultural types (source culture/SC, target culture/TC, international target culture/ITC), supplemented by a semi-open questionnaire with six lecturers. Results show an imbalanced representation: products dominate while practices and perspectives remain underrepresented; SC and TC appear more frequently than ITC. This confirms that Arabic textbooks are still oriented toward linguistic skills rather than intercultural competence. Pedagogical implications include reflective and comparative assignments, the integration of cross-contextual authentic materials (ITC), and the strengthening of lecturers' roles as cultural mediators-providing a basis for improving textbook design to support intercultural competencies.

TI Academic innovative environment and academic innovative behavior of
   university teachers: A moderated mediation model
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic innovative environment; Academic innovative behavior;
   University teachers; SOR theory; Moderated mediation model
ID PSYCHOLOGICAL CONDITIONS; INDIVIDUAL INNOVATION; INTRINSIC MOTIVATION;
   SELF-EFFICACY; ENGAGEMENT; RESOURCES; SAFETY
AB Although the academic environment is an important guarantee for academic innovation, the mechanism of their interaction has not yet been fully understood. This study aims to explore the influence of the academic innovative environment (AIE) on the academic innovative behavior (AIB) of university teachers, as well as the mediating and moderating roles of psychological factors. TI Beyond adoption: Teachers' pedagogical reasoning about generative
   artificial intelligence in schooling
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Pedagogical reasoning; Teachers'
   GenAI use; Teachers' perspective
ID BELIEFS; EDUCATION; QUEST
AB Much of the research on teachers and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has focused on whether teachers adopt or intend to adopt it. This line of work often frames adoption as desirable and treats teaching as uniform practice, rather than as situated decisions shaped by teachers' pedagogical reasoning. In this study, we moved beyond adoption to examine how teachers take GenAI into account and how pedagogical reasoning informs practice across contexts. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 middle-school teachers and analyzed them thematically. We identified four pedagogical reasoning profiles (higher-order thinking, authority and control, content delivery, and flexibility) that reflect how teachers consider GenAI in planning and classroom instruction. Across profiles, teachers described blocking GenAI in specific situations, for example, to preserve students' cognitive effort or to address other pedagogical concerns, even when they supported broader use. We discuss implications for research and practice.

TI AI literacy-related domains and AI-TPACK readiness among preservice
   mathematics teachers: A factor-informed structural equation modelling
   study
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; AI-TPACK; Preservice mathematics teachers; Structural
   equation modelling; Factor analysis; Teacher education
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; TECHNOLOGY; EDUCATION
AB In this factor-informed exploratory CFA/SEM study, AI-literacy-related domains were treated as theoretically informed and empirically tested predictors of AI-TPACK readiness rather than as fully validated independent latent variables. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly entering mathematics education, making it important to understand how preservice teachers become ready to integrate AI-supported tools pedagogically. This study examined AI-TPACK readiness among 130 preservice mathematics teachers at a South African public university. Exploratory factor analysis using polychoric correlations indicated that the AI-TPACK readiness items were essentially unidimensional; one weak design-confidence item was removed. The refined seven-item measurement model fitted better than the original eight-item specification, although discriminant-validity evidence for the broader AI-literacy-related domains was mixed. The primary gender-controlled latent SEM (sample n = 129) showed good approximate fit, chi(2)(602) = 789.92, p < .001, CFI = .981, TLI = .984, RMSEA = .049, SRMR = .082, and explained 53.0% of the variance in AI-TPACK readiness. Positive associations were observed for prior AI use, critical-ethical appraisal, and support/enablers. The support/enablers path had the largest standardised coefficient, but should be interpreted cautiously because the construct had marginal AVE and overlapped with information-source engagement. Year level was significant in the primary model but less stable in sensitivity analysis. Overall, the findings suggest that readiness was associated with direct AI experience and critical-ethical judgement, while the contribution of support/enablers remains provisional. The study contributes a cautious empirical account of AI-TPACK readiness in a Global South teacher education context.

TI Transformations in Children's Play in Rural Areas: Teachers' and
   Parents' Perspectives
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE children's play; digital technology; early childhood education; hybrid
   play ecology; parental mediation; parental perspectives; play
   transformation; rural childhood; rural Indonesia; teacher perspectives
AB Play for young children in rural areas is changing with social, cultural shifts and increased digitaltechnology use. This study explores changes in play among children aged 4-6 in three Gunungkidul villages, from parents' and ECE teachers' perspectives. Using a descriptive qualitative approach, data from 21 parents and six teachers were collected via online questionnaires and analysed thematically. The findings indicate that children's play has evolved into a hybrid play ecology in which physical, social, imaginative, traditional and digital play coexist across homes, schools and communities, rather than shifting linearly towards digital play. However, notable changes were observed in the context and proportion of play, including increased indoor and individual play, reduced spontaneous group play, a weakening of traditional play transmission and shorter durations of imaginative engagement. These shifts were associated with digital access, weakened peer ecosystems, parental safety concerns, changing family time structures, the use of devices as time-filling and calming tools and post-pandemic social habits. The study highlights the need for school-family collaboration and context-sensitive digital parenting and media mediation strategies to support balanced and developmentally meaningful play in rural early childhood settings.

TI Beyond Administration: How School Governance Practices Foster Happiness
   and Belonging Among Primary Students
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE participation; primary education; school governance; school happiness;
   student voice
ID VOICE
AB Schools are not only instructional settings but also critical social environments in which students' emotional well-being, sense of belonging, and agency are shaped. While previous research has emphasized the role of student voice in democratic schooling, limited empirical evidence exists on how governance-oriented practices function in primary education through participatory interventions. This study investigates how governance-based practices influence primary students' school happiness and sense of belonging through an action research approach. Conducted in a public primary school in T & uuml;rkiye, the study involved 15 third- and fourth-grade students and employed semi-structured interviews before and after the implementation of participatory governance practices. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis. The findings reveal that structured opportunities for representation and shared decision-making enhance students' emotional well-being, strengthen their sense of belonging, and foster greater engagement with school life. Students who perceived their voices as valued reported increased confidence, motivation, and psychological security, whereas limited participation and authoritarian practices were associated with feelings of marginalization and reduced attachment to school. The study demonstrates that participatory governance functions not merely as an administrative mechanism but as a socio-emotional infrastructure supporting students' holistic development. Although situated in T & uuml;rkiye, the study offers transferable insights for primary school governance contexts where student voice is emerging. By illustrating how democratic practices can be systematically developed through action research, this study contributes to the literature on democratic school leadership and offers practical implications for embedding student voice within primary school governance.

AB Background and Aims Down syndrome (DS) is associated with intellectual disability, with particular difficulties in expressive language and gross motor abilities, and relative strengths in receptive language. Here, we examine how this profile arises over the first five years of life.Methods A total of 104 children with DS (6-63 months) participated in a standardised developmental assessment (Mullen Scales of Early Learning; MSEL). TI When Cut Scores Impact Human Ratings: An Extended Many-Facet Rasch Model
   for Category-Specific Rater Severity Shifts
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT
LA English
DT Article
ID CROSS-VALIDATION; DEPENDENCE
AB The many-facet Rasch model (MFRM), widely used to analyze and evaluate rater-mediated assessments, focuses on between-rater differences in overall severity or leniency across facets and rating scale categories. Studying within-rater severity differences, particularly abrupt shifts in a rater's tendency to assign harsh or lenient ratings around specific scale categories, requires an extended modeling approach. Specifically, to focus on local, category-dependent severity effects, we propose the "many-facet Rasch model for category-specific severity shifts" (MFRM-CSS). Building on Bayesian parameter estimation, we demonstrate the model's suitability for examining local severity changes at scale categories with special significance as cut scores. In a simulation study and real-data analysis, we found that (a) differences in category-dependent severity levels affected observed score distributions and passing rates, (b) the MFRM-CSS reliably recovered true overall and local rater severity parameters, (c) ignoring local severity shifts biased overall severity and category threshold estimates, and (d) the MFRM-CSS outperformed the baseline MFRM, which does not account for category-specific severity shifts, in data-model fit when applied to essay rating data. In the real dataset, the greatest impact of local severity was observed at the second threshold, where the pass-fail cut score was set. The discussion highlights the practical implications of applying the MFRM-CSS and suggests directions for future research.

AB Introduction As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into university contexts, it is essential to understand students' perspectives of the competencies needed to apply its tools for academic writing. TI The Agentic AI bridge: a perspective on educational leadership, teacher

SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Agentic AI; developmental supervision; educational leadership;
   professional development; reflective practice; sustainability
AB Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming education, with the emergence of Agentic AI introducing new opportunities for adaptive, autonomous, and context-aware support.    satisfaction among educators in southern Peru
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

DT Article
DE educators; emotional intelligence; job satisfaction; teachers; work
   motivation
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; MEDIATING ROLE; TEACHERS
AB <p style="margin-left:0px; margin-right:0px">Background: Job satisfaction among educators has become a relevant concern for both public health and organizational functioning, particularly in socially vulnerable educational contexts in southern Peru. <p style="margin-left:0px; margin-right:0px">Objective: To examine the structural relationships among emotional intelligence, teacher work motivation, and job satisfaction among educators in southern Peru. <p style="margin-left:0px; margin-right:0px">Materials and methods: A cross-sectional study using structural equation modeling was conducted with a latent variable design in a non-probabilistic convenience sample of 294 educators from the Puno region (M = 41.66, SD = 6.51), of whom 58.2% were women. TI Exploring teacher attrition, retention and relocation in a Dutch urban
   context
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE attrition; primary education; relocation; retention; teachers
ID CARD SORTS
AB Introduction Teacher shortages are a growing concern, particularly in urban areas where retaining teachers is increasingly challenging. This study examines the factors influencing teacher attrition, retention, and relocation in Dutch primary education and explores how these factors differ across teachers who leave the profession, remain in urban schools, or relocate to schools outside Amsterdam.Methods A comparative qualitative design was employed, combining semi-structured interviews with a card-sorting task based on the four-capital model of teacher retention and attrition. The sample comprised former teachers (n = 13), current teachers in Amsterdam (n = 9), and teachers who had relocated from Amsterdam to another school (n = 7). Factors supporting retention included enjoyment of working with children, making a societal contribution, and positive collegial relationships. Relocation decisions were primarily driven by housing affordability, long commuting distances, and inadequate travel reimbursement, highlighting the importance of urban contextual factors.Conclusion The findings demonstrate that teacher attrition, retention, and relocation are shaped by distinct but interconnected factors. Strengthening school leadership, improving induction and classroom management support, and addressing housing and commuting barriers may help reduce teacher shortages and improve teacher retention in urban areas.

AB Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, yet comparative evidence from diverse international settings remains limited. This cross-national study examined undergraduate students' adoption and perceived academic impact of generative AI tools at institutions in Indonesia, Tajikistan, and the United States. A harmonized online survey was administered to 584 undergraduates during Spring 2026 (Indonesia n = 235; Tajikistan n = 226; United States n = 123). TI From Affordance to Autonomy Risk: A Dual-Pathway Model of Pedagogical
   Integration of Agentic AI in Higher Education Teaching
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE agentic AI; pedagogical integration; affordance theory; institutional
   capability; autonomy risk; higher education
AB Agentic artificial intelligence (AAI) systems-capable of autonomously executing multi-step instructional tasks with minimal human oversight-are reshaping higher education while exposing the limitations of adoption- and continuance-centred models that treat value and risk as independent predictors. In an environment of widespread AI availability, the more meaningful question concerns how deeply educators integrate delegation-capable systems into teaching, assessment, and instructional workflows. Drawing on affordance theory, institutional theory, and automation risk perspectives, this study develops and tests a dual-pathway framework that conceptualises pedagogical integration as a dynamic value-risk trade-off embedded within institutional and contextual conditions. Survey data from 338 higher-education educators across Global North and South contexts, all of whom underwent a structured screening process to verify exposure to agentic rather than conventional generative AI systems, were analysed using PLS-SEM with robustness and endogeneity checks. The model explains substantial variance in pedagogical integration (R-2 = 0.619), pedagogical value (R-2 = 0.621), and autonomy risk (R-2 = 0.615). Institutional AI capability is positively associated with pedagogical value and negatively associated with autonomy risk, whereas perceived AI complexity shows the opposite pattern. Higher pedagogical value is also associated with lower perceived autonomy risk (beta = -0.445, p < 0.001), suggesting that educators may interpret system autonomy as a manageable pedagogical feature rather than solely as a source of concern. Regulatory clarity weakens the complexity-risk relationship, while AI legitimacy strengthens the value-integration relationship. Given the cross-sectional design, findings should be interpreted as associative rather than causal.

TI Influencing Factors and Mechanisms of the Construction of Practical
   Knowledge for Chinese as a Foreign Language Intern Teachers in an Online
   Internship Program: A Qualitative Study Based on Key Events
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teaching internship stage; Chinese as a foreign language teacher;
   practical knowledge; key events
AB A persistent challenge in teacher education is that intern teachers often struggle to effectively apply theoretical knowledge to classroom practice. While constructing practical knowledge is key to bridging this gap, current research has paid insufficient attention to the dynamic processes and triggering mechanisms through which such knowledge develops among Chinese as a Foreign Language (CFL) intern teachers during the internship stage. This study focuses on the "key events" encountered by 7 CFL intern teachers participating in an online internship program at a teacher education institution in Northeast China, through 83 class observations and semi-structured interviews. Negative key events outnumber positive events in terms of quantity, depth of reflection, and persistence of impact. Reflection is the core mediating mechanism connecting key events and knowledge construction, but the "reflection-in-action" ability of intern teachers is weaker than that of expert teachers. This study reveals the dynamics and cross-cultural particularity of practical knowledge construction for CFL intern teachers, providing empirical evidence for optimizing teacher education internship training.

TI National Institutes of Health-Funded Institutional Training Programs in
   Colleges and Schools of Pharmacy
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB Unlike nursing and dentistry, pharmacy lacks a dedicated institute within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) to support its research and training needs, despite having many NIH-funded researchers within colleges and schools of pharmacy (C/SOPs). As a result, C/SOPs must compete across all NIH institutes for institutional (T-series) as well as individual (F-series) training grants. In 2024, the Council of Deans of the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy tasked a working group with assessing C/SOP participation in NIH-funded institutional training programs. Reviewing NIH RePORTER data from fiscal year 2024, we identified 26 institutional T32 training grants awarded to 18 C/SOPs, with most funding focused on pharmacology, toxicology, and chemical biology. Examining data for the distribution of funding, we observed that 61% of training grants were awarded to schools of medicine, whereas only 1% went to C/SOPs. We identified barriers that reduce pharmacy participation, which include the absence of dual Doctor of Pharmacy/Doctor of Philosophy degree programs, in which research and clinical training are fully integrated and the time to both degrees is shortened. Other barriers include a lack of education about how to develop training programs that are competitive for NIH T32 training grants. The task force developed a set of recommendations that include the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy sponsoring a training grant-writing program and advocating for funding pharmacist-scientist training programs. This may be particularly important for pharmacy-related fields, such as pharmacoepidemiology, pharmacoeconomics, and implementation science.

TI Recognizing, Honoring, and Nurturing Diverse Talents: Enabling Young
   People to Thrive in the World of the 21st Century
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE 21st Century Skills; diversity; talent development; creative problem
   solving; Discovering Intellectual Talents and Skills while Observing
   Varied Ethnic Responses (DISCOVER); paradigm shifts; research on talent
   recognition and development
ID GIFTED EDUCATION; MULTIPLE INTELLIGENCES; DISCOVER; IDENTIFICATION;
   CREATIVITY; STUDENTS; RETHINKING; MODEL
AB The purpose of this article was to present a conceptual framework and research-based methods for recognizing and nurturing a wide range of talents in inclusive settings. These methods (a) honor diversity of abilities, culture, language, income status, disabilities, values, and other personal characteristics and (b) enable students with talents to thrive in the world of the 21st Century. Research has been conducted during many research and development projects in several countries over a 36-year period. The framework and methods evolved through a rigorous process of designing, field-testing, evaluating, revising, and implementing methods for assessing and developing talents in varied domains. The underlying thesis is that creative problem solving and the 21st Century Skills of creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, communication, while using the ten talents wisely, are more important than knowledge and the ability to get the "right answer" to a question presented by the teacher or on a test. Results and methods used in research on indicators of talent in ten domains and tasks to elicit them are presented. Methods for recognizing and developing the talents are the focus for the final section: materials and guidelines for talent exploration centers and talent development principles for use in all classrooms. To make needed changes, educators, policy-makers, parents, psychologists, and others who have an impact on young people need to re-think prevailing ideas about recognizing and developing talents.

TI Frontline Staff Perspectives on Barriers and Facilitators to WIC
   Referrals Among Eligible Refugee, Immigrant, and Migrant Populations
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE food assistance; frontline workers; nutrition policy; immigrants and
   emigrants; refugees
ID FOOD; MEDICAID; SECURITY; FAMILIES; SNAP
AB Objective: To better understand the experiences of frontline staff who work with Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC)-eligible refugee, immigrant, and migrant (RIM) populations, specifically their experiences with the WIC program, role in the WIC referral process, and facilitators of and barriers to the referral process. Design: Qualitative; 3 groups and 11 individual interviews. Setting: In-person or virtual. Participants: Twenty-one frontline staff from 12 local organizations. Phenomenon of Interest: Frontline staff's role in the WIC referral process, and facilitators of and barriers to the process. Results: Ten themes emerged. Facilitator themes focused on easier WIC benefit redemption, RIM family reliance on WIC for food and formula, the essential role of frontline staff in connecting RIM families with WIC, child citizenship eligibility, and health care-based enrollment. Barrier themes focused on stigma related to benefit redemption, cultural and social barriers (e.g., language and transportation), WIC meeting requirements and food restrictions, limited cultural flexibility, and frontline staff unfamiliarity with WIC. Conclusions and Implications: Frontline staff play a crucial role in referring RIM families to WIC, but improvements are still needed in both the referral process and program. The findings can inform frontline staff training, guide future research, and support advocacy for policy change. TI Stakeholder Perspectives on Remote Delivery of a Group-Based Child
   Obesity Prevention Program for Latino Families With Low Income
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE nutrition education; Hispanic Americans; obesity prevention;
   telemedicine
ID IN-PERSON; MOTHERS; INTERVENTION; NUTRITION
AB Objective: To explore attitudes and preferences related to remote nutrition education programming for Latino families in the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) and primary care. Design: Community-engaged, qualitative, thematic analysis of interviews and focus groups. Setting: Prenatal and pediatric primary care and WIC sites in Manhattan, Queens, and Nassau Counties, New York. Participants: Four stakeholder groups: (1) past participants of a primary care-based obesity prevention program (Starting Early Program Prenatal) for Latino families that transitioned to remote delivery because of coronavirus disease 2019 (n = 40), (2) Latina WIC participants, including pregnant women and mothers of young children (n = 40), (3) Starting Early Program Prenatal staff (n = 6), and (4) WIC staff (n = 16). Phenomenon of Interest: Attitudes and preferences related to in-person vs remote nutrition education programming. Analysis: Focus groups and interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed for emergent themes using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Four themes emerged: (1) valuing in-person social connection while recognizing barriers to in-person gathering, (2) navigating distraction-related barriers to remote engagement, (3) consistent content delivery but uncertain quality of remote programs, and (4) coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic-related contextual factors. Conclusions and Implications: Future remote programs in WIC may benefit from incorporating opportunities for social interaction, explicit discussion of anticipated barriers, and strategies to overcome them.

TI Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic and 2022 Formula Crisis on WIC
   Nutrition and Breastfeeding Peer Counseling Services in Connecticut: A
   Qualitative Study
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE Key Words: COVID-19; breastfeeding; peer counseling; WIC; qualitative
   research
ID LACTATION-ADVICE; DISPARITIES; HELP
AB Objective: To describe the impact of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic and the 2022 formula crisis on the Connecticut Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children Design: Qualitative study using in-depth key informant interviews. Setting: The Connecticut WIC Nutrition and Breastfeeding Peer Counseling programs between December 2022 and June 2023. Participants: Twelve WIC staff members: administrators (n = 2), peer counselors (n = 6), nutritionists/ International Board-Certified Lactation Consultants (n = 3), and a breastfeeding coordinator (n = 1). Phenomenon of Interest: The effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on (1) perinatal care for WIC mothers, (2) the provision of nutrition and breastfeeding peer counseling services in Connecticut, and (3) the effect of the 2022 formula crisis on peer counseling services and participants. Analysis: An inductive, iterative approach was used to identify themes from the interviews. Braun and Clarke's 6-step approach was used to analyze transcripts. Results: The pandemic caused disruptions to perinatal care that affected the peer counseling process and required a rapid shift in WIC structure, workflow, and communication approaches. The formula crisis led to uncertainty, confusion, and increased interest in breastfeeding. The WIC program adapted quickly by providing remote/virtual services and flexible service hours. Conclusions and Implications: These findings support the continued use of remote/virtual breastfeeding peer counseling services and operations in the state of Connecticut WIC program.

TI The Impact of Standardized Letter of Recommendation Origin on Orthopedic
   Surgery Residency Match Outcomes
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE letter of recommendation; away rotation; home rotation; match outcomes;
   residency match; orthopedic surgery
AB Objective Orthopedic surgery remains one of the most competitive specialties in the United States residency match processes. Many factors are considered when evaluating applicants, including the Standardized Letters of Recommendation (SLORs). Away rotations play another instrumental role in the match. As both SLORs and away rotation play an important role in the orthopedic surgery match process, it is important to understand how home versus away SLOR writers influence match rates. Setting An individual, academic orthopedic surgery residency program accredited by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education in the United States. Participants Individual applications submitted to the residency program for the 2023 to 2024 orthopedic surgery residency application cycle were reviewed. After identifying 8.9 as the 50th percentile of SLOR scores, SLORs were divided into "high" scores (>8.9) and "low" scores (<= 8.9) (50th percentile) and match rates to orthopedic surgery programs between high and low scoring SLORs were compared using an adjusted odds ratio, while accounting for demographic and academic variables. Results About 350 SLORs were identified from 200 unique applications with an average score of 8.7 +/- 1.2, without differences between scores from home versus away institutions. The unadjusted match rate for applicants with a high home SLOR score was 88.5%, while those with a high away SLOR score only demonstrated a 66.0% match rate. After adjusting for confounding variables, applicants with a high scoring home SLOR were 4 times more likely to match than applicants with a high scoring away SLOR (p = 0.017). There was no difference in match success of applicants with low scoring SLORs from home versus away institutions. Conclusions Applicants with high-scoring home SLORs were associated with significantly improved match rates than those received from away rotations only, despite no significant difference in actual SLOR score.    Among Medical Students Applying to General Surgery
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical student; general surgery residency; scholarly productivity;
   research; residency match; bibliometrics
AB OBJECTIVE To evaluate longitudinal trends in scholarly output among U.S. MD applicants to general surgery and assess associations with match competitiveness. DESIGN Repeated cross-sectional, cycle-level longitudinal analysis of publicly available the National Resident Matching Program data from 2007 to 2024. SETTING United States National Resident Matching Program. PARTICIPANTS U.S. MD senior applicants to general surgery residency programs across 9 match cycles. RESULTS Mean scholarly output among U.S. MD applicants increased from 2.2 in 2007 to 10.9 in 2024. The proportion of matched applicants with 5 or more scholarly products increased significantly over time (beta = 0.037/year, p < 0.001) while those with zero scholarly products declined (beta =-0.015/year, p < 0.001). Matched applicants demonstrated higher scholarly output than unmatched applicants (5.6 vs 3.8 products). CONCLUSIONS Scholarly output among general surgery applicants has increased substantially over time, driven primarily by temporal trends rather than changes in competitiveness. Our findings suggest a shift toward a "productivity culture" in residency applications, with implications for surgical education structure, including equity and residency selection practices. TI Regulating Trainee Workload in Laparoscopic Simulation: Evidence from
   NASA-TLX and Pupillometry Analysis
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE eye tracking; laparoscopic simulation; NASA-TLX; skill development;
   training design; workload assessment
ID SKILL
AB OBJECTIVE: To explore whether a workload-adapted training protocol was associated with differences in trainee workload during laparoscopic simulation, using both self-reported and physiological measures. We hypothesized that adapting task difficulty to trainee progression would be associated with lower workload variability than a fixed-difficulty protocol. DESIGN: A randomized, controlled experimental pilot study. Participants were randomized into an Experimental group (workload-adapted protocol: task difficulty increased from low to high) or a Control group (fixed-medium difficulty). Workload was assessed using NASA-Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) and real-time pupillary response (Tobii Pro Nano). Data were analyzed using mixed ANOVA, Levene's test for equality of variances, and Pearson correlation. SETTING: Surgical Simulation Research Lab, University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta, Canada. PARTICIPANTS: Twenty-two novice participants (university students) with no prior laparoscopic experience were recruited. All 22 participants completed the full training curriculum and subjective assessments; valid pupillary data were obtained from 16 participants. RESULTS: NASA-TLX scores decreased significantly over time in both groups during training (p <0.001). No significant between-group differences were observed in mean NASA-TLX scores or pupil size values (p > 0.05). However, the Control group showed significantly greater variance than the Experimental group for both NASA-TLX scores (p = 0.04) and pupil size (p = 0.03). These findings suggest that the workload-adapted protocol was associated with lower workload variability during training. A weak but statistically significant positive correlation was observed between NASA-TLX scores and pupil size (r = 0.19, p = 0.020). CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that, within this pilot sample, the workload-adapted protocol was associated with lower workload variability during training. The observed association between pupillary response and NASA-TLX scores suggests that pupillometry may serve as a complementary physiological measure of trainee workload. These exploratory findings warrant validation in larger studies.

TI Generative AI literacy as a mediator between lifelong learning and AI
   competence in nursing students: A regression-based cross-sectional study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence literacy; Generative AI; AI competence; Lifelong
   learning; Nursing students
AB Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming nursing education and requires students to develop AI literacy alongside lifelong learning skills. Understanding how lifelong learning tendencies relate to generative AI usage and competence, and the potential mediating role of AI literacy, is essential for preparing digitally competent future nurses. Aim: To determine the lifelong learning tendency among nursing students, their levels of generative AI literacy, and their levels of generative AI usage and competence. Also, to examine the mediating role of generative AI literacy in the relationship between lifelong learning tendency and generative AI usage and competence. Design and setting: An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted at two state universities in the Mediterranean Region. Participants: The study was conducted with 533 nursing students between June and October 2025. Methods: Data were collected using a Personal Information Form, the Lifelong Learning Tendency Scale, the Generative Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, and the Generative Artificial Intelligence Usage and Competence Scale. Results: Students demonstrated high levels of generative AI literacy (36.66 +/- 7.30), lifelong learning tendency (120.61 +/- 22.73), and AI usage and competence (68.43 +/- 12.71). Conclusion: The findings suggest that lifelong learning tendency is positively associated with AI literacy and AI usage and competence, and that AI literacy plays a partial mediating role in this relationship. These findings suggest that supporting lifelong learning and developing generative AI literacy may be important for enhancing AI usage and competence; however, causal interpretations should be made with caution due to the cross-sectional design. Furthermore, these implications are limited to the educational context and should not be directly generalized to clinical practice<bold>.</bold> Further longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to evaluate the real-world applicability of these findings in clinical settings.

AB This study investigates the relationship between lexical features and text quality in analytical writing from a developmental perspective in L1 and L2 Spanish. TI LLM-derived metrics in second language writing assessment: an
   explainable AI approach
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Language education; Automatic language assessment; Large language
   models; Language resource; Explainable AI
ID SYNTACTIC COMPLEXITY; GRAMMATICAL COMPLEXITY; FLUENCY; LANGUAGE; INDEXES
AB Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in educational technology for automated writing assessment, yet most applications rely on prompt-based scoring and feedback generation, which often lack transparency, reproducibility, and interpretability. This study investigates whether model-internal LLM representations can provide interpretable and reproducible metrics for second language (L2) writing assessment. We derived surprisal and perplexity from next-token prediction to quantify linguistic predictability and embedding-based similarity to measure semantic coherence across sentences. These metrics were computed at the token, sentence, and discourse levels using three pretrained Chinese language models and evaluated on 1196 essays written by Chinese L2 learners across four proficiency levels. Their relationships with 11 established linguistic measures of fluency, lexical sophistication, phraseological complexity, and syntactic complexity were also examined. Results showed that surprisal and perplexity generally decreased with proficiency for the two Traditional Chinese-focused models, indicating greater linguistic predictability in more proficient writing, whereas the multilingual model showed weaker sensitivity. Embedding-based similarity increased with proficiency, reflecting stronger semantic coherence. Combining LLM-derived metrics with classical linguistic features improved proficiency classification and prediction beyond either feature set alone. Correlation and qualitative analyses further demonstrated that the proposed metrics capture complementary aspects of writing while revealing conditions under which their interpretations become less reliable. These findings demonstrate the value of interpretable, model-derived metrics for transparent, reproducible, and scalable AI-supported L2 writing assessment, particularly for underrepresented learner populations and lower-resource languages.

TI Enhancing engagement in virtual reality learning: Insights into design,
   usability, and pedagogical impact
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION: X REALITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Immersive learning; Sustainability education; Educational technology;
   Virtual reality in education
AB Virtual reality (VR) and metaverse platforms are now widely used to make difficult topics easier to experience and explore, on both headsets and regular screens. However, problems like dizziness, mixed engagement, and uneven uptake suggest that "more immersion" is not enough. What seems to mat-ter more are specific design choices: how the scene is laid out, how quickly tasks follow one another, and whether students use VR headsets or non-VR devices. In this study, we examined how a metaverse-style learning platform can be designed to feel comfortable, engaging, and worth using again for students with different devices and levels of gaming experience. Thirty-one design undergraduates completed a short sustainable agriculture activity, ei-ther in VR or on a non-VR device, and followed either a U-turn path or a simpler, linear path. We combined survey data with coded open-ended com-ments. Perceived usefulness and enjoyment were the strongest predictors of students' intention to use VR for learning, with attitude also helping, whereas feeling confident using VR alone and judging the interface "intuitive" did not increase intention as expected. Headset use and weekly gaming were both linked to lower immediate intention. A linear layout produced 18 percentage points fewer mentions of dizziness than the U-turn layout, and students who did not mention dizziness reported higher ease-of-use, enjoyment, perceived performance, and intention. Non-VR users and non-weekly gamers also re-ported higher intention than VRheadset users and weekly gamers, with no gender differences observed. Overall, the results highlight three design levers for metaverse-based learning: scenes that avoid unnecessary turning, small-step tasks with clear feedback, and real support for both VR and non-VR devices.

TI Cultural influences on patient safety error responses among nursing
   students: A qualitative study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Patient safety; Nursing education; Cultural diversity; Safety culture;
   Speaking up; Qualitative research
AB Background: Patient safety is a fundamental component of nursing education and professional identity formation. Although safety culture is widely discussed in the literature, limited research has examined how international nursing students interpret and respond to patient safety issues within culturally diverse clinical learning environments. Understanding these perspectives is important for the development of culturally responsive patient safety education. Aim: This study explored how cultural background shapes undergraduate nursing students' moral framing of patient safety, error attribution patterns, and responses to safety violations in clinical practice. Methods: A descriptive qualitative design informed by phenomenological principles was employed. Participants were 25 international undergraduate nursing students enrolled in a four-year nursing programme in T & uuml;rkiye and representing Middle Eastern, African, and European backgrounds. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analysed using Colaizzi's descriptive phenomenological method. Trustworthiness was supported through credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability strategies, including member checking, peer debriefing, and reflexive documentation. Findings: Participants across all cultural groups expressed a shared ethical commitment to preventing harm and viewed patient safety as both a moral and professional obligation. However, differences emerged in error attribution and intervention behaviours. European participants more frequently emphasised system-level contributors, whereas Middle Eastern and African participants initially foregrounded personal responsibility and vigilance. Cultural meanings attached to hierarchy and authority influenced willingness to speak up, and ambivalence toward formal reporting reflected tensions between relational harmony and organisational transparency. Participants also identified theory-practice gaps, limited simulation exposure, and a need for culturally responsive patient safety education. Conclusion: Patient safety behaviours among nursing students are shaped not only by curriculum content but also by culturally embedded moral and relational frameworks. Patient safety education should therefore integrate culturally responsive pedagogy, structured speaking-up practice, and explicit engagement with just culture principles to support safe practice in multicultural clinical learning environments.

TI Learning by leading-Nursing students' experiences with student-led
   simulation in home-based care
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Clinical practice; Home-based care; Nursing education; Student
   experience; Student-led simulation; Qualitative research
ID IN-SITU SIMULATION; INTERVIEWS
AB Background: Research on nursing students' experiences with student-led simulation is limited, underscoring the need for more in-depth exploration. Gaining insight into their experiences may contribute to the further development of student-led simulation as a pedagogical approach. Student-led simulation is a pedagogical approach in nursing education that integrates principles from peer-assisted learning (PAL) and experiential learning theory. Aim: To explore nursing students' experiences of their roles as facilitators of simulation-based training for healthcare personnel in home-based care settings. Design: A qualitative descriptive exploratory study using focus group interviews. Settings: This study was conducted at a Norwegian university and in home-based care settings. Participants: A total of 16 second-and third-year nursing students participated in the focus groups. Methods: Focus groups were recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using thematic analysis. Ongoing discussions among the researchers were used to support reflexivity and investigator triangulation and to develop and refine the themes. Findings: Themes indicate that student-led simulation fosters clinical reasoning, critical thinking, and professional identity. Students report deeper learning through scenario development than through participation alone. Acting as a facilitator promotes autonomy and academic engagement, whereas peer collaboration supports mutual learning and psychological safety. Debriefing emerges as a critical phase, enabling reflection and the integration of theory and practice. Teachers play a supportive yet nonintrusive role, while supervisors' involvement varies due to clinical demands. Organisational challenges, such as time constraints and a lack of coordination, are identified as barriers to optimal learning outcomes. Conclusions: Student-led simulation represents a valuable educational strategy that promotes holistic learning and professional development, empowering students to take ownership of their learning and contributing to improved competence among both students and healthcare personnel. The integration of simulation earlier in the curriculum, along with structured support and clear coordination, is recommended to maximise its pedagogical impact.

TI Nursing students' career intentions towards paediatric nursing: An
   integrative literature review
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing students; Paediatric nursing; Career planning; Nursing
   education; Integrative review
ID PREFERENCES; EMPLOYMENT; PERCEPTIONS; EXPERIENCE; NURSES
AB Objectives: This integrative review explores the factors that influence preregistration nursing students' intentions to specialise in paediatric nursing. The review was undertaken to address the absence of consolidated synthesis focusing specifically on paediatric nursing. Design: An integrative review of qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods studies was guided by the five-step process by Whittemore and Knafl and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement. Data sources: Seven electronic databases - Academic Search Complete, CINAHL Plus, Education Research Complete, MEDLINE, ProQuest Central, Scopus, and Web of Science - were searched using keywords: student nurse, career choice, paediatrics. The initial search was conducted in February 2024 and updated in January 2026 including forward and backward citation searching. Review methods: Studies were eligible if they were peer-reviewed primary qualitative, quantitative, or mixed methods studies published in English and examined factors influencing preregistration nursing students' intentions to specialise in paediatric nursing. All identified studies were independently screened for relevance by two authors, and the JBI Critical Appraisal tools were used to assess the quality of the included studies. A convergent integrated approach was used to synthesise findings across diverse study designs, and the findings were integrated through thematic narrative analysis. Results: Three interconnected domains shaped students' intentions to pursue a career in paediatric nursing: identity, perception, and experience. Students who identified as young women, particularly those with caregiving experience or a strong affinity for children, were more likely to express interest in the specialty. Paediatric nursing was frequently romanticised as joyful, meaningful, and emotionally rewarding - an image reinforced by societal narratives and cultural ideals. Clinical placement emerged as a pivotal influence: positive exposure built confidence and sustained interest, whereas negative or absent experiences prompted students to reconsider previously held aspirations. Conclusion: While educators may not shape students' identities, they can influence how paediatrics is perceived and experienced. Early engagement and deliberate placement strategies offer a critical opportunity to nurture sustained interest and optimise alignment between student aspirations and workforce needs.

AB Background: Due to global demographic changes and transformations of healthcare organizations, nursing students need to be adequately prepared for caring for older persons in home settings and for involving and supporting their family members. However, nursing students feel unprepared for and anxious about interacting with family members. This study is part of a project aiming to advance nursing education on this matter by involving undergraduate nursing students in the development of an educational intervention. TI Latent profiles of role overload and associated factors among nursing
   students: A cross-sectional study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Role overload; Nursing students; Latent profile analysis; Stress; Night
   shifts; Physical exercise; Sleep regularity
AB Background: Nursing students experience role overload due to the dual pressures of academic coursework and clinical internships, which can lead to stress and negative mental health outcomes. However, there is limited research on the heterogeneity of role overload and its effects on nursing students' psychological well-being. Objective: This study aims to explore the latent categories of role overload among nursing students, analyze the characteristics of these categories, and identify factors influencing role overload, providing insights for educational and psychological interventions. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 512 nursing students, and role overload was measured using the Role Overload Scale. Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) was used to classify students into different role overload categories, and multiple regression analysis was performed to identify predictive factors. Results: The analysis revealed three categories of role overload: low, moderate, and high. Significant differences were observed among groups in night shift frequency, physical exercise, sleep regularity, and weekly working days (all p < 0.05). Factors such as night shift frequency, physical exercise, sleep regularity, and the number of patients cared for were significant predictors of role overload. Students in the high overload group reported frequent night shifts, irregular sleep, and a lack of physical exercise. Conclusion: The results indicate that role overload among nursing students varies across individuals, with high overload linked to unhealthy lifestyle habits and high work demands. Strategies such as improving sleep quality, reducing night shifts, and encouraging physical exercise may help alleviate role overload and support students' mental health.

AB Teacher job satisfaction is a growing international concern, with evidence linking declining satisfaction to reduced well-being and poorer classroom functioning. TI Exploring the impact of augmented reality on cognitive load, emotion,
   and creative performance
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Augmented reality; Cognitive load; Emotion; Creativity
AB In recent years, Augmented Reality (AR) has been increasingly applied across various educational domains with promising outcomes. Although previous studies have reported positive effects of AR on learning outcomes, limited research has simultaneously examined its influence on cognitive load, real-time learning emotions, and phase-based creative performance. This study aimed to examine the effects of AR on cognitive load, learning emotions, and creative performance, and to further analyze its predictive power on these variables. A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest nonequivalent group design was employed with 59 high school students. The experimental group received AR-based instruction, while the comparison group received multimedia lecture-based instruction. The results indicated that AR significantly enhanced creative performance in the incubation and illumination phases, but had no significant effect on cognitive load. AR significantly reduced positive emotions across most phases, and creative performance was influenced both directly by AR and indirectly through emotional changes. Practical implications are proposed for AR content design, the timing of emotion measurement, the frequency and duration of AR use, and the characteristics of AR-based learning materials.

TI Designing effective feedback in video lectures using GenAI: The roles of
   feedback type and learner agency in error detection
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Media in education; Mobile learning; Lifelong learning; Adult learning
AB Many learners exhibit low engagement and high dropout rates when using traditional video lectures. With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), these systems are now capable of generating coherent, context-aware, and human-like feedback. However, limited empirical evidence exists regarding how the type of feedback and learners' active involvement in processing feedback affect learning outcomes in video lecture contexts. To address this gap, the present study conducted two experiments to examine how the type of feedback (Experiment 1) and agency in error detection (Experiment 2) influence students' motivation, engagement (as indexed by eye movements and learning behaviors), and performance gains. Across two experiments, the findings consistently showed that feedback combining knowledge of results and knowledge of correct response was more effective than feedback providing either component alone in enhancing learners' motivation, self-regulatory learning processes, and performance gains. Furthermore, when such feedback was coupled with learner-detected errors, learners demonstrated greater attentional engagement with instructional content, more sustained cycles of self-assessment and regulation, and superior performance gains compared with conditions involving GenAI-detected errors or no explicit error detection. Together, these results support feedback theories emphasizing that effective feedback should integrate evaluative and corrective information while engaging learners in generative processes of error detection.

TI "Conversing With a Sheet of White Paper": Imagination in Conceptualizing
   Logical Connectors
SO CULTURE AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE imagination; conceptual development; Vygotsky; French logical
   connectors; classroom interaction
AB Vygotsky remarks that the child who faces the written word must "converse with a white sheet of paper, with an imaginary or conceptualized interlocutor" (1934/1987, p. 202). This can be a challenge in literacy-based schooling. We draw on Vygotsky's work on imagination to further understand how this imagined interlocutor is vital to developing a grasp of linguistic concepts. We compared examples from a corpus of secondary-level French language lessons of two teachers as they scaffold tasks to enable students to master the conscious use of logical connectors expressing cause and consequence. The strategy that allows students to imagine themselves as interlocutors in a face-to-face conversation, as they think through grammar exercises, tends to lead students to further awareness of the logical relations involved.

TI Informal and formal learning experiences of LGBTQIA plus care in
   creating culturally intelligent student pharmacists
SO HEALTH EDUCATION JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
DE LGBTQIA plus; cultural intelligence; pharmacy; education; qualitative
   research
ID HEALTH
AB Objective: To understand the effect of formal and informal LGBTQIA+ educational experiences on cultural intelligence (CQ) and explore how formal and informal experiences relate to perceived LGBTQIA+ CQ, with CQ defined as the ability to effectively understand, adapt, and work in culturally diverse contexts. Methods: Qualitative data was collected from student pharmacists at one school of pharmacy between May 2024 and July 2024. Participants were invited to share previous LGBTQIA+ education experiences and perceived impacts via semi-structured, virtual focus group discussions. Educational experiences were either considered formal (structured, planned), such as classroom learning, or informal (non-structured, unplanned), such as social media. Deductive and inductive thematic analyses were undertaken to describe type of experience, its relationship to Bloom's taxonomy, and the depth of CQ demonstrated. Results: Twenty-one participants were involved in the focus group sessions. Commonly reported educational experiences included coursework, pharmacy work or rotation encounters, and social media. Overall, 78% of high-level responses for LGBTQIA+ CQ (Analyse, Evaluate, and Create on Bloom's taxonomy) came from participants with more educational experiences (>= 4). Participants with a higher percentage of informal experiences (>50%) had a greater amount of high-level responses on Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives (40% of responses), compared to participants with a lower percentage of informal experiences (<50%) who had a lower amount of high-level responses on Bloom's taxonomy (23% of responses). Participants with more educational experiences (>= 4) perceived informal experiences as being more impactful on their learning compared to formal experiences. Conclusion: Integrating greater opportunities for informal or patient-focused experiences into pharmacy curricula may enable student pharmacists to develop greater LGBTQIA+ CQ. To achieve this, educators should utilise experiential learning principles, encourage co-curricular opportunities, and include LGBTQIA+ topics and voices as part of their teaching and learning materials.

TI Unlocking digital entrepreneurial intention: The role of AI adoption and
   entrepreneurship education among university students
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI adoption; Digital entrepreneurial intention; Entrepreneurial
   self-efficacy; Entrepreneurship education; University students
ID SELF-EFFICACY; CHATGPT ADOPTION; CAREER
AB This study explores the mechanism through which artificial intelligence (AI) adoption influences the digital entrepreneurial intention of university students, with a particular focus on the moderating role of entrepreneurship education. Drawing on social cognitive career theory, the research model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) based on survey data from 571 Vietnamese students who had prior experience with AI and had completed at least one technology-related entrepreneurship course. The results reveal that AI adoption positively affects both entrepreneurial self-efficacy and digital entrepreneurial intention, with the effect on entrepreneurial self-efficacy being stronger. Entrepreneurial self-efficacy also positively influences digital entrepreneurial intention, though its effect is weaker than that of AI adoption. Furthermore, entrepreneurship education significantly moderates the relationships, amplifying the effects of AI adoption on both entrepreneurial self-efficacy and entrepreneurial intention. These findings provide novel evidence that AI adoption not only enhances entrepreneurial competence but also directly shapes entrepreneurial aspirations in the digital era. The study contributes by extending social cognitive career theory to the context of digital transformation and by highlighting entrepreneurship education as a critical factor that strengthens the link between technology use, entrepreneurial self-efficacy, and intention.

TI InterdisciplinaryCURE Studying Protein Aggregationwith Super-Resolution
   Fluorescence Microscopy Promotes Student ScientificSelf-Efficacy and
   Sense of Belonging
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate/General; Transfer Student; Biochemistry;
   Physical Chemistry; Curriculum; Interdisciplinary; Laboratory
   Instruction; Collaborative/Cooperative Learning;
   Inquiry-Based/DiscoveryLearning; Protein Aggregation; Single-Molecule
   Fluorescence; Super-Resolution Fluorescence Microscopy
ID PROINSULIN C-PEPTIDE; UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH EXPERIENCES; AMYLOID
   FIBRILS; INSULIN; BINDING; COPPER; ELUCIDATION; KINETICS; BIOLOGY;
   GROWTH
AB Research experiences are a powerful means of engaging students and a critical component of education in STEM fields. However, at large universities, the number of STEM undergraduate students greatly outnumbers the positions available in faculty research laboratories. Course-based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) provide research experiences for larger numbers of students and have been shown to support recruitment and retention of diverse student populations in STEM majors. Here, we describe a new CURE developed for first-year and transfer students to study protein aggregation with single-molecule, super-resolution fluorescence microscopy. Super-resolution fluorescence microscopy (the technique recognized by the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry) is a powerful tool for characterizing the growth and structures of protein aggregates associated with human disease. The CURE is highly interdisciplinary, combining biological and chemical wet-lab work with the chemistry and physics of single-molecule, super-resolution fluorescence microscopy and image-processing and analysis on the computer. Assessments of the CURE indicate that it (1) provides students with authentic research experiences of collaboration, discovery and relevance, and iteration, (2) improves factors such as scientific self-efficacy and sense of belonging that have been linked to improved student outcomes and persistence in STEM majors, and (3) contributes to personal student gains in the context of science. The CURE can be adapted to the study of any aggregation-prone proteins, enabling future adoptions and collaborations.

TI InteractiveRadiative Forcing Learning Tool To ConnectClimate Science to
   Chemistry Curriculum
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate/General; Environmental Chemistry; Web-based
   learning; Atmospheric Chemistry; Thermochemistry; Sustainability;
   Climate Change
ID CLIMATE SYSTEM; KEY INDICATORS; ANNUAL UPDATE; STATE; CO2
AB Radiative forcing, the change in Earth's energy balance since the beginning of the First Industrial Revolution in 1750, is the ultimate driver of climate change and one of the core Earth system processes that determines whether we are living within our planetary boundaries. Substances that are positive radiative forcers increase Earth's energy imbalance and contribute to warming, while negative radiative forcers decrease Earth's energy imbalance and cause cooling. Though radiative forcing is central to understanding the mechanisms that drive climate change, it is an unfamiliar concept to many chemistry students and the public. To bridge this knowledge gap, the King's Centre for Visualization in Science (KCVS) has developed an online interactive learning tool to help students explore these concepts further and connect climate change to their learning of core chemistry content. The learning tool visualizes changes in radiative forcing over time and quantifies how each of the key substances' interactions in the atmosphere have contributed to positive and negative radiative forcing. By engaging with this resource, students, educators, and the public can learn about the sources, impacts, and solutions to mitigate anthropogenic emissions of each radiative forcer. Initial assessment of the learning tool with undergraduate introductory chemistry students demonstrated that the learning tool was successful in increasing their foundational understanding of radiative forcing and its most important contributors.

TI ConstructingCrystal Structure Models with Poly(vinylalcohol) Beads
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE General Chemistry; Inorganic Chemistry; MaterialChemistry; Structural
   Chemistry; Crystal/Crystallography; Hands-On Learning/Manipulatives;
   Collaborative/CooperativeLearning; Discovery-Based Learning;
   Demonstrations
ID CRYSTAL-STRUCTURES; EDUCATION; BALLS
AB This article presents the construction of metallic, ionic and network covalent crystal structure models using poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) beads. With the assistance of the baseplates, the crystal structure models can be easily constructed layer by layer, and they can be decomposed into multiple parallel crystal planes from a specific perspective to uncover the stacking nature of atoms/ions in crystals. Model construction based on the PVA beads can improve students' spatial visualization of crystal structures, helping them conceptualize the structural characteristics of various types of crystals. It can not only stimulate students' enthusiasm for learning but also cultivate their teamwork ability simultaneously. In the teaching practice, students expressed overwhelmingly positive feedback on this model kit, and they exhibited a high level of interest in collaborating with their classmates to construct crystal structure models. In addition, this model kit is cost-effective and portable, and thus it exhibits extremely high practicality for hands-on activities and classroom demonstrations in the teaching of crystal structures.

TI A practical approach to illustrate the importance of the bodily energy
   and heat balances and of the associated regulatory loops to healthcare
   students
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Experimental learning; Thermoregulation; Metabolic rate; Climate change;
   Obesity
ID DISEASE; WEIGHT; WOMEN
AB Background Training medical students is a demanding task, and some contents remain difficult to teach and understand. This also applies to topics that require increasing attention. For instance, obesity rates keep rising, while almost each year turns out to be hotter than the last. Consequently, it is inevitable that current healthcare students will one day be confronted with these challenges. But the underlying physiological principles are concepts that prove difficult to understand. To remedy this situation and improve students' awareness and understanding of impacted patients, we have developed an educational tool to illustrate the concepts of metabolic rate and thermoregulation.Methods Following a 'learning by doing' approach, we designed practical courses covering these topics and comprising data production, collection and analysis. Students measure their heart rates, metabolism rates (indirect calorimetry) and body temperature, at rest and during moderate-intensity exercise. They then (i) quantify the amounts of energy expended as muscular work or heat, (ii) characterize heat dissipation mechanisms, and (iii) estimate theoretical core temperature rise in the absence of thermoregulatory control. Their data are ultimately integrated into a large cohort dataset (N = 89), enabling the study of confounding variables (e.g. sex, body size). This course is evaluated by the students via an anonymized web-based survey.Results Exercise-induced changes in heart rate showed that the test subjects were primarily healthy and challenged at a moderate level only. The measurements and subsequent calculations illustrated that this moderate-intensity exercise induced a strong increase in metabolic rate, and that this additional energy is spent as heat rather than muscle work. A dramatic shift in the relative contributions of the heat dissipation pathways during physical activity were also observed. Finally, average increase rates of core temperature of 1.33 degrees C/h at rest and 4.4 degrees C/h during moderate-intensity exercise were estimated. Only minor differences between female and male subjects were observed. This course has received very positive evaluations in recent years.Conclusions We present a readily implementable approach that integrates education and science. It is designed to favor medical students' comprehension of metabolic balance and thermoregulation while fostering critical evaluation of data quality and analytical rigor.
