TI Integrating Ethnoscience Within Project-Based Learning: Enhancing
   Twenty-First Century Skills of Science Pre-Service Teachers Through
   Lecturer Perceptions
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL OF SCIENCE MATHEMATICS AND TECHNOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Project-based learning; Ethnoscience-based learning; twenty-first
   century skills; Higher education; PLS-SEM
ID KNOWLEDGE; FRAMEWORK; EDUCATION
AB The integration of ethnoscience into project-based learning (PjBL) has gained increasing attention as a culturally responsive approach to fostering twenty-first century skills in science education. However, limited empirical evidence explains how lecturers' knowledge and pedagogical competence shape the implementation of Ethno-PjBL and its impact on students' twenty-first century skills. This study investigates the structural relationships among lecturer knowledge, pedagogical competence, Ethno-PjBL implementation, and students' twenty-first century skills in higher education science programs in Indonesia. A quantitative survey design was employed involving 38 science lecturers from multiple universities. Data were analyzed using partial least squares-structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results demonstrate that lecturer knowledge has a strong and significant effect on pedagogical competence (beta = 0.986) and directly influences students' twenty-first century skills (beta = 1.396). Pedagogical competence significantly predicts the implementation of Ethno-PjBL (beta = 0.885), while the direct effects of pedagogical competence and Ethno-PjBL implementation on twenty-first century skills are not statistically significant. The structural model explains a substantial proportion of variance in twenty-first century skills (R 2 = 0.965), indicating strong predictive power. These findings highlight that the effectiveness of Ethno-PjBL is primarily driven by lecturers' conceptual understanding and pedagogical readiness rather than the mere adoption of instructional models. The study underscores the importance of strengthening lecturers' professional knowledge and pedagogical capacity to ensure meaningful implementation of culturally integrated project-based learning for developing twenty-first century skills in higher education science classrooms.

TI Teaching Subject-Verb-Object Sentences to Students with Autism or Other
   Developmental Disabilities through Matrix Training
SO EDUCATION AND TREATMENT OF CHILDREN
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Combinative generalization; Matrix training; Syntax;

ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; CHILDREN; LANGUAGE
AB Students with autism or other developmental disabilities often experience delays in language development, particularly in constructing syntactically appropriate sentences. This study evaluated the effectiveness of matrix training in teaching Subject-Verb-Object (S-V-O) sentence construction to 14 Chinese-speaking students with autism or other developmental disabilities. The study was conducted in two phases. Phase 1 employed a concurrent multiple-baseline design across three participants to evaluate experimental control. These findings support matrix training as an efficient instructional strategy for promoting recombinative sentence construction in special education settings.

TI Preparing Indonesian Pre-Service English Language Teachers to Develop
   Generative Artificial Intelligence-Based Teaching Materials
SO ENGLISH TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Materials design; Pre-service
   English teachers; Teacher agency
AB The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence technologies presents new opportunities and challenges for learners, teachers, and pre-service teachers in education. While previous studies have focused on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education, including teachers' and learners' experiences, less attention has been paid to how pre-service English language teachers (PELTs) incorporate GenAI into their materials design. Drawing on an ecological perspective on teacher agency, this qualitative study explores four PELTs' experiences in designing GenAI-based teaching materials for their future classrooms. We collected multiple forms of qualitative data, including reflective journals, semi-structured interviews, and photovoice artifacts, which were thematically analyzed. Findings are Findings are organized into two main areas: (a) pre-service teachers' negotiation of the affordances and constraints of generative artificial intelligence in developing instructional materials and (b) their agentive practices in adapting materials, designing lessons, and developing assessment practices. The findings suggest that preparing PELTs for safe and effective use of GenAI requires explicit ethics policies, assessment designs that make learner authorship visible, and collaborative structures that build critical artificial intelligence literacy. This study contributes a practice-anchored account of GenAI-mediated ELT and shows how teacher agency can illuminate the pedagogical and ethical negotiation involved in materials design.

DT Article
DE Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI); AI literacy; Technology

AB As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into educational settings, understanding the factors influencing teachers' adoption of AI technologies has become an important area of inquiry. This study investigated the relationships between AI literacy and technology acceptance among Turkish secondary school English Language Teaching (ELT) teachers. TI Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Dual Perspective From Academics
   and Students on Its Transformative Potential
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academics; artificial intelligence; higher education; qualitative
   research; students
AB This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in higher education institutions in Kazakhstan. It aims to explore students' and academics' perceptions, usage patterns, challenges, and training needs. The findings show that AI is increasingly seen as a transformative academic tool, especially for research, language learning, writing support and problem-solving. Although many participants first encountered AI through media exposure or academic requirements, their engagement has shifted from initial scepticism to routine use, with many reporting daily reliance on AI tools. Participants highlighted AI's potential to create more personalised and interactive learning environments, particularly through applications like chatbots and adaptive learning systems. However, concerns were raised about over-dependence on AI, which could weaken critical thinking and problem-solving skills. These concerns align with previous research warning of passive learning behaviours in AI-supported educational settings. Despite widespread AI adoption, the study identifies significant gaps in institutional infrastructure and the absence of systematic training programmes. Most participants developed their AI skills through informal, self-guided learning rather than formal university instruction, underscoring the urgent need for structured AI literacy initiatives within higher education. Ethical issues, including algorithmic bias and data privacy, were also highlighted, emphasising the importance of responsible AI use and ethical governance in institutional policies and curricula. The results suggest that universities should invest in AI infrastructure, implement comprehensive AI literacy programmes and incorporate AI ethics education into academic curricula to prepare both students and faculty for effective and responsible AI use. This study contributes to the growing body of literature on AI adoption in higher education by providing empirical insights from the Kazakhstani context.

TI The impact of medical student gender on perception of gender bias and
   stereotype threat during the general surgery clerkship: a prospective
   cohort study
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender bias; Stereotype threat; General surgery; Clinical clerkship;
   Undergraduate medical education
ID VALIDATION; CAREER; SENSE
AB Objective Women remain underrepresented in many surgical specialties and leadership positions, despite gender parity among medical school graduates. Given that third-year clerkships are pivotal for career exploration, we investigated whether women who perceived greater gender bias and were more susceptible to stereotype threat reported a lower sense of belonging and worse well-being during their general surgery clerkship. Design Students were invited to participate in this prospective cohort study during clerkship orientation. Participants completed the same survey instrument during orientation and upon clerkship completion. Correlation analysis was conducted, and linear mixed models and regression models were created. Setting Virginia Tech Carilion School of Medicine (Roanoke, Virginia, USA), a tertiary care academic hospital. Participants All third-year medical students on their required six-week general surgery clerkship over an 11-month timeframe were eligible to participate, of which 48/49 students completed the survey at both timepoints. Results Perceived gender bias was negatively correlated with sense of belonging (pre: r = - 0.55, 95% CI (- 0.72, - 0.30), p < 0.0001; post: r = - 0.65, 95% CI (- 0.79, - 0.44), p < 0.0001) and well- being (pre: r = - 0.42, 95% CI (- 0.63, - 0.15), p = 0.003; post: r = - 0.40, 95% CI (- 0.62, - 0.12), p = 0.005); whereas, susceptibility to stereotype threat was less strongly correlated to both domains. Although women students reported higher perception of gender bias, the adjusted mixed-effects model demonstrated a small and imprecise gender effect (beta = 0.37, 95% CI (- 0.02, 0.76), p = 0.018). Women reported increased susceptibility to stereotype threat compared to men (beta = 0.82, 95% CI (0.32, 1.32), p = 0.001). Conclusions Perceived gender bias is a key correlate of medical students' sense of belonging and well-being during the general surgery clerkship. Interventions to reduce perceptions of gender bias may promote entry and success of individuals into surgical careers.

TI The downstream effect of gender bias on academic performance and career
   aspirations amongst female students in STEM via Gender-Professional
   Identity Integration (G-PII)
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender bias; Gender-Professional Identity Integration (G-PII); Women in
   STEM; Computing and Information Sciences (CIS); Academic performance;
   Career aspirations
ID BICULTURAL IDENTITY; POWER ANALYSIS; FIT INDEXES; ASSIMILATION;
   DYNAMICS; CONTRAST
AB Background Gender imbalance in STEM, characterized by a significant underrepresentation of women, remains a significant challenge. Although gender bias is a well-known contributor to women's attrition from STEM, the psychological mechanisms linking gender bias to departure are less well understood. Our research investigates early antecedents of attrition and the psychological processes that precede leaving the STEM pathway in tertiary education. Drawing upon identity integration research, we propose that perceived gender bias exerts undermines female STEM students' academic performance and career aspirations by reducing their Gender-Professional Identity Integration (G-PII), a construct that captures individual differences in the perceived compatibility between a woman's gender identity and her professional identity within a male-dominated STEM field.Results Across two studies, we examined 344 college students from the field of Computing and Information Sciences (CIS). In a cross-sectional study (Study 1), we first demonstrated that gender moderates the relationship between perceived gender bias and G-PII among STEM students. We then conducted a longitudinal study (Study 2) to further examine this moderation effect, assessing how perceived gender bias in CIS influences G-PII, in turn, influences female students' academic performance and future career aspirations in the field. This pathway is not observed among their male counterparts.Conclusion Our findings showed that the perceived bias-G-PII-career aspirations/academic performance link emerged only among female students. This highlights how gender bias within STEM fields undermines the perceived congruity between female students' gender and their STEM identities, negatively impacting their academic performance and reducing their interest in pursuing STEM careers after graduation. These insights reveal the psychological factors driving women's attrition in STEM post-college and highlight the need for educators and practitioners to address gender bias through an identity-focused lens. Strengthening female students' internal congruity through interventions that increase G-PII may enhance their academic performance and confidence in pursuing STEM careers.

AB Background Understanding STEM identity as process oriented may clarify how students form commitments to STEM and how these processes shape motivation. TI Effects of Temperature and Salinity on the Germinationof Triticum
   aestivum
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Graduate Education/Research; Environmental
   Chemistry; Agricultural Chemistry; Laboratory Instruction
AB In this laboratory exercise, students explore the potential impacts of temperature and salinity on agricultural systems. Specifically, wheat seed germination was evaluated across a temperature range of 15-35 degrees C and in the presence or absence of sodium chloride (NaCl), thereby simulating scenarios of rising temperatures and increasing soil salinity. The primary objective of this activity was to raise students' awareness of the challenges that climate change may pose to crop production and, consequently, to promote critical thinking about agronomic strategies that could mitigate these adverse effects. The results indicate that both root and shoot growth of wheat seedlings increase as temperature rises within the tested range. However, at elevated temperatures (35 degrees C), particularly under saline conditions, both root and shoot development were markedly reduced. These findings allow students to examine the interactive effects of temperature and salinity stress while connecting experimental observations to broader environmental and agricultural issues.

TI Experiential and problem-based learning in animation education:
   examining the role of problem-solving strategies in perceived
   effectiveness
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE 3D animation production; Experiential learning theory; Perceived
   effectiveness; Problem-based learning; Problem-solving strategies
AB This study investigates the relationships between design challenges, problem-solving strategies, and perceived effectiveness in 3D animation production within higher education. Grounded in experiential learning theory (ELT) and problem-based learning (PBL), a survey was conducted with 110 undergraduate students in an advanced animation programme at a public university. The findings show that while technical and cinematographic tasks were consistently perceived as challenging, user experience considerations were rated as less critical in academic settings. Students reported relying primarily on industry references, trial-and-error experimentation, reflective documentation, and feedback-driven revision. Regression analysis confirmed that problem-solving strategies were a strong and significant predictor of perceived effectiveness (beta = 0.882, p < 0.001), explaining 61% of the variance, whereas design challenges exerted no significant direct or mediated effect. The results highlight that effectiveness is shaped less by the presence of challenges than by the adoption of structured strategies, refining applications of ELT and PBL by emphasising the role of pedagogical scaffolding. Practically, the study suggests embedding training focused on strategy and reflective assessment into curricula, while strengthening collaboration between academia and industry to prepare students with adaptive skills for professional animation practice.

TI How paramedic degree apprenticeship students experience academic and
   workplace learning and the relationship between these domains
SO RESEARCH IN POST-COMPULSORY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Paramedic education; degree apprenticeships; professional identity;
   work-based learning; situated learning theory; apprenticeship pedagogy
ID CURRICULUM; INTERVIEW; EDUCATION
AB This study explores students' experiences of a paramedic degree-level apprenticeship, a higher education route to paramedic registration for existing ambulance staff. As research in this area is limited, understanding these experiences is vital for evaluating and developing the programme. This small-scale phenomenological study recruited six students from one ambulance trust in southern England. Data were gathered through audio diaries structured around Gibbs' (1988) reflective cycle and follow-up semi-structured interviews, analysed thematically. Findings showed academic and clinical learning were closely integrated, with students applying knowledge between domains. Participants learned through peers, mentors, and communities of practice, highlighting both benefits and inconsistencies. Academic learning transferred effectively into practice, while real-world experience helped students navigate the limitations of simulation-based teaching. However, online learning posed challenges around engagement and participation. With hybrid delivery now embedded in the curriculum, further research into enhancing online student engagement is recommended.

TI Teachers' grade retention beliefs and practices - the role of collective
   teacher culture
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teachers' beliefs; Grade retention; Collective teacher culture; Latent
   profile analysis
ID SELF-EFFICACY; NORMS; BEHAVIOR
AB Teachers have a complex, multidimensional system of socially constructed beliefs that shape their practices. Grade retention beliefs, in particular, are embedded within a broader psycho-pedagogical framework and may be reinforced when shared by the teachers' community. The present study used a person-centred approach to identify teachers' profiles based on their perceptions of collective teacher culture and grade retention beliefs, to examine how these profiles relate to other psycho-pedagogical beliefs, and to their grade retention intentions and practices. An online questionnaire was completed by 1,597 Portuguese basic education teachers, assessing their beliefs about learning, assessment, intelligence, and grade retention; their intentions and practices regarding grade retention; and their perceptions of collective teacher culture. Latent profile analysis identified six profiles, differentiated by teachers' perceptions of the collective teacher culture (two weak, two moderate, and two strong), with three profiles supporting grade retention and three sceptical of it. Covariate analyses showed that teachers in the Grade Retention Support profiles reported stronger transmissive and fixed intelligence beliefs, whereas teachers in the Grade Retention Scepticism profiles reported more malleable intelligence beliefs. Teachers in the Strong Collective Teacher Culture profiles also endorsed more transmissive teaching and summative assessment beliefs. Teachers in the Scepticism profiles showed a lower intention to use this practice. The highest grade retention rates were observed within the Weak Collective Teacher Culture and Grade Retention Scepticism profile. These findings highlight the importance of reflective and collaborative practices among teachers to share effective strategies that enhance student success, strengthen collective efficacy, and reduce grade retention rates.

   support of specific language learner difficulties

AB This research examines how scholars in English Language Teaching (ELT) and Special Education (SE) perceive and tackle Specific Language Learner Difficulties (SLLDs) in teacher education in Turkiye and existing pedagogical deficiencies. It suggests a paradigm for enhancing inclusive ELT methods in global educational settings. The research employed a qualitative methodology. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews with 10 academics chosen by purposive sampling. The interviews were thematically analysed, supported by MAXQDA. TI Expert Judgments as an Approach to Evaluating Items' Instructional
   Sensitivity
SO APPLIED MEASUREMENT IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; STANDARDS; ACCURACY; TEACHERS; ANGOFF; TESTS
AB Instructional sensitivity is an item characteristic that refers to the extent to which an item captures the effects of instruction on student performance. One potentially economical approach to evaluate instructional sensitivity is based on expert judgments. However, little is known about their validity. This study investigates expert judgments from four perspectives: a comparison (1) of teachers and subject matter specialists; (2) of a global and a differentiated rating; (3) of the differentiated rating facets, and (4) of expert judgments to statistical measures of sensitivity. Results indicate that (a) teachers perform better than subject matter specialists, (b) the differentiated rating offers no advantage over the global rating, (c) experts can distinguish the facets of the differentiated rating, and (d) expert judgments and item sensitivity measures are weakly to moderately related. We conclude that expert judgments show potential but are not (yet) sufficiently accurate to replace established procedures for investigating instructional sensitivity.

TI The use of electronic chat in French language teaching to develop
   written interaction skills among faculty of education students
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Electronic chat; FFL teaching; Written interaction; Quasi-experimental
   design; Faculty of education students
AB Written interaction is a core component of foreign language development because it enables learners to negotiate meaning, respond to others, and refine linguistic knowledge in context. This study examined the effect of electronic chat (e-chat) on the development of written interaction skills among students in the Faculty of Education. To this end, the study developed a written interaction skills framework, a student activity booklet, a lecturer's guide, and a written interaction test. Using a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control-group design, the study was conducted with second-year French as a Foreign Language students at Beni-Suef University. After the instructional intervention, quantitative analyses showed a statistically significant difference at the alpha = 0.01 level between the experimental and control groups on the post-test of written interaction in favor of the experimental group, with a large effect size. The experimental group also showed substantial gains from pre-test to post-test. These findings suggest that e-chat, when embedded in structured pedagogical tasks, can support the development of written interactional competence. The study concludes with pedagogical implications, limitations, and directions for future research.

TI Curriculum by design: Enabling early career teachers' summative
   assessment through competence, confidence, and opportunity
SO CURRICULUM PERSPECTIVES
LA English
DT Article
DE Curriculum enactment; Summative assessment; Early career teachers;
   Assessment literacy; Teacher agency; Initial teacher educaiton
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; ASSESSMENT LITERACY; PERCEPTIONS; PRESERVICE;
   SUPPORT
AB Summative assessment is a critical mechanism of curriculum enactment, yet early career teachers often encounter substantial challenges in designing and implementing assessment tasks that meaningfully align with curriculum goals and pedagogical intent. This study investigates the enabling conditions that support early career secondary teachers in Queensland, Australia, to develop confidence and competence in designing effective summative assessments. A cross-sectional survey of 116 early career secondary teachers explored their experiences across four domains: initial teacher education (ITE) preparation, current opportunities for assessment design, confidence in practice, and preferences for professional learning. Quantitative analyses-including frequency distributions, paired t-tests, and correlation matrices-were used to examine patterns across three interrelated constructs: Competence, Confidence, and Opportunity. While most participants had been introduced to assessment theory during ITE, many reported feeling underprepared to independently design new assessment tasks or rubrics at graduation. Confidence in assessment design increased significantly with contextualised, supported practice. Opportunities to engage in assessment creation and receive feedback were strongly associated with growth in both competence and confidence. Despite low interest in formal external professional development, participants expressed strong preference for mentoring and embedded, practice-based support. This study introduces and affirms a conceptual framework in which iterative interactions among Competence, Confidence, and Opportunity underpin early career teachers' curriculum enactment through assessment. Findings have implications for teacher education, school-based professional learning, and curriculum policy, highlighting the importance of relational, practice-embedded support to build teachers' curriculum capacity.

TI A Teaching Experiment on Moisturizing Hydrogels forIvory Protection:
   From a Single-Layer Acrylic Hydrogel to a Silicone-Modified Bilayer
   Hydrogel
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Hydrogel; Cultural Relics Protection; Ivory; Postgraduate Laboratory
   Experiment; Interdisciplinary Education; Materials Characterization
ID CONSOLIDATION; SANDSTONE
AB Chemistry plays an essential role in the conservation of water-sensitive organic artifacts. Unearthed ivory objects from the Sanxingdui site are particularly vulnerable to irreversible damage, such as cracking and powdering, due to moisture loss. This challenge provides a real-world context that naturally stimulates postgraduate students' interest and engagement. To address it, we designed a laboratory project that integrates professional education with research practice. Students prepared both a single-layer poly(acrylamide-co-acrylic acid) (P(AM-AA)) hydrogel and a bilayer hydrogel combined with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) (P(AM-AA)/PDMS). The materials were characterized (e.g., for chemical structure, optical properties, mechanical behavior, and thermal stability), and their performance was tested under 25 degrees C and 50% relative humidity (RH). The bilayer hydrogel outperformed the single-layer hydrogel and an untreated control group in preserving the weight and morphology of ivory and plant sample. Based on a post-experiment questionnaire, students reported significantly strengthened awareness of cultural-heritage conservation and enhanced ability to justify material selection and design. The questionnaire also revealed that students deepened their understanding of four core chemical concepts, which are hydrophilicity, hydrophobicity, hydrogen bonding, and interfacial adhesion, and directly applied them to the bilayer hydrogel design. Overall, students expressed high levels of engagement and satisfaction, noting that the authentic research context effectively improved their integrated experimental competencies in polymer materials chemistry and their research capability to solve real-world protection problems. The proposed hydrogel-based approach also provides a potential material strategy for the conservation of other moisture-sensitive cultural heritage materials.

TI Malpractice fear and career decision regret among resident physicians: a
   cross-sectional study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Resident physician; Fear of malpractice; Career decision regret; Health
   law
ID DEFENSIVE MEDICINE
AB Background Malpractice litigation is increasingly prevalent in contemporary healthcare and may influence both clinical decision-making and physicians' psychological well-being. The present study aims to evaluate the fear of malpractice and career decision regret among resident physicians and to identify factors associated with these constructs. Methods A total of 308 resident physicians (87.7% of the eligible population) from surgical and non-surgical clinical specialties at a university hospital in Turkey were included. Fear of malpractice was assessed via the Malpractice Fear Scale, and career decision regret was assessed via the Decision Regret Scale. We collected data on sociodemographic characteristics, specialty preferences, and exposure to malpractice complaints. Multivariate linear regression identified independent predictors of fear of malpractice and career decision regret. Results High levels of fear of malpractice were reported by 73.1% of the residents, and 73.4% experienced varying degrees of career decision regret, predominantly mild regret (44.2%). Fear of malpractice and career decision regret were modestly (r(s) = 0.228, p < 0.001) but significantly associated. Higher fear of malpractice scores (beta = 0.178, p = 0.001) and prior personal exposure to malpractice complaints (beta = 0.132, p = 0.017) independently predict increased career decision regret. Awareness of colleagues accused of malpractice was strongly associated with greater fear of malpractice (beta = 0.219, p < 0.001). Intrinsic motivations, including interest in the chosen specialty (beta = -0.176, p = 0.001) and professional satisfaction (beta = -0.147, p = 0.007), were associated with lower career decision regret. No significant differences in fear of malpractice were observed between residents in surgical and non-surgical clinical specialties (p = 0.227). Conclusions Fear of malpractice is a prevalent stressor among resident physicians and is significantly associated with career decision regret. While malpractice-related experiences may increase regret, intrinsic motivations for specialty choice-particularly personal interest and professional satisfaction-appear to buffer against career decision regret. These findings suggest that strengthening both medicolegal support and factors that promote professional fulfillment may help improve residents' career well-being. Integrating medicolegal education, psychological support, and institutional risk-management strategies into residency programs may help mitigate these adverse effects.

TI Educators' experiences transitioning from a traditional to an AI-aware
   assignment rubric: a qualitative study in a health and medicine course
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic integrity; AI-aware assessment; artificial intelligence;
   rubric; teaching and learning
AB Assessment strongly shapes student learning and engagement. Traditional assessment rubrics in health and medicine education often fail to account for emerging challenges posed by artificial intelligence. The use of AI tools risks encouraging surface-level learning and undermining academic integrity if not addressed through purposeful assessment design. This study evaluates the impact of transitioning from a traditional to an AI-aware rubric in a Health and Medicine course, examining how this shift influenced educators' grading practices, instructional strategies, and perceptions of student engagement. Methods: A qualitative research design employed semi-structured interviews with three educators who had taught the course using both original and revised rubrics. Educators perceived that the revised rubric supported deeper student engagement with AI, increased their grading confidence, and prompted shifts in instructional approaches. Conclusion: AI-aware rubric design can meaningfully reshape both teaching and assessment practices. However, sustainable implementation requires institutional support, structured professional development, and clearer policy guidance on acceptable AI use. The study also refines the Twelve Tips framework, positioning it as a flexible design heuristic rather than a prescriptive checklist. These findings are particularly relevant for undergraduate health professions programs navigating rapid educational and technological change.

TI Developing and validating a domain-specific instrument for measuring
   physical education teachers' acceptance of artificial intelligence: the
   AI-PEQ
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

DT Article
DE AI-PEQ; artificial intelligence; instrument development; physical

   acceptance; technology acceptance
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY
AB Introduction The growing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational settings has created an urgent need for psychometrically validated instruments capable of measuring educators' acceptance of AI-enhanced tools within specific disciplinary contexts. In Physical Education (PE), this need is particularly acute; despite the proliferation of AI-supported technologies such as motion capture systems, biomechanical feedback platforms, and adaptive performance analytics, no validated domain-specific scale existed to assess PE teachers' acceptance of such tools before this study. This paper reports the development and psychometric validation of the AI in Physical Education Questionnaire (AI-PEQ), a new instrument designed to measure PE teachers' acceptance of AI across five theoretically grounded constructs: AI Awareness, Perceived Educational Value, Ethical Considerations, Perceived Curriculum Integration Feasibility, and Behavioral Intention.Methods Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), item generation followed a systematic, literature-informed procedure. The study contributes to the emerging scholarship on technology-enhanced physical education by providing the field's first validated instrument for measuring AI acceptance and offers a replicable methodological framework adaptable to other specialist education contexts.

TI Blind teachers in the educational system-an oxymoron? A participatory
   research project to identify subjectively reconstructed barriers to
   participation in teacher training in Germany
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ableism; barriers to inclusion; epistemic injustice; participatory
   research; teacher education
ID ABLEISM; STUDENTS
AB Against the backdrop of international discourse on social justice and inclusive education, this participatory research project examines subjectively reconstructed barriers faced by blind teachers during teacher training in Germany. Although the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) guarantees equal access to education, there are clear discrepancies between political aspirations and the reality of pedagogical professionalization in German-speaking countries. While numerous studies take into account the perspective of visually impaired students, the views of blind teachers remain largely unexplored. Drawing on the concept of Epistemic Injustice and the approach of Inclusive Participatory Action Research, episodic interviews were conducted with six blind teachers. Qualitative content analysis identified three central themes: (a) dysconscious and benevolent ableism, particularly in the form of doubts about professional competence; (b) strained social relationships in the second phase, characterized by increased pressure to perform, competition among peers, and critical attitudes on the part of trainers; and (c) lack of accessibility in materials, rooms, and organizational structures, often exacerbated by complex requirements for the use of personal assistance. The results show a clear break between the university and school practice phases and illustrate that inclusion must be understood as an intersubjective experience of belonging, acceptance and value that are dynamic and in flux and systematically anchored in the structures of teacher training. By foregrounding blind teachers as epistemic agents, this study extends inclusion research beyond student perspectives and offers one of the first empirical analyses of teacher training barriers in the German context.

AB Some higher education institutions prohibit beverages in classrooms to protect cleanliness, infrastructure, safety, and discipline. AB We designed this course during the COVID19 pandemic on reverse vaccinology (RV) that utilized authentic online bioinformatics learning tools. We utilized Slack as a free Learning Management System (LMS) to make the resources available to the students. High-impact activities included, but were not limited to, the hands-on exploration of the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) gene search, NCBI genome search, Virulence factor database (VFDB), BepiPred.2, Expasy Prosite, and Open reading frame (ORF) finder. Student to student and student-teacher interaction along with assignment submission happened over Zoom and Slack. All the tools utilized in this course were freely available online. In the post-course survey, students expressed confidence in their bioinformatics skills.

TI Modelling the Impact of Extramural English on Undergraduates' L2
   Achievements: Task Engagement as a Mediator
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE task engagement; extramural English; undergraduates; L2 achievements
AB This exploratory mixed-methods study investigated the relationships among students' engagement with L2 tasks, extramural English, and their self-assessed L2 proficiency. Participants were undergraduate students at a public university in Myanmar. First, qualitative data were elicited from eight students; then, quantitative data were collected from 336 participants. The thematic analysis revealed how students engaged with L2 tasks and extramural English cognitively, behaviourally, emotionally and socially. The quantitative results underpinned with evidence of students' high to moderate levels of engagement with tasks in their English classes and beyond them. These findings highlight the pivotal role of task engagement both in and outside English classes. L2 educators should recommend and integrate extramural English activities to enhance their students' proficiency in English.

TI Designing GenAI-Mediated Mathematics Storybooks: Process Patterns and
   Tool Affordance Uptake Among Pre-Service Early Childhood Teachers
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative AI; digital storytelling; pre-service teachers; teacher
   education
AB Digital storytelling is widely used in education as a multimodal design practice that foregrounds creator agency and audience awareness. Generative AI (GenAI) expands the speed and range of story production but also raises questions about how educators retain pedagogical control over generated content. This exploratory qualitative study used cross-case workflow analysis to examine how 27 pre-service early childhood educators in Hong Kong designed GenAI-mediated mathematics storybooks. Data included video-recorded process presentations, records of interactions with ChatGPT (GPT-5) and Krea 2, and completed storybooks. Analysis traced participant decisions across planning, generation, curation, and integration, focusing on GenAI-related affordance uptake, recurring workflow patterns, and tensions among technical innovation, ethical accountability, and cultural impact. Findings show that participants commonly used GenAI to steer generation through pedagogical constraints; expand narrative and visual alternatives; and select, reject, or revise generated materials. Two recurring process patterns were identified: constraint-guided planning-to-generation, in which pedagogical requirements were established early and used to guide subsequent decisions, and exploration-to-selection, in which participants generated and compared alternatives before progressively stabilizing a preferred direction. Across both patterns, tensions were particularly evident during curation and integration, when participants balanced efficiency with sustained oversight, creative variation with pedagogical coherence, and generic outputs with local contextual fit. The findings show that GenAI-mediated storybook creation is not simply a process of generating text and images, but a pedagogical workflow in which pre-service teachers exercise agency through the critical selection, revision, and integration of AI-generated materials. Implications are discussed for teacher education, AI literacy, and the design of scalable support for teachers' use of GenAI.

TI "Peace Is (Not) a Political Position": Intercultural Competence in
   Higher Education at Times of War
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE peace; teacher training; liberal multiculturalism; trust; dialogue;
   neutrality
ID CONFLICT-RESOLUTION; CULTURE; CRITIQUE
AB This study examines the challenges facing intercultural competence education in higher education during times of intense conflict. Most of the intercultural competence programs in higher education are based on Western liberal multicultural logic that strives to build trust between groups in conflict to promote peacemaking. The common conception of trust is described as a developmental cognitive-emotional effort that is anchored in a reflective and multi-perspective calculation of events and procedures that require a willingness to give up parts of positions and standpoints. The process is supposed to be mediated by a professional and unbiased facilitator who creates a "dialogic space" based on self-reflection and perspective-taking of the "other". Previous findings suggest that these programs were relatively efficient before the 7 October war broke out in Israel. Thus, a joint Palestinian and Jewish program that was conducted at a teacher training college after 7 October challenged these findings. Examining the discursive practices used by the participants during the meetings revealed that the basic liberal multicultural assumptions of the intercultural competence model were rejected by students from both groups. The students interpreted the model as a way to contextualize the term peace in a specific ideological-political context. Understanding peace as a concept with a layered meaning contradicts the intercultural competence model's perception of it as a universal-humanistic-independent position. Thus, the findings further problematize the universal perception of intercultural competence models in order to adjust them to teacher trainees working outside the West during difficult times.

TI Effects of Language Policy and Learners' Sociolinguistic Background on
   Educational Achievement in a Multilingual City in the Philippines
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTBMLE); bilingual
   education; language of instruction; language policy in education;
   regional and minority languages; non-dominant languages; learning
   outcomes; achievement gap; Philippine education
ID MOTHER TONGUE INSTRUCTION; MINORITY LEARNERS; READING GROWTH; GAP;
   TRAJECTORIES; STUDENTS
AB In the Philippines, most children speak regional languages like Ilokano, Cebuano, and Hiligaynon as their first language (L1), but they have historically been schooled in English and Tagalog (i.e., Filipino). In 2012, the Department of Education (DepEd) institutionalized Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTBMLE), designating regional/local languages as the primary medium of instruction in the early grades. Despite this major policy shift, data on how it affected children of different linguistic and ethnic backgrounds remain scarce. This study addresses that gap by examining the effects of language-of-instruction (LOI) policy, child L1, and parental ethnicity on Grade 1 academic achievement in San Fernando, La Union-a multilingual city where Ilokano is the predominant language of the community and Ilocos Region. This quasi-experimental pre-post cohort comparison leverages an exogenous policy change to analyze data from 3002 Grade 1 students across 10 urban public schools in two consecutive school years: the last year of the old English-Filipino bilingual policy (SY 2011-2012) and the first year of MTBMLE (SY 2012-2013). Ordinary least squares and mixed-effects linear regression models estimate the effects of LOI policy, child L1, parental ethnicity, and their interactions on achievement scores. Under the old L2-oriented bilingual policy, L1 Ilokano children (the demographic majority) achieved significantly lower academic ratings than their L1 Tagalog peers, with an estimated gap of approximately 1.17-2.13 points (up to 0.5 standard deviations). Within one year of MTBMLE implementation, this gap decreased to just 0.10-0.18 points (less than 0.1 SD), driven primarily by an increase in Ilokano-speaking children's achievement across all subjects. Parental ethnicity moderates these effects: children with at least one Ilokano parent showed greater achievement gains under MTBMLE than children with no Ilokano parents, but having one Ilokano parent was more advantageous than two. This suggests that multilingual home environments influence outcomes in complex ways. Overall, the findings provide empirical support for MTBMLE's positive impact on educational outcomes and equity, observable even within the first year of implementation. They carry urgent implications as the Philippine government has suspended the policy under Republic Act 12027 of 2024. Policymakers are urged to disaggregate educational achievement data by children's home languages, and incorporate L1s in instruction, assessment, and program evaluation.

TI Student-AI collaboration in peer feedback: Effects on perceived feedback
   quality, emotional responses, and feedback literacy development
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer feedback; Generative artificial intelligence; EFL writing; Feedback
   literacy; Task enjoyment; Task anxiety
ID DESIGN
AB This study investigates how English as a foreign language (EFL) student reviewers engage in openended, dialogic interactions with generative artificial intelligence (AI) during the feedback generation process in peer assessment within EFL writing classrooms. It examines the impact of these interactions on feedback quality perceived by recipients, emotional responses (task enjoyment and anxiety), and feedback literacy. A quasi-experimental design was employed with 60 Chinese undergraduate students, divided into an experimental group (EG) that used generative AI (Doubao) for support and a control group (CG) that did not. Over three intervention cycles, data from chat histories, feedback quality ratings by recipients, and pre/post questionnaires on emotions and feedback literacy were analyzed. Nevertheless, AI support led to significant, progressive improvements in the perceived quality of feedback, particularly in affect, description, justification, and constructiveness. Furthermore, EG students reported significantly higher task enjoyment and lower anxiety compared to the CG. The intervention also positively enhanced all dimensions of feedback literacy: knowledge and abilities, willingness to participate, cooperative learning, and appreciation of peer feedback. The findings suggest that generative AI can serve as a powerful scaffold, reducing the emotional and cognitive burdens of peer assessment while fostering a more supportive and effective feedback environment. This study underscores the value of integrating AI into peer feedback practices to develop students' feedback literacy and improve the overall quality of peer learning experiences.

TI Comparing human and LLM ordered coding of qualitative data: How coding
   differences cascade through temporal analysis
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Ordered data coding; Qualitative coding; Text classification; Large
   language models; Automated feedback systems; Transition network
   analysis; Learning analytics; Artificial Intelligence
AB Automating the process of qualitatively coding text data from learners has been a long-standing ambition of learning analytics researchers since it represents an essential step toward delivering timely and scalable feedback. Automating this process is especially challenging in the case of ordered coding schemes -necessary for temporal analytical methods- where one text utterance can be assigned more than one qualitative code and the assignment order matters. This problem goes beyond multi-class and multi-label classification and, therefore, cannot be easily tackled using classic language models such as BERT. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, especially with the advent of large language models, have -allegedly- created a substantial step forward in making the goal of automatically coding complex temporal data attainable. However, little is yet known about how to implement this process in a way that most closely resembles human coding, i.e., taking into account the context in which the textual data appears for accurate interpretation. Moreover, due to the complexity of the data and its shape, the accuracy of the results cannot be computed using classic accuracy metrics. This study makes two main contributions: first, it presents two evaluation approaches for assessing the quality of ordered data coding and the usability of LLM in automatically coding ordered processes; and second, it demonstrates a method of LLM prompting that leverages a consistent context window. Our results reveal systematic and statistically significant differences between LLM and human coding across structural, transitional, and code-level metrics for binary and ordered tasks. As classification errors can propagate through automated feedback systems, relying on LLM outputs risks amplifying inaccuracies and producing misleading interpretations of learning processes.

TI Institutional structures, digital inequality, and AI integration in
   higher education
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Higher education; Digital inequality;
   Technology adoption; Institutional diversity; Developing countries; AI
   policy
ID COMMUNITY
AB The global diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education raises questions about institutional equity, as adoption patterns shaped by structural factors risk reproducing existing inequalities. This study provides one of the first systematic comparative assessments of AI integration across Nigerian university types, examining how governance structures, resources, and inter-organizational networks shape technology adoption in developing country higher education. This study conducted a comparative content analysis of 45 Nigerian universities (15 Federal, 15 State, 15 Private), assessing AI integration across six dimensions: infrastructure, curriculum, research, industry partnerships, international collaborations, and policy frameworks using structured coding scales with anchored descriptors. Drawing on an integrated framework combining institutional theory, resourcebased view, and network theory, data were analyzed using one-way ANOVA, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple regression. Results reveal moderate overall AI integration (M = 4.79, SD = 1.71) with meaningful variation across dimensions and institution types. Federal universities demonstrated the highest integration (M = 5.25), private universities recorded their strongest performance in curriculum integration (M = 5.87), and state universities showed emerging strength in policy frameworks. Institution age (beta = 0.43, p = 0.016) and geographic location (beta = 0.31, p = 0.029) significantly predicted integration levels, while institution type was not significant when controlling for other factors. The strong correlation between international collaborations and industry partnerships (r = 0.74, p < 0.001) suggests network positions create compounding advantages for well-connected institutions. These findings challenge assumptions that governance structure determines integration capacity and reveal how historical and geographic inequalities perpetuate through technology adoption, with implications for equitable AI deployment and international partnership design in developing country higher education.

TI Human-centered AI for teacher educators: Designing professional learning
   for critical AI literacy
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher education; Critical AI literacy; Human-centered AI; Design-based
   research; AI in education
AB Teacher educators play a pivotal role in shaping how preservice teachers understand, evaluate, and integrate artificial intelligence (AI) in classrooms, yet they rarely receive systematic preparation to lead this work. This design-based study examines how principles of Human-Centered AI (HCAI) and critical AI literacy can inform the design of professional learning resources for teacher educators. Across three cycles of needs analysis, prototyping, and refinement with seven teacher educators, findings identified three convergent design needs: (a) improving instructional efficiency and effectiveness while preserving professional judgment, (b) modeling responsible and ethical AI integration, and (c) reforming teacher education pedagogies with AI. We translate these findings into a five-module curriculum that operationalizes critical AI literacy competencies (foundational AI knowledge; ethics and algorithmic bias; pedagogical integration; implementation, guidelines, and policy; and human-centered AI in education) through seven HCAI-informed activities, including educator-in-the-loop tasks that strengthen professional judgment, transparency, and equity-oriented decision-making. The study identifies teacher educators as the nexus where critical AI literacy and HCAI converge and reframes AI literacy as a design practice through which teacher educators structure how preservice teachers first encounter AI. The study offers an evidence-based professional learning model that positions teacher educators as designers and ethical stewards of AI integration and a scalable pathway for preparing future teachers for responsible AI-enabled practice.

   through the lens of DigCompEdu and TPACK
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Education; Digital competences; DigCompEdu; Technology; TPACK
ID LITERACY
AB Digital competence is a critical skill for teachers in the modern era, as technology reshapes the education ecosystem. The ability to integrate digital tools effectively into teaching practices not only enhances learning outcomes but also equips students with skills that are important for their daily lives. For teachers, fostering digital proficiency is fundamental to addressing the challenges of contemporary education environments, promoting inclusive learning, and addressing the evolving demands of the digital age. This article evaluates the digital competencies of K1-12 teachers in Kosovo using the DigCompEdu framework, providing information on six competency areas in the Digital Competence for Educators Famework (DigCompEdu). TI The experience of using AI-generated social stories as a behavioral
   intervention tool for children
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Social stories; Special education; Professional
   attitudes; Behavioral intervention; Autism spectrum disorder;
   Educational technology
ID AUTISM
AB As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into educational and therapeutic settings, understanding professional user experience with AI-generated interventions is crucial for successful implementation. This study examines how education and therapy professionals experience using social stories created by AI versus human experts for children with special needs. Using a 2 & times;2 experimental design, 227 female professionals in Israel evaluated social stories designed to either promote positive behaviors or reduce challenging behaviors, with authorship randomly attributed to either AI (Claude) or a human speech therapist. All stories were actually AI-generated, allowing isolated examination of authorship perception effects. Results revealed no main effects for creator type or story purpose, but significant Creator & times; Purpose interactions emerged for understanding, feasibility, and overall user experience. AI-generated stories were rated more favorably for behavior promotion interventions, while human-authored stories were preferred for behavior reduction interventions. User experience ratings remained stable across conditions, suggesting fundamental legitimacy of both approaches. Professionals working with younger children reported significantly better user experience compared to those working with adolescents, while professional experience and field showed no influence on user experience evaluations. These findings challenge assumptions about AI resistance in sensitive professional contexts and reveal the importance of strategic alignment between intervention purpose and perceived creator expertise. The results provide evidence-based guidance for integrating AI tools in special education, suggesting that AI may be particularly valuable for promoting positive behaviors while human expertise remains preferred for addressing complex behavioral challenges.

TI Pharmacy student-facilitated prescription writing workshop: Evaluating
   interprofessional peer performance, communication, and collaboration
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer-facilitated learning; Peer-assessment; Self-assessment;
   Prescription writing; Health professional education; Interprofessional
   education
AB Introduction: A peer-led prescription writing workshop was delivered by pairs of fourth-year pharmacy student facilitators (PSFs) to second-year medical (MD) and first-year physician assistant (PA) students. This study assessed PSFs' teaching performance and evaluated participants' perceptions of the workshop's educational value. Methods: A mixed-methods cross-sectional design was used. MD and PA students evaluated the PSFs and the workshop via a Likert scale survey that was developed from validated instruments. PSFs also completed self-assessments and evaluated their co-facilitator's performance. Descriptive statistics were reported (N, %), stratified by discipline, and comparisons were made using chisquare and Mann-Whitney U tests. A post-workshop focus group with PSFs explored experiences and feedback was analyzed using Braun and Clarke's inductive thematic analysis. Results: Ten PSFs led the session for 339 students (289 MD, 50 PA). Quantitative results showed high satisfaction, with 85% of all participants strongly agreeing the session was informative and 84% feeling it met expectations. Most participants rated PSFs' performance at the highest level, and PSFs gave similarly high ratings to themselves and co-facilitators. More PA students (73%) expressed interest in further training compared to MDs (44%, p = 0.0001). Qualitative analysis revealed that PSFs experienced challenges engaging students during the role-play activity. Effective teaching strategies included preparation, collaboration to address knowledge gaps, and using the teach-back method. PSFs found the experience rewarding, valued affirming feedback, and expressed interest in future peer-facilitated teaching. Conclusion: A peer-led prescription writing workshop successfully met learners' expectations and was a valuable experience for both student facilitators and participants.

TI Educational exclusion among India's youth and young workers: Evidence
   from CAMS 2022-23
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational exclusion; Youth; Early-career workforce; Inequality; India;
   Second-chance education; SDG 4; Capability approach
ID VOCATIONAL-EDUCATION; LIFE-COURSE; CHALLENGES
AB This study uniquely quantifies educationally excluded individuals in the labour-market-entry age range (15-34). It investigates the extent of low educational attainment (middle school or less) among Indian youth (15-24 years) and early-career workers (25-34 years), and socioeconomic and regional factors associated with it. Using nationally representative Comprehensive Annual Modular Survey 2022-23 data (N = 455,194), we employ survey-weighted logistic regression to identify correlates of low educational attainment. Approximately 20.1% of youth and 34.4% of early-career workers, totalling 129.7 million individuals, have a middle school education or less. Compared to Other Castes, Scheduled Tribes have 2.50-2.66 times higher adjusted odds of low attainment (p < 0.01), and Scheduled Castes have 1.96-2.22 times higher adjusted odds (p < 0.01). Muslims show 2.43-2.66 times higher adjusted odds compared to Hindus (p < 0.01). Married individuals show substantially elevated odds (adjusted OR 1.95-3.70, p < 0.01) vs unmarried. After controlling for individual and household socioeconomic factors, northern states (Uttar Pradesh, Bihar) show significantly higher adjusted odds of low attainment compared to the reference state, while southern states (Kerala, Tamil Nadu) show significantly lower adjusted odds. These findings identify priority populations (Scheduled Tribes, Scheduled Castes, Muslims, and married women) and high-burden regions relevant for National Education Policy 2020 implementation. The persistent disparities suggest potential relevance of secondary retention programmes and second-chance learning initiatives targeting identified groups. Results contribute to global debates on inclusive education policy in low- and middle-income countries and offer insights relevant to achieving Sustainable Development Goal 4.

TI Associations between self-rated stuttering severity and multidimensional
   stuttering impact
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Stuttering; Self-rated severity; OASES; Life impact
ID RELIABILITY; THERAPY; PEOPLE; ADULTS; LIFE
AB Purpose: Prior research examining stuttering severity and the impact of stuttering has revealed inconsistent findings, partly due to differences in how severity is defined and measured. This study examined bivariate and covariate-adjusted associations between a global self-rated severity (SRS) measure and multidimensional stuttering impact measured by the Overall Assessment of the Speaker's Experience of Stuttering (OASES) among Chinese adults who stutter. Method: Data were collected via an anonymous online survey from 346 adults who stutter in China. Participants completed the Simplified Chinese OASES-Adults (OASES-A-SC) and a singleitem 7-point SRS. Pearson correlations were used to test bivariate associations; multiple linear regression models examined whether SRS was associated with OASES outcomes after controlling for age, gender, speech therapy history, and support-group participation. Results: SRS was positively associated with the OASES Overall Impact Score and all four section scores (rs =.49-.67), with the strongest associations for the Overall Impact Score and Section III (Communication in Daily Situations). In adjusted models, SRS remained significantly associated with all OASES outcomes. Support-group participation was also associated with lower impact scores for most outcomes. Conclusion: SRS was moderately to strongly associated with multidimensional stuttering impact, indicating that the two measures are related but should not be treated as interchangeable. Brief SRS measures may capture clinically meaningful aspects of lived experience and serve as a practical, speaker-centered complement to the OASES, especially in large-scale surveys and crosscultural settings where clinician-administered severity assessment and calibrated listener-based estimates are less feasible.

TI Automated feedback on argumentative writing: The role of secondary
   students' feedback receptivity and feedback perception
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Receptivity to feedback; Perceived feedback usefulness; Motivation;
   Argumentation; Individual differences
ID PEER FEEDBACK; LEARNING PROGRESSION; MODEL; PERFORMANCE; SCIENCE;
   METAANALYSIS; ACHIEVEMENT; MOTIVATION
AB Background: Argumentative competencies are key in secondary school. Feedback can foster competence development, but effects on performance and motivation vary widely across students. Students' feedback receptivity and perceptions are presumed to explain this heterogeneity; however, empirical evidence for automated feedback is lacking. Aims: We investigated how students' receptivity to feedback related to revision performance and interest change during an argumentative writing task, and whether students' usefulness perceptions of the given feedback mediated the relationship. Methods and results: 1507 secondary school students wrote an argumentative text, received automated feedback, and revised their texts. For schools, the results suggest that encouraging students' general receptivity to feedback may be a valuable goal alongside providing high-quality feedback.

TI An entropy-based ARAS approach to identifying teachers' proof schemes
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM); Entropy-based ARAS; Proof
   schemes; Proof evaluation; Mathematics teachers
ID MATHEMATICAL KNOWLEDGE; STUDENTS
AB Background: Although proof is central in school mathematics, task-based, quantitative evidence on how teachers evaluate argument types remains limited. As most literature is qualitative, drawing broader statistical conclusions about teachers' evaluative orientations systematically is challenging. Aims: This study investigates middle-school teachers' proof evaluations by integrating Harel and Sowder's framework with Multi-Criteria Decision-Making. It aims to objectively quantify and rank teachers' proof-related orientations, bridging the gap between pedagogical theory and systematic measurement. Sample: The study involves 30 middle-school mathematics teachers in T & uuml;rkiye. Methods: Participants used a Proof Scheme Identification Form to rate five argument types across five propositions. These 1-5 scale ratings were processed using an entropy-based ARAS method. This approach allowed for the objective determination of criterion weights via Entropy, followed by a final ranking based on ARAS utility coefficients. Results: The results revealed a hierarchy: axiomatic and transformational schemes ranked highest, while authoritarian and empirical schemes ranked lower. These patterns remained stable despite occasional individual preferences for non-deductive justifications. Notably, verbally framed propositions were the most discriminative, whereas symbolically familiar items contributed least. This suggests that a familiar mathematical format may sometimes mask underlying logical insufficiencies. Conclusions: Integrating Entropy and ARAS provides a transparent, quantifiable map of proof orientations that complements qualitative research. The results highlight a critical gap between teachers' ability to recognize formal standards and their tendency to privilege the external form of an argument.

TI Family accommodation of restricted and repetitive behaviors and emotion
   regulation in early childhood: Associations across autistic,
   developmentally delayed, and non-diagnosed groups
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Family accommodation; Restricted and repetitive behaviors; Emotion
   regulation; Autism; Early childhood
ID SPECTRUM DISORDERS; ANXIETY; TEMPERAMENT
AB Family accommodation (FA) of restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) is common in autism and associated with child and family outcomes, yet its relationship to emotion regulation (ER) in both children and parents remains unexamined. This study investigated associations between FA, RRBs, child temperament traits (surgency, negative affect, effortful control), and parental ER strategies (cognitive reappraisal, expressive suppression) across autistic (n = 146), developmentally delayed (DD; n = 44), and non-diagnosed (ND; n = 98) groups of young children (23-60 months). All the children were referred for suspected autism prior to evaluation, and underwent standardized diagnostic assessments (ADOS-2, Mullen/WPPSI). Parents completed measures of FA-RRBs, child temperament (CBQ), and parental ER strategies (ERQ). FA-RRBs were positively associated with child negative affect across all three groups (rho =.37-.54, all p <= .021; four of six parent-group combinations survived FDR correction). These associations were observed across a spectrum of autistic, DD, and ND groups, establishing a broadly relevant link between child emotional distress and parental accommodation of RRBs. Parental ER strategies were not significantly associated with FA-RRBs in any group after FDR correction, and this null result was confirmed under multiple imputation. This is the first study to situate family accommodation of RRBs within the emotion-regulation ecology of the family, and the first to test whether the construct is specific to autism or extends to developmentally delayed and non-diagnosed children referred for the same concerns. These findings establish FA-RRBs as a construct that is not reducible to level of autism characteristics, and identify child negative affect as its most consistent correlate across diagnostic boundaries.

TI Translanguaging optimizes the developmental trajectory of
   beginning-level L2 writing: A sequence analysis study with an
   experimental design
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Translanguaging; Sequence analysis; L2 writing; Developmental
   trajectory; Beginning-level; Experimental study
ID COGNITIVE LOAD; SCHOOL; LIFE
AB Current research in language education predominantly relies on static, cross-sectional assessments, which provide limited insight into the dynamic processes underlying skill development. As an approach to longitudinal data analysis, sequence analysis offers a novel lens for unpacking the developmental "black box" of second language (L2) writing. This study employed sequence analysis to examine the developmental trajectories of L2 writing under a translanguaging intervention. Based on data from a one-semester intervention, dynamic sequences [State 1 -* State 2 -* State 3 -* State 4] were constructed from four consecutive writing tasks completed by an experimental group (n = 125) and a control group (n = 129). Multiple sequence analysis techniques, including state distribution plots, sequence index plots, transversal entropy plots, and state transition matrices, were utilized for visual comparison. Four distinct types of developmental trajectory were identified, and typical trajectories were delineated for each cluster. The results indicated that translanguaging can optimize the developmental trajectories of beginninglevel L2 writing. This study offers a dynamic, sequence-based analytical framework for investigating the mechanisms underlying language proficiency development.

TI Between silence and uncertainty: Exploring what dyslexia teachers
   hesitate to say in Saudi classrooms
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher silence; Dyslexia; Inclusive education; Professional judgement;
   Saudi Arabia
ID INCLUSIVE EDUCATION
AB Teachers play a central role in inclusive education, yet hesitation persists around discussions of dyslexia in contexts shaped by diagnostic uncertainty, stigma, and hierarchical authority. This study examines what teachers avoid saying about dyslexia in Saudi classrooms and the social and institutional conditions shaping this silence. Teacher silence is conceptualised as communicative restraint, how teachers manage what can be said, to whom, and through which channels, rather than absence of talk. Semi-structured interviews with 10 general and special education teachers were analysed inductively. Findings indicate three patterned practices: softening dyslexia through skill-based descriptors, restricting diagnostic language to private professional spaces while avoiding official documentation, and conditional directness shaped by audience and perceived risk. This restraint reflected restricted diagnostic authority, relational considerations, and organisational norms, functioning as professional judgement rather than lack of awareness. The study reframes teacher silence as an ethically grounded, systemically produced practice enacted under real-world constraints.

TI Teachers' growth mindsets and their approaches to teaching: The
   mediating role of epistemological beliefs
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Growth mindset; Epistemological beliefs; Teaching approaches; Mediation
   analyses; Teacher education
ID PERSONAL EPISTEMOLOGY; PRESERVICE TEACHERS; SCHOOL TEACHERS;
   CONCEPTIONS; KNOWLEDGE; COGNITION; METACOGNITION; INTELLIGENCE;
   ACHIEVEMENT; DIMENSIONS
AB This study examines the mediating role of teachers' epistemological beliefs in the relationship between mindset orientations (growth vs. fixed) and teaching approaches. Drawing on personal epistemology theory, it explores how beliefs about knowledge are associated with pedagogical orientations. Data from 339 in-service teachers were analyzed using Hayes' PROCESS Macro (Model 4). Results indicate that a fixed mindset is directly associated with teaching approaches and shows no significant indirect association through epistemological beliefs. In contrast, a growth mindset is associated with teaching approaches through epistemological beliefs, which significantly mediate this relationship in some models. The findings highlight the importance of considering both mindset and epistemological beliefs when examining teaching approaches. Interpreted within an exploratory associational framework, the study contributes to understanding how teachers' belief systems are linked to instructional orientations and offers implications for teacher education and professional development.

TI Pilot Study on Gamification and Digital Comics to Enhance Motivation and
   Understanding in Engineering Education
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital comics; educational gamification; multimodal learning; STEM
   education; student motivation
AB Sustaining student motivation and engagement in technically oriented engineering subjects remains a persistent challenge in higher education, particularly when instruction relies primarily on traditional lecture-based approaches. Digital and computer-supported learning tools offer new opportunities to promote active learning and conceptual understanding in engineering education.This pilot study presents the design and evaluation of a technology-enhanced instructional approach that integrates interactive digital comics, gamification dynamics, multimodal interactive lessons implemented using a web-based authoring platform (Genially), and three-dimensional visualizations to support learning in engineering courses.The intervention was implemented with undergraduate and master's students enrolled in Civil Engineering, Mining and Energy Resources Engineering, and Energy Engineering programs at a public Spanish university, including the full population of students registered in the participating courses. A mixed-methods research design was employed, combining pre- and post-intervention conceptual understanding assessments, learning analytics and digital interaction metrics, and qualitative analysis of student perceptions.The results indicate statistically significant improvements in conceptual understanding, academic engagement, and perceived usability of the digital learning environment. Interaction data revealed differentiated engagement patterns across activities, while qualitative feedback highlighted the contribution of narrative structure, visual design, and interactivity to student motivation and comprehension.These findings suggest that the integration of computer-based gamification and interactive digital comics constitutes a pedagogically sound and contextually valid approach in engineering education. By working with the entire cohort of enrolled students, the study provides ecologically valid evidence of the effectiveness of digital narrative and interactive visualization tools, and establishes a solid foundation for future large-scale implementations in engineering teaching contexts.

TI The Effect of Nursing Students' Metaverse Perception on Flexible
   Thinking in Learning: A Path Analysis
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE flexible thinking in learning; metaverse; nursing students; path
   analysis
ID COGNITIVE FLEXIBILITY
AB It is expected that nursing students will demonstrate flexibility in their thinking as they learn, enabling them to solve problems, produce solutions, and establish cooperation. The development of flexible thinking can be facilitated by the use of the metaverse, which is a technological innovation and a three-dimensional virtual world. This study aims to examine how nursing students' metaverse perception affects flexible thinking in learning and to investigate the relationship between them. This research has a descriptive and exploratory design. The study was conducted between October and November 2024 with the participation of 494 nursing students. Three instruments were employed for the collection of data in a face-to-face setting within the classroom environment. The instruments utilized in the study were the Descriptive Characteristics Form, the Metaverse Perception Scale for Nursing Students, and the Flexible Thinking in Learning Scale. The statistical analysis was conducted with a significance value of p < 0.05, employing the statistical software package SPSS 22.0. The mean age of the students was 20.39 +/- 2.35 years. Of the total sample, 76.5% were female, and 29.1% were first-year students. The male participants, those who engaged in virtual gaming, and those who exhibited a preference for active learning exhibited significantly higher levels of metaverse perception. Those who considered themselves to be academically successful and those who preferred face-to-face, active learning exhibited significantly higher levels of flexible thinking in learning. The results of the path analysis indicated a significant positive correlation between metaverse perception and flexible thinking in learning (beta = 0.653, R = 0.590, p < 0.001). It was determined that the development of metaverse perception is important for nursing students to think flexibly in learning. It is recommended that metaverse technology be used in the nursing curriculum to meet the changing demands of the health system and to improve students' metaverse perception.

AB Educators and researchers have called for systems thinking in chemistry education to prepare future STEM professionals and citizens to address 21st century sustainability challenges.
