TI Spiral Integrationof Organic Synthesis and InstrumentalCharacterization
   Using Ferrocenyl Chalcones
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Organic Chemistry; Analytical Chemistry;
   Laboratory Instruction; InstrumentalAnalysis; Materials Chemistry;
   Ferrocenyl Chalcones; Spiral Laboratory
ID DERIVATIVES
AB Undergraduate chemistry curricula often present organic synthesis and instrumental analysis as disconnected experiences, limiting students' ability to integrate structural, spectroscopic, and materials-focused concepts when interpreting authentic data. To address this problem, we implemented a spiral laboratory experience in a third-year Instrumental Analysis course at a Hispanic-serving research university (n approximate to 48) in which students revisited ferrocenyl chalcones synthesized in a prior organic chemistry course and analyzed them as "unknowns" using complementary chromatographic, spectroscopic, and thermal analysis techniques. This reintegration required students to draw on prior synthetic knowledge while developing new analytical reasoning skills by interpreting data collected across multiple analytical methods. Assessment of laboratory reports and postactivity surveys revealed increased student confidence with analytical instrumentation, improved ability to integrate concepts across subdisciplines, and increased engagement with materials-oriented applications of organometallic compounds. This activity provides a replicable model for addressing curricular fragmentation by combining spiral integration, integrative analytical reasoning, and responsible AI use within the undergraduate chemistry laboratory.

TI Enhancing ScienceCommunication through DeliberativeDiscussions on Water
   Contamination in a General Chemistry Lab at anHBCU
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Undergraduate; General chemistry laboratory; Water contamination; Policy
ID POSTER PRESENTATIONS; SCIENCE; CRISIS
AB In Spring 2023 (pilot study, n = 24) and Spring 2024 (main study, n = 48; survey respondents n = 36), second-semester General Chemistry II laboratory students at Xavier University of Louisiana, a Historically Black College and University (HBCU), participated in a classroom activity designed to enhance science communication skills through deliberative discussions on water contamination issues. Following qualitative analysis experiments on heavy metal ions, students engaged in structured small-group deliberations evaluating real-world water contamination challenges and policy solutions. The activity was explicitly aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) #6: Clean Water and Sanitation, providing a global sustainability framework for student discussions. Survey results indicate increased student engagement, improved understanding of water contamination, and enhanced confidence in communicating scientific concepts to nonspecialist audiences. While most students reported increased interest in science communication and STEM careers, some indicated the need for additional support to build confidence. These findings demonstrate that integrating deliberative, sustainability-focused discussions into laboratory courses effectively connects experimental chemistry to societal challenges while fostering scientific literacy and communication skills.

TI A collaborative global competence intervention: effects on fourth
   graders' perspectives about poverty and interculturality
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Global competence; Interculturality; Intervention; Poverty; Primary
   school
ID ECONOMIC-INEQUALITY; CHILDRENS; ADOLESCENTS; PREJUDICE; ATTITUDES; POOR;
   INTELLIGENCE; ATTRIBUTIONS; METAANALYSIS; CHILDHOOD
AB Although schools are now called to prepare a generation of globally competent students, little is known about the effectiveness of global competence interventions in the classroom. The current study aimed to examine the effectiveness of a collaborative intervention following a global competence framework in fourth-grade children's perspectives on two issues: poverty and interculturality. Participants were 248 fourth-grade children (8 to 11 years old) enrolled in public schools in Portugal. Following a quasi-experimental design, classrooms were assigned to a control group or an intervention group. Within the intervention group, classrooms were dedicated either to the topic of poverty or interculturality. Children participated in structured interviews. Concerning poverty, we targeted children's explanations and solutions to poverty. Concerning interculturality, we targeted references to cultural influences; prejudice; rights, values, and principles; authority and social conventions; and concerns with emotions. No noteworthy effects were found for the intercultural intervention. Findings suggest that a global competence framework may be useful when teaching about social issues in primary school, but more systematic and targeted interventions might be necessary to foster greater effect sizes.

TI Mapping teachers' emotional and pedagogical dimensions: a network
   analysis of teachers' socio-emotional competencies, conceptions of
   teaching and implicit theories of emotions
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teachers' socio-emotional competencies; Conception of teaching; Academic
   emotions; Implicit theories of emotions
AB Teachers' socio-emotional competencies (SEC) are known to contribute to their well-being and classroom climate. Yet, little is known about how these competencies interact with their conception of teaching and their implicit theories about emotions. We addressed this gap using a network analysis from 263 preservice teachers to explore the interrelations between preservice teachers' intra and interpersonal SEC, their conceptions of teaching, and their beliefs about utility, source and malleability of emotions in the classroom. Results show that a constructivist approach to teaching is positively associated with perceiving oneself as a key source of students' emotional experiences, with this association occurring alongside higher valuation of positive emotions in learning contexts. Intrapersonal SEC is associated with beliefs in the malleability of students' emotions and co-occurs with teachers' perceived capacity to support students' emotional regulation. The central position of malleability beliefs and intrapersonal competencies suggests that these dimensions are highly connected within this system and may represent priorities for future longitudinal or intervention research. Overall, the findings provide a basis for examining how emotional competencies and pedagogical conceptions become translated into classroom practices during teacher development.

TI Cultivating Shared Epistemic Agency in AI-Enhanced Classrooms: A
   Duoethnographic Study in China and Japan
SO ENGLISH TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-enhanced language education; Shared epistemic agency; Duoethnography;
   Reflexivity; Human-AI collaboration; Responsibility;
   AI(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic);
   (sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic); (sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)(sic);
   (sic)(sic)(sic); (sic)(sic)(sic)(sic); (sic)(sic)(sic)(sic)
ID TEACHERS
AB This duoethnographic study explores how two university language teachers in China and Japan understood, negotiated, and attempted to cultivate shared epistemic agency in AI-enhanced classrooms. In this study, shared epistemic agency refers to the collaborative capacity to engage in knowledge creation through reflection, judgment, and responsibility in relation to AI-mediated pedagogical practice. Drawing on co-constructed reflexive journals, sustained Zoom and in-person dialogues, and contextual prompts from student artefacts, classroom notes, and selected AI interaction logs, the study traces how the two teachers interpreted the conditions and tensions involved in fostering such agency. Four recurring concerns became central to their dialogue: reflexive task design, recursive reflection on AI use, learner ownership and responsibility, and contextual challenges and strategies in cultivating shared epistemic agency. Their accounts show how local ideologies, language norms, institutional policies, and cultural expectations may shape what counts as responsible and meaningful AI use in each setting. The study highlights the value of duoethnographic reflection for illuminating the situated conditions, tensions, and pedagogical strategies through which shared epistemic agency may be cultivated. It also underscores the need to foreground learners' epistemic participation in AI-era language education while critically attending to the cultural and institutional conditions that mediate human-AI collaboration.

TI School Climate, Teaching Enjoyment, Resilience and Work Engagement Among
   University Teachers in AI-Driven Higher Education: A Multi-Group
   Structural Equation Modelling Study
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-driven higher education; resilience; school climate; teaching
   enjoyment; work engagement
ID OF-FIT INDEXES; ENVIRONMENT; VALIDITY
AB This study investigated the relationships among school climate, teaching enjoyment, resilience and work engagement among university teachers, while further examining gender differences in these relationships. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was adopted. In the quantitative phase, survey data were collected from 658 university teachers and analysed using structural equation modelling and multi-group analysis. The quantitative data were processed using SPSS 27.0 and AMOS 26.0, while the qualitative interview data were analysed with MAXQDA 24 through thematic analysis. In the qualitative phase, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 teachers to further explain the observed gender differences. The results showed that school climate was positively associated with teaching enjoyment, resilience and work engagement, while both teaching enjoyment and resilience were positively associated with work engagement. In addition, significant gender differences were found in two structural paths: the association between school climate and work engagement was stronger among male teachers, whereas the association between teaching enjoyment and work engagement was stronger among female teachers. Interview findings further suggested that male teachers were more sensitive to institutional support and structural conditions, whereas female teachers were more strongly influenced by positive emotional and relational experiences in teaching. These findings enrich current understanding of teacher engagement and provide practical implications for fostering supportive and sustainable professional environments in contemporary higher education.

TI Digital field representations as a holistic approach to experiential
   learning in High Arctic geoscience field education
SO GEOSCIENCE COMMUNICATION
LA English
DT Article
ID TRIPS; ACCEPTANCE; STUDENTS; TOOL
AB Field-based education is a cornerstone of geoscience learning, offering students the opportunity to connect theoretical knowledge with real-world geological contexts. Yet access to such experiences remains limited due to logistical, financial, environmental, and social barriers, especially in remote or extreme environments like the High Arctic. These barriers may be especially salient for people with disabilities. In response to these challenges, Virtual Field Experiences (VFEs) are emerging as promising tools to complement traditional fieldwork. In this study we investigate how VFEs contribute to experiential learning among students at the University Centre in Svalbard (UNIS) in Longyearbyen, Svalbard.Using a mixed-methods approach grounded in experiential learning theory and the Technology Acceptance Model, we surveyed 66 students who used VFEs as part of geoscience courses at UNIS before and after physical field excursions. Results reveal that students found VFEs particularly valuable for pre-field orientation, spatial awareness, and post-field reflection. Students reported improved readiness, deeper conceptual understanding, and enhanced engagement. The virtual representations enabled them to revisit complex sites, identify overlooked features, and consolidate observations made during fieldwork. Importantly, most participants did not see VFEs as a replacement for traditional fieldwork but recognized their role in making field learning more inclusive, repeatable, and accessible.We highlight how VFEs may help students manage perceived novelty by familiarizing them with unfamiliar environments before initial field exposure. Students expressed strong interest in broader applications of VFEs across courses and disciplines, particularly when enriched with interactivity and guided tasks. These findings suggest that digital field representations hold significant promise for expanding access to geoscience education and perceived reinforcement of understanding. Future research should explore co-design practices with students and educators to optimize VFEs for equity, sustainability, and pedagogical impact across diverse learning environments.

TI Validation of an inanimate simulation model for subclavian central
   venous catheterization training
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Simulation-based education; Central venous catheterization; Subclavian
   approach; Validity evidence; Procedural skills training; Medical
   education
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION; INSERTION; COMPLICATIONS; VALIDITY; SKILLS
AB Purpose Simulation-based education is increasingly used to support procedural training while minimizing patient risk. This study aimed to gather validity evidence for a low-cost inanimate simulation model designed for training in subclavian central venous catheterization (CVC).Methods A cross-sectional validation study was conducted following Messick's framework. Twenty participants were included: 10 sixth-year medical students with no prior experience in CVC (novices) and 10 experienced general surgeons (experts). Content validity was assessed using an expert survey and quantified with the Content Validity Index (CVI). Technical performance was evaluated using a 13-item procedural checklist scored by two independent evaluators, with interrater reliability assessed using kappa. Construct validity was examined using a known-groups approach comparing performance outcomes between experts and novices.Results All content validity items achieved an item-level CVI of 1.00, with a scale-level CVI/Ave of 1.00. Interrater reliability for checklist scoring was perfect (kappa = 1.00). The procedural checklist demonstrated moderate internal consistency (KR-20 = 0.63), with ceiling effects in several fundamental steps. Experts achieved higher checklist scores (100.0% vs 85.4 +/- 10.5, p = 0.002), shorter procedure times (5.28 +/- 0.79 vs 11.61 +/- 4.67 min, p = 0.002), higher first-attempt success rates (70% vs 10%, p = 0.020), and greater procedural autonomy (100% vs 10% independent completion, p = 0.0003). No complications occurred among experts, whereas novices experienced simulated complications in 30% of attempts.Conclusions This study provides validity evidence supporting the interpretation and use of scores obtained with a low-cost inanimate simulation model for training and assessment of subclavian CVC placement. The ability of these scores to discriminate between novice and expert performance contributes construct validity evidence consistent with this intended interpretation.

TI The relationship between entrustment and EPA assessment factors in
   general surgery residency training
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrustable professional activities; Assessment; Competency-based
   medical education
ID ENTRUSTABLE PROFESSIONAL ACTIVITIES; OPERATING-ROOM; FEEDBACK; GAP
AB Purpose Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) serve as an assessment framework for core activities of general surgery to inform resident entrustment. Entrustment in general surgery (GS) training has demonstrated feedback and demographic differences. Here, we examine the relationship between GS trainees' entrustment levels and receiving narrative EPA feedback as well as other assessment factors in the full EPA implementation phase. Methods In this multi-institution, retrospective study, all EPA assessments of GS trainees completed by faculty between July 2023 and June 2025 were analyzed. Mixed-effects ordinal regressions were performed to examine the association between entrustment and receiving narrative feedback, year of training, case complexity, assessment phase of care, and faculty and resident demographics. Results A total of 1071 assessments were analyzed with 896 EPAs (83.7%) containing narrative feedback and 175 EPAs (16.3%) without any feedback. Trainees performing at higher levels of entrustment for a given activity were less likely to receive narrative feedback (OR = 0.44, p < 0.001). The likelihood of trainees receiving higher entrustment increased significantly with post-graduate year (PGY), reaching the highest entrustment likelihood in senior training stages. Trainees participating in straightforward cases were more likely to receive higher entrustment than those in complex cases (OR = 1.94, p = 0.002). Pre-and post-operative assessments were more likely granted higher entrustment than intraoperative phases (pre: OR = 4.94, p < 0.001, post: OR = 3.04, p = 0.017). There was no difference in entrustment based on trainee or faculty demographics after controlling for PGY and case complexity. Conclusion Receipt of narrative feedback was associated with significantly lower odds of being in a higher entrustment category. Efforts should be made to ensure all residents receive actionable feedback along the continuum of their training.

TI Harnessing AI and chatbots to develop an interactive learning activity:
   student perceptions and outcomes
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE active learning; artificial intelligence; AI; gamification;
   discovery-based learning; sexually transmitted disease; higher
   education; premedical; Twine; ChatGPT
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed various industries, and education is no exception. This paper details how AI can be utilized to support the development of an interactive, choose-your-own-adventure learning activity for pre-health students. With ChatGPT assistance, we identified and implemented the open-source platform Twine to create a branching, scenario-based activity focused on sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), allowing students to engage with clinical decision-making and apply course concepts. Additionally, ChatGPT's natural language processing capabilities allowed educators to create a script-based learning experience informed by prior student feedback, providing students with immediate, targeted feedback and support. Importantly, the use of AI helped streamline the development of this activity, lowering barriers to creating complex educational activities that may otherwise be difficult to implement. Here, we demonstrate how AI can be leveraged to support the development of interactive, scenario-based learning activities and provide practical guidance for instructors.

TI The role of self-assessment in self-regulated learning in elementary
   education
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-regulated learning; Self-assessment; Elementary education
ID EFFICACY; STUDENTS; CLASSROOM; METAANALYSIS; KNOWLEDGE
AB This study investigates the relationship between self-assessment and self-regulated learning (SRL) in upper elementary education, focusing on the distinctions between product and process-based self-assessment and the role of self-assessment accuracy. A four-week intervention involving 187 students explored whether self-assessment practices enhanced SRL across planning, monitoring, control, and reflection phases. Results revealed that practicing a combination of product- and process-based self-assessment led to greater improvements in self-assessment accuracy over time, compared to practicing only product-based assessment. However, no direct improvements in SRL behaviors were observed, suggesting that self-assessment alone may not suffice to foster comprehensive SRL development. Findings highlight the nuanced relationship between self-assessment accuracy and SRL, suggesting that self-assessment may need to be complemented by additional forms of SRL support to yield broader improvements in SRL.

TI Academic language challenges in EMI: linking EAP-EMI integration,
   self-efficacy, and perceived academic success
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EAP-EMI integration; Self-efficacy; Perceived academic success; Academic
   language learning; English-medium instruction
ID ENGLISH MEDIUM INSTRUCTION; HIGHER-EDUCATION
AB English-medium instruction (EMI) has expanded rapidly in transnational higher education and has become an important site of second and foreign language learning in disciplinary contexts. Yet how EAP-EMI integration is related to students' academic language experience and perceived academic success as an institutional learning condition remains underexplored. This study investigates the relationships among perceived EAP-EMI integration, academic language-related challenges, EMI-related self-efficacy, and perceived EMI academic success in a Sino-US transnational higher education programme. Survey data were collected from 405 undergraduate students with sustained EMI exposure and analysed using structural equation modelling. Results indicate that perceived EAP-EMI integration is strongly associated with lower academic language-related challenges and higher perceived EMI academic success. Academic language-related challenges function as an important experience-near mechanism linking institutional alignment to students' evaluative outcomes. EMI-related self-efficacy is closely calibrated to experienced challenge and operates in a differentiated manner, indicating both facilitative and constraining associations with perceived academic success once institutional alignment and experienced challenge are taken into account. Overall, the findings support a process-oriented account of academic language learning in EMI contexts, highlighting how perceived academic success emerges from the interplay among institutional alignment, language-mediated academic experience, and students' evaluative beliefs in second and foreign language education settings. Future research could extend this work through longitudinal, multi-site, and performance-based designs to examine more robustly how these relationships develop across different EMI contexts and stages of study.

   creativity? Gender differences in knowledge construction
SO JOURNAL OF WORKPLACE LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Social media-enabled fragmented learning; Employee creativity;
   Constructivist learning theory; Knowledge construction; Gender
   differences
ID PERFORMANCE; ENVIRONMENT; MANAGEMENT
AB Purpose-This study aims to investigate how social media-enabled fragmented learning (SMFL) influences employee creativity, the mediating roles of declarative knowledge and procedural knowledge and the moderating role of gender in knowledge construction. Design/methodology/approach-A two-wave survey yielded 311 valid employee responses, which were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and partial least squares multigroup analysis. Findings-Social media-enabled fragmented learning from local communities of practice (SMFLCOP) and social media-enabled fragmented learning from electronic networks of practice (SMFLNOP) positively influence employee creativity. Moreover, examining gender differences extends constructivist learning theory.

SO RESEARCH IN MATHEMATICS EDUCATION

ID CURRICULUM
AB This study analyses the process of co-evolution between the International Baccalaureate (IB) programme and the Polish mathematics education system in the context of global educational changes after 1989. Using qualitative research methodology, the paper documents the phenomenon of pragmatic adaptation of international mathematics teaching standards and the emergence of a new type of mathematical wars between global standards and local educational traditions.    through a structured quality and safety course
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

ID ADVERSE EVENTS; HOSPITALIZED-PATIENTS; CURRICULUM; EDUCATION; ERROR;
   UTAH; CARE
AB Background Patient safety is a fundamental principle of healthcare, yet adverse events remain a major cause of preventable morbidity and mortality worldwide. Human error is a leading contributor to these events. Patient safety education has been shown to improve healthcare providers' knowledge, attitudes, and competencies, but evidence from LMICs remains limited. This study evaluates the effectiveness of a patient safety course implemented among medical interns. Methods A one-arm quasi-experimental study was conducted among postgraduate medical interns at a private tertiary care hospital. Participants completed a structured Quality and Patient Safety (QPS) module consisting of pre-module assessment, two days of interactive didactic and applied learning sessions, and a post-module assessment. Quantitative data were analysed using paired statistical tests, while qualitative reflections underwent thematic analysis. Results A total of 166 medical interns participated, most without prior patient safety training. The intervention led to significant improvements in knowledge test scores, systems thinking, and knowledge efficacy across all cohorts (p < 0.001). Gains were particularly pronounced among interns without previous training. Qualitative reflections highlighted improved confidence, teamwork, and systems-oriented perspectives. Conclusion This study provides evidence that a structured patient safety course introduced into the intern's curriculum significantly increases knowledge, systems thinking and knowledge efficacy regardless of previous patient safety education exposure. The findings support that course should be formally included for early career clinical staff in LMICs where preventable harms remain a major patient safety concern.

TI Social and pedagogical conditions for overcoming professional burnout
   among university teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; institutional support; professional burnout; social
   and pedagogical conditions; teacher well-being; university teachers;
   workload
AB Background Professional burnout among university teachers is increasingly shaped by workload, institutional support, material conditions, pedagogical autonomy, and opportunities for professional development. In higher education, teachers combine teaching, research, administrative reporting, student support, and continuous professional growth, which may intensify emotional exhaustion and mental fatigue. Objective This study aimed to identify the social and pedagogical conditions associated with overcoming professional burnout among university teachers in Kazakhstan. Methods An exploratory cross-sectional mixed-method survey was conducted with 65 university teachers working in higher education institutions in Kazakhstan. Data were collected through an anonymous trilingual Google Forms questionnaire consisting of 12 closed-ended Likert-type items and three open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, and Spearman's rank correlation, while open-ended responses were examined through thematic analysis. Results Burnout was expressed mainly through emotional exhaustion, mental fatigue, workload pressure, dissatisfaction with economic and material conditions, and limited awareness of institutional burnout-prevention measures. A total of 38.5% of respondents reported emotional exhaustion often or very often, and 56.9% felt mentally drained by the end of the working day. However, 66.2% still reported professional motivation and engagement. Burnout was negatively associated with social-organizational conditions (rho = -0.459, p < 0.001), economic-material conditions (rho = -0.329, p = 0.007), professional development and prevention conditions (rho = -0.313, p = 0.011), and combined institutional conditions (rho = -0.430, p < 0.001). Qualitative findings highlighted workload, paperwork, bureaucracy, insufficient support, and financial dissatisfaction as key burnout factors. Conclusion Burnout prevention requires visible university-level mechanisms that reduce workload and paperwork, strengthen collegial and administrative support, improve material conditions, support pedagogical autonomy, and connect professional development with teachers' psychological well-being.

AB The quality of education in East Nusa Tenggara (NTT), Indonesia, remains among the lowest in the country, with teacher competency identified as a critical bottleneck. The primary contribution of this study is the development and theoretical grounding of the ADDIE-NTT framework-a culturally responsive, resource-adaptive adaptation of the ADDIE instructional design model specifically constructed for the geographic, linguistic, and infrastructural realities of eastern Indonesia. To build this framework on empirical rather than speculative foundations, the study adopts a sequential evidencebuilding logic in which three subordinate components-mapping teacher competency baselines, evaluating ADDIE-based professional development, and identifying contextual implementation barriers-each directly inform one or more dimensions of the proposed framework. The competency mapping (n = 312, cross-sectional survey) establishes which ADDIE phases require the greatest contextual adaptation; the quasi-experimental training evaluation (n = 87, pre-post design) suggests that structured ADDIE-based professional development may be associated with substantial gains (Cohen's d = 0.78) even under NTT's constrained conditions, validating the framework's feasibility; and the qualitative barrier analysis (n = 28 interviews) identifies the cultural, linguistic, and institutional conditions that the framework must structurally address. The four components are therefore not parallel objectives but a single integrated evidence chain culminating in the ADDIE-NTT framework's three core mechanisms: Cultural-Linguistic Contextualisation (CLC), Resource-Adaptive Design (RAD), and Community-Embedded Evaluation (CEE). Findings reveal significant gaps in pedagogical competency, particularly in the Analysis and Evaluation phases, attributable to limited access to professional training, inadequate infrastructure, and the absence of systematic instructional design frameworks in school practice. Instructional design competency- operationalized through the validated Teacher ADDIE Competency Scale (TACS) and an independent lesson plan quality rubric scored by two blind raters- showed significant improvement following the professional development programme, though causal attribution requires caution given the absence of a control group [t(86) = 14.23, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.78]. Qualitative data further illuminate contextual barriers unique to NTT, including geographic remoteness and multilingual student populations. The ADDIE-NTT framework synthesizes these findings into actionable design principles and advocates for its integration into regional pre-service and in-service teacher development programmes. Implications for policy, curriculum design, and educational investment in eastern Indonesia are discussed.

TI Supporting parents and early childhood development practitioners through
   a mobile application: The case of CareUp

LA English
DT Article
DE education; early childhood development; m-learning; information and
   communication technology; parents
ID INVOLVEMENT; ENVIRONMENT; EDUCATION; LITERACY; PROGRAM
AB Background: CareUp is a multilingual mobile communication tool connecting practitioners at early childhood development (ECD) centres with parents or caregivers of 4- to 5-year-old children. Aim: The study aimed to measure the uptake and use of the CareUp mobile application among isiXhosa-speaking practitioners and parents, and to extract lessons to inform future m-learning parent-support programmes. Setting: Data were collected from 10 ECD centres in four low-income urban communities in Cape Town, Western Cape, South Africa, where both practitioners and parents were primarily isiXhosa speaking. Practitioners recorded an average of 7.8 interactions per week, while parents averaged 3.4. Both benefits and challenges, as perceived by the beneficiaries, are elucidated. Conclusion: Mobile applications offer promise for supporting communication between parents and practitioners in ECD centres. However, structural and contextual constraints need to be mitigated to ensure broader parental access and use. Contribution: This article provides evidence of how child development practices in low-income urban ECD centres can be enhanced by engaging parents in their home language through mobile technology.

TI Impact of tailored animations on cognitive drive and science literacy in
   Kazakhstan primary education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE culturally responsive pedagogy; educational animation; intrinsic

   quasi-experimental design; science literacy
ID MOTIVATION
AB In Kazakhstan, conventional instructional approaches are becoming less responsive to the learning needs of Generation Alpha students in the elementary grades, and as a result, student engagement with natural science subjects is declining. This study examines the impact of Vyond-based animated videos, developed with cultural and linguistic adaptation for Kazakhstani learners, on the intrinsic motivation and academic performance of primary school students in the World Knowledge subject. A three-month quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group study was conducted with 165 students aged 8-10 across three schools in Kyzylorda. However, animation demonstrated limited effectiveness for tasks involving spatial reasoning. These findings extend the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning and Dual Coding Theory to a linguistically and culturally distinct primary education context and underscore the importance of cultural adaptation and teacher instructional competence for effective digital pedagogy.

TI Does parental involvement affect learning outcomes in students with mild
   special educational needs? Cross-sectional evidence from inclusive
   settings
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE inclusive classrooms; learning performance; parental stress;
   socioeconomic status; survey
AB Background Over 290 million children under the age of 20 live with developmental disabilities that demand tailored pedagogies. In inclusive classrooms, learners with special educational needs (SEN) share space with peers, yet their grades still reflect familial influences. Recent literature spotlights socioeconomic status (SES), parental stress, and involvement as separate levers of achievement, but their interplay remains obscure. This investigation bridges the evidence lacuna by simultaneously examining these variables within a regression framework.Methods The cross-sectional study surveyed 264 parents of school-aged children with mild SEN enrolled in inclusive settings across 14 mainstream public schools. Participants completed validated measures of parental involvement, stress, and SES, while children's academic attainment was assessed via unweighted composite GPA. Data analysis employed confirmatory factor analysis and partial least squares structural equation modeling with bootstrapping to evaluate direct and mediated relationships.Results The measurement model demonstrated good fit and acceptable psychometric properties. Socioeconomic status was positively associated with both parental involvement and academic achievement. Parental involvement was positively related to GPA and partially mediated the relationship between SES and academic achievement. In contrast, parental stress was not significantly associated with either parental involvement or GPA, and no indirect effect through parental involvement was observed. Although several relationships reached statistical significance, the effect sizes were small and the model explained a modest proportion of variance in academic achievement.Conclusion Socioeconomic resources were positively associated with academic achievement among students with mild SEN in inclusive educational settings, both directly and indirectly through parental involvement. However, the observed effects were small, and parental stress was unrelated to either parental involvement or learning success. These findings suggest that family socioeconomic resources and parental engagement may contribute to educational attainment among students with SEN, although their influence appears modest and should be interpreted within the context of broader educational and support systems.

TI Academic leadership beyond hierarchy: balancing autonomy, trust, and
   collaboration in university teams
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic leadership; autonomy; collaboration; higher education;
   qualitative analysis; research management; trust
AB Transformation in Academic leadership, organizational complexity, changing governance structures, growing role of research management and administration (RMA) and limitations in academic leadership let this study to reinterpret academic leadership as a context-dependent and negotiated process. TI Project POEM: fostering inclusive informal education STEM spaces for
   students with visual impairments through project-based learning and
   mentoring
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE career awareness; mentoring; project-based learning; science practices;
   STEM interest; students with visual impairments
ID SCIENCE; EXPERIENCES; TECHNOLOGY; TEACHERS; MODELS; SCHOOL; URBAN
AB This paper reports on an innovative out-of-school program that combined project-based learning and dual-tiered mentoring to engage middle and high school students with visual impairments (VI) in STEM. Project POEM (Project-Based Learning Opportunities and Exploration of Mentorship) supported middle and high school students between 2018 and 2022 to take part in a year-long program that included authentic STEM experiences and project-based learning and engagement with mentors who were university STEM students as well as STEM industry professionals who are blind or visually impaired. We describe the findings from a mixed-method study of middle and high school students (n = 30) and mentors (n = 33) to elucidate lessons learned. Data included pre- and post-surveys of students as well as interviews with students and mentors. By integrating accessible strategies like tactile graphics, audio-based simulations, and virtual mentoring with STEM professionals and university STEM mentors, the project fostered inclusion and enhanced students' outcomes related to interest in STEM and STEM careers. Engaging in Project POEM increased students' self-reported knowledge of accommodations for the workplace, their confidence in doing and presenting science, their attitudes towards STEM, their knowledge of and interest in going into a STEM career, and their confidence in engaging in the world as an individual who is blind or visually impaired. We conclude with practical recommendations based on our lessons learned for others looking to support students with visual impairments in informal education settings.

AB The BIYAHE TA (Let's Ride) extension program was implemented as a university-led community initiative aimed at supporting service-oriented practices among tricycle operators in Daanbantayan, Cebu, Philippines, through training on cleanliness, vehicle upkeep, basic repair and maintenance, and customer service. TI Integrating agent-based modeling and flipped instruction to enhance
   climate-physics learning: a Bloom's revised taxonomy analysis in
   Brazilian high schools
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE agent-based modeling; Bloom's revised taxonomy; climate education;
   complex system; computational thinking; flipped classroom; physics
   education; STEM education
AB Understanding climate-related physical phenomena in secondary education requires instructional designs that integrate thermodynamics, systems thinking and higher-order cognitive processes. To address persistent gaps in climate literacy and the limitations of transmissive physics instruction, this study examines how a nine-session sequence combining flipped classroom methods with agent-based simulations in NetLogo supports student learning across Bloom's Revised Taxonomy (BRT) in a Brazilian public high school.Thirty-four third-year students engaged with computational models of gas behavior, energy transfer and climate dynamics, followed by assessments aligned with six cognitive levels. The study contributes to STEM education by offering a replicable instructional sequence that bridges computational thinking, complex-systems modeling and climate-relevant physics, with implications for curriculum design, teacher preparation and climate education policy.

TI The role of digital learning technologies in enhancing interactive

SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

DT Article
DE artificial intelligence in education; digital learning technologies;
   higher education; in-service teachers; interactive learning;

ID USER ACCEPTANCE
AB This paper seeks to investigate the use of digital learning technologies in fostering interactive learning among education postgraduate students and in-service teachers at Ajman University, UAE. TI Manifestations of emotional agency in teacher education: a
   cross-national comparison of service-learning experiences in Germany,
   Austria, and Greece
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cross-national comparison; emotional agency; emotional competence;
   preservice teachers; service-learning; teacher education
AB Background Emotions play a central role in teacher education, yet research has primarily focused on emotional competence and less on how emotional experiences manifest in professional action. The concept of emotional agency offers a process-oriented perspective for understanding how preservice teachers mobilize emotions in authentic and socially embedded learning environments.Purpose This study investigates the manifestations of emotional agency in preservice teachers' service-learning (SL) experiences and examines how these manifestations vary across teacher education contexts in Germany, Austria, and Greece. Emotional agency is conceptualized as the enactment of emotional competence through professional action and operationalized through the dimensions of Action Regulation, Reflective Processing, and Social Embeddedness.Methods The study draws on 209 reflective diaries collected from preservice teachers participating in SL courses in Germany (n = 94), Austria (n = 60), and Greece (n = 55). Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis following Mayring's structuring approach and combining deductive and inductive coding procedures.Findings The findings show that emotional agency becomes visible when emotional experiences inform behavioral adaptation, professional reflection, and collaborative engagement. Across all three countries, social embeddedness emerged as the dominant manifestation of emotional agency, highlighting the central role of collaboration and interaction in professional learning. At the same time, distinct national profiles were identified. In Germany, manifestations of emotional agency were particularly associated with motivational engagement and collaborative participation. In Austria, emotional agency was more strongly characterized by reflective processing and engagement with emotional complexity. In Greece, manifestations of emotional agency were most evident in collaboration and adaptive responses to professional challenges.Conclusion The study provides a theoretically grounded and empirically applicable operationalization of emotional agency through Action Regulation, Reflective Processing, and Social Embeddedness. By making emotional agency observable and analyzable, the proposed framework offers a foundation for future research on emotions, professional learning, and teacher development across educational contexts.

TI Fostering independence in early adolescents with blindness: a
   qualitative study of caregiver engagement in disability simulations
   during a group-based intervention
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE caregiver engagement; disability simulation; early adolescence;
   independence; visual impairment and blindness
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; YOUNG-CHILDREN; SERVICES
AB Background In the context of visual impairment, involving caregivers is crucial for supporting their children's development, particularly in fostering independence. This study aims to evaluate the impact of engaging caregivers of five early adolescents (ages 11-14) with blindness in disability simulations of visual deprivation during group-based intervention for independence.Methods Five caregivers participated in four disability simulations of visual deprivation with their children with blindness: meal preparation, indoor mobility using safe techniques, mobility with the white cane, and role-playing of daily life scenarios. Following these activities, a focus group was conducted. Qualitative data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, focusing on caregivers' subjective experience of visual deprivation and its influence on their daily lives.Results Key themes that emerged from caregivers included: (1) the physical experience: importance of firsthand engagement in independent tasks while blindfolded; (2) emotional responses, including frustration and anxiety, due to the temporary loss of visual cues; (3) becoming aware: increased understanding of their child's difficulties and strengths; and (4) impact on daily life: integration of new strategies at home, like adjusting timing, using verbal cues, and encouraging their children's independence.Conclusions The use of disability simulations with caregivers of children with visual impairment into family-centered, interdisciplinary, and clinically oriented care programs appears to be an effective strategy for fostering caregivers' awareness of their children's needs regarding independence, promoting the generalization of strategies at home, and ultimately sustaining the development of their children's independence skills.

TI Unequal academics: AI as a threat to the voice and agency of Asian women
   in academia
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE agency; artificial intelligence; Asian women academics; Foucauldian
   discourse analysis; higher education; voice
AB The application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been identified as one of the fastest-growing areas in higher education. While AI improves productivity, it simultaneously shapes knowledge production, distribution and evaluation. Utilising a Foucauldian analytical lens, I use voice, agency and epistemic justice as integrated analytical tools to examine how AI-mediated systems constrain the voice and agency of Asian women academics in Western higher education institutions. This conceptual paper argues that AI is not a neutral tool; it is a discursive force embedded within existing structures of power as it standardises academic expression, mediates scholarly visibility, and reproduces existing gendered and racialised inequalities. When we lose Asian women's voices in academic discourse, we risk inaccurate decision-making and the reproduction of structural inequalities. By presenting Asian women academics as a critical case in the debate about scaling up AI use in universities, it provides a conceptual diagnosis of deeper systemic issues with AI. It calls for institutions to create strong academic leadership and AI governance protocols. Our future should be shaped by governance and leadership, not technology.

TI From production to verification: generative AI, doctoral formation, and
   the leadership of digital education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic authorship; AI policy; boundary work; digital education;
   doctoral education; generative AI; scholarly formation; verification
   literacy
ID ACADEMIC INTEGRITY
AB Introduction Generative artificial intelligence is often framed in higher education as a problem of academic integrity, assessment security, or technology adoption. This framing is necessary but insufficient for doctoral education, where writing, reading, coding, synthesizing literature, and interpreting evidence are not merely academic tasks but formative practices through which students become scholars.Methods Based on qualitative interviews with twenty-one doctoral students at a large research university in the United States, this study examines how doctoral students understand and negotiate generative AI in their scholarly work. The study began with students in education and was extended through purposive and snowball recruitment to include students across a range of other disciplines, so that the account would reflect more than one scholarly context; interviews were semi-structured.Results The findings show that AI functions as an access infrastructure, lowering linguistic barriers for some students and technical barriers for others depending on the demands of their scholarly work. At the same time, students engage in careful boundary work between assistance and authorship, distinguishing grammar support, translation, coding help, and conceptual orientation from intellectual substitution. The analysis further suggests that, among these participants, generative AI is shifting doctoral labor from production toward verification: students' distinctive responsibility increasingly lies in judging the accuracy, legitimacy, ownership, and defensibility of machine-assisted work. Under conditions of policy ambiguity, doctoral students also become primary governors of their own AI use, managing disclosure, caution, verification, and risk.Discussion The article argues that the leadership of digital education should move beyond broad AI policies toward context-sensitive guidance, verification literacy, transparent disclosure norms, and process-based assessment, including the culminating site of doctoral assessment, the dissertation defense. These claims are offered as analytic propositions grounded in a single-site interpretive study rather than as generalizable findings. Generative AI has not made doctoral education less necessary; it has made its purposes more urgent.

TI Bridging algorithmic prediction and teacher judgment: an explainable AI
   framework with institutional fairness calibration for early warning
   systems
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational data mining; explainable artificial intelligence;
   human-in-the-loop AI; institutional fairness calibration; learning
   analytics; SHAP; teacher prediction
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; MEDIATION
AB Prediction models for identifying at-risk students have become technically mature, yet their integration into secondary school practice remains limited by two persistent obstacles: opacity in model outputs, which erodes teacher trust, and uneven predictive performance across institutions, which risks widening rather than closing educational equity gaps. This study develops and evaluates an integrated five-stage framework combining systematic ablation analysis, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based decomposition, and school-level isotonic regression calibration for educational early warning systems. The framework is empirically evaluated on physics assessment data from 497 Grade 11 students across four Indonesian secondary schools (SPHERE dataset; intraclass correlation coefficient ICC = 0.309) and cross-validated on the UCI Student Performance cohort. Ablation results show that, within a school that already has local training data, models trained solely on observable student data achieve R2=0.354 on held-out data, establishing viable backup screening capability when teacher assessments are absent; incorporating teacher prediction raises performance to R2=0.494 [Delta R2=0.140; paired test-set bootstrap 95% CI (0.069, 0.213), positive across 100 independent splits]. However, the teacher prediction variable correlates substantially with the target (rpb=0.626), so its SHAP dominance partly reflects outcome overlap rather than unique professional insight; a single-predictor model using only teacher prediction achieves R2=0.275, confirming that the remaining features contribute additional signal. SHAP analysis reveals a stable three-tier feature hierarchy-teacher-encoded signal, school context, and student attitudes and skills-with Jaccard top-5 rank stability exceeding 0.70 across three datasets. Leave-one-school-out cross-validation (R2=-0.281) demonstrates that the model cannot generalize to entirely unseen schools, while within-school models achieve R2 approximate to 0.39-0.55, confirming student-level predictive capacity when school context is held constant. Gender-disaggregated fairness analysis shows approximate equal opportunity across genders (Delta TPR = 0.048, Delta FPR = 0.017). Isotonic regression calibration reduces institutional performance gaps when per-school training data is sufficient (School 4: Delta R2=+0.082); a minimum of approximately 50 training students per school is identified as a practical deployment boundary condition. Initial cross-context validation across Indonesian and Portuguese datasets supports the framework's methodological transferability, though the specific parameter estimates require multi-country replication before broader generalization can be claimed.

TI AI adoption readiness among Ukrainian education managers: Barriers,
   typologies, and policy implications
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Education management; AI adoption readiness;
   Ukraine; Latent class analysis; fsQCA; Policy analysis; Technology

ID USER ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in education requires strategic leadership from education managers, yet little research examines AI readiness among this stakeholder group, particularly in post-Soviet transitional contexts. As decision-makers who control whether and how AI enters educational practice, managers' readiness is essential for evidence-based policy. This study investigates (1) the current state of AI adoption readiness among Ukrainian edremove ucation managers, including the gap between personal and institutional readiness; (2) the barriers and facilitators that most strongly influence AI readiness; (3) distinct manager typologies based on readiness profiles; and (4) polremove icy implications for scaling AI in education. A cross-sectional survey was administered to 395 education managers across 23 Ukrainian regions in September 2025. The 47-variable instrument covered demographics, AI readiness (personal and system), adoption barriers, tool usage, application potential, and psychological attitudes. Analysis employed descriptive statistics, Latent Class Analysis (LCA) for person-centered typology identification, fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) for configurational analysis of barrier combinations, and exploratory structural analysis. Personal readiness (M = 3.83, SD = 0.96) significantly exceeded system readiness (M = 3.15, SD = 0.93), a 0.68-point personal-institutional gap confirmed by a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p < (.)001, d = 0.73). LCA identified six provisional manager profiles, with the Competency-constrained class being the largest. fsQCA found that no barrier was a necessary condition and no barrier configuration was sufficient for low AI readiness, indicating that low readiness is not reducible to specific barriers or their combiremove nations. Digital competency showed the largest training gap. Ukrainian education managers demonstrate higher personal than institutional AI readiness, constrained primarily by regulatory uncertainty and competency deficits. The identification of six provisional typologies enables targeted policy interventions. Policy priorities should foremove cus on regulatory framework development, institutional capacity building, and differentiated, typology-based training.

TI Academic motivation and self-regulated learning strategies in medical
   students: A cross-sectional comparative study with educational
   implications
SO EDUCACION MEDICA
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Academic motivation; Self-regulated learning; Learning strategies;
   Medical education; Medical students
ID EFFICACY; READINESS
AB Introduction: Academic motivation and learning strategies are key components of self-regulated learning and academic performance in medical students, particularly during the basic cycle, a critical stage for the development of study habits and learner autonomy. Materials and methods: An exploratory, descriptive, cross-sectional study was conducted. The Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) was administered to 152 second-and third-year medical students from two Chilean universities. Descriptive analyses and comparisons of mean scores between institutions were performed. Results: The sample was predominantly female (63.8%). No significant differences were found in intrinsic or extrinsic goal orientations. Differences were observed in task value and control of learning beliefs, with higher scores among students from the University of Magallanes, whereas students from the University of Atacama showed higher academic self-efficacy. No differences were found in cognitive or metacognitive strategies; however, students from Atacama reported greater use of resource management strategies, particularly effort regulation, peer learning, and help seeking. Conclusion: The findings reveal differentiated motivational and strategic profiles between institutions, supporting the contextual nature of self-regulated learning in early medical education. The MSLQis confirmed as a useful tool to inform pedagogical interventions aimed at strengthening self-regulation, academic self-efficacy, and the strategic use of learning resources. TI Effectiveness of guided educational visualization in learning
   embryological content
SO EDUCACION MEDICA
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Embryology; Medical education; Learning
ID CATEGORIZATION
AB Introduction: Embryology is a complex science due to its dynamic and three-dimensional nature, which presents a training challenge compared to traditional teaching based on twodimensional presentations. Guided educational visualization emerges as a promising pedagogical strategy that uses visual mediators to organize and construct developmental learning. This study evaluates the effectiveness of guided educational visualization as an instructional strategy in learning embryological content, with an emphasis on its impact on the cognitive dimension. Materials and methods: A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design was used with 60 medical students from the Technical University of Ambato, divided into an experimental group and a control group. The experimental group participated in guided visualization sessions using 3D animations and ultrasound images, while the control group received traditional lectures. A validated instrument with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.87 was used. Results: Significant differences favoring the experimental group were revealed in all dimensions: conceptual understanding (gain of 33.2 vs. 16.4 in the control group), integration (33.6 vs. 15.3), and application (33.9 vs. 15.5). Effect sizes were large (Cohen's d between 1.12 and 1.45), demonstrating favorable results for the intervention. Conclusions: Guided visualization is an instructional strategy that activates deep cognitive pathways and acts as an essential bridge between theory and clinical practice. TI Building a diagnostic model for misconceptions in physics education
   using eye tracking technology
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID MOTION; ATTENTION; KNOWLEDGE; MOVEMENTS; FORCE
AB Accurate diagnosis of student misconceptions is crucial for effective science instruction. Traditional diagnostic tools, however, often rely on unreliable self-reported confidence levels. This study developed and validated a two-dimensional diagnostic model that integrates objective eye tracking data with test responses to more robustly identify misconceptions in Newtonian mechanics. The study involved three phases: developing a four-tier diagnostic test, conducting an eye tracking experiment to analyze visual attention patterns (fixation duration, revisits, scan paths) among high school students, and constructing the final model by correlating eye movements with confidence judgments. Consistent with previous research, results showed that students with misconceptions had shorter fixation durations on correct options and displayed inefficient scan paths. Conversely, those with scientific conceptions showed focused attention. As a novel contribution of this study, a "reversed U-shaped" pattern was observed between confidence and revisits, indicating that revisits can serve as an objective measure of cognitive uncertainty. Based on these findings, we propose a two-dimensional "eye tracking-test" model. This model offers a more precise method for diagnosing student understanding, providing a foundation for targeted instructional interventions and fostering a dynamic "teach-learn-assess" feedback loop for personalized physics education.

TI Parents' Perceptions of Intellectual Precocity
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE intellectual precocity; parents'; preschoolers; perceptions; concerns;
   parenting strategies
ID GIFTEDNESS; CHILDREN; FAMILY; VALIDATION; EDUCATION; TADI
AB Intellectual precocity refers to the early manifestation of cognitive abilities well above age norms and involves multidimensional developmental needs. Parents play a central role in recognizing and responding to these profiles; however, little is known about how families of young children experience this process, particularly in contexts such as Chile. This qualitative phenomenological study examines parental perceptions of intellectual precocity in 4-5-year-old children through semi-structured interviews with 52 families. Findings conceptualize parenting as a dynamic and relational process shaped by intergenerational continuities, diverse caregiving practices, and children's developmental profiles. Parents frequently recognize their own traits in their children, facilitating understanding but also generating tensions in parenting approaches. A key challenge involves children's questioning of norms, linked to advanced cognitive abilities, which reconfigures traditional authority dynamics. Parents also express concerns regarding educational fit and future trajectories, often perceiving limited institutional responsiveness. In response, families adopt strategies such as intellectual scaffolding in the home, dialogic communication, and active advocacy for differentiated educational opportunities. The study underscores the need for family support and more responsive educational systems to address the multidimensional nature of intellectual precocity.

TI Usage, Benefits and Challenges of Generative Artificial Intelligence in
   Mathematics: The Student Perspective
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE benefits of GenAI; challenges of GenAI; ChatGPT; generative artificial
   intelligence; higher education; mathematics; student perspective
ID ANXIETY
AB The rapid influx of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has resulted in a large number of research studies over the past three years. Much of the research to date has focused on the researcher/educator perspective of the optimal usage, benefits and challenges in the implementation of GenAI, often in a very general sense. The importance of the student voice and discipline-specific results must not be lost in this debate. This study investigates students' decisions to use (or not use) GenAI for mathematics purposes and the reasons they give to support this choice. This was done by surveying almost 700 students in an Irish university, using an online, anonymous survey in March 2025. The students in the sample were all studying at least one mathematics module at the time. In addition, students were asked what they perceive the benefits and challenges to be of GenAI for mathematics in higher education. 91% of respondents were using GenAI for mathematics purposes. Both their reasons for using GenAI and the benefits they perceived for it fell into four main themes: Self-Improvement, Tools, Access, and Support. Their reasons for not using GenAI, and the challenges they perceived, were categorised under Unnecessary/Unknown, Inaccurate, Skill Loss, and Ethical Concerns. Students mentioned using GenAI for self-improvement reasons, such as bettering their understanding of mathematics, and found the lack of interaction with a person to be a benefit rather than a challenge. This study was conducted at a unique moment in time when the usage of GenAI was moving from sporadic to widespread and reflects students' self-reported reasons for this.

TI Beyond the Screen: A Conceptual Framework for Spatial Experiential
   Vocabulary Learning in Digital Language Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE vocabulary acquisition; spatial learning; embodied cognition; situated
   learning; experiential learning; digital language learning; EARR
   framework; object-based learning; immersive environments
ID VIRTUAL-REALITY
AB Despite the rapid growth of AI-based digital language learning platforms, prevailing approaches to vocabulary instruction have remained relatively unchanged. Flashcards, translation drills, and isolated quizzes continue to dominate, and while they may support short-term retention, they tend to strip away the contextual, physical, and spatial dimensions that research identifies as important for durable language acquisition. This paper proposes spatial experiential vocabulary learning as a pedagogically grounded alternative. Drawing on situated learning theory, embodied cognition, and experiential learning theory, it argues that lasting vocabulary acquisition may depend not only on repeated exposure but also on learners engaging actively with language in meaningful, spatially situated contexts. The central theoretical contribution is the EARR framework, a four-phase learning cycle comprising Encounter, Act, Respond, and Reuse, in which vocabulary is embedded within object-rich spatial environments that invite purposeful interaction rather than passive recognition. The paper develops this framework theoretically and draws out its implications for platform design. It concludes by identifying priorities for future empirical research and by considering how digital language learning environments might be redesigned to better support the conditions under which vocabulary acquisition appears to occur.

TI Japanese Language Study Intensity Among Vietnamese University Students:
   Academic Engagement, Career Motivation, and Learning Behavior in a
   Higher-Education Context
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Japanese language learning; study intensity; Vietnamese university
   students; career motivation; academic engagement; self-regulated
   learning; higher education
ID FOREIGN-LANGUAGE
AB Japanese language learning has become increasingly relevant for Vietnamese university students due to expanding academic, cultural, and career-related links between Vietnam and Japan. This study examined lifestyle, social, health-related, and motivational correlates of Japanese language study intensity among Vietnamese university students. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 407 university students studying Japanese in Vietnam. Descriptive and bivariate analyses used the full sample, while the adjusted logistic regression was based on 334 participants with complete data for all model variables. High study intensity was defined as studying Japanese for 8 h or more per week. Descriptive statistics, bivariate analyses, and adjusted logistic regression were used to examine factors associated with high study intensity. Among participants, 185 students (45.5%) reported high Japanese study intensity. In bivariate analysis, high study intensity was significantly associated with higher latest GPA or academic score, career-related reasons for studying Japanese, grammar study frequency, and prioritizing reading. In the adjusted logistic regression model including 334 complete cases, higher latest GPA or academic score and career-related motivation were positively associated with high study intensity, whereas prioritizing reading was negatively associated with high study intensity. Most lifestyle and health-related variables were not significantly associated with study intensity. These findings suggest that intensive Japanese learning among Vietnamese university students may be driven more by academic engagement and perceived career value than by general lifestyle or health-related patterns.

TI Toponymic Knowledge and Territorial Literacy in Pre-Service Primary
   Education Teachers: Effects of a Didactic Intervention in Extremadura
   and La Rioja
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE toponymy; geography education; initial teacher education; spatial
   thinking; higher education
ID SPATIAL THINKING
AB This study analyses the toponymic learning of students enrolled in the Degree in Primary Education programme following a didactic intervention carried out at the Universities of Extremadura and La Rioja. The research was designed as a quasi-experimental study with a pretest and posttest in non-equivalent groups and focused on eight variables related to the identification and location of provincial boundaries, provincial capitals, county seats, and counties. The main objective was to examine the development of toponymic knowledge and to analyse possible differences according to the methodology applied and the group of origin. The results show significant differences between the pretest and posttest in a relevant proportion of the variables analysed, especially in provincial boundaries, provincial capitals, and counties, whereas no significant changes were observed in county seats (i.e., the main towns or functional centres of the Spanish comarcas). In the unadjusted posttest analyses, no statistically significant differences were found between the traditional and interactive methodology; however, exploratory adjusted ANCOVA analyses suggested possible partial methodological tendencies in some specific dimensions, particularly in the identification of counties, although these results should be interpreted cautiously because not all ANCOVA assumptions were met. Likewise, the correlations between identification and location were very high in both phases. Overall, the findings suggest that toponymic tasks based on identification and location can support basic dimensions of territorial literacy in initial teacher education, although they should not be interpreted as a comprehensive assessment of spatial thinking as a whole.

TI Intergenerational Differences in Generative AI Adoption: A Model
   Explaining the Roles of AI Competency, Responsible AI Adoption, and
   Ethical Awareness in Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence (GenAI); AI Competency Capability; AI
   utilisation behaviour; AI ethical awareness; responsible AI behaviour;
   higher education; Generation Y (Gen Y); Generation Z (Gen Z); technology
   adoption; organisational adaptation; AI governance; PLS-SEM; sustainable
   development goals (SDGs)
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming teaching, learning, research, and institutional practices in higher education, increasing the need to understand how university professionals engage with AI technologies in both functional and ethical contexts. This study examined AI adoption among sampled Generation Y (Gen Y) and Generation Z (Gen Z) higher education professionals by investigating the relationships among AI Competency Capability (AICC), AI Utilisation Behaviour (AIUB), Perceived Usability (PU), Perceived Strategic Value (PSV), AI Ethical Awareness (AIEA), AI Self-Efficacy (AISE), Responsible AI Utilisation Behaviour (RAIUB), Academic Engagement (AE), Perceived Performance Outcomes (PPO), and AI Adoption Intention (AAI). Adaptive Structuration Theory (AST) and Dual-Process Theory (DPT) were employed as complementary interpretive perspectives rather than as theories directly tested by the structural model. Data were collected from 870 higher education professionals employed at Saudi Arabian universities and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM), Partial Least Squares Multi-Group Analysis (PLS-MGA), and the Measurement Invariance of Composite Models (MICOM) procedure. The PLS-MGA identified statistically significant between-group differences only for the relationships between AICC and AIUB, which were numerically larger among the sampled Gen Z participants, and between AIEA and Responsible AIUB, which were numerically larger among the sampled Gen Y participants. All remaining differences represented sample-specific numerical variations rather than statistically confirmed between-group differences. Given the cross-sectional design and differences in age, career stage, institutional role, and professional experience, the findings should be interpreted as sample-specific associations rather than fixed generational characteristics. This study introduces the Gen-AI Dual Competency Alignment Framework (GADCAF) as a provisional conceptual and interpretive framework, intended to guide future research on AI competency, responsible AI utilisation, and organisational AI integration rather than as a validated theoretical model. The findings advance understanding of the complementary functional and ethical dimensions of AI adoption in higher education.

TI English Medium Instruction Lectures: A Gender Perspective on
   Comprehension Challenges
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE gender; English medium instruction; lecture; comprehension; language
   processing; content learning; listening
ID SCHOOL; MOTIVATION; ANXIETY
AB Gender has often been overlooked in tertiary English medium instruction (EMI) research. To address this gap, the present study investigates whether gender plays a role in EMI lecture comprehension challenges. The study included 37 participants (21 female and 16 male) who attended EMI lectures in a variety of subjects. Participants used a foot pedal to "time-stamp" comprehension challenges in real time during lectures. After the lectures, students joined stimulated recall interviews guided by the time stamps, where they re-watched time-stamped portions of lecture videos and explained reasons for non-comprehension. Results showed that gender did not play a statistically significant role in relation to a majority of the comprehension challenges, with the exception of top-down >> content-related, where females were more likely to report issues such as lack of prior content knowledge than males. Based on the findings, commentary about the role of gender in EMI and in relation to various language skills is provided.

TI Reexamining the Monitoring and Managing Subdimensions of the Shared
   Metacognition Questionnaire in Online Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE shared metacognition; self-regulation; co-regulation; online learning;
   higher education; scale validation
ID COMMUNITIES; CONSTRUCT
AB The Shared Metacognition Questionnaire (SMQ) is widely used to assess metacognition in collaborative online learning environments. Prior work has supported its two broad dimensions of self-regulation of cognition (SRC) and co-regulation of cognition (CRC), but the lower-order monitoring and managing subdimensions theorized within SRC and CRC have not been empirically supported. The present study used a split-sample exploratory and confirmatory factor analytic approach with graduate students (N = 348) enrolled in 25 fully online courses. For SRC, the results provided tentative support for a two-factor monitoring-managing structure, with the managing factor performing more strongly than the monitoring factor. For CRC, neither the theorized structure nor an empirically informed alternative reached marginally acceptable fit, and item-level diagnostics pointed to potential issues of item clarity, redundancy, and content clustering. The findings (1) provide additional validity evidence supporting the use of SMQ to measure self-monitoring and self-managing; (2) extend the original SMQ development study and broader theoretical models of self- and co-regulation; and (3) offer practical guidance on the current use of the SMQ and suggestions for refining the CRC items.
