TI The psychological effects of teleological thinking training on teachers:
   A quasi-experimental study of self-efficacy, psychological empowerment,
   and job satisfaction
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Teleological thinking; Teacher training; Self-efficacy; Psychological
   empowerment; Job satisfaction; Educational intervention; Teacher
   well-being
ID MOTIVATION
AB Purpose: This study examines the psychological associations of teleological thinking training among teachers, focusing on self-efficacy, psychological empowerment, and job satisfaction. The study further explores whether these psychological resources are statistically associated with indirect pathways linking the training experience to teachers' professional well-being. Design/methodology/approach: A quasi-experimental pre-post design with a control group was employed. The sample consisted of 127 teachers (66 experimental, 61 control). Participants in the experimental group received teleological thinking training, while the control group did not. Data were analyzed using paired and independent samples t-tests, and mediation effects were examined using bootstrapping with 5000 resamples. Findings: The findings indicate that participation in teleological thinking training was associated with significant increases in teachers' self-efficacy and psychological empowerment. Although the between-group difference in job satisfaction did not reach conventional statistical significance, both self-efficacy and psychological empowerment were positively associated with job satisfaction. Bootstrapping analyses revealed statistically significant indirect effects consistent with the proposed mediation framework, suggesting that the relationship between the intervention and job satisfaction may operate through these psychological mechanisms. Originality/value: This study provides an exploratory empirical examination of teleological thinking as an emerging cognitive-developmental perspective within teacher professional development. The findings contribute to the literature by highlighting the potential role of futureoriented and purposive cognitive frameworks in shaping teachers' psychological resources and professional experiences. Rather than presenting teleological thinking as a fully established standalone theory, the study positions it as an emerging integrative perspective that may offer useful directions for future research on teacher cognition, professional development, and educational well-being interventions.

TI The relationship between AI dependency and critical thinking disposition
   in nursing students: The mediating role of metacognitive ability and the
   moderating role of academic self-efficacy
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence dependency; Metacognitive ability; Critical
   thinking disposition; Academic self-efficacy; Moderated mediation model;
   Nursing students
ID COMPETENCE
AB Background: Artificial intelligence tools are increasingly integrated into nursing education. They bring great potential to improve learning efficiency and access to information. However, whether over-reliance on artificial intelligence affects the development of critical thinking remains to be verified. Critical thinking is a core competency for clinical decision-making and safe nursing practice. Although existing evidence suggests a negative association between AI dependency and higher-order cognitive abilities, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In particular, the roles of internal cognitive processes and individual psychological characteristics are not well understood. Existing research has largely focused on external factors related to technology adoption. Less attention has been paid to how AI dependency affects metacognitive functioning or the moderating role of academic self-efficacy. There is a particular lack of in-depth research on nursing students, a group that faces multiple cognitive demands from theoretical study, clinical practice, and professional preparation. Objective: This study aimed to explore the relationship between artificial intelligence dependency and critical thinking disposition among nursing students. It examined the mediating role of metacognitive ability and the moderating role of academic self-efficacy. The goal was to reveal the underlying mechanism of this relationship. Methods: A questionnaire survey was conducted among nursing students using the Artificial Intelligence Dependence Questionnaire (assessing independent variable: AI dependency), the Metacognitive Ability Scale (assessing mediator: metacognitive ability), the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale (assessing dependent variable: critical thinking disposition), and the Academic Self-Efficacy Scale (assessing moderator: academic self-efficacy). Moderated mediation analysis was performed using Model 5 in the SPSS macro program PROCESS. Structural equation modeling and simple slope analysis were used to examine the path relationships and moderating effects among the variables. Results: The direct predictive effect of artificial intelligence dependency on critical thinking disposition was not significant (beta = 0.021, P = 0.325). However, the indirect effect through metacognitive ability was significant. This indicated that metacognitive ability played an indirect-only mediating role in this sample between the two. Academic self-efficacy played a negative moderating role in the path from artificial intelligence dependency to metacognitive ability (beta = -0.008, P < 0.01). It also played a negative moderating role in the path from metacognitive ability to critical thinking disposition (beta = -0.003, P < 0.05). Simple slope analysis showed that for students with low academic self-efficacy, the positive predictive effect of artificial intelligence dependency on metacognitive ability was stronger (beta = 0.218, P < 0.01). Similarly, the positive predictive effect of metacognitive ability on critical thinking disposition was also stronger for this group. For students with high academic self-efficacy, the positive effects in both paths were weakened. Conclusion: Artificial intelligence dependency was indirectly associated with critical thinking disposition in nursing students through the indirect-only mediating role of metacognitive ability. Academic self-efficacy played a negative moderating role in both the first and second halves of the model.
   This model revealed a differentiated mechanism through which artificial intelligence dependency affects critical thinking. For students with low academic self-efficacy, AI dependency may serve as a form of cognitive compensation by activating metacognition. For students with high academic self-efficacy, the positive effects of AI dependency were relatively limited. Rather than simply encouraging or restricting AI use, nursing educators should adopt differentiated guidance strategies based on students' self-efficacy levels-supporting metacognitive engagement for low-efficacy students while fostering critical evaluation of AI outputs for high-efficacy students. The goal is to promote reflective AI use that strengthens metacognitive skills, rather than passive dependence.

TI The impact of career calling on nursing interns' patient safety
   competency: a chained mediating effect of self-directed learning ability
   and clinical thinking ability
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Career calling; Patient safety competency; Self-directed learning
   ability; Clinical thinking ability; Nursing interns
AB Background: Nursing interns serve as a vital backup force for nursing staff, making it imperative to enhance their patient safety competency. While existing research has explored the relationship between nursing interns' career calling and patient safety competency, the underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently substantiated. Aim: This study aims to investigate the impact of nursing intern's career calling on their patient safety competency, and to analyze the chained mediating role of self-directed learning ability and clinical thinking ability in this relationship. Design: This study employed a descriptive cross-sectional design. Settings: This study was conducted at Shanxi Bethune Hospital (a Grade A tertiary general hospital). Participants: The sample size was estimated based on recommendations for structural equation modeling. Of 434 eligible nursing interns who were invited to participate, 392 completed the survey, and after 355 valid questionnaires were included in the final analysis. Method: Career calling scale, Self-Directed Learning Ability Scale, Clinical Thinking Ability Scale, and Patient Safety Competency Scale were used for data collection. Pearson correlation analysis examined relationships between variables, and structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to elucidate mediating effects among variables. Results: The valid response rate was 90.56%. Self-directed learning ability (beta = 0.12; 95% CI [0.07, 0.18]) and clinical thinking ability (beta = 0.09; 95% CI [0.05, 0.14]) mediated the relationship between career calling and patient safety competency, accounting for 22.43% and 16.64% of the total effect, respectively. Furthermore, self-directed learning ability and clinical thinking ability exerted a chained mediating effect in the relationship between career calling and patient safety competency (beta = 0.07; 95% CI [0.05, 0.11]), accounting for 13.83% of the total effect. Conclusion: Career calling is positively associated with nursing interns' self-directed learning abilities and clinical thinking abilities, which in turn are associated with improved patient safety competency. Nursing educators and administrators should establish a comprehensive, multi-level intervention system, including cultivating nursing students' career calling levels, to enhance their self-directed learning ability and clinical thinking ability, thereby improving their patient safety competency.

TI A structured hands-on CSF diagnostic training module improves diagnostic
   knowledge in medical students: a prospective pre-post study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; Neurology; Cerebrospinal fluid; Practical training;
   Pre-post study; Diagnostic skills
ID LEARNING TRANSFORMING THEORY
AB Background Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) diagnostics is an essential component of neurological practice and requires not only theoretical knowledge but also the ability to interpret cytological findings and integrate them into clinical reasoning. Structured, practice-oriented approaches for teaching CSF diagnostics in undergraduate medical education remain limited. This study evaluated the impact of a structured, hands-on training module in CSF diagnostics on medical students' knowledge acquisition and application of diagnostic knowledge. Methods This prospective educational intervention study included fourth-year medical students participating in a mandatory neurology practical course. The intervention consisted of a pre-test, a structured theoretical session, a practical microscopy session using authentic CSF samples, and a post-test conducted during a single teaching session. Knowledge acquisition was assessed using pseudonymized pre- and post-tests covering CSF-related knowledge domains including indications for lumbar puncture, cytological findings, diagnostic interpretation, microscopy-based diagnosis and procedural aspects of CSF diagnostics. Student evaluations were collected immediately after the session using an anonymous questionnaire. Paired data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and McNemar's test, as appropriate. Results Eighty-four medical students completed both assessments. Median test scores increased from 3 to 6 correct answers following the intervention (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Z = - 7.886, p < 0.001). Improvements were observed particularly in procedural knowledge, diagnostic interpretation, cytological assessment, and microscopy-based diagnosis. Baseline performance regarding indications for lumbar puncture was already high and showed no significant change. Student evaluations indicated positive perceptions of the integration of theoretical and practical components. Conclusions A structured, hands-on CSF diagnostics training module was associated with improved short-term knowledge acquisition and application of diagnostic knowledge related to CSF diagnostics among undergraduate medical students. Practice-oriented teaching approaches may complement traditional neurology education and support clinically relevant learning.

TI Transforming curiosity through AR: An empirical study of flow-based
   environmental health education for elementary students
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Augmented reality; Curiosity theory; Flow theory; Environmental
   education; Elementary education; Educational technology design
AB Environmental health education faces the challenge of connecting students with the often-overlooked organisms coexisting in their everyday environments. This study developed and validated an augmented reality (AR)enhanced mosquito vector control curriculum grounded in integrated curiosity-flow theory. The curriculum employed a two-stage design: Session 1 created knowledge gaps to induce deprivation-type (D-type) curiosity, while Session 2 provided AR exploration tools to facilitate transformation into interest-type (I-type) curiosity and foster flow experience. Using structural equation modeling with 423 fifth-grade students, we examined relationships among mosquito-related anxiety, curiosity types, flow experience, and continuance intention. Results demonstrated that anxiety significantly predicted both curiosity types (I-type: (3 = .62; D-type: (3 = .54), which in turn predicted flow experience (R2 = .52). Flow significantly influenced continuance intention ((3 = .53, R2 = .28), with both curiosity pathways showing significant mediation effects. Findings illuminate how AR technologies provide unique affordances, real-time feedback, autonomous navigation, and achievement visualization, that support theoretical mechanisms in environmental education. This research contributes an empirically validated framework integrating curiosity and flow theories for educational technology design.

TI Redesigning Objective Questions for Efficient and Fair Assessment in
   Theoretical STEM Courses
SO IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Modeling; STEM; Design methodology; Cognition; Cognitive systems;
   Learning (artificial intelligence); Testing; Accuracy; Standards;
   Artificial intelligence; Evaluation efficiency; learning assessment;
   multiple-choice questions (MCQ); multiple true-false (MTF); science,
   technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education
ID MULTIPLE TRUE-FALSE; SUMMATIVE ASSESSMENT; EDUCATION; CHOICE
AB Contribution: Despite their logistical advantages, multiple-choice questions (MCQ) and multiple-true-false (MTF) formats are often underused or viewed skeptically in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education due to concerns about superficiality, a lack of depth, and vulnerability to guessing. This study presents redesigned MCQ and MTF formats that aim to improve objectivity, fairness, and efficiency while preserving conceptual rigor. Background: Open-ended questions are traditionally favored in STEM due to their ability to assess reasoning and partial understanding. However, they pose challenges for consistent and efficient grading, especially in large courses. Meanwhile, the literature shows that well-constructed objective items can match open-ended questions in diagnostic power, yet most existing MCQs fail to meet quality standards, and MTFs remain underutilized. Intended outcomes: The intervention seeks to: 1) ensure objective, deterministic grading; 2) reduce the impact of guessing; 3) support partial credit where appropriate; and 4) offer an efficient solution without compromising the depth of assessment. Application design: We propose a ten-option MCQ structure designed to reduce random success rates while enabling richer distractor design, and a sum-based MTF variant where students report the sum of weights assigned to true statements. The combination of both formats enables automatic grading, discourages guessing, and allows nuanced performance measurement. These were applied to two exams in an undergraduate Electrical Circuits II course over a semester. Findings: Results from 52 students indicate that the proposed formats produce balanced precision and effective discrimination between items. Partial credit allowed for better scoring without inflating the results. A parallel evaluation using state-of-the-art large-language models revealed low performance on the proposed questions, suggesting that such structured formats cannot yet be reliably replaced by AI-based grading of open-ended STEM responses. These findings suggest that thoughtfully redesigned objective questions can serve as efficient, fair, and pedagogically rigorous alternatives to open-ended formats in theoretical or foundational STEM courses where conceptual precision is paramount, and should be complemented by project-based or laboratory assessments.

TI AI-Simulated Patients for Training Shared Decision-Making: Feasibility
   Study in Medical Education
SO JMIR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; chatbots; communication; medical education;
   patient participation; professional competence; SDM; self-efficacy;
   shared decision-making; simulation training
ID INVOLVE PATIENTS; OPTION SCALE; KNOWLEDGE; EXTENT
AB Background: Shared decision-making (SDM) is a key element of patient-centered care; however, opportunities for structured and scalable SDM training remain limited in both medical education and clinical practice. Advances in AI have enabled chatbot-based simulations that may support repeated practice and provide automated feedback on SDM-related communication behaviors. Objective: This study aimed to (1) evaluate the agreement between AI-generated and human ratings of SDM performance, (2) compare SDM-related performance and attitudes between medical students and physicians, and (3) explore changes in communicative self-efficacy (CSE) following chatbot-based SDM practice. Methods: We conducted a feasibility study using a pre-post mixed methods design. Medical students and physicians practiced SDM in a 20-minute chat-based interaction with an AI-simulated patient, followed by automated feedback on SDM performance. Prior to the interaction, participants' attitudes toward SDM (IcanSDM) and their CSE (Self-Efficacy in Patient-Centeredness Questionnaire[SEPCQ-24-GER]) were assessed; CSE wasreevaluatedafter the intervention. SDM performance wasmeasured using the validated Observing Patient Involvement in Decision Making (OPTION-12) scale, with the AI evaluating participants' performance from the patient's perspective. These AI-generated ratings were then compared with human ratings to evaluate agreement and rating quality. To further investigate discrepancies between AI and human ratings, a qualitative analysis of selected cases was conducted. Additional measures included demographics, perceived authenticity, and benefits of the interaction. Quantitative analyses included group comparisons, pre-post analyses, and psychometric evaluation of the OPTION-12 scale in an AI-mediated setting. The study was preregistered on the Open Science Framework. Results: A total of 58 participants were included in the analysis, 22 (37.9%) of whom were students, 34 (58.2%) were physicians, and 2 did not declare. Both groups reported similarly positive attitudes toward SDM, but medical students (n=22; mean 28.67, SD 4.32) achieved higher OPTION-12 performance scores than physicians (n=34; mean 22.79, SD 8.14). CSE showed a slight decrease following the intervention. Agreement between AI-generated and human OPTION-12 total scores was high (intraclass correlation coefficient=0.86, df=2,1; P<.001), although AI ratings were systematically higher. The OPTION-12 scale in theAI setting demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach alpha=0.88; mean interitem correlation r=0.43). Participants perceived the AI-simulated interaction as authentic and potentially useful for SDM training. Conclusions: This feasibility study provides preliminary and exploratory insights into the use of AI-simulated patients for SDM training in medical education. The findings contribute to the contextual validation of the OPTION-12 scale in AI-mediated consultations and provide valuable insights into participants' attitudes toward SDM. However, while findings suggest potential for supporting communication skills development and structured feedback, conclusions are limited by the study design and sample size. Further research with larger samples and controlled designs is needed to establish effectiveness and generalizability.

TI Facilitating autistic student voice in reasonable adjustments
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Autistic students; Student voice; Inclusive education; Reasonable
   adjustments; Universal design for learning; Consultation methods
ID SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL-NEEDS; SOCIAL-PARTICIPATION; YOUNG-PEOPLE; CHILDREN;
   DISABILITIES; MAINSTREAM; TEACHERS; EXPERIENCES; INCLUSION; PLAY
AB Purpose: This research addresses the gap between policy requirements for student consultation in reasonable adjustments and actual practice by developing effective methods to elicit autistic students' perspectives on classroom accommodations. Despite international frameworks mandating student voice in educational decisions, autistic students remain largely excluded from planning their own support arrangements. Design/methodology/approach: Fourteen autistic students aged 5-12 years participated in four multi-modal consultation activities: picture book discussions, card sorting, small world play, and creative representation tasks. The study integrated MacBeath et al.'s consultation taxonomy with Universal Design for Learning principles to accommodate diverse communication styles and enable authentic participation across the autism spectrum. Findings: All participants engaged meaningfully across consultation methods, generating 107 distinct accommodation preferences through 740 individual responses. Students demonstrated sophisticated understanding of their learning needs, articulating preferences around sensory regulation, environmental flexibility, assistive technology, and social considerations. Four key themes emerged: embodied learning and sensory self-regulation, environmental agency and spatial control, learning tool sophistication, and social relationship navigation. Originality/value: This study establishes empirical evidence that young autistic students possess valuable insights about their educational needs when provided appropriate consultation methods. The alignment between student preferences and Universal Design for Learning principles suggests that student-informed accommodations benefit broader populations, supporting truly inclusive educational practice rather than segregated adjustment approaches.

TI South Korean immigrant parent and sibling perspectives on physical
   activity participation among adults with autism spectrum disorder
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism spectrum disorder; Developmental disabilities; Physical activity;
   Immigrant families; Siblings; Family systems theory; Qualitative
   research
ID YOUNG-CHILDREN; MOTOR-SKILLS; FAMILIES; INDIVIDUALS; INTERVENTION;
   ADOLESCENTS; INVOLVEMENT; TRANSITION; SERVICES; PEOPLE
AB Background: Although physical activity (PA) participation can promote physical health, social interaction, behavioral regulation, and overall quality of life among adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), South Korean immigrant parents and siblings may face distinctive challenges in supporting PA participation due to caregiving responsibilities, cultural and linguistic barriers, and limited access to supportive community-based resources. Method: Guided by Family Systems Theory, this descriptive multiple-case study examined parent and sibling perspectives from four South Korean immigrant families, with each case including one parent and one sibling of an adult with ASD. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, demographic questionnaires, and the researcher's reflective journal. Within-case and cross-case analyses were used to identify patterns across parent and sibling accounts related to PA participation. Results: Three themes were identified: parents' and siblings' beliefs about the value of PA, parent and sibling burden in supporting PA, and contextual barriers to PA access. Although parents and siblings viewed PA as important, sustained participation was constrained by limited knowledge and confidence, caregiving overload, sibling role strain, reduced post-school opportunities, limited autism-friendly programs, and cultural and linguistic barriers. Conclusions: These findings underscore the need for culturally responsive PA supports that acknowledge parents' and siblings' roles within the family context, address post-school barriers to PA access, and expand sustainable community-based opportunities for adults with ASD.

TI Revisiting the effects of artificial intelligence in education: A
   meta-analysis of academic achievement and student motivation
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence in education; Academic achievement; Student
   motivation pedagogical issues; Teaching/learning strategies
ID LEARNING-SYSTEM; PERSONALIZED INTERVENTION; AI; PERFORMANCE; IMPACT;
   ANALYTICS; IMPROVE; SCIENCE; CHATGPT; BIAS
AB This meta-analytic study examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in education on students' academic achievement and motivation. A total of 215 independent effect sizes (achievement: n = 172; motivation: n = 43) were synthesized using a random-effects model. Results indicate a strong positive effect on academic achievement (d = 0.80, 95% CI [0.68, 0.91]) and a moderate positive effect on motivation (d = 0.64, 95% CI [0.46, 0.82]). Significant heterogeneity was observed among the included studies. Moderator analyses revealed that achievement outcomes varied by subject domain and intervention duration, while motivation outcomes were influenced by educational level and AI tool type. These variations highlight the role of instructional and contextual factors. Overall, the findings suggest that the effectiveness of AI depends on its pedagogical design and implementation, providing important implications for the development and integration of AIsupported learning environments.

TI "Not their real teacher": Exploring teacher-targeted bullying against
   pre-service teachers in the United States during field experiences
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student bullying; Teacher-targeted bullying; Pre-service teachers;
   Teacher education; Field experience; Field placement
ID SCHOOL TEACHERS; KNOWLEDGE; STUDENTS; VIOLENCE; SKILLS
AB Nearly 23% (n = 60) of 271 surveyed U.S. pre-service teachers perceived having experienced bullying by students during their field experiences in K-12 (kindergarten to 12th grade) schools. Relational bullying was the most commonly reported type of bullying perpetrated by students against pre-service teachers. Longer pre-service field experience duration was associated with increased self-reported student-on-pre-service teacher bullying. Self-reported bullying resulted in negative psychological impacts (e.g., worry, sadness, self-doubt), as well as contemplation of changing professional paths. Some participants reported professional growth, support from colleagues, and an increased awareness of student bullying. Participants attributed student bullying of teachers to students' lack of respect for pre-service teachers, the common nature of bullying in schools, and students' personal issues. U.S. teacher education programs must better equip pre-service teachers to address student bullying by integrating evidence-based training into their coursework.

TI Promotion of women at the faculty of medicine at the University of
   Rostock: an archival case study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender equality; Women in medicine; Academic careers; Archival study
ID PHYSICIANS
AB Background Women remain underrepresented in leadership positions in academic medicine, despite decades of formal equality policies. Historical institutional approaches can reveal persistent structural and cultural barriers. This study analyses archival material from the Medical Faculty of the University of Rostock to examine the development of institutional strategies supporting women in academic medicine.Methods Archival sources, including faculty reports, correspondence, equality plans, and committee records from 1950 to 2002, were qualitatively analysed to reconstruct debates, measures, and perceived barriers. More recent material was gathered from institutional websites.Results Early initiatives, including the 1962 Gender Equality Plan, combined support for women's careers with scepticism about their scientific capabilities and family responsibilities. Subsequent plans introduced mentoring programmes, family-friendly policies, and gender-disaggregated monitoring. Despite these efforts, implementation varied across departments, and women remain underrepresented in senior positions.Conclusions Institutional commitment to women's advancement has increased over time, yet women remain underrepresented in senior academic positions. These findings suggest that formal equality measures alone may not be sufficient to achieve sustainable gender equality in academic medicine.

TI Towards a Theory of Inquiry Dialogue Questions
SO EDUCATIONAL THEORY
LA English
DT Article
DE inquiry dialogue; philosophy for children; philosophical questions
ID COMMUNITY
AB The success of an inquiry dialogue depends on the quality of its central question. Yet, evaluating inquiry dialogue questions is harder than it appears. One approach is to maintain that inquiry dialogue questions are philosophical questions, but there is no successful method of identifying all and only philosophical questions. Another approach is to appeal to Peter Worley's influential taxonomy of grammatical and conceptual openness, which builds on Philip Cam's question quadrant model. I advance an alternative that addresses the limitations of previous models while preserving their benefits. This model includes two dimensions: grammatical scope, the extent to which a question's grammar constrains what could count as an answer, and disputational scope, the extent to which a question is subject to reasonable and actual disagreement among the inquirers. Questions fail as inquiry dialogue questions when either dimension is too wide or too narrow, and I show how facilitators can apply this framework when selecting questions and in the midst of an inquiry itself.

TI Consistent fantasy is reality
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE migrant academic; radical theory-making; institutional critique; Black
   feminist epistemology
AB In this article, I am going to recall some memories I collected between 2019 and 2023; this article will follow the footsteps of a doctoral candidate who migrated from her home (Global South) to the West (so-called Australia) to undertake a practice-based PhD. By doing so, I aim to explore "difference" (racial, gender, sexual, or class-based) as the space of radical possibility whose capaciousness can expand even further under impossible circumstances. This does not intend to diminish the violence of impossibility enforced by the normative (institutional) structures, borders, and exclusionary rules and regulations or unsee the violence created by its naturalization, rationalization and refusal. But as Marquis Bey reminds, "our bodies have come to be the site that suffers oppressive forces because that is precisely how oppressive forces wish to construct our subjectivities" (2022, p. 3). Therefore, instead of narrating a journey of a victim/ised migrant, heroic/ised migrant, or heroic-victim migrant, I will be interested in our "figurative capacity" (Snorton, , p. 59) and see how we can use our corporeal and affective labor (embodied knowledge) to "notice" and "breach" the colonial and (neoliberal) plantocratic logics which continuously and repetitively "depict our presently ecocidal and genocidal world as normal and unalterable" (McKittrick, , pp. 2, 3; emphasis mine).

TI Evaluating large language models for rubric-based essay grading in an
   undergraduate biology course
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE large language models; AI-assisted grading; rubric-based evaluation;
   biology education
AB This study examines how three large language models (LLMs), ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, assign grades to undergraduate-level essays in a biology course using a standardized rubric. Each LLM evaluated a data set of 200 essays under two prompting conditions: zero-shot (uncalibrated) and few-shot (calibrated using a small set of exemplar essays). LLM-assigned scores were directly compared with instructor-assigned scores, showing only moderate alignment with instructor grading, with variability observed across models and prompting strategies. Differences in grading behavior were also evident with different items on the rubric, with higher alignment for structural writing components and lower alignment for content- and reasoning-based criteria. Additionally, LLMs showed greater agreement with instructor scores than with one another, indicating substantial inter-model variability under identical grading conditions. These findings suggest that LLM grading outputs vary meaningfully across models, prompting strategies, and rubric components. In this context, LLMs may be best understood as tools that can support specific aspects of structured grading rather than as interchangeable evaluators.

TI An appraisal of small area estimation methods to explore expansion of
   state subgroup reporting on NAEP
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE NAEP; Small area estimation; Large-scale assessment; Disaggregated data;
   Bayesian dynamic borrowing; Machine learning; Empirical Bayes; Subgroup
   achievement
ID MODELS; PREDICTION; ERROR
AB This study explores the use of Small Area Estimation (SAE) methods to expand reporting of state-level subgroup performance on National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) assessments without requiring the assessment program to draw larger samples of students and expand test administration. To evaluate the SAE methods, small area estimates of mean subgroup achievement formed from samples too small to meet NAEP's current reporting requirements are compared with design-based estimates of mean subgroup achievement that satisfy the program's minimum sample size requirement for reporting. Results demonstrate that several SAE methods yield estimates of mean achievement that are more accurate and reliable than estimates of mean achievement that satisfy NAEP's current reporting requirement. Policy implications and future directions for research are discussed.

TI Equal Access, Persistent Divides: Gender Segregation in Italian Higher
   Education across Three Decades (1995-2022)
SO RESEARCH IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender disparities; Higher education; Field of study; Care-technical
   divide; Italy
ID FIELDS; GAP; DISCIPLINE; ATTAINMENT; INEQUALITY; ENROLLMENT; EXPANSION;
   KNOWLEDGE; SCIENCE; CHOICE
AB Adopting an "equal but different" perspective, this study investigates long-term changes in gendered patterns of university enrolment and field-of-study choice in Italy, focusing on the care-technical divide among cohorts of upper secondary school graduates from 1995 to 2022. Leveraging a unique longitudinal harmonization of survey data from the National Institute of Statistics with administrative educational databases, the analysis accounts for gender differences in prior secondary school track choice and academic performance. Results show that the female advantage in Higher Education (HE) participation largely disappears once differences in prior schooling are considered, suggesting that the gender reversal in enrolments reflects gendered educational pathways rather than a net advantage for women. However, a modest and persistent female advantage emerges in the second half of the 2000s, after the incorporation of traditionally feminized fields such as teaching and nursing into HE. Most importantly, gender disparities in field-of-study choice, particularly along the care-technical divide, have remained strikingly stable across cohorts, despite profound changes in overall participation levels. These findings highlight the resilience of horizontal gender segregation in HE and call into question the extent to which the expansion of women's access to university has translated into more gender-equal educational outcomes.

TI Where Do Women Exit the Academic Pipeline?: Evidence from a Decade of
   National Data in Japan
SO RESEARCH IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender inequality; Applicant-stage attrition; Academic pipeline;
   Gendered organizations; Japan
ID SEX-DIFFERENCES; GENDER; SCIENCE; INEQUALITY; ADVANCE; TENURE
AB Gender disparities in academia persist worldwide, yet empirical evidence remains limited on where, at which stages, and to what extent women exit academic careers. Using a uniquely comprehensive, decade-long national dataset from Japan (2014-2023), this study provides system-level evidence of gendered attrition across six disciplinary fields and four academic ranks. By distinguishing among the potential pool, applicant pool, and hiring outcomes, the analysis separates application-stage processes from hiring-stage outcomes-an analytical distinction rarely possible in other national contexts due to data limitations. The findings indicate that the application stage constitutes the primary bottleneck in women's academic careers. Across fields, women's underrepresentation appears to be driven less by disadvantage at the point of selection than by the fact that many qualified women do not apply for academic positions. Once applications are submitted, hiring outcomes are generally neutral or, in some cases, favorable to women, with lecturer-level recruitment showing evidence of proactive intervention. Rank-level analyses further indicate that women's attrition is pronounced at career entry and continues at mid- and senior-career stages in most fields. Field-level analyses highlight substantial heterogeneity in how and when attrition occurs. By separating application-stage attrition from hiring outcomes and examining patterns across ranks and disciplines, this study refines existing accounts of gender inequality in academia. The results highlight the importance of organizational and structural factors shaping application behavior and cumulative disadvantage, and underscore the policy relevance of collecting detailed applicant-flow data. Overall, the findings suggest that stage-specific and discipline-sensitive interventions are essential for addressing persistent gendered disparities in academia.

TI EFL student teachers' AI self-efficacy across different countries
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Self-efficacy; English as a foreign language;
   Student teachers; Cultural comparison
ID ENGLISH
AB The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has identified the need to understand how future educators perceive and engage with these technologies. This study investigates the AI self-efficacy of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) student teachers across three distinct educational contexts: Japan, Poland, and Slovakia. Recognising the crucial role of self-efficacy in technology adoption, this research aims to compare how pre-service teachers in these countries perceive their capabilities in utilising AI tools for language learning and teaching. The study employed a mixed-method design to collect quantitative data using a specifically designed evaluation scale and qualitative data via an open-ended questionnaire. The sample comprised 98 EFL student teachers from the selected countries. Results revealed observable differences in AI self-efficacy scores among participants from Japan, Poland, and Slovakia, with Japanese participants reporting higher confidence levels than their Polish and Slovak counterparts. The findings highlight a need for further research examining which contextual, educational, or experiential variables may underlie these cross-country differences.

TI Disparities in academic enrollment and achievement: an empirical and
   literature-informed study of undergraduate organic chemistry in Lebanese
   higher education
SO CHEMISTRY TEACHER INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE chemical education; academic achievement; sex differences; enrollment
   parity; SDG 4; higher education in Lebanon
ID GENDER-DIFFERENCES; MATHEMATICS; ATTITUDES; BIAS
AB This quantitative case study examines sex-based differences (female vs. male, as recorded by university registrar) in enrollment and academic achievement (course grades) across two undergraduate organic chemistry courses at a private university in Lebanon. Using official grade records for 256 students (177 females, 79 males) enrolled in Organic Chemistry across three consecutive semesters (2023: Spring and Fall, 2024: Spring), we describe sex-disaggregated enrollment patterns and compare distributions of course outcomes. Females accounted for 69.1 % of enrollments, while male students accounted for 30.9 %. Across the collected sample, males had higher mean course scores; an independent-samples t-test indicated a statistically significant difference (t = -2.35, p = 0.043), with a large standardized mean difference (Cohen's d = 1.36). Grade-band analyses further showed a higher proportion of males in the high-achieving category (B-A) and a higher proportion of females in low-achieving and failing outcomes. Because the dataset is administrative and limited to a single institution and course context, the analyses are descriptive and comparative; they do not identify causal mechanisms underlying the observed differences. Findings are discussed in relation to prior work on sex/gender gaps in chemistry and STEM, and implications are framed as context-specific recommendations for further evidence-based instructional support and research.

TI Gender Differences in Reciprocal Associations Between Parenting Styles
   and Preschool Children's Executive Functioning: A Cross-Lagged Study in
   China
SO EARLY EDUCATION AND DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
ID EARLY-CHILDHOOD; DISCIPLINE; FAMILIES; CONTEXT; GIRLS
AB Research Findings: Although recent research has explored the reciprocal relationships between parental behaviors and children' s self-regulation, few studies have examined the bidirectional associations between parenting styles and preschool children' s executive function (EF) observed in everyday contexts. Moreover, the moderating role of children' s sex in these reciprocal relationships remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, this study employed a cross-lagged design to investigate the prospective reciprocal associations between parenting styles and children' s EF, as well as the moderating effects of children' s sex in China. Data were collected in two waves, eight months apart, from children aged 3-6 years and their parents. The results indicated that (1) authoritative parenting and preschool children' s EF showed reciprocal longitudinal associations, (2) authoritarian parenting and children' s EF exhibited mutual predictive relationships, and (3) child sex showed suggestive moderation of the association between authoritarian parenting and children' s EF. Specifically, EF deficits positively predicted authoritarian parenting style among boys. Conversely, authoritarian parenting positively predicted EF deficits among girls. Sex did not moderate the reciprocal relationship between authoritative parenting and children' s EF. Practice or Policy: These findings may offer a reference for parents when responding to EF-related difficulties among preschool children of different sexes. Educational authorities could also consider strengthening home-school-community partnerships and providing brief, feasible parenting guidance.

TI School Leadership Perspectives on Policies Related to Open Educational

DT Article
DE digital resources; education policy; open educational resources (OER);
   school leader; territory-wide study
ID TEACHERS; OER; PERCEPTIONS; BARRIERS
AB To ensure inclusive and equitable quality education for all, high-quality open educational resources (OER) are essential. However, the lack of appropriate policies governing the development and adoption of OER presents a barrier to their application in schools. Based on relevant UNESCO guidelines of OER, this study aims to inform policy development by leveraging insights from school leaders in Hong Kong. The implications of this study are relevant not only for policymakers in Hong Kong but also for those in other regions who aim to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) through the development and implementation of policies related to OER, while also recognising that these policies operate within schools' broader use of digital resources.

TI Evolving from necessary evil to learning partner: glocalization and
   learning-oriented assessment in GEPT and BESTEP
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning-oriented assessment; Socio-cognitive framework; Glocalization;
   CEFR linking; AI; Evolving assessment
AB This article examines how two English proficiency tests-the General English Proficiency Test (GEPT) and the BEST Test of English Proficiency (BESTEP)-have evolved from traditional gatekeeping instruments into learning partners. Anchored in the principles of Learning-Oriented Assessment (LOA) and the glocalization imperative, both tests illustrate how domestically developed assessment systems balance local educational priorities with international standards of test quality and fairness. Central to this evolution has been the adoption of the socio-cognitive framework, which provides a foundation for construct definition, test design, and empirical validation, enhancing validity and reinforcing stakeholder trust. The GEPT, launched in 2000, was designed as a level-based examination aligned with major educational stages to support lifelong learning. To promote positive washback and enrich score interpretation, the GEPT conducted Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) linking studies and integrated technological innovations to enhance score reports with diagnostic information, learning suggestions, and personalized insights into learners' strengths and weaknesses, fostering autonomy and engagement. Drawing on this foundation, the BESTEP was introduced in 2023 under the Ministry of Education (MOE)'s Program on Bilingual Education for Students in College (BEST program), which seeks to strengthen bilingual education in higher education. From the outset, BESTEP integrated technology-enhanced feedback, adaptive resources, and cross-disciplinary collaboration, benefiting from innovations developed through GEPT projects. Its design and validation, guided by the socio-cognitive framework, ensure contextual relevance and international comparability. By linking curriculum and assessment, BESTEP contributes to the evolution of context-specific assessment practices, supporting pedagogy while meeting policy goals. The transformation illustrates how language assessment can be understood through the lens of glocalization: local policy responsiveness, learner-centered design, and contextualized tasks are combined with frameworks and validation evidence that ensure international recognition. Still, challenges remain, including balancing accountability with learning impact, upholding fairness and accessibility in AI-based services, and sustaining collaboration across test developers, educators, and engineers. Additional complexities arise in deploying AI scoring models and maintaining their long-term operational validity. By reflecting on these challenges, the article identifies pathways for sustaining innovation while safeguarding validity, fairness, and educational impact. The evolving practices of GEPT and BESTEP demonstrate how a local testing organization can reimagine assessment as a catalyst for learning, dialogue, and reform. More broadly, the adaptive experience offers insights into the evolution of language testing across Asia, where local-global integration continues to shape new trajectories of practice.

TI Assessing Generative AI Adoption, Tool Preferences, and Cognitive
   Reliance Among Medical Students: A Cross-Sectional Study
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; education; medical; students; natural language
   processing; cross-sectional studies
AB Background and Objectives: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have entered medical education faster than guidance for their responsible use. Although a rapidly expanding 2024-2026 literature has examined generative AI adoption, attitudes, and AI literacy among healthcare students, comparatively little is known about which specific tools medical students prefer or whether reliance on them carries measurable cognitive risks. We characterized adoption patterns, tool preferences, perceived benefits, and determinants of cognitive overdependence among medical students. Methods: A single-center cross-sectional survey was administered to 141 medical students across preclinical and clinical years at a single institution. A 28-item instrument captured usage patterns, perceived learning benefit, output trust, verification behavior, and AI overdependence risk. Analyses included t-tests, ANOVA, chi-square tests, Pearson correlations, and hierarchical regression. Results: Unless otherwise specified, values are reported as group mean scores on 1-5 Likert agreement scales or as percentages of respondents. ChatGPT was the primary tool for 69.5% of respondents, followed by Claude (12.1%). Daily users reported greater perceived learning benefit than infrequent users (4.14 vs. 3.36; p < 0.001). Clinical students verified AI outputs more often than preclinical students (3.69 vs. 3.21; p < 0.001), while preclinical students showed higher reliance (p = 0.002); verification moderated overdependence risk across academic years (interaction p = 0.041). AI familiarity (beta = 0.31) and verification habit (beta = -0.22) were the strongest predictors of integration acceptance (R-2 = 0.34). Conclusions: Reliance and verification habits diverge by training stage; curricula should pair AI literacy with explicit verification training to mitigate overdependence. As a single-center, self-report study, these findings require multi-center confirmation; nonetheless, to our knowledge, this is among the first studies to jointly profile students' tool-specific reliability perceptions and to identify verification behavior as a moderator that buffers familiarity-driven overdependence.

TI Designing an Immersive 360° Video Learning Environment for Virtual
   Chemistry Study Visits: Exploring Authentic Chemistry Research
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE 360 degrees video; chemistry education; immersion; TPACK; virtual study
   visits
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; FIELD TRIP; REALITY; EXPERIENCES
AB Immersive technologies offer new possibilities for chemistry higher education. The field benefits from secondary education study visits that enable decision making for future careers. However, access to authentic laboratory visits is often limited by geographical constraints. Synchronous 360 degrees videos provide an immersive virtual alternative, but the educational value of this technology remains unclear. Using a design-based research approach, this study explored the opportunities and challenges of immersive 360 degrees video in virtual chemistry study visits, developed a synchronous 360 degrees learning environment through co-design, and generated a pedagogical model for its implementation. The resulting design solution was examined through a qualitative case study. The data (n = 7) were gathered via semi-structured interviews and observations and analyzed through theory-driven content analysis. This study suggests that 360 degrees videos may enhance accessibility, support learning, and improve the visual representation and perceived relevance of chemistry. Participants perceived immersive visits as engaging and reported an increased sense of presence and improved focus. Challenges include technical constraints, limited authenticity of interaction, resource demands, and certain limitations of virtuality for experimental work. These findings extend previous research on immersive environments by suggesting that synchronous 360 degrees video may promote focus and presence. Also, the study generated a theory-informed framework and practical guidelines for designing immersive chemistry learning environments. The framework offers a starting point for future research and supports the integration of modern technology into higher education.

TI A dynamic framework of professional identity formation in trainees for
   low-resource settings: a qualitative study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional Identity Formation; Low Resource Settings; Focus Groups;
   Medical Education; General Practitioners
ID RING-THEORY; PERSONHOOD
AB Background Professional Identity Formation (PIF) is a dynamic and context-dependent socialisation process; while existing research identifies various influencing factors, there is a paucity of cohesive frameworks that capture the stage-related internalisation of identity elements within practice. This gap is particularly salient in low-resource settings, such as China's Rural-Streamed Medical Education Programme (RMEP), where substantial turnover and tenuous professional identity among trainees present significant challenges. Drawing upon the Ring Theory of Personhood (RToP) as a theoretical lens, this study aims to construct a dynamic framework for understanding PIF among RMEP trainees, thereby offering insights to enhance PIF for healthcare professionals in low-resource settings.Method Informed by a pragmatic paradigm, nine focus groups were conducted with 42 RMEP trainees across various training stages in China. Drawing upon the RToP as a sensitising concept, data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis to construct a dynamic framework.Results A framework comprising 11 themes was constructed across three dimensions: the Societal Domain, encompassing working conditions, policies, attitudes of others, formal teaching and discipline development; the Relational Domain, including relationships with role models, close ones, patients, and peers; and the Individual Domain, incorporating reflective experience, personal character and values. This framework emphasises the dynamic interaction of these themes and the stage-related shifts of PIF, highlighting a shift from external to internal elements while also acknowledging the prominent influence of early external experiences in low-resource settings.Conclusions By proposing a dynamic framework that maps PIF across different training stages, this study extends existing conceptualizations and provides valuable insights for strengthening it among healthcare professionals in low-resource settings.

TI Visioning Forward: School Leadership Dispositions and Actions in
   Regional, Rural and Remote Australian Schools
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE school leadership; regional; rural and remote education; staffing
AB In this research paper, we outline school leadership dispositions and actions for developing teacher supply pipelines in Australia. In the context of attracting and retaining quality teachers in regional, rural and remote schools, and within the complexity of leading contemporary schools, school leaders require mindsets, strategies, and practices beyond what is acquired during a model of apprenticing. As a constructivist inquiry, the school leaders identified the power of partnerships that are peer supported and situated in place-based consciousness. Our findings illustrate the knowledge, dispositions, training, and professional experience regional, rural and remote school leaders require. As a contribution, we outline implications for school leaders as they navigate the multifaceted dimensions of staffing schools.

TI Abstract Language Use in Gifted and Typically Developing Pre-School
   Children During Free Play: A Comparative Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE gifted children; abstract language; free play; educator-child
   interactions
AB This study examines the characteristics of abstract language use in gifted preschool children during natural free-play activities and compares them with those of typically developing children. The aim is to enhance our awareness of characteristics of gifted children language use and support them in everyday conversations and activities. Abstract language refers to expressions that describe decontextualized situations or that convey causal reasoning and prediction. It is closely related to the development of children's language, cognition, and thinking. A total of 16 gifted children (10 boys and 6 girls; M = 73.06 months) were identified using two standardized instruments, the Combined Raven's Test (Chinese revised version) and the Test of Nonverbal Intelligence, Second Edition (TONI-2). All identified children completed both assessments and scored at or above the 99th percentile on the Combined Raven's Test and the 98th percentile on the TONI-2. Another 16 typically developing children (10 boys and 6 girls; M = 72.81 months) from the same classes were selected as matched controls based on teacher reports and their typical developmental performance. Drawing on corpus analysis, the study analyzed 2778 utterances produced by the gifted children and 2879 utterances produced by the typically developing children during 30-min free-play sessions. The results showed that, as the level of abstract language increased, both groups displayed a similar declining trend in the frequency of language use. However, a cumulative logit mixed-effects model showed that gifted children had significantly higher odds of producing language at higher levels of abstraction than typically developing children. In addition, gifted children demonstrated higher levels of abstract language during educator-child and peer interactions, whereas their private speech was more concentrated at lower levels of abstraction than that of typically developing children. Based on these findings, the study proposes educational recommendations in three areas: recognising children's advanced thinking, addressing their specific language needs, and leveraging their communicative strengths. These recommendations may help create a more supportive educational environment for gifted children and better foster their developmental potential.

TI From Technological Exposure to Pedagogical Engagement: A Case Study of
   Pre-Service Teachers' Digital Profiles and Methodological Orientation
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher education; educational technology; digital literacy; teaching
   methods; active learning; pedagogical innovation
AB (1) Background: Pre-service teachers enter university with extensive digital experience, yet this familiarity does not guarantee pedagogically grounded ICT integration. (2) Objective: This study examines the sociodemographic profile, digital trajectory, ICT perceptions, and methodological orientation of 295 students in the Primary Education Degree and the Secondary Education Teacher Training Master's program at CES Don Bosco, a Spanish university. (3) Method: A quantitative, descriptive-correlational, cross-sectional design was used, combining non-parametric statistics with cluster analysis and multiple regression. (4) Results: Teaching specialization was significantly associated with age profile (chi(2)(1) = 67.46, p < 0.001, phi = V = 0.478). Daily ICT exposure showed a weak, negligible association with tool familiarity (rho = 0.155, p = 0.008), and no asymmetry emerged between the technological and methodological repertoires once expressed proportionally (Wilcoxon Z = 1.32, p = 0.186, r = 0.08). Cluster analysis identified two digital profiles differing not in tool familiarity but in how experience was acquired. Regression showed specific ICT training, not daily exposure, modestly predicted methodological orientation (R-2 = 0.055). (5) Conclusions: Findings do not support a large technology-pedagogy gap; deliberate training, not passive exposure, predicts methodological orientation. As a single-institution case study, results should not be generalized beyond this context.

TI Attending to Teacher Considerations in I-STEM Curriculum
   Supplementation: The Case of Chip Kids
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE integrated STEM; curriculum supplementation; teacher conceptions
AB To address a projected workforce gap in microelectronics, numerous companies and universities are introducing programs that bring authentic, industry-focused practices into K-12 education. Integrated STEM has emerged as an innovative approach to address the urgent push to improve STEM education. Teachers, often trained in a single discipline, are tasked with supplementing their existing curriculum to achieve this interdisciplinary approach. To better understand, we examined the conceptions and considerations of K-12 teachers who were engaged in an industry-led I-STEM professional development and were given supplemental curriculum materials. Teachers were provided with a high-quality, integrated STEM supplemental curriculum, given time to engage with it, and asked how they would use it in their classrooms. This qualitative study sought to understand the factors teachers consider when implementing integrated STEM curriculum supplementation. We found that the primary factors teachers consider during the initial stages of integrated STEM curriculum supplementation are: (1) the curriculum's potential to enhance students' knowledge and students' skill development, (2) the quality of curriculum attributes, and (3) the necessary adaptations for integration into their classroom instruction. Furthermore, teachers rarely mentioned applications across STEM disciplines, which means that meaningful I-STEM PD should be grounded in integrated frameworks that explicitly guide the desired integration and use the curriculum supplement to apply knowledge and practices from other disciplines. Our findings underscore the need to explore how meaningful I-STEM professional development can be designed and delivered using levels of I-STEM integration as a framework.

TI Effect of the "Neuro-Adapter" generative AI environment on ninth-grade
   students' spatial imagination skills across analytical and visual
   cognitive processing styles
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cognitive scaffold; generative AI; hemispheric dominance; Neuro-Adapter;
   spatial imagination
AB Introduction This study investigated the effectiveness of a GenAI-based intelligent learning environment, "Neuro-Adapter," as a cognitive scaffold for developing spatial imagination skills and reducing performance gaps based on cognitive processing styles.Methods A quasi-experimental design was used with 45 ninth-grade students (control group, n = 23; experimental group, n = 22). Data were gathered using a Cognitive Processing Style Inventory and a Pre/Post Spatial Imagination Test over a 4-week timeline.Results Pre-test results favored holistic-visual styles (0.05 >= alpha). On the post-test, the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group with a large effect size (eta & sup2; = 0.86). Within the experimental group, a non-significant post-test difference (Sig = 0.067, Cohen's d = 0.58) indicated that the environment successfully leveled the skill gap for sequential-analytical thinkers.Discussion The "Neuro-Adapter" functioned effectively as an operational cognitive equalizer. We recommend integrating adaptive GenAI algorithms and tailored software scaffolding strategies into spatial education curricula.

TI Creating spaces for norm-critical reflection: lessons from the NormDay
   initiative in health and healthcare education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE awareness; conference; equity in health; higher education; inclusion;
   norm-critique; norms; reflective space
AB In a context where academic freedom is increasingly challenged and exclusionary norms are gaining renewed strength; there is a growing need for educational approaches that foster critical reflection and inclusive perspectives. Conferences have traditionally been viewed as sites for disseminating research, yet their potential as spaces for experiential and transformative learning remains underexplored. This perspective article presents a practice-based case analysis of NormDay as a student initiated educational and organisational innovation, drawing on observational material and participant survey data. Drawing on a norm-critical framework, NormDay combined keynote lectures with participatory workshops, exhibitions, and experience-based activities aimed at disrupting taken-for-granted assumptions and encouraging perspective taking. The initiative brought together researchers, educators, students, practitioners, policymakers, and civil society actors, creating a shared arena for dialogue across sectors. Participant evaluations indicated high levels of engagement and perceived relevance, as well as a self-reported increase in norm awareness. Rather than positioning NormDay as an intervention in the experimental sense, the article conceptualizes it as an awareness-oriented academic practice that may initiate processes of change over time. Key lessons include the importance of participatory formats, cross-sector collaboration, and the integration of embodied learning experiences. At the same time, challenges related to participant reach and the sustainability of impact are highlighted. The article contributes to ongoing discussions on academic freedom and norm-critical pedagogy by illustrating how higher education can create reflective spaces that address exclusionary norms and support more equitable health and healthcare practices.

TI An integrated Jazz-classical piano pedagogy model to enhance student
   creativity in undergraduate music education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE experiential learning; improvisation; Jazz-classical integration;
   musical creativity; piano pedagogy; reflective learning; undergraduate
   music education
ID SKILLS; SELF
AB Introduction Current piano pedagogy in higher education has not adequately integrated jazz improvisation with classical technique to foster musical creativity. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an integrated pedagogical model combining jazz and classical piano approaches to support creativity among undergraduate music education students.Methods A qualitative single-case study was conducted with 64 undergraduate music education students at a public university in Guangdong, China. Data were generated through students' written reflections, semi-structured interviews conducted one month after the intervention, and focus group discussions exploring shared learning experiences. The data were analysed using thematic analysis.Results The findings identified three interrelated dimensions of musical creativity: cognitive-creative, reflected in expanded musical understanding and critical interpretation; exploratory-musical, reflected in improvisation, experimentation, and expressive flexibility; and reflective-contextual, reflected in heightened self-awareness and interpretive consciousness. Authentic performance experiences, structured feedback, and collaborative reflection supported the development of these dimensions, whereas performance anxiety and inconsistent participation constrained them.Discussion These findings suggest that an integrated jazz-classical pedagogical model provides a productive framework for linking technical proficiency with creative development in undergraduate music education. The study highlights the pedagogical value of combining structured rehearsal, improvisational practice, and critical reflection in fostering students' musical creativity.

TI Development and validation of SARA: an AI-assisted reading assessment
   tool for primary school children in low-resource Spanish-speaking
   contexts
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; automated scoring; Dominican Republic;
   low-resource contexts; normative data; psychometrics; reading
   assessment; Spanish
ID SIMPLE VIEW
AB Low reading achievement is a persistent challenge in Latin American education, particularly in the Dominican Republic, where most primary school students perform below minimum proficiency levels. Standardized, culturally adapted assessment tools are scarce in Spanish-speaking low-resource contexts, limiting early identification of reading difficulties at scale. This paper presents the development and validation of SARA (Self-Applied Reading Assessment), an AI-assisted tablet-based tool for autonomous administration and automated scoring of reading assessments in Dominican primary school children (grades 2-6). SARA integrates ECLEC (Evaluaci & oacute;n Centroamericana de la Lectura), a battery grounded in the Simple View of Reading and the Dual-Route Model, covering decoding (letter identification, syllable, word, and pseudoword reading) and oral and reading comprehension. Following convergent validity testing against the PROLEC-R and two pilot studies, SARA was administered to 1,860 students from randomly selected public and private schools in Santo Domingo. Oral responses were scored by two independent human rater teams, yielding an overall inter-rater agreement of 86.11% (73.07%-94.70% across subtests) and a Cohen's Kappa of.550, a conservative estimate reflecting the class imbalance inherent in reading assessment data rather than poor rater reliability. Machine learning models were trained using the expert rater team's labels and evaluated against a conservative human consensus, defined by cases in which both teams agreed. Results showed good to excellent internal consistency across decoding subtests and adequate reliability for reading comprehension. Structural equation models confirmed construct validity by replicating the predicted developmental shift from decoding (beta = .70 in 2nd grade) to oral comprehension (beta = .60 in 6th grade) as predictors of reading comprehension. On the held-out test set, AI scoring achieved 91.97% overall accuracy, comparable to the 86.11% agreement between human raters, with class-specific accuracy higher for correct (90.0%-96.2%) than incorrect responses (73.9%-80.1%). Grade- and school-system-differentiated norms were established, reflecting the documented performance gap between public and private schools. SARA shows promising initial evidence of validity and reliability as a reading assessment tool for Spanish-speaking low-resource contexts and may constitute a scalable solution pending further validation in other regions and contexts.
C1 [Cubilla-Bonnetier, Daniel; Casamassima, Enzo; Marte-Santana, Hugo; Sanchez-Vincitore, Laura V.] Univ Iberoamericana UNIBE, Inst Invest en Neurociencias Aplicadas IINA, Santo Domingo, Dominican Rep.

TI Gamification as an educational strategy in life sciences
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE active learning; gamification; life sciences; motivation;
   self-sufficiency
ID ENGAGEMENT
AB In recent years, educational methodologies have undergone a significant transformation. Strategies such as e-learning, project-based learning and the flipped classroom have been implemented, while more traditional approaches have lost their effectiveness and ability to motivate students. In this context, gamification has emerged as a complementary approach to conventional strategies and is increasingly being adopted in higher education, providing a motivating element that leads to meaningful learning in contrast to the traditional lecture. In this study, we used various gamification tools in undergraduate and master's courses in Life Sciences, analysing their effectiveness in increasing student interest as well as the acquisition of skills in each subject through various assessment tools. The results show that students have found these teaching tools very positive and that they were more engaged, cooperative and participatory than with traditional methods. Therefore, this study suggests that gamification can increase interest and learning at the university level.

TI Inter-rater agreement in Korean constructed-response writing assessment:
   a large-scale empirical baseline from the AI Hub 2024 writing evaluation
   dataset
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI Hub dataset; automated essay scoring; elementary education;
   inter-rater agreement; Korean writing assessment; Many-Facet Rasch
   Measurement; Quadratic Weighted Kappa; rubric specificity
ID WEIGHTED KAPPA
AB Introduction Inter-rater agreement is the principal quality criterion for large-scale human-annotated datasets used to train and benchmark automated essay scoring (AES) systems. Despite rapid growth in Korean AES research, no study has provided a comprehensive, criterion-level inter-rater agreement baseline for a publicly available Korean writing dataset. This study addresses that gap using the AI Hub 2024 Writing Automated Evaluation and Feedback Dataset, comprising 12,873 elementary fifth-grade responses across four subjects and two formats (short-answer, essay), scored by 42 raters on nine criteria, yielding 204,894 individual rater-item judgments.Methods We report Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK), Pearson r, and ICC(2,1) for each criterion, decompose agreement by format and subject via bootstrap inference, and apply Many-Facet Rasch Measurement (MFRM) to estimate and compare criterion-difficulty, rater-severity, and format/subject facet parameters. A secondary exploratory analysis examines whether an a priori coding of scoring-rule abstractness (rubric specificity) is associated with criterion-level QWK.Results Criterion-level QWK ranges from .432 to .924, with a 3:1 ratio of criterion-difficulty range to rater-severity range indicating that criterion-level variation structurally dominates rater-level variation. Rubric specificity is associated with inter-rater agreement (Spearman rho = -.686, p = .041, N = 9 criteria): rule-based criteria show near-ceiling agreement (mean QWK = .915) while judgment-based criteria show substantially lower agreement (mean QWK = .528). Given the small number of criteria, this association should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as a hypothesis test. Format effects are significant for six of nine criteria. The within-one agreement rate of 95.4% across all criteria provides a practical benchmark for evaluating AES models under a one-point tolerance criterion.Discussion These findings provide the measurement-theoretical infrastructure for designing rubric-specificity-stratified AES models, format-aware training protocols, and distributional scoring outputs for Korean constructed-response writing assessment.

TI Perceptions of the blended learning environment, student engagement, and
   academic satisfaction: the mediating role of cognitive and emotional
   engagement
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic satisfaction; blended learning; emotional engagement; higher
   education; learning processes; student engagement
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY
AB Blended learning has become a prominent modality in higher education; however, empirical evidence remains limited regarding the mechanisms through which characteristics of the technological learning environment influence student engagement and academic satisfaction. This study aims to examine how features of blended learning environments shape students' cognitive and emotional engagement and how these engagement processes, in turn, influence academic satisfaction. A quantitative approach was adopted using a non-experimental, explanatory research design. The sample consisted of 99 undergraduate students enrolled in Probability and Statistics courses delivered through a blended learning modality. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that perceived usefulness and perceived interaction have significant effects on both cognitive and emotional engagement. Furthermore, emotional engagement shows a significant direct effect on academic satisfaction, supporting a partial mediation model. These findings highlight the central role of emotional engagement as a key explanatory mechanism linking learning environments and academic outcomes. Beyond providing empirical evidence, this study contributes to a better understanding of how cognitive and emotional engagement operate as mediating processes shaping academic satisfaction in blended learning contexts.
