TI Artificial intelligence literacy, creative thinking, and entrepreneurial
   readiness: the mediating role of learning achievement among generation Z
   business students in Thailand
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; creative thinking capability; entrepreneurial readiness;
   generation Z entrepreneurs; learning achievement
AB This study investigates the structural relationships among Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy, creative thinking capability, learning achievement, and entrepreneurial readiness among prospective Generation Z entrepreneurs in Thailand. Drawing on the growing importance of digital competencies and higher-order cognitive skills in entrepreneurial development, the study employs a quantitative research design using questionnaire data collected from 506 university students. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) using SmartPLS 4 was applied to examine both the direct and indirect relationships among the proposed constructs. The empirical results indicate that AI literacy exerts a strong positive influence on creative thinking capability and a moderate positive effect on learning achievement. AI literacy also demonstrates a smaller but statistically significant direct effect on entrepreneurial readiness. Furthermore, creative thinking capability significantly enhances both learning achievement and entrepreneurial readiness, highlighting the role of cognitive flexibility and idea generation in entrepreneurial development. Learning achievement, in turn, emerges as a key predictor of entrepreneurial readiness, suggesting that students' learning performance and academic engagement contribute meaningfully to their preparedness for entrepreneurial activities. In addition to these direct effects, AI literacy indirectly influences entrepreneurial readiness through the sequential roles of creative thinking capability and learning achievement. Overall, the findings emphasize the importance of integrating AI literacy and creativity-oriented learning strategies into higher education to strengthen students' entrepreneurial readiness in an increasingly digital and innovation-driven economy. The study extends Human Capital Theory by conceptualizing AI literacy as digital human capital and explaining its sequential contribution to entrepreneurial readiness through creative thinking capability and learning achievement.

TI Faculty mentoring program: an instrumental case study of an agricultural
   education and communication department
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE case study; faculty mentoring; higher education; mentoring programs;
   SWOC
ID SWOT ANALYSIS; CAREER
AB Introduction Faculty mentoring programs are essential for professional development in higher education. This study examines faculty perceptions of a mentoring program within an Agricultural Education and Communication (AEC) department at a U.S. land-grant university, utilizing a Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Challenges (SWOC) framework to assess its effectiveness and identify areas for improvement.Methods An instrumental case study approach was employed, involving semi-structured interviews, document analysis, and observations. Data were collected from 14 faculty members (mentors and mentees) and the department head. Thematic analysis was used to identify key patterns and insights.Results Findings revealed two major strengths: a supportive departmental culture and the prevalence of informal mentoring relationships. Weaknesses included limited program awareness, a lack of formal structure, minimal accountability, and inconsistent engagement between mentors and mentees. Opportunities for enhancement included centralized resources, recognition and incentives, and cross-disciplinary learning. Key challenges were time constraints and evolving tenure and promotion processes.Discussion The mentoring program is rooted in collegiality and informal support, which faculty value highly. However, its impact is limited by structural and procedural gaps. Addressing these through targeted improvements, such as clearer guidelines, accountability mechanisms, and institutional recognition, could significantly enhance the program's effectiveness and sustainability. As a single-institution case, these findings offer context-specific insights while also highlighting considerations relevant to similar academic departments.

TI Explainable machine learning for early classification of middle school
   student performance
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE classification; explainable AI (XAI); interpretable machine learning;
   middle school education; SHAP; student performance
ID EARLY PREDICTION; MODELS
AB Identifying students at risk of academic underperformance early is a longstanding difficulty for school systems, and the difficulty is sharpest where socioeconomic inequality is severe. This study presents an interpretable machine learning framework for predicting academic outcomes in middle school. The framework was developed on a dataset of 561,538 student records. Preprocessing, feature engineering, and stratified sampling were used to keep the sample representative across subgroups, and class imbalance was handled through class weighting during training together with threshold tuning for each outcome category. Several algorithms were compared, and model selection relied on the Borda Count method, which aggregates each model's ranking across multiple evaluation metrics instead of privileging a single criterion. CatBoost performed best on the test set, with a balanced accuracy of 88.8%, MCC of 70.6%, G-Mean of 88.7%, and F1-score of 91.4%. Explainable AI (XAI) techniques were then applied so that predictions can be interpreted at the global and individual levels. Assessment and examination scores were the strongest predictors of outcomes; poverty and class size mattered too, though less. The practical use of the framework is straightforward: making the model's reasoning visible lets educators and administrators flag at-risk students earlier and direct support to the schools and students most affected by socioeconomic disadvantages.

TI Critical reflections on AI integration in graduate research writing
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI tools; artificial intelligence; ChatGPT; critical thinking; research
   writing
ID CHATGPT
AB This study explores graduate students' critical reflections on their use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in a Research Writing course, focusing on their perceptions of the associated risks and ethical issues, as well as their views on the inclusion of AI in academic writing education. The study was conducted at a university in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, and involved MA students enrolled in a graduate-level Research Writing course. Course activities included class discussions, case studies, problem-solving exercises, peer and instructor feedback, scaffolded writing assignments, and a short research project. Nine MA students volunteered to participate in the study and were interviewed using semi-structured methods, and the interviews were then analyzed using thematic analysis. Results indicate that the course supported students' development of research writing skills, critical thinking, and AI literacy, although these findings should be interpreted with caution, given the small qualitative sample size. Students reported using AI tools cautiously, verifying AI-generated content against scholarly sources, and appreciating AI for brainstorming, vocabulary enhancement, and outlining, while emphasizing the ongoing need for instructor guidance, peer engagement, and critical assessment. Participants also imagined a hybrid instructional model in which AI supplements rather than substitutes for human teaching. This study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-integrated writing pedagogy by providing context-based insights into the ethical and pedagogically informed integration of AI in graduate-level academic writing instruction in an EFL setting.

TI Interpreting environmental education through religious values: teachers'
   practices in Yogyakarta's nature-based schools
SO ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Environmental education; sekolah alam; nature-based education; quality
   education; religious values; ecological learning
ID CHILDREN
AB This study examines how teachers in Yogyakarta's elementary-level sekolah alam (nature-based schools) conceptualize religious values as a framework for environmental learning and enact them through everyday pedagogical practices. Using a phenomenological qualitative design, data were collected between March and June 2025 through semi-structured interviews, classroom and outdoor observations, and document review involving 18 teachers from three schools. The study illustrates how culturally embedded religious ethics shape ecopedagogical practice and mediate early environmental learning in Indonesian nature-based schools.

TI That's a wrap: Longitudinal exam reflections for pharmacy student
   self-awareness
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Exam wrappers; Exam post-mortems; Reflection; Metacognition;
   Self-awareness; Self-confidence
AB Introduction: Exam wrappers are a metacognitive tool that provides a framework for students to practice reflection on their assessment process and performance. The purpose of this study was to explore changes in pharmacy students' self-awareness, confidence, and exam performance longitudinally with the use of an exam wrapper process within a course sequence. Methods: Pharmacy students enrolled in a pharmacotherapeutics course complete an exam wrapper as a survey series with each exam. This multi-part survey asks students to predict their exam score, provide baseline information such as time spent studying, and reflect on exam results and confidence in each topic on the exam. Correlational analysis of predicted to actual exam scores was used, alongside an analysis of confidence rankings within topics to examine students' self-awareness and predictive confidence over time. Similarly, students' confidence in their performance on exam topics positively aligned with their actual performance on those topics. Conclusion: Results indicate students' awareness of knowledge being aligned with performance. In turn, course faculty are granted a view into students' self-awareness and anticipation of performance.

TI Developing prompt design competence in management education: Exploring
   generative AI as a cognitive tool for business problem-solving
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Strategic problem-solving;
   Management education; Prompt design; Cognitive tools
AB The rapid integration of generative AI (GAI) into management education raises questions about its impact on strategic problem-solving, yet little research has examined how structured GAI interaction supports core managerial competences. This study examines prompt design as an externalisation of strategic reasoning when GAI functions as a cognitive tool rather than a solution generator. It involved 373 MBA students at a fully online Spanish university completing an openended prompt design activity in a Business Strategy course, guided by the CRETA-R framework. A quantitative, correlational, cross-sectional design examined relationships between prompt design performance, examination results, and course grades, and compared instructor-based and AI-based evaluations using non-parametric analyses. These findings position prompt design as a higher-order cognitive meta-skill and provide empirical support for structured, AI-mediated tasks in MBA programmes.

TI Connecting the Dots: Visual Accessibility and Depictions of Change in
   Statistics Education Graphs
SO JOURNAL OF STATISTICS AND DATA SCIENCE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Accessible design; Data communication; Pretest-posttest; Visualization
ID PSYCHOLOGY; VISUALIZATION
AB Data and statistical findings can be communicated effectively using graphs, often better than could be done with numbers or words. In pretest-posttest designs, graphs can be especially useful for visualizing patterns of change. In this study, we sought to examine the quantity of graphs, how variability and error were visualized, and the visual accessibility of graphs used in statistics education literature. Data came from all articles with a two-timepoint design published in three statistics education research journals (Journal of Statistics and Data Science Education, Statistics Education Research Journal, Teaching Statistics) between 2012 and 2024. Results indicate that over half of all published articles implementing pretest-posttest designs had an associated graph. Variability was frequently depicted using distributional methods, but individual-level data and trajectories were rarely shown, limiting the ability to fully represent change over time. Visual accessibility was often poor: small text size and missing or uninformative alt-text were the most common barriers, and many graphs were inaccessible to individuals with color vision deficiencies or reduced contrast sensitivity. To support improved graphing practices, we developed an open-source Shiny web application that allows users to create publication-ready, accessible graphs for pretest-posttest data and provides guidance on effective visualization practices.

TI Learning from Experience: A Systematic Review of Early
   Multi-Institutional EPA Studies Across US Medical Specialties
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competency-based education; residency; Accreditation Council for
   Graduate Medical Education; educational milestones; core competences;
   Entrustable Professional Activities
ID ENTRUSTABLE PROFESSIONAL ACTIVITIES; COMPETENCE
AB OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the design, implementation strategies, and outcomes of early multi-institutional studies evaluating newly implemented Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) across U.S. residency and fellowship programs to inform future EPA implementation. DESIGN: PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched for peer-reviewed U.S.-based multi-institutional or national studies evaluating EPA implementation in residency or fellowship training. Single-institution studies, undergraduate medical education studies, and non-U.S. publications were excluded. Screening and data extraction were performed independently and in duplicate. SETTING: Graduate medical education programs in the United States. PARTICIPANTS: Residency and fellowship programs, faculty assessors, and trainees participating in multi-institutional EPA implementation or evaluation studies. RESULTS: Of 121 records identified, 5 studies met inclusion criteria. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 represented general surgery, pathology, anesthesiology, endocrine surgery, and pediatrics. Study duration ranged from 2 to 36 months, with participation ranging from 6 to 28 programs in pilot studies and 23 programs in one multi-institutional pediatric evaluation study. EPA assessments ranged from 698 to 25,503 per study. EPA implementation was feasible, with entrustment ratings increasing with trainee level. Digital platforms improved evaluation capture. Common barriers included variable faculty engagement, workflow friction, sampling bias from voluntary completion, and redundant evaluation systems. CONCLUSIONS: Early multi-institutional EPA studies demonstrate feasibility but reveal consistent implementation challenges. Future EPA implementation efforts should prioritize workflow integration, digital assessment platforms, and faculty development to support sustainable competency-based assessment. TI Exploring the nature of classroom discourse in multilingual classrooms:
   Questioning for higher-order thinking skills, translanguaging, and
   knowledge construction
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Classroom discourse; Competence-based education; Critical thinking;
   High-order thinking; Questioning; Translanguaging
ID TEACHERS; SCHOOLS; IMPACT; STYLE
AB This study investigates how teachers incorporate higher-order thinking skills (HOTs) into their questioning strategies during classroom discussions, connecting them to knowledge construction processes in 22 sixth-grade math and science classrooms in Kenya. Data were analyzed using a mixed methods approach guided by a coding framework based on Bloom's Taxonomy. The results show that, although teachers aimed to include HOTs in line with Kenya's Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC), questions that involved lower-order thinking skills were prevalent. This study implies that strengthening classroom discourse practices in multilingual contexts through intentional higherorder questioning and translingual dialogic engagement has the potential to shift teacher-centered classrooms and enhance transformative pedagogical practices.

TI Behind the Skills Lab: A Qualitative Study of Skills Lab Faculty
   Workload
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Burnout; Equity; Faculty; Skills laboratory; Workload
AB Objective: Pharmacy skills laboratories are essential courses in the curriculum and require a significant workload from faculty to ensure that students are adequately prepared for pharmacy practice. The objective of this study is to determine skills laboratory faculty perceptions of workload demands, institutional equity, and factors influencing job satisfaction and burnout in pharmacy education. Methods: Following a national quantitative survey of skills laboratory faculty, semistructured interviews were conducted with 10 skills laboratory faculty members (9 women, 1 man) from geographically diverse US pharmacy programs who elected to participate. Interviews lasted 30 to 60 min and explored faculty workload experiences, institutional expectations, workload policy perceptions, perceived equity compared with didactic faculty members, and job satisfaction. Transcripts were analyzed using team-based coding with consensus building across three iterative stages. Results: Seven themes were identified: volume of demands in skills lab, challenges with time, value and understanding of skills laboratories, prioritizing students, burnout and work-life management, institutional differences and instability, and collaborative work culture. Participants described substantial invisible labor, including coordination, scheduling, curriculum preparation and maintenance, individualized student support, and advocacy efforts. Faculty unanimously expressed dedication to student development but reported difficulty quantifying workload, navigating unclear promotion expectations, and experiencing burnout from sustained high-touch engagement. Institutional budget constraints, leadership transitions, and limited lab support compounded workload pressures. Collaborative relationships with colleagues were an essential support mechanism. Conclusion: Skills laboratory teaching demands intensive faculty effort, contributing to burnout and inequitable workload distribution. Transparent policies, adequate staffing, and formal recognition of invisible labor should be considered.

TI Influence of Board-Certified Preceptors on Pharmacy Students' Intention
   to Pursue Specialty Certification
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy students; Board of Pharmacy Specialties; Preceptorship; Career
   aspirations; Middle East
AB Objective: As clinical pharmacy expands, Board of Pharmacy Specialties (BPS) certification is increasingly recognized as a gateway to advanced practice. However, little is known about how pharmacy students in the Middle East perceive this credential or how exposure to board-certified preceptors shapes their career ambitions. This study examined students' awareness of BPS certification, intention to pursue specialization, and the educational impact of training under board-certified preceptors. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was administered to senior pharmacy students at multiple Middle Eastern and North African universities. The validated questionnaire explored demographics, awareness, preceptor exposure, and perceived educational impact. A total of 684 eligible responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression. Results: Among the respondents, 386 (56.4%) reported awareness of BPS certification, while 308 (45.0%) expressed interest in pursuing board certification. Nearly half (47.5%) had trained under at least 1 board-certified preceptor during clinical rotations. They also reported stronger mentorship experiences (mean score, 4.21/5), greater confidence in clinical decision-making (mean, 4.18/5), and enhanced communication and interprofessional skills (mean, 4.09/5). Students frequently described board-certified preceptors as inspiring mentors who simplified complex clinical concepts and encouraged professional curiosity. Conclusion: Exposure to board-certified preceptors was significantly associated with students' confidence, professional identity, and intention to pursue BPS certification. Strengthening preceptorship structures and increasing access to highly experienced clinical educators, including board-certified practitioners, may support the development of a more confident, skilled, and specialty-oriented future pharmacy workforce.

TI The role of psychological contract in sustaining learner engagement with
   AWE systems
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Psychological contract; Engagement; Automated writing evaluation; L2
   writing
ID AUTOMATED FEEDBACK; ACCEPTANCE
AB This study investigates L2 writers' engagement with an Automated Writing Evaluation (AWE) system through the lens of psychological contract theory. Using a mixed-methods approach, this research examined the development of transactional and relational psychological contracts between students and an AWE system over a semester, and analyzed their impact on behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement. Through a latent profile analysis of 153 students' submission patterns, we identified six students as focal participants for in-depth interviews and iterative draft analyses. The findings reveal that transactional contracts, particularly expectations of score improvement, were frequently fulfilled, motivating repeated revisions. However, this fulfillment often prompted strategic system "gaming" rather than genuine writing development. Conversely, relational contracts were routinely breached. Faced with unmet expectations, students adapted their strategies by reducing engagement with the AWE. They supplemented this system with Gen-AI tools and human feedback. The study underscores the dynamic and often fragile nature of learner-AWE relationships, highlighting that engagement is strongly influenced by the perceived expectations and obligations between learners and technologies. Implications include the need for AWE designers to enhance feedback transparency and support for higherorder writing skills, and for instructors to complement AWE use with multi-source feedback to sustain engagement and meaningful writing development.

TI Observing children's self-regulation across play situations and peer
   effects on self-regulation during play in preschool classrooms
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Early childhood; Preschool; Self-regulation; Peer effects;
   Observational; Play
ID EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; ENGAGEMENT; GAINS; BLOCK; LITERACY; LANGUAGE
AB Self-regulation holds increasing importance in early childhood education, as evidenced by its positive influence on a range of skills critical for child learning and development. Prior research also emphasizes that children's self-regulation is contingent on the situation and support level provided by peers. The current study extends prior research by using an ecologically valid observational approach to examine self-regulation variation across common play situations in the preschool setting and to analyze peer effects on children's display of self-regulation. Participants were 95 preschoolers (Mage = 60 months, SD = 10) enrolled in 13 preschool classrooms in an urban area of Portugal. In each classroom, two groups of children were observed in three play situations (kitchen play, free play with blocks, and blocks with instruction). To observe children's self-regulation during play, we used the attention control and inhibitory control subscales of the Regulation-Related Skills Measure. Results showed significant variation in children's observed attention and inhibitory control across the three play situations. Additionally, peers' self-regulation was associated with individual children's observed self-regulation. The current study provides valuable theoretical insights for framing self-regulation as a contextual skill and practical insights by giving important information about how teachers can intentionally use playtime to promote self-regulation while supporting and building on peer interactions.

TI Tell me how: Teaching science with narration vs exposition
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Narrative texts; Science education; Text comprehension processes; RAND
   characteristics; Construction-Integration model
ID TEXT; COMPREHENSION; COMPLEXITY; MEMORY; EDUCATION; STORY; VIEW
AB Background: Narrative texts can support science comprehension. Yet, it remains unclear under which conditions they are beneficial. Aims: We compared the comprehension benefits of science narrative versus expository texts across comprehension levels and retention intervals and identified reader and activity characteristics predicting science comprehension. Sample: A sample of 125 university students with low prior knowledge of the content of the texts volunteered to participate. Methods: Participants read both a narrative and an expository text and then completed comprehension questions targeting different levels of comprehension. The contents were related to math or chemistry. Participants completed the comprehension items on that session, and one week after reading the texts. We also assessed participants' pre-reading perceived prior knowledge of the science topics and their post-reading perceptions of the texts' difficulty and interest. Results: Comprehension scores were higher for the narrative than for the expository text only with the chemistry topic, at all comprehension levels. Scores were higher in immediate comprehension assessments than in delayed assessments. Exploratory analyses suggest that narrative texts support comprehension in part by increasing perceived interest and lowering perceived difficulty. Conclusion: The narrative advantage was specific to the less familiar content, boosting comprehension across all levels of representation, partly by reducing perceived difficulty and increasing interest - underscoring the importance of aligning text type with learners' prior knowledge and task demands.

AB Creativity has long occupied an important place in gifted education theory, yet much of the most recent empirical work on creative development has emerged in adjacent disciplines. TI Teachers' Perspectives on Visual Proofs: Assessing Validity,
   Anticipating Peer Views, and Considering Classroom use
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mathematics teachers' perspectives; Proofs; Proof standards; Visual
   proofs
ID CONCEPTIONS; MATHEMATICS; STUDENTS
AB This study explores high school mathematics teachers' perceptions of visual proofs, or Proofs Without Words (PWWs). Using a mixed-methods design combining semi-structured interviews (n = 8) and questionnaires (n = 122), we examined (1) teachers' acceptance of visual proofs as valid, (2) their perceptions of colleagues' likely evaluations, and (3) their preferences regarding classroom use. Interviews first revealed two distinct levels of acceptance: Unconditional Acceptance, in which the student-produced visual proof was judged sufficient as presented, and Explanation-required Acceptance, in which teachers accepted the proof but preferred it to be accompanied by a verbal explanation. In questionnaire responses, 40% of respondents unconditionally accepted their assigned visual proof, and an additional 29% expressed explanation-required acceptance. However, many participants anticipated that their peers would assign lower grades to the visual proof than they would (58%). Notably, 93% indicated willingness to incorporate visual proofs into their teaching, citing pedagogical, aesthetic, and epistemological benefits. These findings indicate broad pedagogical endorsement of visual proofs, alongside tensions regarding proof standards that warrant further discussion in mathematics teacher education.

TI Toward a Multidimensional Understanding: Computational Chemistry and
   TPACK Framework in Elucidating the Hydrolysis of Methyl Acetate under
   Alkaline Conditions
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Computational Chemistry (CC); Hydrolysisof Esters; Density Functional
   Theory (DFT); TPACK Framework; BOPPPS Teaching Model
AB The hydrolysis of esters under alkaline conditions represents a core and challenging topic in high school chemistry education. Students often struggle to achieve a deep understanding due to the disconnection among macroscopic phenomena, microscopic mechanisms, and symbolic representations. To address the limitations of traditional teaching methods in visually presenting microscopic reaction mechanisms, this study, taking the hydrolysis of esters under alkaline conditions as an example, develops an innovative instructional model that integrates the technological pedagogical and content knowledge (TPACK) framework with computational chemistry (CC). Based on density functional theory (DFT) investigations on the hydrolysis of methyl acetate, methyl chloroacetate, and methyl dichloroacetate under alkaline conditions, an inquiry-based teaching approach grounded in the bridge-in, objective, preassessment, participatory learning, postassessment, summary (BOPPPS) teaching model was designed. By effectively transforming CC results, including molecular structures, energy diagrams, and charge distributions, into instructional materials, the approach helps students build a cognitive framework that bridges macroscopic phenomena and microscopic mechanisms. The results of pre- and postassessments based on this instructional design show that students significantly improved their abilities in two fundamental dimensions: describing reaction mechanisms and analyzing energy diagrams. Improvements were also observed in areas such as interpreting charge distributions, explaining reaction irreversibility, comprehensive discrimination, and metacognitive strategy awareness. This study provides a practical pathway for integrating the pedagogical value of CC-using visual evidence to support abstract concept understanding-into high school chemistry classrooms.

TI Exploring ChatGPT's Career-Based Contextualization of Chemistry Content
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE General Public; High School/IntroductoryChemistry; First-Year
   Undergraduate/General; Internet/Web-Based Learning
AB Contextualizing chemistry problems to connect disciplinary ideas with real-world or career settings has long been an instructional goal, yet analyses of widely used general chemistry textbooks suggest that such a framing is often limited or absent. This exploratory study examines how generative AI produces career-contextualized versions of general chemistry problems using elaboration prompting and how features of the underlying task may influence those outputs. Three second-semester topics differing in chemical specificity and the presence or absence of an explicit problem purpose were used to analyze chatbot-generated questions across six career domains. The chatbot frequently preserved the original chemical systems, calculations, and answer structures while introducing professional narratives, indicating that the model often treated the original problem as a template for contextual variation. Patterns of contextual integration appeared to vary across both chemistry topics and career domains. Problems involving defined chemical systems and explicit purposes more often supported professional decision-making scenarios, whereas problems focused on reporting numerical results tended to retain procedural structures even when narratives were introduced. These findings suggest that AI-generated contextualization often preserves the disciplinary structure of the original chemistry task while layering professional narratives around it, highlighting both the potential and the limitations of generative AI for career-based contextualization.

TI "Hey Prof, I Saw This and Thought of Our Class": A Generation of
   Sociology Teachers Reflect on the Rewards and Challenges of Teaching
SO TEACHING SOCIOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE empathy; conflict management; sociological imagination; skills
ID GRADUATE-STUDENTS; FACULTY; EXPERIENCES; INSTRUCTORS; EFFICACY;
   PEDAGOGY; PROGRAM; SUPPORT
AB This study examines narratives about rewarding and difficult teaching experiences of former students from our graduate teaching program. We interviewed former students from 13 classes from 2004 to 2022 and had a 42 percent response rate. These sociology teachers work across a variety of public and private universities and community colleges and tenure track and contingent contracts. Despite varying positions in the teaching profession, they all uniformly report empathy for their students and not only a commitment to excellence in instruction but also deep commitment to students' well-being. Their difficult experiences were routinely met with a straightforward effort to learn from mistakes and improve their teaching to benefit students. We interpret these findings in light of higher education as a "greedy institution" that needs empathetic skilled teachers. We recommend future research explore whether mid-career teachers and scholars feel mentored and supported for their dedicated teaching work.

TI Impact of Rotation Timing on Emergency Medicine Sub-Internship Course
   Outcomes
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
ID SELECTION CRITERIA
AB Background Emergency medicine sub-internships traditionally occur in summer months to facilitate letters of recommendation for residency applications, although it is unknown whether sub-internship timing impacts course outcomes. The purpose of this study was to identify seasonal trends in course outcomes.Methods This retrospective observational study examined 84 EM-bound medical students during a 4-week EM sub-internship between 2021 and 2024. During the rotation, students received on-shift evaluations graded on a Likert scale from 0 (inadequate) to 4 (outstanding) and completed an online SAEM exam (scored 0-100), both of which contributed to the final course grade. Course outcomes included the number of evaluations, average evaluation score, SAEM score and final course grade. Outcomes were compared between students rotating in May-July (25 students) and August-October (59 students). Analysis was completed in SPSS using independent t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests and regression analysis to adjust for confounders.Results There were no significant differences in outcomes between the May-July and August-October subgroups when comparing average evaluation score (p = 0.11), SAEM score (p = 0.32) and final course score (p = 0.21).Conclusion No performance differences were observed between early summer (May-July) and fall (August-October) rotations. These findings suggest that early summer rotations do not offer a significant advantage over fall rotations. Limitations include a single site study. Future research is needed to investigate factors contributing to seasonal variation in sub-internship performance.

TI Diffracting Childhood Memories, Place and Local Grassroots Mo(v)ements:
   Towards a Relational Environmental Education
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE climate change; community; land; water; wetlands
ID CHILDREN; POSTHUMAN; THINKING; MATTER; LAND
AB This paper employs autoethnography and poetic inquiry to examine how childhood experiences along the west coast of India were entangled with early understandings of environmental education. Drawing on memories of growing up in a rural region, it traces everyday intra-actions with land, sea, plants and community practices to illustrate how environmental awareness emerges through relational, place-based learning/unlearning rather than through universalized frameworks. By weaving poetic inquiry and becoming-with literature, the article disrupts linear and Western epistemologies of research and learning. This article argues that environmental education can benefit from recognizing situated, relational and place-based ways of knowing. In doing so, it contributes to conversations on decolonizing research practices and (re)thinking how environmental education is understood, narrated and enacted within educational contexts.

TI Teaching Machine Learning Concepts to Engineers: A Practical Approach
   With Free Software
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial neural networks; data mining; machine learning; materials
   engineering; ORANGE
AB In recent years, materials engineering education has undergone significant reform due to the transformative impact of computer simulations. This shift towards a more digital curriculum requires accessible and intuitive software for both educators and students. This study evaluates the use of a free and user-friendly data mining and machine learning platform (Orange Data Mining) as a possible pedagogical tool to teach basic concepts of artificial neural networks (ANNs) in materials engineering education. The platform enables the creation of customized workflows and simplifies complex data analysis without requiring programming skills. As a practical application, the study investigates the prediction of inorganic compound solubility in water (412 compounds) and the dissolution rates of inorganic glasses (295 entries from 19 compositions) using experimental data obtained from the literature. Input features comprised elemental composition, temperature, and pH conditions. The best-performing model consisted of an ANN with 30 neurons in a single hidden layer, using the ReLU activation function-selected for its computational efficiency and suitability for nonlinear modeling-and 400 iterations, chosen to balance model capacity and generalization in a teaching-oriented scenario. The results demonstrated high predictive accuracy, with a mean squared error (MSE) of 0.5 for solubility and 0.03 for dissolution rates. Additionally, the study illustrates both classical and modern interpretations of ANN behavior, including overparameterization effects. Overall, the findings indicate that Orange is an effective and accessible tool for teaching machine learning concepts in introductory classrooms, allowing the exploration of complex chemical and physical relationships using simple computational resources.

TI Paternal involvement and children's approaches to learning: the
   mediating role of maternal parental stress and maternal parental burnout
SO EARLY CHILD DEVELOPMENT AND CARE
LA English
DT Article
DE Paternal involvement; Maternal parental stress; Maternal parental
   burnout; Approaches to learning; Chain mediation
ID SCHOOL READINESS; FATHER INVOLVEMENT; MOTHERS; FAMILIES; ENVIRONMENTS;
   FLEXIBILITY; BEHAVIOR; CONTEXT; INCOME; URBAN
AB Grounded in the Family Systems Theory and the Balance between Risks and Resources framework, this study examined associations among paternal involvement, maternal parental stress, maternal parental burnout, and children's approaches to learning in the Chinese context. A chain mediation model was tested with 795 parents and their children aged 3-6 years (M=4.31, SD=1.12). Structural equation modelling revealed paternal involvement was associated with children's approaches to learning both directly and through two indirect pathways: solely through maternal parental stress, and sequentially through maternal parental stress and maternal parental burnout. These findings advance understanding of cross-subsystem family dynamics and provide support for intervention programmes that promote paternal involvement as a protective resource for alleviating maternal psychological distress and supporting children's early learning development.

TI Exploring the Educational Linguistic Landscape Through Cultural Capital
   Theory: A Case Study of a Rural Primary School in China
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cultural capital theory; educational linguistic landscape; rural
   education; student perception; visual discourse
AB Research on linguistic landscapes in educational settings has highlighted their role in reflecting institutional ideologies and shaping school culture, yet little attention has been paid to rural schools, where signage may carry heightened symbolic significance. Grounded in Bourdieu's theory of cultural capital, this study aims to examine how cultural capital is represented and transmitted through a campus linguistic landscape of a rural primary school. Adopting a mixed-methods design, the study collected data from a rural primary school, combining quantitative analysis of sign features with qualitative interpretation of students' perceptions. A total of 180 signs were collected, and interviews were conducted with 30 students to capture both visual patterns and lived experiences. Data were processed through content, discourse and thematic analyses. Five types of cultural capital emerged, namely institutionalised, educational, social normative, symbolic identity and participatory. Students demonstrated varied attitudes towards these messages, ranging from compliance to emotional resonance and aesthetic participation. The study contributes to understanding how linguistic landscapes mediate cultural reproduction and offers insights into creating more inclusive and participatory educational spaces in rural contexts.

   minority mentorship program: are we meeting expectations?

   Medical student

AB Purpose Pipeline programs that offer clinical exposure and mentorship are essential to increasing the recruitment of students underrepresented in medicine (URiM) into surgery. The ASPIRES (Advancing Student Preparedness and Involvement for Representation and Equity in Surgery) Program was established at our institution to address this need. TI The Effect ofa Flipped-Classroom-Enhanced Guided-InquiryCurriculum on
   Attitudes and Course Satisfaction of First-GenerationUnderrepresented
   Minority Students in Chemistry Courses
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate/General; Second-Year Undergraduate; Chemical
   Education Research; Organic Chemistry; Collaborative/Cooperative
   Learning; Computer-Based Learning; Distance Learning/Self Instruction;
   Inquiry-Based/DiscoveryLearning; Minorities in Chemistry;
   QuantitativeAnalysis
ID LEARNING-MODEL; SELF-CONCEPT; INSTRUCTION; ACHIEVEMENT; SCIENCE; EQUITY;
   INSTRUMENT; REDUCE; GAP
AB A quasi-experimental intervention presurvey/postsurvey design study was conducted with undergraduate college students in general chemistry and organic chemistry courses to reduce large educational equity gaps in STEM fields that are experienced by Hispanic and other underrepresented minority (URM) students who live in California's Central Valley. This study encompasses undergraduate student populations from two Hispanic Serving Institutions (HSIs) in the San Joaquin Valley, specifically, a California State University campus and a local community college. A novel combination of two pedagogies was implemented into the course: flipped classroom and guided-inquiry group work (including POGIL and new activities inspired by POGIL). The study compared attitudinal change and change in satisfaction with the chemistry courses via a within group analysis. Findings showed that at the conclusion of the course following implementation of the flipped-classroom-enhanced guided-inquiry curriculum, attitude toward chemistry (for Hispanic and Latino students, M = 29.81, SD = 4.37; for non-Hispanic or Latino students, M = 29.42, SD = 4.71) and satisfaction with chemistry course (for Hispanic and Latino students, M = 12.17, SD = 5.97; for non-Hispanic or Latino students, M = 10.76, SD = 5.46) were higher for Hispanic and Latino students but not statistically significant. For satisfaction with chemistry course, an independent samples t test showed that there was no significant difference (t(179) = -0.038, p >= 0.05) for satisfaction with chemistry course for first-generation (M = 11.56, SD = 5.63) and non-first-generation students (M = 11.59, SD = 5.98) at the conclusion of the course following implementation of the flipped-classroom-enhanced guided-inquiry curriculum. However, an independent samples t test indicated a statistically significant difference (t(179) = 2.25, p <= 0.05) following implementation of the flipped-classroom-enhanced guided-inquiry curriculum in attitude toward chemistry for first-generation students (M = 30.22, SD = 4.81) and non-first-generation students (M = 28.71, SD = 3.74). These findings suggest that the flipped-classroom-enhanced guided-inquiry model in undergraduate college chemistry courses may potentially lead to a decrease in equity gaps and consequently lead to an increase in first-generation underrepresented minority students who enter STEM workforce careers.

   Development and Validation of an Innovative LearningPacket

LA English
DT Article
DE organic chemistry; chemical education research; active learning; systems
   thinking; environmentalchemistry; curriculum; problem solving
ID STUDENT PERFORMANCE; GREEN CHEMISTRY; SCIENCE
AB This study developed and provided initial evidence on the use of an environmental justice-integrated learning packet in organic chemistry. The instructional material was evaluated using a multidimensional framework assessing accuracy, inclusivity, instructional effectiveness, and usability, as well as its potential to promote skills development and civic responsibility. TI Three-Dimensional Printing of Metal-OrganicFramework Crystal Structure
   Models for Chemical Education: Methodsand Applications
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Crystal Structure Visualization; Hands-OnLearning; Metal-Organic
   Frameworks; CrystalStructure Models; Outreach Activities
ID ORGANIC FRAMEWORKS
AB Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) pose a substantial challenge for creating high-fidelity physical models for educational use because of their intricate structures. Here, we report two 3D printing strategies designed to overcome limitations in structural accuracy, dynamic visualization, and cost-effectiveness. Using stereolithography, we fabricated millimeter-scale monolithic models of representative MOFs including UiO-66 and MOF-303. To improve color differentiation, scalability, and structural flexibility, we developed a modular "disassemble-then-assemble" approach based on multicolor fused deposition modeling. This method enabled the construction of flexible MOF models (MOF-808, MOF-5, BUC-88, and BUC-95) using PVC tubing as connectors. These interactive models allow students to simulate framework dynamics and explore structure-property relationships. In a small science outreach activity, retrospective pre/post-self-assessment showed a notable improvement in students' self-perceived understanding: 16 of 17 participants reported higher comprehension levels following the intervention.

TI Covalent OrganicFramework for Uranium Detection UsingColorimetry: A
   Simple Chemistry Experiment for Undergraduate Students
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE covalent-organic framework; undergraduate training; condensation
   reaction; colorimetric uranium detection
ID AQUEOUS-SOLUTION; ADSORPTION; TOXICITY; DEMAND
AB The objective of this study was successfully achieved by engaging undergraduate students in the preparation and application of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) for the colorimetric detection of uranium. The COFs were synthesized via a one-step condensation reaction followed by nucleation, both of which were accessible and manageable for undergraduate training. Characterization of the COFs and the subsequent experimental procedure were conducted with students, and the resulting data were analyzed and plotted using Origin software. The interaction between COFs and uranium ions demonstrated their effectiveness as a sensor, with a UV-visible absorption spectrophotometer used as the primary detection method. This approach achieved an average limit of detection (LOD) of 1.74 mu M with a concentration range of 2.1-13.8 mu M. This work highlights several key advantages: (i) the use of a straightforward and environmentally friendly condensation method for COFs preparation, (ii) the feasibility of a 72 h nucleation process suitable for undergraduate laboratory practice, and (iii) the adoption of a colorimetry detection method that is sensitive, cost-effective, and easy to operate. Overall, this experiment provided students with valuable experience in material synthesis, data analysis, and application of UV-visible absorption spectroscopy for real-world environmental challenges, thereby strengthening both their experimental and conceptual understanding of chemistry.

TI Facilitating Meaningful Work: How Career Wisdom Relates to Well-Being
SO JOURNAL OF COUNSELING PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE career wisdom; work meaningfulness; well-being; time-lagged; mediation
ID AMBIGUITY TOLERANCE; ENGAGEMENT; SATISFACTION; MEDIATION; QUESTIONNAIRE;
   PERSONALITY; MODEL; FIT
AB While prior research has highlighted the promising role of career wisdom in facilitating career development, the mechanisms through which career wisdom fosters well-being remain unclear. To address this gap, the present study employed a time-lagged design to examine the longitudinal associations between career wisdom and three indicators of well-being-job satisfaction, life satisfaction, and work engagement-using work meaningfulness as a mediator. Based on a sample of U.S. workers (N = 995), the study found that work meaningfulness (measured at Time 2) mediated the positive relationships between career wisdom (Time 1) and subsequent job satisfaction and work engagement (Time 3). The mediating effect of work meaningfulness in the relationship between career wisdom and subsequent life satisfaction was relatively small. These findings provide important insights into the role of career wisdom and its underlying mechanisms in contemporary career development, particularly in the cultivation of work meaningfulness and workplace well-being. Limitations and directions for future research are also discussed.

TI Patterns of Agentic Engagement, Autonomy Support, and Extrinsic
   Motivation in Middle School Science
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE agentic engagement; autonomy support; motivation; science education;
   mixed methods
ID STUDENTS MOTIVATION; EPISTEMIC AGENCY; LEARNING PROGRESSION; TEACHERS;
   CLASSROOM; SELF; PERSPECTIVE; PERCEPTIONS; FRAMEWORK; KNOWLEDGE
AB This mixed methods study examined teachers' autonomy-supportive versus thwarting responses to instances of student agentic engagement and changes in students' extrinsic motivation over time. We qualitatively coded videos from three middle school classes (two taught by the same teacher) and integrated those findings with a quantitative analysis of pre-/postunit student survey data. The qualitative analysis revealed differences in the frequency and type of agentic engagement initiated by students, and in the proportion of teacher responses to agentic engagement that were autonomy supportive, thwarting, or mixed in each class. Responses to students' epistemic agentic engagement, a code we developed to align with research on epistemic agency in science education, mirrored the overall patterns. However, there was variability within the three classes, with both teachers making unique instructional decisions in the lessons that promoted more epistemic agentic engagement. Quantitative findings indicated that students' postunit extrinsic motivation for science was higher in the classroom of the less autonomy-supportive teacher and that extrinsic motivation increased from pre- to postunit more in one of her two class sections. When integrated, findings illustrate the theorized relation between controlling teaching practices and externalized forms of motivation while illuminating ways that teachers might use autonomy-supportive responses to encourage students' epistemic agentic engagement and promote deeper science learning.

TI Measuring what matters: Operationalizing neurodiversity-affirming
   practices through participatory design of STEM workshops for autistic
   youth
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE fidelity; neurodiversity-affirming; participatory; social validity;
   student engagement
ID UNIVERSAL DESIGN; COLLEGE-STUDENTS; IMPLEMENTATION; PREVENTION;
   STRATEGIES; ENGAGEMENT; KNOWLEDGE; FIDELITY; OUTCOMES
AB Limited research has examined how neurodiversity-affirming approaches are (1) co-created with autistic people, (2) operationalized, (3) implemented, (4) assessed and (5) iterated. Across a 3-year program of research, we co-developed and iterated game design and employment workshops for and with autistic youth. After encountering difficulties enacting authentically neurodiversity-affirming approaches during the Year 2 workshop, we developed neurodiversity-affirming principles that guided hiring, training, curriculum development and student and staff advocacy opportunities in Year 3 workshops. We assessed fidelity to these principles. This paper examines if these changes were associated with increases in: 1) neurodiversity-affirming staff practices and (2) student engagement with workshop content. Masked coders analysed the following data sources from Years 2 and 3: (1) video recordings of staff teaching practices, (2) pre- and post-workshop staff surveys and (3) students' ratings of engagement with workshop activities. Staff used neurodiversity-affirming practices more frequently after the aforementioned changes. Student-reported engagement did not differ across years and was generally high. However, in Year 3 only, student engagement improved within workshops following intentionally advocacy-oriented student feedback loops. Findings show that redefining fidelity as a flexible, values-driven process offers a model for inclusive program design that fosters socially valid, responsive learning environments.

TI Resource centres as a support measure for inclusion: The voices of
   special education professionals
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE inclusion; mainstream and special education relationship; placement;
   special education; special needs students
ID STUDENTS
AB The right to education for all students is difficult to reconcile with the persistence of segregated schooling modalities. Thus, special schools can no longer be justified as separate settings for certain students. In Spain, a reform process is under way that reorients these institutions as support structures for mainstream schools. This article examines how special school professionals understand and evaluate the resource-centre role performed by their institutions and its perceived contribution to inclusive education. A qualitative study was conducted with 142 professionals, all employed by the 13 special schools in the Region of Murcia (Spain). Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analysed inductively using ATLAS.ti. Participants perceive the main strengths of this role to be specialized guidance, training and advisory support; digital and material resources; and its perceived contribution to collaboration and inclusive practices. While the study draws exclusively on service providers and offers an insider perspective, participants consider that the resource-centre role strengthens mainstream schools' capacity to respond to learner diversity and to support students' presence, participation and learning in ordinary settings. Further research incorporating the perspective of those who receive this support in mainstream schools would contribute to a holistic understanding of its scope and implementation.

   Environments for People with Differing Abilities
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING IN SOCIAL WORK
LA English

DE Pedagogy; experiential learning; disability justice; social work

AB Given the growing number of individuals with disabilities on college campuses in the U.S., social work educators must address and challenge disparities in education related to disabilities. TI Toward Culturally Sustaining Korean as a Foreign Language (KFL)
   Textbooks: A Critical Discourse Analysis of Linguistic, Cultural, and
   Racial Ideologies Across Earlier and Revised Editions
SO MODERN LANGUAGE JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
DE critical discourse analysis; culturally sustaining pedagogy; ideologies;
   Korean as a Foreign Language; textbook analysis
ID REPRESENTATION; AGREEMENT
AB This article critically examines Korean as a Foreign Language (KFL) textbooks published by major Korean universities and widely used around the world. Using critical discourse analysis and a culturally sustaining pedagogy (CSP) perspective, this article analyzes how earlier and revised textbooks represent language, culture, and race, and whether these representations align with CSP principles. Findings reveal that although revised editions introduce more nationalities and visibly diverse characters, the underlying racial logics of the earlier editions remain unchanged, where whiteness remains the default Western norm, Korean ethnonationalism persists, and racialized hierarchies are reproduced in subtler forms. Similarly, cultural representation remains static. Despite the inclusion of contemporary examples, culture continues to be framed as fixed, homogeneous, and nationally bounded, with little attention to hybrid, diasporic, or learners' lived cultural practices. In terms of language, despite minor gestures toward multilingual awareness in the revised editions, the textbooks continue to privilege standard Seoul Korean while erasing regional, diasporic, and hybrid varieties, thus reinforcing a monolingual ideology that marginalizes learners' diverse linguistic repertoires. Together, these patterns illustrate the persistent dominance of monolingual and monocultural ideologies in materials intended for linguistically and culturally diverse learners. Through a CSP lens, this article underscores the need for more inclusive KFL curricula that fully reflect and sustain the diverse linguistic, cultural, and migratory experiences of contemporary KFL learners.

TI Acquisition of subject restrictions and inference in Japanese emotional
   adjectives among Chinese JFL (Japanese as a Foreign Language) learners
SO READING AND WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Japanese emotional adjectives; Subject restriction; Inference markers;
   Chinese JFL learners; language proficiency
ID VISUAL WORD RECOGNITION; FREQUENCY; MODEL
AB This study examined how Chinese JFL (Japanese as a Foreign Language) learners perceived and used Japanese emotional adjectives, focusing on subject restrictions and the role of inference markers. In Japanese, emotional adjectives are typically restricted to first-person subjects, while third-person expressions require inference markers such as -s & omacr; or rasii to indicate indirect emotional inference. To investigate this, we compared the acceptability judgments of 48 native Japanese speakers and 67 Chinese JFL learners across different proficiency levels, analyzing how learners adapted to these linguistic constraints. The results (see Fig. 1) indicate that Chinese learners were more likely to reject third-person emotional expressions without inference markers, adhering more strictly to traditional Japanese norms compared to native speakers. As proficiency increased (see Fig. 2), learners gradually developed a more refined understanding of subject restrictions and inference markers. Nevertheless, even among high-proficiency Chinese JFL learners, judgments of third-person emotional adjective sentences remained more conservative than those of first-person sentences, with ratings generally narrow ranging between - 1 ('rather unnatural') to + 1 ('rather natural'). Additionally, the study highlights the influence of contemporary Japanese usage, where younger native speakers would exhibit greater acceptance of third-person emotional expressions without inference markers. This evolving linguistic trend appears to shape Chinese JFL learners' adaptability, influencing how they navigate both formal and informal contexts in Japanese. These findings emphasize the importance of targeted instruction and exposure to diverse language input in facilitating learners' acquisition of Japanese emotional expressions.

TI Prologue: language abilities in persons with dyslexia
SO ANNALS OF DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
ID UNDERSTANDING DYSLEXIA
AB The purpose of this special issue is to showcase current research on language abilities in persons with dyslexia. Although dyslexia is most often defined as a word-level reading and spelling disorder rooted in phonology, a large and growing body of evidence shows that the language difficulties of dyslexia extend well beyond phonology and are too often overlooked in research and practice. The articles in this issue (a) examine how broader oral language has and has not been accounted for in dyslexia research and policy, (b) characterize the language profiles of children with dyslexia with and without co-occurring developmental language disorder (DLD), (c) trace early language markers and subtypes that precede and predict reading difficulty, and (d) consider practical tools for detecting language vulnerability and for tailoring intervention to it within populations with reading and language difficulty. Read together, these contributions converge on a single message: dyslexia is best understood as a language learning disability, and assessment and instruction that ignore broader oral language risk leaving the needs of many children unmet. Universal screening, evaluation, and intervention for children with or at risk for dyslexia should routinely include measures of and stimulation for all components of oral language.

TI Epilogue: language abilities in persons with dyslexia
SO ANNALS OF DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Dyslexia; Developmental language disorder; Comorbidity; Research design
ID DEVELOPMENTAL DYSLEXIA; READING-DISABILITY; SIMPLE VIEW; FOLLOW-UP;
   IMPAIRMENT; CHILDREN; DISORDER; DEFICITS; SPEECH; ACQUISITION
AB Language difficulties are common among individuals with dyslexia and warrant greater consideration across research, advocacy, and clinical practice. For almost a hundred years, language difficulties have been observed in individuals with dyslexia (e.g., Orton, 1928). However, in approximately half of all individuals with dyslexia, language difficulties meet the clinical criteria for developmental language disorder (DLD), an impairment in the comprehension and use of oral language (Bishop et al., 2017; Catts et al., 2003, 2005; Ramus et al., 2013). Even when language difficulties in dyslexia do not meet the clinical threshold for DLD, many subclinical language difficulties persist beyond the point of word-reading remediation (Gallagher et al., 1996). In light of these patterns, this epilogue synthesizes contributions from the special issue on language abilities in persons with dyslexia and identifies four priority areas for the field. First, research design should systematically measure and account for language comorbidity. Secondly, legislative screening policy should be expanded to include broader language comprehension measures alongside current predictors of word reading. Third, special education evaluation practices should incorporate cognitive-linguistic markers, such as nonword and sentence repetition, to differentiate dyslexia from DLD in comorbid presentations. Finally, word-reading intervention research should address the semantic and morpho-syntactic dimensions of language, in addition to phonological and orthographic instruction, to improve automatic word reading. Taken together, these priorities support a more complete account of dyslexia, one that reflects the full range of language profiles and accounts for comorbidity in this population, and is in line with the new definition of dyslexia (IDA, 2025).

TI Task repetition in oral assessment: differential effects in monologue
   and dialogue
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Speaking assessment; Task repetition; Task type; Dialogue; Monologue
ID SPEAKING PROFICIENCY; PERFORMANCE; COMPLEXITY; FLUENCY; ACCURACY
AB Oral assessment is a challenging issue as various factors may play a role in language learners' production. Task repetition and task type are among factors that may influence oral performance. Previous studies have produced contradictory results about the effect of these two factors. Furthermore, such studies have only focused on one of these factors. Thus, it is yet unclear how these two factors may function in tandem to affect oral performance. The present study was, therefore, aimed at filling this gap. Thirty-two EFL learners carried out four tasks made by combining task repetition and task type: Monologue with exact repetition, dialogue with exact repetition, monologue with procedural repetition, and dialogue with procedural repetition. Four raters evaluated the participants' speaking performance using the Common European Framework of Reference speaking scale, including descriptors of range, accuracy, fluency, interaction, and coherence. A two-way repeated measures ANOVA was conducted to compare the participants' performances across the four tasks. Results indicated no significant interaction effect for task repetition and task type on test takers' performance after applying the Bonferroni adjustment. Additionally, the test takers received significantly higher scores on range and fluency when tasks involved exact repetition as opposed to procedural repetition. The findings further revealed that participants achieved significantly higher scores on accuracy in dialogue compared to monologue tasks. The findings hold implications for language teachers on how to use task types and task repetition in improving language learners' oral production.

TI Unveiling the Fluid Impact of Self-Concept and Self-Efficacy Upon
   English Achievement: A Perspective of the Island Ridge Curve
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

ID GOODNESS-OF-FIT; LANGUAGE; MOTIVATION; BELIEFS; PREDICTORS
AB Self-concept and self-efficacy have received much attention from second/foreign language (L2) researchers. However, very few studies have empirically deciphered their similarities and distinctions. Even fewer have investigated how their contributions to L2 achievement vary across L2 proficiency levels. The current study examined the commonality and specificity of self-concept and self-efficacy and their relative contributions to English achievement and their fluid effects on English achievement across different proficiency groups based on the Island Ridge Curve theory. TI Examining the Role of Perceived Teacher Support on Left-Behind Students'
   Well-Being in China: The Mediation Role of Motivation and Resilience
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE left-behind students; motivation; resilience; teacher support;
   well-being
ID SOCIAL SUPPORT; DISCRIMINATION; EXPERIENCE; ENGAGEMENT; CHILDREN
AB Since learners believe that their teachers can offer them chances to choose, support them in autonomous problem solving, and comprehend their internal feelings, teacher support results in the feeling of being loved and cared for. At the same time, the significance of motivation and resilience on the well-being of left-behind students (LBS) has been emphasized within the educational sphere. The present research investigated the way teacher support affects learners' well-being, with internal motivation and educational resilience as mediators. A total of 258 LBS were surveyed in the present research. The results revealed that teacher support significantly predicted both resilience and motivation (explaining 26.4% and 46.6% of their variance, respectively). Both mediators, in turn, significantly predicted well-being. The model explained 18.7% of the variance in well-being. The study indicated the significance of teacher support to the LBS's well-being; therefore, maintaining the theoretical importance for enhancing their motivation and resilience.

TI Linking the stages of teaching skills based on the dynamic model of
   education effectiveness with student outcomes in Taiwan
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Dynamic model of education effectiveness; Quality of teaching; Stages of
   teaching skills; Student achievement; Teacher development
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; SOCIOECONOMIC-STATUS;
   QUALITY; PROGRAMS; SALTUS
AB Understanding how teaching quality influences student achievement offers insights for the design and implementation of professional development programs. Drawing from an adapted version of the Dynamic Model of Educational Effectiveness for the Taiwanese educational context, this study aims to investigate the relationship between teaching quality and student outcomes in Taiwan. Data for this study were collected through a questionnaire and mathematics tests, involving 55 Taiwanese primary school teachers and 1480 students. Teachers were classified into three stages of teaching quality, which were then linked to students' mathematics performance. Results showed that students taught by teachers in the highest-quality teaching stage generally achieved higher final mathematics scores, regardless of their initial performance. The outcomes highlight the necessity of considering cultural and contextual factors when identifying stages of teaching quality. Additionally, the findings reaffirm that teaching quality is an important factor in student achievement, as students in high-quality learning environments tend to achieve better academic outcomes. Suggestions related to teacher professional development are proposed, encompassing the development of a student feedback instrument to support teachers in optimising the quality of their teaching and enhancing the overall learning environment.

TI Interconnected third spaces: collective inquiry into spaces that honour

   CPD; scholarship; online collaboration
ID SECTOR
AB Empirical research examining the efficacy of online communities within Further Education (FE) contexts remains limited. TI Critical Thinking Conceptions, Attitudes and Practices Among Ideological
   and Political Theory Course Lecturers in Chinese Higher Education
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE critical thinking; ideological and political theory courses; teacher
   beliefs; teaching practices; belief-practice gap; Chinese higher
   education
ID TEACHING CRITICAL THINKING; DISPOSITIONS
AB Critical thinking is a stated priority of higher education reform in China, yet its enactment in everyday teaching remains uneven. This study investigated how lecturers of ideological and political theory courses (IPTCs) understand and value critical thinking, and how they report teaching it. To our knowledge, few studies have modelled lecturers' conceptions, attitudes, reported practices and contextual constraints jointly within these courses. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed. A validated questionnaire was completed by 362 IPTC lecturers across 20 universities in Anhui Province, and semi-structured interviews were subsequently conducted with 34 lecturers. The survey data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including multiple and moderated regression, whereas the interview data were examined thematically. Reported classroom enactment fell below the scale midpoint. Conceptions did not predict practice; attitudes predicted it only weakly (standardised beta = 0.13), and contextual constraints did not moderate the attitude-practice relationship. The regression models accounted for almost none of the variance in reported practice. These findings indicate a broad belief-practice gap that is shaped by structural conditions rather than by individual beliefs. The single-province, self-report design constrains wider generalisation. The findings direct reform attention towards assessment design and sustained, practice-based professional learning, since belief change alone appears unlikely to alter classroom practice.

TI From Dissonance to Emotional Regulation: Pre-Service Teachers' Lived
   Experiences of the SEL Loop in Role-Based Simulation
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE simulation; social-emotional learning; teacher education;
   self-awareness; self-management
AB Simulation-based learning (SBL) is recognized as a transformative methodology in teacher education, yet the social-emotional processes through which pre- and in-service teachers navigate role dissonance remain underexplored. Drawing on the Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) framework proposed by CASEL, this study conceptualizes simulation as a cyclical SEL loop across three phases, pre-briefing, simulation, and debriefing, each activating distinct competencies: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making. This qualitative phenomenological inquiry examines the lived social-emotional experiences of pre- and in-service teachers participating in The School of Valtance, a large-scale, multi-role international simulation embedded in a postgraduate teacher qualification program. Participants from 9 international faculties were deliberately assigned to roles, such as pedagogue, head of studies, and parent, divergent from their professional backgrounds, generating the cognitive-emotional disruption known as the "valley of despair". Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews, reflective journals, and facilitator field notes across all three simulation phases and subjected to thematic analysis. The findings reveal that role dissonance disrupts participants' emotional equilibrium, activating self-awareness and social awareness competencies that precede and enable metacognitive growth. The debriefing phase emerges as the space in which the SEL loop closes, as participants articulate and consolidate both the emotional turbulence and relational learning generated during the simulation, transforming affective experience into transferable social-emotional competence. These findings offer practical guidance for simulation designers seeking to embed SEL intentionally across all phases of the pedagogical cycle in intercultural teacher training contexts.

TI Language Learning Strategies, Motivational Beliefs, and English Learning
   Achievement Among Thai University EFL Learners: A Structural Equation
   Modelling Analysis
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE language learning strategies; motivational beliefs; English achievement;
   structural equation modelling; Thai EFL learners
ID SELF-REGULATION
AB This study investigated the structural relationships among language learning strategies (LLSs), motivational beliefs (MBs), and English language achievement (ELA) among first-year Thai university students learning English as a foreign language (EFL). Grounded in self-regulated learning, social cognitive, and expectancy-value theories, the study examined how LLSs and MBs jointly contribute to ELA. A quantitative cross-sectional design was used, with 913 participants from a public university in Thailand. Data were collected via a structured questionnaire measuring learners' cognitive, metacognitive, and social strategies; intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, task value, and self-efficacy; and overall assessment of their perceived English learning achievement and self-rated English proficiency across the four language skills. Descriptive statistics, Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), and Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) were conducted. Results indicated moderate use of LLSs, with cognitive and metacognitive strategies used more frequently than social strategies. Students reported moderate-to-high motivational beliefs, with task value emerging as the strongest dimension. EFA and CFA supported the reliability and construct validity of the measurement model. SEM analysis demonstrated excellent model fit and revealed that intrinsic motivation, task value, and self-efficacy significantly predicted strategy use and ELA. LLSs showed the strongest direct effect on achievement, whereas extrinsic motivation had no significant direct effect. In addition, LLSs partially mediated the effects of intrinsic motivation, task value, and self-efficacy on achievement. The SEM results indicated that ELA is shaped by the combined influence of adaptive motivation and effective strategic behaviour. Therefore, instructional interventions should synchronously enhance strategic language learning and increase learners' motivational beliefs to promote English learning achievement.
