TI Digital participation outside institutional provision: implications of
   the access-competence gap for digital transformation in Ghana's basic
   education system
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE access-competence gap; basic education; digital inequality; digital
   literacy; Ghana; online safety; vulnerability
ID INTERNET
AB Digital literacy has become a foundational competence for participation in contemporary educational, social, and economic life. However, debates surrounding children's digital engagement often oscillate between concerns about online vulnerability and assumptions that expanding connectivity automatically promotes digital inclusion. This study examines how digital access, digital literacy, educational engagement, and vulnerability intersect among Basic 8 students in Ghana. The study employed a mixed-methods design involving a cross-sectional survey of 823 students drawn from 24 public schools across three districts in Ghana's Central Region, complemented by a six-week ethnographic study in three selected schools. Composite indices were developed to measure digital access, digital literacy, educational engagement, and vulnerability, all demonstrating acceptable reliability (Cronbach's alpha = 0.76-0.88). Correlation and regression analyses were used to examine relationships among key constructs, while qualitative data provided contextual insights into students' digital experiences. Findings reveal a paradoxical pattern of digital inclusion. Despite limited ICT infrastructure within schools, students reported substantial engagement with digital technologies through home-based access and mobile devices. Digital access was positively associated with digital literacy (r = .174, p < .001) and educational engagement (r = .444, p < .001), while vulnerability was negatively associated with digital access (r = -0.692, p < .001), digital literacy (r = -.105, p < .01), and educational engagement (r = -0.284, p < .001). Importantly, an access-competence gap was identified among 21.6% of students, indicating that access exceeded competence. Regression analysis further demonstrated that this gap was the strongest predictor of vulnerability (B = 0.326, p < .001), suggesting that exposure to digital environments without corresponding competencies increases susceptibility to online risks. The findings challenge access-centred approaches to digital inclusion by demonstrating that connectivity alone does not guarantee safe, meaningful, or empowering digital participation. The study argues for competence-centred digital inclusion policies that integrate digital literacy, online safety, information verification, and critical media education within basic education systems. By operationalising the concepts of vulnerability and the access-competence gap, the study advances understanding of digital inequality in Ghana and comparable low-resource contexts across sub-Saharan Africa.

TI Teacher professional procrastination as a well-being and self-regulation
   challenge: development and validation of the Arabic teacher professional
   procrastination scale
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Arabic scale; confirmatory factor analysis; exploratory factor analysis;

   professional procrastination; teachers
ID FIT INDEXES; WORK; QUESTIONNAIRE; PERFORMANCE; INVENTORY; STUDENTS
AB Background/objective Educator well-being and resilience are increasingly recognized as critical for sustainable teaching and professional effectiveness. Professional procrastination may undermine teachers' occupational functioning through difficulties in self-regulation, emotional coping, and motivation. This study aimed to develop and validate the Arabic Teacher Professional Procrastination Scale (TPPS) and examine its associations with factors relevant to educator well-being and resilience.Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 1375 Tunisian middle- and high-school teachers (mean age = 44.84 +/- 6.78 years). Findings highlight professional procrastination as a multidimensional challenge linked to educator well-being, self-regulation, and resilience-related resources.

TI Gravitational inequality in academia: a call to reimagine institutional
   influence
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academia; career; graduate school; higher education; inequality
ID PRESTIGE; GRAVITY
AB Academic systems across the globe are under pressure from demographic shifts, geopolitical turbulence, and technological disruption. In the United States, long-standing hierarchies of institutional prestige shape the pathways through which talent and knowledge circulate. Recent developments - federal constraints on indirect-cost reimbursement at R1 universities, restructuring of major NIH and NSF program announcements, and political and legal challenges to private endowment governance - suggest that the conditions historically sustaining elite dominance are under measurable strain, though it remains an open question whether the underlying hiring and citation hierarchies will shift in response. This piece proposes a generative framework, academic gravity, to conceptualize how institutional prestige shapes opportunity. Building on gravity-equation traditions in economic geography and migration research, the framework treats pairwise flows of scholars, citations, and funding as a parametric function of institutional mass and distance - a formulation designed to be fit to, and falsified against, dyadic data such as the hiring matrix seen in previous studies - a program of empirical testing this Perspective motivates rather than completes. Drawing on insights from network science and complex systems theory, I outline a roadmap for reimagining academic mobility and equity, with implications for faculty hiring, doctoral training, and the long-term health of public research institutions.

TI Reducing L1 and L2 transfer in L3 English acquisition: an intervention
   study in Kazakhstani trilingual education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE communicative and cognitive approach; grammatical patterns; lexical
   errors; statistics; systemic approach
AB This study examines interlanguage interference within the context of foreign language education in Kazakhstan. Drawing on an analysis of pedagogical practices and statistical data, this study identifies the primary error types and methods for preventing interlanguage interference. Interlanguage interference occurs when learning Kazakh, Russian, and English within a trilingual education setting. Difficulties arise in phonetics, grammar, and lexis, manifesting as pronunciation errors (e.g., substituting/theta/ with/s/) and non-canonical word order. The lexical difficulties included the translator's "false friends." A survey on the level of lexical skills development in the context of interlanguage interference, which was conducted on the basis of the Nazarbayev Intellectual School (116 people) and the Nurmakov specialized boarding school (146 people), indicated the following results: a high level of lexical skills-50%, a medium level of lexical skills-40%, and a low level of lexical skills-10%. Thus, the combination of systemic and cognitive-communicative approaches has reduced the impact of interlanguage interference in the study of Kazakh, Russian, and English.

TI Gesture-controlled presentation systems in STEM education: associations
   with student participation and classroom interaction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational technology; gesture-based interaction; interactive learning
   environments; STEM education; student participation
AB This study examined the implementation of a gesture-controlled presentation system in STEM education and its association with student participation and classroom interaction. The system enables hands-free control of presentation content through computer vision and a supervised machine learning model for gesture classification. The study involved 84 undergraduate students (experimental group, n = 42; control group, n = 42) across four STEM subjects: computer science, biology, chemistry, and physics. In the experimental group, gesture-based presentation control was used during lessons and student presentations, whereas the control group used conventional presentation methods based on standard input devices. Data were collected through structured classroom observations, and differences between groups were analyzed using the chi-square (chi & sup2;) test. The results showed significantly higher levels of student participation in the experimental group, whereas no statistically significant changes were observed in the control group (p < 0.05). Classroom observations also indicated more continuous interaction with presentation materials and smoother instructional flow during presentation activities. The gesture recognition system achieved a classification accuracy of 0.93 with an average response latency of 94 ms, supporting reliable real-time classroom use. Unlike previous studies that primarily evaluated gesture recognition from a technical perspective, this study examined its implementation in authentic STEM classrooms involving both teacher-led instruction and student presentations. The findings suggest that gesture-controlled presentation systems may serve as an additional instructional tool to support interactive teaching practices and student participation in STEM education.

TI Motivation and well-being: exploring the relationships
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE flourishing; flow; grit; growth mindset; meaning in life; passion
ID SELF-EFFICACY; LIFE; PERFORMANCE; EXPERIENCE; MINDSETS; PASSION; GRIT;
   PERSEVERANCE; COHERENCE; HAPPINESS
AB Drawing on positive psychology and motivation science, this study examined whether grit, growth mindset, and passion represent interrelated motivational traits associated with holistic well-being, conceptualized through flow proneness, flourishing, and meaning in life. A cross-sectional online survey was completed by a Norwegian convenience sample of 585 participants, including 222 males (37.9%) and 363 females (62.1%; mean age = 33.2 years, SD = 15.2). The study explored whether motivational traits clustered together, whether well-being indicators formed a coherent latent factor, and whether personal motivation was associated with holistic well-being. Correlational analyses showed moderate-to-strong positive associations among grit, growth mindset, and passion, and among flow proneness, flourishing, and meaning in life. Regression analyses indicated that grit and passion were consistently associated with well-being outcomes, whereas growth mindset contributed uniquely to flourishing. Structural equation modeling supported a significant association between the latent personal motivation factor and latent holistic well-being factor, beta = .65, SE = .04, p < .001, with acceptable model fit, chi(2)(7) = 39.43, p < .001, CFI = .974, TLI = .945, RMSEA = .089, 90% CI [.063,.117], and SRMR = .032. These findings suggest that perseverance, passion, and adaptive beliefs may represent related but distinct motivational resources associated with engaged, meaningful, and flourishing lives. However, because the study used a cross-sectional convenience sample that was predominantly female and Norwegian, the findings should be interpreted as associational and generalizability across populations needs to be further examined. The results suggest that efforts to support well-being may benefit from considering multiple motivational traits, and that longitudinal and experimental research are warranted to examine potential causal pathways.

   learners' fluency, interactional competence, and autonomy

LA English
DT Article
DE AI-mediated speaking; generative artificial intelligence; interactional

AB Introduction: The growing availability of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools has created new opportunities to enhance language learning, particularly speaking practice. However, studies on the effectiveness of AI voice-chat applications in enhancing English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners' speaking skills and autonomy remain limited. Methods: This mixed-methods quasi-experimental study investigated the effects of Microsoft 365 Copilot voice chat on speaking fluency, interactional competence, and learner autonomy of 52 university English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners over eight weeks. TI Translanguaged lexical-pragmatic scaffolding makes pragmatic vocabulary
   knowledge visible in Jordanian EFL classrooms
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

   vocabulary knowledge; Jordanian secondary education; L2 pragmatics;
   multilingual pedagogy; pragmatic usability; translanguaged

ID ENGLISH
AB This study examines translanguaged lexical-pragmatic scaffolding in Jordanian secondary EFL classrooms. Vocabulary teaching often makes translation, recognition, and controlled sentence use visible, while pragmatic usability remains less inspectable. Using a non-experimental, embedded mixed-methods case design, the study traced how Arabic-English classroom movement mediated selected English lexical items beyond form-meaning recognition. Data came from three anonymized schools, four Grade 10-11 EFL classes, and 120 learners. The evidence base included 20 audio-recorded lessons, 51 lexical-pragmatic teaching episodes, fieldnotes, 40 textbook or teacher-material records, worksheets, quizzes, exam-oriented artifacts, 20 stimulated-recall excerpts, and learner lexical-pragmatic tasks at three time points. Arabic-English movement became most clearly lexical-pragmatic when it extended semantic translation toward register marking, contrastive explanation, metapragmatic explanation, repair, and production support. Learner task-score patterns showed short-term, uneven variation across items and dimensions. The study offers a bounded account of multilingual classroom mediation as a resource for making pragmatic vocabulary use teachable and partially assessable.

   in statistics using Kruskal-Wallis H-test statistic: a nonparametric

   students
AB Purpose The study sought to investigate whether variations in information technology students' achievement across four related classes were statistically significant, thereby addressing concerns about performance consistency and instructional effectiveness in statistical results.Methodology/design/approach This study adopted a quantitative comparative research design to examine the differences in Statistics achievement among Information Technology Education (ITE) students, involving 40 purposively sampled second-year students enrolled in a statistics course. TI Generative artificial intelligence and the epistemology of medical
   learning: from cognitive augmentation to epistemic dependency
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cognition; education; generative artificial intelligence; knowledge;
   medical education
ID EDUCATION
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly transforming medical education by expanding access to information, enabling personalized learning, and improving measurable educational outcomes. Systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and experimental studies consistently report gains in learner satisfaction, communication abilities, practical skills, and short-term academic performance following GAI-assisted educational interventions. Yet these benefits have largely been evaluated through performance-centered metrics, while the cognitive and epistemological implications of algorithmically mediated learning remain insufficiently examined. This Perspective explores how GAI may be reconfiguring the conditions under which medical knowledge is acquired, interpreted, and integrated. Drawing on medical epistemology, philosophy of science, educational theory, and evidence-based medicine, we argue that the educational significance of GAI extends beyond efficiency and information accessibility. By increasingly participating in explanatory, interpretive, and inferential activities, generative systems are redistributing forms of cognitive work that have traditionally contributed to the development of autonomous clinical judgment. We propose that the relationship between GAI and medical learning is best understood as a continuum that extends from cognitive augmentation to epistemic dependency. Along this continuum, algorithmic systems may expand opportunities for learning and reasoning while simultaneously altering the intellectual dispositions through which critical evaluation, uncertainty management, and independent judgment are cultivated. The principal challenge for contemporary medical education is therefore not whether future physicians will learn alongside intelligent systems, but how educational environments can harness the benefits of AI-mediated learning while sustaining the cognitive capacities that underpin responsible clinical reasoning. Cultivating epistemological resilience may become a central objective of medical education in the age of GAI.

TI Navigating the hidden academic job market: a descriptive phenomenology
   of racial and ethnic minority STEM scholars in a structured
   train-and-retain postdoctoral program
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE biomedical postdoctoral job search; faculty diversification ecosystems;
   faculty job search; postdoc-to-faculty conversion programs; postdoctoral
   appointments; postdoctoral hiring; postdoctoral job search process
ID CAREER; PHD
AB Introduction This descriptive phenomenological study examines how racialized ethnic minority (REM) scholars experienced the academic job search while pursuing tenure-track faculty careers in the biomedical sciences. Previous research has documented disparities in faculty representation, relational hiring practices, and the increasing centrality of postdoctoral training within academic career pathways. However, less attention has focused on how scholars navigate structured programs towards faculty diversification. Within an ecosystem framing, the National Science Foundation AGEP PROMISE Academy Alliance (APAA) is understood as the broader faculty diversification ecosystem within a state university system, while the PROMISE Academy fellowship is the embedded train-and-retain (T-RT) postdoctoral-to-faculty pathway through which REM scholars discovered and evaluated a pathway into faculty careers.Methods Drawing on interviews with 11 PROMISE Academy biomedical postdoctoral scholars, this study explores how participants navigated faculty job searches and interpreted T-RT opportunities within informal academic hiring systems. Participants entered the T-RT program from multiple career stages across the five participating institutions.Results Participants described faculty pathway discovery as a network-dependent process shaped by mentoring relationships, sponsorship, professional networks, institutional conditions, and family considerations. Faculty pathways emerged through informal channels rather than through centralized-transparent hiring systems. Differences in guidance influenced how participants understood opportunities and assessed institutional fit. Cohorts entering between 2019 and 2023 navigated job searches at different stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, creating uncertainty about faculty hiring, geographic mobility, and long-term career stability.Discussion Rather than approaching postdoctoral appointments as a sequential career stage, participants described evaluating opportunities in relation to long-term faculty aspirations, institutional support, geographic stability, and family responsibilities. Perceptions of mentorship quality, institutional climate, and the likelihood of transitioning into faculty roles influenced their decisions to enroll in the APAA program. By centering participants' descriptions, this study contributes insight into REM scholars' experiences of faculty pathway discovery within a T-RT pathway.

TI Integrating AI literacy into information culture formation for
   pre-service teachers: a quasi-experimental study with a
   reflexive-adaptive model
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; blended learning; delayed post-test; information culture;
   integrative model; pre-service teachers; quasi-experimental design;
   reflexive-adaptive component
AB Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) transforms education, pre-service teachers require competencies beyond traditional information literacy. Existing information culture models lack AI-specific components, and most empirical studies in this domain lack control groups, fail to account for the Hawthorne effect, and do not assess long-term retention. This study reconceptualized information culture by integrating AI literacy as a distinct component, developed a six-component integrative model with a reflexive-adaptive mechanism, and validated formation criteria with psychometric rigor. Methods A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control group design was implemented across four universities in Uzbekistan (N = 498; experimental n = 249, control n = 249) over 16 weeks. The control group received equal instructional hours (44 h) using traditional methods to control for the Hawthorne effect. A validated diagnostic instrument (Cronbach's alpha = 0.87; test-retest r = 0.84; Kendall's W = 0.83) assessed three criteria: motivational-axiological, cognitive-operational, and reflexive-creative. A delayed post-test was administered 3 months post-intervention. Results The experimental group showed significant improvement: high-level students increased from 8% to 35% (t = 7.64, p < 0.01; chi(2) = 52.8, p < 0.01; Cohen's d = 0.99). The control group showed modest improvement (7-10%). The delayed post-test confirmed 86% retention of gains (t = 6.82, p < 0.01), indicating durable competency formation. Discussion The study contributes a validated framework for integrating AI literacy into information culture formation in teacher education. As a single-country quasi-experimental study with cluster-level assignment, its findings should be interpreted cautiously and require replication in other contexts.

TI Designing curriculum-aligned digital assessment infrastructures: a
   design-based case study of Naviskore in Flemish secondary education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment infrastructure; competency-based education; curriculum
   alignment; design-based research; digital assessment; educational
   technology; human-in-the-loop; teacher agency
ID TECHNOLOGY
AB Background Competency-based education requires assessment infrastructures that make evaluation evidence visible, curriculum-linked, and usable in professional deliberation. In Flanders, existing digital tools often remain fragmented across evaluation input, feedback, reporting, and high-stakes decision-making workflows.Purpose This article presents Naviskore as a design-based case study of a curriculum-aligned digital assessment infrastructure developed in Flemish secondary education. Rather than evaluating the platform's impact on learning outcomes, fairness, workload, or assessment reliability, the study examines how iterative co-design with educators informed the development of infrastructural design principles for transparent, teacher-mediated assessment.Method Over four years, Naviskore was developed through iterative co-design, prototyping, implementation, and technical verification cycles involving teachers, school leaders, administrators, and IT staff. The analysis focuses on design artefacts, stakeholder feedback, platform features, and implementation experience.Results The case identifies five design principles: curriculum-embedded evaluation, structured multi-modal feedback, distributed professional agency, interpretability-by-design, and human-in-the-loop data infrastructure. Implementation across four schools and more than two million evaluation records demonstrates practical adoption and infrastructural scale, but these data are not used to make causal, psychometric, or fairness-outcome claims.Conclusion The study contributes a theoretically informed design model for curriculum-aligned assessment infrastructures in competency-based education. It shows how digital assessment systems can be designed to support traceability, curriculum coherence, and teacher-led deliberation, while identifying the need for future empirical research on reliability, fairness, usability, workload, and educational impact.

TI Immersive learning promise and classroom practice: a qualitative study
   of cultural barriers and human factors in UAE VR integration
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE curriculum localization; immersive learning; K-12 education; qualitative
   research; teacher experiences; technology integration; UAE; virtual
   reality
AB Virtual Reality (VR) being an promising tool for immersive learning nowadays, nevertheless, in K-12 classrooms across the UAE, it's still underexplored thus highlighting a research gap in VR in the UAE context. This study collected data from twenty-five teachers in a single UAE private school who used VR with their students. Using qualitative focus group interviews and data thematic analysis, the study explores the teachers' hands-on experiences, perceived educational impacts, challenges, and practical considerations regarding VR integration in the UAE educational context. The findings discussed the discrepancies of VR's perceived educational benefits and the issues associated with integrating VR into education. Themes identified include student involvement and engagement in VR learning, lack of cultural-related curriculum for Arabic implementation, strategies used by teachers to create innovative solutions for classroom delivery with the lack of resources, technical barriers for both students and teachers, and safety-related issues concerning young children using VR technology. One point that emerged was the difference in what VR was presumed to accomplish regarding teaching and learning and how effective VR is when being actively implemented in an actual educational environment. This study highlights the need for Emirati localized content development, robust infrastructure, and continuous educational support to benefit from the VR's full potential. This paper contributes to the growing body of literature on immersive learning by providing a detailed, context-specific model for VR adoption in a non-Western educational system, offering valuable understandings for educators, policymakers, and technology developers.

TI Omani college students' and lecturers' perceptions of Turnitin and
   artificial intelligence in relation to academic integrity
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic integrity; artificial intelligence; ChatGPT; plagiarism;
   Turnitin
ID PLAGIARISM
AB Academic integrity is a fundamental principle in higher education that plays a key role in supporting students' learning and research. Although Turnitin and Artificial Intelligence (AI) supported tools such as ChatGPT are used by higher education institutions, their relation to academic integrity needs to be investigated in various educational contexts. This study explores Omani college students' and lecturers' perceptions of Turnitin and ChatGPT in relation to academic integrity. This research was conducted using questionnaires and focus group interviews with students and lecturers from different disciplines. The questionnaire results were analysed by employing Chi-square and ANOVA tests while interview results were analysed thematically. The average questionnaire ratings were more than 3 out of 5 on Likert scale which is an indicator of their positive perception. This is further supported with an overall effect size of 1.01 obtained among General Foundation and Undergraduate programme students, indicating a large effect based on variance in perception. However, the effect size was found to be lower among the Postgraduate students. Furthermore, interview results revealed that AI use enhances learning, and interviewee quotes suggested that a balanced approach should be considered to prevent plagiarism and to foster critical thinking. The findings from both questionnaire and interview results indicate significant impact of Turnitin and AI on academic integrity which shows students' and lecturers' positive perception of AI use. This research underscores the fact that institutions play a pivotal role in shaping academic integrity provided they have clear AI policies, integrate AI literacy into curriculum, and promote responsible use through training and awareness raising. As a limitation, the findings are based on a heterogeneous sample of three different disciplines and levels. Future research should involve larger homogeneous samples along with other AI supported tools.

TI Factors Influencing Interest in General Surgery Among Medical Students:
   The Role of Discouragement and Sex Differences
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE career choice; General Surgery; medical education; medical students;
   mentors; sex factor
ID IMPACT
AB BACKGROUND: Interest in surgical careers is shaped by personal and contextual factors. Although women represent a growing proportion of medical students, they remain underrepresented in surgical specialties. This study evaluated factors influencing interest in General Surgery among medical students, with a particular focus on discouragement and sex differences. METHODS: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Brazilian medical students using an anonymous electronic questionnaire distributed through social media. Students who reported General Surgery as their initial specialty choice were included. Sociodemographic characteristics, experiences of discouragement, sources and reasons for discouragement, and factors influencing specialty choice were analyzed. RESULTS: Among 706 respondents, 82 students (11.6%) reported General Surgery as their initial specialty choice. Overall, 65.9% reported experiencing discouragement regarding a surgical career. Women were significantly more likely to report discouragement than men (78.2% vs 40.7%, p < 0.001), and female sex remained independently associated with discouragement after adjustment for age, type of medical school, and having a physician in the family (adjusted odds ratio 5.62, 95% CI 1.96-16.09, p = 0.001). Among women who reported discouragement, 62.8% indicated that at least one discouraging message was explicitly related to their sex. Family members or friends were the most frequently reported sources of discouragement (70.4%). Extracurricular activities were the only factor influencing specialty choice that differed significantly between sexes (p = 0.040). CONCLUSIONS: Interest in General Surgery is frequently accompanied by discouragement, particularly among women. Positive exposure to surgery through extracurricular experiences may represent an important avenue for supporting sustained interest in surgical careers. ( J Surg Ed 83:104075. TI Impact of a Structured Peer Feedback Program in Surgical Residency: A
   Multi-Institutional Mixed-Methods Study
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Feedback; Peer feedback; Surgery; Residency; Nontechnical skills;
   Residency
ID SURGERY RESIDENTS; COMPARING PEER; FACULTY; IMPLEMENTATION; MEDICINE
AB OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the impact of a structured peer feedback program on resident feedback satisfaction, cul-ture, and practices across multiple general surgery resi-dency programs. DESIGN: Multi-institutional mixed-methods study using pre-and post-intervention surveys, session-level assess-ment data, and qualitative analysis of open-ended responses. SETTING: Three general surgery residency programs dur-ing the 2023 to 2025 academic years. PARTICIPANTS: Clinical general surgery residents (n =85 eligible; 62 respondents, 72.9%). RESULTS: Residents reported significant improvements in overall program feedback satisfaction (3.68 +/- 0.71 vs 3.95 +/- 0.37, p = 0.041) and satisfaction with the amount of feedback received (3.14 +/- 0.83 vs 3.86 +/- 0.47, p < 0.001). Measures of peer feedback culture improved, including mutual support (3.86 +/- 0.83 vs 4.27 +/- 0.45, p = 0.008), empowerment (3.68 +/- 0.78 vs 4.00 +/- 0.82, p = 0.035), and comfort providing feedback to senior residents (2.68 +/- 1.04 vs 3.73 +/- 0.98, p < 0.001). Most residents (82.9%) reported changes in feedback behavior, including increased frequency, comfort, and confidence. Qualitative findings demonstrated a shift toward more intentional, structured feedback practices, improved communication and teamwork, and increased comfort with bidirectional feedback. Feedback exchanges most commonly addressed nontechnical domains, including communication (55.1%), team dynamics (52.8%), and leadership (36.0%). Despite these improvements, perceived feedback quality did not signif-icantly change. CONCLUSIONS: A structured peer feedback program was associated with improved feedback satisfaction, feedback behaviors, and a more supportive feedback cul-ture across multiple residency programs. These explor-atory findings suggest that addressing structural and cultural barriers through routine, bidirectional feedback opportunities may strengthen feedback practices in sur-gical training, although improving feedback actionability remains a key target for future interventions. ID CONTEXT AVAILABILITY; COGNITIVE LOAD; SCIENCE TEXT; REPRESENTATIONS;

AB Background: Knowledge abstractness is one of the factors affecting learning outcomes, particularly in learning from multimedia texts. However, most previous studies on multimedia learning have focused on manipulating pictorial abstractness, while the role of text topic abstractness remains largely unexplored. Aims: 1. TI "When, why, and at what cost?" Towards a trauma-informed pedagogy for
   learning about family violence in nurse education
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Family Violence; Domestic Violence; Intimate Partner Violence;
   Trauma-Informed Pedagogy; Teaching; Ethics; Nursing Education;
   Resilience
AB Learning how to recognise and respond to disclosures of family violence is a core component of nurse education, yet this learning often occurs in classrooms and clinical environments where some students and educators may themselves be survivors. Across nursing programs, pedagogical approaches often emphasise recognising and responding to patients affected by family violence yet give limited attention to the vulnerabilities of students and academic faculty or the potential for re-traumatisation when the topic arises in educational settings. Using a trauma-informed lens, we examine the ethical dimensions of disclosure within classroom and clinical learning environments, focusing on how power, professional expectations, and institutional cultures shape what can be safely disclosed. We argue that unsolicited invitations to "share our stories", as well as blanket appeals to "professional boundaries", both risk harming those already living with family violence and obscuring the educator's duty of care. We propose principles for safer pedagogical practice, including explicit attention to role boundaries, advanced framing of sensitive content, meaningful opt-out options, and clear pathways for support when disclosures occur. While grounded in nursing, the issues explored are relevant across health professional education internationally, where family violence is taught within trauma-exposed student and academic faculty populations.

TI Multi-domain assessment of childhood attention-deficit/ hyperactivity
   disorder of the combined presentation
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE AD/HD; Combined presentation; EEG; Assessment; Classification;
   Sensitivity; Specificity
ID SELF-REPORT MEASURE; DEFICIT/HYPERACTIVITY DISORDER;
   CONFIDENCE-INTERVALS; CHILDRENS REPORT; SLEEP PATTERNS; SINGLE-CHANNEL;
   RATING-SCALE; ADHD; PARENT; EEG
AB Screening children for Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (AD/HD) often relies upon subjective behaviour ratings which are susceptible to biases. A brief (35-40 min) post-screening assessment that does not directly address symptoms, increases objectivity, and accurately discriminates children with AD/HD from typically developing peers, could serve as an adjunct to symptom-focussed screening to support decisions about referral for comprehensive specialist assessment. This study examined the classification performance of the subjective parent-reported SNAP-IV screening questionnaire and the multi-domain Neurocognitive Assessment Tool (NCAT), both alone and in combination, in children with and without AD/HD of the Combined presentation (AD/HD-C). The SNAP-IV and NCAT were administered to 46 children with AD/HD-C and 138 typically developing children. The NCAT assessed executive function performance, brain electrical activity, quality of life, psychological needs satisfaction, sleep habits, self-regulation and social behaviour. Discriminant function and receiver operating characteristic analyses evaluated classification performance for SNAP-IV, NCAT, and combined (NCAT+) models. The SNAPIV (97.8% accuracy; 91.3% sensitivity; 100% specificity; AUC =.990) and NCAT+ (95.1%; 87.0%; 97.8%; AUC =.993) demonstrated high classification performance; the NCAT showed lower but robust performance (88.0%; 78.3%; 91.3%; AUC =.966). The SNAP-IV showed the highest classification performance based on subjective ratings of symptoms, which are susceptible to a range of biases. The NCAT exhibited strong classification, particularly in specificity, highlighting its capacity to discriminate children with AD/HD-C from typically developing children using objective measures and non-symptom-specific subjective assessments. Combining the SNAP-IV and NCAT yielded superior performance to NCAT alone, supporting integrated use as screening and decision-support tools to identify children warranting comprehensive specialist assessment. External validation in diverse clinical populations, including those with co-occurring diagnoses, is needed.

TI Assessment of higher-order thinking in education-A systematic review of
   empirical studies
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher-order thinking; Evaluation methodologies; 21st century skills;
   Pedagogical theory; Summative assessment; Formative assessment
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT; MULTIPLE-CHOICE; STUDENTS;
   SKILLS; INVESTIGATE; KNOWLEDGE; SELECTION; GUIDANCE
AB With growing emphasis on Higher-Order Thinking (HOT), assessing HOT has become a critical research frontier. This systematic review analyzed 73 empirical studies to examine how HOT is conceptualized and assessed. Findings show: (a) HOT assessment is concentrated in higher education and subjects like science and mathematics, with limited representation in early education and online contexts; (b) Two main conceptualizations dominate: a hierarchical model rooted in Bloom's taxonomy, and a parallel model centering on critical thinking, problem-solving, and creativity; (c) Assessments remain largely outcome-based, relying on scales, constructedresponse questions, and multiple-choice questions, while process-oriented tools like think-aloud protocols and computer log analyses are underused; (d) Formative assessment is underdeveloped; (e) Reporting on validity and reliability is often insufficient, constraining the interpretive rigor of HOT assessment findings. These findings reflect conceptual tensions and practical limitations in HOT assessment. The review also discussed several critical topics for future HOT assessment design and practices.

TI Exploring the relationship between ICT practices and creative teaching
   practices among different teacher demand-resource profiles: A latent
   profile analysis and network analysis approach
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Use of digital resources; ICT; Creative teaching
ID JOB DEMANDS; WORK ENGAGEMENT; BURNOUT; INNOVATION; MODEL
AB Teachers'use of digital resources, emphasis on ICT competencies, and use of creative pedagogies are increasingly important for high-quality education, yet their relationships may depend on teachers' working conditions. Guided by the Job Demands-Resources model, this study examined how teachers' use of digital resources, emphasis on ICT competencies, openness to creativity, creative values, and use of creative pedagogies were associated across different teacher demand-resource profiles. Data were drawn from the PISA 2022 teacher questionnaire. Latent profile analysis identified two distinct groups of teachers: a low-demand, high-resource group and a high-demand, low-resource group. These findings suggest that teachers'digital engagement and creativity-related beliefs and practices are shaped not only by individual capability, but also by the balance between job demands and available resources. From a practical perspective, schools and policymakers should reduce excessive work demands while strengthening instructional support, access to digital resources, and opportunities for professional development, so that teachers can more effectively integrate digital resources and foster creativity in classroom practice.

TI AI-generated podcasts and learning outcomes: The role of behavioral
   engagement and scaffolding
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-Generated podcasts; Engagement; Scaffolding; Learning analytics;
   Higher education
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; TECHNOLOGY; FRAMEWORK
AB The growing presence of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education raises questions about their effectiveness in fostering learning. This study examines whether AI-generated podcasts can support student learning in a predominantly in-person course. Using data from two semesters with near identical course designs (n = 171), we compare learning outcomes between a semester without podcasts and a semester in which students had access to AI-generated podcasts aligned with course chapters and supplemented by study guides. Exam performance was higher in the semester with podcast availability, while final course grades were similar across semesters. To explore how podcasts relate to learning outcomes, we analyze variation in student engagement with the podcasts during the semester with podcast availability using learning management system analytics. To mitigate potential endogeneity in engagement, we employ an instrumental-variable approach in which access to study guides serves as an instructional scaffold that encourages podcast use. The results indicate that greater engagement is positively associated with both exam performance and final course grades, though the estimated effects are modest in magnitude. Overall, the findings suggest that AI-generated podcasts, when paired with scaffolding such as study guides, can enhance engagement and support learning in higher education.

AB Introduction: Thailand's pharmacy profession is undergoing rapid transformation driven by demographic, technological, and health-system changes. Updating national competency standards requires an understanding of regional and cross-professional benchmarks. Objective: To compare Thailand's pharmacy competency framework with those of ASEAN countries and other major health professions including medicine, dentistry, and nursing and to identify similarities, gaps, and strategic directions. Methods: A structured desk review of regional and international competency frameworks was conducted. Conclusion: Aligning Thailand's framework with ASEAN and global trends, particularly digital health, interprofessional collaboration, and lifelong learning will strengthen future pharmacy education and practice.

These findings bear implications for EFL teacher education and curriculum development.

TI Exploring empathy revitalization in nursing education: A game-based
   study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Empathy; Education; Nursing; Game-based learning; Compassion fatigue;
   Qualitative research
ID EMOTIONAL LABOR; PATIENT SAFETY; NURSES; COMPASSION
AB Background: Empathy is fundamental to nursing practice, yet sustaining empathic engagement remains a pedagogical challenge in demanding clinical environments. This study introduces a novel game-based intervention designed to facilitate emotional expression and reflection through guided interaction. Objectives: This study evaluated an empathy-focused board game, specifically developed by the authors, as a pedagogical strategy. We explored participants' meaning-making during scenario-based play and examined the perceived value of this approach in supporting clinical practice. Finally, we considered the implications for nursing education and professional development. Methods: A qualitative study using interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) was conducted. Purposeful sampling recruited 82 registered nurses from five hospitals in northern and central Taiwan (aged 21-41 years). Learning sessions included free writing, role play, and guided discussion. Results: Findings were organized into the Empathy Competence Cycle in Nursing, comprising depletion and revitalization phases. The depletion phase included three interrelated themes: (1) compassion fatigue exhausting empathy; (2) perceived medical hierarchy shaping empathic expression; and (3) emotional burden arising from societal and professional role expectations. The revitalization phase comprised three processes: facilitating emotional expression, promoting reflection, and fostering empathic re-engagement. Conclusions: Empathy was experienced as a fluctuating, context-dependent relational capacity. The board game provided a novel, non-evaluative "third space" for emotional articulation and peer reflection, which participants linked to sustaining empathic engagement in challenging clinical contexts. Integrating structured reflective game-based learning into nursing education and professional development could support nurses' ongoing empathic practice and well-being.

AB The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the ways in which English for Academic Purposes (EAP) course materials are developed, adapted and evaluated.    human-centered care
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Nursing education; Continuing education;
   Ethical AI; Clinical judgment; Human connection; Nursing competencies;
   Nursing ethics
ID CLINICAL JUDGMENT
AB Problem: Although artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming nursing continuing education, excessive reliance on AI-based learning may undermine essential skills such as critical thinking, clinical intuition, and the relational and ethical aspects that are fundamental to nursing practice. Background: From virtual patient simulations to adaptive learning platforms, AI tools are increasingly integrated into continuing education for nurses. These technologies provide unparalleled opportunities for efficiency, accessibility, and personalized learning; however, their widespread use raises important questions about maintaining core nursing skills. TI Pragmatic competence among non-native learners of Arabic: a
   cross-sectional mixed-methods study of refusal strategies across
   proficiency levels
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pragmatic competence; Refusal strategies; Arabic as a foreign language;
   Interlanguage pragmatics; Proficiency; Mixed methods
AB This study examined how refusal strategy use varied across proficiency levels among non-native learners of Arabic enrolled in an Arabic as a Foreign Language (AFL) program at the University of Ha'il, Saudi Arabia. Using a cross-sectional mixed-methods design, the study analyzed written Discourse Completion Test (DCT) responses from 65 international AFL learners distributed across four proficiency levels. Of the 780 responses initially elicited, 716 valid coded responses were retained after the exclusion of 64 blank, incomplete, illegible, or otherwise non-codable responses. Quantitative analysis classified refusals into three macro-categories-direct, indirect, and adjunct strategies-and summarized their distribution across levels. Results showed a clear proficiency-related pattern: lower proficiency learners relied more heavily on direct refusals, whereas higher proficiency learners used indirect strategies more frequently. A Pearson chi-square test indicated a significant association between proficiency level and refusal strategy category, chi & sup2;(6) = 37.051, p < .001, Cram & eacute;r's V = 0.161. Because each participant contributed multiple responses, this finding is interpreted as associational and descriptive rather than as strict participant-level inference. Qualitative descriptive analysis further identified three recurrent realization patterns: minimal-move refusals, supportive-move packaging through regret, gratitude, reasons, and alternatives, and the use of formulaic sociopragmatic routines as mitigation or stance. The findings suggest that increased proficiency was associated with greater use of supportive and relationally managed refusal forms. However, because the design was cross-sectional and no native-speaker baseline was included, the study does not claim developmental stages or native-like attainment. Pedagogically, the findings support the value of explicit pragmatics-focused practice in AFL instruction.

TI Utilising a web-based e-learning platform for orthodontic case analysis
   training: a randomised controlled trial
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Technology-enhanced learning; Digital dental education; E-learning;
   Teaching innovation; Diagnostic analysis; Diagnostic reasoning
ID COGNITIVE LOAD; CONSTRUCTION; EDUCATION
AB Background In orthodontic case analysis, structured clinical reasoning is required to achieve a diagnosis and establish a treatment decision. In this randomised controlled trial, a web-based training app was compared with conventional analogue case planning in undergraduate dental students. Methods Twenty-eight undergraduate dental students from RWTH Aachen University were randomised to either a digital training group, using the web-based app Orthotrainer, or an analogue training group, performing conventional case analyses with physical models and printed diagnostic records. After a baseline knowledge and online readiness assessment, both groups completed two standardised training sessions. Following the sessions, the ease of use was assessed using the System Usability Scale and the User Experience Questionnaire. The final analogue module exam tested knowledge transfer. Additionally, 27 orthodontic educators from four university orthodontic departments were surveyed regarding analogue correction practices.Results Baseline orthodontic knowledge was comparable between groups (analogue: M = 13.07 +/- 3.15 vs digital: M = 12.86 +/- 2.41, p = 0.842). Both groups demonstrated significant performance improvement across training sessions separated by three weeks, ss = 8.31, 95% CI [2.66, 13.96], p = 0.005, without overall group differences. Exploratory subarea analyses revealed analogue superiority in extraoral assessment (b = 23.37, 95% CI [7.31, 39.42], p < 0.001), digital advantage in radiographic evaluation (b = -17.34, 95% CI [-33.40, -1.29], p = 0.002) and no difference in the model analysis. There were no differences between the groups in the final module exam. The usability assessment yielded a mean SUS score of M = 78.89 +/- 14.11 for digital training (compared to the analogue training, M = 40.30 +/- 11.19, p < 0.001), while students rated the UEQ for the digital version higher in the dimensions of pragmatic, hedonic quality and overall quality (all p < 0.001). Among 27 surveyed educators, analogue correction was rated time-intensive, with preference for digitalisation. Conclusions The Orthotrainer web application delivered diagnostic performance equivalent to that of conventional analogue training, proving particularly effective in radiographic analysis. Higher usability and user experience ratings support its integration into routine teaching. These findings suggest that structured digital tools can support the development of diagnostic reasoning and serve as a valuable addition to traditional orthodontic education.

TI Microbiology students' relatability to scientists is impacted by
   scientists' identities and exposure to brief scientist highlights during
   class time
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE science identity; microbiology; diversity; representation
ID SCIENCE; WOMEN
AB Representation in the classroom and students' ability to relate to scientists are essential for promoting engagement and success in STEM programs. Incorporating information about scientists from diverse backgrounds in the form of assignments increases student relatability to scientists and changes students' views of who can be a scientist toward non-stereotypical identities. However, building new assignments in an already filled curriculum, and identifying scientists from marginalized backgrounds who specifically fit foundational topics in the General Microbiology classroom may be difficult. Here, we evaluated an intervention to increase representation in the classroom that can be easily incorporated during classroom time. We developed 15 short scientist highlights to accompany the content of a General Microbiology course. These highlights included scientists from historically marginalized backgrounds by gender, race/ethnicity, country of origin, and gender identity. Our main research question was to determine if this intervention could increase students' ability to relate to scientists and increase their sense of belonging. We used a modified survey based on Schinske et al. (J. Schinske, M. Cardenas, and J. Kaliangara, CBE Life Sci Educ 14:ar35, 2015, https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.14-12-0231) and Estrada et al. (M. Estrada, A. Woodcock, P. R. Hernandez, and P. W. Schultz, J Educ Psychol 103:206-222, 2011, https://doi.org/10.1037/a0020743) to measure relatability to scientists and sense of belonging as a construct of students' scientific identity. We demonstrate that showcasing scientists from marginalized backgrounds during lectures and without the need to incorporate related assignments can be a simple yet effective strategy to increase students' ability to relate to scientists, while a sense of belonging appears to be a more complex construct with other factors to consider. Additionally, while all students were interested in learning about scientists' contributions to science, those who identify as women were also interested in the scientists' identities, especially when those identities reflected their own.

TI Morphological awareness in TOEIC word-form questions: an item-type
   analysis of EFL learners' performance and perceptions
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Morphological awareness; TOEIC; Word-form items; EFL; Language
   assessment; Korea; Reading confidence
ID SELF-EFFICACY
AB This study investigates Korean EFL learners' performance on TOEIC-style word-form items from the perspective of morphological competence. Although morphological awareness has been widely discussed in relation to second language reading and vocabulary development, less attention has been paid to how learners handle different morphological item types in standardized grammar and vocabulary tasks. To address this gap, 277 Korean university students completed a 30-item TOEIC-style word-form test covering five item types: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and participial/comparative forms. The study also examined the association between test performance and learners' global perceived reading confidence. A repeated-measures analysis showed that accuracy varied across morphological item types. Noun and verb items showed relatively higher accuracy, whereas participial/comparative items showed comparatively lower accuracy than the other categories. In addition, perceived reading confidence was modestly but positively associated with overall test performance. These findings suggest that TOEIC-style word-form items require learners to integrate morphological, syntactic, and semantic cues under time constraints. The study contributes to L2 morphological assessment research by showing that performance in standardized test contexts is not evenly distributed across morphological categories and that morpho-syntactically complex forms may require more targeted instructional attention. Pedagogically, the findings point to the need for explicit instruction on word-form selection, participial modification, comparative structures, and form-function relationships in TOEIC preparation and broader EFL reading instruction.

   review
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Glocalization; Language tests in Vietnam; Test evolution; Test
   devolution
AB This article takes an ecological perspective to discuss language tests in Vietnam in the early twenty-first century. The major facts and figures are about VSTEP, but the discussion also includes a wide range of other important language tests that have been developed, evolved and devolved, during this period in the country. The article will first revisit the discussion on the plethora of implications of the terms such tests are often named after in the literature - as 'locally-produced', 'localized', or simply 'local' tests, which were first asserted by the author in 2019 (Nguyen, ). Based on these multifaceted accounts in light of an ecological approach, the article will suggest some potential areas for further research on glocalized language tests, not only in Asia but also in other parts of the world.

   demands-resources perspective
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

   support from colleagues; Social support from supervisors
ID PERCEIVED AUTONOMY SUPPORT; SCHOOL CONTEXT; EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE; WORK
   ENGAGEMENT; SELF-EFFICACY; BURNOUT; COMMITMENT; EXHAUSTION; MOTIVATION;
   ADAPTABILITY
AB The wellbeing of teachers has emerged as a significant global concern, prompting a substantial body of research examining the individual and contextual determinants of factors such as burnout and mental health. Although much research has focused on the precursors of burnout and the factors associated with attrition, comparatively less attention has been given to the role of interpersonal resources in shaping these processes. Collectively, the findings echo those made by previous research and support the JD-R model, while demonstrating support from parents as an important job resource for teachers.

TI Collaborative Assessments and Conversations: Implementing a Pedagogical
   Partnership
SO TEACHING SOCIOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE pedagogical partnerships; engaged pedagogy; discomfort; vulnerability;
   sense of belonging
ID HAWTHORNE; ENGAGEMENT; COLLEGE
AB Student engagement and collaboration are important for student success. Pedagogical partnerships, or the pairing of a professor and an undergraduate student who engage in ongoing dynamic pedagogical reflection, increase student engagement and expand collaboration in the classroom. Drawing on field notes, feedback session data, and professor and student partner reflections, we demonstrate how pedagogical partnerships effectively address course problems, attenuate the generational gap between professor and students, and help the professor "settle into" the semester. Pedagogical partnerships embody what bell hooks considered education as a practice of freedom.

TI Bridging university and family support: a moderated mediation model of
   career adapting responses
SO EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE Career adaptability; Career adapting responses; University support;
   Parental support; Sustainable career ecosystem
ID ADAPTABILITY; CONSTRUCTION
AB Purpose- Drawing on career construction theory (CCT) and sustainable career ecosystem theory (SCET), this study examines when and under what relational conditions university support translates into students' career adapting responses. We propose a moderated mediation model in which perceived university support (PUS) influences career adapting responses (CAR; crystallization [CR], exploration [EX], decision-making [DE] and preparation [PR]) through career adaptability (CA), with this indirect effect conditioned by perceived parental support (PPS). Design/methodology/approach- Survey data were collected from 390 university students using a two-wave time-lagged design and multi-stage sampling. Structural equation modeling was used to test the proposed model. Findings- PUS was positively related to CA and directly promoted EX, DE and PR, while its effect on CR was fully mediated by CA. PPS moderated the PUS-CA relationship, and moderated mediation analyses showed that the indirect effects of PUS on CR, EX, DE and PR through CA were stronger when PPS was higher. Research limitations/implications- The time-lagged design limits causal inference, and the Chinese sample may constrain generalizability. Practical implications- Universities can foster students' CA and sustainable school-to-work transitions by strengthening institutional support and aligning career development initiatives with family contexts. Originality/value- This study extends career development research by showing how institutional and familial resource alignment shapes CA and CAR. Integrating CCT with SCET, it conceptualizes CA as an ecosystem-dependent capacity and offers insights into sustainable career development.

TI Instructional Design and Practice of an Interactive Animation Course for

SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cognition; computational thinking; flowcharts; practice; visualization
   tool
ID INTELLIGENT TUTORING SYSTEM; STUDENTS; VALIDITY; SKILLS
AB Computational thinking (CT) has received considerable attention as a key competency in education, yet effective approaches for developing CT remain limited. This quasi-experimental study included 63 undergraduates to examine the effects of flowchart-supported learning on CT. The experimental group received flowchart scaffolding and was split into high- and low-scoring subgroups based on flowchart application scores, while the control group received conventional instruction. Results showed no significant between-group differences in general CT after one semester, indicating that general CT is a relatively stable construct. This study provides empirical support for flowcharts as cognitive scaffolding in engineering education and their integration into courses emphasizing project-based practice and logical reasoning.

TI Anti-Racism and Liberal Humanism in Social Work Education: A
   Philosophical Dialectic on Curriculum, Pedagogy and Practice
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING IN SOCIAL WORK
LA English
DT Article
DE Anti-racist pedagogy; Capability Approach; dialectical engagement;
   intellectual pluralism; liberal humanism; social work education
ID CRITICAL RACE THEORY; CRITICAL REFLECTION; JUSTICE
AB Social work education is increasingly shaped by debates over the role of anti-racism versus liberal humanist approaches in preparing students for ethical and effective practice. This article examines the philosophical debates shaping contemporary social work education. It analyses the anti-racist paradigm grounded in critical theory, and the liberal humanist rooted in Enlightenment traditions of universalism, reason, and individual dignity as influential pedagogical orientations in social work education. While anti-racist frameworks emphasize structural analysis, power, and the deconstruction of dominant knowledge systems, liberal humanist approaches prioritize intellectual pluralism, objective evaluation, and competence-based education. Rather than presenting these paradigms as mutually exclusive or fully reconcilable, we present their relationship as a productive dialectic. Drawing on examples from curriculum design, pedagogy, and field education, we examine how each paradigm conceptualizes knowledge, professional competence, and ethical practice. We argue that while some philosophical assumptions between these approaches are incompatible, particularly regarding universalism, truth, and the nature of oppression, their interaction can strengthen the preparation of social workers for ethical and effective practice. Using the Capability Approach as a case study, we illustrate how elements from both traditions can form a nuanced framework for preparing social workers. The article contributes to ongoing debates by moving beyond binary positions and offering a structured account of how epistemic differences can be pedagogically productive in social work education.

TI Teacher narratives in high-concentration multicultural schools: a K-12
   case study in Korea's industrial cluster
SO MULTICULTURAL EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Multicultural education; high concentration multicultural schools;
   curriculum adaptation; teacher professional development; Korea
AB As Korea transitions into a multicultural society, schools with a high concentration of multicultural students have emerged, presenting urgent educational challenges. This qualitative case study explores the practical difficulties and support needs of 20 K-12 teachers from eight schools in a representative high-density immigrant area. The findings reveal systemic challenges across four critical domains: 1) Curriculum: rigid, assimilationist structures and insufficient language support; 2) Teachers: lack of practical training, excessive workloads, and burnout; 3) Administration: ineffective student placement, rigid budgets, and parental communication gaps; and 4) Community Linkages: isolated schools lacking sustainable local partnerships. This study concludes that these schools grapple with 'de facto segregation' unsupported by the current framework. It calls for a paradigm shift toward curriculum autonomy, specialized teacher support, and integrated, community-based support systems to ensure equitable education.

TI Application of an AI-enabled personalized medical education model for
   improving clinical thinking among cardiovascular surgery trainees
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Medical education; Large language model;
   Clinical thinking; Cardiovascular surgery
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE
AB Objective Cardiovascular surgery involves complex clinical scenarios and high demands on clinical judgment. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled personalized teaching model in cardiovascular surgery training. Methods From February to June 2025, 158 trainees in the department of cardiovascular surgery at our hospital were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 79) or a control group (n = 79). The control group received conventional teaching, including lectures, bedside teaching, and case discussions. The experimental group received a personalized teaching model integrating an intelligent question bank, staged case-based teaching, and AI-based standardized patient training. Outcomes included theoretical examination scores, the Chinese version of the California Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory (CTDI-CV), clinical interview performance, and teaching satisfaction. Results The experimental group achieved significantly higher theoretical examination scores than the control group (84.56 +/- 5.07 vs. 77.95 +/- 9.04, P < 0.001). CTDI-CV results showed significantly higher total scores and higher scores in truth-seeking, open-mindedness, analyticity, systematicity, and inquisitiveness in the experimental group (all P < 0.05). In the clinical interview assessment, the experimental group scored significantly higher in completeness of information collection, communication skills, diagnostic reasoning, and overall performance (all P < 0.001), while the between-group difference in empathy was not significant (P = 0.328). Teaching satisfaction in the experimental group was high, with an overall satisfaction score of 4.68 +/- 0.39. Conclusion The AI-enabled personalized teaching model may represent a feasible and effective approach for cardiovascular surgery education. It was associated with higher theoretical examination scores, better critical thinking disposition, higher scores in several dimensions of simulated clinical interview performance, and high learner satisfaction. Further studies are needed to confirm its broader applicability and long-term educational value.

TI Association between ScholarRx Qmax question bank engagement and NBME
   CBSE and USMLE Step 1 performance
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ScholarRx; Step 1; CBSE; Academic support; Practice questions; Medical
   education; External resources; Third-party resources; Assessment
ID RETRIEVAL PRACTICE
AB Background In recent years, the pass rate of the USMLE Step 1 exam has declined. Failing or delaying Step 1 can cost students time, money, and morale. Undergraduate medical curricula are increasingly supplemented with third-party resources to support successful completion of the curriculum and board exams. Empirical research on the utility of specific third-party resources for student success is needed to inform evidence-based resources and strategies to support students' success on standardized exams. To contribute to filling this gap, the present study examined the relationship between usage of specific components of the third-party resource ScholarRx and student performance on the Comprehensive Basic Science Exam (CBSE) and passing the USMLE Step 1 exam before clerkships began. Methods Two cohorts of students from a public medical school in the United States were included in the study: one from a Traditional discipline-based curriculum (n = 97) and one from an Integrated Organ System-based (IOS) curriculum (n = 103). ScholarRx data including usage of bricks, practice Qmax questions, flash facts, and express videos; biomedical science course averages; CBSE scores; and Step 1 outcomes were matched, de-identified, and analyzed (Traditional curriculum n = 97; Integrated Organ System curriculum n = 103). Multiple linear regression was performed to assess associations between engagement with specific ScholarRx tools and CBSE performance. Multiple logistic regression was used to investigate statistical predictors of taking and passing Step 1 on time. Results Multiple linear regression revealed that student use of ScholarRx practice questions (Qmax; Unstandardized B = 0.004-0.005) and biomedical science grades (Unstandardized B = 1.414-1.610) were significantly, positively associated with CBSE scores (R2 = 0.64-0.79, p < 0.05) but bricks, flash facts, and express videos were not. Similarly, logistic regression found that Qmax usage (Unstandardized B = 0.002-0.003) and biomedical science grades (Unstandardized B = 0.342-0.401) were statistically significant predictors of taking and passing Step 1 on time in both curricula (Traditional: x (2)( (2)) = 52.800, p < 0.001; Nagelkerke R-2 = 0.575; IOS: x (2 )((2)) = 36.706, p < 0.001; Nagelkerke R-2 = 0.532). Conclusion This study found that students' voluntary use of ScholarRx practice questions was associated with higher performance on the CBSE and taking and passing the Step 1 exam on schedule in both a Traditional curriculum and an IOS curriculum.

TI Aligning medical student training with rural community needs: academic
   and rural workforce outcomes of a rural longitudinal integrated
   clerkship in Australia
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Rural medical education; Longitudinal Integrated Clerkship (LIC);
   Public-nonprofit partnership; Rural workforce
ID EDUCATION; SCHOOL; LEARN; MODEL
AB Introduction The Australian Government continues to provide sustained investment in rural medical education. Despite this investment, rural and remote populations continue to experience health inequities, including persistent workforce shortages and limited access to health services. In response, Griffith University, in partnership with Rural Medical Education Australia, established the Longlook Rural Medical Program in 2010. Longlook is delivered through a Longitudinal Integrated Clerkship model and is designed as a socially accountable rural training program. This study examined academic performance, rural practice intentions, and workforce outcomes among Longlook graduates. Methods This descriptive observational study used cross sectional analysis of academic records, student survey data, and longitudinal workforce tracking for graduates from 2010-2023. Academic outcomes for Longlook graduates were compared with those of metropolitan-trained peers. Rural practice intentions were assessed using survey data from five consecutive cohorts between 2019 and 2023. Graduate practice locations and specialty choices were identified through the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency register and classified using the Modified Monash Model. Results Of the 2,274 students graduating from Griffith University's medical program between 2010-2023, 384 completed at least one year in the Longlook program. Longlook graduates demonstrated higher academic performance compared to their metropolitan peers (p=0.012) and showed a stronger intention to pursue rural practice (p<0.001). In 2024, 65% of graduates who completed the two-year Longlook were practising in rural areas. Additionally, 30% of graduates who undertook a one-year Longlook placement were practising rurally, while 32% of those completing a one-year Longlook placement in Year 3 followed by a 7-week rural General Practice block in Year 4, were also practising rurally. Among Longlook graduates who have completed specialty training and are practising in rural areas, 80% undertook general practice training, aligning with community needs for broad-scope practitioners. Conclusion The Griffith University Longlook program demonstrates educational excellence and sustained rural workforce participation among its graduates. The findings suggest that socially accountable, community-engaged approaches to medical education can be associated with strong educational outcomes and improved rural workforce participation. The program's partnership model, involving collaboration between a public university and a locally governed nonprofit organisation, may contribute to the program's implementation and community integration; however, further research is needed to determine the specific impact of this partnership structure on outcomes.

TI Integrated Teaching Model Based on Project-Based Learning for Physics
   Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE project-based learning; physics education; simulation; artificial
   intelligence; ChatGPT; Rutherford; integrated teaching model
ID ENGAGEMENT
AB This study examines the effectiveness of an integrated teaching model that combines project-based learning (PBL), interactive simulations, and ChatGPT in the teaching of physics. This study was conducted in the context of teaching Rutherford's atomic model and Bohr's postulates, and it aimed to assess the impact of the proposed model on students' academic achievement, the development of research skills, motivation to learn, engagement, and digital competence. A quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test design was employed involving 39 Year 11 students from a specialised secondary school with a focus on physics and mathematics in Kazakhstan. Participants were assigned to one control group (CG, n = 16) and two experimental groups (EG1, n = 12; EG2, n = 11). Academic achievement was assessed using a physics comprehension test, while students' perceptions of the intervention were examined through a 16-item Likert-scale questionnaire administered to students in the experimental groups (n = 23). Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) revealed a statistically significant effect of group membership on final test results after controlling for pre-test scores. Post hoc comparisons revealed significantly higher adjusted final test scores in EG2 than in the control group, whereas no significant differences were observed between CG and EG1 or between the two experimental groups. Normalised measures of knowledge gain were higher in both experimental groups than in the control group. Also, Hake's gain showed improvement in learning outcomes. The results of questionnaires showed an overall positive perception among students. The findings are of significant importance for the training of future physics teachers. The model developed demonstrates the potential for the effective integration of project-based learning, digital simulations, and artificial intelligence tools into school science education.

TI Designing the Clinical Experience of Principal Preparation for
   Equity-Oriented Aims
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE principal preparation; preparation programs; clinical experience;
   internships; principals; equity; school improvement; mentor; leadership
   coaching
ID LEADERSHIP PREPARATION PROGRAMS; SCHOOL LEADERS; CONTEXT; EXPECTATIONS;
   DIVERSITY; EXEMPLARY
AB This manuscript considers the design of equity-oriented clinical experiences within principal preparation programs as a salient mechanism for supporting equity-oriented school improvement in PK-12 schools. This manuscript presents an integrative review of the literature that has examined equity-oriented principal preparation and clinical experiences. While prior reviews have examined principal preparation clinical experiences broadly, this review extends that work by examining how the clinical experience has been and might be designed to cultivate leadership that better serves equity-oriented purposes, specifically. Given that principal leadership is widely recognized as a critical lever for school improvement, and that the clinical experience is arguably the most consequential component of preparation, how programs design that experience for equity-oriented aims has direct implications for whether school leaders are prepared to do the improvement work that marginalized students most need. Our analysis attends to key design features of the clinical experience, including its form and format, clinical work tasks, and developmental supports, with attention to how each has been or might be reoriented for equity-oriented aims. This review highlights broad recommendations advanced by the more conceptual and theoretical literature as well as more granular insights from individual programs' experiences, making it a comprehensive and actionable starting place for programs interested in strengthening the clinical experience for equity-oriented aims.
