TI Using a Storybook App to Promote Latino Preschoolers' Literacy Skills: A
   Pilot Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE digital family literacy; dialogic reading; elaborative reminiscing;
   preschool; Latino
ID MATERNAL REMINISCING STYLE; DUAL LANGUAGE LEARNERS; READING
   INTERVENTION; BOOK; CHILDREN; KINDERGARTEN; ELABORATION; NARRATIVES;
   PARENTS
AB Parents play a central role in the development of preschoolers' literacy skills. Prior parent-focused literacy interventions have promoted preschoolers' literacy skills through either dialogic reading or elaborative reminiscing, but rarely have these approaches been combined. This is a pilot study of Cu & eacute;ntame Cuentos, a 6-week app-based intervention for Latino families, which included digital storybooks with embedded conversational prompts promoting dialogic reading and elaborative reminiscing. Associations between conversational prompt engagement during app use and gains in preschoolers' literacy skills from pre- to post-intervention were examined. At moderate levels of conversational prompt engagement, the associations with gains in story memory were positive. However, at higher levels of conversational prompt engagement, the associations became negative, suggesting unproductive cognitive effort. No associations with other literacy skills were found. While preliminary, these findings underscore the importance of considering not only whether parents and children engage with app-based conversational prompts but also their level of engagement. Implications for the design of digital family literacy interventions are discussed.

TI Zooming on Mental States: Developing the Mentalization and Interaction
   Skills of Early Childhood Education Student Teachers
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE mentalization; interaction; early childhood education; blended learning;
   video reflection; book reading interaction
ID MIND-MINDEDNESS; SENSITIVITY; LANGUAGE; CARE
AB Early childhood education (ECE) professionals' reflections on mental states have been associated with staff-child interaction quality and child development. However, experimental evidence from mentalization training in ECE teacher education is limited. Fifteen Finnish student teachers with a caregiver background, enrolled in a higher education program, participated in a Video Enhanced Reflective Practice (VERP) intervention. The training was integrated in two blended learning study modules, where the focus was to support children's language, cognitive, and social-emotional development. The student teachers' observed mental state talk increased during trainer-guided peer discussions as well as student-guided discussions with two children during picture book reading interactions. The student teachers' self-reported general interaction skills also improved. In the pilot study, growth was observed in mentalization and interaction skills, following a higher education program that combined VERP with evidence-based content. The preliminary data suggest that future interventions should focus on the transfer of training and on improving ECE student teachers' talk about emotional states during interactions with children.

TI Exploring Authentic Assessment in the GenAI Era: The Efficacy of
   Student-Created Screencasts, an Exploration Using Explainable AI (XAI)
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE learner-generated; higher education; multimedia learning; dual coding;
   elastic net
AB The proliferation of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education necessitates a shift towards more authentic assessment methods that can genuinely measure student understanding. Student-created screencasts are a potentially valuable yet underexamined assessment format in higher education. A screencast is a screen capture video, which records all the activities on a computer screen. This study examines the efficacy of student-created screencasts as an authentic assessment. Using data from 84 undergraduate students, Elastic Net regression and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis were applied to examine predictive relationships across assessment types: screencasts with audio narration (SWAs), screencasts without audio (SNAs), written assignments, and group project presentations. The findings reveal that SWAs have a moderate-to-strong positive association with test performance, acting as a significantly stronger predictor than both traditional written work and SNAs. The results suggest that narrated screencasts may serve as a useful assessment format for gauging student understanding, supporting the early identification of at-risk students, and providing a platform for developing crucial communication skills. This assessment strategy holds promise for enhancing academic integrity and learning in the GenAI era. This study contributes to assessment research by demonstrating the predictive value of narrated screencasts in identifying at-risk students in AI-supported learning environments. Future research should extend this work through multi-institutional designs, longitudinal analysis, and qualitative investigation of student perceptions in various courses other than artificial intelligence.

TI A socio-technical framework for educational excellence: Empirical
   validation of artificial intelligence and Jidoka integration in
   accounting pedagogy within emerging financial markets
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Pedagogical technology integration; Socio-technical systems theory;
   Artificial intelligence augmentation; Lean manufacturing principles in
   education; Jidoka implementation; Multivariate statistical
   methodologies; Accounting curriculum development; Educational quality
   assurance mechanisms; Structural equation modeling; Confirmatory factor
   analysis
ID SYSTEMS
AB The focus of this research is on how AI instrumentation affects quality-assurance systems based on the concept of Jidoka within the ecosystem of accounting education in an emerging financial-market environment. The study fills a void regarding technology use beyond traditional financial-center locations by addressing an existing ev idence gap. It was conducted in Kuwait, which represents an early-stage financial center (Technology Adoption Index = 0.72), and cross-sectional surveys were collected in 2021 from three groups of participants: 86 educators, 231 senior students, and 28 auditing professionals. A structural equation model (SEM) corrected for measure ment error was used as the analytical technique. The integrated AI-Jidoka model explained 73% of the variance in perceived educational quality (R-2 = 0.73; chi(2)/df = 2.18, GFI = 0.93, CFI = 0.94, RMSEA = 0.058). Jidoka quality protocols had a significant positive relationship with educational quality (/3 = 0.27, p = 0.013) and a positive association with assessment accuracy (a 31.4% improvement). The outcomes suggest that benefits from using AI can be achieved by integrating AI with both institutional preparedness and structured quality-control protocols. Because this study is a cross-sectional survey of perceptions at one time point in one country, the results are inter pretive rather than causal; however, they do provide empirical evidence supporting an integrated socio-technical adoption model for accounting pedagogy in developing countries

TI Evaluating an Iteratively Revised Assessment for a Global Pediatric
   Surgery Short Course Using Mixed-Effects Modeling and Item-Level Rasch
   Analysis
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE pediatric surgery; global surgery; surgical education; short-course;
   Rasch modeling; assessment validity
ID SKILLS
AB Objective To evaluate changes in learner performance after a global pediatric surgery short course, measure consistency of scores across 4 iteratively revised assessment versions, and examine item-level performance and language-related bias. Design Prospective pre-and postcourse assessment study with generalized linear mixed-effects models for whole-test and domain-level analyses and many-facet Rasch modeling for item-level analyses and language bias. Setting Five rural hospitals (2 districts, 3 regional) in Rwanda (January-March 2025). Participants Sixty nonspecialist physicians (26 interns, 23 junior physicians, 11 senior physicians). Most preferred English (n = 54), with a minority preferring French (n = 6). Two-thirds had prior pediatric surgery exposure (n = 40). Results Overall scores improved significantly from pre-to postassessment, from 71.3% to 86.5% (+15.2 percentage points; p < 0.001). Across domains, mean percentage correct increased from 73.4% to 94.0% in Diagnosis, 69.7% to 83.4% in Transfer, and 70.9% to 84.7% in Management (all p < 0.001; partial eta squared 0.47-0.88). Across the 4 assessment versions, there were no significant differences in baseline scores, postcourse scores, or pre-to postcourse change for total or domain-specific scores (p > 0.05). In mixed-effects models, language preference was associated with total scores and the Management domain (p = 0.03-0.05; partial eta squared, eta & sup2;p >= 0.41), while training level, prior pediatric surgery exposure, hospital site, and assessment version were nonsignificant (all p > 0.05). Item-level analyses identified items with misfit and language-related differential item functioning, including bias disadvantaging French-preferring learners for several items. Conclusion A single-day pediatric surgery short course was associated with significant improvements in postcourse knowledge across all domains, while iterative assessment revisions preserved score comparability across versions and sites.

TI Profiles of self-directed learning and learning engagement among
   undergraduate nursing students in blended learning environments: A
   cross-sectional cluster ensemble study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Blended learning; Self-directed learning; Learning engagement; Learner
   profiles; Cluster ensemble analysis
AB Background: Blended learning requires nursing students to regulate their learning while maintaining meaningful engagement. However, learner-profile research jointly examining self-directed learning and learning engagement remains limited, leaving heterogeneity in how these constructs co-occur among nursing students insufficiently understood. Objectives: This study aimed to identify heterogeneous learner profiles among nursing undergraduates based on self-directed learning and learning engagement, and to examine factors associated with learner-profile membership. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among nursing undergraduates from two universities in China. Data were collected using the Self-Rating Scale of Self-Directed Learning (SRSSDL) and the Blended Learning Environment Student Engagement Scale. Learner profiles were identified through cluster ensemble analysis, which included voting and consensus matrix methods. Multinomial logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with learner-profile membership. Results: Four learner profiles were identified: competent proactive learners (32.37%), developing transitional learners (47.40%), passive and disengaged learners (6.36%), and autonomous and committed learners (13.87%). Competent proactive learners exhibited relatively high levels of self-directed learning and learning engagement but less-developed strategy use. Developing transitional learners demonstrated moderate engagement but limited self-directed learning, whereas passive and disengaged learners reported the lowest levels of both constructs and constituted a potentially vulnerable profile. Autonomous and committed learners exhibited the highest levels of self-directed learning and learning engagement. Gender, grade, reasons for choosing nursing, residence, and monthly family income were associated with learner-profile membership (P < 0.05). Conclusion: Nursing students showed substantial heterogeneity in self-directed learning and learning engagement within blended learning environments. Profile-specific instructional strategies could be considered, including open-ended learning tasks and clinical simulations for autonomous and committed learners; collaborative learning activities combined with explicit strategy support and a gradual transfer of learning responsibility for competent proactive learners; clear guidance and metacognitive strategy training for developing transitional learners; and early identification with targeted motivational support for passive and disengaged learners.

TI Metic matriarchs: Cunning intelligence and the parasocial ethos
   of the grandfluencer
SO COMPUTERS AND COMPOSITION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital Rhetoric; Influencer; Grandfluencers; Metis; YouTube; Parasocial
   relationships
ID COMMUNICATION
AB Grandfluencers-elderly content creators-are one of the fastest growing demographic groups in the social media landscape. Drawing on the YouTube presence of nonagenarian Lillian Droniak (@LillianDroniak), this article examines the multimodal construction of the grandfluencer digital ethos. By synthesizing the classical Greek concept of metis (an embodied, cunning intelligence) with feminist rhetorical theory, I argue that Droniak employs an affective voice-characterized by authenticity, humor, and wisdom-to negotiate agency within a medium dominated by digital natives. This performance functions as a site of intergenerational social circulation (Royster and Kirsch), fostering a digital space where Droniak's audience cultivates strong parasocial bonds with her as a "digital grandmother." This attachment is distinctly reciprocal; Droniak leverages this collective social capital to combat the invisibility and loneliness common at the end of the life. Ultimately, this study demonstrates how Droniak's "slay" aesthetic serves as a rhetorical intervention, bridging the affective gap between Gen Z and the Silent Generation through the strategic authoring of a life lived in public.

TI Reframing school leadership for the digital age
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Technology integration; Transformative leadership; Digital leadership;
   Inclusive; Cultural transformation
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; CULTURE
AB The role of school leadership in digital transformation is increasingly recognised as central to creating inclusive, adaptive, and future-proof schools and education systems. However, the complexity of this task is often underestimated in policy, research, practice, and professional development. This article explores school leaders' roles as key agents in co-designing inclusive and adaptive digital learning cultures within diverse sociocultural, technological, and educational contexts. Building on contributions from Thematic Working Group 2 (TWG2) at EDUsummIT 2025, this paper introduces a leadership framework comprising six inter-related parts: transformative and strategic leadership; capacity building; equity and inclusivity; policy and governance; leading change; and future-proofing. This framework reflects the evolving demands placed on leaders in digitally enhanced, constantly changing educational environments. Contributions include reflections on theoretical approaches, empirical studies, conceptual analyses, policy-focused pieces, and international cases. Together, they provide a synthesis of current challenges and innovative responses to leadership in the digital age, with a focus on practical tools, inclusive and adaptive strategies, and contextual variations in reframing schooling for the digital age.

TI Entrustable Professional Activities and Competencies for Experiential
   Learning: A Delphi Study
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrustable professional activities; Experiential learning; Delphi
ID CONSENSUS
AB Introduction: There is a need for competency-based assessment of pharmacy students during experiential learning (EL). Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) originated in Medical Education and have been adopted by other health professions globally. This research sought consensus on entrustment levels, EPAs and competencies for use in assessing student pharmacists during EL. Methods: Six EPAs with competencies were developed based on previous research: NHS England entrustment levels were adopted. A Delphi questionnaire was distributed to EL facilitators (n = 1685), final year student pharmacists at the University of Strathclyde and Robert Gordon University (n = 240), and academic and National Health Education Scotland (NES) pharmacists involved in initial education and training of pharmacists (n = 58). Participants could agree or disagree with the appropriateness of entrustment levels and competencies using yes/no responses. "No" responders could suggest alternative wording/comment/explain their answer. There was also space for general comments. Consensus was set at 75%. For primary analysis response percentages were calculated with respondent subgroups as secondary analysis. Comments were analyzed for themes. Results: Response rate was 15.8% (313/1983) and consensus was achieved on all EPA competencies and Entrustment Levels on the first round. Secondary analysis showed one entrustment level and two EPA competencies in the Academic/NES subgroup, and one other EPA competency where both Hospital Facilitator and Academic/NES subgroups did not reach consensus. Themes identified were student knowledge, placement duration, guidance required, supervision/checking of work, missing EPAs/competencies and overlap of EPAs. Conclusion: Consensus was reached on entrustment levels and EPA competencies for use in student pharmacist EL.

TI Just the right amount of caution? Remote instruction and student
   performance in Sweden during the COVID-19 pandemic
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Remote instruction; Distance learning; School performance; COVID-19
ID ONLINE; EDUCATION
AB This study investigates how distance learning during COVID-19 affected educational outcomes of lower secondary students in Sweden. In contrast to most previously studied contexts characterized by prolonged and fully remote school closures, Sweden represents a school system with a high level of digital preparedness, in which distance learning was implemented for a limited period, often combined with in-person instruction, and accompanied by exemptions for students with special needs. Using a difference-in-differences design with entropy balancing, we compare pre-pandemic and pandemic-affected cohorts. Our findings suggest that students in schools that adopted remote instruction performed similarly on standardized tests to those in schools that maintained in-person teaching throughout the pandemic. Moreover, progression to upper secondary school was not negatively affected. In some cases, we even find positive effects of remote instruction.

   Educational interventions; Educational policy; adult learning; adult
   education
ID REVIEWS
AB Self-directed learning (SDL) is widely promoted to strengthen students' capacity to manage their own learning. Yet, evidence on the effectiveness of SDL-oriented interventions remains fragmented across educational contexts. This second-order meta-analysis synthesises experimental and quasi-experimental meta-analytic evidence on SDL-oriented interventions and their effects on student learning outcomes. Using an overview-of-reviews approach, we identified 12 first-order meta-analyses, yielding 13 independent overall effect sizes and data from approximately 43,775 students across formal education. Random-effects modelling indicated a moderate, statistically significant overall effect of SDL-oriented interventions on learning outcomes (ES = .56, 95% CI [.46, .65]). Heterogeneity was substantial. Publication-bias analyses did not indicate meaningful distortion of the pooled estimate. Moderator analyses showed that effect sizes differed by educational level, with larger effects in K-12 and mixed-level samples than in higher education-only samples, and by methodological quality, with smaller effects in high-quality than in medium-quality reviews. By contrast, effects did not differ significantly by learning environment. Outcome-category analyses showed positive effects for self-regulated learning strategies (ES = .47), academic achievement (ES = .43), and skill-based outcomes (ES = .61), although differences across outcome categories were not statistically significant. Overall, the findings indicate that SDL-oriented interventions produce educationally meaningful benefits across formal education and support SDL as a valuable framework for structuring learner regulation.

DT Article
DE online medical education; self-assessment; simulation training; surgical
   education; technical skills training; video-based learning
ID EDUCATION; SIMULATION; STUDENTS; TOOL
AB OBJECTIVE: To evaluate an online surgical skills course integrating structured video-based self-, peer-, and tutor feedback designed to enhance individualized feedback during early surgical training. DESIGN: Prospective observational study evaluating 4 course iterations following an iterative course development phase conducted between 2020 and 2023. SETTING: Online surgical skills course delivered at the Department of General, Visceral, and Vascular Surgery, Universita & euro;tsklinikum Jena, Germany. PARTICIPANTS: Seventy-three undergraduate medical students participated in 4 course iterations between February 2024 and March 2025. TI Message Received? Applicant Insights on Preference Signals in General
   Surgery Residency Recruitment
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE preference signaling; general surgery; graduate medical education;
   residency recruitment
AB OBJECTIVE: We aimed to understand general surgery applicants' experiences with and attitudes toward preference signaling. DESIGN: Qualitative analysis of de-identified transcripts from semi-structured interviews of general surgery residency applicants was performed. SETTING: A general surgery residency program at an academic hospital in the United States. PARTICIPANTS: All applicants to one general surgery residency program in the 2024 to 2025 recruitment cycle were invited to participate. Twenty-seven applicants participated in semi-structured interviews (59% female, 63% MD graduates, 11% DO graduates, 26% international medical school graduates). RESULTS: While applicants decided where to signal differently, applicants noted that they signaled across a range of program competitiveness and made strategic choices based on interest versus likelihood of matching. While applicants highlighted the importance of a good advisor, they noted that disagreements were common between advisors regarding signaling strategies. Applicants additionally noted a disparity in advising for IMG and DO applicants, as their schools often did not have surgery-specific advisors or a track record of matching into surgical specialties. Applicants focused on several signaling pitfalls, including difficulty judging their competitiveness and determining where they would "fit" before their interviews. While applicants did not expect to receive interview offers from non-signaled programs, they found these interviews could go 2 ways: either non-signaled programs were a good fit, or they experienced quasi-adversarial interactions about their potential lack of interest. With respect to future changes, applicants wanted more transparency regarding each program's screening process and felt that signal number changes should be data-driven to ensure applicants receive enough interviews to match. CONCLUSIONS: Applicants had varied experiences with signaling, reporting different allocation strategies and guidance from advisors. Applicants highlighted a need for transparency regarding how applicants should signal and how programs interpret signals. This transparency can break down the hidden curriculum of signaling, improving applicant trust in the recruitment process. ( J Surg Ed 83:104096. (c) 2026 The Authors. TI Structural Determinants of Underrepresented in Medicine Residents in
   Orthopedic Surgery Residency Programs: Impact of Visiting Student
   Scholarships and Political Policy
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE orthopedic surgery; residency education; underrepresented in medicine;
   visiting student scholar-ships; diversity; graduate medical education
AB OBJECTIVE: Visiting student scholarships are increasingly offered by orthopedic surgery residency programs to reduce financial barriers to away rotations. We sought to determine the prevalence of these scholarships, characterize programs offering them, and evaluate whether scholarship availability is associated with underrepresented in medicine (URiM) resident representation after accounting for program size and state-level anti-DEI legislation. DESIGN: Cross-sectional observational study using publicly available program-level data from the 2024 to 2025 application cycle. Associations were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression, negative binomial regression, and binomial generalized linear models. SETTING: U.S. Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME)-accredited orthopedic surgery residency programs. PARTICIPANTS: Of 210 orthopedic surgery residency programs listed on the AAMC Residency ExplorerTM tool, 187 programs with complete demographic and program characteristic data were included. RESULTS: Seventy-four programs (39.6%) offered visiting student scholarships, with availability concentrated in larger, university-based programs. After adjustment, scholarship availability was not independently associated with the presence of >= 1 URiM resident (OR 1.01; 95% CI, 0.28-3.62; p = 0.985) or with URiM resident count (IRR 1.13; 95% CI, 0.78-1.64; p = 0.527) or proportion (OR 1.14; 95% CI, 0.95-1.36; p = 0.156). Program size was consistently associated with both scholarship availability and URiM representation across all models. State-level anti-DEI legislation was not independently associated with URiM outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Although visiting student scholarships may reduce financial barriers to away rotations, they were not independently associated with URiM representation after accounting for structural program characteristics. Program size, used as a proxy for institutional capacity, was the strongest predictor of URiM representation across all models. These findings suggest that scholarships may be a necessary but insufficient component of a comprehensive diversity recruitment strategy, and that surgical educators should consider embedding financial access mechanisms within broader institutional efforts that include mentorship, holistic review, and inclusive training environments. AB Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), specific learning disorder (SLD), and their comorbidity are associated with weaknesses in cognitive efficiency; however, the diagnostic utility of WISC-V index patterns remains unclear. This study examined WISC-V cognitive profiles in children with newly diagnosed ADHD, SLD, ADHD-SLD comorbidity, and typically developing controls (N = 133; 6-16 years), with emphasis on Working Memory and Processing Speed. DT Article

ID SELF-EFFICACY; WORK; BELIEFS; STUDENT; CHOOSE
AB The present study investigated varied and interrelated factors among teacher efficacy, professional commitment, and career decision-making difficulties during the practicum period in pre-service teachers. Based on the Preservice Teacher Commitment Model, this research aimed to determine how beliefs concerning efficacy and commitment interact over time and how they relate to pre-service teachers' career decisions. TI Building data literacy and decision-writing with structured
   evidence-based reasoning: A repeated-measures study
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Data literacy; Decision-writing; Structured pedagogy; Cognitive load
   theory; Evidence-based management
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; DESIGN; INSTRUCTION; RELIABILITY; STUDENT; IMPACT;
   TESTS; POWER; WORK
AB This study examines how management educators can develop and evaluate two transferable competencies: data literacy and decision-writing. The study was conducted in an intact classroom using authentic, context-based tasks. I designed and implemented WRAP pedagogy: Warm-up, Read & Research, Application, and Post-assessment. WRAP integrates evidence-chain procedures, source credibility checks, and a standardized decision memo template. The study compared WRAP with baseline lecture-based instruction across eight two-week phases (N = 70). Data literacy was measured through phase-end micro-quizzes. Decision-writing was assessed using analytic-rubric scores for decision memos. Linear mixed-effects models were used as the main analytic approach. The findings suggest that structured WRAP pedagogy is associated with higher data literacy and decision-writing scores than baseline instruction. Interaction terms further indicate that, under structured instruction, outcomes are less dependent on baseline language proficiency and prior knowledge. These patterns are interpreted as longitudinal associational classroom evidence rather than definitive causal evidence. Overall, the study provides inspectable longitudinal classroom evidence. It also proposes a replicable bundled instructional model for evidence-to-decision tasks. The study further clarifies the interpretive boundaries of an intactclass crossover repeated-measures design.

TI Introducing exampling: A communicative strategy behind students' use of
   examples in mathematical argumentation
SO JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICAL BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE Mathematical identity; Positional identity; Relational identity;
   Argumentation; Examples; Mathematics education
ID PARTICIPATION; ACHIEVEMENT
AB Empirical justification schemes - often viewed as an epistemological limitation or instructional shortcoming - are pervasive in student argumentation. This study offers the term exampling to describe a previously unnamed phenomenon: the strategic use of examples in mathematical arguments rooted in students' awareness of audience and shaped by their mathematical identities. Drawing on frameworks of positional and relational identity, we explore how students choose to include examples in ways that reflect their perceptions of authority, ability, belonging, and communicative purpose.    peer feedback quality measures
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer feedback quality; Review; Measurement; Conceptual framework
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; STUDENTS; PERCEPTIONS; IMPACT; ENGAGEMENT; ANONYMITY;
   TAXONOMY; SCIENCE; LEVEL
AB Peer feedback, especially when of higher quality, can support many kinds of learner outcomes. However, peer feedback quality has been conceptualized in diverse ways, and the field still lacks a unifying framework for understanding and measuring this construct. This study reviews 218 peer-reviewed articles that conceptualized and measured peer feedback quality to identify the major dimensions and subdimensions examined in the literature. Six major dimensions were identified and organized along an overarching causal chain: inputs to feedback, the feedback message itself, and outputs of feedback. This review provides a conceptual basis for future theory development and measurement design.

TI Probing High School Students' Knowledge and Cognitive Structures in
   Electrochemistry: A Combined Use of Concept Mapping and Epistemic
   Network Analysis
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE High School Chemistry; Knowledge Structure; Cognitive Structure;
   Electrochemistry; Chemical Education Research
ID MISCONCEPTIONS; DIFFICULTIES; INSTRUCTION; SCHEMA; FLOW
AB The interconnected nature of concepts in electrochemistry (EC) poses significant challenges for students. This study distinguished knowledge structure (KS)-alignment with an intended knowledge system-from cognitive structure (CS)-the mental network that organizes and guides domain knowledge. Using concept mapping (CM) and epistemic network analysis (ENA), this study probed high school students' KS and CS in EC and compared high- versus low-achieving groups. KS was examined through segment mastery, morphological patterns, and cross-links. CS was characterized via clustering patterns, associative strength, and cognitive emphasis. Group comparisons employed KS typology (classifying students' maps and comparing distributions), alongside ENA subtracted networks and centroid positions for CS. Six knowledge segments were identified from CM, with the "electrode reaction equation" segment as the primary bottleneck due to superficial recognition and few cross-links. Organized into principle, application, and representation clusters, the CS model exhibited "principle" as the cognitive hub, strongly co-occurring with the others. High-achievers demonstrated more coherent KS and broadly distributed associations, with centroids shifting toward the "representation" dimension; low-achievers showed scattered KS and localized associations, with centroids near the "application" dimension. The findings informed high school EC teaching and helped university educators bridge learning transitions by revealing students' prior knowledge.

TI Smartphone Application throughout Comprehensive Chemistry Experiment: A
   Case Study of Tofu Preparation Video Recording and Quantitative
   Detection of Protein in Tofu
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Analytical Chemistry; Biochemistry;
   Hands-On Learning; Multimedia-Based Learning; Proteins; Colloids; Food
   Chemistry; Quantitative Analysis
AB Traditional challenges in chemistry laboratory instruction, such as equipment scarcity, limited real-time supervision, difficulty in tracing error sources, and underdeveloped student skills in scientific expression and reflection, have long been recognized. To address these gaps, a smartphone-integrated teaching model was developed for a comprehensive chemistry experiment involving tofu preparation and protein quantification. Students were engaged with concepts of protein chemistry, colloid stability, and quantitative analysis through hands-on activities using homemade photoboxes, smartphone video recording, and mobile video editing. A quasi-experimental design was employed, in which 166 undergraduate chemistry education students were divided into an experimental group (n = 130) that followed the smartphone-integrated model and a control group (n = 36) that used traditional methods with a UV-vis spectrophotometer and paper-based reports. Student perceptions were overwhelmingly positive, with the model recommended by 96% of students. Implementation challenges were manageable through targeted instructor interventions. This work illustrates an effective smartphone-integrated experimental design for resource-limited settings, through which students are trained in laboratory skills, digital literacy, scientific communication, and reflective practice-competencies essential for future science educators.

AB The purpose of this qualitative study was to examine preservice early childhood teachers' (PSTs) epistemic framing of integrated STEM pedagogy as represented through children's picture books they designed as part of a 14-week mathematics education course grounded in the Early STEM Integrated Teaching Framework. TI Programme-level redesign and student outcomes in specialist
   post-registration ophthalmic nursing education: a cohort study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Health professions education; Nursing education; Ophthalmic nursing;
   Post-registration education; Curriculum design; Assessment; Programmatic
   assessment; Competency-based education; Educational outcomes
ID DESIGN
AB Background Post-registration specialist nursing programmes must balance academic standards with workforce responsiveness, but fragmentation often persists across learning outcomes, assessment structures, and workload distribution. Although theoretical models including constructive alignment, programmatic assessment, competency-based education, and cognitive load theory promote coordinated design, empirical evaluation of integrated programme-level reforms remains limited, particularly regarding structural change and its association with measurable educational outcomes.<br /> Methods This retrospective observational cohort study examined the association between a theory-informed programme-level structural redesign and student academic achievement in a United Kingdom (UK) post-registration specialist ophthalmic nursing programme. The study also introduces the Integrated Programme Reform Model (IPRM) as a framework for programme-level educational reform. Nine sequential cohorts of registered nurses were included (N = 106). Six cohorts completed the traditional programme structure (2018-2021; n = 73), and three cohorts completed the redesigned programme (2022-2023; n = 33). The redesign integrated strategies derived from alignment, programmatic assessment, competency-based progression, and workload redistribution. First-attempt summative assessment outcomes were compared using Welch's t-tests, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Fisher's exact tests. Effect sizes were calculated using Cohen's d.<br /> Results Following programme redesign, mean student achievement increased from 57.4% (SD 10.6) to 71.1% (SD 8.1), with a mean difference of 13.7% points (95% CI 10.0-17.4; p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 1.39). The proportion of students achieving distinction (>= 70%) rose from 15.1% to 60.6% (p < 0.001), while the proportion of scores below the standardised 50% pass threshold fell from 19.2% to 0% (p = 0.005). These findings indicate a distribution-wide upward shift in achievement across the full performance spectrum, alongside reduced variability following redesign.<br /> Conclusions Coordinated programme-level structural redesign was associated with sustained higher first-attempt academic achievement across successive cohorts. Causality cannot be inferred: the redesign coincided with a transition to master's-level provision and a change in assessment modality, the evaluation was conducted within a single programme by an author professionally involved in the redesign, and the data are historical. The IPRM is offered as a conceptual design heuristic for organising programme-level reform and requires prospective, independent, multi-site evaluation before any claim of effectiveness or transferability can be made.

DT Article

AB This mixed-methods study examined the effects of DeepSeek-powered genre-based instruction (GBI) on argumentative writing performance, ideal L2 writing self, and writing enjoyment among 71 low-proficiency EFL undergraduates. A quasi-experimental design was employed, with an experimental group (N = 32) receiving 6 weeks of AI-powered GBI and a control group (N = 39) receiving traditional instruction. TI Seeing the Research, Not the Researcher: The Effect of Research Literacy
   Training on Evaluations of Research Credibility
SO JOURNAL OF PUBLIC AFFAIRS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE gender; diversity; learning outcomes; survey research; quantitative
   methodology
ID ANCHORING BIAS; GENDER; MITIGATION; MANAGEMENT; CLASSROOM; WOMEN
AB How does (perceived) author's gender affect students' evaluation of the credibility of research related to public administration? We conducted a two-round survey experiment, testing if students' assessment of public administration/political science research rigor is influenced by author's gender, the controversiality of the argument, and the presence of academic research methods before and after long-term research literacy training. The findings reveal that prior to research literacy training, students' perceptions of research rigor was shaped by the controversial nature of the research and author's gender. However, after long-term research literacy training, students became more reliant on methodological cues to assess research credibility. This shift suggests that deliberate pedagogical strategies can help students align their evaluations with core values of fairness, analytical rigor, and respect for diversity. Further, as restrictions are being placed on DEI initiatives, these findings illustrate that there are neutral strategies that still achieve important DEI outcomes.

TI Does Saying "I Am Human" Make Me a Racist?
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING IN SOCIAL WORK
LA English
DT Article
DE Human; racism
ID SOCIAL-WORK RESEARCH; AFRICAN-AMERICANS; RACE
AB At a recent annual convention of a major social work organization, I attended a presentation with a number of speakers. Near the end of the session, one editor (Professor X) said "I do not pay much attention to White supremacist journal metrics." I politely asked "Could you give us an example of a White supremacist journal metric?" She replied "Journal Impact Factors & mldr; Bruce, what is your race?" Rather shocked at this inappropriate question, I replied "I am a human being." She then repeated herself, "No really, Bruce, what is your race?" I replied "I define myself as human, and I find this question a microaggression and feel threatened." The meeting ended then with no further discussion. Later I received an e-mail from a Professor Z who said what I did was aggressive and racist, and she sent me a copy of the organization's anti-harassment policy. In this editorial, I describe what happened in greater detail, and my reasons for saying I was a human being. Among these is the idea that racial categories are not scientifically supported, that categorizing people by their so-called race is actually harmful, and why asking me my race in a public forum is a form of microaggression, as inappropriate as asking someone their gender, religion, or sexuality. I provide many examples of how historically significant persons from around the world identified as human, and that to assert that such statements reflect aggressive racism minimizes the very real problems of racism and oppression.

TI Student achievement and self-confidence in mathematics and science:
   evidence from TIMSS 2023
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID PERFORMANCE; UNAWARE; GENDER
AB This paper examines whether underachieving students systematically overestimate their abilities and explores how confidence patterns vary across different contexts. Drawing on grade eight mathematics and science data from TIMSS 2023, we fit two-level regression models by country. Findings challenge the "unskilled and unaware" narrative: low-performing students typically reported muted, stable confidence, while high performers demonstrated strong positive achievement-confidence associations. Results align more with calibration theory and the Reciprocal Effects Model, which emphasize developmental feedback processes, than with inherent metacognitive deficits that align with the Dunning-Krueger theory. Further, cross-national contrasts underscore cultural variation: East Asian students reported modest confidence despite high achievement, whereas European systems exhibited steep calibration slopes. Gender differences were robust in mathematics, with boys reporting higher confidence net of performance, while immigrant effects were inconsistent. Overall, results highlight that confidence is socially and culturally structured, warranting context-sensitive approaches to motivation and feedback.

   skills and motivation in English language classes
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Dialogic pedagogy; Argumentative skills; Motivation; EFL; STEM
ID CLASSROOM; ENGAGEMENT; TEACHERS; SPEAKING
AB One of the goals of educational institutions is to make students problem-solvers. Hence, they design various tasks and initiate extracurricular activities to support learners' thinking skills. Argumentation skill is one part of thinking and problem-solving skills, which support learners' creativity, innovation, persuasion, and academic performance. Thus, the purpose of this research was to examine the effects of dialogic pedagogy on STEM students' argumentation skills and motivation in learning English language courses. The participants were Bahir Dar University Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) students. The study was designed through a quasi-experimental design, in which two groups were selected and assigned to different groups. The data were gathered through oral presentation, key informant interviews, observation, and questionnaire, and the quantitative data were analyzed through independent t-test, One-Way Manova, and Paired sample t-test, and the qualitative data were analyzed through narration. The data indicated that dialogic pedagogy had a great impact on STEM students' argumentation skills and motivation. The experimental group outperformed the comparison group in their oral argumentation skills and employed a higher level of claim formulation, provided reasons and evidence, supported their arguments, and had audience awareness. The data also confirmed that the experimental group improved their motivation skills, which the instruction supported the learners' emotional engagement, interest and taking intellectual risks, active participation, and collaboration. Therefore, the researcher suggested that dialogic pedagogy could be an alternative instructional methodology to improve learners' argumentation skills and motivation in learning English language skills.Clinical Trial Number Not applicable.

TI Educational Multisim - LabVIEW Co - Simulation of the Theory of Images
   in Groundwater Engineering
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE groundwater; image theory; LabVIEW; multisim RC
ID FLOW
AB This study employs a co-simulation module combining Multisim and LabVIEW as an educational tool in the classroom to teach the method of images in groundwater engineering. It evaluates students' use of digital technology through quantitative data, supported by qualitative analysis. The Multisim module creates RC networks to simulate virtual one- and two-sided bounded aquifers, featuring recharge, barrier, and mixed boundary types. LabVIEW acts as a data acquisition system, visualizing and analyzing simulation results. Data transfer occurs via hierarchical connectors. Inspired by image theory, the physical boundaries are replaced with imaginary wells to mimic the flow effects of actual boundaries. A key achievement is the RC analogs' ability to demonstrate and verify the hydraulic principles of image theory in a virtual confined aquifer with various boundary configurations. The strong agreement between the RC analogs' results and analytical solutions verifies their accuracy. This approach is novel in classrooms, as previous studies have not used digital technology to validate analytical solutions in image-theory hydraulics.

TI From Environment to Engagement: Innovative Insights Into AI-Mediated
   Language Learning Through Psychological Mechanisms
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-mediated language learning; growth mindset; psychological mechanisms;
   student engagement; teacher enthusiasm
AB AI is increasingly used in language learning, yet the psychological mechanisms underlying student engagement remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates the associations among teacher enthusiasm, learner growth mindset, and student engagement in AI-mediated language learning, with a focus on the mediating roles of willingness to communicate, resilience and creative self-efficacy. A total of 699 university students participated in a cross-sectional survey, and the data were analysed using structural equation modelling and psychological network analysis to examine indirect pathways and networked associations among environmental, cognitive and psychological factors. The results indicate that higher levels of teacher enthusiasm and stronger growth mindset are positively associated with psychological variables, which in turn are linked to higher engagement. Network analysis further reveals that willingness to communicate, resilience and creative self-efficacy are interconnected, with engagement occupying a central position within the network. These findings highlight the importance of considering multiple psychological mechanisms when exploring engagement in digitally enhanced learning contexts and extend social cognitive theory by illustrating the interactive contributions of environmental and individual cognitive factors. These findings extend social cognitive theory by showing how environmental and individual factors jointly shape engagement through multiple psychological mechanisms.

TI Immersive Learning in Business Education: The Impact of Metaverse
   Technology
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE business education; cognitive load theory; experiential learning;
   immersive learning; Metaverse technology; virtual reality
ID ENVIRONMENTS
AB Metaverse technology, supported by advances in Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, Mixed Reality and Extended Reality, offers new possibilities for immersive business education. However, existing research remains fragmented across individual technologies, educational contexts and learning outcomes, providing limited explanation of how the distinctive affordances of the Metaverse can be translated into theoretically grounded instructional design for business education. Through a structured review of the literature and theoretical analysis, this study examines how Metaverse-based environments can support student engagement, practical skill development, business decision-making and cross-cultural collaboration. AB As higher education transitions from Industry 4.0 to 5.0 amid global instability, universities face a profound paradox. While processing big data is effortless, potentially millions of gigabytes of student-generated intellectual capital like essays, theses and projects remain trapped behind closed institutional repositories. TI Perceived Educational Utility of Hands-On 3D-Printed Models for Teaching
   MRI Image Quality Concepts to Radiography Students
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE three-dimensional printing; medical education; radiography; teaching
   tool
AB Objectives: The aim of this study was to investigate radiography students' perceptions of the usefulness of hands-on 3D-printed models for supporting their understanding of key image quality concepts in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Students' views on the perceived contribution of these models to their learning experience, confidence, and independent learning were also evaluated. Methods: This questionnaire-based study included 79 students. Three 3D-printed MRI model sets were designed and fabricated for use in hands-on teaching sessions. Following the sessions, participants completed a seven-item questionnaire divided into two sections. The first section assessed students' perceptions of the teaching value of each model set, whereas the second section assessed students' perceived learning benefits. Likert-scale responses were summarized descriptively, and the internal consistency of the seven-item questionnaire was assessed using Cronbach's alpha. Results: In terms of the perceived teaching value of the models, the highest proportion of "strongly agree" responses were observed for pixel-voxel dimensionality and voxel geometry model sets, with 58 (73.4%) and 55 (69.6%), respectively. Regarding students' perceived learning benefits, students strongly agreed that the 3D-printed MRI models supported their confidence, independent learning, and learning experience in understanding MRI image-quality concepts, with 49 (62%), 47 (59.5%), and 46 (58.2%), respectively. The seven-item questionnaire demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.896, 95% CI [0.835, 0.957]). Conclusion: Radiography students expressed strong favorable views regarding the hands-on use of 3D-printed models and perceived them as helpful tools for visualizing core MRI image quality concepts.

AB This study investigates a secondary science teacher's beliefs and attitudes toward marginalized minority students and examines how these beliefs and attitudes influenced students' science identity development. The study focused on an experienced Black female biology teacher with an MEd in STEM education and her students at an urban high school in a U.S. state where anti-diversity, equity, and inclusion influences on curriculum were particularly strong. All students in the class (N = 21) identified as marginalized minority students. Data sources included teacher interviews, classroom observations, field notes, and student surveys. These data were analyzed and interpreted through the frameworks of Critical Race Theory and culturally responsive teaching. Findings showed that students expressed a strong sense of belonging when their diverse voices, backgrounds, and experiences were acknowledged in the classroom. However, many students also described feeling disconnected from the traditional image of a scientist, which contributed to self-doubt about their potential participation in scientific careers. This study highlights the importance of educators actively engaging with students' identities, promoting diverse representations within science, and creating supportive and inclusive classroom environments. At the same time, the findings reveal the limits of classroom-based support for science identity development when broader structural barriers and dominant stereotypes about science remain strong influences.

TI Geomaniguras: A Manipulative Resource for Supporting Conceptual
   Understanding in Geometry Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE geometry education; manipulative materials; mathematical reasoning;
   geometric thinking; conceptual understanding; Van Hiele theory
ID MATHEMATICS
AB Manipulative materials are widely considered valuable resources in geometry education because they may support visualization, spatial reasoning, and conceptual understanding when implemented within appropriate instructional contexts. However, many existing resources focus on isolated concepts and provide limited opportunities for connecting geometric relationships through transformation and decomposition. This study presents Geomaniguras, a manipulative material designed for upper primary and lower secondary education. The research adopts a design and development approach focused on pedagogical design and expert-based validation rather than measuring student learning outcomes. The study combined prototype construction, expert evaluation, and iterative refinement. Twelve specialists in mathematics education assessed the material using a structured validation guide addressing pedagogical usefulness, conceptual coherence, usability, visual design, and classroom applicability. Results indicate that experts perceived Geomaniguras as a potentially valuable resource for exploring polygon classification, area relationships, geometric decomposition, circumference, and the Pythagorean theorem. The findings provide preliminary evidence regarding the pedagogical plausibility and classroom applicability of the material, although no direct conclusions can yet be drawn about instructional effectiveness. The originality of the proposal lies in its integrated conceptual framework, which connects multiple geometric learning experiences within a single manipulative system.

ID CHEMISTRY
AB Esters are widely present in everyday materials, and their study is important for understanding fundamental concepts in organic chemistry. TI Density Calculation Using Cubic Equations of State: A Python-Based
   Framework for Thermodynamics Education
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Thermodynamics; Physical Chemistry; Python Programming; Computational
   Chemistry; Cubic Equationsof State; Open-Source Learning; Data Literacy;
   Chemical Engineering Education
AB Density is a critical thermodynamic property in chemical engineering and physical chemistry. However, many undergraduate students encounter equations of state (EoS) only symbolically, without connecting them to practical computations or visualizations. This work introduces an open-source Python framework for calculating and comparing fluid densities via four classical cubic EoS-van der Waals, Redlich-Kwong, Soave-Redlich-Kwong, and Peng-Robinson methods. This resource advances computational and conceptual learning in thermodynamics, supporting reproducible and code-based chemistry instruction.

TI Multimodal digital production and the negotiation of identity: a
   critical pedagogy case study of agency and resistance in EFL writing
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical digital pedagogy; Identity negotiation; Digital literacies;
   Multimodality; Agency and resistance; EFL writing
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; LANGUAGE; TECHNOLOGY; LITERACY
AB The integration of digital technology into English Language Teaching (ELT) has become standard practice. However, research often emphasizes the instrumental benefits of technology for skill acquisition, while neglecting how technology supports critical engagement with the world. This study addresses this gap by exploring the implementation of a critical digital pedagogy in a university academic writing course. Using a qualitative case study design, this research investigates how learners experience this approach and how they use multimodal digital creation to express their identities. Data were collected over one academic semester from fourteen students through semi-structured interviews, analysis of student-produced digital artifacts, and a reflective journal. Thematic analysis of the data revealed five primary findings: (1) a shift in student roles from passive recipients to active authors; (2) the development of critical practices for evaluating the validity of digital information; (3) the expression of personal and cultural identities through multimodal composition; (4) an awareness of the emotional exposure associated with public dissemination; and (5) the presence of resistance and technical distraction that at times hindered linguistic development. The results suggest that critical digital pedagogy encourages agency and provides a valuable space for identity work in a second language, though it requires intentional support to address technical challenges. This paper concludes by outlining pedagogical implications for ELT practitioners on how to move beyond functional uses of technology toward more transformative educational experiences.

TI Breaking Barriers in Large Classes: Using Cloud Computing and
   Computational Biology to Implement Research-Inspired Curricula in
   Biochemistry I
SO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID LIBRARIES
AB Course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) are a high impact instructional approach but are challenging to implement in large lecture courses due to class size and content demands. We describe the evolution of a research-inspired project in a large-enrollment (70+ students) Biochemistry lecture course. Our goal was to integrate a project that complements the rigid content while providing experience working on a novel research project. We addressed access barriers by expanding the use of cloud-based computational techniques, notably Google Colaboratory (Colab), to ensure software accessibility across diverse student devices. The semester-long project is divided into four modules focusing on protein structure and function, culminating in an individual project that studies a novel protein variant and its effects on structure and function. These projects are further supported by a science and math librarian to teach information literacy and data management skills. Since Fall 2024, over 250 students have participated. Student self-assessments demonstrate gains in confidence, particularly in analyzing molecular structures, connecting genetic mutations to protein function, and using scientific databases like UniProt. This model shows that research-inspired curricula can be successfully integrated into large, content-heavy lecture courses by leveraging accessible cloud-computing resources.

TI Embedding, Copilot, or Agent? L2 Teachers Modes of Collaboration With
   Generative AI in Providing Feedback on Writing Assignments: Rubric
   Influences, Workload Dynamics, and Barriers to Integration
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE collaborative strategies; GenAI chatbot; human-AI collaboration; LLM
   Chatbot; teacher feedback; written corrective feedback (WCF)
AB Drawing from the established human-AI collaboration framework (Mosqueira-Rey et al., 2023), this study investigated how L2 teachers at a research-intensive university collaborated with Generative AI chatbots to provide feedback on tertiary-level written assignments over 9 weeks. Data from thirteen teachers included 278 interactions with GenAI, 876 feedback instances, and reflective accounts of their experiences. Findings revealed three Teacher-GenAI collaboration modes-embedding (human-led), copilot (interactive), and agent (GenAI-led)-with a MANOVA indicating that rubric dimensions significantly influenced their frequency of use. Post hoc comparisons indicated that teachers used the agent and copilot modes more frequently in the "language use" dimension. Conversely, the embedding mode was used most frequently in the "content" and "overall evaluation" dimensions. Although the agent mode reduced teachers' workload in providing feedback on mistakes at the micro level, the embedding mode demanded more effort from teachers to give feedback at the macro level of students' assignments. Guided by Ertmer's framework (1999) on the barriers to educational technology integration, we found that teachers tried to claim more control over human-AI collaboration by adopting embedding and copilot modes for four concerns: GenAI agents' misalignment with task requirements, inconsistency with external expectations, inadequacy in addressing students' emotional needs, and cautious attitudes toward technology.

TI Language Experience Shapes Creative Idea Generation
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE alternate uses task; bilingualism; creativity; divergent thinking;
   proficiency
ID CHAINED EQUATIONS; LEXICAL ACCESS; BILINGUALS; PROFICIENCY;
   COACTIVATION; IMPUTATION; THINKING
AB Bilinguals often outperform monolinguals on creative tasks, suggesting a positive link between bilingualism and creativity. However, the inconsistent definitions of both bilingualism and creativity have made it difficult to understand the precise factors driving the association. Here, we examine the relationship between creativity and bilingualism by focusing on the effects of language proficiency and dominance on divergent thinking. Spanish-English bilinguals and English monolinguals completed the Alternate Uses Task (AUT, a measure of divergent thinking) in each of their languages. Responses were assessed in three ways: number of ideas generated (fluency), the length of each idea (elaboration), and how original each idea was (originality). The originality of each response was scored automatically with a fine-tuned, multilingual large language model. Results revealed that AUT performance was influenced by the language of testing and by participants' language proficiency, indicating a relationship between language experience and divergent thinking. Specifically, higher proficiency and dominance in each language were associated with more original ideas, demonstrating that people's capacity for creative expression is tied to their linguistic abilities. We conclude that verbal creativity assessments, whether in research or real-world settings, should take into account language experience, especially in multilingual populations and contexts.

TI Migration and social mobility: a qualitative longitudinal study
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATION AND WORK
LA English
DT Article
DE Migration; social mobility; longitudinal study
ID LABOR-MARKET; EDUCATION; DISCRIMINATION; STRATEGIES
AB This article examines how adult migrants in Sweden navigate the complex and shifting conditions surrounding labour-market integration over time. Drawing on a qualitative longitudinal study involving 55 participants interviewed twice between 2017-2021, the analysis explores social mobility as a dynamic, relational and non-linear process shaped by structural constraints and personal aspirations. Four interrelated themes emerge: the profound impact of legal status and protracted asylum procedures on migrants' capacity to plan for the future; the widespread mis-recognition of foreign qualifications, often resulting in downward mobility or extended requalification pathways; experiences of labour-market exploitation, particularly among those whose residence permits depend on employment; and the decisive role of social networks in enabling language learning, accessing opportunities and fostering a sense of belonging. The study contributes to a deeper understanding of how policy frameworks, institutional practices and relational resources interact to facilitate or constrain migrants' social mobility trajectories in contemporary Sweden.

TI Engaging with theoretical models in social science education
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE models; second-order concepts; social science education; theory
AB In citizenship education, subjects like social science aim to enhance students' reasoning about social issues through disciplinary knowledge, skills and abilities. One key ability is using theories and models to better understand and reason about societal phenomena. Given the limited research on students' use of theory, this article explores the potential of theoretical models in social science education. We analysed 117 final essays from students who participated in an inquiry-based segment on political trust and its significance for democracy, where they engaged with a theoretical model. The thematic analysis identified four distinct ways in which theory helps students organise, analyse and critically examine their arguments. These include using theory to analyse social phenomena, construct arguments, problematise issues and assess conclusions. The study was conducted in two Swedish high schools with diverse socio-economic backgrounds, involving students in year 11. The findings suggest that theoretical models can scaffold students' learning processes, enabling them to develop powerful knowledge and engage deeply with complex social issues. This article discusses how these insights can guide teachers in leveraging models in social science education, highlighting both opportunities and challenges. The implications for teaching include the need for explicit instruction on using theoretical models and the importance of addressing the limitations of these models in representing real-world complexities.Context and implications Rationale for this study: Research highlights the importance of theory and scaffolding in social science education, yet little empirical work shows how students use theoretical models in their reasoning or how powerful knowledge is enacted in classroom practice. Why the new findings matter: The study demonstrates how a theoretical model can function as a disciplinary scaffold that deepens students' analytical, argumentative and evaluative reasoning about democracy. Implications for practitioners, researchers and teacher educators: For practitioners, the findings suggest that explicit modelling of how to analyse, argue, problematise and assess using theoretical frameworks can strengthen students' social scientific reasoning and democratic competence. For teacher educators, the study highlights the need to prepare future teachers to work consciously with second-order concepts and disciplinary scaffolds. For researchers, the findings indicate the value of further empirical studies examining how powerful knowledge is enacted and transformed in everyday classroom practices across different social science topics and contexts.

TI Understanding complexity: Insights from Seashell's sector-wide survey on
   education provision for young people with complex learning disabilities
SO SUPPORT FOR LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE complex needs; data-informed planning; education and health care plans
   (EHCPs); learning difficulties; special education
AB This article shares findings from Seashell's 2024 complex needs survey, which aimed to address the critical lack of reliable cross-sector data on children and young adults with learning disabilities and complex needs in England. The absence of consistent definitions and data collection methods across education, health and social care has long hindered inclusive strategic planning at local, regional and national levels. This project gathered data from 18 specialist providers through a national survey. Findings reveal that approximately 1800 children and young adults with learning disabilities and complex needs are currently educated by these providers, with autism spectrum condition and severe learning difficulty being the most reported primary needs. Respondents also reported a marked increase in the complexity of needs among their cohort, particularly in health and behavioural challenges, placing growing demands on specialist environments and staff. In response, some providers are expanding their capacity, with projected increases of 15.67% in education placements and 25.21% in residential placements. These findings align with national trends, including a rise in Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), improved diagnostic practices and advances in neonatal care improving life expectancy for extremely premature infants and those born with complex disabilities. Despite ongoing inconsistencies in national data systems, this study offers a valuable benchmark for understanding this population and highlights the urgent need for integrated, inclusive data strategies. This paper offers a practical, data-informed perspective on how inclusive practice can be enhanced through improved understanding of learner needs.

TI Wargame-based learning in management education: The use of
   Diplomacy board game
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Art of negotiations; Artificial intelligence; Betrayal; Strategy
   building; Strategic decision making; Thinking out-of-the box; Wargames
ID BUSINESS; ALLIANCES; STRATEGY; FOG
AB Can wargames be used in management education to provide students with agency? To answer this question, we draw on narrative transportation theory and develop an immersive learning experience by using Diplomacy boardgame. As a novel theoretical contribution, we extend narrative transportation theory into management education by introducing the idea of wargame narrative world based on the evolving narrative created by student teams who acted as empires during the Great War. The master course aimed to strengthen students' business negotiation knowledge and skills. Through wargaming, teams practiced strategic analysis, resource management, and decision-making under conditions of the 'fog of war'. By granting students agency to negotiate alliances, Diplomacy's immersive setting exposed how quickly they adapted, and sometimes compromised, their behaviors, responsibilities, and ethical standards. As a result, they improved their adaptive thinking skills and critical reflection on competitive assumptions. As a practical contribution, we design a course that uses a wargame as an educational tool to deepen students' understanding of business concepts and practices. Although wargames require significant time and energy to implement, we argue they deserve wider adoption because they help students develop strategic thinking, make pressured decisions, and evaluate trade-offs more effectively.

TI The use of 3-dimensional (3D) printing in teaching musculoskeletal
   oncology for medical undergraduates
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical Education; Educational Outcomes; Musculoskeletal Oncology;
   Osteosarcoma; 3D Printing
ID EDUCATION; STUDENTS; ANATOMY
AB Introduction The approach to integrating relevant anatomy in the medical curriculum has been debated for many years. Current literature has explored the broad impact of 3D printing in medical education. However, there is little evidence on 3D printing for the teaching of musculoskeletal oncology (MSO). This is a self-controlled case series (SCCS) study that aims to analyse the effectiveness of 3D printed models in MSO in enhancing the learning experience, engagement and understanding of clinical and surgical anatomy for medical students. Method A cross-sectional cohort study involving 75 clinical year medical students across 3 years from 2 medical schools that rotated through a single teaching hospital's orthopaedic department. Participants first viewed a set of computed-tomography (CT) images of a large pelvic osteosarcoma from a free open-source database, the Cancer Genome Atlas Sarcoma Collection (TCGA-SARC). A standardised 10-minute pre-intervention questionnaire which comprised 15 questions categorised by: 4 questions in 'anatomical knowledge', 7 questions in 'spatial awareness', 4 questions in 'surgical planning and complications', was administered to assess the baseline knowledge in their interpretation of the pathology via CT images only. Next, a 3D-printed model of the pelvic osteosarcoma, which included colour-coded adjacent structures, was provided as an adjunct to answer the same questionnaire. This concluded with a 5-point Likert scale feedback survey to gauge their perspectives and experience. Results The mean scores comparing their pre- and post-intervention assessment questionnaire increased by +1.34 from 8.15 (SD = 1.85) to 9.49 (SD = 1.7) (p < 0.001). The final year students had the greatest improvement of +1.54 from 8.00 (SD = 1.89) to 9.54 (SD = 1.59) (p = 0.004). There was no significant difference between the scores amongst the 2 medical schools. 91% of students agreed that the 3D model had helped them further their understanding of the anatomy of the sarcoma and 87% would want 3D printing models to augment their learning in anatomy. Baseline weaker students demonstrated significantly greater improvement in scores compared with baseline stronger students (mean difference +2.04 vs +0.30, p < 0.001). Conclusion 3D printing is an effective teaching adjunct for musculoskeletal oncology surgical anatomy for medical undergraduates and could be used to enhance their understanding and learning experience. 3D models could be integrated in the teaching curriculum of surgical anatomy for undergraduate students.

TI Developing de-encapsulated hybrid activity in a school: Making inclusion
   a shared responsibility
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Change laboratory; Cultural-Historical Activity Theory;
   De-encapsulation; Hybrid schooling; Inclusion; Disability; School garden
ID PERSPECTIVES
AB Change Laboratories are a means to support transformation in schools, grounded in CulturalHistorical-Activity Theory (CHAT). They can enable schools to become agents of social change by connecting learning to what happens outside of school, and organising schooling in collaboration with community. This is referred to as de-encapsulation or hybridity. Recent developments in Change Laboratories have seen strengthened engagement with knowledges from the Global South. This paper reports an adapted Change Laboratory in a rural Bhutanese school. Participants identified two desired axes of development towards de-encapsulation: a shift from inclusion being the responsibility of specialists, to being a shared responsibility; and a shift from low to high school-community collaboration. The idea of Phentshen Dhumra (garden benefitting everyone) emerged, grounded in Bhutanese spiritual and cultural values relating to compassionate awakening, mutual obligation, and virtuous actions. Parents, shopkeepers, farmers and local government supported the initiative, which became a site for students with disabilities to contribute alongside peers, but also a basis for parents to become actively involved in school and in their children's education. This study shows how movement towards de-encapsulation and hybridity were part of the development of gardening activity in which inclusion became whole-ofcommunity responsibility and benefit, even while other aspects of schooling remained encapsulated. The paper offers insights into how CHAT can be brought into meaningful dialogue with spiritual and traditional knowledges from the Global South.

TI AI as Scaffold or Shortcut? Metacognitive Regulation in Graduate
   Students' Educational App Design
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence in education; generative AI; educational
   technology design; metacognition; teacher education; technology
   integration
AB The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has raised important questions about how learners and teachers regulate their thinking when interacting with AI-supported tools. This study investigates metacognitive regulation during the design of AI-supported educational applications by graduate students (N = 12) in a UAE teacher education programme. The qualitative research adopted a multiple-case study method to analyse six student design teams involved in designing educational applications as part of a technology integration course. Data were collected from three main sources: the educational apps themselves, the corresponding Teacher Guides, and reflective interviews conducted using a semi-structured interview guide. Data analysis combined deductive qualitative coding based on the regulation-of-cognition dimensions of the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (MAI) framework with inductive thematic analysis of participants' experiences and conceptualisations of AI. The findings show that AI was used differently across the six cases. It appeared to function more as a cognitive scaffold when participants questioned, checked, revised, or justified AI-generated outputs, and more as a shortcut when outputs were used mainly for convenience with limited further reflection. Planning was the most visible regulatory process, while stronger regulatory engagement was evident when AI-generated outputs were examined, questioned, and refined rather than accepted without further consideration.
