TI "Precision", "Approximation", and Experimental Mathematics at School in
   the Age of Digital Educational Technology
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE epistemic shift at school; error as a learning opportunity; weighing
   digital outputs; informal introduction of advanced mathematical
   concepts; guided inquiry based on experimental mathematics
ID CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; TEACHERS
AB This paper explores the interrelations between "precision", "approximation", and experimental mathematics supported by digital educational technology in the classroom. It examines the epistemic and pedagogical challenges and opportunities these links create in school mathematics and what is required of teachers to address them. Instances of "approximation" mathematics, emerging from experiments performed with digital tools, are analyzed and evaluated from the standpoint of "precise," deductive mathematics. The study presents examples where "approximate" computations-or inferences based upon them-are incorrect from the standpoint of "precision" mathematics. It also shows how to correct or further investigate such discrepancies and how school mathematical practices would profit from such approaches. In addition, it discusses instances where experimental mathematics reveals issues typically outside the school curriculum but still conceptually accessible, yielding unexpected or unfamiliar results. The paper also considers recurrent sequences and their hands-on exploration in the context of the interrelation between the three realms of mathematics. The analysis of the examples through the prism of three realms of mathematics linked by digital technologies outlines the ensuing epistemic shift in the mathematics classroom. The teachers' expectations in view of this shift are analyzed and presented.

TI Teachers' self-efficacy and its role on effective classroom management
   at secondary schools in Johannesburg, South Africa
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE effective classroom management; learners' performance; secondary
   schools; skill development; teacher self-efficacy
AB Teacher self-efficacy and its influence on effective classroom management are fundamental aspects of teaching, learning and learners' academic outcomes. It is, therefore, crucial to have qualified, skilled, trained and effective teachers in classrooms. Hence, this study intended to identify the influence of teacher self-efficacy on effective classroom management. The research employed a generic qualitative research approach to investigate the phenomenon, using semi-structured interviews as the data collection method. A purposive sampling technique was used to identify 18 participants from six Johannesburg schools: 12 teachers and six school heads. It was found that physical and material resources are important for effective classroom management, but they cannot replace teachers' personal self-efficacy. In addition, some beginner and in-service teachers lacked classroom management skills, as they were not offered many skills improvement opportunities. It is thus recommended that teachers be provided with professional development opportunities to increase their effectiveness in classroom management.

TI Digital transformation in higher education: a theory-guided systematic
   literature review linking learning outcomes, entrepreneurial innovation,
   and SDG 4
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE bibliometric analysis; content analysis; emerging technologies;
   entrepreneurial skills; higher education institutes; sustainability;
   theories
ID TASK-TECHNOLOGY FIT; ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; USER ACCEPTANCE; SKILLS;
   MOTIVATION; UNIVERSITY; KNOWLEDGE; IMPACT
AB Introduction Digital transformation in higher education represents not only a technological shift but also a fundamental change in pedagogy, aligning with the demands of a globalized society. This systematic literature review (2020-2024) examines how emerging technologies in higher education impact learning outcomes, foster entrepreneurial innovation, and advance Quality Education (SDG 4). Methods Conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search of Scopus and Web of Science databases was performed. This process yielded 41 relevant studies, which were subsequently appraised for quality using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) checklist. Results Using bibliometric analysis and network mapping, we identified four major thematic clusters in the literature. Based on these clusters, we propose an integrative theoretical framework that links digital transformation initiatives to educational outcomes, innovation, and sustainability goals. Discussion We outline crucial future research directions (e.g., addressing infrastructure challenges, enhancing digital pedagogy, and scaling innovation labs) to guide scholars and practitioners. Our review provides a timely synthesis of current knowledge and offers actionable insights for leveraging digital transformation to improve global educational quality and equity.

TI Teaching parabolic functions using GeoGebra in senior high school:
   evidence from a one-group pretest-posttest study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE activity theory; constructivist theory; GeoGebra; mathematics education;
   parabolic functions; technology integration
AB This study examines the effectiveness of using GeoGebra in teaching parabolic functions in Senior High School mathematics. It responds to persistent challenges associated with traditional teacher-cantered approaches, which often limit students' understanding of abstract mathematical concepts such as quadratic functions. A quasi-experimental one-group pretest-post test design was adopted, supported by qualitative classroom observations and interviews to provide a richer understanding of students' learning experiences. The study involved Senior High School Form Two students who were taught parabolic functions using GeoGebra after an initial pretest assessment. Students' performance was measured before and after the intervention, while qualitative data captured their engagement, collaboration, and conceptual understanding during classroom activities. The findings revealed a significant improvement in students' post-test scores compared to their pre-test results, with mean performance increasing from low achievement levels to high mastery levels after the intervention. The paired-sample t-test showed that students' post-test scores were significantly higher than their pre-test scores (p < .001), indicating substantial improvement in performance following the GeoGebra intervention. Qualitative findings showed increased student engagement, active participation, and improved ability to connect algebraic expressions with graphical representations. Students demonstrated better understanding of intercepts, vertices, and axes of symmetry through interactive exploration. Guided by Constructivist and Activity Theories, the study demonstrates that GeoGebra supports active learning through visualization, interaction, and collaboration. The study concludes that integrating GeoGebra into mathematics instruction enhances students' conceptual understanding and engagement in learning parabolic functions. It recommends the adoption of dynamic technological tools in mathematics classrooms to promote more effective and meaningful learning experiences.

TI From understanding to advocacy: the journey framework as an enactment
   architecture for neuro-affirming autism education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE co-regulation; design-based research; family-school collaboration;
   inclusive early support; journey framework; neuro-affirming education;
   relational neuroscience; translational pedagogy
ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; CHILDREN
AB This conceptual paper proposes the Journey Framework as an enactment architecture for neuro-affirming practice in autism education, situated within a broader translational pedagogical lens. It addresses a persistent gap between established frameworks and their consistent application in family and school contexts, particularly under conditions of diagnostic uncertainty and system complexity. Its contribution lies not in replacing existing frameworks, but in organising them within a coherent pedagogical architecture for sustained implementation. In this paper, translational pedagogy is used to describe the pedagogical problem of how established developmental, relational, and neuro-affirming educational principles become understandable, enactable, and sustained in practice. The Journey Framework addresses this problem through the alignment of co-regulatory conditions, accessible design, and sequenced support. Informed by developmental, relational, and design-based perspectives, including the SCERTS Model and Autism Education Trust (AET) guidance, now continued through the Neuroinclusive Education Network (NEN), the paper conceptualises early intervention as Early Support: a process through which complex theory becomes accessible, relationally safe, and usable in practice. At the macro level, the Journey Framework organises learning across six interlinked domains: Understanding -> Connection -> Regulation -> Communication -> Identity -> Advocacy, reflecting both child development and adult learning through shifting patterns of emphasis rather than fixed stages. At the micro level, enactment is organised through a co-regulatory pedagogic mechanism, Connection -> Clarity -> Confidence, which shapes the moment-to-moment experience of learning. The framework operates across interacting levels of practice, including child development, parent learning, practitioner implementation, and whole-school systems. The central hypothesis is that alignment between relational safety, accessible design, and sequenced support increases the likelihood that adults will understand, implement, and sustain evidence-based educational practices. Developed through practitioner-research contexts including parent-learning programmes and school partnerships, the Journey Framework offers an account of how such alignment may reduce fragmentation, support shared understanding, and strengthen confidence in practice over time. It is therefore presented as a testable conceptual framework with implications for family learning, professional learning, and whole-school implementation.

TI An integrated perspective on students' interdisciplinary learning
   process and interdisciplinary learning outcomes
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE constructive alignment; education design; higher education;
   interdisciplinary education; learning outcomes
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION
AB Research has suggested that well-designed interdisciplinary education, based on constructive alignment, can support the development of interdisciplinary knowledge and skills. However, teachers in interdisciplinary education tend to struggle with how to effectively design interdisciplinary education based on such an outcome-based model. At the same time, the learning process through which students develop interdisciplinary skills remains insufficiently theorized. Drawing on interdisciplinary integration techniques to integrate current literature on interdisciplinary learning outcomes and existing theories and frameworks on learning processes, combined with practice based insights on interdisciplinary education itself, the Levels of Interdisciplinary Learning Model is proposed. The model provides a meta-perspective on interdisciplinary learning by integrating previously fragmented conceptualizations of interdisciplinary learning outcomes and the interdisciplinary learning process into a single pedagogical framework. The model conceptualizes that interdisciplinary learning is a three-dimensional process: learning occurs in a cognitive, attitudinal and social-interactive dimension. Furthermore, it proposes that interdisciplinary learning develops over time at different levels of competency and that students as such progress through an 'interdisciplinary learning process'. By offering a structured and integrated framework for understanding how interdisciplinary learning outcomes relate to one another and develop over time, the model advances the theorization of interdisciplinary learning and extends existing literature on interdisciplinary outcome-based education. In addition, the model is intended to provide teachers with concrete guidance in educational practice. To facilitate this application, the article introduces a didactical design tool derived from the model that could inform and strengthen choices in the design, development and implementation of interdisciplinary education.

TI Motivations, consequences, and concerns about the use of artificial
   intelligence in higher education: empirical evidence
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; CHAID models; decision trees; higher education;
   student; universities
AB Introduction The article analyzes the motivations, consequences, and concerns regarding the use of artificial intelligence (AI) among university students, with the aim of determining its influence on teaching-learning processes mediated in higher education.Methodology A quantitative analysis of the variables was conducted through the establishment of CHAID (Chi-square Automatic Interaction Detection) relationships among the motivations, consequences, and concerns perceived in students' educational dynamics. An intentional sampling was applied to 268 students from universities in El Salvador.Results The nine decision trees generated reveal heterogeneous yet consistent patterns. The most robust models show that academic cycle and perceived academic workload are the most relevant initial predictors, leading to pathways where difficulties in retaining information and intensive use of ChatGPT emerge as compensatory mechanisms.Discussion The findings open a problematic field concerning the diverse socioeducational processes and adjustments influencing higher education, confirming trends documented in previous international and regional studies.Conclusions The results highlight the urgent need to strengthen digital competencies, establish clear ethical guidelines, and promote a pedagogically oriented use of these technologies in Salvadoran higher education.

TI Understanding continuance intention towards e-learning platforms: a
   structural model based on expectation confirmation and individual
   innovativeness
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE continuance intention; e-learning; expectation confirmation theory;
   individual innovativeness; PLS-SEM; satisfaction
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; USER ACCEPTANCE; UNIFIED THEORY; ADOPTION
AB Introduction The rapid growth of e-learning platforms in higher education has increased the need to understand the factors influencing students' continuance intention toward online learning systems. Drawing upon Expectation Confirmation Theory and integrating individual innovativeness, this study examines the relationships among expectation confirmation, perceived usefulness, satisfaction, and continuance intention, with gender as a moderating variable.Methods A quantitative research design was employed. Data were collected from 166 students with prior e-learning experience in Indian higher education institutions using a structured questionnaire. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyse the measurement and structural models.Results The findings indicate that satisfaction is the strongest predictor of continuance intention toward e-learning platforms. Expectation confirmation and perceived usefulness significantly enhance satisfaction; however, their direct effects on continuance intention were not significant. Mediation analysis revealed that satisfaction fully mediates the relationships between expectation confirmation, perceived usefulness, and continuance intention. Additionally, individual innovativeness demonstrated a significant negative direct effect on continuance intention, while gender significantly moderated the relationship between innovativeness and continuance intention.Discussion The study extends post-adoption e-learning research by highlighting the central role of satisfaction in sustaining continued usage of e-learning platforms. The findings further suggest that individual innovativeness and demographic characteristics shape continuance behaviour in online learning environments. The study offers theoretical contributions to continuance intention literature and practical implications for higher education institutions and e-learning platform developers seeking to improve long-term learner engagement.

TI Does artificial intelligence predict scientific productivity? Machine
   learning evidence from university research seedbeds
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; emerging economies; higher education; machine
   learning; Peru; research seedbeds; scientific productivity
AB This study examines the relative predictive contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) learning and use, compared with academic trajectory and sociodemographic variables, in explaining scientific productivity profiles among undergraduate students participating in university research seedbeds in an emerging Latin American context. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional design with supervised predictive modeling was employed, using census data from 57 students at a Peruvian university. Six dimensions of AI learning and use, along with composite indices and academic trajectory variables, were evaluated against a binary scientific productivity profile. Four machine learning classifiers (penalized logistic regression, Random Forest, Extra Trees, and XGBoost) were compared using repeated stratified cross-validation, and model interpretability was assessed through permutation importance. Results indicate that penalized logistic regression achieved the highest predictive performance (accuracy = 0.842; balanced accuracy = 0.845; F1-macro = 0.835; AUC-ROC = 0.894). The most influential predictors were time of participation in the research seedbed, age group, and gender, whereas AI-related composite indices exhibited negligible or marginally negative contributions. These findings suggest that, in this sample, self-reported AI capabilities were not the dominant predictors of scientific productivity once formative trajectory variables were considered. Instead, sustained formative engagement and academic trajectory emerge as stronger determinants, challenging the prevailing assumption of AI as a universal accelerator of research performance. The study highlights the need to reorient institutional strategies toward strengthening research training environments and integrating AI within the full scientific production cycle.

TI Designing "The League Of Wise Guardians": a narrative-based
   co-research training model with children and adolescents in Chilean
   public schools
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE child and adolescent participation; children and adolescents as
   co-researchers; co-research; design-based research; participatory
   research; school-based research
AB Children and adolescents are increasingly recognized not only as participants in research but as knowledge producers capable of shaping the questions, methods, and meanings of inquiry. However, in practice, their participation is often limited by adult-centered designs, institutional constraints, and a lack of pedagogical models to support research decision-making. This Brief Research Report presents the design and preliminary validation of The League of Wise Guardians, a narrative-based training model developed to support children and adolescents as co-researchers in Chilean public schools. Adopting a qualitative Design-Based Research approach, the study drew on documentary analysis, exploratory work with children and adolescents, expert review, participatory pilot testing with upper primary students, and facilitator reflection. The design and preliminary validation process identified four core components of the model: (1) a playful narrative universe that makes research concepts accessible; (2) a structure for progressive decision-making across the research process; (3) a four-phase training cycle integrating methodological learning with research action; and (4) facilitation principles attentive to children's agency, methodological rigor, and school conditions. The study contributes a situated pedagogical model for translating participation rights into concrete research practice. It suggests that meaningful co-research requires more than child-friendly materials; it requires a pedagogical architecture through which children and adolescents can gradually understand, exercise, and share decision-making power. Further research is needed to examine the model's implementation, how children and adolescents take up co-research roles, the quality of participation, and how decision-making power is negotiated across the research process.

TI Trust and help-seeking judgments in everyday relationships: a
   qualitative study of Cambodian pre-service teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cambodia; help-seeking; interpersonal trust; mental health; pre-service
   teachers; Southeast Asia; university students; qualitative research
ID MENTAL-HEALTH; SELF; COGNITION; CONTEXT
AB In post-conflict settings such as Cambodia, weakened social trust may hinder supportive relationships and access to mental health care. Trust and help-seeking are important for mental well-being, yet little qualitative research has examined how Cambodian pre-service teachers develop interpersonal trust and seek help in everyday relationships. This study explored the judgment criteria that Cambodian pre-service teachers used to evaluate trust towards specific relational targets and to select sources of help. An exploratory qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 15 pre-service teachers in Cambodia. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using inductive qualitative content analysis. The analysis identified relationship-specific criteria shaping trust toward family members, friends, teachers, and neighbors. Trust in family members was associated with emotional security and long-term cohabitation. Trust in friends depended on relational closeness and reciprocity but could be undermined by negative interpersonal experiences. Trust in teachers was influenced by perceived approachability and supportive behavior, while trust in neighbors was conditional and linked to relational distance. Help-seeking choices varied by perceived support needs. Family and friends were the primary sources for emotional and practical support, while doctors were consulted for professional care. Self-coping was preferred for manageable problems. Across relational targets, participants applied several common evaluative judgment criteria, including psychological safety, reciprocity, relational closeness, perceived expertise, and problem-source fit. These findings suggest that trust and help-seeking are shaped by both relationship-specific and cross-cutting judgment criteria and highlight the importance of psychologically safe and supportive interpersonal environments for Cambodian pre-service teachers.

   justice in the novel Journey to Jo'burg

DT Article
DE reading club; empathy; diverse literature; social justice; critical
   thinking; agency; mirrors
ID MULTIPLE-PERSPECTIVES; EMPATHY; CLUBS; BOOKS
AB Background: Despite the growing recognition of the importance of diverse narratives, children's literature sometimes lacks substantive representation of social justice themes, thereby limiting opportunities for critical engagement and awareness. The study seeks to investigate how exposure to such literature can cultivate critical thinking, empathy, and a heightened social consciousness among children. Through an analysis of their reflections, the research underscores the potential of literature as a transformative medium for fostering awareness and empowering young readers to recognise and question systemic inequalities. TI Children's performance in math and language: Examining the role of
   maternal education and home language
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Elementary education; Mathematics; Mathematical language; Language
ID MATHEMATICS VOCABULARY; ACHIEVEMENT; STUDENTS; PROFICIENCY; KNOWLEDGE
AB Regression-based studies concluded that children's general language abilities, mathematical language abilities, and mathematical abilities are positively related to each other. However, additional approaches are needed to better understand these relationships. A k-means cluster analysis based on 692 first, second, and third grader's general language abilities, mathematical language abilities, and their mathematical abilities identified four distinct profiles of children. In a second step, group membership in these clusters in terms of maternal education level and home language use was examined. In Cluster 1, children attained a low performance on all three abilities, had low maternal education levels, and often spoke a different language than the instructional language. In Cluster 4, children attained a high performance on all three abilities, had high maternal education levels, and often only spoke the instructional language at home. Clusters 2 and 3 are situated between these extremes. These clusters exhibit similar mathematical language abilities, both representing intermediate performance levels. Children in Cluster 2 had intermediate general language abilities and low mathematical abilities. Children in Cluster 3 had low general language abilities and high mathematical abilities. Children in both clusters differed in their home language use but showed comparable maternal educational levels (i.e., medium to highly educated mothers). Our results indicate that the previously reported positive associations between these three abilities are more nuanced. In addition, children with lower maternal education levels (and especially those growing up with a different home language as well) may require more targeted support.

TI Study on semantic diagram intervention for declarative knowledge
   learning in students with elevated learning anxiety
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Declarative knowledge; Learning anxiety; Semantic diagram; Deep reading;
   Cognitive load
ID COGNITIVE LOAD
AB Learning anxiety is a prevalent psychological issue among university students in contemporary China, significantly affecting academic performance. Semantic diagram, as an innovative knowledge visualization tool, can be integrated into learning processes as a potential cognitive scaffold for students in high-anxiety contexts. This study investigates the effects of semantic diagrams on learning outcomes in declarative knowledge among Chinese university students screened for moderate-to-severe learning anxiety. The study involved 94 first-year non-Chinese major students who were screened for moderate to severe learning anxiety using the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS). Participants were randomly divided into a control and an experimental group (n = 47 each). The control group engaged in self-directed learning using their preferred methods, while the experimental group utilized semantic diagram tools. After a 15-week intervention period, both groups completed a standardized assessment with acceptable reliability and content validity. Independent samples t-test revealed a significant difference between groups (p < .001, Cohen's d = 1.81), suggesting that the experimental group achieved a markedly superior understanding of declarative knowledge. The significant improvement in the experimental group suggests that the integrated intervention-combining semantic diagram visualization with iterative feedback-provides a robust instructional scaffold for declarative knowledge acquisition in high-anxiety contexts. Qualitative feedback suggests that this scaffolding provided students with a greater subjective sense of structure and perceived control over their learning process. However, as no post-intervention anxiety measure was administered, these qualitative accounts do not constitute evidence of anxiety reduction and are limited to descriptions of perceived cognitive ease.

AB Educational neuroscience offers valuable insights for teaching, yet preservice teachers' understanding is often impeded by misconceptions or "neuromyths." TI Longitudinal associations between dispositional envy, need for
   popularity, and bullying and cyberbullying in adolescence
SO REVISTA DE PSICODIDACTICA
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Adolescence; Dispositional envy; Need for popularity; Bullying behavior;
   Cross-lagged structural equation modeling
ID BEHAVIORS
AB From a social comparison perspective, emotions and motivations related to social status may play an important role in understanding aggressive behavior during adolescence. In particular, dispositional envy may motivate adolescents to pursue higher popularity within peer hierarchies, potentially increasing their involvement in aggressive behaviors such as bullying. However, longitudinal evidence examining the processes linking envy, status-related motivations, and aggression remains limited. The present study investigated the longitudinal associations among dispositional envy, need for popularity, and both bullying behavior and cyberbullying behavior in a sample of 707 adolescents (ages 11-17 years; M = 13.35, SD = 0.93) assessed across three waves. Cross-lagged structural equation modeling was used to examine the temporal relationships among these variables. Results showed that dispositional envy at Time 1 positively predicted need for popularity at Time 2. In turn, need for popularity was associated with higher levels of bullying behavior at Time 3, but not with cyberbullying behavior. The indirect effect linking envy to bullying through need for popularity was small and should therefore be interpreted with caution, and no mediation effect was observed for cyberbullying. Multi-group analyses indicated that the structural relations among the variables were similar for boys and girls. Overall, the findings suggest that dispositional envy may contribute indirectly to bullying behavior through adolescents' motivation to achieve social status. These results highlight the relevance of status-related motivations in the development of bullying during adolescence and underscore the importance of addressing such socio-motivational dynamics in prevention efforts. TI Are school strategies based on information useful to increase
   adolescents risk perception about alcohol? Moderated mediation analyses
   of individual, peers and parental drinking
SO REVISTA DE PSICODIDACTICA
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Alcohol use; Risk perception; School information; Parental influences;
   Peer influences
ID SUBSTANCE USE
AB Following McLero & yacute;s socio-ecological model, the present study tested whether school strategies based on information about substance use moderated the mediational effect of adolescent risk perception of alcohol use in the association between peers/parental alcohol use and adolescent drinking. Data were analyzed from a national representative survey that included 35,369 participants aged 14-18 (50.1% female). Data were weighted and standardized. Moderated mediation models were conducted. Across four models tested, school information had a significative effect increasing risk perception. Mediation models were significant at the two levels of the moderator, confirming the protective effect of high risk perception of alcohol use in the relation between peers/parental alcohol use and adolescent drinking. School information about substance use did not buffer the impact of parental alcohol use on adolescent risk perception. In contrast, school information about substance use potentiates the protective effect of risk perception in the relationship between peers drinking and adolescent alcohol use. School information about substance use moderates the impact of peer alcohol use on adolescent drinking by increasing the risk perception of alcohol consumption. Therefore, educational strategies are needed to weaken peer influences. The attenuation of parental influences might require intervention in other settings or including elements other than just giving information.

TI Understanding students' mathematical achievement through feature
   selection and machine learning: Evidence from PISA 2018
SO REVISTA DE PSICODIDACTICA
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Machine learning; Feature selection; Classification; Mathematical
   achievement; Educational data mining; Explainable artificial
   intelligence
ID LITERACY; CLASSIFICATION; PERFORMANCE; IMPUTATION; EDUCATION
AB The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) provides a framework for examining academic achievement. Using the Turkish sample of PISA 2018, this study investigates mathematics achievement, focusing on students performing below and above the baseline proficiency level (Level 2). To address this objective, a machine learning classification approach is adopted, integrating feature selection, supervised algorithms, and model interpretation techniques. The analysis includes 6,863 students from 186 schools and 62 student-and school-level variables derived from the PISA questionnaires. Three feature selection methods - Boruta, Mutual Information, and ReliefF - are used to identify subsets of variables that serve as inputs for five classification models: Decision Tree, Bagging, Random Forest, AdaBoost, and Support Vector Machine. Model performance is evaluated using repeated stratified cross-validation across plausible values and multiple classification metrics. The results indicate that models built on substantially reduced feature sets can achieve predictive performance comparable to models using all variables. Among the evaluated configurations, the combination of Mutual Information feature selection with the top 20 variable subset and the Random Forest classifier provides a stable and practical useful balance between prediction performance and model parsimony. Model predictions are examined using conditional SHAP values, partial dependence plots, individual conditional expectation plots, and accumulated local effects plots. Results show that socio-economic background, perceived test difficulty, occupational expectations, school stratum type and behaviors hindering learning are among the variables most strongly associated with model predictions. These analyses capture predominantly non-linear associations between predictors and model predictions, and these relationships vary across students, indicating heterogeneous model responses.

TI Resisting eurocentrism and preserving hmong cultural ways of being:
   Narratives shared by Wisconsin's Hmong early educators and cultural
   caregivers
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Hmong early educators; Cultural caregiving; Wisconsin; AsianCrit; Racial
   equity; Asian Americans
ID MODEL MINORITY; OUTSIDER; QUALITY
AB Adopting a counter-storytelling paradigm, this qualitative study examines the workforce experiences of 10 Hmong women in Wisconsin who serve as early educators in formal early education settings and as cultural caregivers within family- and community-based contexts. Grounded in Critical Race Theory, Asian Critical Theory, Intersectionality, and Community Cultural Wealth, the study centers Hmong educators' narratives to illuminate how race, gender, refugee history, language, and structural power coalesce to shape their professional lives. Findings reveal that Hmong early educators navigate Eurocentric definitions of quality, licensing practices, and professional norms that marginalize culturally rooted caregiving, linguistic knowledge, and intergenerational forms of care, while simultaneously bearing significant emotional, physical, and financial strain associated with racial gendered caregiving labor. Participants resisted these conditions by sustaining Hmong cultural practices, language, and relational caregiving traditions. This study addresses a critical gap in the early education scholarship by foregrounding the distinct experiences of Hmong educators, challenging dominant assumptions embedded in policy and practice, and offering culturally responsive recommendations to advance equity, visibility, and well-being within early education systems.

TI Does virtual service delivery make home visiting more accessible yet
   still provide benefits to families?
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Home visiting; Parenting; Social-emotional development; Medical home;
   Virtual service delivery; Accessibility
ID RANDOMIZED CONTROLLED-TRIAL; EMPOWERMENT
AB Home visiting has been shown to be an effective support for families with young children. However, intensive inhome models often face persistent challenges with engagement and retention, which may limit their effectiveness for some families. A light-touch home visiting model-offering fewer visits over a shorter duration-delivered in a virtual setting presents an alternative opportunity for families to participate in home visiting and receive needed support with lower expectations for engagement. This paper explores the benefits of a light-touch home visiting program offered virtually to families with newborns through 9 months of age. Using administrative data from the Welcome Baby program, the study found increased enrollment and completion rates after the program's transition to virtual implementation. The study also surveyed 910 families with new babies in Los Angeles County when their babies were 10 months and 18 months old. Those who had received Welcome Baby virtual visits demonstrated greater parenting confidence and parent-child interactions and had babies with stronger social and emotional development than families who did not receive Welcome Baby virtual visits. Differences were not observed for other measures of parenting behaviors. Families in Welcome Baby also were more likely to have consistent access to medical care, though this did not translate into greater use of well-care services. Findings suggest that virtual visits may make home visiting more accessible and offer important benefits for families.

TI Health and social characteristics of autistic adults in the UK-wide
   Adult Autism Spectrum Cohort (ASC-UK): A cross-sectional study
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autistic adults; Mental health; Physical health; Social; Cohort
ID EXPERIENCES; NEED
AB Purpose: This study aimed to characterise the health, social, and demographic circumstances of autistic adults in the UK using data from the Adult Autism Spectrum Cohort-UK (ASC-UK), a large, cross-sectional, population-based cohort. It sought to identify age-and gender-related differences in mental and physical health, healthcare access, employment, social relationships, and support needs. Methods: Between 2015 and 2021, 2129 autistic adults (diagnosed or self-identified), aged 16 years and older, were recruited via diverse routes including NHS services and community organisations. Data were collected using a 78-item registration questionnaire covering ten domains of daily life and the Social Responsiveness Scale-2 (SRS-2). Responders were grouped into four age categories and compared using appropriate statistical tests including ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis, Chi-square, and effect size measures. Results: Autistic adults reported high rates of physical (e.g., gastrointestinal, obesity, arthritis) and mental health conditions (e.g., anxiety, depression), with notable gender and age variation. Females reported significantly more mental and physical health issues than males. Employment was lowest in the youngest and oldest groups and unemployment was associated with poor mental health. A substantial gap was found between needed and received support, particularly among females and those with complex health needs. Social deprivation was not significantly associated with health diagnoses. Conclusion: Autistic adults across the UK experience substantial health disparities and unmet support needs. Gender and age influence outcomes, and healthcare services must adapt to improve access and equity. This study offers critical, lifespan-wide insights to inform policy, practice, and future longitudinal research.

TI Effects of a mindfulness-based intervention on study and learning
   processes in a sample of university students
SO REVISTA DE PSICODIDACTICA
LA English
DT Article
DE Mindfulness; Academic motivation; Learning strategies; Procrastination;
   Self-regulation
ID ATTENTION
AB This study analysed the effects of a mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) on motivation, learning strategies and approaches, procrastination, and mindfulness in university students. Forty-two students (22 in the experimental group and 20 in the control group) participated in an experimental design with pre-test, post-test, and four-month follow-up measures. The results showed that the intervention was associated with a significant increase in deep motivation, deep learning strategies and approaches, and mindfulness levels, as well as an observed decrease in superficial motivation and strategies, and academic procrastination. These findings indicate that mindfulness training appears to favour a more autonomous and self-regulated motivational profile, may promote deep learning, and tends to contribute to the reduction of maladaptive behaviours associated with studying, such as procrastination. AB The main purpose of the study is to evaluate the theoretically ordered mediating roles of valuing mathematics and confidence in mathematics in explaining the relationship between students' liking for learning mathematics and mathematics achievement. TI Development and Implementation of a Tiered Mentorship Program in a
   General Surgery Residency
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE mentorship; surgery residency; surgical education; career mentorship
ID FORMAL MENTORSHIP; WOMEN
AB OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to describe the development, implementation, and longitudinal evaluation of a structured, tiered mentorship program within a general surgery residency. DESIGN: This was a single-institution descriptive study using anonymous annual resident surveys conducted from 2024 through 2026. SETTING: The study was conducted within the General Surgery Residency Program at a tertiary academic training center in Charlotte, North Carolina. PARTICIPANTS: General surgery residents participating in a formal mentorship program were surveyed annually. Approximately 32 residents were included each year, with an overall response rate of approximately 70%. Mentorship was consistently regarded as highly important to surgical training, and most residents reported that the program positively impacted both residency training and career planning. CONCLUSIONS: A structured, tiered mentorship program in general surgery residency is feasible, sustainable, and highly valued by trainees. Integration of peer, faculty, career, and alumni mentorship may provide longitudinal support throughout residency training and professional development. ( J Surg Ed 83:104080. TI The value of pilot and feasibility studies in nursing education
   research: a worked example
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Pilot study; Feasibility study; Virtual reality; Simulation-based
   learning; Nursing education research
ID SAMPLE-SIZE; CLINICAL-TRIAL; RECRUITMENT; POPULATIONS
AB Background: Feasibility studies play a critical role in determining whether clinical or educational interventions can be implemented as intended before progressing to large-scale trials. In nursing education, many innovative teaching strategies, particularly complex interventions such as simulation-based learning, are often advanced directly to full trials without first establishing feasibility. This premature progression creates recruitment, acceptability, fidelity, and protocol adherence challenges, which may compromise study quality and valuable resources. This paper addresses this gap by clarifying the purpose and value of feasibility studies in nursing education research and outlining key considerations for designing an early-stage feasibility study that aligns with contemporary evidence and best-practice methodological guidance. Methods: A practical, step-by-step methodology is presented for designing rigorous early-stage feasibility studies in nursing education, based on a worked example, structured around the four phases of the Medical Research Council Framework for complex interventions: (1) Development, (2) Feasibility and Piloting, (3) Evaluation, and (4) Implementation Planning. Implication: As a methodological paper, we focus on insights rather than empirical outcomes. Examples from the working feasibility trial demonstrate how feasibility data informs judgments about readiness for a larger study. Funding bodies increasingly value feasibility evidence when assessing readiness for large-scale trials. Conclusion: This methodological paper highlights key considerations for evaluating feasibility and demonstrates how preliminary feasibility data guides decisions about if a study is ready to progress to a larger-scale trial. The examples provided illustrate how feasibility indicators, rather than effect size estimates or hypothesis-driven analyses, support transparent and appropriate decision-making in early-phase research.

While previous research has identified various factors influencing technology acceptance, their complex interplay in shaping continuance intention requires further investigation. This study examines how teacher support, peer support, AI learning self-efficacy, and perceived enjoyment collectively influence learners' continuance intention for AI-enhanced EFL learning. By integrating structural equation modeling (SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), the study moves beyond net effects to uncover conjunctural causality. Analyzing data from 705 Chinese university students, SEM results show that teacher support operates only indirectly via self-efficacy and enjoyment, whereas peer support exerts both direct and indirect effects. Complementing the SEM results, fsQCA reveals five equifinal configurations for high continuance intention, with perceived enjoyment as a core condition in most pathways. Notably, teacher and peer support can compensate for each other in specific contexts, a finding that linear models cannot capture. These insights advance technology acceptance theory by demonstrating that social, cognitive, and emotional factors combine in nonlinear, configurational ways to sustain AI-enhanced language learning. Practical implications for designing adaptive support systems are discussed.

TI Utilization of Escape Room Gamification for Medical Toxicology Education
   of Emergency Medicine Residents
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE education; emergency medicine; gamification; simulation; toxicology
AB Background Medical toxicology is a core area of competence laid out by the American Board of Emergency Medicine (EM). While traditional lecture-based education is crucial for knowledge acquisition, innovative approaches such as escape room gamification may enhance resident engagement. Objectives The authors aimed to compare the effectiveness of in-person escape room gamification with traditional didactic teaching for toxicology education among EM residents. Methods A randomized crossover study was conducted at a large urban academic simulation center. EM residents were assigned to receive medical toxicology education through escape room gamification or traditional lecture. Knowledge acquisition was assessed using a 10-item multiple choice test administered pre- and post-intervention, with knowledge retention at 4-6 weeks. A Likert-Scale survey was utilized to assess participant satisfaction and perceptions. Paired two-tailed t-tests were used for analysis. Results Fifty-one EM residents across various post-graduate years (PGY 1-4) participated in the study. Average knowledge scores graded from 0 to 10 improved significantly after both gamification (6.67 +/- 1.90, p = 0.043) and lecture-based education (7.04 +/- 1.46, p = 0.001) compared to pre-intervention (5.78 +/- 1.53). Most participants (73.5%) preferred escape room gamification. No difference was detected at 4-6 weeks retention assessment, with scores remaining significantly higher than baseline (p < 0.001). Conclusion Escape room gamification demonstrated comparable knowledge acquisition and retention to traditional lectures. Gamification was preferred by learners. Gamification is a feasible, effective, and engaging adjunct for teaching medical toxicology to EM residents.

TI Bridging the Gap to Access? Impact of Pre-Collegiate Summer Program on
   College Outcomes
SO EDUCATION FINANCE AND POLICY
LA English
DT Article
ID MATCHING ESTIMATORS
AB U.S. colleges face persistent inequities-not only in who enrolls, but in who ultimately graduates. While institutions have expanded efforts to diversify incoming classes, students from historically underserved backgrounds, including those who are first-generation and economically disadvantaged, continue to face several barriers that affect their rate of degree completion. This paper evaluates the causal impact of a bridge program called Bridge Scholars Program (BSP), an eight-week pre-collegiate summer initiative at a large public land grant university designed to support such students in their transition to college. Leveraging a fuzzy regression discontinuity design within a local randomization inference framework, highlighting its value for credible causal inference in settings with limited effective sample sizes near the cutoff, I find that BSP substantially improves first-year completion and second-year persistence. While participants receive a $2,500 annual scholarship, comparative analyses of similar financial aid programs suggest that the bundled nature of BSP-including structured summer programming, academic mentoring, and peer support-is central to its effectiveness. These findings underscore the importance of holistic interventions that address both financial and non-financial barriers to student success.

TI Academic Benefits to Full-Time Schools: Evidence from Fortaleza
SO EDUCATION FINANCE AND POLICY
LA English
DT Article
ID MOTHERHOOD
AB Although full-time schools are increasingly available in developing countries, there is a lack of consensus on their effectiveness. Motivated by this gap, this paper studies the effect of enrolling in a new set of full-time schools in the city of Fortaleza, Brazil. For identification, enrollment is instrumented with the distance from the student's graduating primary school to the closest full-time school in operation at that time. The results show that enrollment in a full-time school increases lower secondary-school graduation by 11 percentage points and improves math test scores at the end of this schooling level by 0.22 standard deviation. These findings highlight the potential of full-time schools to significantly improve both student progression and learning outcomes.

TI The Effect of Compulsory Education on Age at First Marriage and Age at
   First Birth: Evidence from a Difference-in-Discontinuity Design
SO EDUCATION FINANCE AND POLICY
LA English
DT Article
ID HEALTH EVIDENCE; SCHOOLING LAWS; MIDDLE-INCOME; FERTILITY; INFERENCE;
   OUTCOMES
AB Using a difference-in-discontinuity research design, this study estimates the causal impact of Turkey's 1997 extension of compulsory schooling-from five to eight years-on girls' age at first marriage and age at first birth. In contrast to previous studies of the reform, this design uses a narrower bandwidth to minimize bias, eliminates general effects associated with being born in January or December, and includes all relevant cohorts in the analysis to produce more accurate and population-representative estimates. The findings show that the increase in mandatory schooling substantially raises girls' educational attainment and improves their labor market outcomes, primarily by reducing their employment in the agricultural sector. Higher educational attainment is also associated with a later age at first marriage and a decline in teenage childbirth. However, the effect on age at first birth disappears after age 19, consistent with the increase in high school graduation rates driven by the reform.

TI The Path of Student Learning Delay During the COVID-19 Pandemic:
   Evidence from Michigan
SO EDUCATION FINANCE AND POLICY
LA English
DT Article
AB Educators and policy makers have been concerned that the COVID-19 pandemic led to substantial delays in learning due to disruptions, anxiety, and remote schooling. We study student achievement patterns over the pandemic using a combination of state summative and higher frequency benchmark assessments for fifth and sixth grade students in Michigan. Comparing pre-pandemic to post-pandemic cohorts, we find that math achievement growth dropped by 0.20 standard deviation more than expected between 2019 and 2022. These drops were larger for Black, Latino, and economically disadvantaged students, as well as students in districts that were at least partially remote in 2021-22. Benchmark assessment results are consistent with summative assessments and show sharp drops in 2020-21 with a partial recovery in math. Reductions in English language arts growth were generally small and statistically insignificant. Both assessments and subjects, however, show recovery stalling at a level below pre-pandemic achievement.

TI The Unintended Consequences of an International Student Shortage:
   Evidence from South Korea
SO EDUCATION FINANCE AND POLICY
LA English
DT Article
ID IMMIGRATION; IMPACT
AB We study the role of international students in the higher education sector and the local economy by exploiting a policy reform in South Korea that restricted the admission of foreign students to local universities. By comparing the pre-and post-reform differences across universities with different pre-reform shares of international student enrollment, we show that an international student shortage resulting from this policy reform significantly worsened the financial outcomes ofuniversities and consequently led to reduced investment in their students. We also document that a reduction in the number of international students in local areas decreased native employment, mainly in low-skilled sectors such as business support services. Our findings suggest that limiting the inflow of international students can have unintended negative spillover effects on both universities and local labor markets.

TI Teacher Effectiveness in Remote Instruction
SO EDUCATION FINANCE AND POLICY
LA English
DT Article
ID ACHIEVEMENT
AB The effect of remote learning on student performance has been a frequent topic of research and discussion in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, yet little is known about the impact of remote instruction on the performance of teachers. This study documents how relative effectiveness of teachers changed when moving from in-person to remote instruction and analyzes the characteristics of teachers associated with greater relative effectiveness during remote instruction. Using matched student/teacher-level data from three large metro-Atlanta school districts, we estimate teacher value-added models to measure the association between teacher characteristics and a teacher's relative contribution to test score growth before and during the period of virtual instruction in the 2020-21 school year. We find evidence of increased variation in overall teacher effectiveness during remote instruction, driven largely by changes in the relative performance of early elementary (K-2) and middle school teachers. Veteran teachers appear relatively more effective in virtual instruction than their less experienced peers, with less experienced teachers performing relatively worse regardless of in-person teaching ability. Finally, we find that the very best in-person teachers are more likely to experience large declines in relative effectiveness when shifting to remote instruction compared with a baseline period with in-person instruction.

TI The Evolving Landscape of Legacy Preference Bans in Postsecondary
   Admissions: Evidence and Policy Implications from Case Studies
SO EDUCATION FINANCE AND POLICY
LA English
DT Article
ID RACIAL COMPOSITION; OUTCOMES
AB "Legacy preferences," the practice of giving admissions bonuses to college applicants with relationships to alumni, have recently fallen under sharp criticism. Critics argue that this practice perpetuates racial and socioeconomic inequality in higher education admissions, and there is a growing policy movement to eliminate legacy preferences. In this brief, we document the evolving landscape of legacy preference bans occurring at the federal, state, and local levels. TI A Web-Based Curricular Inventory of Emergency Medicine Clerkships in the
   United States
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
AB Background Since rotation data were last cataloged in 2013 by Khandelwal et al., there have been significant events that impacted emergency medicine (EM). Investigators sought to determine characteristics of EM experiences offered at US medical schools. We anticipated that, compared to data collected in 2013, there would be more required clinical rotations, but variability in timing and length.Methods We conducted an internet search of publicly available EM curricula for 224 accredited, degree-granting (158 MD, 66 DO) US medical schools. We examined if an EM clinical experience was required, when it occurred, rotation length, and the number and length of shifts.Results We identified that 61.2% (137/224) of schools had a required EM clerkship, most frequently occurring after core clinical rotations. Advanced electives (sub-internships/acting internships) were offered at 110/224 schools (49.1%). These experiences were typically 4 weeks in length. Additional information regarding the number of shifts, shift length, and preceptorship, was limited and variable.Conclusions Most US medical schools require EM rotations, an increase over the prior decade. The Structure and timing of rotations vary, and many curricular details are not publicly available. A direct survey of clerkship directors and continued maintenance of existing repositories are needed to completely assess national trends.

TI The Moderating Effects of Classroom Social Support on the Relationship
   Between Peer Victimization and Children's Emotional-Behavioral
   Functioning
SO CANADIAN JOURNAL OF SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE peer victimization; social support; internalizing symptoms;
   externalizing symptoms; elementary school
ID ADOLESCENT MENTAL-HEALTH; EARLY ELEMENTARY-SCHOOL; LONGITUDINAL
   ASSOCIATIONS; EXPERIENCE QUESTIONNAIRE; INTERNALIZING SYMPTOMS;
   FRIENDSHIP QUALITY; PROSOCIAL BEHAVIOR; TEACHER; CLIMATE; DIFFERENCE
AB Healthy relationships are essential for children's emotional and behavioral development. However, difficulties in peer relationships can negatively affect children's adjustment. This longitudinal study examined whether social support moderates the association between peer victimization and children's internalizing and externalizing symptoms in a sample of Canadian elementary school students in Grades 4 and 5 (N = 399, M age = 9.91). Results indicated that peer support moderated the association between both physical and relational victimization and children's externalizing symptoms, such that higher levels of peer support weakened these associations. Teacher support buffered the association between relational victimization and children's externalizing symptoms. The findings highlight the protective role of social support in mitigating externalizing problems at low and medium levels of peer victimization. Implications for school psychology are discussed, including the importance of fostering supportive peer and teacher relationships, promoting social inclusion, and providing targeted support for students experiencing high levels of victimization.

TI Bridging Theory and Practice: Digital Twin Simulation of a Heat
   Exchanger in Laboratories for Engineering Students
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE CFD; digital twin; engineering education; heat exchanger; laboratory
   simulation; Python
AB Digital twins serve as virtual replicas of physical systems. They can be used as a tool for engineering education by revealing the underlying principles behind unit operations. The project aimed to integrate digital twins into university engineering lab courses, complementing traditional methods by bridging the gap between experimentation and the underlying physical phenomena behind this unit operation. An intuitive application was created using Python, enabling Chemical Engineering students to perform computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations with Ansys while experimenting, connecting the app with the laboratory heat exchanger. Unlike conventional approaches limited to discrete temperature measurements, these simulations provided comprehensive visualizations of temperature profiles across the entire equipment. The app is successfully implemented, delivering reliable simulations that accurately reflect experimental conditions. One of the main challenges consists of the time-intensive nature of the calculations, due to high computational demands. Despite this, this work shows that digital twins can help transform engineering education by incorporating digital solutions. This method could improve educational outcomes and could be extended to other unit operations, although improving computational efficiency will be necessary in future iterations. This project is presented as a technical infrastructure to enable future large-scale educational assessment.

ID ENGINEERING DESIGN; QUESTION PROMPTS; SCIENCE; CLASSROOM;

AB Understanding how groups interact with the task during face-to-face collaborative problem solving in STEM classrooms is central to the task design process of ill-structured tasks. TI Numeracy skills development through indigenous games in pre-school
   learners: a teacher perspective
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF CHILD CARE AND EDUCATION POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous games; Numeracy; Early learning; Play-based learning
ID PEDAGOGY; PLAY
AB This study explores the effectiveness of indigenous games (IG) in fostering numeracy skills among pre-school learners in Chibombo District, Zambia. With an increasing global emphasis on play-based learning, IG offer a culturally relevant and engaging pedagogical approach in Early Childhood Education. Despite the growing recognition of play-based pedagogies, the integration of IG in formal ECE curricula remains under-researched, particularly in African contexts. This study employed a Participatory Action Research (PAR) design within an interpretivist paradigm. The research was conducted with ten ECE teachers from four primary schools in Chibombo District, who were selected purposively. Data were collected through focus group discussions (FGDs) and lesson observations. The study found that IG played a significant role in the acquisition of key numeracy skills, including counting, seriation, problem-solving, and number recognition. Teachers observed increased learner engagement, improved understanding of mathematical concepts, and enhanced critical thinking abilities among children when IG were used in the classroom. Additionally, the games provided a context for integrating cultural knowledge, fostering a sense of identity and connection to local traditions. The study concludes that IG are a valuable pedagogical tool for teaching numeracy in ECE, contributing to child development and preservation of cultural heritage. The paper recommends incorporating indigenous games into teacher training programs to equip educators with the skills to integrate culturally responsive teaching methods into their practice. The study underscores the potential of indigenous games as a transformative educational resource for early childhood numeracy development.

TI The impact of an LLM-based educational agent on learning achievement,
   cognitive dynamics, and student perceptions in computer science
   education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Large language model; Educational agent; Human-AI interaction; Cognitive
   engagement; Lag sequential analysis
AB Background While Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into educational settings, the transition from passive chatbot to autonomous LLM-based agents-characterized by tool use, memory retention, and goal-directed reasoning-remains underexplored. To address this gap, this study designed a domain-specific educational agent (DBagent) for an undergraduate database course, and examined its impact on learning achievement, cognitive engagement patterns, and student perceptions. A large-scale quasi-experiment was conducted with 313 sophomore students across four authentic classes (three experimental and one control) over a four-week period.Results We employed statistical analyses to examine learning achievement and the distribution of cognitive engagement levels, lag sequential analysis (LSA) to analyze cognitive behavior sequences from interaction logs, and structural equation modeling (SEM) to interpret survey data. Findings indicate that (1) the agent-enriched environment significantly improved learning achievement compared with traditional instruction; (2) LSA revealed distinct cognitive trajectories: while student-instructor interactions fostered balanced cognitive levels, student-agent interactions were characterized by high-frequency engagement driven by a specific "Query-Evaluation-Query" verification loop; and (3) SEM analysis confirmed that learners' positive perceptions of the educational agent promoted sustained engagement through the mediating role of satisfaction.Conclusion Taken together, the findings indicate that educational agents can improve learning achievement, foster distinctive cognitive engagement patterns, and sustain learner participation through positive user perceptions. These findings provide empirical evidence for the pedagogical value of educational agents and offer practical implications for the design of GenAI-enriched learning environments.

TI How STEM social capital shapes secondary school students' STEM
   aspirations: the roles of STEM expectations and mathematics competency
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF STEM EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM aspirations; STEM social capital; Parental STEM occupations;
   Homeroom teachers' STEM backgrounds; STEM expectations; Mathematics
   competency; Chinese secondary school students
ID PARENTAL EXPECTATIONS; ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; CAREER-DEVELOPMENT;
   SCIENCE; PARTICIPATION; ACHIEVEMENT; PERSISTENCE; CLASSROOM; CHOICE
AB Background Secondary students' STEM aspirations strongly predict later STEM degrees and careers. Understanding how these aspirations are shaped is therefore critical. Family and school contexts are widely recognized as important influences, but the specific pathways through which these influences operate remain underexplored. Grounded in science capital theory, this study conceptualizes STEM social capital in terms of parental STEM occupations and homeroom teachers' STEM backgrounds, and examines how these factors relate to Chinese secondary school students' STEM aspirations, the mediating pathways involved, and heterogeneity across sex and urban-rural contexts.Results Using data from the 2014-2015 follow-up wave of the nationally representative longitudinal data from the China Education Panel Survey (CEPS), this study analyzed a restricted sample of 5,123 eighth-grade students in 122 classrooms across 61 schools. The sample was restricted to schools with random classroom assignment in seventh grade and no performance-based reshuffling in eighth grade to better identify homeroom teacher effects. Balance checks suggest that the restricted analytical sample is broadly comparable to excluded cases on most school-level characteristics, although it includes fewer rural and socioeconomically disadvantaged schools and students. Linear probability models with school fixed effects were estimated while controlling for student, family, and classroom characteristics, followed by mediation and heterogeneity analyses. The results showed that Chinese secondary school students with greater STEM social capital were more likely to report STEM aspirations. Parental STEM occupations influenced aspirations through STEM expectations, with students' perceived parental STEM expectations exerting a stronger mediating effect. Homeroom teachers' STEM backgrounds were linked to aspirations through mathematics competency, with mathematics performance showing a slightly stronger mediating effect than students' self-assessment of mathematics competency. Heterogeneity analyses showed that parental STEM occupations, particularly fathers' STEM occupations, were more strongly associated with girls' STEM aspirations, whereas homeroom teachers' STEM backgrounds were more strongly associated with boys' STEM aspirations. In addition, parental STEM occupations were significant only in urban schools, whereas homeroom teachers' STEM backgrounds were more pronounced in rural schools.Conclusions This study provides a relational and contextually grounded account of how multiple sources of STEM social capital shape secondary school students' STEM aspirations in the Chinese context. By revealing family- and school-based pathways, this study provides practical guidance and insights for parents, teachers, and policymakers on how to support students' STEM aspirations in China and other similar educational contexts.

TI Applying the CRADLE Method: An Undergraduate Case Study on Machine
   Learning for Chiral Noble Metal Nanoparticles Using Literature-Mined
   Data
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Data Science;
   Interdisciplinary/Multidisciplinary; Machine Learning; Nanoparticle
   Synthesis; Chirality; Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experience
   (CURE)
ID RESEARCH EXPERIENCES; CIRCULAR-DICHROISM; GOLD
AB Integrating artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) into undergraduate chemistry curricula is essential for preparing students for modern research, yet a central challenge remains: providing students with meaningful, research-ready data sets without prohibitive resource demands. To address this challenge, we present CRADLE (Creating Research-ready Data set from Literature for Education), a pedagogical framework in which students construct machine learning-ready data sets through systematic mining of the chemical literature. We demonstrate CRADLE through an undergraduate case study on predicting chiroptical responses in chiral noble metal nanoparticles. Students mined 67 publications to build a 201-entry database, developed a chemically informed feature-encoding strategy, and trained machine learning models. The optimized Extra Trees model (R2 = 0.93) guided the synthesis of gold nanoclusters with an anisotropic g-factor of 0.0035, surpassing the highest literature-mined value in their data set by 95%. Rubric-based course-performance data and anonymous pre/post-project self-assessments suggested that students successfully completed the major project tasks and reported increased confidence in research-related skills; all eight students endorsed the project-based approach. The CRADLE framework is practical and adaptable, offering a scalable model for embedding authentic, data-driven research experiences into undergraduate chemistry courses.

TI Hydrogel Biomaterials Laboratory Modules for Biotransport Education
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Polymer; Swelling; Degradation; Diffusion; Cross-Linking; Inclusive
   Teaching
AB Biotransport, the movement of molecules, energy, and momentum within biological systems, is a foundational concept in biomolecular science and chemical engineering. Acquiring a thorough understanding of biotransport phenomena is essential for the next generation of scientists and engineers to advance applications such as tissue engineering, gene and drug delivery, and biomedical device design. Practical exposure to biomaterial transport phenomena can help develop an intuitive understanding of these concepts. There is a need for accessible, hands-on, and cost-effective laboratory modules to teach biotransport principles at multiple educational levels. As water-swollen macromolecular networks, hydrogels serve as an ideal model system due to their tunable properties and physiological relevance. Here, we present a collection of laboratory modules designed to introduce students to the principles of biotransport and factors influencing molecular diffusion using hydrogel biomaterials. In these laboratory activities, students learn to fabricate both natural and synthetic hydrogels and investigate molecular diffusion as a function of temperature, polymer cross-linking density, polymer concentration, and molecular weight of substance. These modules demonstrate the influence of polymer properties on diffusion but also provide a platform for introducing fundamental polymer chemistry concepts such as polymerization, cross-linking, swelling, and degradation. The experiments are designed to be performed using widely available laboratory materials and equipment, making them suitable for a broad range of educational settings. Together, these hydrogel-based laboratory modules offer an accessible approach for teaching biotransport phenomena, enhancing student engagement, and improving learning outcomes for students with limited background in biomaterials science and engineering.

TI Development and validation of subscales for assessing first-generation
   university students' experiences
SO JOURNAL OF NEW APPROACHES IN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE First-generation university students; Retention; Persistence;
   Undergraduate trajectories; Higher education
ID EXPLORATORY FACTOR-ANALYSIS; COEFFICIENT ALPHA; INTEGRATION
AB This article presents the results of the development and validation of a novel First-Generation University Students Scale (FGUS Scale). It represents the first psychometrically tested set of subscales within a multidimensional framework in Latin America, designed to assess the experiences of FGUSs. Scale development and validation are critical to document these experiences, and to provide a foundation for informing future improvements in the educational experiences of non-traditional higher education students, such as FGUSs. An instrumental design was implemented to develop and examine the psychometric properties of the scale. The sample comprised a total of 530 FGUSs. This included a pre-pilot phase (n = 28), with cognitive interviews conducted with six participants. An analytic sample of 502 participants was then used for psychometric validation, which was split for exploratory (EFA; n = 200) and confirmatory (CFA; n = 302) factor analyses. The final version of the scale consists of 25 items organized into theoretically-meaningful subfactors. Adequate validity and reliability were demonstrated in several subfactors, with a more limited performance in others, supporting their internal structure within each domain. The use of purposive, non-probabilistic samples limits the generalizability of the findings. Future research should focus on implementing a stratified sampling to strengthen the scale's utility and contribute to comparative research on FGUSs across Latin America.

TI The role of instructional quality in explaining socioeconomic
   disparities in mathematics achievement: a multilevel structural equation
   modeling of Swedish TIMSS 2019 data
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational equity; Instructional quality; Instructional clarity;
   Classroom management; Socioeconomic status; Mathematics achievement;
   Multilevel structural equation modelling; TIMSS 2019; Sweden
ID TEACHING QUALITY; COGNITIVE ACTIVATION; ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; SCHOOL
   CHOICE; STUDENT; MOTIVATION; CLASSROOM; TEACHERS; SWEDEN; SEGREGATION
AB Background Socioeconomic status (SES) is an important predictor of achievement, yet the classroom processes through which it may be associated remain debated. This study examines whether student-perceived instructional clarity and classroom management are associated with eighth-grade mathematics achievement in Sweden, and whether these dimensions of instructional quality are associated with SES differences in achievement at the student and classroom levels.Methods Using nationally representative TIMSS 2019 data (Grade 8), we estimated two-level structural equation models in Mplus, incorporating student weights and the plausible-value methodology. We modeled student-perceived instructional clarity and classroom management as latent constructs at within- and between-classroom levels. We tested the direct associations with achievement, indirect pathways between SES and achievement, and a random-slope model for the within-class SES effect, followed by cross-level interactions.Results Instructional clarity was positively related to achievement within classrooms, whereas classroom management showed a stronger association between classrooms; SES remained a robust predictor at both levels. Evidence for indirect associations was limited, as within-class indirect effects via clarity or management were negligible. A small between-class indirect path via classroom management was marginal only. The random-slope variance for the SES-achievement relationship was not statistically significant, indicating little cross-class heterogeneity. Accordingly, cross-level interactions with class-mean SES, clarity, and management were also nonsignificant. Class-mean SES and classroom management showed positive associations with mean achievement at the between-level.Conclusions Findings suggest instructional clarity was more strongly associated with individual-level achievement, while classroom management was more strongly associated with classroom-level achievement. However, these features were not strongly associated with SES-related disparities. Higher levels of instructional quality with higher overall achievement, but closing SES gaps requires combining classroom improvement with broader, equity-oriented policies.
