TI Business Chinese vocabulary learning strategies among international
   undergraduates: usage patterns, group differences, and strategic
   interrelationships
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Vocabulary learning strategies; Business Chinese; Chinese as a second
   language; International students; Self-regulated learning; Quantitative
   research
AB As Business Chinese gains prominence in international language education, understanding how learners acquire its specialized vocabulary becomes increasingly important. This study investigates the vocabulary learning strategies (VLS) employed by 105 international undergraduate students enrolled in Business Chinese courses at four universities in Shanghai. Drawing on Schmitt's (1997) VLS taxonomy, the research aimed to identify the most and least frequently used strategies, examine differences in strategy use based on learner background variables, and analyse interrelationships among strategy categories. A cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted, and data were analysed using descriptive statistics at both category and item levels, t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Pearson correlations. The findings reveal a moderate overall frequency of VLS use (M = 3.08), with metacognitive, determination, and memory strategies being the most commonly used. At the item level, sustained vocabulary study and contextual guessing were among the most frequently used strategies, whereas flashcards and asking teachers to check self-made vocabulary lists were among the least used. Significant differences in strategy use were observed across academic majors, universities, and years of study, with students in Chinese-related majors and upper-year levels demonstrating more diverse and frequent strategy use. Only one gender-related difference emerged, with female students reporting higher use of determination strategies. However, no significant differences were found for age, ethnic background, or duration of learning. Significant positive correlations were identified among all five strategy categories, ranging from moderate to very strong (r = 0.529-0.806), suggesting that Business Chinese learners tend to use vocabulary learning strategies in an interrelated and coordinated manner. These findings highlight the need for more targeted strategy instruction in Business Chinese, particularly for students in non-Chinese-related majors and lower-year learners, as well as more systematic support for underused strategies, such as those related to collaboration and vocabulary review.

TI An AI-Enabled Integrated Blended Teaching Framework for Civil
   Engineering Education: A Case Study From an Undergraduate Program in
   China
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; blended learning; civil engineering education;
   engineering practice; teaching evaluation
ID CONSTRUCTION
AB The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping engineering education by promoting more adaptive, data-informed, and practice-oriented learning paradigms. To address persistent challenges in undergraduate civil engineering education, including insufficient personalized support, limited integration of authentic engineering practice, and over-reliance on summative assessment, this study proposes an AI-enabled integrated blended teaching framework. The framework integrates large language model-assisted learning support, blended instructional design, authentic engineering practice scenarios, and a multidimensional process-oriented assessment system. It was implemented in the undergraduate course Principles of Concrete Structure Design, where mainstream large language models, including Wenxin Yiyan, ChatGPT, and Tongyi Qianwen, were integrated with the Rain Classroom platform to support question answering, learning guidance, resource recommendation, and feedback generation. Course materials, engineering codes, and case documents were incorporated to constrain AI responses, while instructor review and weekly verification were adopted to reduce hallucination risks. Dynamic student profiles were constructed based on learning behavior data to support differentiated learning recommendations. Evaluation using platform logs, academic performance, questionnaires, and inferential statistical analyses showed that the framework was associated with improved engagement, more stable participation, better understanding of engineering practice, and more timely instructional feedback. The findings suggest that embedding AI into instructional mechanisms can support personalized learning, engineering-oriented teaching, and process-based evaluation in civil engineering education.

TI An AI-Driven Framework for Evaluating the Quality of Mechanical
   Engineering Undergraduate Capstone Topics: Development and Empirical
   Validation
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE DeepSeek AI model; dual-dimensional evaluation model; evaluation
   framework; mechanical engineering; topic quality; undergraduate capstone
   project
ID DESIGN
AB Undergraduate capstone projects were a critical component of mechanical engineering talent cultivation, as the quality of topic selection directly determined both the overall quality of the project and the effectiveness of students' competency development. However, the absence of scientific and operable evaluation criteria for topic selection review led to formalistic assessments, ultimately compromising the quality of graduation projects. To address this issue, this study established an evaluation system for mechanical engineering undergraduate capstone project topics based on a dual-dimensional subjective-objective assessment model. A total of 150 graduation projects from the 2024 cohort of the Mechanical Engineering program at Wuhan University of Technology were used as samples. The effectiveness of the proposed evaluation system was validated using the DeepSeek AI model. The results indicated that the predicted topic quality grades generated by the evaluation system achieved a 73.3% consistency rate with students' actual graduation project performance grades. These findings demonstrated that the proposed system could effectively enhance the standardization and reliability of topic selection reviews, providing a practical and valuable theoretical framework and tool for ensuring the quality of undergraduate capstone projects.

TI Epigenetic Pathways to Giftedness: Bridging Biology and Talent
   Development
SO GIFTED CHILD QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE epigenetics; DNA methylation; histone acetylation; BDNF; talent
   development; giftedness; creativity; cognitive function;
   gene-environment interaction; systematic review; equity
ID DNA METHYLATION; NEUROTROPHIC FACTOR; BRAIN-DEVELOPMENT; STRESS; MEMORY;
   BDNF; INHERITANCE; MECHANISMS; PLASTICITY; MODEL
AB Contemporary talent-development models recognize that ability is malleable and shaped by experience, yet lack a mechanistic explanation of how environmental factors biologically enable or constrain cognitive and creative potential. Epigenetics provides that missing layer but has largely been absent from gifted-education scholarship. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from 70 human, animal, and multi-cohort studies, following PRISMA guidelines, to examine how epigenetic mechanisms interact with the conditions shaping the development of cognitive and creative potential across the lifespan. Findings across five thematic domains converge on a consistent pattern: intellectual and creative potential are shaped by cumulative environmental exposures rather than fixed at birth, with early adversity and enrichment leaving biologically detectable signatures that influence learning-related development over time. These findings challenge snapshot-based identification practices, support trajectory-based and context-sensitive assessment, and reframe underrepresentation not as a student deficit but as a constrained developmental opportunity. Epigenetic evidence strengthens the scientific case for equitable, enrichment-first approaches to talent development while reinforcing the field's long-standing commitments to growth, opportunity, and developmental justice.

TI Understanding academic integrity challenges among non-native
   english-speaking students in higher education: a teacher-informed
   reflective analysis
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL FOR EDUCATIONAL INTEGRITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Plagiarism; Academic misconduct; Higher education; Thematic analysis;
   Qualitative research; Academic integrity; NNES students
ID PLAGIARISM; TECHNOLOGY; KNOWLEDGE
AB Academic misconduct and weak academic writing remain persistent concerns for higher education assessment. Although extensive research has examined plagiarism and academic integrity, fewer studies have considered how experienced academic practitioners interpret misconduct among non-native English-speaking students in English-medium higher education contexts. This study adopts a qualitative exploratory case-study design informed by reflective practice. It draws on semi-structured reflective interviews with eight academic practitioners who had taught and assessed NNES students across multiple higher education contexts. Using reflexive thematic analysis, the study identifies three connected themes: forms of academic misconduct, perceived causes of misconduct, and preventive responses. The findings suggest that misconduct among NNES students should not be treated only as deliberate cheating. Rather, intentional academic misconduct, unintentional academic misconduct and poor academic practice may overlap in practice, particularly where students face challenges with academic literacy, citation, paraphrasing, time management and assessment expectations. The paper argues for a preventive response based on explicit academic-integrity education, early writing support, transparent assessment guidance and proportionate institutional handling of low-level poor academic practice.

AB Although coherence is widely cited as an important feature of professional development (PD), few initiatives provide teachers with agency to adapt PD to be coherent with their contexts and experiences. DT Article
DE Quality of homework involvement; Homework procrastination; Homework
   motivation; Parental education level; Students' grade level
ID ACADEMIC PROCRASTINATION; SELF-EFFICACY; CHILDRENS ACHIEVEMENT;
   SOCIOECONOMIC-STATUS; ELEMENTARY-SCHOOL; AUTONOMY SUPPORT; BELIEFS;
   HELP; EXPECTATIONS; ADOLESCENCE
AB Students' homework procrastination significantly affects the quality of homework completion, learning satisfaction, emotional responses to homework, and even academic performance and workload. Reducing homework procrastination is therefore critical for fostering students' academic development and well-being. This study investigated the relationships between three distinct types of parental homework involvement-autonomy support, content support, and structure-and students' homework procrastination. Additionally, the study examined the mediating role of homework motivation, specifically competence beliefs and subjective task value, as well as the moderating effect of parental education level and students' grade level on these relationships. A total of 5394 elementary and middle school students (grades 3-8) participated in the study by completing validated survey measures. However, although competence belief mediated the link between parental content support and homework procrastination, subjective task value did not significantly mediate this relationship; (3) parental education level moderated several relationships among quality of parental homework involvement, homework motivation, and students' homework procrastination and (4) students' grade level moderated the relationship between parental content support and students' homework procrastination. These findings provide important implications for parental strategies to enhance homework-related motivation, foster effective home-school collaboration, and mitigate students' tendencies toward homework procrastination.

TI VETTING: A dual-LLM framework for in-loop safety verification via policy
   isolation in educational AI
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Large language models; AI in education; AI safety; Educational
   technology; LLM guardrails; Runtime security
ID HELP-SEEKING
AB Educational AI systems increasingly rely on large language models to support student writing and inquiry, yet enforcing safety and instructional constraints during open-ended, multi-turn interaction remains challenging. Existing approaches commonly embed such constraints within conversational prompts or rely on static filtering. Over time, these approaches may become sensitive to user interaction, making it difficult to monitor and audit when students are able to circumvent or otherwise attempt to violate such measures. We introduce VETTING, a dual-LLM framework that separates response generation from policy verification and applies explicit policy checks at runtime. The framework is illustrated through a grounded instantiation that enforces instructional and safety constraints without exposing policy specifications during interaction. We evaluate VETTING through an in situ deployment in a middle school writing activity, combining analysis of student-AI interaction behavior, human audit of verification outcomes, and characterization of computational overhead. In this deployment, VETTING achieved a precision of .943, recall of .913, and F1 score of .928, and was associated with an estimated 91.2% reduction in inappropriate content exposure with a 19.6% increase in token usage (628,011 tokens). These results suggest that policy-isolated runtime verification can support the analysis and management of educational AI behavior under authentic classroom use.

TI In the AI era: A project-based digital storytelling framework for art
   and design education
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Project-based learning; Digital storytelling; Creative thinking; Higher
   education; Art and design; Artificial intelligence
ID TORRANCE TESTS; CREATIVITY
AB The ascent of generative artificial intelligence (AI) challenges art and design education to reaffirm the value of human creativity. This study proposes and examines a pedagogical response: a project-based learning (PBL) model with digital storytelling (DS) at its core, designed to cultivate the emotional, cultural, and narrative capacities that AI lacks. Conducted through an embedded case study of the 15-week "Creative Shanzhou" project with 426 Chinese undergraduate students, the research implemented a theoretically-grounded PBL-DS framework. Digital storytelling served as the primary methodology for students to translate local cultural heritage into emotionally resonant, multimodal narratives. Quantitative results revealed strong performance, particularly in novelty (M = 4.21), while effectiveness (M = 3.96) and wholeness (M = 3.68) pointed to areas requiring more extended scaffolding, while qualitative analysis of exemplars illustrated how the DS process, from narrative construction to contextual immersion, facilitated original expression and critical problem-solving. The findings affirm that embedding digital storytelling within an authentic PBL context effectively bridges theory and practice, creating a learning ecology where technology amplifies rather than automates human creativity. This study offers a transferable model for leveraging digital storytelling to develop AI-resistant competencies, with implications for creative education and beyond.

TI Which factors matter in data-driven peer learning: Social intimacy,
   proficiency gaps, or selection autonomy?
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer learning; Social intimacy; Data-driven system; Partner selection;
   Learner autonomy; Knowledge gap
ID PERFORMANCE; FEEDBACK
AB Peer learning is a promising strategy that encourages knowledge co-construction and reflection, while biased partner choice may hinder effective collaboration. Data-driven systems with interpretable learning analytics create new affordances for optimizing peer selection through knowledge awareness. Grounded in a technology-enhanced learning environment, this study investigates how social intimacy, knowledge proficiency gaps, and partner-selection autonomy affect peer learning in a Japanese university academic reading course. The data-driven conditions that underscored proficiency gaps in partner selection mitigated the influence of social intimacy and improved efficiency without compromising learning outcomes, although they alone were insufficient to inherently enhance engagement or learning quality. Helper-initiated pairing demonstrated relatively higher efficiency when learners could autonomously identify knowledge gaps and select partners. This study contributes a substantial implementation of computer-supported peer learning, an empirical analysis of key determinants of peer interaction, and a pedagogically aligned framework for integrating data-driven support into higher education to promote collaborative learning experiences. It also leads to future exploration of balancing these factors through contextualized design and continuously updated learner models incorporating multimodal data, thus extending applications to broader educational contexts.

TI Mothers' work schedules and children's participation in center-based
   early care and education: The role of publicly funded early care and
   education programs
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Early care and education; Work schedules; Child-care subsidy program;
   Head Start; Public pre-kindergarten
ID EARLY-CHILDHOOD EDUCATION; ARRANGEMENTS; QUALITY; ENROLLMENT; IMPACTS
AB A key goal of publicly funded early care and education (ECE) programs-i.e., child-care subsidy, Head Start, and public pre-kindergarten programs-is to increase children in low-income families' participation in high-quality and center-based ECE in order to improve children's development and reduce income-based disparities in child outcomes. Yet, one reason why low-income children might be less likely to participate in center-based ECE than their higher-income counterparts is because their mothers are more likely to work a nonstandard schedule, and these programs typically operate on a daytime weekday schedule. Although publicly funded ECE programs have increased participation in center-based ECE among children from low-income families, it is unknown whether these effects are concentrated among children whose mothers work a standard schedule or also translate to children whose mothers work nonstandard schedules. In this study, we used data from the Survey of Income and Program Participation to estimate associations between public spending on ECE programs and children's participation in center-based ECE, focusing on heterogeneity by mothers' work schedules. We found that public ECE spending was associated with higher rates of center-based ECE participation among young children whose mothers worked standard and nonstandard schedules. Among 3-4-year-old children, gaps in center-based ECE participation between children whose mother worked a nonstandard versus standard schedule were small or nonexistent at high levels of ECE spending. Our findings suggest that publicly funded ECE programs increase lowincome children's center-based ECE participation regardless of mothers' work timing.

TI School-based support staff and chronic absenteeism: Evidence from North
   Carolina
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE K-12 public schools; Chronic absenteeism; School-based support staff
ID MENTAL-HEALTH; CHILD; ABSENCES; OUTCOMES; NURSES
AB In this paper, I investigate the causal impact of school-based support staff on student absences and chronic absenteeism using the introduction of the Child and Family Support Team (CFST) program in North Carolina. Introduced during the 2006/07 school year, the CFST program funded two-person teams composed of a nationally-certified school nurse and a state-licensed school social worker in 43 elementary schools. The teams worked in schools to identify and intervene with students who faced economic, health, and social barriers to academic success. Taking advantage of two sources of variation, I estimate impacts for students in directly treated schools, which received CFST teams, and indirectly treated schools, which experienced staffing increases through district reallocation and hiring responses to CFST. Using event-study and difference-in-differences approaches, I find that high-risk students in directly treated schools experienced reductions in absences of 0.4 days per year (6%) and a 0.9 percentage point reduction in the likelihood of chronic absenteeism (12%). Students in indirectly treated schools experienced smaller declines in absences of 0.2 days per year (3%) but no statistically significant effects on the likelihood of chronic absenteeism. Although I interpret the estimates from indirectly treated schools with caution, the pattern and magnitude of effects corroborate the main findings from directly treated schools. Overall, the main results indicate that intensive, team-based school-based support staffing models are effective for identifying and supporting high-risk students. The findings highlight the role of health and social services in reducing chronic absenteeism and inform education policy related to school-based support staff in K-12 public schools.

TI How I Do It: OpenTrainer, An Open-Source Laparoscopic Surgery Simulator
   With a Smartphone Endoscope
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE surgery simulator; smartphone; endoscope; surgical education;
   laparoscopic training; Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery Exam
AB OBJECTIVE: To develop a low-cost DIY laparoscopic surgical simulator that uses a smartphone and can easily be replicated. DESIGN: (1) utilize fabrication methodologies available at most university or community makerspaces (2) utilize hardware and software that is easy to access and install (3) include training modules for the Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) exam. (4) provide a framework for developing surgery training modules. SETTING: Nonclinical collaboration between biomedical engineering and surgery departments at an academic medical center. PARTICIPANTS: N/A. RESULTS: The FLS trainer, a commercial surgical simulator commonly used to prepare for the FLS exam, costs $4686.1 We designed OpenTrainer as a low-cost alternative. OpenTrainer utilizes the following materials and manufacturing methods to enable broad accessibility: a smartphone screen as the display, a smartphone-linked industrial endoscope as the camera, laser-cut acrylic as the device body, and 3D printed plastic as trocars and FLS exam modules. OpenTrainer costs less than $150 in materials (Appendix A). Design features enable easy manufacturing and use while maintaining the fidelity of traditional simulators: (1) trocars are based on an existing design from Thingiverse, (2) binding pins enable quick assembly and disassembly for portable use, and (3) the endoscope holder allows the user to adjust the viewing angle as needed. We also developed modules that replicate each FLS task: (1) 3D-printed pegs for peg transfers, (2) a gauze holder for precision cutting, and (3-5) a laser-cut EVA foam holder for ligation and suturing. CONCLUSIONS: By utilizing fabrication methodologies available at most university and community makerspaces, the OpenTrainer surgical simulator is readily made at low cost, enabling more trainees to access laparoscopic training, and potentially earlier in training. Within the OpenTrainer footprint, new training modules can be designed for students to practice techniques beyond the traditional FLS exam. AB In response to the global spread of English, China has promoted a competence-based agenda in English curricula to cultivate students who will become well-rounded, adaptive and inclusive on the international stage.    Design Variable in Refugee Education

LA English
DT Article
DE AI in refugee education; conceptual framework; cultural identity;
   ethical AI design; displaced learners; multilingual NLP; affective
   computing; SDG 4.7
ID MENTAL-HEALTH
AB More than 43 million children are currently displaced globally, yet the artificial intelligence (AI) systems deployed in their education are rarely designed with cultural identity, linguistic continuity, or belonging as architectural concerns. Existing frameworks treat identity as a contextual consideration surrounding educational technology; this paper argues that identity should be treated as a design variable within AI system architecture itself. The paper develops the AI-Based Identity Support Framework (AISF), a conceptual model constructed through interdisciplinary synthesis across bodies of literature including cultural bereavement theory, narrative identity, ethical AI design, and multilingual AI systems, and informed by the author's practitioner engagement with displaced communities (2018-2023). The AISF specifies three interlocking domains (cultural anchoring, emotional co-construction, and adaptive belonging), each defined operationally and accompanied by diagnostic indicators, design principles, and a preliminary assessment rubric. The framework is differentiated from trauma-informed pedagogy, culturally sustaining pedagogy, and principle-based AI ethics as a system-architectural rather than pedagogical construct. The paper engages critically with risks internal to identity-supportive AI architectures, including essentialization, surveillance, and algorithmic identity-fixing, and addresses low-resource deployment constraints. The AISF is intended to provide a structured diagnostic instrument for designers, evaluators, and policymakers, aligned with Sustainable Development Goals 4.7, 10, and 16.

TI Beyond Vocabulary Breadth: Homonym Knowledge and Reading Comprehension
   Among Multilingual Learners and English-Monolingual Elementary Students
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE homonym knowledge; vocabulary depth; multilingual learners; reading
   comprehension; lexical quality
ID METALINGUISTIC AWARENESS; LANGUAGE LEARNERS; WORD KNOWLEDGE; CHILDREN;
   GROWTH; INSTRUCTION; PROFICIENCY; OUTCOMES; SKILLS; DEPTH
AB This study examined (a) the development of vocabulary breadth and vocabulary depth, operationalized as homonym knowledge, across one academic year (fall to spring) in Grades 1-4 for multilingual learners and English monolinguals and (b) the concurrent and longitudinal relations between homonym knowledge and reading comprehension. Participants were 758 elementary students (60% multilingual learners) who completed measures of vocabulary breadth, homonym knowledge, word identification, and reading comprehension in fall and spring. Two 2 (Time) & times; 2 (Language) & times; 4 (Grade) mixed ANOVAs and hierarchical regressions were conducted. Both multilingual learners and monolinguals showed significant growth in vocabulary breadth and homonym knowledge over the academic year, but growth rates were comparable across language groups and grades, indicating a persistent vocabulary gap between multilingual learners and monolinguals. Hierarchical regressions showed that fall homonym knowledge uniquely contributed to fall reading comprehension after controlling for fall vocabulary breadth and word identification. Longitudinally, fall homonym knowledge also predicted spring reading comprehension after accounting for fall reading comprehension, word identification, and vocabulary breadth. These results highlight homonym knowledge as an aspect of vocabulary depth that is associated with reading comprehension in early elementary grades for both multilingual learners and monolinguals, and point to the potential value of explicit instruction on homonyms to support multilingual learners' literacy and content-area learning.

TI Assessing Student Motivation in Financial Literacy in Higher Education:
   Adaptation and Preliminary Psychometric Evaluation of the Financial

SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

DT Article
DE academic motivation scale; amotivation; intrinsic motivation; extrinsic

   MODEL; SEM
AB This quantitative study adapted the Academic Motivation Scale (AMS) to the Financial Calculus context in higher education. It examined the preliminary psychometric properties of the resulting Financial Literacy Academic Motivation Scale (FLAMS). The 28 AMS items were translated, contextually adapted, and administered to 164 Portuguese undergraduate students enrolled in Financial Calculus during the 2023/2024 and 2024/2025 academic years. Future research should replicate the model in larger independent samples, test measurement invariance across cohorts and institutional contexts, and examine associations with external criteria, including Financial Calculus grades, financial-literacy learning outcomes, engagement, and persistence.

TI Re-Mapping Teacher Mentoring in Dynamic and Challenging Educational
   Contexts: A Longitudinal Bibliometric Landscape Analysis (2010-2025)
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher mentoring; professional learning; teacher identity; teacher
   training; induction; bibliometrics; VOSviewer; science mapping;
   co-occurrence analysis; overlay visualisation; density visualisation
ID SCIENCE
AB Mentoring has become a central mechanism of teacher support and professional learning, while the conditions of teaching have been reshaped by socio-political uncertainty, teacher shortages, digitalisation, increasingly diverse student needs, and the COVID-19 pandemic itself. This study aimed to map the conceptual structure and temporal evolution of research on teacher mentoring and professional learning. A longitudinal bibliometric and science-mapping analysis was conducted on 2843 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus database and published between 2010 and 2025, using co-occurrence (co-word) analysis of author and indexed keywords in VOSviewer 1.6.20, complemented by network, overlay and density visualisations. The final co-word map comprised 123 keyword elements organised into four clusters, with 3312 links and a total link strength of 17,024. The central node was 'mentoring' (532 occurrences; 121 links; total link strength = 2212; average publication year = 2019.40). Four thematic lines structured the discourse: (1) professionalisation in the wider sense, including health education mentoring; (2) initial teacher education and the induction of new teachers; (3) higher education and digitally mediated environments of professional learning; and (4) bridging concepts of collaboration and professional identity formation. The findings indicate that, within the literature mapped, mentoring functions as a relational, context-sensitive form of support connecting several arenas of professional learning. This study contributes a longitudinal conceptual map of the field; the results describe the intellectual structure of the literature and do not constitute evidence of the effectiveness of mentoring practices.

TI Reconceptualizing the L2 Writing Process: GenAI-Human-Mediated Feedback
   Through Ecological Languaging Competencies
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE GenAI; human assistant; higher education; GenAI-mediated writing;
   ecological languaging competencies; L2 writing
ID DYNAMICS
AB Generative AI (GenAI) has transformed L2 writing, producing human-like prose but often impersonal feedback. This study explores the potential of GenAI-human collaborative feedback, focusing on the first author's experience as a teaching assistant in a Hong Kong public university's Bachelor of Education (English language track). Grounded in Ecological Languaging Competencies (ELC) and its affordance framework, this study employs an ethnographic approach informed by narrative inquiry and phenomenology. Data were drawn from Zoom tutoring sessions incorporating interview-style questions to investigate participants' perspectives and experiences, GenAI-student conversation logs, and final assignments in order to analyze two multilingual students' GenAI-human-mediated L2 writing processes. In both cases, GenAI demonstrates consistent limitations in facilitating the situated, embodied, and affectively attuned dimensions of languaging that effective L2 writing entails. This study makes two contributions: it extends ELC's affordance network to tertiary-level GenAI-human-mediated L2 writing, and it reconceptualizes writerly authorship as a distributed yet agentively orchestrated practice. Moreover, co-agentic GenAI-human feedback foregrounds ecological embeddedness, writerly agency, and ethical GenAI integration.

TI Collective identity development in higher education teacher teams: a
   realist synthesis study protocol explaining how collective identity
   develops in and shapes co-creative practice
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE co-creation; collective identity; higher education; realist synthesis;
   study protocol; teacher teams
ID COLLABORATION
AB This article presents a protocol for a realist synthesis that aims to explain how collective identity develops in higher education teacher teams, and how it enables or constrains co-creation under different contextual conditions. Teaching in higher education increasingly requires teachers to jointly design and enact complex, open-ended learning environments. This demands sustained processes of shared sensemaking, negotiation, and alignment that go beyond mere coordination. In this study, collective identity is conceptualized not only as an outcome, but as a generative mechanism within these processes. It is understood as a shared interpretive frame comprising shared language, values, and practices through which teacher teams develop a shared basis for co-creative practice. Using realist synthesis methodology and guided by initial programme theories, the review will identify and refine context-mechanism-outcome configurations that explain how collective identity develops and functions in different contextual conditions. The findings will contribute to a more refined understanding of educational collaboration as a complex social system by clarifying how collective identity develops and functions as a mechanism for co-creation in higher education teacher teams. In doing so, the study provides a theoretical foundation for the design of context-sensitive interventions aimed at strengthening co-creative practice.

TI Do teachers differentiate materials, lessons, or children? A
   mixed-method study on differentiated (reading) instruction of Austrian
   primary school teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE differentiated instruction; differentiation; digital tools; inclusive
   practices; mixed methods; reading instruction; reading promotion
ID LITERACY; ACHIEVEMENT; EDUCATION
AB Differentiated instruction is promoted to address student diversity, yet little is known about its implementation within the context of digitalization and reading promotion. This mixed- methods study examines Austrian primary school teachers' conceptions and practices of differentiated (reading) practices. Survey data (N = 252) and interviews (N = 10) reveal differentiation as an approach to address individual needs and promote equity, primarily through tiered assignments and worksheets during the practice phase of lessons mainly based on teachers' experience. Systematic integration of differentiated reading promotion is lacking regarding subskills: reading accuracy, fluency, and strategies. The findings hold implications for teacher education and policy decisions.

TI A lightweight multi-scale deep separable network for early dropout
   prediction in MOOCs: balancing accuracy and educational deployability
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE deep learning; depthwise separable convolution; learner behavior
   modeling; MOOC dropout prediction; multi-scale feature learning
AB Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) have expanded access to higher education, yet high dropout rates persist. Early identification of at-risk learners is essential for timely support, but current predictive models often prioritize technical accuracy over practical applicability in educational contexts. This study investigates a lightweight multi-scale deep learning model for early dropout prediction in MOOCs, designed for use on typical school and university hardware. The proposed Multi-scale Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural Network (Multi-scale DSCNN) features decision-tree-based data cleaning to reduce noise, parallel multi-scale feature learning to capture relationships in learner behavior, and a symmetric architecture that reduces computational requirements. Evaluated on the KDD Cup 2015 dataset, the model achieved 91.5% accuracy, 97.7% recall, and 95.1% F1-score. High recall ensures few at-risk students are missed, while the efficient design allows near-real-time prediction on common devices. Balancing accuracy with deployability (0.16M parameters, 1.8M FLOPs, CPU-only inference, 85 MB RAM), this approach enables practical integration of dropout prediction in educational settings, supporting timely and equitable interventions, (97.7% recall, 2.3% miss rate), and is suitable for standard school computers (runs on Intel i5-8250U with 1.82 ms per sample inference time).

AB <p style="margin-left:0px; margin-right:0px">This study examines how full-time undergraduate and graduate students at a leading technical university in Uzbekistan engage with generative AI tools and how this relates to cognitive regulation, motivation, self-regulation, and ethical awareness. Using a quantitative exploratory design, an online survey was administered to 381 participants during the first (autumn) semester of the 2025-2026 academic year. A preliminarily screened 30-item instrument was developed across seven scales AI Use, Digital Attention, Cognitive Load, Motivation, Self-Regulation, Neuro-AI Pedagogical Competence, and Ethics and Academic Autonomy with internal consistency ranging from alpha = 0.717 to alpha = 0.895; content and discriminant validity have not yet been confirmed on independent samples. Group comparisons were conducted using Mann-Whitney U with Cohen's d on a balanced subsample (n = 302; 151 per group), constructed to avoid confounding group-size asymmetry with substantive group differences. Significant between-group differences were found on six of seven scales (p < .001): Ethics and Academic Autonomy (d = 1.47), AI Use (d = 1.29), Self-Regulation (d = 1.14), Neuro-AI Pedagogical Competence (d = 1.14), and Digital Attention (d = 0.99) showed large effects; Motivation showed a medium effect (d = 0.70). Cognitive load did not differ significantly (p = .296). Multiple regression (n = 372) identified Ethics and Academic Autonomy (beta = 0.446), Self-Regulation (beta = 0.279), and Motivation (beta = 0.178) as the strongest predictors of Neuro-AI Pedagogical Competence (R-2 = 0.799). The findings suggest that higher scores on Neuro-AI Pedagogical Competence were associated with stronger ethical awareness, self-regulation, and motivation, rather than with frequency of AI use. The study contributes empirical evidence from Central Asian higher education and supports the design of level-differentiated AI-integrated curricula.

TI Succeeding at Defining Success: How Governing Organizations Frame
   Student Success in U.S. Higher Education
SO JOURNAL OF POSTSECONDARY STUDENT SUCCESS
LA English
DT Article
DE student success; higher education; literature review; university
   governance
ID INTERVENTIONS; ENGAGEMENT; PROGRAM
AB Student success has become a buzzword in higher education, with many governing organizations now incorporating this metric into strategic plans and faculty evaluations. The extant literature varies in how this construct is defined and measured in modern education. This study offers a contextual overview of how student success has been defined in research throughout the 20th and 21st centuries. Further, the study analyzes guidelines and policies related to student success found in publicly available documents from a purposive sample of 21 higher education governing organizations across the United States. Results reveal myriad approaches to defining student success, often centered on retention, progression, and graduation, but with limited transparency around how definitions were developed or which stakeholders contributed. Recommendations include using more precise and descriptive language to clarify how student success is defined and measured across contexts. The study also finds that both academic research and policymaking efforts oftentimes fail to reflect the views of all stakeholders (e.g., students, faculty, administrators), supporting the recommendation to include all perspectives when appropriate.

TI Roommates, Floormates, and Success: Multilevel Analyses of the Role of
   International Peers
SO JOURNAL OF POSTSECONDARY STUDENT SUCCESS
LA English
DT Article
DE international students; roommates; academic achievement; retention;
   graduation
ID STUDENT SATISFACTION; INTERGROUP CONTACT; SOCIAL NETWORKS; COLLEGE;
   ACCULTURATION; FRIENDSHIPS; EXPERIENCE; COMMUNITY; EDUCATION; AMERICA
AB The increasing internationalization of higher education brings opportunities for international and domestic students to interact with one another in productive and meaningful ways. This study examined residential environments in which international and domestic students may be placed in close physical proximity and spend a great deal of time together. Using an institutional dataset of 1,340 international students and 20,323 domestic students from a large research university in the United States, this study explored the extent to which having at least one international roommate and the percentage of international floormates predicts success outcomes among international and domestic students. The results of multilevel regression analyses showed that domestic students living with international roommates tended to have lower grades, retention rates, and graduation rates than domestic students living with domestic roommates; similar adverse findings were observed for the percentage of international floormates. In contrast, the presence of international roommates and floormates was unrelated to success outcomes among international students.

TI A Novel Association and Ranking Approach Identifies Factors Affecting
   Educational Outcomes of STEM Majors
SO JOURNAL OF POSTSECONDARY STUDENT SUCCESS
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM education; student success in college; graduation outcomes;
   academic performance predictors; multifactor analysis; STEM; D-basis
ID STUDENTS; COLLEGE; SCIENCE; PERSISTENCE; GAPS
AB Improving undergraduate success in STEM requires identifying actionable factors that impact student outcomes, allowing institutions to prioritize key leverage points for change. Based on Astin's Input-Environment-Output model, we examined academic, demographic, and institutional factors that might be associated with graduation rates of STEM majors at two private four-year colleges in the northeastern United States using a novel association algorithm called D-basis to rank attributes associated with graduation. Importantly, the data included outcomes of students who left their original institutions. Key attributes associated with graduation included performance in introductory STEM courses, the choice of first mathematics class, and flexibility in major selection. Specifically, high grades in introductory biology, general chemistry, and mathematics courses were strongly associated with graduation. Students who changed majors-especially from STEM to non-STEM-also had higher overall graduation rates. Financial need and demographic factors, although less predictive overall, revealed disparities in time to graduation. The findings highlight the importance of early academic support to enhance student success in STEM gateway courses and the implementation of institutional policies that provide flexibility in major selection. This study offers data-driven insights to guide strategies to increase bachelor's degree completion.

TI Fostering collaborative futures: Multidisciplinary approaches to AI
   integration in educational ecosystems
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Educational ecosystem; Data needs; Adaptive
   learning; Ethics; Privacy; Policy recommendation; Learning analytics;
   Delphi study
AB With the rapid evolution of AI and data-driven technologies, AI integration in the educational ecosystem requires careful consideration. This paper aims to facilitate the process of fostering collaborative futures with AI agents in education by examining the impact of AI on education from the perspectives of researchers, practitioners, and policymakers. The authors conducted a Delphi study involving a survey administered to N = 70 international professionals, followed by in-depth face-to-face discussions with a panel of international experts from policy, research, and practice to identify key trends and challenges for deploying AI in education. Additionally, top importance included (4) the ongoing imperative to explainability and trustworthiness of AI agents and (5) accessibility and equal access to AI agents. Based on these findings, the paper outlines policy and action recommendations for collaborative AI initiatives in education and proposes a research agenda to address identified research gaps.

TI Alignment Between Assessment Processes and Active Methodologies in
   Primary Education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Active methodologies; Formative assessment; Assessment literacy; Primary
   education; Mixed methods
AB Active Methodologies and formative assessment are two fundamental components of contemporary competency-based educational approaches. Although both have been widely studied independently, limited evidence is available regarding how they are articulated in teaching practice and which factors facilitate or hinder coherence between active methodologies, assessment, and grading in primary education. This study examined such coherence from teachers' perspectives, as well as the influence of training-related, professional, institutional, and disciplinary factors. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed. The quantitative phase involved 500 Spanish primary school teachers and included descriptive, correlational, and inferential analyses using the OCDUMA and MAEV-G instruments. Subsequently, the qualitative phase analysed open-ended responses through Grounded Theory procedures to gain a deeper understanding of the quantitative findings. The results revealed positive associations between favourable perceptions of active methodologies and assessment and grading practices. Specific training in active methodologies emerged as one of the factors most closely associated with greater methodological and assessment coherence. Differences were also observed according to professional experience, school ownership, and teaching area. Qualitative findings indicated positive perceptions of self-assessment, peer assessment, and continuous feedback, alongside barriers related to administrative workload, time constraints, and training needs. The findings suggest that coherence between active methodologies, assessment, and grading is not an automatic consequence of pedagogical innovation but rather a process shaped by training-related, professional, and institutional factors. The study provides empirical evidence on the conditions that promote such coherence and highlights the importance of strengthening assessment literacy and the organisational conditions required for the sustainable implementation of competency-based approaches in primary education.

TI International insights into the academic mindset of economics students
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF ECONOMICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic mindset; Self-efficacy; Growth mindset
ID GROWTH MINDSET; SELF-EFFICACY; PERFORMANCE; VALIDATION
AB This paper investigates the academic mindset of economics students across eight countries using a large-scale dataset collected through the Economic Education Network for Experiments (EENE) in 2023/24 and 2024/25. Surveys from 1188 students and 13 instructors across 18 modules at 11 universities outside the United States measured four dimensions of academic mindset - belonging, self-efficacy, growth mindset, and perceived relevance - at the start and end of a teaching term. We find that students' mindsets are dynamic and context-dependent rather than uniformly improving over time. While perceptions of belonging within economics and the discipline's relevance tended to increase, general self-efficacy and beliefs about the accessibility of economics declined during the academic term. Gender consistently emerged as an important source of heterogeneity: non-male students reported lower self-efficacy and weaker perceived relevance of economics, with several gaps remaining evident by term's end. Pedagogical context was also associated with outcomes: active learning environments and intermediate-level courses were often linked to stronger mindset measures, while larger institutions and later academic years were sometimes associated with weaker outcomes. Cross-national variation was substantial. These results highlight that student self-efficacy and identity with economics are associated not only with individual characteristics but also with pedagogical practice and institutional context. The findings point to the potential value of inclusive, interactive teaching and culturally sensitive approaches to support diverse participation in economics education worldwide.

AB OBJECTIVE: The Dunning-Kruger effect is a well-researched influence on the abilities of individuals to accurately estimate their competence in any given domain, such that those with less expertise overestimate their abilities and those with more expertise under estimate their abilities. TI The attention crisis in nursing education predates generative AI
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing education; Generative artificial intelligence; Sustained
   attention; Attention economy; Digital pedagogy
ID MEDIA
AB Generative artificial intelligence [GenAI] is increasingly treated as a primary explanation for students' perceived difficulties with sustained attention in nursing education. The author contends that such a framing risks misdiagnosing a longerstanding educational concern. While GenAI raises legitimate issues related to misinformation, overreliance, academic integrity, privacy, and critical thinking, students' attentional difficulties should also be understood within the broader history of the attention economy, short-form media, and digitally saturated learning environments. Drawing on literature on sustained attention, cognitive effort, attention regulation, digital distraction, short-form media, and GenAI in healthcare education, the author highlights a chronological mismatch between the recent emergence of widely accessible GenAI tools and earlier shifts in digital environments that reward novelty, rapid attentional switching, and low-friction engagement. Rather than reducing the issue to shortened attention span, the author examines how digitally saturated learning environments reshape sustained attention, attention regulation, and tolerance for cognitive effort in nursing education. This reframing matters because nursing education depends on students' capacity to sustain attention during clinical reasoning, patient assessment, communication, documentation, simulation-based learning, and safe decision-making. GenAI may amplify or make visible pre-existing challenges, but restriction alone is unlikely to address the broader attentional conditions shaping students' learning. Thus, the author calls for attention-supportive pedagogy that scaffolds cognitive effort, makes reasoning visible, supports digital and AI literacy, and deliberately cultivates sustained attention, critical evaluation, and clinical judgment in nursing education. Rather than treating declining attention span as a fixed cognitive trait or uniform population-level decline, the paper focuses on difficulties with sustained attention and attention regulation in contemporary nursing education. This reframing matters because nursing education depends on students' capacity to sustain attention during clinical reasoning, patient assessment, communication, documentation, simulation-based learning, and safe decision-making. GenAI may amplify or make visible pre-existing challenges, but restriction alone is unlikely to address the broader attentional conditions shaping students' learning. The paper therefore calls for attention-supportive pedagogy that scaffolds cognitive effort, makes reasoning visible, supports digital and AI literacy, and deliberately cultivates sustained attention, critical evaluation, and clinical judgment in nursing education.

TI Easy-to-difficult transfer improves long-term motor learning of complex
   skills in autistic children: A randomized controlled trial
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Motor learning; Easy-to-difficult transfer; Bicycle riding;
   Skill retention; Skill transfer
ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; ACQUISITION
AB Autistic children frequently experience motor coordination difficulties that, together with environmental barriers such as limited availability of trained professionals and inclusive physical activity settings, restrict participation in physical activities and reduce opportunities for social interaction. Despite the importance of motor skill development in this population, few studies have examined teaching strategies that optimise long-term skill acquisition and generalisation. Few studies have examined motor learning strategies that optimize long-term skill acquisition and generalization in this population. This study investigated whether an easy-to-difficult transfer framework would enhance the acquisition, retention, and transfer of a complex motor skill-two wheel bicycle riding-compared with a traditional training-wheels approach. Fifty children aged 5-8 years (24 with autism, 26 typically developing [TD]) were randomly assigned within their diagnostic groups to either the easy-to-difficult transfer condition (balance bike to assisted wheels to independent riding) or the traditional condition (training wheels progression only). Participants completed six acquisition sessions over two weeks, followed by retention and transfer tests two weeks later. Riding performance was measured using a validated 15-item questionnaire (maximum score = 75). During acquisition, both TD groups performed equivalently and superior to both autism groups. Within the autism groups, the conventional approach produced significantly higher scores from Session 2 onward. However, the easy-to-difficult transfer group showed markedly superior retention and transfer performance across both populations. For autistic children, the easy-to-difficult group outperformed the traditional group in retention (M = 62.17, SD = 7.17 vs. M = 48.50, SD = 13.88) and transfer (M = 62.25, SD = 5.85 vs. M = 40.50, SD = 11.38). Parallel advantages were observed in the TD sample. Although traditional practice accelerated short-term gains during acquisition of complex skills, the easy-to-difficult transfer framework promoted more robust long-term retention and generalization, particularly in autistic children. This theoretically grounded approach offers a promising strategy for motor skill interventions in developmental disabilities.

DE Online composition; Student success; Validating experiences; Academic
   outcomes; Holistic contexts; High-context communication
AB This case study examines factors that significantly affect student success in online first- and second-year composition at an open-access community college and, in doing so, contributes to scholarship on online composition and student success by empirically linking community and communication through high-context communication and students' holistic contexts to indicators of academic outcomes and validating experiences. TI Developing consensus on entrustable professional activities for bachelor
   of pharmacy graduates in Namibia: A modified Delphi study
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrustable professional activities; Pharmacy education;
   Competency-based education; Delphi technique; Undergraduate pharmacy;
   Namibia
AB Background: Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) translate competencies into observable workplace tasks and are central to competency-based pharmacy education. However, context-specific EPAs for undergraduate pharmacy training in low-and middle-income countries, including Namibia, remain limited. Objective: To develop and achieve stakeholder consensus on core EPAs required of University of Namibia Bachelor of Pharmacy (BPharm) graduates prior to internship. Methods: A two-round modified Delphi study was conducted with Namibian pharmacists from academia, public and private sectors, and regulatory bodies who had experience supervising intern pharmacists. Round 1 evaluated 40 draft EPAs derived from Namibia's 2010 National Pharmacist Competency Framework using a five-point Likert scale and open-text feedback. EPAs achieving >= 75% consensus progressed to Round 2, where they were assessed for essentiality, clarity, and observability using retention thresholds of >= 70% essential and >= 90% observable. Descriptive statistics and qualitative comment analysis informed refinement of the final framework. Results: Of 33 invited pharmacists, 18 completed Round 1 and 10 completed Round 2, with participant attrition occurring between rounds. Eleven EPAs were excluded after Round 1, mainly those related to veterinary medicines, disaster response, and selected management functions. In Round 2, 17 of the 29 EPAs failed observability or essentiality thresholds and were considered overly specialized, unclear, or insufficiently observable. The final 12 EPAs covered compounding and manufacturing, patient care, clinical pharmacy, supply chain management, and pharmacovigilance. Conclusion: A contextually relevant EPA framework for Namibian BPharm graduates was developed and may support curriculum development, workplace-based assessment, and graduate preparedness.

LA English
DT Article

   education
ID CHALLENGES
AB Parental educational anxiety is increasingly visible in competitive education systems, but less is known about how family resources may be linked to both lower and higher worry. Using a 2020 parent survey from Suzhou, China (N = 91,967), this study examines how family socioeconomic status (SES) is associated with parents' education-related worry through extracurricular tutoring intensity and parental involvement. TI Sustainability education in business schools: From responsible
   management identity to sustainable marketing competency
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sustainability education; Responsible management identity; Perceived
   sustainable marketing competency; Experiential learning; Management
   education
AB Although there is increasing adoption of sustainability in business education, there is a paucity of empirical studies that describe the process of sustainability education transferring to domain specific managerial skills. Based on the Transformative Learning Theory, Experiential Learning Theory, and Social Identity Theory, this paper constructs and empirically validates an integrative model, which connects exposure to sustainability education with perceived sustainable marketing competency via the mediating variable of responsible management identity. The model also investigates the moderating relationship of the intensity of experiential learning and the Teaching Approach Quality. 1154 business students in Jordan, Palestine, and Saudi Arabia were used to gather data and analyzed through PLS-SEM. Multigroup analysis indicates structural invariance across the three countries. The research contributes to the responsible management education literature by demonstrating that sustainability education is associated not only with what students know, but also with how they perceive themselves as future managers, with responsible management identity playing a central role in the development of perceived sustainable marketing competency.

TI Exploring the Interface of Hyperconjugation and Polarizability-Enhancing
   Pedagogies for Charge Stabilization in Organic Chemistry
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate/General; Organic Chemistry; Physical Chemistry;
   Misconceptions/Discrepant Events; Alcohols; Alkanes; Ammonium Compounds;
   Carbocations; Covalent Bonding; Computational Chemistry
ID CORRELATED MOLECULAR CALCULATIONS; GAS-PHASE ACIDITIES; GAUSSIAN-BASIS
   SETS; ATOMS; CATIONS; DONOR
AB The stabilization of positive and negative charges by alkyl groups (in particular) in organic compounds is often described as polarizability, but it can also be described as hyperconjugation (and related stereoelectronic effects). To a large extent, how one describes charge stabilization depends on the bonding model used. One can only talk about hyperconjugation in the context of a localized bonding model (hybridization). However, using this bonding model, it is less intuitive to talk about polarization of the whole molecule, which requires full molecular orbitals. It is important in chemical education to be aware of the limitations and intersections of the models we are using. In this work, we show that the polarization of alkyl chains in representative molecules, either by a computationally applied field or by a charge in the molecule, is reflected in changes in hyperconjugative interactions throughout the structure in a logical and predictable manner. This makes a clear and accessible point that hyperconjugation and polarizability are simply two models (at least for charge stabilization) that explain the same phenomenon. In this work, we identify advantages and limitations of each explanation, giving educators examples that can be used in teaching at various levels.

TI Perceptions of Pre-Clerkship Surgical Scrub Training and Operating Room
   Orientation Among Medical Students: A Needs Assessment and Pilot
   Implementation
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE clinical clerkship; curriculum; medical; medical education; operating
   rooms; students; surgical education
AB OBJECTIVES: Early clinical exposure is essential for medical students, yet the degree varies across institutions. At UC Irvine School of Medicine, pre-clerkship students lacked a formal surgical scrub training program. This limited their operating room (OR) participation to shadowing, potentially hindering preparation for surgical rotations and competitiveness for surgical residencies. This study aimed to assess student attitudes and experiences regarding OR etiquette and sterile technique, with the goal of informing recommendations for a formal preclerkship scrub training and OR orientation program. DESIGN AND SETTING: A cross-sectional survey paired with a single-group pre-post pilot intervention was conducted at UC Irvine School of Medicine. Following the needs assessment survey, a formal OR introduction session was implemented for first-year medical students, covering essential OR topics and including a hands-on demonstration of scrubbing, gowning, and gloving techniques. Unpaired preand post-surveys assessed student interest and self-reported confidence. PARTICIPANTS: In Phase 1, 81 medical students (MS1-MS4) responded to an anonymous survey (18% response rate; 30 MS1s, 13 MS2s, 10 MS3s, 28 MS4s). Among MS1s, 100% supported pre-clerkship implementation. The majority of MS3s (80%) and MS4s (69%) agreed earlier training would have been at least somewhat helpful. Following the pilot session, the proportion of MS1s feeling very confident in their ability to scrub in increased from 5% to 27%, and those very confident in maintaining sterility increased from 14% to 40%. CONCLUSIONS: Medical students across all class years strongly support formal pre-clerkship scrub training, and a pilot 1-hour OR introduction session substantially improved MS1 confidence. These findings support implementing optional pre-clerkship OR preparation programs and may inform similar curriculum initiatives at other institutions. ( J Surg Ed 83:104079. (c) 2026 The Authors. TI What is involved in being retained as a teacher? Early career teachers
   in England show relational activism in their retention decision-making
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Early career teacher; Retention; Social networks; Agency; Relational
   activism
ID ATTRITION; PROFESSIONALS; RESILIENCE; NETWORKING; IDENTITY; SUPPORT;
   WORK
AB Retaining early career teachers is a challenge across the Global North, making it vital to understand what shapes teachers' decisions to remain. This paper draws on nine interviews with early career teachers in England, using socio-network maps from their training year and three or four years later. Findings show that teachers actively shaping their professional lives through decisions which can be viewed as invisible retention activity. TI Impact of mathematical attitudes and growth mindset on pharmaceutical
   calculations exam performance
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Growth mindset; Pharmaceutical calculations; Mathematical attitudes;
   Pharmacy calculations; Mathematical confidence; Student engagement
AB Objective: Pharmacy calculations are a crucial skill set in patient care. In an effort to improve best practices in teaching, identifying student cognitive abilities may impact their performance is critical in identifying students needing additional support to reach competency in this area. This study sought to examine the relationship between growth mindset and math confidence on pharmacy student performance on a comprehensive, must-pass pharmaceutical calculations exam. Methods: This study was conducted in fall semesters between 2022 and 2024. 212 PharmD students completed the Dweck Mindset Instrument and an Attitudes in Mathematics scale prior to, and after, participation in a required pharmaceutical calculations course. At the end of the course, students took a comprehensive, must-pass calculations exam. Student growth mindset and attitudes towards mathematics were compared to their results on the comprehensive calculations exam. Results: There was no meaningful change in Growth Mindset or Mathematics Attitude from precourse to post-course. There was a significant correlation of Mathematics Attitude with calculations exam performance, but there was no correlation between student growth mindset and exam performance. Conclusion: Student confidence regarding mathematics did directly correlate with their performance on the calculations exam. Student belief that they can generally improve their abilities and knowledge (growth mindset) did not have an association with their performance on a high-stakes, calculations exam. Further research is needed to determine if math performance impacts their feelings on the subject of mathematics, or if vice versa.

TI Exploration of Literature-Based Discussion Teaching in Biology and Cell
   Biology Laboratory Courses
SO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE biology and cell biology laboratory courses; interest-driven; laboratory
   teaching reform; literature-based discussion teaching
AB The teaching team optimized and reformed the teaching methods and assessment strategies of Biology and Cell Biology laboratory courses to enhance students' interest and teaching quality. This reform was based on the existing theoretical framework and experimental content of the course, introducing cutting-edge research topics related to the curriculum for discussion. Students selected topics of interest, conducted literature searches and readings in teams, and reported on their findings in class. Students' satisfaction with the seminars exceeded 95.0% (>= 58/61), with evaluations indicating that the seminars played a positive role in providing learning opportunities, understanding academic frontiers, and improving comprehensive abilities. In conclusion, the literature-based discussion teaching has promoted teaching practices and laid the foundation for further deepening teaching reforms.

TI Making student mistakes didactically useful in bedside teaching:
   relevance of learning content, teacher and patient presence
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Bedside teaching; Medical education; Student mistakes; Teacher
   reactions; Teaching methods; Teacher presence; Patient presence; Video
   study
ID CLINICAL SKILLS; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; FOCUS-GROUP; ROUNDS; STRATEGIES;
   ERRORS
AB Background Student mistakes are common in bedside teaching (BST) and can serve as important learning opportunities. However, little is known about how frequently mistakes occur in authentic clinical settings, what types of learning content they involve, and how teacher and patient presence shape teachers' handling of these mistakes. This study investigated (RQ1) the relevance of learning content during student mistakes, (RQ2) associations between mistake types and teachers' reactions, and (RQ3) whether patient presence influences clinical teachers' responses to mistakes.Methods We conducted an observational study based on video recordings of 36 BST sessions across internal medicine, neurology, and orthopaedics (78.4 h). Using a hierarchical coding scheme, we identified mistakes, classified their learning content and mistake types, and coded teacher reactions as well as teacher and patient presence. Interrater reliability ranged from substantial to excellent. Descriptive statistics were used to determine the frequency of mistakes per hour and their distribution across the learning content. Associations between mistake types and teacher reactions were analysed via Spearman's rank correlations (RQ2). Mann-Whitney U tests (RQ3) were used when examining whether teachers' mistake-related behaviours differed depending on the presence or absence of the patient.Results Across all BST sessions, the students made an average of 4.9 mistakes per hour. Mistakes occurred most often during theoretical knowledge and clinical reasoning, predominantly as reproduction mistakes, whereas an incorrect application of skills was most frequent during clinical examination and case presentations. Teacher presence was positively associated with the number of observed mistakes, particularly reproduction mistakes. During the physical examination, the students were supervised for only 72% of the active practice time. Teachers' reactions - including elaboration, directness of feedback, and time provided for correction - did not differ significantly depending on patient presence.Conclusions Student mistakes are common in BST and hold considerable didactic value; however, this value is not fully realised when supervision is inconsistent or when feedback remains limited. Enhancing clinical teachers' capacity to detect errors, providing structured and supportive feedback, and adapting their approach to the presence of patients may strengthen their ability to learn from mistakes. Interventions that cultivate psychological safety and promote effective error-management practices could further improve the pedagogical quality of BST.

TI AAUC: A Feedback-Centric Framework for Automated Assessment of UML
   Use-Case Diagrams
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE automated assessment; diagrammatic answers; engineering education;
   formative feedback; UML use-case diagrams
ID ALGORITHM
AB Assessing diagrammatic artifacts such as UML use-case diagrams is a core yet challenging task in engineering and software engineering education. In large classes, manually evaluating such diagrams is time-consuming, subjective, and difficult to scale, particularly when student solutions exhibit structural variations and diverse labeling choices. These challenges limit the consistency of grading and the timeliness of feedback provided to students. This article presents Automated Assessment of Use-Case Diagrams (AAUC), a feedback-centric framework and tool for the automated assessment of UML use-case diagrams, designed to support assessment practices in engineering education. The proposed approach integrates label and structure matching, along with instructor-configurable marking rules, within a level-aware assessment model that supports partial credit and differentiated evaluation. Unlike approaches that focus solely on correctness detection, AAUC emphasizes the generation of meaningful formative feedback by identifying specific modeling issues, such as missing actors, incorrect relationships, and inconsistent or incomplete labeling. The framework has been evaluated using a dataset of 445 student-generated use-case diagrams collected over multiple academic years from undergraduate software engineering and systems analysis courses. The evaluation demonstrates that the system can robustly assess diverse student submissions, apply consistent marking policies, and generate both quantitative scores and qualitative feedback aligned with instructor expectations. By combining automated assessment with explicit feedback generation, AAUC addresses scalability challenges while supporting iterative improvement in student modeling work. The framework provides a practical, extensible solution for instructors seeking to integrate automated support into engineering education contexts involving diagrammatic design tasks.

AB The purpose of the study is to holistically identify the protective factors that contribute to students' academic resilience and examine the mediating role of protective factors between school burnout and school attachment using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, one of the mixed-methods research designs. TI Global citizenship education within virtual global engagement: Ethical
   challenges and possibilities
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE global citizenship education (GCE); virtual education; ethical
   education; higher education; internationalisation at home; ethical
   global citizenship education (EGCE)
ID UNIVERSITY SOCIAL-RESPONSIBILITY
AB This case study considers the ethical challenges faced by programme developers leading a virtual engagement programme aimed at developing global citizenship that reaches from the university to communities around the world. The programme is IGlobal, which was launched by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign's College of Education during the COVID-19 pandemic as a virtual replacement for teach abroad programming. It is a virtual global engagement project that links participants from over 20 countries spanning the Global North and Global South. Applying the framework for ethical global citizenship education (EGCE) proposed by Emiliano Bosio and Hans Schattle, this qualitative study used interviews, focus group discussions, document analysis and programme observation to consider the ways in which the framework can guide practice and illuminate particular challenges in global community engagement, as well as the areas that the framework may not reach. Since the focus was on the programme developers' experience, the pupils being taught through the IGlobal programme were not themselves surveyed for this case study. The author's analysis reveals the challenges of ethical virtual global engagement as well as the value of the framework for addressing these challenges. The article discusses the implications for ethical international university-to-community engagement, internationalisation at home, and virtual programming.

TI "Young Scholar[s] on the Beat": Multimodal Composition as a Form of
   Critical AI Literacy Pedagogy
SO JOURNAL OF ADOLESCENT & ADULT LITERACY
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; critical AI literacy; critical pedagogy; critical
   posthumanist literacy; multimodal composition
ID CLIMATE-CHANGE; PEOPLE
AB "AI literacy" includes both technical competencies and critical engagement with social and ethical dimensions of AI, but literacy approaches are underrepresented in how we conceptualize and teach its core components. In this paper, we focus on youth multimodal composition as a form of AI literacy pedagogy, analyzing the video products and written reflections of 22 11th grade students who composed video public service announcements about AI ethics issues of their choosing. In our findings, we report on trends in student video content, including (1) the overwhelmingly negative portrayals of AI, especially related to school-based surveillance and punitive treatment relating to AI; (2) the complex interdependence of human and machine responsibility for harm; and (3) the persistence of students' messages of hope in the face of their cynical representations. Next, we show how students (1) experienced composition as joyful, creative collaboration and (2) connected composition and AI literacy learning. We discuss the implications of these findings for critical AI literacy pedagogy, offering suggestions for future practice and highlighting areas for further development and pedagogical innovation.

   Families of Children With Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities

DT Article
DE families; intellectual and developmental disabilities; overnight respite
ID MARITAL QUALITY; CARE; STRESS; UPLIFTS; HEALTH
AB Background Overnight respite care can be a lifeline for parents of children with intellectual and developmental disabilities. We explored the multifaceted parent-reported outcomes of respite and potential demographic variations related to this broad impact.Method Parents (n = 178) reported respite effects on their personal well-being, spousal relationships, family relationships, spiritual needs and ability to complete other activities, which correspond to five subscales of the novel Respite Impact Survey.Results Most parents agreed/strongly agreed with 22 of 23 items, particularly related to rest, recharge and relationships.
