TI ExperimentaQuimica: Evaluating an Experimental Continuing
   Professional Development Program for Primary Chemistry Teaching
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Elementary/Primary School; Chemical Education Research; Hands-On
   Learning/Manipulatives; Teacher Training/ProfessionalDevelopment
ID UTILITY VALUE INTERVENTION; SCIENCE
AB This study examined the impact of the ExperimentaQuimica program on the teaching of chemistry in Portuguese primary education, designed as a continuing professional development initiative centered on experimental methodologies and individualized support. The aim was to understand the extent to which participation in the program fostered changes in teachers' perceptions, pedagogical practices, and motivation, as well as to identify the design features that supported these transformations. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, involving 16 female teachers at this educational level. Data collection included pre- and post-test questionnaires and semistructured interviews, analyzed through descriptive and inferential statistics and qualitative content analysis using a hybrid deductive-inductive coding strategy. The results revealed significant changes in perceptions of experimental teaching, positive emotions associated with chemistry teaching, the perceived importance of instructional resources and institutional support, and teachers' self-perceived preparation for chemistry teaching, as well as an increase in enthusiasm for teaching chemistry. Quantitative findings also indicated reduced agreement with traditional gender-related stereotypes associated with chemistry teaching. The interviews confirmed these trends, highlighting improvements in classroom practices, greater teacher motivation, and positive effects on pupils, notably in increased curiosity and engagement. The design of the program proved decisive, with particular emphasis on the value of individualized support and the provision of tailored laboratory kits. Despite limitations related to sample size and intervention duration, the study suggests the potential of continuing professional development initiatives that integrate experimental practices and personalized support. These findings offer relevant contributions to the promotion of early chemistry education and to the international debate on teacher education and scientific literacy.

TI How the Konkur, principals, and parents shape novice EFL teachers'
   classroom assessment in Iran?
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Language Assessment Literacy; Novice EFL teachers; Washback; Classroom
   assessment; Systemic constraints; Iran
ID ASSESSMENT LITERACY
AB This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study investigates the classroom assessment realities of novice EFL teachers in Iran's public secondary schools-a context defined by large classes, limited resources, and the pervasive washback of the Konkur (university entrance examination). Drawing on Xu and Brown's () Teacher Assessment Literacy in Practice (TALiP) framework, the study integrates survey data (N = 158), semi-structured interviews (n = 20), and document analysis (n = 18 tests) to address three questions: the challenges teachers face in constructing classroom achievement tests; how teachers navigate between assessment principles from pre-service education and daily practical demands; and what supports teachers identify as critical for their development relative to current availability. Findings document a constrained assessment ecology where time scarcity (M = 4.62) was the most strongly endorsed challenge, and a triad of stakeholder accountability pressures-Konkur expectations, principal oversight, and parental demands-was consistently associated with assessment decisions. A substantial gap emerged between principle endorsement and implementation (e.g., formative assessment: 91.1% endorsement vs. 28.5% implementation), with constraint intensity negatively associated with implementation frequency (r = - .62). Four navigation approaches were identified: recalibrating priorities toward practicality, identifying manageable proxies for complex constructs, preserving communicative elements within examination-aligned formats, and developing localized knowledge through informal collegial networks-the last varying substantially by school location. Support priorities centered on structural investments-protected collaboration time, curated resources, and structured mentorship-where importance-availability gaps were substantial (e.g., collaboration time: gap = 3.14, d = 4.64). Findings challenge deficit-oriented interpretations by documenting that primary barriers are institutional rather than individual, carrying implications for teacher education and systemic support design in examination-driven settings.

TI Emotional and Cognitive Mechanisms Impacting Reading Skills in Autistic
   and Non-Autistic Children
SO MIND BRAIN AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE anxiety; ASD; autism; reading comprehension; reading decoding; word
   reading
ID COMPREHENSION; DISORDERS; LANGUAGE; ANXIETY
AB This study focuses on the influence of anxiety on reading decoding and reading comprehension in autistic and non-autistic children, while also investigating the cognitive mechanisms underlying reading. Eighty-three participants (7-13 years of age, 46 autistic and 37 non-autistic) underwent neuropsychological assessments of reading skills. TI Exploring associated factors of differentiated instruction practices in
   Australia: a pilot partial least squares structural equation modelling
   study
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Differentiated instruction; Differentiation; Structural equational
   modelling; Inclusive education; Teacher attitudes; Teacher self-efficacy
ID TEACHERS; EDUCATION; EFFICACY
AB In Australia, teachers are required to differentiate to meet the needs of students across the full range of abilities. However, research conducted in Australia has shown that the implementation of differentiated instruction (DI) in Australian classrooms is varied, and that teachers' self-efficacy beliefs, attitudes, preparedness and contextual factors can influence teachers' implementation. To date, these factors have typically been examined in isolation in Australia, limiting understanding of how they interrelate to shape DI enactment. Addressing this gap, this pilot study, novel in the Australian context, involved 87 primary and secondary school teachers to examine associations among teacher experience, attitude, self-efficacy, readiness and preparedness and DI practices. Using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM), the findings revealed that teacher efficacy (beta = 0.290) and preparedness (beta = 0.498) were associated with DI practices. Teacher attitudes were strongly associated with readiness (beta = 0.621) and efficacy (beta = 0.528), suggesting hypothesised associations through which attitudes relate to DI implementation, while teaching experience was positively associated only with teacher efficacy. Overall, the model explained 44% of the variance in DI practice, highlighting preliminary associations among psychological and contextual factors related to DI implementation. Implications are drawn for professional development and teacher education.

TI Safe harbours in treacherous waters: Leading pride groups in schools
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Pride groups; School inclusion; LGBTIQA plus youth; Student leadership;
   Educational equity
ID GAY-STRAIGHT ALLIANCES; POSITIVE YOUTH DEVELOPMENT; LGBTQ; INVOLVEMENT;
   RESPONSIBILISATION; VICTIMIZATION; STUDENTS
AB Pride groups are widely recognised in international literature as fostering inclusion, improving school climate, and reducing bias-based bullying for LGBTIQA + youth. This qualitative study explores how leadership of school-based pride groups in Tasmanian public schools is understood and practised by key stakeholders. Drawing on the thematic analysis of interviews with school staff and focus groups with pride group participants, the research highlights the transformative potential of these student-led groups. Our findings affirm this outcome in the Tasmanian context, with students describing pride groups as essential spaces of safety, belonging, and affirmation in school environments that often remain hostile or unsupportive. At the same time, the findings highlight the structural limitations that constrain these groups. Pride groups are frequently hampered by reliance on voluntary staff labour, inconsistent institutional recognition, and narrow policy framings that valourise visible, student-led leadership while overlooking the relational and emotional labour young people perform. The findings caution against responsibilising LGBTIQA+ students to lead cultural change without adequate support, and foreground the need to recognise care-based, relational forms of leadership that are central to how these groups operate. This study contributes to a growing body of research that calls for a more nuanced understanding of student leadership and systemic responsibility in fostering inclusion in schools. Ensuring that pride groups serve both as refuges from hostile environments and platforms for agency will require sustained institutional commitment, recognition of diverse leadership practices, and structural support for the staff and students who carry the important work of pride group leadership.

TI 'Strong in Will but Weak in Power': University Teachers' Perceived
   Values and Pedagogical Approaches to Values Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE pedagogical approach; teacher agency; university teachers; value
   perception; values education
ID AGENCY
AB This qualitative study investigated university teachers' value perceptions and pedagogical approaches to values education. Drawing on semi-structured interviews, classroom observations and document analysis with 10 Chinese university teachers, the study identified five main value types emphasised by the participants (i.e., benevolence, security, tradition, conformity and self-direction values) and three approaches adopted in values education (i.e., traditional, constructivist and critical approaches). The findings show that university teachers actively incorporated curricular values into their teaching and enacted these values through their own interpretations and pedagogical decisions. However, their practices displayed an imbalanced pedagogical pattern, characterised by relatively extensive content knowledge but less developed pedagogical content knowledge related to values education. These findings further highlight teachers' struggling agency in a standardised accountability context, where insufficient professional support constrained their capacity to enact values education in pedagogically meaningful ways. The study offers implications for values education reform and teacher development in higher education institutions.

TI Psychological Mechanisms of Emotion-Cognition Interactions in Secondary
   Mathematics Learning: An Empirical Study based on Large-Scale
   Educational Behavioral Data
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational behavioral data; Emotion-cognition interaction; Secondary
   mathematics learning
AB This study analyzed EdNet and ASSISTments datasets (131,441 middle school students) to develop a behaviorally grounded psychological model of emotion-cognition interaction in mathematics learning. Using ensemble learning for the behavioral inference of emotional states (87.3% classification accuracy), Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, and Hidden Markov Models, four interaction patterns were identified: synergistic facilitation (35%), competitive inhibition (28%), emotion-dominant (20%), and cognition-dominant (17%). Emotion-cognition interaction explained 23.6% of learning performance variance, surpassing emotional (12.4%) or cognitive factors alone (15.8%). Temporal analysis revealed a U-shaped trajectory: interaction intensity peaked initially (beta = 0.51), reached minimum mid-stage (beta = 0.29), and rebounded during challenging tasks (beta = 0.46). Significant individual differences emerged between high (coefficient = 0.42) and low emotional regulation groups (0.18), emphasizing metacognitive abilities' role in modulating interactions.The model demonstrated robust cross-dataset validation (correlation = 0.89). These findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding mathematics learning psychological mechanisms and inform personalized educational interventions and intelligent tutoring system design. The research highlights that emotion-cognition interaction, rather than isolated factors, critically determines learning outcomes, with temporal dynamics and individual regulation abilities as key moderators.

TI "Teach in English or retire": linguistic, pedagogical and career
   consequences of English medium instruction
SO LANGUAGE POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Career injustice; EMI approaches; Language policy; Multilingual schools;
   Professional survival
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; CHALLENGES
AB This study examines how teachers in Basic Community schools in rural Nepal, a non-colonised country where English has no historical administrative roots, experience, interpret, and enact English medium instruction (EMI) policy. A qualitative inquiry approach was employed, utilising semi-structured interviews and classroom observations to collect data from teachers. Findings indicate that schools' independent decision to adopt EMI in non-English-speaking multilingual contexts presents challenges for teachers, complicating their professional practice. Despite low English proficiency among both teachers and students, schools' EMI policy raises concerns about curriculum goal achievement. While the intention of these community schools to attract more students by implementing EMI, akin to private schools, may seem appealing, the approach appears counterproductive regarding competencies intended to be developed in students, and the performance schools aim to demonstrate through students' exam results. EMI policy promotes social injustice and educational inequality within rural multilingual communities. Findings highlight linguistic and pedagogical challenges faced by teachers, raising serious concerns about career injustice. This study presents three key theoretical contributions: career injustice, which refers to marginalisation based on English proficiency rather than pedagogical competence; performative compliance with substantive resistance, where superficial EMI protects jobs while undermining policy goals; and within-school institutional hierarchies, characterised by the devaluation of local language teachers in English versus Nepali blocks. This study offers insights for policymakers and other stakeholders, encouraging them to engage in comprehensive dialogue and analyse sociolinguistic contexts before adopting a specific medium of instruction, including EMI, in schools.

TI The Role of Mental Health Problems in the Relationship Between Spelling
   Skills and School Anxiety
SO ZEITSCHRIFT FUR ENTWICKLUNGSPSYCHOLOGIE UND PADAGOGISCHE PSYCHOLOGIE
LA English
DT Article
DE spelling disorder; mental health problems; school anxiety; mediation
   analysis; Rechtschreibst & ouml;rung; psychische Auff & auml;lligkeiten;
   schulische Angst; Mediationsanalyse
ID PSYCHIATRIC-DISORDERS; GENDER-DIFFERENCES; WORKING-MEMORY; CHILDREN;
   DIFFICULTIES; STUDENTS; PERFORMANCE; DISABILITY; DYSLEXIA
AB : The study examines the relationship between spelling, mental health, and school-related anxiety in a sample of 291 third-graders. It investigated whether children with spelling disorder differ from their peers in comorbid mental health problems and school-related anxiety, and whether the relationship between spelling and school-related anxiety is mediated by mental health problems or whether a direct relationship exists. Analyses of group differences using independent samples t tests showed that children with a spelling disorder exhibited significantly more symptoms of mental health problems as well as more pronounced school-related anxiety. A mediation analysis using a structural equation model revealed partial mediation, suggesting that part of the relationship between spelling and school-related anxiety is mediated by comorbid mental health problems, while the other part can be attributed to a direct relationship. These findings suggest that children with spelling disorder are at increased risk for school-related anxiety, even in the absence of comorbid problems.

   Psychiatric Hospitalization

ID MENTAL-HEALTH PROBLEMS; CHILDREN; ADOLESCENTS; DISORDERS; CARE;

AB : This study examined teachers' needs in dealing with students with mental disorders and in collaborating with hospitals for school reintegration. Survey data from 265 teachers from 13 primary and secondary schools show that most teachers experience challenges working with students with mental disorders and would like to acquire more knowledge and skills. In addition, almost all teachers reported they would like to consult clinical professionals regarding students returning to their classrooms after psychiatric hospitalization. Central aspects of discussion in the additional focus group with school principals were the teachers' need for more knowledge on how to deal with mental health problems as well as more interdisciplinary collaboration and aftercare. These results indicate that there is a high and unmet need among teachers for further training and hospital-school collaboration in dealing with students with mental disorders. Results can be used to develop tailored support services for teachers in this area.

TI Parent interaction in and attitudes towards Zoom-mediated heritage
   language maintenance: a mixed methods investigation of Farsi-speaking
   migrants in Australia
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Heritage language; First and second-generation Australians; Farsi;
   Zoom-mediated heritage language maintenance
ID BILINGUALISM; CHINESE; SLA
AB Many minority language speaking migrant families living in Australia are located broadly across the country. Due to this circumstance, computer-mediated language learning, especially that involving video-conferencing platforms like Zoom, represents one way to systematically address concerns around first- and second-generation children's heritage language attrition. Despite the crucial role of parents in heritage language transmission and the strong potential of videoconferencing in facilitating distance heritage language learning, there is sparse research investigating parents' involvement in and attitudes towards Zoom-mediated heritage language learning. Mixed methods were used to describe seven Farsi-speaking parents' involvement in and attitudes towards six Zoom-mediated language learning sessions aimed at supporting their children's heritage language development. First, the recorded videos of the lessons were systematically analyzed to enumerate various factors indicative of the extent and nature of parent involvement during the lessons. Second, after the completion of the six lessons, semi-structured interviews were undertaken and thematically analyzed to describe parents' attitudes towards the lessons. Data was triangulated to establish a generalized picture of the types of parental interaction evident during the lessons and the parents' attitudes toward them. Findings reveal that while parents were consistently present and supportive, differences in children's agency and family dynamics shaped the nature and effectiveness of parental involvement. The discussion presents key takeaways that can be applied in future efforts to maintain heritage languages through computer-assisted means.

SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MENTORING AND COACHING IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Inclusion; Communities of practice; Special education; Research practice
   partnership; Students with disabilities
ID SPECIAL-EDUCATION; LEADERSHIP; KNOWLEDGE; ATTITUDES
AB Purpose This article explores the complicated process of developing a research practice partnership (RPP) seeking to support systemic change in a public school district. The specific reform at the heart of this RPP involves strengthening how elementary and secondary schools across the district engage in "inclusion." Drawing from our personal reflections as leaders of this RPP, we provide perspectives on how communities of practice can scaffold the learning of coaches seeking to advance social justice. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper applies the sociocultural learning theory of communities of practice as an analytical lens for understanding coaching toward inclusion. This RPP was situated in a large urban public school district in the United States. The reform involves strengthening how schools engage in "inclusion" through coaching. We extend coaching scholarship by theorizing coaching as a sociocultural learning process within nested communities of practice, structured by five dualities of learning architecture, as a conceptual framework for mentoring coaches toward equity-centered inclusion. Findings We find the five dualities of the learning architecture create a useful lens for unpacking practices that expand our understanding of the communities of practice in which coaching practices unfold. Research limitations/implications Scholars analyzing coaching can benefit from explicating the learning theory undergirding this work. Practical implications A helpful strategy for mentoring coaches toward social justice is to explicitly situate this work in the context of nested communities of practice. Originality/value Coaching that expands inclusive practices in schools is complex and multifaceted. Understanding how this occurs within nested communities of practice can help coaches navigate these complexities.

TI Social justice mentoring in the borderlands of academia: developing a
   transnational mentoring network for mutual scholarly support
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MENTORING AND COACHING IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Transnational; Cosmopolitanism; Mentoring; Academia; Social justice
ID KNOWLEDGE
AB Purpose This research examines both the possibilities of establishing mutual learning and dialogue beyond the confines of academic discipline, rank and geographical location, and developing transnational mentoring networks (TMNs) from the experiences of three scholars of color from different academic traditions in three different parts of the world. Design/methodology/approach Utilizing cartas and pl & aacute;ticas as methods, we collaboratively created and analyzed our data through textual reflections on guided topics, reflections and conversations. Our approach yielded 12 cartas and over 12 h of discussion about our mentoring relationships. Findings Given the current state of mentorship in academia and our willingness to engage in solidarity, we sought dialogue and mentorship beyond the borders that confine our disciplines, ranks, geographical locations and epistemologies. Our epistemological foundations presented an opportunity for us to initiate a TMN from which we organically established an (un)anchored academic safe space from which lessons were drawn. Originality/value In an academic era of polarization, less collaboration, performativity and transactionality, our TMN highlights how an alternative space can overcome geopolitical and academic borders and foster solidarity through cosmopolitan dialogue and transnational mentoring.

TI Transnational language teachers' identity construction in the USA:
   insights from an intercultural context
SO JOURNAL FOR MULTICULTURAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Transnational language teachers; Language teacher identity (LTI);
   Intercultural teaching environment; Foreign languages other than English
   (FLOE)
ID EFL TEACHERS; AGENCY; NEGOTIATION; NNES
AB Purpose Increasing global mobility has enabled language teachers to work across national, linguistic and cultural boundaries, leading to processes of professional identity construction and negotiation in transnational educational contexts. While previous studies on transnational language teachers' identity development have largely focused on EFL teachers (Liu and Li, 2025), transnational teachers of foreign languages other than English (FLOE) remain critically underexplored (Zhu et al., 2025). This study aims to investigate how transnational language teachers construct their professional identities in the USA. Design/methodology/approach This qualitative exploratory case study investigates how two tertiary-level transnational language teachers construct their professional identities in the USA, using Yazan's (2018) Conceptual Framework for Language Teacher Identity (LTI). The participants were two transnational language instructors from a Pacific Northwest university, one teaching Turkish as a foreign language (TFL) and the other Italian as a foreign language (IFL). Data from semi-structured face-to-face interviews, classroom observations and reflection reports were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's (2006) thematic analysis to capture how professional identities were constructed across participants' retrospective and current teaching experiences and contexts. Findings The findings indicated that the participants' professional identity development was shaped by six interconnected factors: teacher cognition, teacher learning, previous learning experiences, contextual factors, emotional conflicts and participation in communities of practice (CoP). Research limitations/implications This study has several limitations. First, it was a small-scale study with only two participants, restricting the breadth of insights into transnational FLOE teachers' identity construction. Second, data were collected over a single month, which is a limited timeframe given that identity formation is an ongoing process. A longitudinal design would better capture shifts in professional identity over time. Third, one participant was unable to complete the reflection report during the data collection period. Future studies replicating this design should allow greater time between data collection stages to accommodate participants' demanding academic schedules and enable richer, more complete data. Practical implications Teacher educators can support transnational teachers by fostering awareness of their life histories as language learners and teachers. Self-introspection tasks such as critical reflections, autobiographies and critical multilingual language awareness activities should be incorporated into teacher education programs. Innovative multimodal practices, including language portraits, collages, dioramas and photo-elicitation, can further empower teachers in their identity construction. Pre-service and in-service teachers should engage in discussions and critically examine hegemonic discourses such as native speakerism. Additionally, teacher education courses should introduce potential micro-, meso- and macro-level challenges transnational teachers may encounter, fostering professional coping mechanisms to manage emotional vulnerability in intercultural teaching environments.
   Originality/value This study extends current research beyond EFL-dominated contexts, offers practical implications for language teachers and teacher educators engaged in transnational language teaching and contributes to ongoing discussions on identity development in intercultural settings.

TI Revisiting Learning Styles in the Age of Generative AI: A Conceptual
   Framework for Regulation and Agency
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; learning styles; neuromyths; epistemic agency;
   metacognitive regulation; higher education
AB This conceptual paper revisits the learning styles debate in the context of generative and adaptive artificial intelligence in higher education. It does not seek to rehabilitate classical learning style taxonomies, whose prescriptive claims have been widely challenged as a neuromyth. Instead, it argues that AI-mediated learning creates new conditions under which patterns of regulation, delegation, verification, iteration, epistemic control, and ethical responsibility may become more observable and pedagogically relevant. Drawing on research on learning styles, neuromyths, AI literacy, adaptive learning, assessment, self-regulated learning, metacognition, and epistemic agency, the paper proposes a conceptual framework for regulation and agency styles in AI-mediated learning. In this framework, style is not treated as a fixed psychological trait or as a category into which learners should be sorted, but as a situated and modifiable profile of decisions and actions distributed across learners, tasks, and intelligent systems. Three analytical dimensions are proposed: epistemic control and metacognitive orchestration, adaptive regulation and generative iteration, and socio-algorithmic agency and ethical governance. The paper concludes with implications for task design, assessment, teacher education, and equitable AI integration.

TI Mathematics for the Arts and the Arts for Mathematics: Promoting Soft
   Skills Through the STEAM Approach in Early Childhood Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE mathematics; arts; STEAM approach; interdisciplinarity; soft skills;
   early childhood education
AB This article links Mathematics and the Arts through the STEAM approach to highlight the potential of this interdisciplinary approach in early childhood education. From this perspective, the aim is to present the design and implementation of the STEAM activity, We Build Trees with Cuisenaire Rods, and to analyse how soft skills are promoted within a group of 18 five-year-old pupils. Using the Thick Description approach and an analytical model, it has been identified that: (1) Mathematics and the Arts maintained an ongoing dialogue throughout the sequence of seven tasks included in the STEAM activity; (2) the STEAM activity contributed to the development of soft skills such as critical and creative thinking, problem-solving, collaboration and teamwork, technological and digital literacy, curiosity and autonomy, and design and design thinking. We conclude that, from the interdisciplinary STEAM perspective, the Arts are not an instrumental discipline serving Mathematics, nor is Mathematics merely a setting for working on art; rather, both disciplines enrich one another to promote soft skills in early years education.

TI Don't Panic! And Other Principles for Environmental Educators in an Era
   of Authoritarian Extractivism
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE authoritarianism; extractivism; education; resistance; affect
ID HOPE
AB This paper, based on a keynote given at the Nordic Environmental and Sustainability Educators Conference, explores a set of principles that might inform the responses of environmental educators, in particular those working in Europe, to the growth in political authoritarianism allied with climate denial and ecological extractivism. Taking the form of a manifesto and intended to prompt debate and mutual support, the piece proposes 11 principles: Don't panic; Acknowledge your own emotions; Explore Possibilities Beyond the Classroom; Work with hope as praxis; Proliferate stories of change; Nurture alternatives; Name and protect gains; Diversify resources and tactics; Practice simple sabotage; See the bigger picture; and Don't forget the dancing.

TI Who Teaches Introductory Biology? National Patterns of Contingent and
   Ladder Faculty Assignments in Gateway Courses
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE introductory biology; gateway courses; contingent faculty; tenure-track
   faculty; faculty assignment
ID STUDENTS; POLICIES; SCIENCE
AB Introductory biology courses play a pivotal role in shaping students' exposure to STEMM disciplines and in influencing persistence along life science pathways, yet relatively little is known about who teaches these gateway courses at a national scale. The collective effort to cultivate inclusive experiences for STEMM students relies on the professional and political structures within which instructors of this key course operate in. This study examines the distribution of faculty appointment types in introductory biology across several hundred U.S. colleges and universities sampled to approximate the national landscape by geographic region and institutional type. Using a large, multi-sheet dataset of class sections, we systematically coded instructor titles into contingent (non-tenure-track), ladder (tenure-track/tenured), and other categories and generated both section-level and institution-level estimates of faculty assignment. We then addressed three questions: (a) whether contingent or ladder faculty teach the majority of introductory biology sections nationally; (b) how the distribution of faculty types varies by institutional characteristics; and (c) how estimates of faculty representation differ when each course section versus each institution is weighted equally. Results indicate that, in this sample, ladder faculty teach a majority of introductory biology sections, although there is substantial variability across institutions and clear contrasts by institutional type and context. Comparisons of section-level and institution-level estimates further show that conclusions about "who teaches" introductory biology depend on the analytic lens, with section-weighted analyses emphasizing the typical student experience and institution-weighted analyses emphasizing typical institutional practice. These findings contribute discipline-specific evidence to broader conversations about how the academic workforce is constituted, and by extension creates inclusive environments and provide methodological guidance for studying faculty roles in gateway STEM education.

TI Understanding Teacher Professional Development in Social Music Projects:
   Experiences from the Spanish Context
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher professional development; music education; social music
   projects; community music; qualitative research
ID REFLECTIONS; PERCEPTIONS
AB This study explores how teachers working in social music projects in Spain understand their professional development and which elements they identify as central to their learning processes. Although teacher professional development (TPD) has been widely studied in formal music education contexts, less is known about how it unfolds in socially oriented and community-based settings. The study adopts a qualitative design based on in-depth semi-structured interviews with seven music teachers involved in social music projects across Spain. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis to identify recurring themes and patterns in participants' accounts. The findings show that teachers understand professional development as an ongoing and situated process closely linked to their daily practice. Experiential learning, adaptation to uncertainty, collaboration with others, and continuous reflection emerge as key elements in their development. In addition, participants highlight the importance of expanding beyond strictly musical training to include pedagogical, social, and relational competences. These results suggest that professional development in social music projects differs from more traditional models by emphasising context, experience, and community engagement. The study contributes to current discussions on music teacher development by highlighting the need for more flexible, collaborative, and context-sensitive approaches to TPD.

TI Developing a Theory of Effective Parental Engagement in Family Literacy
   Programmes
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE parental engagement; family literacy; Constructivist Grounded Theory;
   disadvantaged community; collaborative practice; partnership
ID INVOLVEMENT; INTERVENTIONS; EDUCATION; SCHOOLS
AB This study develops a theory of parental engagement by exploring the perspectives of both parents and practitioners within a socio-economically disadvantaged area in Dublin, Ireland. Using Constructivist Grounded Theory, data were generated through focus groups with participants involved in the family literacy programme Breakfast Buddies. Analysis resulted in the development of a substantive theory, The Dance of Engagement, which conceptualises parental engagement as a relational, non-linear, and co-constructed process. The findings identify three foundational tenets-safety, equality and trust-as essential conditions underpinning effective parental engagement. Four interconnected categories describe how engagement unfolds in practice: choosing to engage, co-creating engagement, connecting to engage and sharing. These categories illustrate how engagement is initiated, sustained and extended beyond programme settings into home and community contexts. The study demonstrates that personalised practitioner approaches, relational environments and shared ownership of engagement processes support greater parental confidence, sustained participation and reciprocal learning between parents and practitioners. The resulting theory challenges deficit-oriented and participation-based models of parental engagement by focusing on collaboration and contextual responsiveness. The Dance of Engagement offers a theoretically grounded framework with clear implications for policy and practice, particularly for designing inclusive family literacy practices to improve outcomes for children and families in disadvantaged communities.

TI From Contradictions to Solutions: An Expansive Learning Analysis of
   Culturally and Linguistically Diverse (CALD) Parents Navigating Digital
   Exclusion in Western Sydney
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE digital exclusion; contradictions; modelled solutions; expansive
   learning; parental engagement
AB Digital exclusion compounds the challenges that migrant and refugee parents already face in supporting their children's education. As schooling becomes increasingly digitally mediated, this shift can intensify existing inequalities, particularly when the school and home systems present contradictions that these parents must navigate simultaneously. Grounded in expansive learning theory, this study examines the experiences of 18 migrant and refugee parents in Western Sydney, Australia. It draws on interview data to illuminate the contradictions encountered when supporting their children's home learning. Through this theoretical lens, we highlight how parents take agentic actions and work to develop solutions tailored to their families' specific needs and circumstances. The findings identify three broad types of contradictions and the strategies parents employed to overcome barriers to supporting home learning. We argue for a co-construction approach in which schools, parents, and community actors collaborate to promote expansive learning, positioning migrant and refugee parents as active participants in the redesign of school-home-community partnership systems.

TI Gender differences in high school students' mathematics performance,
   attitudes, and career aspirations in Northern Ghana: the mediating roles
   of equal chance, equal treatment, and caliber of instruction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE attitudes; caliber of instruction; career aspirations; equal chance;
   equal treatment; gender; goals
ID SEX-DIFFERENCES; EDUCATION; PATTERNS; PROGRESS; SCIENCE
AB This study examined the relationship among mathematics performance, attitudes, and career aspirations of Senior High School (SHS) students based on gender in the Northern Region of Ghana. A concurrent triangulation mixed method research approach was employed to gather qualitative and quantitative data through the use of closed and open-ended items. A stratified sampling technique was used to select 366 students (183 male and 183 female) as participants. Thematic coding, structural equation modeling (SEM), and Descriptive and independent sample t-test were used in analyzing the data. An independent-samples t-test revealed a statistically significant difference in mean mathematics performance between male (M = 9.41, SD = 1.093) and female students (M = 8.50, SD = 1.169), t(364) = 7.70, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.80 (large effect). Structural equation modeling showed that Caliber of Instruction had the strongest direct effect on mathematics performance (beta = 0.51, p < .001), followed by Equal Chance (beta = 0.31, p < .01) and Equal Treatment (beta = 0.23, p < .05). A moderate positive relationship existed between career aspirations and mathematics performance (beta = 0.43, p < .001). The study recommends gender-equitable career guidance to support students' aspirations in mathematics-related fields. Implications for policy, theory, and practice are discussed.

TI Building trust: two cluster randomized controlled trials of professional
   development to strengthen family engagement as an essential aspect of
   high-quality early childhood education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE culture; early childhood education; family engagement; poverty; trust
ID SCHOOL; INTERVENTIONS; ELEMENTARY; IMPACTS; TEACHERS; EQUITY
AB Introduction Despite robust evidence and policy recognition that family engagement is essential to student success and well-being, the extant literature includes few rigorous evaluations to inform how to support educators in building inclusive school environments and trusting relationships with families.Methods To evaluate the impact of a novel approach to professional development, we conducted two parallel cluster randomized controlled trials in New York City pre-Kindergarten (pre-K) programs across 61 schools and 70 early education centers serving primarily Latine and Black children living in concentrated poverty, with samples of similar to 4,500 parents in each study. In partnership with the school district, we randomized pre-K programs to intervention arm: ParentCorps professional development for pre-K leaders and teachers or comparison (professional development-as-usual in the district). Both studies utilized a repeated cross-sectional cohort design, with administrative data from consecutive independent cohorts of parents whose children attended pre-K in study schools/centers over a four-year time span: two cohorts prior to randomization (2016, 2017) and two during professional development (2018, 2019). Difference-in-differences models assessed the impact of ParentCorps professional development on pre-K parent responses to the district-administered annual survey of school climate and quality, which included three scales relevant to family engagement: Communication and Trust in Teacher, Trust in School Leader, and Inclusive Leadership.Results Relative to comparison, ParentCorps professional development led to significantly stronger family engagement outcomes in both studies. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the primary analysis, with significant impact in four of six models; for two of the six primary models, there was a potential violation of difference-in-difference assumptions (in Study 1, for Trust in Leader; in Study 2, for Communication and Trust in Teacher).Discussion This is the first demonstration that professional development impacts family engagement from the perspective of parents. Confidence in intervention effectiveness is strengthened by reliance on a system-wide survey of school climate and quality, use of inverse probability weighting procedures to estimate population-level effects, and findings of impact across both pre-K settings. Professional development represents a scalable strategy to help educators build trusting relationships with families and inclusive environments, with potential for systems change and reduction of disparities in education.

TI Paper versus pixels: comparing pre-service teachers' experiences of low-
   and medium- technology simulation modalities
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE initial teacher education; pre-service teachers; simulation design;
   simulation-based learning; technology
ID COGNITIVE LOAD THEORY; EDUCATION; FIDELITY; DESIGN; ENGAGEMENT; PREPARE
AB Amid ongoing global concerns regarding teacher recruitment and retention, the importance of preparedness for practice remains a priority across Initial Teacher Education (ITE). The integrated use of technology and simulation-based learning offer a potential means of addressing these issues. However, existing research in ITE contexts is yet to establish the relative impacts of different simulation modalities. Adopting a sequential mixed methods design, this study is therefore the first to explore the value of low- and medium-technology simulation modalities as a means of preparing pre-service teachers (PSTs) for professional practice. Findings demonstrate a consistent pattern of no significant difference in PSTs' experiences and engagement across both simulation modalities. These are complemented by deepened analysis of qualitative data indicating that these experiences are influenced by perceptions of authenticity, accessibility, and learning preferences. The study indicates that careful pedagogical consideration is required to establish whether less advanced or more sophisticated technological platforms provide the best value option for PST learning.

TI The problem of early school leaving-socioeconomic causes and potential
   solutions: a systematic literature review
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE early school leaving; educational disadvantage; policy interventions;
   school segregation; socioeconomic determinants
ID EDUCATIONAL-ACHIEVEMENT; RISK-FACTORS; IMPACT; SEGREGATION;
   INEQUALITIES; ADOLESCENTS; NETHERLANDS; PERFORMANCE; DISPARITIES;
   RESOURCES
AB Early School Leaving (ESL), defined within the European Union policy space as individuals aged 18-24 who leave the education system without attaining upper secondary qualifications, affects approximately 3.1 million young people annually across EU. The repercussions of ESL are profound, such as diminishing tax revenues, increasing reliance on social services, and perpetuating cycles of poverty and poor health. Through a systematic literature review of 80 peer-reviewed papers published between 2003 and 2023, the purpose of this paper is to examine the socioeconomic causes of ESL. These causes include factors such as parental level of education and occupation, poverty leading to educational disadvantage, and lack of educational motivation. They also include factors related to schooling, such as school segregation, unsuitable curricula, teacher attitudes and expectations, and inflexible pathways through education and training. The findings reveal the complex interplay between socioeconomic status and educational outcomes. The discussion, while highlighting the interaction of social determinants contributing to underachievement and ESL, also outlines policy measures and interventions designed to counteract ESL's impact, emphasizing a joined-up approach to tackle these challenges. The paper concludes with specific recommendations for policymakers and practitioners aimed at reducing ESL and enhancing educational equity across Europe and beyond.

TI Psychological symptoms and learning adaptation in college students: the
   mediating role of learning engagement
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE college students; learning adaptation; learning engagement; mediating
   effect; psychological symptoms
ID ADAPTABILITY; BURNOUT
AB Background As an important indicator of higher education quality, college students' learning adaptation is crucial for their academic development and personal growth. Currently, college students generally face multiple psychological pressures, and the relationship between psychological symptoms and learning adaptation has attracted considerable scholarly attention. However, the mediating role of learning engagement in this relationship has not been systematically explored. This study aims to examine the mediating role of learning engagement in the relationship between psychological symptoms and learning adaptation, providing a reference for universities to formulate evidence-based educational strategies. Methods A total of 418 college students in Zhejiang Province completed the Symptom Checklist-90 (SCL-90), the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale-Student (UWES-S), and the College Student Learning Adaptation Scale. Descriptive statistics and correlation analyses were conducted using SPSS 27.0, and the mediation effect was tested using PROCESS v5.0 with gender included as a control variable. The 95% confidence interval of the indirect effect was estimated using the Bootstrap method. Results (1) Psychological symptoms were negatively correlated with college students' learning adaptation. (2) Psychological symptoms were negatively correlated with both learning engagement and learning adaptation, while learning engagement was positively correlated with learning adaptation (all p < 0.01). (3) Learning engagement partially mediated the relationship between psychological symptoms and learning adaptation, accounting for 28.51% of the total effect. Conclusion This study identifies the partial mediating role of learning engagement between psychological symptoms and learning adaptation. These findings may serve as a reference for colleges and universities to design mental health and learning support programs correlated with stronger learning adaptation.

TI Examining the links underlying learning disposition among future
   professionals in Southern Peru: the roles of teachers' effectiveness,
   purpose in life, perceived social support, and spiritual experience
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE learning disposition; teachers' effectiveness; purpose in life;
   perceived social support; spiritual experience; higher education;
   development; learning
ID PLS-SEM; WILLINGNESS; EDUCATION; EFFICACY; STUDENTS
AB Introduction: In the contemporary context of higher education, training professionals capable of facing academic challenges and those of the future job market requires not only the development of cognitive skills, but also emotional, social, and spiritual resources that foster more integral and sustainable learning processes. In this context, the objective of this study was to evaluate whether teachers' effectiveness, purpose in life, perceived social support, and spiritual experience are associated with learning disposition. Method: An explanatory study was conducted on a sample of 600 university students from southern Peru. Participation was evenly distributed between women and men, with ages ranging from 18 to 45 years (M = 21.8; SD = 3.3). The data were analyzed using PLS-SEM, and the internal consistency coefficients showed adequate values, confirming the internal robustness of each construct in the model. Results: The hypotheses were confirmed, showing that teachers' effectiveness, purpose in life, and perceived social support are associated with learning disposition. Furthermore, it was validated that spiritual experience is associated with learning disposition, teachers' effectiveness, purpose in life, and perceived social support. In addition, empirical evidence was found demonstrating that purpose in life is associated with teachers' effectiveness, and that perceived social support is associated with purpose in life. Discussion: The model presented suggests a reevaluation of existing models, especially those aimed at improving the management of higher education in Peru. Its main contribution lies in proposing and empirically validating an integrated model that conceives of learning disposition as the result of the convergence not only of academic factors, but also of existential (purpose in life), psychosocial (social support), spiritual (spiritual experience), and professional (teachers' effectiveness) dimensions. By transcending fragmented explanatory approaches, this research provides a broader conceptual framework for understanding learning disposition in higher education. It contributes novel evidence from a Latin American context to the international literature.

TI Educational participation in children with developmental language
   disorder: associations with co-occurring developmental difficulties
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE (pre-)school; co-occurring difficulties; developmental difficulties;
   developmental language disorder; parent-report; participation
ID CHILDHOOD; OUTCOMES
AB Participation in education refers to children's attendance and involvement in educational activities and is central to their development. Educational activities are highly language-dependent, making children with developmental language disorder (DLD) potentially vulnerable to participation barriers. However, DLD is heterogeneous, and many children show co-occurring nonlinguistic difficulties. Little is known about how educational participation varies within this population in relation to these difficulties. Parents of 72 children with DLD aged 5-10 years, recruited from a specialized inpatient rehabilitation clinic in Germany between March and September 2023, completed the Participation and Environment Measure for Children and Youth. Children were grouped according to whether they had no, one, or at least two co-occurring nonlinguistic difficulties, as assessed by standardized measures in visual-perceptual, motor, and behavioral domains. Group differences were tested with Kruskal-Wallis tests, and associations with Spearman correlations. Participation frequency and involvement in individual educational activities were largely similar across groups. However, mean participation frequency across activities decreased with increasing numbers of co-occurring difficulties and was significantly lower in children with two or more difficulties than in the other groups. Higher motor coordination was associated with higher mean participation frequency, whereas visual-perceptual and behavioral abilities were not. Involvement was high across groups, with no significant group differences or associations. Within the context of this clinical sample, findings suggest that co-occurring difficulties in DLD, particularly more complex developmental profiles and lower motor coordination, may contribute to reduced participation frequency in educational activities. Supporting educational participation in children with DLD requires a holistic, context-sensitive approach that considers co-occurring difficulties.

TI Teaching scientific thinking and science literacy in primary: exploring
   their impact on scientific and critical thinking skills
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational intervention; quasi-experimental design; scientific skill;
   thinking skill; younger school age
ID RATIONALE
AB This study evaluates the impact of an educational intervention aimed at teaching scientific thinking to fifth-grade elementary school students and its effect on critical thinking skills. The main concepts of scientific and critical thinking, along with evidence from educational research regarding their connections are reviewed. A longitudinal quasi-experimental design was employed, featuring two pre-existing fifth-grade classroom groups (n = 60) established by the school prior to the study and we randomized only the assignment of intervention (control and experimental group). Specific tests were administered to assess critical and scientific thinking skills both before and after a 14-week intervention. The experimental group received explicit instruction in five scientific skills: observation, questioning, hypothesis formulation, experimentation, and conclusions. In contrast, the control group received standard instruction. Results indicated that the intervention led to large effect sizes in scientific thinking and moderate-to-large improvements in critical thinking skills, particularly in problem-solving and logical reasoning. Analysis of changes from baseline highlights the significant added value of the intervention compared to standard education. Both boys and girls benefited from the intervention, with some small gender differences observed. Furthermore, a positive correlation was found between scientific thinking and critical thinking, as well as school grades. Predictive models suggest that scientific thinking skills can forecast critical thinking skills. Overall, this study provides empirical evidence that explicit instruction in scientific thinking in primary education enhances both scientific and critical thinking skills, supporting its integration into early science education. TI The great need for migrants in the Italian economy: overcoming
   educational barriers, skills mismatch, and socio-economic integration
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Italy; labour-market inclusion; migration; skill mismatch; skill
   partnership
ID MIGRATION
AB Introduction Migration has become a structural component of the Italian economy, particularly in sectors such as construction, manufacturing, elderly care, and service activities. Despite persistent demand for migrant labour, significant barriers continue to hinder the full integration of foreign workers, including educational gaps, skills mismatches, and bureaucratic obstacles related to the recognition of qualifications.Methods This study adopts a qualitative multi-method approach, combining an online open-ended questionnaire with company representatives (human resource managers) and focus groups with employers and key stakeholders-including vocational education and training providers, higher education institutions, NGOs, and organizations engaged in migrant reception and inclusion in Italy. The analysis explores sector-specific factors shaping migrants' employment trajectories.Results Findings indicate that labour market dualism and ethnic segmentation remain widespread, with migrants frequently channelled into occupational roles based on nationality rather than skill level. These patterns are consistent with the "Mediterranean capitalism" model (Amable), as the Italian case exhibits relatively strong employment protection alongside comparatively weaker social protection mechanisms. The study further examines the opportunities and limitations of skill partnership initiatives involving selected African countries, including Tunisia (construction) and Egypt and Ghana (manufacturing). While these programmes provide targeted benefits, they appear insufficient in promoting long-term employment stability and career progression.Discussion The findings point to the need to reform qualification recognition mechanisms, expand sector-specific vocational training, strengthen workplace-oriented language education, and design more inclusive skill partnership frameworks. Such measures are essential to ensuring that migration functions not only as an economic resource but also as a socially sustainable process.

TI Digital literacy as a mediating factor and generation as a moderating
   factor on continuance to use digital technology for early childhood
   education teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE continuance to use; digital literacy; generation; government policy;
   intention to use; job relevance; perceived ease of use; perceived
   usefulness
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE MODEL; INTENTION; CONFLICT; ADOPTION
AB This study examines factors influencing early childhood education (ECE) teachers' continuance intention to use digital technology by extending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) 3. The study combines four exogenous variables-Perceived Ease of Use, Job Relevance, Government Policy, and Digital Literacy-along with the endogenous variable Continuation of Use, with digital literacy as a mediator and generational cohort as a moderator. Data analysis employed a two-stage approach: measurement model assessment verified instrument reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity, while structural model assessment tested hypotheses using path coefficients, the epsilon V statistic, and PLS Multi-Group Analysis. Results from 365 ECE teachers revealed three of the four significant direct relationships. Job relevance, government policy, and digital literacy positively influenced continuance of use, while perceived ease of use did not show a significant direct effect. Digital literacy significantly mediated the relationships between Perceived Ease of Use and Continuation of Use, and between job relevance and Continuation of Use, but not between government policy and Continuation of Use. Generational cohort significantly moderates the relationship between government policy and sustained adoption. The model exhibits moderate predictive quality. These findings suggest increasingly convergent technology acceptance across generations in the workplace context, with government policy playing a significant role in sustained adoption. Practical implications emphasize establishing digital literacy standards for early childhood teachers and strengthening digital infrastructure. Policymakers can leverage carefully designed regulations and incentives to increase technology adoption across generations. This study contributes to the educational technology literature by demonstrating that while traditional TAM constructs remain relevant, contextual factors such as policy frameworks and digital literacy are increasingly becoming important determinants of sustained technology integration in early childhood education settings.

TI Automated software scoring of senior school certificate examination
   mathematical items in economics using a contextual similarity model
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; assessment; contextual similarity; economics;
   mathematical items; software model
AB Education is a key driver of national development, and technology is transforming assessment methods globally. Although traditional examination formats, such as multiple-choice and essay tests, dominate assessment, subjective human scoring often leads to inconsistencies. Artificial intelligence-based automated scoring systems offer a promising solution. Therefore, this study uses a developed artificial intelligence software based on a contextual similarity model to score mathematical items in secondary school Economics and validates the AI-generated scores against human experts. A correlational research design was adopted for this study. The population comprised 274,978 Economics students from South-west Nigeria, 1,008 of which were sampled through a multi-stage sampling procedure. An AI-based software was developed based on the waterfall model. It was validated by three software experts, and a Cronbach alpha of 0.86 was determined. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics and a Pearson Correlation Coefficient at an alpha level of 0.05 significance. The study's findings revealed a significant relationship between the AI software and the 12 human experts in scoring Economics Mathematical items. The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) indicated a high level of agreement (r = 0.86), P < 0.01). The study concluded that the scoring model possesses the ability to award scores to mathematical computation items in economics that are equivalent to the scores awarded by human expert markers. The study, therefore, recommends that teachers, evaluators, and various examination bodies use this Artificial Intelligence software in scoring mathematical computation items in economics to ensure consistency and save on cost and time.

ID PSYCHOMETRIC PROPERTIES; DDST-II; CHILDREN; VERSION
AB Introduction Cultural adaptation of developmental screening tests often prioritizes psychometric outcomes, overlooking administration-related errors. This study proposes a process-oriented quality assurance model for adapting the Denver II Developmental Screening Test in Kazakhstan.Method Designed as a qualitative case study, the adaptation process was structured using the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle. TI Measuring impact of crucial role of emotional and social intelligence
   among university leaders: towards faculty job satisfaction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE emotional intelligence; job satisfaction; university leaders; ordered
   probit regression model (OPRM); regression tree analysis (RTA); social
   intelligence; university leadership
ID WORK ENGAGEMENT; RESOURCES; TEACHERS; SUSTAINABILITY; MODEL; STYLE
AB In the context of higher education institutions facing increasing pressures from rapidly changing policies and performance evaluations, understanding the role of leadership in faculty well-being remains underexplored. Despite growing interest in leadership competencies, there is limited empirical evidence about the joint impact of emotional and social intelligence (ESI) of university leaders on faculty job satisfaction, particularly in GCC higher education contexts. This study examines the extent to which ESI of university leaders is associated with faculty job satisfaction at King Faisal University, Saudi Arabia. Using a purely quantitative methodology based on ordered probit regression models and regression tree analysis, we surveyed 100 faculty members (academic staff responsible for teaching, research, and student assessment) at King Faisal University, Saudi Arabia, to assess their perceptions of their leaders' ESI and their own job satisfaction levels. Results revealed that both emotional intelligence (EI) and social intelligence (SI) significantly predict faculty job satisfaction, with SI demonstrating a particularly strong influence. Regression tree analysis identified specific ESI competencies-particularly empathy, effective communication, and relationship management-as statistically significant predictors of satisfaction levels. This study's originality lies in its simultaneous examination of both EI and SI constructs in the GCC higher education leadership context and its application of regression tree methodology to identify item-level patterns and micro-contributors to faculty satisfaction. The findings provide evidence-based guidance for academic institutions to prioritize ESI competency development in leadership training programs to enhance faculty morale, reduce turnover, and strengthen institutional sustainability.

TI Low-threshold interdisciplinary encounters across boundary objects:
   early insights from an exploratory study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competency development; curriculum design; education for sustainability;
   higher education; interdisciplinarity; learning activity; graphical
   abstracts
AB Introduction Sustainability challenges are characterised as "wicked" problems that cannot be tackled by one discipline but depend on collaboration between interest holders with multiple, sometimes competing, perspectives. Learning to work effectively in such circumstances is among the most valuable capabilities university students can develop and is therefore appropriately situated within the core curriculum. However, interdisciplinary encounters are demanding for students and educators alike, calling for low-threshold approaches that can adapt to changing circumstances without requiring extensive curriculum redesign. We designed and piloted a theoretically informed learning activity pattern to facilitate encounters between students from different disciplines. The design drew on concepts of epistemic stability and epistemic adaptability to support integrative competency development, alongside boundary object theory which highlights the capacity of artefacts to create shared problem spaces while retaining interpretive flexibility.Methods To examine the design, we took an inductive, theory-building approach comprising three strands: an observation and focus group with students piloting the activities; interviews with three educationalists; and interviews with two module leads who adapted the activities for their own students. Data were thematically analysed to appraise the design's potential in practice.Results The student pilot successfully demonstrated a proof of concept of the activities, providing indicators of competency development and insights about pace, instructions, and other operational considerations. Educationalists and educators identified benefits, challenges, and conditions for successful implementation.Discussion Participants valued the interdisciplinary encounters and expressed appetite for more such opportunities. The activity pattern shows potential to support interdisciplinary competency development. We also identified qualities of graphical (visual) abstracts that enable them to function effectively as boundary objects.

TI Collaborative online international learning (coil) and global mindset

   Global South university

DE collaborative online international learning; cultural intelligence;
   global mindset; intercultural competence; internationalization at home
AB Introduction: Internationalization at home has emerged as an inclusive strategy for developing intercultural competence without requiring physical mobility. Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL) enables digitally mediated intercultural collaboration; however, limited empirical evidence has examined the relationships among student engagement, cultural intelligence, multicultural personality traits, and global mindset development within Global South higher education contexts. Methods: This study examined the relationships among COIL engagement, intercultural competence, and global mindset development among undergraduate students in a Philippine public university implementing internationalization-at-home initiatives. Method: We analysed the content of the PrimTEd Mathematics Knowledge and Practice Standards', from a 'language(s) in mathematics education' perspective. All instances where language is explicitly referenced or implicitly invoked are identified and categorised. In critically reflecting on the findings, we note what is absent and illustrate how the policy framework could be strengthened. Results: Three approaches to language(s) are evident: through general pedagogical standards; through standards related to mathematical acting and thinking; and through the specification of knowledge of various problem types. However, the standards remain generic and high level, offering limited guidance for mathematics course design. We make two contributions towards greater specification. Firstly, we propose performance-level descriptors that articulate levels of attainment for language-responsive teaching (using the example of addition and subtraction). Secondly, we provide illustrative examples of 'gap-generating' words and phrases known to contribute to learner confusion in this domain. Conclusion: We argue for more explicit identification of gap-generating language and research that supports language-responsive teaching within the multilingual context envisaged for South African teacher education. Contribution: This article clarifies how language and mathematics are conceptualised in the PrimTEd standards and offers illustrations that could be used to inform mathematics course design and programme strengthening.

TI Reflections on designing multiple-choice items for largescale
   assessments of student teachers' visual and critical visual literacy
   knowledge and practices
SO READING & WRITING-JOURNAL OF THE READING ASSOCIATION OF SOUTH AFRICA
LA English
DT Article
DE reflective case study; assessing visual and critical visual literacy;
   multiple-choice questions; student teachers; PrimTEd Assessment project
AB Background: The current Curriculum and Assessment Policy Statement (CAPS) for teaching languages and literacies in South African schools includes visual literacy components in all grades and thus teachers need to be visually literate, to be critical viewers of the visual, and to know how to teach visual and critical visual literacy. Objectives: The aim of this research was to investigate the possibilities of designing multiplechoice items that attempt to assess student teachers' visual and critical visual literacy content and pedagogic knowledge. Method: In this reflective case study we present, discuss, and reflect on examples of multiplechoice items designed for the assessment of components of the Primary Teacher Education Project (PrimTEd). Contribution: The article contributes to the field of visual and critical visual literacy assessment in initial teacher education through an investigation of the affordances and limitations of the multiple-choice format commonly used in large-scale assessments.

TI Assessment of classification accuracy in endodontics by dental students:
   a comparative study of holographic imaging and conventional radiography
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Education; Dental; Endodontics; Holography; Radiography;
   Three-dimensional imaging
ID SAMPLE-SIZE; APICAL PERIODONTITIS; PILOT; ANATOMY
AB Background Dental students must master endodontic anatomy, radiographic diagnostics, and treatment strategies early in their clinical training-yet traditional teaching methods, including two-dimensional radiographs, often fail to effectively convey complex spatial structures. Hologram technology has emerged as a promising tool for three-dimensional visualization in dental education. The aim of the study was to compare the classification accuracy of dental students using holograms versus conventional periapical radiographs in identifying endodontic structures. Methods This randomized single center-controlled trial included 79 dental students (years 4-6). After a calibration seminar and pre-test each of the 79 students assessed six tooth cases-three presented as holograms and three as periapical radiographs. Holograms were created from cone-beam computed tomography data, annotated by two calibrated examiners to establish reference points regarding the number of canals, Vertucci classification, and treatment complexity. Students evaluated each case for these parameters; responses were compared to the reference points to assess classification accuracy. The final evaluation form captured their subjective perceptions of the new hologram system. Primary binary outcomes were analyzed using logistic mixed-effects models. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results After Benjamini-Hochberg correction, holography significantly improved root-canal number identification in three multi-rooted cases (adjusted p <= 0.007). For Vertucci classification, only the maxillary anterior tooth remained significant (adjusted p = 0.044). Treatment-complexity assessment showed case-dependent results, favoring radiography in two cases (adjusted p = 0.045 and p = 0.006) and holography in one case (adjusted p = 0.013). Conclusions Holographic visualization demonstrated case-and task-specific effects in endodontic training. Holograms were able to improve classification accuracy in certain endodontic tasks. However, they did not outperform conventional periapical radiographs in all outcomes. Holography could be an effective, supplementary tool for teaching certain endodontic tasks, but its application requires further investigation.

TI AI-mediated authentic assessment and metacognitive reflection: A
   mixed-methods study of the AAIWA model
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Authentic assessment; Condition-Responsive AI feedback; Metacognitive
   reflection; Pre-service teacher education; Academic writing;
   Mixed-methods R&D
AB This study introduces the Authentic AI-Assisted Writing Assessment (AAIWA) model, integrating authentic rubric-based assessment, condition-responsive AI feedback, and structured metacognitive reflection as a unified recursive architecture within Indonesian pre-service teacher education. Existing models treat these components additively, creating a critical design gap particularly in underrepresented Global South contexts. AAIWA addresses this by computationally embedding rubric criteria within the feedback engine and positioning structured reflection as a dynamic input into subsequent feedback cycles rather than a post-hoc add-on. The AAIWA prototype is a constrained hybrid system: a rule-based NLP layer governs all pedagogically consequential decisions while GPT-3.5-turbo serves exclusively as a language-articulation module. Claims of 'condition-responsive feedback' therefore denote rule-conditioned responsiveness, not autonomous LLM reasoning. A mixed-methods R&D design engaged 75 pre-service teachers across three universities in four iterative writing cycles. Significant improvements were observed in academic writing performance (d = 0.92, 95% CI [0.65, 1.19]) and metacognitive reflection (d = 0.98, 95% CI [0.69, 1.27]). A moderate writing reflection correlation (r = .54, 95% CI [.36, .68]) offers partial mechanistic support for the integrated design. Thematic analysis (n = 15) identified three themes: enhanced metacognitive awareness, motivational benefits of immediate feedback, and progressive internalisation of reflection. Expert validation yielded strong content validity indices (rubric: CVI = 0.84; inventory: CVI = 0.82). These pilot findings associated with rather than causally attributable to AAIWA indicate a theoretically grounded, empirically promising framework warranting controlled replication across diverse educational contexts.
