TI Levels of AI awareness and pedagogical skills among Nigerian teachers:
   The differentials of gender and teachers' experience
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE AI awareness; AI pedagogical skills; Nigerian teachers; Gender; Teaching
   experience; AI in education
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; TECHNOLOGY; EDUCATION
AB The rapid diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) across educational systems has intensified the need to assess teachers' readiness to engage with AI-informed pedagogy, particularly in underrepresented contexts. This study investigated the levels of AI awareness and AI pedagogical skills among secondary school teachers in Nigeria, with specific attention to gender and teaching experience differentials. A cross-sectional survey design was employed, drawing on a stratified random sample of 2,586 teachers across Nigeria's six geopolitical zones. AI awareness was measured using an eight-item binary scale, while AI pedagogical skills were assessed using the 20-item Educators' AI Literacy (EDAIL) scale (alpha = .977). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, independent samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, correlation analysis, and ANCOVA. Findings indicate moderate levels of AI awareness (M = 3.13, SD = 1.79 on a 0-8 scale) but comparatively lower AI pedagogical skills (M = 2.47, SD = 0.86 on a 1-5 scale), suggesting a gap between conceptual familiarity and pedagogical application. Significant gender differences were observed, with male teachers reporting higher AI awareness (d = 0.17) and pedagogical skills (d = 0.31), although effect sizes were small. Teaching experience did not significantly predict AI awareness; however, early-career and mid-career teachers reported significantly higher AI pedagogical skills than experienced teachers (eta 2 = 0.008). A moderate positive correlation (r = .378, p < .001) was found between AI awareness and pedagogical skills. These patterns remained robust after controlling for school type. These patterns may suggest that Nigerian secondary school teachers are navigating an early-to-intermediate phase of AI integration, conceptually familiar with AI technologies, yet not fully equipped to enact them pedagogically. The study contributes large-scale empirical evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa. It underscores the need for structured, equity-sensitive, and pedagogically grounded professional development frameworks to advance sustainable AI integration in education.

TI Within arm's reach: Exploring the effects of hand-based augmented
   reality on presence and spatial distance estimation
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION: X REALITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Augmented reality; Spatial computing; Psychological distance
ID PERCEIVED DISTANCE; PLACE ATTACHMENT; INTERACTIVITY; JUDGMENTS;
   RESPONSES
AB Perceived distances to social targets, such as international communities in need, shape social judgments and helping behaviors. In lieu of a direct visit to such communities, bridging perceived spatial distances via narrative or traditional media is limited due to the inability to simulate the audiovisual experience of being in the depicted spaces. However, augmented reality (AR) can overlay virtual content onto a user's physical environment, creating the illusion of being in a virtual rendering of the depicted community, potentially reducing the perceived distances. This work investigates how learning about distant communities, via a charitable giving AR application, shapes perceived spatial distance and evaluations of a distant community. In study 1, a withinsubjects experiment (N = 39) found the AR experience significantly reduced the perceived spatial distance between users and the depicted community. Study 2 (N = 69) employed a 2-condition (input modality: hand-based vs. screen-based) between-subjects experiment using two versions of the app to understand how perceived distance estimates vary as a function of the mode of exploration. Counter to our hypothesis, neither the hand- nor screen-based experience reduced distance estimates, with the hand-based version increasing distance estimates, an effect potentially explained by device-specific factors. Overall, this work contributes to spatial cognition research and demonstrates how AR can distort perceived distances between audiences and distant communities in need. Implications and future research are discussed.

TI Adaptive objective structured clinical examinations across a pharmacy
   curriculum
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING

DT Article
DE Adaptive learning; OSCE; Clinical skill assessment; Critical thinking
ID LEARNING PLATFORM; STUDENTS; EDUCATION
AB Background: Adaptive learning in objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs) allows realtime modification of cases, creating personalized learning trajectories tailored to individual student performance. Objective: To describe and evaluate the implementation and perceptions of adaptive OSCEs throughout a pharmacy didactic curriculum. Methods: Pharmacy students in their first through third (P1, P2, P3) professional years participated in an adaptive OSCE specific to their respective course content. Students completed a baseline OSCE, followed by an OSCE for remediation or advanced practice based on performance. Conclusion: Adaptive OSCEs offered students greater exposure to clinical scenarios tailored to their abilities. Benefit from this assessment style was perceived by students and faculty, with students reporting greater benefit regarding clinical and critical thinking skills.

TI Protecting academic performance: A school-based randomized crossover
   trial of a digital neuropsychological program in 'red zones' of
   Guatemala
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Pediatric neuropsychology; Child development; Vulnerability; Cognitive
   stimulation; Emotional competence; Randomized controlled trial
ID EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; CHILDREN; VERSION
AB Introduction: Guatemala is among the poorest countries in Latin America, with high levels of social inequality, poverty and extreme violence. This socioeconomic context poses a risk for cognitive and emotional development in children. In addition, the socioeconomic gap faced by its inhabitants increased during the COVID-19 pandemic. This article presents the results of the implementation of a neuropsychological stimulation program aimed at improving academic performance. Methodology: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of a cognitive and emotional stimulation program focused on Attention, Language, Executive Functions, and Social Cognition, through a digital neurorehabilitation platform using tablets inside classrooms. Participants from 5th grade (n = 352, 45.5% females) were randomly divided into an experimental and control group. Pre- and post-intervention assessments were conducted, along with a follow-up assessment one year later with role reversal between the experimental and control groups. Results: The program had a significant positive impact on the primary functional outcome: academic performance (GPA). Specifically, GPA significantly increased in two of the four participating schools during the main intervention (beta = 0.42 and 0.51, p < .001). Follow-up assessments confirmed this protective effect, with one school showing a significant improvement in GPA after receiving the program (beta = 0.42, p < .001). After applying strict statistical corrections for multiple comparisons, improvements in individual cognitive and emotional measures did not reach the threshold for significance and were treated as positive tendencies. Discussion: These findings suggest that the intervention's success is driven by an aggregate effect, where sub-threshold improvements across multiple cognitive and emotional domains accumulate to produce a measurable boost in global academic performance. This RCT supports the use of this neurorehabilitation tool as an effective school-based "digital shield" to safeguard academic trajectories in high-vulnerability contexts, mitigating educational gaps in children following systemic disruptions.

ID MORAL FOUNDATIONS THEORY; BUSINESS ETHICS; EDUCATION; STUDENTS; GENDER
AB Management ethics education requires instructional approaches that go beyond merely transmitting norms to support ethical judgment in context. This study examines how a theoryinformed, case-based instructional sequence implemented through EthicApp, a digital learning environment, is associated with shifts in students' judgments about a prosocial academic misconduct dilemma. The sequence translates Schwartz's Integrated Ethical Decision-Making (IEDM) model into instructional phases that cue intuition, emotion, duty-based reflection, rationalization, and peer consultation. Using an instructional quasi-experimental design with repeated measures, the study examines how systematically varied prompts are associated with shifts in ethical judgments rather than directly measuring cognitive processes. Drawing on Moral Foundations Theory (MFT) and repeated-measures data from 1080 students at two Chilean universities, the findings show that initial intuitive judgments are primarily associated with Binding foundations; emotionally framed prompts increase willingness to help, duty-oriented prompts reduce support for misconduct, and peer consultation moderates polarized positions. Differences by seniority and gender indicate heterogeneous responses. The study contributes to management ethics education, moral psychology, and instructional design by showing how a process model of ethical decision-making can be operationalized as a sequenced pedagogical intervention, and how moral foundations shape initial intuitive judgments, offering guidance for ethics instruction in management education.

TI More than a continuum: Distinct pathways to mathematics learning
   difficulties and mathematical giftedness
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Domain-general factors; Dyscalculia; Heterogeneity; Mathematical
   giftedness; Motivational and emotional factors; Socio-economic status
ID NUMBER SENSE; METAANALYSIS; ACHIEVEMENT; STUDENTS; DYSCALCULIA;
   PREDICTORS; NUMERACY; CHILDREN; ACCESS
AB This editorial paper introduces a special issue presenting thirteen papers investigating the factors related to exceptionally high and low mathematics performance across diverse age groups and educational contexts. Despite the variety of approaches, several consistent findings emerged. One important finding is that early numerical competencies are reliable predictors of later mathematics achievement. While domain-general factors are associated with mathematics performance, their predictive power diminishes when considered together with numerical skills. Additionally, both shared and distinct predictors of low and high attainment have been identified. The studies also highlight substantial heterogeneity within the high- and low-achieving groups. Overall, these findings challenge the idea that differences along the mathematics attainment continuum are purely quantitative. Instead, they support a multidimensional perspective where different pathways underlie low and high performance. These results have important implications for theory, early identification, and targeted interventions, emphasizing the need for approaches that account for both between-group differences and withingroup variability.

TI Gamification of learning and instruction-Learning processes and
   individual differences
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Gamification; Gamified learning; Leaderboards; Personalization; Young
   learners
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; MOTIVATION; GAMES
AB Gamification has become a prominent approach in educational research and practice, yet its effectiveness remains inconsistent and insufficiently understood. This Special Issue addresses key gaps by advancing a more differentiated perspective on gamified learning, focusing on heterogeneity in design, adaptivity, and individual learner differences. The Special Issue is structured around three interconnected themes: personalized gamification, competition-based gamification with leaderboards, and gamification in young learners. Across these areas, the studies highlight that effects of gamification are context-dependent and often driven by complex interactions between design features and learner characteristics. Overall, the contributions emphasize the need for rigorous, theory-driven research that moves beyond average effects toward understanding for whom and under which conditions gamification works.

TI Diagnostic reasoning in the RN-to-NP transition: An interpretive
   description study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Diagnostic reasoning; Nurse practitioner education; Professional
   identity formation; Interpretive description; RN-to-NP transition
AB Aim: To explore how nurse practitioner (NP) students understand, experience, and develop diagnostic reasoning (DR) during their NP education, and to examine how prior nursing experience and clinical learning environments shape this development. Background: DR is a core competency for NP practice and represents a significant shift in responsibility during the transition from registered nurse (RN) to NP. While existing literature has focused primarily on teaching strategies, limited research has examined DR from the learner perspective. Methods: This qualitative study employed Interpretive Description. Twenty-four NP students in their final semester from two Canadian universities participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed using a five-phase qualitative analytic process. Themes were developed through iterative coding and constant comparison. Results: Four themes emerged: (1) structured sense-making and professional identity transformation (2) prior RN experience as a double-edged influence (3) developing DR under conditions of complexity and constraint, and (4) scaffolded and iterative pathways to diagnostic development. Participants described DR as the "biggest leap" in the RN-to-NP transition, representing not only systematic hypothesis refinement but also diagnostic accountability as the most responsible provider. DR was experienced as inherently relational and co-constructed within the clinical encounter. Prior RN experience provided experiential foundations that supported pattern recognition, while at times narrowing diagnostic breadth due to specialization and habituated practice patterns. Developing DR in primary care was experienced as intellectually taxing, shaped by cognitive load, uncertainty, and contextual fragmentation. Students actively strengthened their DR through self-regulated strategies, while simulation, engaged preceptors, and iterative reassessment functioned as scaffolded supports for DR development. Conclusion: NP students experience DR as a cognitive, relational, and identity-forming process that extends beyond technical skill acquisition to encompass diagnostic accountability. Educational approaches that explicitly address role transition, relational competencies, and structured reasoning may better prepare learners to assume diagnostic responsibility and navigate clinical uncertainty in NP practice.

TI The impact of transition shocks on career aspirations during nursing
   internships: A moderated mediated effects model
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing students; Occupational stigma; Occupational respect; Transition
   shock; Career aspirations
ID STIGMA; RESPECT; PROGRAM
AB Background: During the transition from theoretical learning to clinical practice, nursing students frequently experience substantial transitional stress, potentially undermining their professional aspirations and even leading to turnover intentions. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Therefore, exploring effective coping strategies and guiding nursing students in developing sound professional values are critical for enhancing their career stability. Aims: To investigate whether occupational stigma moderates the mediating effect of nursing students' sense of occupational respect on the relationship between transition shock and career aspirations. Design: This was a cross-sectional study employing a moderated mediation model. Participants: A total of 408 undergraduate nursing students from a university in Zhejiang, China, participated in this study. Methods: Participants were surveyed using the Occupational Stigma Scale, the Nurses' Sense of Occupational Respect Scale, the Career Ambition Scale, and the Transition Shock Scale. Additionally, occupational stigma moderated the relationship between transition shock and sense of occupational respect. Specifically, nursing students who perceived lower levels of occupational stigma showed a stronger correlation between transition shock and occupational respect. Conclusion: This study clarifies the mechanisms involved in the relationship between transition shock and career aspirations among nursing students during practical training. These findings may assist in reducing transition shock during clinical practice and enhancing nursing students' career aspirations.

AB Research on mathematics development has identified a multidimensional network of individual- and contextuallevel predictors. TI University students' evolving conceptual metaphors of AI in English
   academic writing: An actor-network perspective
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Conceptual metaphors; Artificial intelligence; English academic writing;
   Actor-network theory
ID FEEDBACK
AB Students' metaphors of AI describe and actively configure learner-AI relationships in academic writing. Prior research has identified recurring framings of AI as tool-based or human-based, yet has largely relied on cross-sectional designs that tended to treat metaphors as static representations. This longitudinal study draws on Actor-Network Theory (ANT) as an interpretive lens to examine how ten university students' metaphorical conceptualizations of AI evolved over a oneyear period. Data were collected through two rounds of semi-structured interviews, triangulated with students' AI-use artifacts. The findings reveal three trajectories: maintenance of tool-based metaphors with enhanced recognition of AI capabilities; shifts from tool-based to human-based conceptualizations; and processes of intensified or reduced personification. These shifts of metaphors appear to reflect not individual cognitive change alone but negotiated relationships among tools, teachers, peers, policies, and tasks. Effective and ethical human-AI collaborative writing is less an individual achievement than a network accomplishment, dependent on alignment among student literacies, AI capabilities, institutional policies, and task demands. This study demonstrates the value of an ANT perspective in AI research, showing how human and non-human actants mutually shape learning relationships. Creating opportunities to make students' AI metaphors visible can facilitate responsive institutional policy-making and inform pedagogical strategies. The tensions between students' explicit tool-based metaphors and their implicit affective characterizations highlight AI's emotional dimension, inviting further investigation. The study underscores the importance of longitudinal designs for capturing the dynamic evolution of human-AI interaction.

TI The role of motivational beliefs in pre-service teachers' technology
   integration intentions: Longitudinal findings over one year
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Situated Expectancy-Value Theory; Pre-service teachers; Teacher
   motivation; Digital competence beliefs; Prospective technology
   integration; Teacher education; Longitudinal study
ID ACCEPTANCE MODEL; EXPECTATIONS; COMPETENCE; IMPACT; ICT
AB Understanding how pre-service teachers' motivation toward educational technology develops during teacher education is essential for fostering classroom technology integration. Drawing on Situated Expectancy-Value Theory, this longitudinal study examined the stability of technology-related expectancies for success and task values, as well as their prospective and reciprocal relations with intended technology integration. Data were collected from 314 pre-service teachers in Germany at two measurement points one year apart. Confirmatory factor analyses supported scalar measurement invariance across time. TI Spanish Validation of the Self-Regulation for Learning Online (SRL-O)
   Questionnaire for University Students
SO JOURNAL FOR THE STUDY OF EDUCATION AND DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE self-regulated learning; online learning; university students;
   cross-cultural validation
ID STRATEGIES; FIT
AB As online learning becomes increasingly prevalent, understanding how students regulate their learning in digital contexts is crucial. This study validated the Spanish version of the Self-Regulation for Learning Online (SRL-O) questionnaire, originally developed in English to assess motivational beliefs and learning strategies in online and blended learning. A total of 1,880 university students from a fully online Spanish institution completed the 44-item SRL-O, which measures 10 factors: online self-efficacy, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, negative achievement emotion, planning and time management, metacognition, study environment, effort regulation, social support, and task strategies. The SRL-O shows conceptual and psychometric robustness in Spanish and offers a practical tool for identifying students at risk of poor academic outcomes and promoting self-regulated learning in online education.

TI The Effects of Blended Learning on Undergraduate Students Conceptual
   Understanding of Chemical Bonding and Molecular Geometry
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Blended Learning Environment; Technology-Enhanced Learning; Conceptual
   Change; Chemical Education Research; Chemical Bonding; Molecular
   Geometry; Undergraduate Education
ID MISCONCEPTIONS; DIFFICULTIES
AB Understanding how blended learning (BL) influences undergraduate students' conceptual understanding of chemical bonding and molecular geometry (CBMG) remains an important yet underexplored area in higher education, particularly in developing contexts. This study examined the effects of the BL approach on undergraduate students' conceptual understanding of CBMG. A mixed-methods approach with a nonequivalent control group quasi-experimental design was employed. A total of 86 undergraduate students (59 male and 27 female) from Bahir Dar University in Ethiopia participated in the study. Two intact classes were randomly assigned to an intervention group (IG; n = 42), which received BL instruction, and a comparison group (CG; n = 44), which was taught using conventional teaching methods (CTM). Quantitative data were collected using a Three-Tier Conceptual Understanding Diagnostic Test (TTCUDT), while qualitative data were gathered through semistructured interviews. The results showed a statistically significant difference in posttest conceptual understanding scores between the groups, favoring students in the BL condition. The findings further indicated that BL enhanced students' scientific knowledge and reduced misconceptions (MCs) regarding CBMG concepts compared with CTM. However, no statistically significant gender differences were observed in students' conceptual understanding. Overall, the results suggest that BL is an effective instructional strategyfor improving undergraduate students' conceptual understanding of chemistry, and supports the integration of technology to promote meaningful learning.

TI Closing the Theory-Practice Gap in Analytical Chemistry: A Gas
   Chromatography Simulator for Enhanced Student Learning
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Analytical Chemistry; Instrumental Methods; Gas Chromatography;
   Separation Sciences; Distance Learning; Self Instruction; Laboratory
   Instruction
ID DETECTOR; PERFORMANCE
AB Chromatography is a core technique in undergraduate instrumental analysis courses; however, student understanding of chromatographic optimization is often limited by restricted access to instrumentation, time constraints, and the abstract nature of theoretical parameters, such as temperature programming, column dimensions, and detector selection. We report the development and pedagogical evaluation of a MATLAB-based gas chromatography (GC) simulator designed for analytical chemistry courses in science degrees and master's programs. The simulator allows users to manipulate column characteristics (stationary phase type, length, internal diameter, and film thickness), temperature conditions (isothermal and programmed gradients), carrier gas parameters, and detector types, generating simulated chromatograms that reflect realistic chromatographic behavior. The tool was implemented in a cohort of approximately 200 students enrolled in Pharmacy and Chemistry programs and accompanied by a structured teacher guide, installation instructions, and a student activity manual. Its educational effectiveness was evaluated through a postactivity satisfaction survey and qualitative feedback. Results indicate high levels of student engagement and perceived improvement in understanding chromatographic resolution, selectivity, and detector response. This open-access tool (Zenodo repository - ) provides a flexible and scalable strategy to enhance conceptual learning in instrumental analysis courses where hands-on access to GC instrumentation is limited.

TI Humanising Web-Based Learning for Academically Transitioning Students
   Through Their Voices
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic transition; English reading; humanising learning; students'
   voices; web-based learning
ID 1ST YEAR; EDUCATION
AB Web-based learning (WBL) has been widely used to support students' learning and has demonstrated its role in boosting students' academic success. Little research has focused on strategies that students can use to humanise this mode of learning, especially academically transitioning students. To fill this gap, this study explores the pedagogical use of student voice to humanise WBL during students' academic transition. Informed by a qualitative case study approach, the study involved a group of female students (N = 12) from a university in China who were academically transitioning to content-based English reading learning while participating in WBL for out-of-class learning. During their semester-long learning, data were collected naturalistically, including student-instructor dialogues as well as the students' written reflections and interviews with the students as ways of eliciting their voices. No additional interventions were made. By mainly employing inductive thematic analysis of data sources, the study shows that over time, voice-making seemed to empower students to agentively participate in learning, reflect upon their learning, and offer critical insights into their interaction between WBL and the constraints on their academic transition. Their voice-making, coupled with their and their instructor's action-taking (which is a further crucial component of the pedagogical use of student voice), gradually formed a relatively stable loop through which WBL was being humanised. That is, the WBL was flexibly tailored to meet the students' diverse needs during their academic transition. The study concludes that the pedagogical use of academically transitioning students' voices could be gradually helpful in humanising WBL, creating a learning environment that was caring and effective enough to bridge their previous and ongoing learning.

DT Article
DE Supernumerary registrar; Supernumerary medical training; Foreign medical

AB Background The Supernumerary Registrar (SNR) training program has been instrumental in providing non-South African medical practitioners, particularly from other African nations, with essential postgraduate training opportunities. However, despite its long history, there is a notable absence of formal evaluations that assess the program's academic and clinical impact on both South African healthcare systems and the healthcare services in the registrars' home countries. The aim of this study is to objectively evaluate the clinical and academic impact of University of Cape Town (UCT) SNRs in Orthopaedic Surgery by assessing theatre clinical outputs and academic research contributions and career progression post-graduation.Methods A cross-sectional study involving Registrars and Registrar Alumni attached to the Division of Orthopaedic Surgery at the UCT was done. Further research could explore if this pattern exists across UCT's Surgery Department and re-examine registrars' experiences at UCT.

   re-implementation and engagement strategy in a general surgery residency
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrustable professional activities; SIMPL; Change management; Surgical
   education; Resident assessment; Faculty engagement
ID ENTRUSTABLE PROFESSIONAL ACTIVITIES
AB Objective Entrustable professional activities (EPAs) are now required for general surgery residency assessment, typically through the SIMPL platform, but adoption has been limited by inconsistent engagement. We evaluated whether a structured re-engagement strategy guided by the ADKAR change-management framework increased EPA assessment activity.Design Single-center before-after quality-improvement study reported per SQUIRE 2.0. A faculty survey mapped barriers to ADKAR domains and informed a multicomponent intervention (faculty and resident re-education, a monthly leaderboard, and recognition of high participation) delivered from August to December 2024. EPA activity was compared between matched calendar quarters before (January to March 2024) and after (January to March 2025) the intervention, using count-data regression adjusted for postgraduate year and resident type and accounting for residents present in both periods.Setting A single urban academic general surgery residency program.Participants Twenty-four residents per period (48 resident-periods, 31 unique residents) and 66 surveyed faculty.Results Total EPA assessments rose from 36 to 100; residents completed approximately 2.6 times as many assessments after the intervention (incidence-rate ratio 2.58, 95% CI 1.17 to 5.73; p = 0.019), an interval spanning a modest to a large effect. About 40% of the increase reflected resident cohort turnover, and the within-resident change was not statistically significant.Conclusions A structured, ADKAR-guided re-engagement strategy was associated with substantially greater EPA assessment activity. Because gains partly reflected cohort turnover and a concurrent national trend, these uncontrolled results warrant caution, and the study measured EPA utilization only, not feedback quality, learning, or competency. Nonetheless, the reproducible bundle offers a practical template for programs facing low EPA engagement.

AB This study explores how college undergraduate students read young adult literature through a critical gender lens in a general education course. TI Mistake-Based Learning (MBL): A Mistake-Tolerant Teaching Approach for
   Developing Innovation-Related Competence in Undergraduate Chemistry
   Laboratories
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Chemical Education Research; Undergraduate/General; Laboratory
   Instruction; Student-Centered Learning; Innovative Literacy;
   Mistake-Based Learning; Mistake-Tolerant Teaching; MBL; PBL
ID SCIENCE
AB This study presents Mistake-Based Learning (MBL), an instructional approach grounded in Mistake-Tolerant Teaching and aimed at fostering students' innovation literacy through the development of observable competencies in undergraduate chemistry laboratories. MBL is organized around a core cycle of mistake emergence, trial-and-error, and mistake transformation. It integrates innovation-literacy development, a mistake-tolerant learning environment, and structured laboratory practice through a five-stage pathway supported by three interacting drivers, with a four-part evaluation providing continuous formative feedback, guiding students to transform naturally occurring experimental mistakes into opportunities for inquiry, analysis, revision, and reflection. In a cocurricular "second classroom" setting with pharmacy-related undergraduates, MBL was implemented, with phenol nitration serving as an illustrative experimental case. Data were collected from pre-, mid-, and postimplementation questionnaires, student reports and presentations, students' reflective materials, and records of key learning episodes. Under clearly defined safety boundaries and phased instructor support, students identified and worked through recurring problems in controlling reaction conditions, implementing procedures, and responding to unexpected outcomes by examining possible causes and refining their experimental decisions. Descriptive questionnaire results indicated a shift toward more process-oriented views of innovation, accompanied by stronger innovation-related self-efficacy and self-reported growth in adaptive inquiry, iterative resilience, and reflective integration. These findings suggest that MBL may provide a way to turn bound experimental uncertainty into a productive resource for inquiry, revision, and reflection, thereby offering a valuable pathway for cultivating innovation literacy in undergraduate chemistry laboratories.

TI "Relationships Are the Key": How First-Year Teachers Apply the
   Trauma-Informed Lessons of Their Teacher Training
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE elementary teacher education; equity; preservice teacher education
ID EDUCATION; MODEL
AB Equity-centered, trauma-informed education (ECTIE) provides educators with a framework for supporting all students, especially those impacted by trauma. This study examines how first-year teachers implement ECTIE practices after being introduced to ECTIE during preservice teacher training. Employing interpretive description through the lens of sociocultural theory, researchers interviewed eight first-year teachers and conducted three classroom observations. Through thematic analysis, we found participants engaged in multiple ECTIE practices, including connecting with students and building safety. Participants engaged in praxis by integrating ECTIE theory in everyday teaching practices that interconnected and supported one another, which we used to develop an ECTIE teaching model to visualize these connections. However, philosophical mismatches created barriers to implementing ECTIE. The ECTIE teaching model, along with stories from first-year teachers, demonstrates the complexity in building ECTIE praxis and provides a conceptual tool for embedding ECTIE in teacher education.

TI Neurodivergent Social Work Educators: A Collaborative Autoethnography on
   Teaching, Power, and Inclusive Pedagogy
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING IN SOCIAL WORK
LA English
DT Article
DE Neurodivergence; social work education; inclusive pedagogy;
   collaborative autoethnography
ID AUTISM
AB Neurodivergent educators remain largely absent from scholarship on higher education, despite growing attention to neurodiversity among students. This absence has implications for pedagogy, institutional practice, and inclusion in social work education, where teaching is shaped by implicit norms of professionalism, communication, and relational labor. This collaborative autoethnography examines how neurodivergent social work educators experience and navigate these conditions within everyday teaching practice. Guided by the neurodiversity paradigm and double and triple empathy theories, we draw on iterative collaborative reflection and analytic dialogue among four neurodivergent social work educators across career stages. Through vignette-based narratives and collective sensemaking, we identify four interrelated themes: professionalism as a neurotypical standard, hidden curriculum and learning through consequences, chrononormativity, and the gap between empathy and capacity under institutional constraints. Findings illustrate how institutional norms and power relations shape not only student experiences, but also the conditions under which educators teach, respond, and sustain their work. This paper contributes to social work education by centering neurodivergent educators' lived experiences and extending empathy-based frameworks to faculty labor, institutional design, and inclusive pedagogy.

TI Co-Designing Multimodal, Multilingual Text Sets: Centering Caregiver
   Choice
SO READING TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
DE early literacy; family literacy; linguistic justice; multilingual
   learners; multimodal texts
ID ENGAGEMENT
AB Early literacy instruction in the U.S. often centers monolingual, English-dominant practices that marginalize multilingual learners and their families. This qualitative design-based research study examines a family literacy initiative that engaged caregivers and teachers as co-designers of a multilingual, multimodal literacy resource bag. Using the MultiSemiotic Architecture Framework, we analyzed qualitative data to explore how collaborative text selection can advance linguistic justice in early childhood education. Findings highlight five themes that shaped intentional text selection and supported multilingual home literacy practices: content, language, cultural relevance, curricular alignment, and collaborative modifications. The study offers practical implications for educators and researchers seeking to design family literacy initiatives that sustain home languages and affirm multilingual families' expertise.

TI "I'ma Superhero Too.": A Critical Case Study of a Black Student's
   Biliteracy Journey
SO READING TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Black language; Black students; multilingualism; raciolinguistics;
   translanguaging
ID BILINGUAL-EDUCATION; DUAL-LANGUAGE; IMMERSION; EQUITY; RACE
AB This article explores the biliteracy journey of Jamaal, an African American, in an elementary dual language bilingual education (DLBE) classroom. Although scholars have researched the biliteracy development and identity construction of bilingual children for decades, limited research has explored the biliteracy trajectory of African Americans in DLBE, including how they maintain biliteracy identities while also resisting historical stigmatization of their linguistic practices. This qualitative study draws upon raciolinguistic perspectives, translanguaging, and liberation literacies. These theoretical lenses provide a foundation to explore the complexity of how African American children navigate racialized biliteracy development in DLBE and illuminate the fullness of their linguistic repertoires. Data were collected from an ethnographic case study in a Midwestern elementary DLBE program primarily serving Latine/x and African American children. Findings demonstrate how African American children are capable of employing their linguistic resources for linguistic liberation. In one vignette, Jamaal demonstrates this by drawing upon features of Black Language to participate in a retelling of a read-aloud. In another, he combats raciolinguistic ideologies that labeled him a "non-reader" by reconstructing his own story using features of Black Language in a space that often renounced his linguistic identity. This article has implications for practitioners and researchers as it demonstrates how bilingual African American children agentively leverage their linguistic resources in DLBE classrooms, and how their teachers furnish supportive platforms for the totality of their identities.

TI Agentic AI in Education: Whose Agent? Whose Agency?
SO TECHTRENDS
LA English
DT Article
DE Agency; Agentic AI; AI agents; Rights; Education; Generative AI; Student
   agency; Teacher agency
AB This article examines a linguistic shift with significant stakes for education. As the technology industry markets increasingly autonomous software as "agentic AI," it draws on a vocabulary (agent, agency, agentic) that has done centuries of work in moral and educational thought. We argue that agent and agency are different kinds of words. Agent is a role-word that extends easily to software, while agency is a rights-word whose moral weight was won through centuries of struggle to widen the circle of who counts as a person whose voice matters. When vendors sell "agentic AI" to schools, they borrow the moral weight of the second word to legitimize the extension of the first. Tracing this distinction through the history of agency as a hard-won right and through educational traditions that center learner and teacher voice, we show that so-called agentic learning platforms are structurally double agents, serving institutional principals under the vocabulary of serving the learner. The result is a slow erosion of the vocabulary educators need to defend student and teacher self-determination against the very systems now marketed under its name.

TI From Machines to Algorithms: A Short History of Technical Rationality in
   Education
SO TECHTRENDS
LA English
DT Article
ID INSTRUCTIONAL-DESIGN; TECHNOLOGY
AB This brief historical essay argues that one of the most consequential shifts in educational technology has been conceptual rather than technical: the ascendancy of technical rationality as the design logic of pedagogy. Tracing three moments (mechanical instruments, computational systems, and algorithmic infrastructures) the piece highlights how optimization, management, and prediction have tended to reframe what teaching and learning are imagined to be. By reading past innovations as carriers of rationalities, not just tools, the essay urges educators to recognize-and exnovate-inherited assumptions that privilege automation and control over interpretation and encounter.

TI Exploring ESL pedagogical strategies across diverse learning styles:
   insights from English language educators
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ESL; Engineering education; Learning styles; Teaching practice; VARK
ID TEACHING STYLES
AB Learning styles remain an important consideration in ESL instruction, particularly in engineering education contexts where accommodating diverse learner preferences is crucial for effective technical and professional communication. Despite growing recognition of learner diversity, limited empirical research has examined how ESL teachers in engineering colleges translate this awareness into actual classroom practice. This study employed a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, combining a VARK (Visual Auditory Read/Write and Kinesthetic) based questionnaire administered to 40 ESL instructors with semi-structured interviews conducted with 15 participants across five engineering colleges in the Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu, India. Read/Write and Auditory modalities were the most consistently accommodated learning styles across all institutions, reflecting a shared emphasis on traditional lecture-based and text-centered instruction. Visual and Kinesthetic modalities showed considerable variation, with some institutions demonstrating significantly stronger implementation of hands-on and visual learning strategies than others. Qualitative findings revealed that resource limitations, assessment misalignment, and the absence of targeted professional development represent the primary barriers to balanced learning style accommodation. Although ESL instructors broadly recognized the importance of accommodating diverse learning styles, implementation consistency varied significantly across institutions. The findings suggest that multimodal instructional approaches, assessment reform, and institution-level professional development are essential for improving learning style accommodation in engineering ESL contexts.

TI Bridging the Python Training Gap for Bioscientists in Brazil:
   Improvements and Challenges
SO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE biological data; introductory programming; python; workshop
AB The rapid evolution of high-throughput technologies in biosciences generates vast and diverse datasets, demanding that bioscientists develop advanced data manipulation and analysis skills. Python, with its versatility and powerful libraries, has become a crucial tool for managing these datasets. However, a significant lack of programming training for bioscientists persists in many countries. To address this knowledge gap in Brazil, the Brazilian Python Workshop for Biological Data was introduced several years ago, focusing on fundamental programming concepts and data handling techniques using popular Python libraries. Despite positive feedback from earlier editions, persistent challenges necessitated continuous adaptation to meet the evolving needs of bioscientists. This work describes the advancements implemented in the 2021 and 2022 editions of the workshop and discusses suggestions for its ongoing enhancement. Key innovations were introduced in the workshop's structure and coordination, including new committees and a code of conduct. Feedback forms were updated for real-time adjustments, and the event's reach was expanded to increase geographical diversity. New didactic strategies, such as pair-teaching, code clubs, and the integration of ICTs, were implemented to enhance learning outcomes. Programming best practices and scientific reproducibility were emphasized through talks and hands-on activities guided by PEP8 conventions. Furthermore, scientific dissemination was intensified through an increased social media presence and participation in international events. Finally, we present updated recommendations for students, researchers, and educators interested in organizing similar initiatives.

TI The Affective Power of the Imagination: Vygotsky With Spinoza
SO CULTURE AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Spinoza; affect; necessity; Shklovsky; pere & zcaron;ivanie
AB Vygotsky, basing himself on Spinoza, identifies the driver of the differentiation of psychic functions as the development of the affects themselves. This transformation of affectivity is played out through the ludic imagination of the child. Since, according to Spinoza's Ethics, one affect may only be overcome by a stronger affect, the child can free herself or himself from the temptations of reality and from his or her own affective tendencies only by opposing them with a stronger affectivity, born of the imaginative pleasures of playing by rules-born, therefore, from the transformation of a concept into an affect. It is this concept becoming an affect that brings the child to a zone of proximal development-to "a notch above himself/herself." We examine, through this use of Spinozism by Vygotsky, in what sense the ludic imagination of the child, but also the esthetic imagination of the poet, is a true work of de-realization-what Vygotsky also called, from Shklovsky, "enstranging" [making strange]-such that the experienced emotions become intelligent ones.

TI A study of the interplay between educational policy, research and
   teaching in the context of a mathematics curriculum reform
SO RESEARCH IN MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mathematics curriculum reform; interacting activity systems;
   transformative agency
AB School mathematics curriculum reforms are deeply influenced by political considerations, reflecting societal goals and ideological conflicts. This study examines an ongoing reform of the mathematics curriculum, with a focus on fostering students' active engagement with powerful mathematical ideas to develop as critical citizens. Using a fourth-generation activity theory framework, the study analyses interactions among three interrelated activity systems: research, teaching, and policymaking. Data were collected through an autoethnographic approach, including official documents and reflections shared via email and in in-person and online meetings among three lead coordinators and two educational policy counsellors involved in the design process. Research activities are prioritised when scientific evidence is required to resolve tensions, whereas teaching activities gain emphasis when tension resolution entails macro-political risks.

TI Exploring factors influencing self-advocacy in students with learning
   disabilities: A qualitative study
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE educational inclusion; factors; influences; learning disabilities;
   self-advocacy; students
AB Self-advocacy is a central component of educational inclusion for students with learning disabilities because it enables students to recognize their learning needs, communicate those needs, request accommodations and participate more actively in decisions affecting their education. However, students often develop self-advocacy within emotionally demanding and institutionally inconsistent contexts. This study aimed to explore the lived experiences of students with learning disabilities and identify the internal, relational and institutional factors that shape their self-advocacy in secondary and post-secondary educational settings. A qualitative descriptive-interpretive design was used. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 26 students aged 14-22 years in Richmond Hill, Canada, all of whom had a formal learning disability diagnosis. Participants were recruited from secondary and post-secondary educational settings and support networks. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed in NVivo-15 using open, axial and selective coding. Trustworthiness was enhanced through member checking, peer debriefing, analytic memoing, audit-trail documentation and consensus coding. Five interrelated themes were identified: internal psychological factors, social and relational influences, structural and institutional conditions, personal growth and coping strategies and empowerment through self-advocacy. Participants described self-advocacy as a developmental process shaped by fear of judgement, disability identity, communication confidence, teacher responsiveness, peer and family support, accommodation procedures, access to legal-rights knowledge, technology use and prior successful advocacy experiences. The findings indicate that self-advocacy among students with learning disabilities is not merely an individual skill but a situated process produced through the interaction of emotional readiness, relational validation and institutional accessibility. Schools and post-secondary institutions should therefore provide explicit self-advocacy instruction, consistent accommodation systems, teacher training and supportive opportunities for students to participate in their own educational planning.

TI Reinstituting teacher agency and classroom resilience amid geopolitics
   of AI homogenisation
SO PEDAGOGY CULTURE AND SOCIETY
LA English

DE Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd); algorithmic homogenisation;
   technological dependence; classroom resilience; AIEd geopolitics
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; HIGHER-EDUCATION; OPPORTUNITIES; CHALLENGES
AB The development of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) is often presented as a narrative of technological neutrality, sustained by the logic of efficiency and deterministic inevitability. TI Exploring Artificial Intelligence Through Robotics and Machine Learning:
   Perceptions of Pre-Service Teachers, Elementary School Students, and
   In-Service Teachers
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE elementary education; educational technology; higher education; machine
   learning; robotics
AB This study examined how educational robotics and machine learning activities contributed to the understanding of artificial intelligence (AI) among elementary school students, pre-service teachers, and practicing teachers. The intervention involved 1207 participants, including 1009 fifth-grade students, 93 practicing elementary school teachers, and 105 pre-service teachers. Participants engaged in a series of structured activities focused on educational robotics, visual block-based programming, and machine learning concepts. A pre-experimental design was employed to assess changes in understanding and to explore participants' perceptions of the learning experience. Statistical analyses included Student's t-tests, the Kruskal-Wallis H test, and Bonferroni-corrected post hoc comparisons. Results indicated pre-post gains in elementary school students' understanding of machine learning, AI modeling processes, and fundamental computational concepts following participation in the intervention. Across the three groups, participants reported positive perceptions of the activities and recognized their value for learning about AI. Elementary school students reported higher motivation and stronger engagement in coding-related tasks, likely reflecting their previous experience with Scratch in school settings. Practicing teachers expressed a more interdisciplinary perspective on the educational applications of AI, whereas pre-service teachers demonstrated stronger conceptual understanding of the underlying principles. Overall, the findings suggest that educational robotics and machine learning activities are associated with positive learning experiences and observed gains in AI-related understanding. However, given the pre-experimental design without a control group or random assignment, the results should be interpreted as evidence of observed changes and participant perceptions rather than demonstrated effectiveness.

TI University Education in Ukraine in Conditions of Russian Aggression
SO ACADEMIA Y VIRTUALIDAD
LA English
DT Article
DE Russian aggression; organization and delivery of education; Ukrainian
   universities; digital technologies; distance and blended learning;
   martial law
AB The article examines the peculiarities of organizing and delivering education at Ukrainian universities in the context of Russian aggression. The purpose of the study was to analyze the transformations in the educational process of higher education institutions in Ukraine under wartime conditions and to identify the main challenges and prospects for their development. The study is based on a qualitative analytical approach, including the methods of analysis, synthesis, comparison, and generalization of scientific sources and empirical data. It is shown that, during the war, the organization and delivery of education at Ukrainian universities have undergone significant changes due to security risks, destruction of infrastructure, and forced displacement of participants in the educational process. As a result, the vast majority of higher education institutions have switched to distance learning, while some have implemented blended learning formats combining online and face-to-face instruction. The findings indicate that the effective organization of education under wartime conditions requires appropriate technical resources, stable internet access, and well-developed digital competencies among both students and teachers. At the same time, a significant number of participants in the educational process still face difficulties in adapting to distance and blended learning formats, with teachers demonstrating a lower level of adaptation compared to students. It is concluded that distance and blended learning will remain relevant in Ukraine in the post-war period due to ongoing digital transformation. These conditions necessitate comprehensive reforms of the higher education system aimed at improving the quality of education, developing digital competencies, and integrating international, particularly European, experience.

TI Tailoring assistive technology training for ASD: a moderated mediation
   model of students' perceived needs and disciplinary contexts
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE assistive technology; autism spectrum disorder; educational needs;
   moderated mediation model; professional training
ID CHILDREN; AUTISM; DISABILITIES; PROGRAM
AB Background: The integration of assistive technologies (AT) in the intervention for children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is critical. However, the mechanisms through which professional training translates into practical competence remain under-explored. This study examines a moderated mediation model to understand how academic domain and educational expectations influence this transition. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 227 students (97.4% female, ages 18-45) from the University of Bucharest, specializing in Special Psychopedagogy (48%), Pedagogy (25.1%), and Primary/Preschool Education (26.9%). Participants completed assessments regarding their preparation/training, perceived educational needs/expectations, and practical experience in AT. Data were analyzed using moderated mediation analysis (Delta method) to assess conditional direct and indirect effects. Results: Moderated mediation analysis revealed that all interaction paths were significant (p < .05). A key finding was the "filter effect" of educational expectations: as student needs increased, the conditional indirect effect of training on practice significantly strengthened (beta Low = 0.230, p = .020; beta High = 0.511, p < .001). Conversely, the conditional direct impact of training on practice weakened as expectations rose (beta Low = 1.395, p < .001; beta High = 0.805, p < .001). Notably, while 70.5% of students reported below-average formal training, 100% demonstrated above-average practical application, indicating a heavy reliance on subjective expectations and domain-specific context. Conclusions: Professional training in AT does not produce uniform outcomes. Its efficacy is maximized when calibrated to the specific academic domain and the individual motivational structure of the students. For clinical and educational practice, these findings suggest that "one-size-fits-all" training programs are suboptimal. To effectively translate theoretical knowledge into high-quality interventions for children with ASD, programs must integrate students' subjective expectations and the unique requirements of their specialization.

TI Pedagogical conditions for adapting primary school students to learning

AB The process of adapting primary school students to learning depends on many factors. The aim of this study was to theoretically substantiate and experimentally test the proposed set of pedagogical conditions that contribute to the successful adaptation of primary school students to learning in the primary education system. The study employed a quantitative quasi-experimental design involving experimental and control groups. The participants included 99 first-grade primary school students aged 6-7 years. The results of the study may be applied not only by primary school teachers and administrators, but also by researchers.

   of mathematics preservice teacher education in open distance e-learning

SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

DT Article
DE digital pedagogy; Global South; mathematics education; ODeL; preservice
   teachers; technology integration
ID PEDAGOGICAL CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; FRAMEWORK
AB The expansion of Open Distance e-Learning (ODeL) systems across the Global South has transformed access to teacher education, yet this transformation has not been matched by corresponding pedagogical innovation. Despite the centrality of digital technologies in ODeL environments, technology integration in mathematics preservice teacher education remains largely peripheral, often treated as an optional or supplementary component. This article adopts a conceptual and reflective analytical approach to interrogate this misalignment and to advance a reconceptualisation of technology integration as a foundational element of teacher preparation. The study is positioned as a theory-building and conceptual analysis article rather than an empirical investigation. Drawing on contemporary scholarship in educational technology, digital inclusion, and mathematics education, the study argues that existing frameworks, particularly Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), are necessary but insufficient for explaining technology integration in ODeL contexts, given their limited engagement with structural and disciplinary dimensions. In response, the article proposes a Contextualised Technology Integration Framework that integrates technological access, institutional support, the ODeL learning environment, digital pedagogical competence, and mathematical content mediation. The framework is used to analyse current practices and to demonstrate how fragmented curricula, limited pedagogical modelling, and structural inequalities constrain meaningful integration. The article concludes by arguing that repositioning technology integration as the backbone of mathematics preservice teacher education requires systemic alignment across policy, curriculum, and practice. This study contributes to theory by advancing a context-sensitive, discipline-specific model and provides a foundation for future empirical and design-based research on ODeL systems.

   stress tolerance
AB Background Adolescents with dyslexia are particularly vulnerable to emotional strain, especially in contexts of armed conflict where learning difficulties intersect with ongoing environmental stressors. AB Introduction The 2023 Organic Law on Personnel and Discipline of the Armed Forces strengthened the connection between military education and Ecuador national higher education system. TI From thriving to self-reliance: latent profiles of mental health
   attitudes in engineering culture
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering education; help-seeking; latent profile analysis; stigma of
   mental health; thriving
ID HELP-SEEKING
AB Background Mental health challenges among undergraduate engineering students are well documented; however, existing research has primarily relied on variable-centered approaches that overlook how stigma, help-seeking attitudes, mental health, and perceptions of engineering culture co-occur within individuals. Understanding these interrelationships from an ecological perspective is essential for informing educational practices that support student wellbeing.Methods Guided by Bronfenbrenner's bioecological Process-Person-Context-Time (PPCT) model- this study employed a person-centered approach using latent profile analysis (LPA). Survey data were collected from 1,151 undergraduate engineering students at two large public U.S. universities. Demographic analyses indicated that women and students with minoritized sexual orientations were disproportionately represented in higher-risk profiles.Conclusion These findings demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in engineering students' mental health experiences, highlighting the importance of situating wellbeing within disciplinary and institutional contexts and exploring their interactions with an ecosystem lens. Implications for engineering education include the need for targeted, context-sensitive interventions that address both individual help-seeking behaviors and departmental climate. This study contributes to an ecosystem-oriented understanding of student mental health and supports the development of more inclusive and responsive educational environments.

TI A cognitive resource trade-off model of AI-assisted language learning in
   Chinese undergraduates
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-assisted English learning; cognitive load; learner identity;
   metacognitive monitoring; sustained usage intention
ID SELF-EFFICACY; INFORMATION; LOAD; INVESTMENT; ACCEPTANCE; IDENTITY;
   DESIGN
AB Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly embedded in language learning, yet its psychological consequences remain insufficiently understood. In a cross-sectional survey of 4,010 Chinese undergraduates who used AI tools for English learning, this study examined the associations among AI-assisted learning engagement, cognitive load, metacognitive monitoring, reinforcement experience, English learner identity, and sustained usage and investment intention. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the six-factor measurement model, and structural equation modeling showed excellent fit. AI engagement was positively associated with both metacognitive monitoring and cognitive load, indicating simultaneous facilitative and constraining pathways. Cognitive load was negatively associated with metacognitive monitoring and learner identity, whereas metacognitive monitoring and reinforcement experience were positively associated with learner identity. The decomposition of indirect effects further showed that AI engagement was positively associated with learner identity through metacognitive monitoring but negatively associated with learner identity through cognitive load. An alternative model adding a direct path from AI engagement to learner identity did not improve model fit, supporting the more parsimonious theoretical model. Reinforcement experience and learner identity were positively associated with sustained usage and investment intention. These findings suggest that the educational value of AI-assisted language learning depends not only on the extent of AI use, but also on whether AI feedback can support reflective regulation without imposing excessive cognitive burden.

TI Development and validation of a competence level model for elementary
   algebra at the transition to higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competence level model; conceptualization; elementary algebra; higher
   education; item response theory
ID KNOWLEDGE
AB Elementary algebra is a critical prerequisite for mathematics-intensive degree programs, yet many students continue to struggle with it at the transition to higher education. While conceptual models of algebra exist, empirically validated competence levels remain scarce. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating a competence level model for elementary algebra, grounded in a three-aspect conceptualization that integrates three content areas (expressions, equations, functions), three algebraic activities (generational, transformational, global/meta-level activity; following Kierans framework), and three tiers of task demand. The competence level model provides a fine-grained framework for diagnostic assessment and targeted instructional support, contributing to means of supporting the critical transition to higher education in mathematics.

TI Mitigating algorithmic bias in educational prediction systems using
   reweighting and adversarial learning
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adversarial debiasing; algorithmic fairness; bias mitigation;
   educational data mining; learning analytics
AB The increasing integration of machine learning models into educational decision-making processes has raised concerns regarding algorithmic bias, particularly when sensitive attributes such as gender or socioeconomic status influence learning outcomes and assessment predictions. Models trained on historical educational data may reproduce structural inequalities, leading to disparities in automated decisions across student groups. This study presents an empirical fairness-evaluation framework for educational prediction systems, comparing a baseline classifier with demographic reweighting and adversarial debiasing. The approach is evaluated through statistical testing, subgroup analysis, and robustness assessment using standard fairness metrics, including Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD), and Disparate Impact (DI), together with predictive indicators such as accuracy and F1-score. Experimental results show that mitigation effects are dataset- and metric-dependent. In ASSISTments, the adversarial configuration improves predictive performance but increases SPD and EOD relative to the baseline, whereas reweighting produces nearly identical behavior to the unmitigated model. In OULAD, the adversarial configuration slightly reduces predictive performance while widening the observed fairness disparities. Under Gaussian perturbations (sigma=0.05), the adversarial model preserves most of its predictive capacity. Overall, fairness-aware mitigation should be evaluated as a trade-off between predictive utility and subgroup equity rather than as a single optimization objective, contributing to more transparent educational decision-making in learning analytics systems.

DE curriculum; reading skills; multimodal transversal learning unit
AB The Autonomous University of the State of Morelos designed a multimodal curricular strategy known as the multimodal transversal learning unit for the reading, analysis, and synthesis of written texts, which has been incorporated into the curricula ofvarious educational programs. This study aims to understand and interpret the results of the device in its virtual modality in relation to reading competence, through the convergence of the student profile and the performance of virtual advisors. To this end, a non-experimental, cross-sectional, and explanatory case study was conducted in a science degree program using triangulation of information from 89 surveyed students and 10 interviewed students, e-observation of five virtual classrooms, and two interviews with virtual advisors. The results showed that, of 105 enrolled students, 38 completed the course, with an average grade of 44.98%. The factors with the greatest weight in this outcome were identified in the performance of the virtual advisors, which resulted in low student achievement. It is concluded that the device meets the requirements of curricular and instructional design; however, contextual factors affecting its implementation lead to unsatisfactory results for the development of reading competence.

TI Technostress, Attitudes, Knowledge and Use of ICT in High School (Upper
   Secondary Education) Students in Mexico

LA Spanish
DT Article
DE student attitudes; upper secondary education; technological stress;
   information and communication technologies

This study aims to analyze police mediation as a training strategy to enhance police service competencies, particularly in assertive communication, conflict resolution, decision-making, and professional ethics.    Literary Texts
SO ACADEMIA Y VIRTUALIDAD
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE argumentation; historical thinking; literary texts; didactics
AB The article of this article was to strengthen students' historical thinking through the production of argumentative essays based on literary texts that address socially relevant issues.    A retrospective post-survey

LA English
DT Article
DE Problem-solving; Pharmacy; Education; Empathy; Advocacy
AB Introduction: To assess patients-as-teachers (PAT) as an instructional method, including the impact on ability to perform skills-based learning outcomes, and student perception of it in comparison to other instructional methods. Methods: A retrospective, post-survey was used to evaluate student pharmacists' perceptions of PAT in a Rare Genetic Disorders elective course during the Spring 2024 semester. The data from items related to learning outcomes were examined using both descriptive statistics and t-tests for comparison at pre and post. PAT had the highest overall rating as an instructional method utilized in the course. C onclusion: PAT demonstrated a positive impact on student skills-based learning outcomes and was rated higher than other instructional methods.

TI Understanding contemporary digital childhoods in Australia: A bounded
   scoping review of transdisciplinary research of the ARC Centre of
   Excellence for the Digital Child
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital technology; Digital child; Early childhood; Australia; Review
AB Childhoods are shaped by people, experiences, and contexts that, increasingly, include if and how children connect with digital technology. This scoping review, bounded by the research of a national Centre of Excellence that is currently the largest critical mass of transdisciplinary research about Australian digital childhoods, asked: What insights and understandings about contemporary digital childhoods in Australia can be drawn from the research of the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child? Sixty-one studies (15 reviews and 46 primary studies) met the inclusion criteria of being a peer-reviewed publication of primary research or a structured review associated with the Centre. Results were synthesised in three clusters, derived from the trial of various inductive and deductive classification schemes, as (1) children (k = 16), (2) children's adults (k = 30), and (3) surrounding systems that shape digital childhoods (k = 15). Within-cluster inductive narrative synthesis enabled thematic analysis that accounted for the breadth of design, discipline, focus, and methodologies within the archive. Results offer novel transdisciplinary insights into areas including: child outcomes associated with use of digital technologies; knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, and practices of children's adults regarding digital technologies; and influence/s of systems that shape families' digital engagement and experiences, including issues of political economy, datafication, privacy, rights, digital design, and digital inequalities. While bounded by a predefined (yet broad and responsive) program of Centre research, we identified thematic trends, consistencies, contradictions, and future agendas related to evolving digital childhoods in Australia that can inform ongoing research, policy and practice.

TI Towards a standardized competency-profile for peer-to-peer-teachers in
   medical education - a systematic mapping review
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer-to-peer-learning; Student as a teacher; Tutoring; Competency;
   Qualification; Mapping review; Systematic map; Medical education;
   Research; Empirical
ID STUDENT-AS-TEACHER; PROGRAM; BELIEFS
AB Background Medical education research acknowledges "P2P-teaching" as an effective, scalable, and cost-effective possibility for educating students in human medicine. At the same time, the medical field is yet to form an empirically founded and overarching description of necessary P2P-teaching competencies across medical subjects. In order to create an overarching picture of relevant student P2P-teaching competencies in medical education, this article raises the question, "What are the relevant teaching competencies in qualification measures for P2P-teachers in medical education?".Method We performed a systematic mapping review. Our search strategy applied the PICOS-Scheme and the semantic fields "student tutor", "qualification", "competency", "medical" and "empirical" to medical and educational databases, over the period from July to November 2024. A snowballing-system enriched the results, and a selection process according to PRISMA systematically reduced search results from 322 down to 18 peer-review articles for in-depth analysis. This final sample includes peer-reviewed studies from North America, Europe and Australia, drawing from many medical disciplines and published in English and German. For synthesis, we extracted key study characteristics and qualitatively analyzed contents of qualification measures for P2P-teachers.Results The analysis brings three medical and 12 student P2P-teaching competencies to the fore. Together these competencies form a competency-profile for student P2P-teachers. The competency-profile shows overlaps with relevant medical teaching frameworks. The relevant studies not only show a weak grounding of P2P-teaching research in learning and teaching theories, but also that they tend to be limited to low levels of evidence.Conclusions Our results are limited to the peer-reviewed and English- and German discourse. This specific discourse on P2P-teaching does not show an overarching consensus as to what the focal competencies for student P2P-teachers are, but it shows a remarkable number of implicit and explicit overlaps. Therefore, the P2P-teaching competency-profile for student tutors might serve as a starting point for (and invitation to) an open-discussion across medical schools to create and elaborate on an interrelated evidence-based research strategy on P2P-teacher-training. Against the background of the current state of research methodology, systematically investigating competencies of student P2P-teachers is a fruitful research area.

TI Developing and evaluating an in situ, simulated emergency training
   course for nurses with low seniority
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE High fidelity simulation; Junior nurse; Emergencies; Training; Effect
ID CRITICAL THINKING; PATIENT-CARE; STANDARDS; PRACTICE(TM); IMPACT
AB Objectives This study aimed to construct and implement an in situ simulated emergency training (SET) course for nurses with low seniority and evaluate its effectiveness. Methods This was an experimental study, and a purpose-sampling method was adopted. We selected 82 nurses with less than 5 years of experience working in a grade -III Class A hospital in Hubei province from August to December 2023 as the research objects, and randomly divided them into intervention group (n = 37) and control group (n = 45). The control group underwent routine stratified training, whereas the intervention group underwent in situ SET based on routine stratified training. Before and after training, we compared differences in the scores of the intervention and control groups in terms of critical thinking (CT), clinical communication (CC), clinical reasoning (CR), and first aid (FA). Results The constructed in situ simulated emergency training course consisted of nine courses, each of which covered one theme. The nine themes were acute myocardial infarction, diabetic ketoacidosis, secondary shock due to acute transfusion anaphylaxis, post-operative respiratory depression combined with pulmonary edema, unplanned extubation, impulsive violence, chemotherapeutic drug extravasation, patient suicide, and acute pulmonary embolism. The results of the empirical study showed that before training, there were no differences between the intervention and control groups in the scores for the following abilities: CT, CC, CR, and FA (p > 0.05). After training, the scores for CR and FA in the intervention group were higher than those in the control group (p < 0.05), while the scores for CT and CC did not differ from those in the control group (p > 0.05). Conclusions The content of the in situ SET course is comprehensive, which is helpful in improving junior nurses' CC and FA abilities and can serve as a reference for establishing a training course for them. However, the effects on the CT and CC were not significant. Further empirical studies are required to explore the targeted training courses.
