TI Temporal dynamics of online learning interactions: A learning analytics
   study within the CoI framework
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital literacy; Older adults; Peer support; Community of Inquiry (CoI)
   framework; Online learning
ID COMMUNITY; INQUIRY; SATISFACTION; ENVIRONMENT; OUTCOMES; SYSTEM
AB Understanding how online learning unfolds over short time spans is essential for improving the design and facilitation of digital learning environments. This study examines the temporal dynamics of online learning interactions through the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework in two two-week online courses for older adults. Using Moodle log data from an instructor-led edition (n = 27) and a peer-facilitated edition (n = 45), 4,276 behavioural traces were mapped to teaching, social, and cognitive presence and transformed into daily time series. Cross-correlation analyses (f3-day lag) were conducted to explore short-term temporal associations. The patterns observed suggest that synchronous videoconferencing may precede increases in cognitive engagement, and that learning guides may be followed by brief sequences of individual exploration and forum participation. Peer facilitation appears to be associated with higher levels of social presence, although temporal coupling patterns across presences remain broadly comparable. While exploratory in nature, these findings offer preliminary indications of short-term temporal structures in online engagement and may inform the timing of instructional scaffolds and facilitation strategies in courses designed for older adults.

TI Academic performance, background and pre-existing quantitative skills of
   economics starters: Mind the Gap!
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF ECONOMICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education; Educational inequality; Awarding gaps; Quantitative
   skills; Diagnostic tests
ID MATH SKILLS; STUDENTS; SUCCESS
AB We examine differences in early academic performance among economics entrants by gender, ethnicity and origin (home versus overseas), and assess the role of existing skills before entering university in explaining these differences. Using diagnostic test scores, assessment marks, and demographic data from three student cohorts (over 1000 observations), we identify sizeable attainment gaps between home and overseas students and across ethnic groups. By contrast, we find little evidence of differences by gender or socioeconomic status alone, except for an advantage of state-school over privately educated students and an advantage for men in Microeconomics among home students. These findings highlight the importance of targeted support at university entry to improve equality of opportunity and academic outcomes.

TI Predictors of foundational reading competence in speaking and
   non-speaking children with intellectual disabilities
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Intellectual disabilities; Word decoding abilities; Predictors;
   Eye-tracking measures; Students who use AAC
ID PHONOLOGICAL AWARENESS; DOWN-SYNDROME; EYE-TRACKING; LANGUAGE; STUDENTS;
   AUTISM; SPEECH; SKILLS
AB Phonological awareness, knowledge of grapheme-phoneme correspondences, working memory, and broader linguistic factors are well-established predictors of the acquisition of foundational reading skills in students with and without intellectual disabilities. However, empirical evidence remains limited regarding the specific factors that contribute to literacy learning difficulties in children with intellectual disabilities who rely on augmentative and alternative communication (AAC). The present study aimed to examine predictors of basic reading abilities in children with intellectual disabilities, both with and without spoken language, using standardized assessments and eye-tracking measures during word decoding tasks. The variable "spoken language" did not account for additional variance beyond these predictors. The findings are discussed with regard to their implications for the design of evidence-based reading instruction. In particular, phonologically oriented interventions are recommended for children with mild to moderate intellectual disabilities, irrespective of their spoken language abilities.

AB Leveraging the potential of Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) environments for creativity enhancement, this randomized controlled experiment explores the impact of a novel IVR-based cognitive figural creativity training on creative thinking, engagement, and user experience among young adults. TI Does vocational education and training act as a safety net in labour
   markets? Some recent evidence from India
SO EMPIRICAL RESEARCH IN VOCATIONAL EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE Vocational education and training; Formal education; Labour market
   outcomes; Safety net hypothesis; Casual employment; Regular salaried
   employment; I21; I24; I26; I28; J24
ID SCHOOL; TRANSITION; CASTE; INEQUALITY; TRACKING; RETURNS; EXPLAIN;
   CHOICE
AB This study revisits the "safety net" hypothesis of vocational education and training (VET), which posits that vocational training reduces the risk of unemployment, albeit potentially at the cost of lower wage outcomes. Using unit-level data obtained from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS, 2023-24), the paper examines the relevance of the safety net hypothesis in explaining labour market outcomes of VET-trained individuals in India. In order to do that, we employ a multinomial probit model to analyze employment status and estimate the Mincerian earnings function to examine wage outcomes of VET trained and untrained individuals using a sample of individuals aged between 25 and 59 years. It is also evident from the estimation results of Mincerian earning function that both formal and informal training yield higher monthly earning from wages and salaries compared to untrained persons. Combining these estimation results, this study proves that the safety net view holds only partially in the Indian labour market.

TI Finding Voice Across Platforms: Asian American and Asian Transnational
   Youths' Identity Negotiation in Social Media Spaces
SO JOURNAL OF ADOLESCENT & ADULT LITERACY
LA English
DT Article
ID LITERACY
AB Despite being one of the largest immigrant groups in the United States (U.S.), Asian heritage youth are often essentialized by dominant literacy ideologies as quiet, obedient, or culturally foreign, leaving their identity negotiation underexamined and insufficiently supported. This qualitative study examines how first- and second-year Asian American and Asian transnational college students use social media literacy practices to sustain heritage connections and navigate bicultural identities across platforms. Drawing on a qualitative research design that includes surveys, in-depth interviews, and youth-generated social media diaries, the analysis identifies two clusters of practices. Our findings position social media as a Third Space (Bhabha 1994; Guti & eacute;rrez 2008) constructed through Asian heritage youths' agentive digital literacy practices, where they draw on cultural and linguistic resources and make hybrid identities visible.

TI Development and Implementation of a Cloud-Based HPLC Teaching Platform
   Enhanced by Artificial Intelligence
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Undergraduate education; Laboratory instruction; Computational
   chemistry; Distance learning
ID LIQUID-CHROMATOGRAPHY; MS; CHEMISTRY; EDUCATION; PRODUCTS; LAB
AB High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) is a fundamental component of undergraduate chemistry curricula. However, the high cost of instrumentation and limited laboratory hours often restrict students' hands-on access. This lack of practical experience hinders their ability to deeply understand HPLC principles, master instrument operation, and develop problem-solving skills. To address these challenges, we developed an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cloud HPLC experiment platform, termed C-HPLC. Specifically, a deep learning model was constructed to predict compound retention time (RT); then, a refined 3D model was established to illustrate the HPLC instrument structure, and a web-based architecture was implemented to enable cross-platform interoperability. C-HPLC allows students to freely explore mixture separation under varied experimental parameters through accurate RT prediction. The platform is accessible on multiple devices, including smartphones, tablets, and computers, and provides online visualization of HPLC instrument structures and operating principles. Through online exploratory learning, students can deepen their understanding of HPLC principles and instrument configurations. Subsequent hands-on laboratory experiments reinforced and validated this knowledge, leading to an improvement in the effectiveness of HPLC experimental teaching. Usage data and questionnaire results demonstrated the reliability and usability of the platform. Among 105 trial users, 94 reported an enhanced understanding of HPLC, and 100 expressed overall satisfaction. C-HPLC offers a promising solution to current challenges in HPLC experimental teaching and supports the achievement of instructional objectives.

TI School Readiness, Learning Challenges, and Lifestyle Changes Among
   Children During the COVID-19 Pandemic
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE COVID-19; learning difficulties; lifestyle; school readiness
ID FIT INDEXES; ACHIEVEMENT
AB Background The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted schooling worldwide. While there is evidence of declines in academic performance, the links between early vulnerabilities in school readiness, learning difficulties, and lifestyle changes during the pandemic and their impact on postcrisis academic achievement are not well understood.Methods This longitudinal study followed 3871 children across three time points over 6 years (50.3% boys). TI Students' perceptions of music teachers' instructional decision-making
   in urban and rural China: a mixed-methods study informed by culturally
   relevant pedagogy
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE China music education; Culturally relevant pedagogy; Learning
   environments; Music teacher decision-making; Student perceptions;
   Urban-rural disparities
AB This mixed-methods study examines junior high school students' perceptions of music teachers' instructional decision-making in urban and rural China. Music classrooms are conceptualised as culturally and institutionally situated learning environments shaped by teaching resources, teacher professional background, curriculum design, student interest, school support, and socio-cultural context. Data were collected from 404 students across six schools in Jinan using a validated 19-item questionnaire covering six contextual factors, supplemented by semi-structured interviews with 36 students. The findings indicate that students' evaluations of instructional decision-making are shaped by the interaction of cultural, material, and socio-cultural conditions within learning environments. This study contributes to learning environments research by offering a student-centred perspective on instructional decision-making and highlights the importance of culturally responsive and context-sensitive approaches in addressing urban-rural disparities in music education.

TI Awareness of belief change predicts information seeking
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Memory; Belief change; Information seeking; Metacognition; Learning
ID METACOMPREHENSION ACCURACY; NEED; COMPREHENSION; METAANALYSIS;
   CONSISTENCY; MOTIVATION; SCIENCE; MODEL; LEADS; MOOD
AB When people change beliefs, they generally exhibit poor awareness of that change. Two experiments examined the extent that awareness of belief change predicted information-seeking preferences and behavior. Participants' initial beliefs were recorded during a prescreening session 2-11 weeks prior to the experiment, and again in the experiment after they had read a text that presented evidence and arguments that were inconsistent with those initial beliefs. Participants also recalled their initial beliefs before completing measures of information seeking. Experiment 1 examined beliefs related to TV violence and asked participants to rate their level of interest in reading articles with titles that were either related or unrelated to that topic. Using a similar procedure, Experiment 2 examined beliefs regarding gun control and assessed information-seeking via an open-ended reading task where participants could read articles that were either related or unrelated to the topic. Both experiments showed that participants changed beliefs after reading belief-inconsistent texts and that recollections of previous beliefs were biased towards current beliefs. Awareness of belief change, as measured by recollection accuracy, predicted interest in reading further information on TV violence in Experiment 1 and the number of gun control related articles read in Experiment 2. In both experiments, the information-seeking behavior was specific to the topic studied and did not extend to the control topics. The results of these findings build upon past research that shows poor awareness of belief change by documenting its relationship with information-seeking behavior.

TI Teachers' perceived competence and professional uncertainty when
   managing micro-exclusions and identity-related classroom dynamics
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher perceived competence; Professional uncertainty;
   Micro-exclusions; Identity-related classroom dynamics; Classroom
   climate; Mixed-methods research
ID RELATIONAL AGGRESSION; PEER RELATIONSHIPS; EARLY-CHILDHOOD; SCHOOL;
   LGBTQ; GENDER; MICROAGGRESSIONS; INTERVENTIONS; EXPERIENCES; ENGAGEMENT
AB Teaching is increasingly recognised as emotionally and relationally demanding work, particularly when teachers manage subtle peer dynamics and identity-related classroom interactions. While research on teachers' social and emotional competence has highlighted its importance for classroom climate, less is known about how teachers experience competence and uncertainty in specific, high-stakes situations involving micro-exclusions and identity-sensitive dynamics. This study examines teachers' perceived competence and professional uncertainty in managing micro-relational classroom processes and identity-related interactions, and explores how these domains intersect across levels. The sample comprised 346 in-service teachers from primary, lower secondary, and upper secondary schools in Italy. A convergent mixed-methods design was adopted. Teachers completed two self-report measures assessing perceived competence in managing micro-relational processes (MEPRC) and identity-sensitive classroom dynamics (I-ISEC), alongside open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and correlational analyses, while qualitative data were examined through reflexive thematic analysis. Integration was achieved through a joint display. Teachers reported relatively high perceived competence overall, alongside lower confidence in post-conflict repair, protection from peer pressure, and prevention of microaggressions. Micro-relational competence showed a school-level gradient, with increasing difficulty in secondary settings, whereas identity-sensitive competence did not vary by school level. Qualitative findings highlighted invisible peer dynamics, identity-related language, and professional uncertainty linked to boundary negotiation. Teachers' difficulties in managing micro-exclusions and identity-sensitive dynamics reflect situated professional dilemmas rather than attitudinal deficits. These findings refine conceptualisations of teacher competence by foregrounding the normative and relational conditions under which emotionally demanding classroom work is enacted.

TI Bullying through prejudice: the role of heteronormativity, racism, and
   ageism
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Bullying; Prejudice; Heteronormativity; Racism; Ageism;
   Intersectionality; Critical and queer pedagogy
ID RAPE MYTH ACCEPTANCE; INTERCULTURAL SENSITIVITY; AMBIVALENT SEXISM;
   SEXUAL DIVERSITY; ATTITUDES; GENDER; STUDENTS; SCHOOL; HOMOPHOBIA;
   EDUCATION
AB Bullying is a complex phenomenon that is fed by social discourses on normative and non-normative identities. However, it has so far been studied from a simplistic perspective, especially focused on micro variables related to the individual, the family, or the school. In this study, we analyzed the profile of students who engage in bullying behavior, examining how this profile differs by gender and is influenced by several forms of prejudice, considering bullies' adherence to gender stereotypes and their sexist (hostile and benevolent), homophobic, racist (blatant and subtle), and ageist (hostile and benevolent) attitudes. Likewise, the data show greater similarities between male and female bullies, whereas the group of boys and girls who do not bully their peers is more heterogeneous. The results of our work highlight the urgency of going beyond generic bullying prevention programs by designing interventions that recognize the influence of prejudices about normative and non-normative identities in the genesis of violence, aimed at disrupting normality regimes and following an intersectional, critical, and queer pedagogy.

   Analysis
SO TECHTRENDS
LA English
DT Article

AB Immersive Virtual Reality (iVR) is a transformative technology in education, offering unique opportunities to create engaging and authentic learning environments. While its potential for Foreign Language Learning (FLL) is widely acknowledged, a comprehensive, macro-level overview of the scientific landscape of this specific domain remains underexplored. This study provides a quantitative foundation that complements existing qualitative reviews, offering valuable insights into the field's historical trajectory, key players, and emerging trends, thereby guiding future research and collaboration.

TI A cultural-context framework of AI-mediated formative assessment:
   perceptions and proficiency in Iran's TEFL context
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-mediated assessment; Cultural-context framework; TEFL; Iran;
   Collectivism; Self-regulated learning; Proficiency levels; Teacher-led
   assessment
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; FIT INDEXES; LEARNERS
AB This convergent mixed-methods study introduces a novel cultural-context framework to explore Iranian TEFL learners' perceptions of AI-mediated formative assessments compared to teacher-led assessments, emphasizing validity, reliability, fairness, and their links to self-regulated learning (SRL) and proficiency gains. Data from 346 learners (B1-C1) across Tehran, Isfahan, and Shiraz were collected over 12 weeks using surveys, interviews, focus groups, and Cambridge tests. The proposed cultural-context framework highlights AI's perceived usefulness and associations with proficiency gains in Iran's collectivist TEFL setting. Qualitative findings suggest that these perceptions are likely shaped by cultural norms and infrastructure, supporting calls for hybrid AI-teacher models to enhance equitable technology-enhanced language learning in high-context educational settings.

Students perceived Daily SPARKs to have strengthened concepts, clarified misconceptions, enhanced exam readiness, offered new explanations, were visually engaging, sustained attention, and is a low-cost scalable learning method.

TI Education Beyond the Program: Exploring the Eventive Possibilities of
   Education
SO EDUCATIONAL THEORY
LA English
DT Article
DE John Caputo; deconstructionism; program; event; Jan Masschelein; Gert
   Biesta
AB Modern education has often been criticized for reducing teaching and schooling to a matter of "program." Critiques of this programmatic approach to education come from a variety of perspectives with a wide range of underlying reasons. This article presents a perspective that might contribute to the prevailing ways of theorizing about how education could be taken beyond the program: namely, a deconstructionist perspective derived from the work of American philosopher and theologian John D. Caputo. This article begins with a discussion of the relation between the program of education and the "name" of education by posing the question: can a program of education (ever) be worthy of its name? The answer I give, in short, is "no." Next, I engage with the question of the ontological status of the program and argue that there is, properly or ontologically speaking, nothing beyond the program. The two sections that follow discuss how education could go beyond the program of being and becoming on the one hand, and the program of education itself on the other. Overall, I present and argue for a Caputo-inspired deconstructionist way to theorize about education that tries to take education beyond the program by exploring its possibilities for the event without being hostile to the inherent program-ness of education.

AB The rising prevalence of twin births has created distinct developmental and educational dynamics that remain insufficiently theorized in psychological and educational research. TI The Smoothness Advantage: Session Quality and Symptom Change in a
   Training Clinic
SO JOURNAL OF COUNSELING PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE session depth; session smoothness; multilevel modeling; symptom change;
   productive distress
ID PSYCHOMETRIC PROPERTIES; WORKING ALLIANCE; PERSONALITY; IMPACT;
   VALIDATION; QUESTIONNAIRE; DISORDERS; CLIENTS; MODELS
AB While both emotional depth and relational smoothness are considered therapeutic, their relative contributions to symptom change remain debated. This study disentangles the within-person (state) and between-person (trait) effects of client-rated session depth and smoothness on symptom trajectories in a university training clinic. Utilizing longitudinal data from 84 clients (1,338 session observations) treated by 33 novice therapists, this study employed multilevel modeling with two complementary specifications: an autoregressive model testing immediate session-to-session effects and a baseline-adjusted model testing cumulative change from pretreatment levels. Findings revealed distinct pathways for immediate versus cumulative change. Within-person fluctuations in session depth were associated with cumulative symptom reduction (b = -0.06, p = .015), suggesting that sessions deeper than a client's average provide incremental long-term benefits. Conversely, within-person smoothness was associated with a slight increase in next-session symptoms in the autoregressive model (b = 0.05, p = .001), potentially reflecting regression effects or the temporary disruption that accompanies productive therapeutic work. However, the most robust finding across both models was the between-person smoothness effect (b(AR) = -.34, b(Base) = -.36, p < .001); clients who generally experienced smoother, more comfortable therapeutic interactions demonstrated significantly better overall symptom trajectories. Findings challenge the "no pain, no gain" assumption in short-term psychotherapy and counseling with young adults. While depth contributes to cumulative change, establishing a consistent "smoothness advantage," a comfortable and safe relational foundation, appears critical for symptom relief in this population. For novice therapists, prioritizing relational safety over premature depth may optimize outcomes.

TI Use of a 3D-printed smartphone microscope adapter in a general biology
   lab course
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE 3D-printed; microscope; images; video; smartphone; camera; handsfree;
   undergraduate laboratory
AB High school and undergraduate students often use personal cell phones to document experimental data or to capture images of microscopic observations on their phones. We utilized a 3D-printed smartphone mount adapter for microscopes in a predominantly first-year undergraduate general biology classroom. The hands-free mount is low-cost, works with different brands of phones, different kinds of microscopes, and does not damage the phone or microscope. At the start of the semester, a 10-question pre-use survey was conducted using a 4-choice Likert scale (n = 330). 73% of respondents strongly agreed with wanting to use their personal cell phone to record laboratory experiment data. Over a semester, students used 3D-printed cell phone microscope adapters as a part of four different general biology lab modules. As examples, the adapters were used to take stable microscopic images of pond water, Gram stain results, and live Daphnia pulex organisms to measure heart rate. At the end of the course, students were asked to participate in a post-use survey (n = 186). Students believe the adapter helped them engage with lab content. The adapter was most often used to visualize microscopic items live and simultaneously with their lab partner. The survey data show that use of a 3D-printed device to hold phones steady on a microscope was viewed positively by students.

SO LANGUAGE ASSESSMENT QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
AB Despite its significance, the research supporting the calibration of many of the CEFR illustrative descriptors has not been systematically replicated. TI "Okay tengo estas flores": Exploring urban multilingual children's
   perspectives on nature in cities amidst the climate crisis
SO ENGLISH TEACHING-PRACTICE AND CRITIQUE
LA English
DT Article
DE Urban ecopedagogy; Multilingualism; Critical literacy; Climate literacy;
   Children's photography
AB Purpose- Drawing from a larger study of young children's climate justice literacies, the purpose of this paper is to explore the perspectives that urban, multilingual children hold toward nature in cities and to share how a critical urban ecopedagogies approach can be responsive to students' lived histories, experiences and the natural world around them. Further, the article shows how adults can elicit and learn from urban multilingual children's alternative ecological epistemologies about their natural environment that often challenge dominant environmental narratives. Design/methodology/approach- Blending practitioner inquiry and ethnography in a study conducted in a first-grade classroom, this study adopted urban ecopedagogy specifically by foregrounding children's engagement with diverse environmental picturebooks that centered on nature in cities and providing children with digital cameras to elicit children's perspectives on nature across their social worlds of their school, home and community. Moving beyond mononational and monolingual environmental sensemaking, children also revealed how their transnational and translingual language and literacy practices intrinsically shaped their conceptions of and connection to their natural worlds. Through their documentation of the nature around them, children also showed how digital tools (e.g. digital cameras, social media platforms) allowed them to challenge adult-driven narratives of their danger of technology by enhancing and deepening their connection with nature, rather than distracting them from it. Originality/value- This paper shows the importance of challenging dominant, adult-regulated environmental narratives by eliciting the perspectives of multilingual children on the urban spaces that they experience in their everyday lives. It also reveals how a focus on nature in urban landscapes can be a way to nurture young children's thinking about the environment, providing an entryway into and supporting discussions of climate justice literature more broadly.

TI Experiential and Collaborative Learning to Engage Youth in STEM and
   Agriculture: A Design Case Study
SO TECHTRENDS
LA English
DT Article
DE AI education; Data science education; Design case; Experiential
   learning; Spiral learning structure; Smart agriculture; STEM education
AB Emerging technologies such as sensor networks, data analytics, and artificial intelligence are rapidly transforming agriculture into a data-driven, highly automated domain, yet these innovations remain underrepresented in secondary STEM education. To address this gap, we designed and implemented a two-week Smart Agriculture Summer Camp for middle and high school students, guided by experiential and collaborative learning frameworks. The camp's design incorporated a spiral learning structure across four modules, indoor/outdoor farming, IoT-enabled sensing, data processing and visualization, and machine learning/artificial intelligence. Advisory board feedback led to iterative refinements, including icebreakers, gamified learning, and virtual reality experiences. Pre- and post-surveys provided preliminary descriptive evidence of changes in students' understanding, confidence, and interest, while low-stakes quizzes, cumulative open-ended assignments, reflections, and observations were embedded primarily as learning, reflection, and instructional feedback tools to support the camp's iterative design. Preliminary results demonstrated that authentic, technology-rich activities fostered engagement, collaboration, and confidence, while highlighting logistical challenges such as equipment access, technical support, and variability in student prior knowledge. This design case contributes to the growing body of research on integrating smart agriculture into STEM education and provides practical guidance for educators seeking to develop interdisciplinary, technology-enhanced learning experiences.

TI The Dual Landscape of Clinical Placements for Nursing Students:
   High-Quality Learning and Bullying
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE clinical placements; learning environment; supervisory practices; team
   cohesion; inclusion; bullying and harassment; organisational culture
ID WORKPLACE VIOLENCE; MIXED METHODS; EXPERIENCES; INCIVILITY; PERCEPTIONS;
   RESILIENCE; COMMUNICATION; HARASSMENT; NURSES; IMPACT
AB Background: Nursing students spend a substantial proportion of their education in clinical practice; hence, the quality of these environments plays a critical role in shaping students' learning outcomes. While research finds that nursing students often encounter bullying and harassment during clinical placement, the characteristics of positive and high-quality learning situations during these placements are less clearly described in the literature. Methods: A convergent, quantitative-dominant mixed-methods study was conducted between April and June 2024. Quantitative and qualitative data were collected concurrently; statistical analysis described prevalence and associations, while thematic analysis explored students' experiences and contextualised the quantitative findings. Results: Statistical and thematic analyses indicated that high-quality learning emerged from the interplay of inclusion, mastery and active participation. A gradual transition from observation to independent practice, combined with appropriate challenges and opportunities for reflection, characterised the most effective learning situations. Approximately 50% of the students perceived themselves as victims of bullying or harassment, which impaired learning and prompted some to consider leaving nursing programs. The juxtaposition of positive and negative experiences highlighted team inclusion as the pivotal factor for both enhancing learning and preventing bullying. Conclusions: Being included as part of the team emerged as the main driver of positive clinical learning, whereas feeling isolated from the team was interpreted as bullying or harassment. These results indicated that well-prepared students, empowered supervisors, and inclusive organisational cultures supported by transparent reporting and response systems can provide the foundation for both high-quality learning and the prevention of bullying and harassment in clinical education.

TI Developing purposeful observation during early clinical exposure in
   anesthesiology: a cluster-randomized study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Purposeful observation; Early clinical exposure; Workplace-based
   learning; Anesthesiology; Medical students
ID MEDICAL-STUDENTS
AB Background Early clinical exposure allows undergraduate medical students to encounter authentic clinical practice, but novice learners may not know what to observe or how to interpret complex clinical events. This challenge is particularly relevant in anesthesiology, where many professional activities are embedded in perioperative workflow and are not immediately visible to beginners. This study examined whether a structured perioperative observation model was associated with improved learning objective clarity and self-reported purposeful observation during early anesthesiology clinical exposure. Methods This prospective cluster-randomized educational study included 154 s-year undergraduate medical students from 12 clerkship groups. Six groups were assigned to a conventional lecture-observation-question-and-answer clerkship, and six groups were assigned to a structured perioperative observation model organized according to the Bridge-in, Objectives, Pre-assessment, Participatory learning, Post-assessment, and Summary (BOPPPS) framework. The primary outcome was the post-clerkship score for learning objective clarity and self-reported purposeful observation ability. Secondary outcomes included anesthesia-related awareness, knowledge test scores, post-clerkship learning experience, and open-ended feedback. A linear mixed-effects model was used to account for clerkship group clustering. Results Seventy-six students were assigned to the conventional group and 78 to the structured observation group. Academic track distribution differed between groups, while other baseline characteristics were comparable. The structured observation group had a higher primary outcome score than the conventional group (22.55 +/- 1.17 vs. 16.74 +/- 1.36, P < 0.001). The association remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, academic track, prior operating room exposure, and baseline interest in anesthesiology. The structured group also showed greater gains in anesthesia-related awareness and knowledge and higher post-clerkship learning experience scores. Findings were consistent across academic track and prior operating room exposure strata. Conclusions Structured perioperative observation was associated with higher learning objective clarity and self-reported purposeful observation during early anesthesiology clinical exposure. By guiding students to observe perioperative workflow, anesthesiologists' responsibilities, patient safety, and team collaboration, this model may help novice medical students transform passive clinical exposure into more goal-directed learning.

TI Lived experiences of parents of school-age children and young people
   with autism spectrum disorder regarding education in Kuwait
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE autism spectrum disorder; inclusive education; Kuwait; lived experience;
   parents; qualitative research; thematic analysis
AB Background Parents of children and young people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) frequently report barriers to equitable, safe, and meaningful educational participation. In the Gulf region, inclusive education policies are expanding, yet implementation challenges persist and Kuwait-specific qualitative evidence for school-age learners remains limited.Aim To explore the lived experiences of parents of school-age children and young people with ASD regarding the education of their children in Kuwait.Methods We conducted individual semi-structured interviews with eight parents/caregivers of children/young people with ASD. Interviews were conducted in Arabic, lasted approximately 60 min, and were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis guided by Braun and Clarke's approach. Reporting was aligned with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ).Results Five themes were developed: (1) Navigating educational access; (2) Differentiated inclusion and varied access; (3) Variability in school readiness and autism-specific capacity; (4) Parents as case managers, advocates, and co-educators; and (5) The cost of accessing specialised provision. Parents described their experiences as a mix of administrative complexity and meaningful gains: where placement, parent-school communication, and intervention intensity aligned, parents reported substantive improvements in their children's communication, independence, and social participation; where these conditions were not met, they described delay, financial strain, and advocacy fatigue.Conclusion Parents' accounts highlight both the strengths of existing services in Kuwait-including intensive specialised provision, supportive school-home pairings, and dedicated allied health input that produced observable gains-and the structural challenges that continue to shape family experience, including procedural complexity, conditional eligibility, and uneven capacity across settings. Building on these strengths, further progress requires transparent placement pathways, scaled-up access to high-quality provision, sustained teacher and aide development, and affordable supports integrated with allied health services.

TI Teachers as designers of gamified pedagogical infrastructure: ClassPoint
   use in language classrooms
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Arabic language and Islamic studies education; ClassPoint; classroom
   response systems; digital pedagogy; gamification; teacher design agency
ID GAMIFICATION
AB Gamified classroom response systems (CRSs) have been studied for student engagement and assessment; however, little attention has been paid to how teachers of Culturally Located Arabic Language and Islamic Studies design, negotiate, and legitimize gamified interaction in discipline- and culture-specific classrooms. This interpretive qualitative study examined the implementation of gamification by 15 Grade 9 teachers of Arabic Language and Islamic Studies in Abu Dhabi public schools through the adoption of a ClassPoint-based process comprising professional development workshops over a 4-month implementation period. Informed by the theory of reflexive thematic analysis, semi-structured interviews conducted with teachers were analyzed. The findings revealed that teachers enacted ClassPoint-supported gamification as a form of pedagogical infrastructure by designing participation routines, embedding formative feedback cycles, and aligning gamified activities with curriculum goals and cultural values. Teachers also reported broader participation opportunities, iterative professional learning, and implementation challenges related to infrastructure, time, and institutional support in the context of pedagogical infrastructure and teacher design agency theories, this paper offers an innovative conceptualization of CRSs as tools for engaging students and as designed interactions between teachers and students. This study provides insights into the dynamic interactions among facilitating conditions, teacher design agency, and classroom enactment in the design, implementation, and sustainment of gamified lessons in culturally oriented contexts.

TI Exploration of practical teaching reform for machine vision courses
   based on comprehensive innovative experiments
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE comprehensive experiments; improved YOLOv8n algorithm; machine vision;
   practical teaching reform; senior undergraduate students
AB This experimental course is designed for senior undergraduate students and employs a strawberry detection task in real agricultural scenarios as the experimental vehicle to construct a student-centered comprehensive innovative teaching case. The course curriculum encompasses the complete research workflow, including literature review, dataset collection and annotation, software and hardware environment configuration, model training and improvement, design of ablation and comparative experiments, result analysis, and project presentation. Throughout the instructional process, the instructor introduces inquiry-based learning tasks to guide students in independently formulating hypotheses, designing improvement strategies, and conducting systematic comparative experiments, thereby cultivating their critical thinking and innovative practical abilities. A comprehensive assessment system is designed for this course, integrating formative, summative, and collaborative evaluation approaches to holistically measure student learning achievements in knowledge application, engineering practice, innovative inquiry, and team collaboration. Feedback collected through questionnaires and individual interviews upon course completion indicated that the majority of students reported that the use of real agricultural scenarios enhanced their engagement and interest, that the inquiry-based tasks effectively stimulated innovative thinking, and that the group collaboration and role-rotation mechanism improved their communication skills and sense of responsibility. This experimental course has demonstrated significant effectiveness in stimulating students' research interest and cultivating their innovative practical abilities, thereby laying a solid practical foundation for their subsequent graduation projects, research endeavors, and career development.

TI Amplifying silent voices: a qualitative study of female Islamic boarding
   school leaders' (Nyai) perspectives on preventing gender-based
   violence in Indonesia
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE gender-based violence; <italic>pesantren</italic>; female leadership;
   Indonesia; <italic>Nyai</italic>; Islamic feminism; educational
   leadership; <italic>Maqashid Shariah</italic>
ID STRATEGIES; MIGRANTS
AB Gender-based violence in educational settings persists across Southeast Asia, yet the perspectives of female religious leaders within Indonesia's Islamic boarding schools (pesantren) remain largely absent from scholarly discourse. This qualitative study centres the voices of Nyai, female pesantren leaders, through in-depth interviews with four Nyai from different institutions across Java. Drawing on Keadilan Hakiki Perempuan (Women's Authentic Justice), feminist institutionalism, and preventive socialisation theory, thematic analysis reveals six key themes: theological foundations grounded in Maqashid Shariah; daily practices cultivating respect through classical texts; identification of structural risks including power imbalances and surveillance gaps; reimagining power relations through love-based obedience; challenges encompassing toxic seniority and intergenerational tensions; and visions for pesantren as peace laboratories. The inclusion of a younger-generation Nyai illuminates generational shifts in approaching prevention, including internal resistance and strategic reform initiatives. This study demonstrates that Nyai articulate prevention approaches representing indigenous Islamic feminism, offering authentically local resources for addressing gender-based violence while maintaining fidelity to Islamic tradition. The findings contribute to understanding how female religious leaders in Asian contexts navigate tradition and transformation to protect those entrusted to their care.
